finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Wall Street Peers Into Abyss of AI Trade as Midterms Expose Risk
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Jeran Wittenstein and Ryan Vlastelica

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- For months, investors have been worrying about a long list of risks to the gravy train of artificial intelligence spending.
Most Read from Bloomberg
This week, they hit the panic button.

Fears of the worst-case scenario for the AI trade kicked in after the US midterm elections on Tuesday, in which Democrats secured majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives and won control of state houses and governor's mansions across the country. Many of the winning candidates ran on anti-AI platforms, raising the possibility that the development of data centers could grind to a halt in many places.

That realization sent traders racing for the exits starting on Thursday, dumping shares of everything tied to the hundreds of billions of dollars in projected AI spending. The Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index plunged 12% while the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index fell 6.4%, the biggest one-day drops for both since the Covid pandemic hit in March 2020. And AI poster child Nvidia Corp. led the market lower, tumbling more than 9% and losing more than $440 billion in market value.

"People are questioning the growth assumptions for data center suppliers and pulling back pretty broadly," said Peter Tuz, president of Chase Investment Counsel, whose fund owns shares in chipmakers Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. as well as major AI spenders like Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. "It is easy to draw a line from the election results to increased uncertainty toward the regulatory environment, and from there to the growth outlook for these companies."

Anxieties about AI spending had been mounting for much of the year amid rising interest rates, higher levels of debt being raised to fund the build-out and an increasingly vocal backlash against data center development. That spending has been key to the rise in the S&P 500 Index and has insulated the benchmark from macroeconomic problems, including high oil prices, elevated inflation and risks from the war in Iran.

It remains to be seen how efforts to rein in data center development and regulate AI will play out, of course, considering how slowly the gears of government often move. But the selloff shows the level of fear that the heart of the bull market is in trouble.

"It feels like the economy is firing on one cylinder, and that cylinder is not only not pumping as fast as it used to, but it may even slow further due to the election," said Barry Knapp, managing partner at Ironsides Macroeconomics. "I'm not a buyer of anything right here."

Nearly one-third of computing power projected to come online in the US in 2028 is now at risk, according to estimates by strategists at UBS Group AG. A majority of that is from data centers planned in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa, who has vowed to halt new data center approvals, defeated Republican Greg Abbott to become the first Democrat to win a governor's race in the state since 1990.

Those concerns are prompting a rethink of the AI trade's valuations, which were already under pressure. Take Nvidia, which has been the biggest beneficiary of AI investment. It's trading at 13 times profits estimated over the next 12 months, down from more than 32 times a year ago. Broadcom Inc., the second-most valuable US chipmaker, is priced at 15 times estimated earnings, down from a peak of 42 times in December.

"People were acting like data centers were a new state of affairs that could be projected out years into the future," Knapp said. "If we only build data centers for a couple more years, then chips go back to a slower pace of growth over time, what price should you pay for that?"

The selloff has been particularly brutal in the riskiest corners of the AI trade. CoreWeave Inc., the provider of AI-computing services, has tumbled 20% this week, leaving it down more than 75% from a June 2025 peak and just a few dollars from its March 2025 initial public offering price. And debt-laden neocloud provider Nebius Group NV lost 15% on Thursday, bringing its decline from a June high to 58%.
To make things even more challenging, uncertainty surrounding regulation and oversight of AI and the data center build-out has left investors wary of stepping in to buy the dip.

"It is difficult to say that this has gotten excessive, since we don't know what the regulatory outlook is going to look like," Chase Investment Counsel's Luz said. "It seems like the move has gotten overdone, but we would not be buyers until the situation clears up some."

One upside to a slowdown in data center development is tech giants like Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft Corp. and Meta Platforms Inc. would be forced to curb their spending. Selloffs in those stocks following the companies' recent earnings reports showed how intolerant investors are of capital spending that's outstripping cash generated from operations.

Those four companies, along with Apple Inc., saw their shares soar on Wednesday, adding more than $800 billion in combined market value, before giving up some of the gains on Thursday amid the broad selloff.
"If they cut back on spending, maybe they don't have to borrow as much, maybe cash flow rises," Luz said. "But at the same time, maybe growth slows. There are so many questions right now."
• Technology stocks plunged the most since 2020 on Thursday as investors exited the sector on concerns over the artificial intelligence trade after Democrats swept the US midterm elections.

• Microsoft helped create the "neocloud" boom, signing tens of billions of dollars in contracts with upstart data center operators in an effort to sate the crushing appetite for its cloud and AI services.
• SoftBank Group Corp. founder Masayoshi Son and other tycoons across Asia saw billions erased from their fortunes as a global tech selloff rippled through their companies on Friday.

• OpenAI said it will avoid nondisclosure agreements when it negotiates data center deals and ensure residents don't pay for the electricity to power those projects, part of a framework the company believes should be adopted into laws governing the expansion of AI.
• Apple raised $7.5 billion from its high-grade bond offering, attracting solid demand from investors seeking a break from a glut of AI-related debt deals despite a broader selloff across markets.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: AI Elite Lose $18 Billion as Chip Stock Rout Spreads to Asia
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Cindy Wang and Pui Gwen Yeung

paragraphs.text: Cindy Wang and Pui Gwen Yeung
Thu, November 5, 2026 at 11:22 PM PST 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- SoftBank Group Corp. founder Masayoshi Son and other tycoons across Asia saw billions erased from their fortunes as a global tech selloff rippled through their companies on Friday.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Twenty-two billionaires from China, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea who rank in the world's 500 richest lost more than $21 billion in combined wealth as of 10 a.m. Hong Kong time, before paring that to more than $18 billion, according to calculations from the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Son was the biggest loser, with his fortune declining by $3.9 billion to about $29 billion.

Among the hardest hit were the firms at the heart of the AI boom. Those who lost $1 billion or more include Takemitsu Takizaki of electronic sensor maker Keyence Corp., and Singapore's richest person Jason Chang of ASE Technology Holding Co., which assembles and packages semiconductors.
Samsung Electronics Co. shareholders Jay Y. Lee, his mother and sister - one of Asia's richest families - collectively lost about $2.5 billion from their fortunes.

The turmoil also last month hit hedge funds including Tiger Global Management and Whale Rock Capital Management, as concerns over AI investments roiled markets. In Asia, wealthy clients of brokers from Taiwan to Hong Kong faced margin calls on leveraged bets, people familiar with the matter said.

Expectations that a Democrat-controlled House of Representatives and Senate will work to slow construction of data centers — a critical component of AI infrastructure — helped drive technology stocks lower across Asia Friday, following a record $2.3 trillion wipeout in market value of the Nasdaq 100 index. The losses extended a wealth reversal that saw Nvidia Corp.'s Jensen Huang drop out of the world's top ten richest.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Wall Street Traders Wrong-Footed After Bullish Equity Calls
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Natalia Kniazhevich

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Wall Street's biggest trading desks spent weeks saying the stock-market rally would resume once the election was done. On Thursday, that call backfired spectacularly.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Trading desks at JPMorgan Chase & Co., Citadel Securities and UBS Securities had said the midterm vote would be a clearing event for markets that had been jittery going into the vote. With plenty of cash on the sidelines, investors would be inclined to rebuild their positions, the trading desks said.

Of course, one day doesn't make a trend in the stock market and the trading desks' bullish views may still materialize. Thursday's selloff highlights the traps of trying to estimate the stock market's direction, even for Wall Street's pros. US equities advanced on Wednesday before anxiety around the artificial intelligence trade after Democrats swept the elections wiped out $2.3 trillion from the Nasdaq 100 Index the next day. The S&P 500 plunged 4.4%, with every sector finishing the day in the red.

On Wednesday, Goldman Sachs Group Inc.'s equities trading desk had one of its busiest sessions of the year, according to John Flood, the bank's head of Americas equities execution services. Thursday was "the exact opposite," he wrote in a note to clients. "Our phones are exploding with asks for color. Unfortunately we aren't seeing much."
Earlier: Goldman Traders Say Phones 'Are Exploding' as AI Selloff Worsens

The long-only investment community was "frozen" again, he said in the note. Investors had aggressively reduced stock exposure ahead of the midterms and were caught off guard by Wednesday's rally, he said. Hedge funds were now selling some of the AI hyperscaler stocks they had bought the day before.

The bullish calls ahead of the vote had been tied to the idea that investors were positioned so defensively heading into the vote that the removal of election uncertainty could encourage them to rebuild exposure. Hedge funds, for instance, cut equity risk in October at a pace not seen since March, according to data from Goldman's Prime Services desk.

Citadel Securities' Scott Rubner, head of equity and equity derivatives strategy, said the election could help clear the way for a year-end advance. "With the election behind us and volatility potentially normalizing, there is considerable capacity for investors to rebuild risk," Rubner wrote in a note to clients on Wednesday. "With uncertainty fading and several of the market's largest buyers returning, we believe the path of least resistance for US equities is higher into year-end," he said.
Futures on the S&P 500 gained 0.1% at 8:37 p.m. in New York, while contracts on the Nasdaq 100 jumped 0.7%.

UBS Securities' Davide Montoni similarly argued that the vote could provide an upside catalyst after a volatile stretch for technology stocks. "Hyperscaler earnings clearly did not provide the all-clear investors were hoping for, but getting through the election could be the catalyst that unlocks a year-end squeeze," he said.

JPMorgan's trading desk also expected technology stocks to rebound and the rally to broaden beyond a narrow group of megacap stocks. The bank's US Market Intelligence team said it was tactically bullish, arguing that the recent tech selloff had created an opportunity for a near-term rebound.
But the election did little to resolve the other forces weighing on stocks.

Barclays Plc's global head of equities tactical strategies Alex Altmann was one of few skeptics across Wall Street's major trading desks. He had warned that the midterms were unlikely to be the clearing event investors were looking for, with the biggest pressures on equities, such as AI's payoff and the cost of financing its buildout, wouldn't be resolved by the vote.
Systematic Flows Add Pressure
The scale of Thursday's decline was amplified by the so-called systematic strategies, many of which follow the stock market direction rather than fundamental drivers.

Volatility-control funds could reduce equity exposure by about 30 percentage points, one of the largest one-day adjustments since the Covid-era market turmoil, Barclays Equities Tactical Strategies models show. Those funds could sell roughly $135 billion in US equity futures over the next 24 to 48 hours, the models show.
"We expect this to continue tomorrow as unwinds spread through the real money channels of retail and Long Only investors," Altmann added.
ETF rebalancing added to the pressure. Thursday was estimated to be the largest-ever levered ETF rebalance for sale, Barclays noted.

Retail investors, another source of demand during previous market dips, were reluctant to dive in. Retail traders were on track for their largest day of selling in individual stocks since the Covid-19 pandemic, Vanda Research said. As of 3 p.m. in New York on Thursday, they had sold a net $338 million of single stocks, according to the firm.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261105.headline: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years

paragraphs.text: Scientists have discovered remarkably preserved traces of dinosaur blood inside 115-million-year-old bones, revealing that delicate biological molecules can survive far longer than previously believed. The breakthrough could transform how researchers study prehistoric animals and even influence the search for ancient life beyond Earth.

An international team led by Curtin University found fossilized red blood cells and chemical evidence of blood molecules in the remains of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating theropod dinosaur discovered in northeastern Brazil. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, also include amino acids associated with collagen, an important structural protein found in bones and other connective tissues.

The discovery provides the first definitive chemical confirmation of molecules derived from hemoglobin inside fossilized dinosaur red blood cells. Earlier research had identified structures resembling blood cells in ancient fossils, but scientists had not conclusively demonstrated the presence of these particular molecular remains within them.
Ancient Dinosaur Blood Preserved Inside Fossilized Bones

When researchers examined the dinosaur's limb bones, they identified numerous mineralized red blood cells inside vascular canals, the tiny passages that once contained blood vessels. Chemical analysis revealed preserved heme molecules, which are components of hemoglobin, the protein that allows red blood cells to transport oxygen.

Finding these molecules provided direct chemical evidence that the fossil contained remnants of ancient blood. It also demonstrated that some biological materials once thought too fragile to survive for millions of years can remain detectable under exceptional conditions.

The study was led by John Curtin Distinguished Professor Kliti Grice, founding director of Curtin University's WA-Organic and Isotope Geochemistry Centre and an Australian Research Council Laureate Fellow.
"To detect intact heme-derived molecules in 115-million-year-old red blood cells is astonishing: this really is a landmark discovery," Professor Grice said.

"It not only extends the known fossil record of blood, but also offers a direct molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals so we may better understand them and the world they lived in."
How Dinosaur Blood Survived 115 Million Years

The extraordinary preservation appears to be connected to a mineral called hausmannite. This mineral helped stabilize the fossilized blood cells and preserve their molecular components (including amino acids of collagen) over an immense span of geological time.
In effect, the mineral created a natural time capsule that protected microscopic evidence of the dinosaur's biology long after its death.

Researchers believe the conditions surrounding the dinosaur's burial were also crucial. They suspect the animal was quickly covered by sediment in an environment with little oxygen and abundant microbial activity. These conditions may have helped preserve biological material that would ordinarily have broken down and disappeared.

The international research effort brought together scientists from Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, the Brazilian National Museum, the Regional University of Cariri, and Johns Hopkins University.
A Discovery That Challenges Fossil Preservation Limits

The findings challenge a longstanding assumption in paleontology that molecules associated with blood, particularly those derived from hemoglobin, could not remain preserved across such enormous periods of time.
Beyond confirming the survival of ancient blood components, the discovery raises the possibility that other fossils may contain molecular information that conventional examinations have overlooked.
"These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time," Professor Grice said.
"It opens exciting new avenues for molecular-level paleontology, allowing us to investigate the evolution of blood, metabolism and even activity levels in ancient animals."

Such information could eventually help researchers better understand how extinct animals functioned, including aspects of their metabolism and physiology that are difficult to reconstruct from bones alone.
Implications for Ancient Life Beyond Earth

The significance of the discovery may extend well beyond dinosaurs. Understanding how fragile biological structures can survive for millions of years could also help scientists identify possible traces of ancient life in other extreme environments, including those beyond Earth.

Professor Martin Van Kranendonk, head of Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, said the results are changing how researchers understand the preservation of molecular structures over vast timescales and under harsh conditions.

These insights could be valuable to astrobiology, a field that investigates the possibility of life elsewhere in the universe. If biological molecules or their chemical signatures can persist under the right conditions for more than 100 million years, scientists may need to reconsider where and how they look for evidence of ancient organisms.
"This study exemplifies how coordinated efforts across institutions, continents and scientific disciplines can unlock extraordinary insights into ancient life," Professor Van Kranendonk said.
The research was supported by a 2021 Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship awarded to Professor Grice.

The study, titled "Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115- million-year-old dinosaur bone," was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

wsj.com/finance/commodities-futures/taiw.headline: Taiwan Activates Market-Stabilization Measures to Stem AI Bleeding

paragraphs.text: Taiwanese authorities activated market-stabilization measures on Friday, joining South Korea in moving to stem the bleeding in local equities caused by the global selloff in artificial intelligence-related stocks.
At an emergency meeting on Friday afternoon, the National Financial Stabilization Fund of Taiwan authorized the executive secretary to deploy funds as needed to stabilize the market.

Officials cited the sharp downturn in Taiwan's stock market in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections, and continued selling by foreign investors, indicating a significant lack of investors' confidence.

The benchmark Taiex index shed 12% this week, tumbling alongside other tech-heavy indexes as the Democrats' victory in the U.S. midterms stoked concerns about tighter regulations that could slow the AI infrastructure buildout, hurting demand for AI-related hardware.
The Taiex is now down about 20% from its 2026 high, putting it in bear-market territory and underscoring the downside of breakneck, AI-fueled growth.

Home to the world's largest contract chipmaker, TSMC, Taiwan occupies a critical role in the semiconductor supply chain. It has reaped the windfall of the global AI investment boom: The stock market has scaled record highs, while exports have surged, spilling over into broader economic growth.

The Taiwan fund alluded to AI concentration vulnerability on Friday, saying that the island's economic fundamentals remain sound but that the market is dominated by high-tech stocks and closely correlated with the U.S. Philadelphia Semiconductor Index.
South Korea, Asia's other chip-making powerhouse, has suffered from the AI rout too. Earlier on Friday, authorities in Seoul also stepped up efforts to steady Korea's battered stock market.

Established in 2000, Taiwan's stabilization fund is tasked with stepping in to quell market turbulence. It has a maximum deployable capital of 500 billion Taiwan dollars at its disposal, or about US$15.11 billion.
During the Covid-19 pandemic, the fund's presence in the stock market lifted the Taiex by more than 40%, according to the National Treasury Administration.
Officials on Friday said "market confidence is clearly insufficient in the short term," vowing to take the necessary measures to restore order.
Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission said it will tighten short-selling restrictions from Nov. 9 to combat volatility.
The FSC also encouraged listed companies to consider share buybacks and hold investor briefings to replenish confidence.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/tesla-will-sto.headline: Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck in 2027
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/tesla-will-sto.author: Sean O'Kane

paragraphs.text: Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, according to CEO Elon Musk, who said on X that the company will use the factory space to build more two-seater Cybercab robotaxis.

The decision to wind down the futuristic, steel-clad EV comes after just a few short years of underwhelming sales. When Musk handed over the first few Cybertrucks in late 2023, he predicted Tesla would sell around 250,000 per year. It was supposed to be such a cornerstone of Tesla’s future that, before construction began, the company talked about its Texas factory as the “Cybertruck factory.” But Tesla has instead sold just tens of thousands — total — over the last three years.
Tesla is killing off the Cybertruck at a moment when it is trying to become an AI- and robotics-focused company. A big part of that is its robotaxi ambitions.

The company has spent the last two months putting Cybercabs on the streets in its hometown of Austin, Texas. With no major incidents to date, the company has said it plans to expand the Cybercabs operations to other cities, starting with Dallas later this month. (Tesla also operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUVs in Austin, Houston, and Dallas, as well as three cities in Florida.)

This is the third product Tesla has discontinued in order to fuel those greater ambitions. Earlier this year, the company decided to end production of the Model S sedan and Model X SUV and instead use the factory space dedicated to those vehicles to make Optimus humanoid robots.
First announced in 2019, the Cybertruck was a product that Musk had long obsessed over.
“Probably my personal favorite for the next product is the pickup truck, and we are going to just do an amazing pickup truck,” he said on one of Tesla’s earnings calls that year.

Musk promised the Cybertruck would be radical, inspired by the designs of cyberpunk sci-fi stories like Blade Runner. While that certainly bore out in the design, the company overpromised on the basics of the Cybertruck from the jump. During the now-infamous reveal event in 2019, when head designer Franz von Holzhausen cracked the Cybertruck’s windows with steel balls, Tesla said the EV was supposed to start at under $40,000 and have up to 500 miles of range. It achieved neither of those figures.

Instead, the truck was delayed for two years, in part because of the Covid-19 pandemic. When it finally did hit the market in late 2023, Tesla handed over the first few Cybertrucks to customers in a short, somewhat odd for Tesla event (by the company’s own standards, at least), which saw a poorly-lit Musk standing in a truck bed promising the truck was “the finest in apocalyptic equipment” fit for “late civilization vibes.” The base price had inflated to around $60,000, and the top-end range had shrunk by over 100 miles.

The truck has struggled on the market ever since. The polarizing design never seemed to sit well with buyers, especially at a higher-than-expected price. Then, during its first full year of sales in 2024, Musk became a major financial backer of Donald Trump, which turned the instantly recognizable Cybertruck into a target for protesters. That continued into 2025 as Musk led the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, which fired thousands of federal workers.

Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane.

latimes.com/lifestyle/story/2026-11-06/s.headline: How to have the best Sunday in L.A., according to B-Real
latimes.com/lifestyle/story/2026-11-06/s.author: Marah Eakin

paragraphs.text: Life’s a lot different for Cypress Hill rapper B-Real than when he was a kid.

Born in Los Angeles and raised in South Gate and Bell, B-Real — whose real name is Louis Mario Freese — says he was always surrounded by people he knew and members of his family. “It’s very tight-knit,” he says. “Back in the day, we were trying to go everywhere together, like whatever clubs were popping off that were playing hip-hop. Any sort of event that was hip-hop-related, we’d try to get to it.”

That sort of access and exposure served B-Real well, with Cypress Hill finding mainstream success with its self-titled LP in 1991. The group’s biggest single, “Insane in the Brain,” became a crossover hit in 1993, garnering the group both its first Grammy nomination and its first — and last — appearance on “Saturday Night Live.” The trio was banned from the show after DJ Muggs lit a joint during the act’s second song, something that was seen as wildly scandalous at the time.

Years later, though, Cypress Hill and B-Real are still tight. Over the summer, the group released its 11th studio record, “Dios Bendiga,” which the trio says is a tribute to its Latino heritage, roots and community. A tour of Latin America is scheduled to start Nov. 5 in Bogotá, Colombia.

When B-Real’s not on the road, though, he’s a resident of Moorpark in Ventura County, where he says life can feel slower and more isolated than it did in his youth. Fortunately, he says, he still gets to the city often, whether it’s to his gig as a host on Shade 45, Eminem’s Sirius XM channel, or to hang out with his pals.
With all that in mind, here’s how B-Real would spend a perfect Sunday in Los Angeles.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
6:30 a.m. Gym, then breakfast at the spot with a shorter line
I’ll hit the gym and then, if we’re having a “family Sunday,” then that’ll mean we’re getting up and heading out to breakfast, either at El Torito or Brent’s Deli in the Valley.

I know El Torito is generic, but their brunch is pretty good. We started going there because at Brent’s, if you don’t go early, you’re going to be sitting there for 30, 40 minutes. One week we got there kind of late and were going to have to sit too long, so we went over to El Torito. They usually have a line and a wait too, but this day there wasn’t and the breakfast buffet was really popping off. I was pleasantly surprised.

Brent’s has been a staple in the Valley for a long time, though. When we moved into the area, a lot of our friends that already lived there recommended Brent’s to us. Now we know the owners, who are very cool people and who have embraced us in a great way. I generally do a build-your-own omelet there or maybe steak and eggs. The pastrami and eggs is awesome too.
9 a.m.: Bowling for 200

If I’m not hanging out with my family or working on a Sunday, I’ll call up a couple of my guys at [my digital platform] BRealTV that are into bowling and we’ll go to one of the various bowling alleys that we frequent to get our rolling in.

If we’re downtown, we’ll bowl this place called Shatto 39 and when we’re out in the Valley, we’ll do either Corbin Bowl or Winnetka. Winnetka’s the really good spot. They’ve got really well-kept lanes and a pro shop. The lanes are key, because sometimes you go to these places and the lanes are overworked or underworked and it’s nothing but frustration.

I used to bowl a lot when I was a kid and I just recently got back into it three or four years ago. My average is about 150, but I’ve been trying to get back up to the 200s, which is what it was when I was a kid. To get those big numbers, you’ve got to bowl with frequency and we only go maybe once or twice a week.

It’s a release for us, though. Our squad does all sorts of things together. Sometimes we go on bike rides as a group too, like we’ll do 20, 30, or sometimes 50 miles together. As of late, though, it’s been bowling. It’s a little frustrating when you’re not hitting the pins the way you want to, but it’s still good to be doing something.
Noon: K-BBQ

After bowling, we typically end up at any one of our favorite Korean barbecue restaurants. We’ll go and get a fair amount of protein after expending all that energy and frustration, depending on whether we had a good game.
We try different spots. Parks is a good spot for Korean barbecue and that’s off Vermont by Shatto 39. If we’re at Corbin or Winnetka, though, we’ll do Ayce Gogi.

I’ve been eating Korean barbecue since 1994. There was a spot off of La Cienega here called Woo Lae Oak that was a high-end Korean barbecue spot. We had a business meeting there with our manager or agent or lawyer or something and then we had just started going there religiously every Friday.
2 p.m.: LAFC all day

A lot of times on a Sunday there’ll be a LAFC match so I’ll take myself down to support our guys. I’ve been a season ticket holder for many years now. It’s always good because it’s a different kind of energy and usually we’re on our feet the whole time so we’re burning off what we just had at the Korean spot.

The first few years LAFC was around, we were on tour a lot so I didn’t get a chance to go to any matches or anything like that, which was tough because when you’re a fan of a team, you want to try to go and to absorb the atmosphere and be around the other fans. You want to see the level of appreciation and adulation that the team gets.

What really sparked me getting season tickets was that I had a few friends that were season ticket holders and they had been pretty close with some of the team reps. They asked me to do some music for them and I obliged because I was a fan. We made a song with DJ Flict — who produced it — Kid Ink and myself as a theme song for the team and it just so happened that they won the Cup that year. That sort of locked me into the team and to the organization, and I went on to do more songs for them. I’ve even played in the drum lineup in the supporter section.
6 p.m.: Movie time

After the game, it’s most likely time for movie night with the family, whether that means we’re going to a movie or if we’re popping one off at the house. It just depends on the vibe. If I have Shade 45 on Monday, then it’s got to be an early night but if I don’t have a shift, then we might go to an actual theater to see a movie, which is a better experience.
10 p.m.: Off to bed

If I’ve got Shade 45 on Monday, then I’ll probably conk out anywhere between 10:30 and 11 so that I can get enough sleep to get up early enough to get my workout in before I go to the station. If it’s not a Shade 45 night, then I might stay up a little longer, like maybe 11:30.

It’s tough because as a young adult, I was always pretty much an insomniac. I didn’t go to sleep ‘til maybe 3 in the morning and then I woke up at 6 to go do my workouts. I was just running on very little. As I got older, I realized that I needed more sleep, so I would force myself to go to bed and now I’m finally in the rhythm of it for the most part. Now I’m trying to master that 10 o’clock sleep hour but it still feels like I’m missing s— if I go to sleep too early.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5yne5984l0o.headline: Shakahola deaths: Kenya court doomsday cult leader Paul Mackenzie sentenced to life in prison
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5yne5984l0o.author: Basillioh Rukanga

paragraphs.text: A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.
Alongside 27 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.
Ahead of sentencing, prosecutors in the court in Mombasa had argued for the death penalty for Mackenzie because of the gravity of the crimes.
The prosecutors also cited what they described as Mackenzie's lack of remorse for the crimes. They requested life sentences for his co-accused.

Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives in Shakahola forest, including two grandchildren, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".
Mackenzie and the co-accused have formally pleaded for mercy and asked for leniency from the court.
Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.
Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Diana Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.
Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.
One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".
Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.
The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.
Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.
The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.
"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen", says Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.

Wanje says a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.
"It was his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."
The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.
Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.
The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.
Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.

latimes.com/travel/story/2026-11-06/clif.headline: Clifton’s quietly reopens with plans to become an immersive megaspace
latimes.com/travel/story/2026-11-06/clif.author: Todd Martens

paragraphs.text: At Clifton’s in downtown Los Angeles, a Halloween wedding is taking place, a courtship between a woman and a demon lord. Modantus is his name, his head a skull, with brassy adornments ascending like a satellite dish. He doesn’t talk so much as click, growl and grunt as if clinging to life.

Before dinner is served, a masked man approaches people in the crowd — half in costumes, half in formalwear — in Clifton’s second-story ballroom, once a swing dancing haven. He’s in a vested suit, his mask, a sort of triangular sundial, reflecting light off of the candles at a head table.

“I’m collecting fears,” the man says, as a singer nearby performs a Gothic rendition of Soundgarden’s “Black Hole Sun.” Nightmare creatures from the netherworld feast on the worries of mere mortals, he explains, and so he invites guests to unload some of their own.

Clifton’s, the famed institution that dates to 1935, once a Depression-era oasis designed to look like a woodsy, Northern California lodge, has quietly started operating again after years of post-pandemic fits and starts. Its new operators, Neil Biondich and Alex McCullough, are ramping up events to activate the myriad spaces inside the building, all five stories of forest-themed kitschy wonder. That means magic shows in a mystical basement, karaoke in a lavish tiki bar, and live immersive theater parties in the main room, like its Halloween weekend event “The Dark Weekend.”
And for those who miss Clifton’s as a casual hangout space, their vision also includes two restaurants, the first of which they hope can come online in early 2027.

Their dream — a grand one — is to turn the space into an immersive entertainment venue, one where a live action role playing game (LARP) is running daily. Clifton’s, with its collection of oddities, be it a taxidermied bear or a bartop meteorite, is just the sort of fantastical place, they reason, to house a never-ending “Dungeons & Dragons”-inspired game.

“We’re not looking to radically change what this place looks and feels like,” says Biondich, an entrepreneur who has worked in 3D animation and directed commercials. “It should feel just like coming to Clifton’s. There just happens to be some decor that takes you deeper into an urban fantasy.”
Except, for now, maybe don’t call it Clifton’s.

Here’s where the story becomes more complicated. Biondich and McCullough do not have access to the Clifton’s name. They’re attempting to rebrand the building as Sanctuary, and running all events and ticketing via Sanctuarydtla.com. If one goes to the official Clifton’s site or social media pages, it will tell you programming at the space is paused.

Prior owner Andrew Meieran recently sold the building to real estate investment firm Robhana Group. Meieran, however, retained the name Clifton’s and its intellectual property (IP). He hasn’t ruled out reviving the brand elsewhere someday.

He bought downtown’s Broadway location in 2010 and invested more than $14 million in renovating it, including building out its heavily detailed tiki bar, complete with a vintage speedboat. Meieran has been outspoken about the challenges of running a large nightlife business downtown but held onto the brand, he says, because Clifton’s is a rarity, a unique only-in-California business.

“It’s not a restaurant,” Meieran says. “It’s not a bar. It’s not a theme park. It’s sort of in between all these things. It’s hard for both an operator and a guest, in terms of appealing to everybody. It wants to be the cafeteria for the people who want the cafeteria. It wants to be an immersive nightlife destination for the people who want that. It also wants to be a tourist destination and a place for families.”

Both Biondich and Meieran are careful when speaking about the other party, and hesitant to do so on the record. The relationship, it’s safe to say, is challenged. Both want to see Clifton’s revived but have yet to come to an agreement. After initially declining to comment on the talks, Meieran later emailed a statement.

“Clifton’s has never been just a building — it’s a concept that’s endured more than ninety years of upheaval: the Depression, a world war, riots, a pandemic, and a city whose people and tastes have changed many times over,” he wrote. “We’re working with the building’s owners to put a foundation in place that allows Clifton’s to thrive for another ninety years, bringing Clifton’s special brand of magic to Broadway for generations to come.”

Biondich is, for now, moving forward with the Sanctuary name, even developing an app that will bring augmented reality monsters to the venue. He describes his vision for the LARP as something between “Dungeons & Dragons” and “Pokémon Go.”

“We’ll eventually have glasses where you can see people in neighboring dimensions,” Biondich says. “We call it a dimensional tuner. You can look at higher frequencies and see if there’s any fae spirits around, or down-tune it and see if there’s any undead spirits or demons around.” Once the game launches, those who play it will receive rewards, such as discounted food or drinks.

It’s a welcome moment for Clifton’s to reemerge. Downtown has struggled since the end of the pandemic, with many workers not returning to its plethora of office space and a significant number of business abandoning the neighborhood, jeopardizing what was once a robust community. There are some smattering signs of life right now, however. Cole’s, for instance, is set to reopen in the coming weeks, and there’ve been rumblings that the Original Pantry will also soon return.

“Everybody who works and lives down here loves downtown,” Biondich says, “and they’re doing everything they can to bring it back and make it a more palatable place for people to come and enjoy. I really enjoy the passion of people who live downtown. It’s infectious.”

Biondich envisions a day when the building now known as Clifton’s operates as a restaurant in the day and early evening, then “wakes up” at night with actors in monster garb in its core bar spaces. Long term, he is planning a late-2027 opening of a second, more upscale restaurant in the venue. He intends for the comedy, magic and karaoke events to continue.

Biondich wants people to speak of Sanctuary in the same way they would talk of other noteworthy immersive venues. He cites art collective-turned-experiential firm Meow Wolf as an inspiration, only Sanctuary would have a more linear narrative that would emphasize game-inspired socializing.

“Our goal is to make this an international destination,” Biondich says. “If you’re going to Los Angeles, you’re going to check out Clifton’s for Sanctuary, in a similar way one would go to a Meow Wolf.”

But he’s also trying to walk a line, to assure longtime fans of the space, as well downtown residents, that Clifton’s will still primarily cater to them. He’s hired a chef, he says, and Clifton’s serves a limited menu — a burger, fish tacos — on days it’s open. While many of the early events, such as a “Dungeons & Dragons” social club or a “Super Smash Bros.” tournament, have courted the geek community, Biondich, a Northridge resident, says once the lower-level restaurant is open, it will honor the Clifton’s legacy.
That means that yes, there will be a Jell-O dish.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Williams Says Fed Should Gather Data to Judge Price Risks
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Maria Eloisa Capurro and Craig Stirling

paragraphs.text: Maria Eloisa Capurro and Craig Stirling
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 2:31 AM PST 3 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams endorsed the US central bank's statement saying that this is the time to collect information on the risks to prices.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Speaking at an event at the European Central Bank in Frankfurt on Friday, he said that inflation is "absolutely too high," though other indicators so far aren't signaling concern.

Monetary policy "does have a critical role in making sure that these relative price shocks don't translate into broader or more persistent inflation," Williams said. "Inflation expectations remain well anchored. We're seeing wage growth be consistent with our 2% goal."

Fed officials held interest rates steady last month, saying the "accumulation of more information" would allow them to determine the best level for policy. The 10-2 decision to stay put followed a unanimous move to lift their benchmark rate in September by a quarter point to a target range of 3.75%-4%.

Several policymakers speaking since the meeting have touted the need for additional rate hikes but advocated for a gradual approach. The public statements followed comments from Chairman Kevin Warsh, who pointed to a strong economy and warned about persistent inflation, but continued to abstain from sharing his outlook for rates.

"Our FOMC statement last meeting, I think, captures correctly that this is an appropriate time to accumulate more information to help us determine what the appropriate stance of policy is to make make sure we achieve a timely return to our 2% target," Williams said.

The Fed's preferred inflation measure, the personal consumption expenditures price index, rose by 3.6% in September from a year earlier, and gauges of underlying inflation excluding food and energy items also rose. Data also showed the US economy expanded at the fastest pace in a year in the quarter ending September.

"A couple of themes are really interesting, both for us and around the world: a very unusual set of relative price shocks affecting our economies, at the same time very strong resilience at least our economy through these shocks," Williams said.

He spoke just days after US Democrats saw decisive victories in Tuesday's midterm elections, taking control of Congress in a shift that Fed watchers said could protect the central bank and give officials more room to fight inflation without political interference.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Fast-Money Systematic Funds Stoked $2.3 Trillion Tech-Stock Rout
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Natalia Kniazhevich

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- As investors rushed out of US technology stocks on Thursday, selling by trend-following systematic strategies amplified what quickly became a record plunge by market value in the Nasdaq 100 index.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The tech benchmark sank 6.4%, erasing $2.3 trillion in market value, the most ever in a single day. Concerns that a Democratic sweep could mean tighter regulation of the AI buildout, crimping growth for chipmakers and data-center suppliers at the heart of the equity market's bullish run, drove the move.

As those worries pushed major indexes below key technical levels, systematic funds were forced to cut exposure, speeding the decline, according to equity derivatives strategists at JPMorgan Chase & Co. Unlike traditional investors, these quantitative funds typically follow the direction of the stock market, responding to price movements and momentum signals rather than company fundamentals.

Commodity trading advisers, or CTAs, as well as other trend-following strategies likely deleveraged sharply, turning net short US equities, the JPMorgan strategists led by Bram Kaplan said in a note. The decline broke several key momentum signals across major US indexes during the morning session, triggering additional selling by CTAs.
Net selling in S&P 500 futures totaled about $11 billion during the first hour and a half of cash trading, according to JPMorgan data.

Selling pressure from systematic strategies may not be over. Volatility-targeting portfolios have an estimated $50 billion of equity exposure to sell over the next few days, as they cut target leverage to around the 30th percentile from the 67th, according to the JPMorgan team's model.

Separately, Barclays Equities Tactical Strategies models show that these funds could reduce equity exposure by about 30 percentage points, one of the largest one-day adjustments since the Covid-era market turmoil. The funds could sell roughly $135 billion in US equity futures over the next 24 to 48 hours, the models show.

The JPMorgan team said that leveraged exchange-traded funds also sharply reduced exposure for the second time in a week, with the latest selling once again concentrated in technology. The funds sold more than $60 billion of stocks into the close, with about 90% of this tied to technology-related products, including semiconductors, Nasdaq 100 and technology-sector ETFs, they said.

With leveraged ETFs having already cut exposure sharply, their potential rebalancing flows should be smaller going forward. Their implicit short-gamma exposure has declined to about $6.5 billion per 1% market move from roughly $7.5 billion, the strategists' estimates show.
"Investor dip-buying inflows may have offset some of this rebalancing need, as in past selloffs," Kaplan wrote.

latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-06/mi.headline: Midterm results could shape 2028 presidential dialogue
latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-06/mi.author: Justine McDaniel, Ana Ceballos, Kevin Rector

paragraphs.text: WASHINGTON — Democratic upsets in this year’s midterms, which stretched from the suburbs of Atlanta to rural Kansas, could reshape the electoral map that governs presidential politics — and, with it, the calculus for each party in the fight for the nation’s top office in 2028.
Democrats were already cautioning against overconfidence, discussing how to translate their midterm success into more lasting power and to draw back Tuesday’s voters in 2028.

For Republicans, the defeat set off something close to an existential crisis, with would-be contenders for the party’s presidential nomination openly debating what had gone wrong and how the party should regroup after voters rebuked President Trump’s agenda.

And members of both parties were taking stock of the deep reach Democrats demonstrated Tuesday, with Senate, House and state legislative seats flipped in red strongholds that have not been up for grabs in a presidential race in years.

The midterm results have “enlarged the competitive map” for 2028, said Alex Keyssar, a professor at the Harvard Kennedy School, who has written books about voting rights and the electoral college. States such as Texas and Georgia may no longer be considered long-safe GOP territory, he said, leaving Republicans with fewer states they can count on and more ground they will have to spend money to defend.

“The number of states that the Republicans can feel secure that they have has diminished,” he said. “And the flip side of that is that there are more states that the Democrats can compete in. And that’s a shift.”

Presidential hopefuls typically begin putting together exploratory committees soon after the midterms, announce their candidacies after the new year and begin fundraising by midyear. Potential candidates began putting down markers swiftly this week.

On Thursday, allies of Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont) launched a fundraising committee for his potential candidacy. Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is considering a run, commuted the death sentences of all California’s death row prisoners. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker this week released a road map with recommendations for the new Congress.
And party leaders in Washington were nodding to 2028 as they outlined broad plans for their House and Senate majorities.

“As we look to 2028 and beyond, we need to start identifying now, in 2027, to solidify our position in the states we won and build our party infrastructure in those areas,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told an audience Wednesday at the think tank Center for American Progress, “and continue to expand the map into new states.”

Meanwhile, Republican leaders moved swiftly to assert authority within their party with analyses and prescriptions after Tuesday’s battering. Vice President JD Vance, long seen as a potential Trump heir, on Wednesday rushed to blame the sweeping losses on the president’s war in Iran.

Sen. Ted Cruz, whose state of Texas saw a historic blue wave, faulted his party for ignoring the economic pain many voters face. And Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, one of the few states where Republicans held the line, called the midterms an “extinction level event for Republicans” that will last beyond 2028.

“Once you have the [midterm] election results, that’s when like the real literal politicking begins, and you have to move quick,” said Matt Gorman, a Republican strategist who worked for the National Republican Congressional Committee and the presidential campaigns of Jeb Bush and Mitt Romney.
For the GOP, Tuesday’s results will mean spending more money in places such as Texas that the party has traditionally counted on to get their candidates to 270 electoral votes, Keyssar said.
“When the map shifts, the strategies have to shift, and that includes the allocation of money,” he said.

For Democrats, the midterms demonstrated that the party should be “investing heavily in the coastal South,” said Keneshia Grant, a Howard University political scientist. The party needs to “recognize the moment and meet it,” she said, pointing to the unexpectedly close Senate races in Florida and Mississippi.
“If you’re the Democratic Party at the national level, you now have to ask yourself different questions about the calculus,” Grant said.
It is generally difficult to predict the next presidential election outcome based on the results of the preceding midterms, said Justin Grimmer, a political scientist at Stanford University.

“Right now there’s this incentive or dream of Democrats to think, like, ‘Well, what if this were 2028? Then it’s a landslide.’ And then Republicans are fearful that if this map were to carry forward, that they would get ransacked in ‘28,” Grimmer said.
But “it’s hard to know what the major issues are gonna be in 2028, who the candidates are, and what sort of world we’ll be in.”
‘No silver lining’
President Trump has so far declined to endorse a successor, saying it is “too early” to make the call, though he has praised both Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
“We’ll see what happens,” Trump said Wednesday. “You can have maybe a lot of people running, maybe nobody is going to run. ... I don’t know who is going to run.”
Trump cast doubt on whether Vance would eventually run. But Vance appeared to be signaling 2028 aspiration with a post that pinned the GOP defeats on the Iran conflict launched by Trump this year.
The scale of the midterm losses may be the most useful thing for Republicans moving toward 2028, Gorman argued.
“The silver lining is that there’s no silver lining,” Gorman said.
That’s because there is nothing to cling to. “It’s a bottoming-out,” he said, which frees the party to begin “rebuilding conversations.”

The larger danger for whoever leads the party next is assuming that Trump’s voters come with the nomination, he argued, saying the 2028 nominee will have to create their own voter coalition. The same applies to Democrats, Gorman said, pointing to Latino voters who swung toward Trump in 2024 and back toward Democrats this year.
Such groups of swing voters, said California Republican consultant Mike Madrid, care about economic and quality-of-life-issues, not culture-war and partisan issues.

Madrid said that if he were advising a 2028 presidential contender, he would tell them, “Quit talking about these differences, or at least set these differences in the construct of a class-based, top down model — not a right left model.”
Time to ‘deliver’

With Democrats set for a wide-open presidential primary with a large array of candidates, the sweeping success on Tuesday of the party’s populist platform could influence how 2028 contenders run their campaigns.

Democratic leaders in Congress have said they intend to make affordability a centerpiece of their legislative agenda as soon as they take control of both chambers next year. But any measure will still need Trump’s signature, setting up an early test of whether Democrats can hand voters tangible results before 2028 — or end up with a stack of vetoes to campaign on instead.

“We have won immense amounts of political power, and now it’s the most important time in which to deliver,” Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.) told reporters Wednesday, “so we can keep that political power.”

Now that voters expect Democrats to clean up the nation’s problems in the next session, the party has to ensure that is “backed up by real results” — something anyone who is preparing a 2028 run will need to have in mind, strategist Rob Flaherty said at the Center for American Progress event Thursday.
“That is a huge thing that whoever we nominate has to be thinking about: quick delivery, quick change that people can substantively feel in their lives,” Flaherty said.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), who has not ruled out a presidential run, told reporters Thursday that some states may now be more “swing-ish” and that the Democrats will need to “take in” and analyze Tuesday’s data.
But, he said, voters’ top issues will remain the same.
“The candidates ... that can answer those things authentically and well for the voter,” he said, are “going to be the more successful” ones.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.headline: 'Godzilla Minus Zero' review: Stomp, smash, sob, sob, sob
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/st.author: Amy Nicholson

paragraphs.text: Takashi Yamazaki directs the best monster attacks in the multiplex: “Godzilla Minus Zero,” his follow-up to the 2023 period picture hit “Godzilla Minus One,” opens with a ground-eye view of the decimation of Matsumoto, a midsized mountain town that also happens to be where Yamazaki was born. One local calls its shellacking by winged, dragon-necked Ghidorah a “cruel twist of fate,” moaning that the village was never bombed during World War II. The moralistic film takes no pleasure in destroying Matsumoto; it’s pro-human to a fault. But boy, does the audience shiver with delight watching Ghidorah stomp buildings to rubble while the sound design rattles our seats.

The filmmaker François Truffaut once insisted that it’s impossible to make a truly anti-war film, since its images of combat simply pack too much of a visceral thrill. I’ll add to that: It’s impossible to make an anti-Godzilla film when we’ve all bought tickets to watch the big lizard smash.

Nevertheless, Yamazaki wants to try making a genuinely empathetic disaster movie and he’s earned the right. He’s the rare filmmaker to win his own Oscar for visual effects after Stanley Kubrick did so with “2001: A Space Odyssey.” This decent sequel works very hard to make us feel sad about its mass deaths; the only blood Yamazaki is willing to show is when the injured pack the hospitals. But he’s exponentially better at directing action sequences than he is at emotional ones, and as soon as composer Naoki Satô’s dynamic orchestral score crescendoes up, up, up into Godzilla’s theme music, I couldn’t wait to see the monster explode onto the screen to wreak more havoc.

It’s now 1949 and “Godzilla Minus One’s” core trio is back: reluctant former kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) and his family of an orphaned little girl, Akiko (Sae Nagatani), and the woman he’s teamed up with to raise her, Noriko (Minami Hamabe), a prickly urchin who fast pivots to a sweetie pie. Noriko, you may remember, miraculously survived Godzilla’s rampage through Tokyo. This script justifies that lame happy ending with a clever idea about the radiation sickness that results from suffering a blast of the creature’s atomic breath.

The now-married couple are too wan to take up as much of the running time as they do. While they’re meant to be in love, their screen chemistry feels closer to roommates. That would be a bracing statement on their need to cling to their hastily settled home life if Yamazaki was actually making it. Instead, there’s just an awful lot of tears — and young Nagatani is by far the best at sobbing. When the small girl wails, “Something scary is coming again!” the intensity of her terror shatters your heart.

Naval engineer Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka) also returns with a new promotion to director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau. There, he welcomes two more scientists: Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a plucky meteorologist, and Tanaka (Kanji Murakami), a vengeful biologist who comes with such a compelling backstory that the film would be more interesting if he was the lead. Tanaka also explains his reasoning behind Ghidorah’s name — it’s a Japanese portmanteau of the mythological Greek beasts Hydra and Chimera.

The post-World War II geopolitical landscape is reconstructing itself faster than the Ginza district, which was devastated in the last film and continues to look like a battlefield. The U.S. military has pivoted from fighting against Japan to helping the county fight the kaiju, as long as the Japanese are the ones risking their necks on the front lines. The United States prefers to team with Japan against Russia; Japan, in turn, would rather ally with Godzilla over Ghidorah. However, when the film begins, its characters sincerely think that Godzilla, last seen crumbling to smithereens in the Pacific, is dead. What fun it is to see people realize for the first time that the monster is going to keep coming back.

This is a war film in style and substance, emphasizing the mental exhaustion of a country that cannot handle any more carnage. Kōichi even describes Ghidorah in war terms as “a bomber with guns everywhere and no blind spots” — and that’s before the flying creature sprouts two more heads. One aerial fight is a dazzler with long takes of planes swooping through the clouds accompanied by the teeth-rattling clatter of lightning bolts that crash against your ears like metal trashcan lids. (The muscular cinematography and sound design are, respectively, by Kôzô Shibasaki and Natsuko Inoue.)

Yet a fascinating element of “Godzilla Minus Zero” — as well as director Hideaki Anno’s 2016 “Shin Godzilla” — is how they make a point of featuring saviors who are adamantly dull. The people trying to save the day are never macho or quippy. They wear drab suits and work out of drab offices; the dramatic montages are of people working intently at their desks. When their plans go badly, they take full responsibility. When they succeed, they pause to honor everything sacrificed in the effort, and would find it barbaric if anyone dared to pump their fists.

The focus on shared burdens over individual heroics extends even to the civilians who are forever being told how to stifle their feelings for the common good, whether that’s young Akiko lectured not to hug her adopted daddy in front of other orphans, or, conversely, the parents of a dead child who are asked to cry quieter.

At its core, “Godzilla Minus Zero” drills at the core difference between King Kong and a kaiju: A King Kong movie is about respecting nature while a Godzilla film is about confronting cold and indiscriminate death. Fittingly, the showdown between Godzilla and Ghidorah plays like a ghastly cockfight.

Still, the movie’s tone is so guilt-inducing and grim that when one character insists that there will be time to grieve later, I wanted to blurt out that everyone onscreen has been grieving the whole time. At the risk of sounding monstrous, can we please get back to the smashing?

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Fed’s New Schedule for Rate-setting Meetings Turns Back the Clock for ‘Strategy’ Sessions
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Catarina Saraiva

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- In 2027, the Federal Reserve will begin a transition to holding fewer policy meetings a year, a change that seems monumental for such a staid institution, but one that will actually return the US central bank to bygone ways of operating.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Chairman Kevin Warsh, who has promised to enact sweeping change at the Fed, said that by 2028 the Fed would use two of its eight annual meetings to discuss broad strategy instead of voting on interest rates.

It's the first change to the Fed calendar since the early 1980s, when it moved to eight meetings from 12. Though investors have raised worries that a new schedule could disrupt markets, defenders have dismissed those concerns and said it will give policymakers back time — used in the past to deliberate special topics — that it lost through a series of incremental changes.

"This is not unprecedented for the FOMC, even in recent times," said Loretta Mester, who joined the central bank in 1985 and served as president of the Cleveland Fed from 2014 to 2024, attending most Federal Open Market Committee meetings since 2000.

It harkens back to the years before the financial crisis, a time familiar to Warsh, who was a Fed governor from 2006 to 2011. In those years, six of the Fed's eight annual meetings were single-day affairs reserved mostly for talking about the economy and monetary policy, and voting on interest rates. The two remaining gatherings included a second day to wrestle with larger economic themes.
The crisis, which exploded in 2008, commanded all the Fed's attention and necessitated longer meetings more frequently.

In 2012, the Fed officially adopted a permanent, two-day meeting schedule. But half of those were followed by the chair's press conference — introduced by Chairman Ben S. Bernanke in 2011. Those usually ended early, allowing Bernanke time to prepare for the podium.

When Jerome Powell became chair in 2018, he expanded the press conference to every meeting. The bulk of the work then took place on day one, with day two typically wrapping up after officials voted on rates.

In the discussion time that remained it became harder, Mester said, to address big, meaty topics while also making difficult calls on monetary policy. "Taking a bit more time to actually have those conversations is a good thing," she said.

Warsh has said he wants to re-examine much of how the Fed operates, from the data it uses to assess the economy, to how it communicates. Many of his bigger ambitions will require deliberation and approval by his colleagues.
Earlier this year Warsh established task forces of outside experts to look at five key areas of Fed operations and propose new ideas. Those reports are due around the end of this year.

"If they're going to make progress on broader issues, they've got to create some time to do that," said Ellen Meade, an economics professor at Duke University and a former Fed adviser who attended many FOMC meetings from 2011 to 2020.

Yet the details of the new calendar will be important, Meade said. The Fed could keep to its current cadence of one meeting every six-to-seven weeks, and simply designate two as non-voting sessions. Or it could completely revamp the schedule, with the six voting meetings evenly spaced out every two months and two special-topic meetings tucked in around them.
Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin on Thursday praised the idea of scheduling meetings every two months.

"I really don't like having FOMC meetings and then walking out and getting a jobs report on Friday," Barkin said of the current calendar. "If you did it every two months, then you could, in fact, have the full suite of data twice in a row and make decisions based on two cycles of data."

Barkin said the shift is otherwise not a big departure for the central bank. William Dudley, who served as New York Fed president from 2009 to 2018, echoed that sentiment, saying there's no magic number of meetings. What's more important, he argued, is that markets understand how the Fed is likely to react under different economic conditions — what economists call the reaction function.
"I'm not sure if these things are really going to be that substantive in terms of making the Fed more effective as an institution," Dudley said of the changes.

Warsh has said the current meeting frequency, and the inclusion of press conferences after each FOMC gathering, drives Fed watchers and markets to focus too narrowly on policymakers' incremental actions.
He said the big questions — like what's happening with productivity or demographics, or how the economy is weathering shocks — ultimately matter more.

Holding fewer voting meetings, intentionally spaced out throughout the year, would allow policymakers to gather more economic data between each rate decision, both Mester and Meade said. It could also avoid awkward dates, like last week's, when officials voted on rates just a day before the release of key third-quarter economic data. That gathering also came just days before the midterm elections, casting a political shadow over the Fed's decision.

But there are also drawbacks to fewer rate-setting gatherings. For starters, shifting the cadence might force the Fed to alter the release of economic forecasts and rate projections, which currently fall on a neat, quarterly schedule in line with every other FOMC meeting.

With fewer live meetings, officials might also more frequently move rates by larger amounts than the traditional quarter percentage point, Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, wrote in a note to clients. Even the expectation of larger moves could trigger greater market volatility.

Georgetown University economist Masaaki Yoshimori, a proponent of moving to fewer but better-timed meetings, said the Fed should accompany such a decision with an explicit readiness to convene additional gatherings, if needed.

"The risk associated with moving from eight to six meetings is not necessarily that six normal-period meetings are insufficient on average," Yoshimori, who met with Warsh in August, said in a research paper. "It is that an unexpected disturbance may occur during the longer interval between meetings."

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/underdog-shows.headline: Underdog shows off a 32MB speech model in new demo
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/underdog-shows.author: Ivan Mehta

paragraphs.text: AI companies across the world are racing to make bigger and better models, but the problem is all of them need massive amounts of processing power. On the other end, some researchers and startups are creating smaller models that can run on edge devices, like your phone or computer.
One such startup, Underdog, has released a game built with its new voice model called Woof that’s only 32MB large.

The game features a room with a retro tech theme, a typewriter, and a CRT monitor. There is a desk lamp, which makes a sound when you click its switch. The intro warns users about “intrusive” cloud providers in the town — ostensibly a jab at cloud-based models.
You can interact with the typewriter and music tuner.
You can type anything on the typewriter using your keyboard, and the game will speak it back. You can also rotate the tuner to generate different kinds of music.

All of this works within the browser through Underdog’s speech generation model, which, the company says, can run on most devices without any internet connection. The model has 31 million parameters and is open for everyone to download.
While such a small model likely won’t replace bigger models, it may still be enough to drive local assistant experiences or create personalized podcasts.
This demo comes weeks after Underdog launched Bark, a 167 MB speech-to-text model also designed to run on edge devices for transcription and dictation.

Sigil Wen, the founder of Underdog, told TechCrunch that he started building the app because, instead of using notetakers like Granola, he wanted to build his own system with AI models that can run on users’ devices and let them own their data.

“I think we will be able to run most capable models of today on the devices you already own within months. We just want to train the best open models that are American-made, that are open, that are capable and allow people to have private AI,” he said, referring to his manifesto.

In addition to the two voice models mentioned above, Underdog has also released a 27-billion-parameter model that can run on laptops, along with a waitlisted app that the company is positioning as a locally-hosted alternative to Muse and Instinct.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/anc-fa.headline: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/anc-fa.author: Rachel Savage

paragraphs.text: The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

For The American Scholar, Lisa Russ Spaar offers us beautiful litany of loss in all its various shapes and forms. From those we love to objects like keys, from our teeth to our moral compass, Spaar takes a close look at what we go through when we experience loss at various times in our lives, and how losses tend to stack up as we age.

I’ve informally polled several friends, colleagues, and family members about their first remembered losses. For most, it was when a milk tooth fell out, usually around the age of six. (Surely there are primal reasons many of us dream throughout our lifetimes about our teeth, as important as they are to speaking, eating.) More than 20 years ago, one of my talented undergraduates, Molly, wrote a poem about losing her first tooth while sledding in winter. Upon tonguing the little bloody socket that remained, she wrote, “I taste my death.” That line has haunted me over the decades. Again, our bodies: made for loss. Language: our ability to articulate what that might mean.

I often wonder what was happening in my late mother’s mind as she sank, over a period of 10-plus years, into the tangled ambages of dementia. She lost the names of things and people. She lost any memory of who we were, those of us who cared for her, even her devoted husband, my father. She finally even forgot that she was not only an alcoholic with a fifth of Scotch hidden in the breadbox but also a chain smoker, though she’d occasionally hold a drinking straw to her lips and take a long, deep drag.
