cnbc.com/2026/11/06/automakers-rising-co.headline: Where's the growth? Legacy automakers face a tougher 2027 as costs rise, market tightens
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/automakers-rising-co.author: Michael Wayland

paragraphs.text: DETROIT — There's a growing concern that the global automotive industry may be stuck in neutral, if not reverse, heading into 2027.

The auto industry — from the companies to their customers — has been surprisingly resilient this decade, but there are fears that rising costs, weaker vehicle pricing and a more challenging market could threaten profits and growth going forward.

Automakers also face pressure outside the U.S. from an onslaught of Chinese carmakers, a thinner new-product pipeline after retreating from some all-electric plans, and company- and region-specific challenges.

"With investor focus increasingly shifting to 2027, the setup appears challenging," Barclays analyst Dan Levy said in an investor note last month. "Rising inflation, continued China pressure, affordability concerns in the U.S., and a flat global production outlook suggest another year of limited earnings growth."

Several Wall Street analysts have said automakers will need continued pricing strength and additional cost savings to offset inflation, higher investment spending and a potentially weaker economy just to maintain their current levels.
"It's a little bit more optimistic in the U.S. and then very pessimistic in Europe," RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan told CNBC. "As a whole, there's some negativity on '27."
Guidance cuts, increased costs
Automakers from the U.S. to Europe to Asia have been facing a growing list of headwinds.

For U.S.-based legacy automakers, Ford Motor said it expects next year's results to be in line with 2026, while General Motors grew more cautious about its ability to continue growing earnings as much as it had previously expected.

"We continue to believe that 2027 will be another strong year and better than 2026, assuming customer demand remains strong, and commodity, logistics and other recent cost pressures moderate," GM CEO Mary Barra told investors Oct. 20.

GM CFO Paul Jacobson said that while it's too early to officially forecast, the company is facing additional inflationary costs that could lead to another $2 billion headwind in 2027, like it expects this year. He specifically cited costs of commodity inflation, logistics and DRAM, or dynamic random-access memory chips as challenges.
Those chips are critical components in modern vehicles and are used for everything from temporary data storage and real-time processing from infotainment systems to safety-critical systems.

GM and others have been able to offset outside pressures through cost cuts, operational efficiencies and resilient consumer demand for higher-margin vehicles. However, there's a limit to what companies can do.
"There's only so much pricing you can push to consumers," Narayan said. "They're already at pretty high pricing."
European automakers including Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW in recent weeks reduced their 2026 earnings forecasts in response to U.S. tariffs, the growth of Chinese automakers and rising costs.

Most recently, BMW this week said accelerated restructuring measures would reduce its automotive pretax earnings margin this year by 2.5 percentage points. The company said the restructuring should support "positive effects" into 2027 and a 3% to 5% pretax profit margin for 2028. That compares with a 5.3% automotive margin last year and 3.4% during the third quarter.

Chrysler parent Stellantis, which has large operations in Europe and the U.S., is facing its own challenges, as it's in the midst of a restructuring that aims for a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin this year. It has maintained a 2026 guidance that includes a mid-single-digit percentage increase in net revenue and a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin.

In Asia, South Korean automaker Hyundai Motor, which has experienced notable growth in recent years, also cut key metrics when it reported earnings late last month. The company lowered its 2026 wholesales target to 4 million vehicles, down from 4.16 million, and cut its operating-margin target to between 5.5% and 6.5%, down from a previous goal of 6.3% to 7.3%.

Toyota Motor is an outlier for its most recent quarter and outlook, as the world's largest automaker increased its full-year operating income forecast by 500 billion Japanese yen (about $3.2 billion) on Thursday.
Toyota's results were boosted by weakness in the Japanese yen as well as strong hybrid vehicle demand in the U.S. However, the increase in operating income was its first in six quarters.
Broadly, the changes to earnings and outlooks come as production for the global industry slows.

Consulting and insights firm GlobalData expects global light-vehicle production of about 90.96 million units in 2026, down 2.1% compared with last year. It forecast a production increase of less than 1% next year. That comes on the heels of strong annual growth earlier this decade, led by China.
Caution lights
Cox Automotive reported the average transaction price of a new U.S. vehicle in September was more than $50,500. That was just shy of the record of $50,614 in December 2025.
Lofty vehicle prices have led to record-high and record-long financing deals, as well as concerns that customers are getting priced out of the new-vehicle market.
The typical U.S. new-vehicle payment reached $776 a month in September, the highest since December 2023, according to Cox Automotive.
Cox Automotive chief economist Jeremy Robb, discussing the third quarter for the automotive industry, rated the overall economy, buyer ability and borrowing costs as cautionary "yellow lights."

But he did have some "green lights," such as good credit availability and employment conditions, which could give some relief for automakers and consumers, many of whom need vehicles for their everyday lives.

Robb said there's a "tug-of-war" between headwinds such as rising costs, interest rates and fuel prices and tailwinds such as growth in liquid assets and savings that has helped offset some of the additional costs.

"Consumers remain under financial pressure, but the vehicle demand continues to hold, showing more resiliency in the auto industry than we've seen in other parts of the economy," Robb said during a Sept. 24 call, noting consumer sentiment remains low.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/physicl-raises.headline: Physicl raises $10M to make the digital world real enough for robots
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/physicl-raises.author: Tim Fernholz

paragraphs.text: Alex de Vigan’s last business got swamped by the rise of generative AI, but now he’s betting the tech that team had built, a platform for creating tempting product renderings for e-commerce, can be re-purposed to make robots more useful.
His new venture, Physicl, has raised $10 million in seed funding from Inovia Capital to help world model designers and robot builders solve thorny training problems with more realistic simulations.

Founder and CEO de Vigan spent the last decade building nfinite, which made it easy for brands and retailers to create 3D models of their goods and display them online. The arrival of transformer-based AI models led that company to focus more on generative imagery, but de Vigan saw a new purpose for his team and the tech stack they’d built to faithfully render 3D environments.
“What we were super unique about doing in 3D, AI was going to replace, but something was missing in AI: its ability to understand, interact, and manipulate space and objects,” de Cigan says.

Researchers developing physical AI models to make robots more capable of tasks like handling diverse, small objects have been frustrated by the returns of training them on video, and the expense of gathering data through remote operations.

Simulations in digital worlds are seen as a promising solution, but ensuring that these simulated worlds are faithful to real-world physics has proven difficult. de Vigan believes that the pipeline his previous company built to “transform unstructured, incomplete, heterogeneous real-world information into a high-fidelity physical representation… with correct geometry, materials, and physics” can now be used to make physical AI models more effective.

Physcl is entering a crowded category of startups vying to provide data and tooling to foundation model builders and robot operators. “The space is very young and and and very blurry sometimes,” de Vigan admits. There are a variety of companies collecting, labeling, or generating data in different modalities as their customers try to figure out the secret sauce that will make robots live up to their promise.

In particular, Phyiscl wants to focus on post-training models on difficult edge cases. The startup is releasing a product called Studio with 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 assets that represent various objects. It lets users create scenes to generate synthetic data for training robots on specific problems. For example, Studio could be used to generate training data to help a robot that has trouble discerning a cup on a cluttered counter-top, or while the cup is in shadow.
Loading the player…

SpAItial, a world model builder, collaborated with Physicl as an early customer to improve the fidelity of its products, the latest of which, Echo-3, was released last week. SpAItial’s tool generates 3D simulations from 2D imagery, and to do that effectively, its CEO and founder Matthias Niessner said they needed to train on the kind of high-fidelity synthetic data Physicl offers.

However, Physicl wants to be more than a data provider; it sees itself as the tooling for ongoing synthetic data generation. “What we created 10 years ago, without knowing it, was basically an agentic workflow to transform unstructured information into high fidelity 3D,” de Vigan said. He imagines customers bringing trillions of images or millions of hours of LIDAR capture data to feed into his platform and turn them into high-quality 3D representations that can be used to generate billions of permutations to train their models.

“The real challenge is, you have to curate the data by hand, and this is a very long cycle,” Niessner, also a professor of robotics at the Technical University of Munich, told TechCrunch. “To us what seems very attractive is you can just do this on the fly […] You’re running Claude, and it checks, ‘Oh, I need more data of this in my training,’ and then it auto generates that data, depending on the training state. That, to me, is super exciting, and this is exactly what Physicl is offering.”

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/flavio.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro battles to remain relevant as he speaks at rightwing conference at Mar-a-Lago
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/flavio.author: Tom Phillips

paragraphs.text: Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s presidential election last month, has insisted his defeat is not “the end for Brazil” as he battles to maintain political relevance after fleeing to the US.
Bolsonaro absconded early last week shortly after losing the 25 October election to the leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than 4m votes.

On Thursday night Bolsonaro made his first major public appearance since arriving in the US, speaking at a rightwing gathering at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property where he claimed “great things” were still to come.

“I know this wasn’t the end for Brazil and I know it wasn’t the end for America,” Bolsonaro, 45, told a gala dinner at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC)’s four-day “gathering of visionaries” event, where the former British prime minister Liz Truss is also due to speak.

“Even when what seems like the end isn’t what we’d hoped for, we must thank God and have even more faith that this isn’t yet the end,” he added. “No one shuts the door that he opens – and the door he shuts, no one opens.”
Earlier, in his first post-election interview, Bolsonaro made a series of unsubstantiated claims about election fraud and insisted he received “help from absolutely no one” to flee.

“It was all me,” Bolsonaro told the New York Times, contradicting reports that he was helped by the Trump adviser Jason Miller and Santiago Caputo, a close aide to Argentina’s rightwing president, Javier Milei.

He said he would “take to the grave” the full story of how he had fled Brazil, where he faces federal police investigations for money laundering and corruption. Bolsonaro is a member of congress who has held elected office for more than 20 years but he will lose parliamentary immunity early next year when his term ends, meaning he could then be prosecuted.

Brazilian analysts agree that by skipping the country after an election in which he received 59m votes, Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, abdicated leadership of the opposition and sabotaged his political future.

Thomas Traumann, an author and pundit for the TV network GloboNews, said: “Flávio was foolish enough to throw away the leadership of the opposition that he could have exercised had he stayed in Brazil. But the [Bolsonaro] family is still a player.”

Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, also lives in self-imposed exile in the US and will have to serve a four-year sentence for coercion if he returns to Brazil. Four other members of the Bolsonaro family were elected to congress in last month’s election, including their brothers Carlos and Jair Renan and stepmother, Michelle Bolsonaro.

Traumann believed it was not inconceivable that Jair Bolsonaro would attempt a political comeback if he managed to negotiate his way out of his 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. However, as things stand, the 71-year-old is banned from running for office until 2060 and must live under house arrest.
Many doubt the Bolsonaro family can continue to control Bolsonarismo, the populist political movement that takes their name, with two key members in exile and one imprisoned.
“[The movement] is mortally wounded because of its mistakes and its crimes,” the political scientist Sérgio Abranches told the newspaper O Globo this week.

Abranches said democratic rightwing politicians now had a chance to “detach” themselves from the Bolsonaros’ anti-democratic movement and break off in a new direction before the next presidential election in 2030.
Flávio Bolsonaro told the New York Times he would “obviously” be a candidate in future elections but said his future lay in the US “at least for now”.

It is unclear where Flávio Bolsonaro, who has been granted a US visa by Trump, will live. His brother Eduardo set up home in Southlake, Texas, after leaving Brazil last year – although some expect him to move after the traditionally conservative state elected the Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor in this week’s midterms.

In a video posted on CPAC’s social networks before Thursday’s event, Eduardo Bolsonaro played down the risk posed by the “blue tsunami” to their ability to stay in the US. “They [Democrats] will try [to make trouble for us] – but it’s not up to Congress … to revoke visas or citizenships,” he said.
Likening their plight to that of a female asylum seeker fleeing Iran for fear of being killed after refusing to wear a hijab, he added: “I am 100% legal – as is my brother and his family.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tesla-cybertruck-tex.headline: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas next year to ramp Cybercab, Musk says
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/tesla-cybertruck-tex.author: Michael Wayland

paragraphs.text: Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Friday said the electric vehicle maker will "be winding down" production of the Cybertruck at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year.

Musk, who hailed the Cybertruck as the future of the pickup truck segment, said in a post on X early Friday morning that the end of production at the massive facility would make room for production of its Cybercab robotaxi.
The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward.

Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an "end of an era" and said the Cybertruck was the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made."
"True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time," Musk said.
Tesla began Cybertruck deliveries in late 2023. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.
The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000.
"Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019. "Like 100 years. Trucks have been basically the same. We want to try something different."
While Tesla does not break out its sales by model or region, Cox Automotive estimated sales of the Cybertruck last year at 20,237 units in the U.S., down 48% from 38,965 in 2024.

The Cybertruck's specifications also fell short of those Tesla advertised early on, and in some cases fell short of those offered by leading fuel-burning pickups. There have also been many quality and production problems, including several recalls.

cnbc.com/2026/11/05/nasdaq-drops-into-co.headline: Nasdaq drops into correction territory — here’s what typically happens next
cnbc.com/2026/11/05/nasdaq-drops-into-co.author: Deena Zaidi, Nicholas Wells

paragraphs.text: The Nasdaq Composite plunged into correction territory on Thursday. History shows more selling can follow in the near term, but a recovery eventually takes hold three months later.

The tech-heavy index slid more than 5% on Thursday, closing more than 11% below its record reached last month. On Wall Street, any decline greater than 10% is a correction. A 20% pullback qualifies as a bear market.

Across 10 previous correction episodes over the last decade, selloffs in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 were followed by further rough selling over the next one month. But the Nasdaq was back to rally mode again after six months for all those occasions except one: 2022.
Overall, the Nasdaq gained an average of 9.41% from the correction bottom over the following three months and 17.03% over six months.
The January 2022 correction was the one that offered a harsher outcome. The Nasdaq lost another 18.3% over the next six months and was down 24.3% a year later.

The catalyst for this correction was Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party also made significant gains in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor after campaigning on an immediate moratorium for data center development.
Investors are now weighing whether tighter state-level restrictions could slow data center construction, putting pressure on companies tied to the artificial intelligence trade.
Frank Cappelleri, founder of CappThesis, pointed to past midterm election cycles for guidance and found that points to more volatility in the near term as well.
The chart analyst said the Nasdaq was higher 12 months after the election in all but one of 13 midterm cycles since 1974.
"The caveat is that the path can be a volatile one," he said.

Cappelleri pointed to 2018, when the Nasdaq rallied the day after Democrats won the House. A sharp December sell-off followed, but the index was ultimately about 15% higher a year after the election, he said.
Chip stocks tumbled Thursday, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) falling 12% and for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.
— CNBC's Fred Imbert contributed to the report

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: US and Iran Edge Closer to Deal With Nuclear Issue Back in Play
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Fiona MacDonald

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The US and Iran are moving closer to a potential breakthrough in efforts to end the war, with Tehran showing a willingness to discuss issues related to its nuclear program that were previously off the table, according to a diplomat with knowledge of the talks.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Iran is studying proposals related to its atomic activities that were presented by chief mediator Qatar, according to the diplomat, who asked not to be identified discussing sensitive information. Any concession on that issue could lead to a significant step forward in negotiations, which have been stagnating since the collapse of an interim peace deal agreed in June.

US President Donald Trump recently spoke by phone with Qatar's leader about efforts to de-escalate tensions, an indication of his desire to end a war that helped propel a Democratic sweep against his Republican party in the US midterm elections this week.

Trump and Emir Sheikh Tamim Bin Hamad Al-Thani discussed Qatar's efforts to resolve differences between the warring sides and secure a comprehensive agreement to end the conflict, the emir's office said on Friday.

Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu started the war with attacks on Iran at the end of February, triggering a retaliation by the Islamic Republic against US allies in the Middle East and triggering a surge in energy prices and global inflation. Talks to end the war have repeatedly broken down, with Iran demanding the US lift a naval blockade against its ports, among other concessions.

Trump has long said the chief aim of the war was to prevent Iran from building a nuclear weapon, though little is known about the extent of the country's atomic activities since the start of the conflict. While Iran has always said its nuclear work is strictly for non-military purposes, any commitment to allow more transparency could be enough to move the peace process forward.
Reuters and the New York Times previously reported on Iran's willingness to compromise on the nuclear issue.

Qatari officials had been shuttling back and forth between Doha and Tehran to solidify a potential deal in the run up to the US midterms on Tuesday, which saw the Democrats take control of Congress in a landslide win over Trump's Republican party. One of the reasons for the reverse was the American public's opposition to the war, in part due to its impact on gasoline prices.

In the aftermath of the vote, Trump said he had no immediate plans to launch fresh strikes on Iran, sending oil prices lower. Brent crude has plunged below $100 for the first time since September as investors wager that the Democratic sweep eases the prospect of a return to all-out fighting, which Trump had repeatedly threatened before the vote.

In other recent diplomatic moves, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi discussed "efforts aimed at establishing stability in the region" in separate phone calls with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts on Thursday, according to a statement on his official Telegram channel. He also spoke to his opposite numbers in the United Arab Emirates, Turkey, Kuwait, Cyprus and Jordan.

Mohsen Rezaee, Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, according to a statement on Russia's presidential website. Rezaee delivered a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei addressed to Putin, Iran's state-run IRIB reported, without giving more details.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.headline: Bitcoin Selloff Eases as Investors Explore Cautious Recovery
finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.author: Emily Nicolle

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Bitcoin edged back into the green after a bruising selloff on Thursday swept through cryptocurrencies and other risky assets, pressured by lackluster chipmaker earnings and a Democratic sweep of Congress.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The largest cryptocurrency was trading at around $76,000 on Friday morning in New York, having tumbled almost 6% from a position above $80,000 a day earlier. Smaller cryptocurrencies were also broadly up on Friday, with BNB, ZCash and HYPE all trading up between 1 and 3%.

The S&P 500 recorded its steepest drop in more than a year on Thursday as investors forecast a Democrat-led clampdown on data center expansion, pushing chipmaker stocks lower. Futures for the benchmark and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 crept up on Friday, helping to bolster trader optimism that spilled into crypto bets.

"Bitcoin appears to be finding some relief after yesterday's sharp selloff, although I would be cautious about calling this a reversal just yet," Dean Chen, an analyst at crypto exchange Bitunix, said in an email. "I would describe the current move as selling pressure easing, rather than fresh accumulation taking hold."

Crypto remains on shaky ground after a $6.3 billion hack on digital-asset exchange Binance Holdings Ltd. rocked the sector on Oct. 29, dampening investor enthusiasm for the asset class. Volatility in the broader market has only worsened the blow, with routs in artificial intelligence stocks spilling over to crypto as a result of many of the industry's mining companies pivoting to the AI industry in recent years.

"The selloff reflects growing doubts over the returns from huge AI spending, fears that tighter regulation could slow data-center construction and a broader retreat from highly valued growth assets," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG. "Yet with stock markets continuing to slide, Bitcoin is so far holding its ground, suggesting buyers are stepping in to defend current levels. That relative strength could be an important test of whether Bitcoin is starting to decouple from the technology trade, rather than simply following it lower."

Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds in the US recorded $430 million in outflows on Thursday, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund led the pack with about $200 million of that figure, followed by BlackRock Inc.'s IBIT with about $105 million in outflows.
"The selling does seem to be easing, but the recent bounce looks more like brief relief than sustained recovery," said Samuel Leyne, co-head of crypto trading at Marex.

"You need a real catalyst to bring confidence back, whether that's geopolitics cooling off, oil coming down or the macro picture improving," he added. "Until then, we have to watch stocks, ETF flows and the basis levels. Bitcoin needs to get back above $77,000 to build any momentum, and if equities keep sliding, $75,000 is right back in play."

finance.yahoo.com/real-estate/articles/f.headline: New Florida Property-Tax Cut May Bring an Unwanted Side Effect
finance.yahoo.com/real-estate/articles/f.author: Leslie Kaufman

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Florida's newly approved property-tax cut is designed to make homes more affordable. But it could also push up another punishing cost of homeownership: insurance.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Homes in the Sunshine State are already among the most costly to insure in the US because of their exposure to hurricanes, floods and other natural hazards, risks that are being compounded by climate change. Florida's property taxes, although rising fast, are less exceptional: The mean effective rate on owner-occupied homes ranks 27th among states.

But amid a nationwide rebellion against property taxes, a ballot measure championed by Governor Ron DeSantis and passed Tuesday by Florida voters will cut them. And by so much that it is projected to strip billions of dollars from local governments, potentially squeezing fire departments, building safety offices and other services that help protect homes and reduce losses.

That could have a knock-on impact on home insurance rates. "You ostensibly are going to pay for living in a high-risk area, either as a taxpayer or as a ratepayer," said Jesse Keenan, a professor of sustainable real estate and urban planning at Tulane University. "It's just shifting the burden."

The measure, Amendment 3, narrowly cleared the 60% threshold required to amend Florida's constitution. It increases the property-tax exemption on a homeowner's primary residence from $50,000 to $150,000 next year and up to $250,000 in 2028. School taxes are excluded.

"Florida passed Amendment 3. The governor and the Legislature own what comes next," Jeff Brandes, a former Republican state senator who opposed the ballot initiative, said Wednesday on X. "They have the responsibility to manage the fallout."
In his post, Brandes cited Dunedin, a small city in Pinellas County, which is doing contingency planning for having fewer firefighters working per shift.
Florida Realtors, a trade association for real-estate agents, spent heavily to support the measure, promoting it as a way to ease housing costs.

"This Election Day, Florida homeowners chose property-tax relief," Chuck Bonfiglio Jr., president of Florida Realtors, said after the vote. He said the measure could be implemented "without compromising the essential services our communities depend on."

But Florida TaxWatch, an independent, nonpartisan taxpayer research group, says the amendment will cost counties, cities and special districts tens of billions of dollars in lost revenue over its first five years. Unless the money is found elsewhere, it will necessitate significant cuts to local services.

Insurers care about the strength of local fire departments because the speed and effectiveness of their response can determine whether a small fire causes limited damage or destroys a home. Many insurers rely on ratings produced by the Insurance Services Office, a private insurance-data company owned by Verisk Analytics Inc., to help assess that risk.

ISO evaluates local fire protection, including firefighter staffing, training, equipment, water supply and emergency communications, and assigns communities a rating that insurers can use in underwriting.

"A reduction in fire protection services in a community can lead to a lower ISO rating," said Mark Friedlander, a spokesman for the Insurance Information Institute, an industry-funded research group. "The ISO rating is among numerous risk factors property insurers use to underwrite homes in Florida and could potentially cause premiums to increase if the rating is downgraded."
Keenan, of Tulane, said tighter local budgets could also mean fewer resources for building inspectors, code enforcement and disaster mitigation.
"This will greatly impair local governments' ability to make investments in risk reduction," he said.
Keenan and other observers argue the amendment may ultimately shift costs rather than eliminate them, as cities and counties turn to sales taxes, special assessments and fees to replace the revenue.

The Tax Foundation, a tax-policy research organization, similarly concluded that Amendment 3 doesn't eliminate the cost of local services but changes who pays for them. Businesses, landlords and second-home owners will not get the expanded homestead exemption, which applies only to primary residences. But they will benefit from a separate provision that caps annual increases in assessed values at 5%, down from 10%. Renters, meanwhile, could face higher rents if landlords pass along higher costs.
The governor's office and the Florida Insurance Council, a trade group, didn't respond to requests for comment.

Florida localities say it is too soon to know how they will respond. Cragin Mosteller, deputy executive director of the Florida Association of Counties, which opposed the measure, said Wednesday that counties will work with the governor, legislature and state Taxation and Budget Reform Commission "to make the transition carefully and to protect the quality of life Floridians expect."

technologyreview.com/2026/11/06/1148154/.headline: The Download: a humanoid cleans house and Samsung builds for the AI boom
technologyreview.com/2026/11/06/1148154/.author: Thomas Macaulay

paragraphs.text: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
—Grace Huckins
When I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.

The device that arrived at my building belongs to Tau Robotics, a local startup. Its long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but the technology isn’t quite there yet. For now, humans pilot the robots remotely, watching them work through onboard cameras.
There were some unexpected challenges along the way, but also moments that felt like a glimpse of the future.
Find out how well the machine cleaned my home—and how close we are to truly autonomous domestic robots.
A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
Generative AI models depend on stacks of specialized memory chips. To meet soaring demand, Samsung is building a vast new semiconductor manufacturing campus in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.
I visited the sprawling campus south of Seoul, where three fabs already operate around the clock, a fourth is coming online, and thousands of workers are racing to build a fifth.
Step inside the vast chipmaking complex powering the AI boom.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/furthe.headline: Further bomb threats disrupt at least another 18 flights across Europe
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/furthe.author: Rory Carroll

paragraphs.text: A fresh wave of bomb threats has disrupted air traffic across Europe but the affected planes landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices.

The latest alerts affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Czechia, France, Italy, Hungary, Cyprus, Romania, the UK and Portugal. Danish police investigated a threat against Copenhagen airport but the airport said it was operating normally.

The warnings followed separate threats on Tuesday and Thursday that forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched, raising questions over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.

The latest threats affected at least nine flights to and from Prague, four flights over France, two flights en route to Sofia and a flight from Lisbon to Rome. Hungary scrambled fighter jets three times to escort civilian flights in its airspace, the defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said on Facebook.

The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny percentage – just 0.0674% – of the 26,709 flights that according to the air traffic control agency Eurocontrol were scheduled in Europe on Friday.
A separate spate of threats on Friday against media organisations in Ireland disrupted broadcasts and prompted staff evacuations and police searches of offices and newsrooms.
The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, told RTÉ Radio 1 after it resumed scheduled broadcasting that such threats had to be taken seriously and were an effort to sow fear and anxiety.

“It shows how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and undermine the normal operation of society.” European security agencies would seek to identify those responsible and hold them accountable, said Martin.
The British broadcaster ⁠Sky said on Friday it had also received a ⁠security threat and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.
Earlier this week, cyber-attacks targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

Investigators have said there was no evidence that hoaxes against airlines and other targets were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, but that inquiries continue.
Some of the threats on Thursday were signed “fighters of the Male State”, a reference to a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016.
Some officials suspect the waves of disruption are linked to European support for Ukraine in its war against the Russian invasion.

Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, said authorities needed more time to identify culprits but that there appeared to be a pattern. “It ⁠cannot be mere coincidence that so many incidents with exactly the same modus operandi are happening across Europe,” he told the national broadcaster TVE.
“The most reasonable assumption is that we are facing an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare,” he said, adding that Europe must be prepared for more such challenges.

npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6030867/jobs-la.headline: Hiring jumps: The economy added 165,000 jobs last month
npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6030867/jobs-la.author: Scott Horsley

paragraphs.text: The U.S. job market picked up steam last month.
Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, according to a report Friday from the Labor Department. The unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%, from 4.2% the previous month.
Employment gains for August and September were revised up by a total of 84,000 jobs.
Industries adding jobs last month include health care, manufacturing, and business services. Meanwhile, restaurants and construction companies cut jobs during the month.

One sign of the strengthening job market was slightly larger wage gains. Average wages in October were up 3.1% from a year ago. That's a bigger annual increase than the previous month, but still probably not enough to keep pace with rising prices.
Inflation climbed to 3.7% in September. The cost of living has been going up faster than wages for much of this year, since the war with Iran triggered a sharp jump in energy prices.
"Workers are losing ground right now," says Cory Stahle, an economist with the Indeed job-search website. "The longer it wears on, the more and more they're going to feel that."
Voters' frustration with high prices was a big factor in the midterm elections, which cost Republicans their majorities in both the House and Senate.

The unemployment rate remains historically low, which has allowed the Federal Reserve to focus its attention on fighting inflation. The central bank held its benchmark interest rate steady last week, but investors expect the Fed to raise rates when policymakers meet in December.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: Anti-fire ant eradication activist convicted after using legal arguments ‘similar to sovereign citizens’
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Andrew Messenger

paragraphs.text: The Queensland leader of a group opposing the eradication of fire ants in Australia has been convicted of obstructing government officers, after a magistrate threw out his argument that the commonwealth-funded program is illegal.

Trevor Hold was fined $1,500 but a conviction was not recorded. Hold has described himself as an “ultrapreneur”, a mental health counsellor, an organic cattle farmer and the chief executive officer of the anti-program group the Australian Advocacy Group – and as self-employed.
He was convicted last month of two counts of obstruction for attempting to prevent fire ant treatment at his property, in what is believed to be a Queensland first.

His organisation and others held a series of well attended meetings last year across south-east Queensland to advise residents on what the group called their legal rights to refuse or prevent access to their properties to the program.
Under Queensland’s Biosecurity Act, landholders must permit program officers to access their property to treat fire ants, which are a declared priority pest.
But the organisations advised landholders to use a provision in the act allowing them to obstruct an officer if they had a “reasonable excuse” to refuse access, a provision in the Biosecurity Act.

On 16 April at about 9.20am, Hold prevented officers from entering his property in Adare in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane. The property was in the treatment zone and due for its annual treatment.

The eradication program had informed Hold in advance that it would treat his property that day. A small group of supporters gathered to film and yell at them while they did so, according to court documents.
The scene was later described as “an increasingly rowdy and crowded and dynamic situation” in the Ipswich magistrates court, which heard Hold’s charges last month.

He was arrested by Queensland police after about 40 minutes for obstructing them by not allowing a gate to be opened. He was then un-arrested. Despite being warned again, he was again arrested after another interaction with program officers.
Hold made three arguments to the magistrate, Leanne Scoines, in his defence.
He argued that he was intimidated by the police and the program officers and “withdrew his consent for their attendance”, describing himself as “frazzled”.
“It was put to Mr Hold that he was not frazzled, and that he had said on three occasions, as heard in the body-worn camera footage, that ‘this is the Trevor Hold show’,” Scoines said.
Through his lawyer, solicitor Beatrice Ludwig, Hold argued that the police had failed to take into account his “reasonable excuse” and were therefore acting outside their powers.

Hold based part of his argument on emails he sent to the Department of Primary Industries in December 2024 and January 2025, notices the magistrate described as “unilateral”, “quasi-legal documents … seeking tacit approval by non-response”. The magistrate found they were of no legal effect.
Finally, he challenged the validity of the program, arguing that the prosecution had not proven it was properly authorised under the Biosecurity Act, Scoines said.

All three arguments were dismissed and the magistrate found that the officers were entitled to proceed on the basis that the DPI officers were exercising powers conferred on them by the Biosecurity Act.
“I am not satisfied that Mr Hold was a credible or liable witness on the critical issues in dispute,” she said.
A police prosecutor told the court “In my respectful submission it was clear he was actually enjoying this incident”.
Hold has appealed against the judgment to the district court.
On his website, Hold advertises fundraising efforts for his defence, and also a mooted class action lawsuit against the program.
Hold would not comment on the case.

Southern Cross University professor David Heilpern compared some of the arguments used by Hold to sovereign citizen cases he used to judge as a magistrate in the NSW Northern Rivers region, particularly his claim that he hadn’t consented to fire ant treatment.

“That is a tried and tested argument in terms of many of those who are on the fringe of or deep into the sovereign citizen movement; that you have a right to remove consent from the operations of various laws,” Heilpern said.
“Whether you consent or don’t consent is completely immaterial under the biosecurity legislation.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/wall-streets-fear-ga.headline: Wall Street's fear gauge may be flashing a buy sign
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/wall-streets-fear-ga.author: Oliver Renick

paragraphs.text: There's nothing like a good selloff to turn a trader into an investor – so the saying goes. It's an adage that echoes the sentiment of an even older one: buy when there's blood in the streets. The maxims ring true after Thursday's selloff in stocks that sent the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) to its biggest one-day move since April 2025's "Liberation" week for tariffs, according to data from Bespoke Investment Group. In the 19 instances since 1990 in which the VIX rose at least five points from under 20 – it surged more than 11 points from 16.6 to 28.2 Thursday – the median return for the S&P 500 Index three months later was 4.2%, and 4.8% six months later, according to Bespoke analysis that also showed returns were positive 68% and 79% of the time over each period, respectively. "These types of sharp spikes from placid levels are like a line of thunderstorms coming through in summer," said Paul Hickey, co-founder of Bespoke. "The sky quickly darkens and wind gusts, but the loudest thunder and brightest lightning doesn't last long."

To be sure, the data do show the storms can be disruptive near-term. While the median return one month after such events was 2.1%, the average return was negative 0.4%, thanks to a few big downdrafts following volatility surges in 1990 and more recently, Feb. 24, 2020, when the Covid selloff was just getting started. According to X account OddStats, there were only 12 other days in stock market history prior to Thursday when the S&P 500 lost 4% and the Nasdaq 100 Index lost 6% – including one during Liberation week 2025 and three instances during the 2020 pandemic.Tech volatility was even more pronounced as the Nasdaq 100 posted its worst day since March 2020. The Cboe Nasdaq Volatility Index VXN jumped more than 13 points to 38.3, the highest since April 11, 2025. The selling was so intense in chipmakers that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) traded below its net asset value. Yet options traders were still leaning bearish in their trades into the bell Thursday, with 670,000 puts traded out of the total 900,000 options on the ETF. Of the total $1.7 billion options premium exchanged, $1.5 billion of it was in puts, according to SpotGamma.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: The Victorian Liberals’ campaign bus was supposed to be a reset. Instead it became the symbol of a rough week
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Benita Kolovos

paragraphs.text: Jess Wilson has barely put a foot wrong since becoming Victorian Liberal leader a little under a year ago. That was until this week, which ended with her campaign bus reversing into a small business.
The bus was launched on Friday, a few days earlier than planned, in what appeared to be an effort to reset Wilson’s relationship with the Spring Street press pack.

A day earlier, journalists had been left waiting for an hour as Wilson announced a $100m investment in medical research to an enthusiastic room of researchers at the Burnet Institute. But when it came to questions she stayed for just four minutes and 39 seconds – answering a single question from each of the nine journalists present before cutting the press conference short.
The pack had been keen to press Wilson on Labor’s claim that the Coalition’s election policies would cost $6.35bn more than they had disclosed.

The treasurer, Colin Brooks, had earlier spent 20 minutes taking journalists through a glossy booklet Labor titled “Jess Wilson’s Dodgy Costings”, which detailed 30 Coalition promises it claimed had not been costed and dozens it said the opposition had underquoted.

It was an interesting stunt given Labor has its own cost blowouts and financial problems – including net debt that is forecast to reach $199bn within four years. But they are not the only ones questioning how the Coalition plans to deliver a surplus by 2032 while making $8bn worth of election promises, offering tax cuts and vowing not to cut frontline services.
The Liberals have made much of their credentials as better economic managers than Labor and Wilson, as shadow treasurer, should have been prepared to stay and defend her own numbers.
The moment played into Brooks’s suggestion earlier in the day that the Liberals “don’t want to be subject to the scrutiny of having journalists … asking questions during the day”.
“They’re thinking they’re going to coast home to this election result, and that’s treating the Victorian people with contempt,” he said.
A similar thing happened last week, when Wilson’s team cancelled a press conference amid confusion over the Coalition’s plan to “pause and review” the multibillion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop project.

Then there is the debate brouhaha. Both News24 and Nine had requested a debate involving Wilson, the Labor premier, Ben Carroll, and the One Nation leader, Warren Pickering – given the latter is now commanding about 20% of primary votes in most polls.

Wilson has refused, instead insisting on a traditional one-on-one format with Labor, arguing that only the two major parties could form government. Carrollwants Pickering to be included, seemingly keen to keep alive the idea of a Liberal-One Nation coalition despite polling suggesting the Liberal-National Coalition should be able to win government in its own right.
Last week, News24 seemed to resolve the impasse by also inviting the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell.

But no agreement has been reached on Nine’s proposal. Wilson issued a statement on Thursday saying she had agreed to debate Carroll next week. This time Labor refused, claiming Nine has offered Pickering the opportunity to appear in a separate 10-minute segment during the same broadcast.
The Liberals reset on Friday, unveiling the “Jess Express” campaign bus.

Wilson was joined by her team and recruits from Canberra – including her close friend and federal Liberal senator James Paterson, and Kane Silom, who has taken leave from his role as communications director for the federal Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, to work on the Victorian campaign.
She chatted with journalists on the bus before it arrived at a Bentleigh cafe, where she made coffees and served brunch before a press conference, this time clocking in at more than 20 minutes.
Pressed again on her party’s costings, she said voters would have to wait until after early voting begins to see them.
“We cannot release our costings until the government has released its pre-election budget update,” Wilson said.

She batted off questions about the Liberals’ latest election commitment – to sell $1.3bn worth of government-owned land. Labor says this is more “dodgy costings” as it includes land earmarked for first home buyers, and a plot where radioactive cow carcasses were buried that would cost millions to clean up.
“Those costs have been factored in as part of the independent costings by the Parliamentary Budget Office,” Wilson said.
Then it was back on the bus and to the Centre Road shops – one of which became the victim of the Jess Express.
But perhaps there’s a glimmer of hope. Despite the damage, the store owner wasn’t too fussed, provided his awning is repaired.
Nor was it enough for him to rule out voting Liberal – he said he was still undecided.
It will take a little more to stop the Coalition momentum at this stage of the campaign.
• Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

politico.com/news/2026/11/06/democratic-.headline: The size of Democrats’ wave surprised even their top House super PAC
politico.com/news/2026/11/06/democratic-.author: Aaron Pellish

paragraphs.text: Even the head of House Democrats’ top super PAC didn’t fully anticipate the size of their massive midterm wave.

Heading into Election Day, House Majority PAC president Mike Smith told POLITICO Tuesday’s results, which have netted them a whopping 252 House seats with more yet to be called, was “on the very high end” of the group’s expectations.

The group spent at least $283 million on ads this cycle, per ad-tracking firm AdImpact, making them the largest Democratic spender in House races this cycle and a significant force behind the party’s big night.
As Democrats turn their attention to 2028, Smith remains optimistic the party can hold on to its majority.
His confidence stems in part from a projection that Democrats will respond to the affordability concerns that were the core of the party’s promise to voters.
If Democrats don’t make efforts to address the rising cost of living, “then it's a totally different story,” Smith said.
Q: How were you feeling in the final days before Tuesday?

Obviously this would have been on the very high end of what we expected. Over the last three months, overall our polling has been pretty consistent. Our whole thought was, with the right environment, if we have the right message and the right types of candidates in, not just the 50-50 districts, but like deeper in the map, that we could put those seats in play and we could potentially win.

Going into Election Day, our whole feeling was there's a clear path to like 235-plus [seats]. We were playing in districts that, if you were to rank them from like one to 435, some of those districts were like 250, 255, right? And I would throw IN-05, CO-03, KY-06, SC-01, some of the Florida races. SC-01 wasn't ever going to be seat 225. That was always in the 240s and maybe even 250s. But we took a chance because we saw what the national environment looked like. We saw what the data was coming back in within these individual races. So I think we were optimistic. But to be totally honest, in our heads, you have to play in seat 255 to get to seat 240. You have to spread out the map. You have to force Republicans on their heels, and then you start piecing together how you get to the 240-245 range. Once the numbers started coming back, that was the best case scenario for us. Everything came together.

You guys cut reservations in some reach districts, only to go back up in the final few days. On the outside, it appeared like cutting spending in those reach districts was a bad sign. What went into those last-minute spending decisions?

A lot of the places we made reservations back in April, and then continued to add on to that over the course of the summer. Partners and allies in a bunch of different places took over our reservations. We tried to be smart by locking in the lowest possible rates in very expensive markets, [so that] even if HMP wasn't the entity spending, we still had partners and allies that were taking over their reservations. In doing all that we saved about $130 million that we could reinvest.

The challenge with some of the races was by a week out, our money was spent. And in some of those districts, there weren't any partners willing to step up and do it. Florida is a good example of that.

That’s where we just had to make a decision that there weren't the resources there, and we had to leave the reservations on the table. Around that time, Mayor Bloomberg was like, "We can't let these races get away from us. We need to do everything we can," and that's where we went back into some of those places.
Did you feel the need to adjust your messaging at all once MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s PAC joined CLF on the airwaves?

The short answer is no. The messaging was fairly consistent. Early on, our whole feeling was we need to reframe how voters perceive Democrats. When voters think about what Democrats are fighting for, the first thing we want them to think about is cost of living, the economy. At the same time, bringing to light Republican policies that are increasing the cost of living, or focus on things that are anything but that.

Over several months, we did a bunch of battleground research looking at ‘how does corruption tie into that,’ which culminated in what we would describe as the cost of Republican corruption, and how that is impacting your day to day and your cost of living. That's what we went into Election Day with.

Overall, we ran, I don't know, 1300 different types of ads, whether TV, digital, direct mail, or whatnot. 76% of those ads talked about the economy. 60% of those ads focused on corruption, because in so many of them, those two things were interlinked in voters' minds.

Republicans continued to focus on the same thing. It was trying to paint Democrats as out of touch or extremists. And again, the theory of the case from the beginning was us focusing on economic concerns, especially when we figured out we could tie that corruption lens into it. That's going to be more important to voters than folks talking about socialism or anything else.
Democrats were able to prevent Republicans from capitalizing on their redistricting gains. Are you worried about those gains bearing fruit in a less favorable environment, maybe as soon as 2028?

In a different environment, these races are going to come together in a much different way. So I do think it's something that we need to be hyper-focused on. That said, I don't think redistricting is going to go away.
I'm actually pretty hopeful that these huge shifts across every demographic group that we just saw, as long as Democrats continue to focus on the issue that matters most to voters.
If we don't, then it's a totally different story.

Are you saying the fate of Democrats' House chances in 2028 to keep these seats is predicated on Congress passing something, even with the current president still in the White House, that addresses affordability issues?
I wouldn't say passing. Soon-to-be Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, since we won, his message is that Democrats are focused on three things: costs, care and corruption.

When we come into power, we are going to be hyper-focused on fighting to bring down the cost of living for voters. I think Donald Trump is still this outsized X-factor in everything. He's still the sitting president in the White House. So I wouldn't say it's like, “Oh we have to pass 300 bills. That's the only way we're going to be successful.” I think we just need to show voters that we are willing to get stuff done, and in instances where we need to, work across the aisle to pass stuff that's going to be helpful to voters. I think if we do that, then I think we're setting ourselves up for success going into ‘28, both with the White House and the House and the Senate. Donald Trump is still going to be this huge factor in all of this, and I don't think voters are going to be like, “Democrats weren't able to accomplish this,” and think that that was us. They're going to continue blaming Donald Trump going into Election Day 2028.
To go back to redistricting, do you want Democrats in these states where they have newly-won trifectas to take up redistricting even if Republicans don’t push for it again?

I think Democrats need to do everything that it will take to win, and if that means that in states where we control the state house, the state senate, a governor's race, we have an opportunity to redraw the map, I think we need to do it.
What were the seats Democrats flipped that surprised you the most?
I would say NJ-02 [Rep. Jeff Van Drew’s seat], It was a district where we had looked at it — we did not think that it was credibly possible, to be totally honest.

I'd say North Carolina as a whole, probably. We felt good about NC-01, NC-11 for a while…. [NRCC Chair and North Carolina Rep.] Richard Hudson, we looked at that district. There was a clear path to winning it. There just wasn't money, at the end of the day. NC-13, NC-14, same thing. The makeup of the districts, they're not bad targets for Democrats. It was just, how much can we spread resources out? But the total implosion in North Carolina by Republicans at the federal level, at the state level — that was probably one of the biggest surprises.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/after-blocking.headline: After blocking Muse, Amazon now lets users text Alexa to help them shop
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/after-blocking.author: Ivan Mehta

paragraphs.text: Amazon is jumping on the currently most popular bandwagon for interacting with AI agents: texting. The company on Friday said it is launching a feature that lets customers chat with its Alexa AI agent over text messages to help them shop, much like you can with AI agents like Muse or Instinct.
The move comes after Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from querying its site in September. The company is rolling the features out just before the start of the holiday shopping season.

The e-commerce giant said select U.S. customers will get a text asking them to enable the shopping feature. Those with access can text Alexa to shop on Amazon using natural language queries, spanning everything from searching for items, adding them to cart, and purchasing.

The text agent builds on the recent shopping-focused upgrades to Alexa, and so can manage lists, keep tabs on prices, search for items across the web, compare products, and check the status of orders. Users can also share a picture of an item or someone wearing an outfit to search for similar listings on Amazon.
The company said over time, Alexa will learn users’ preferences and suggest items accordingly.
The company said users who don’t get invited to use this feature can sign up to a waitlist. The feature will be rolled out more broadly in the coming weeks.

As the market for consumer-focused AI agents balloons, platforms like Amazon are building their own to tap this new avenue of user interaction. Last month, delivery company DoorDash said that third-party agents had so far only placed hundreds of orders in total on its platform, and that it plans to concentrate on developing its own text-based agent, launched in September, further.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Anthropic IPO Valuation Expectations Pressured After AI Rout
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Bailey Lipschultz, Julien Ponthus and Levin Stamm

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Prospective investors in Anthropic PBC's initial public offering are facing a weekend of uncertainty ahead of the kickoff of formal marketing, after a punishing post-election selloff in AI stocks prompted a rethink of the company's expected valuation.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Investors previously told bankers on the IPO that their estimate of a fair valuation had moved to around $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion, Bloomberg News has reported. That has shifted again after the Nasdaq 100 index plunged 6.4% on Thursday, wiping out $2.3 trillion in market value, a record for a single day.

Some potential backers are discussing a $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion range for the company, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified as the information isn't public.
Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions have been made, the person said. A spokesperson for Anthropic declined to comment.

A volatile environment for tech stocks has already dented the outlook for what would be the first IPO by a so-called frontier AI model maker. Investors estimated a fair valuation for Anthropic as high as $2 trillion in early October, people familiar with the matter have said. The retreat to around $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion came after a company briefing on its latest financials in October, Bloomberg News reported at the time.

Questions about the Claude chatbot maker's valuation in the IPO accelerated after the Democratic sweep of Congress triggered the prospect of greater scrutiny over the pace and impact of data center expansion. The Cboe Volatility Index rose to the highest since April 2025 on Thursday, making any IPO more difficult for investors to stomach.

"I would expect, based on the derating we saw in the AI space, valuations might need to be at least at the very low end of the rumored target range of $1.5 to $2 trillion, maybe some 10% to 15% below that," said Stephan Kemper, chief investment officer at BNP Paribas Wealth Management Germany.

Michael Alfaro, the chief investment officer of Gallo Partners, a long-short and event-driven hedge fund, told Bloomberg News before Thursday's market rout that Anthropic needed to target a valuation between $1.3 trillion and $1.4 trillion "in order to build a quality book."

"If they set a valuation toward the bottom of the range, say $1.2 trillion, they shouldn't have a problem finding investors," said David Rainville, a technology portfolio manager at Sycomore Asset Management.

Still, Max Kettner, chief multi-asset strategist at HSBC Holdings Plc, said around $1 trillion could be a more comfortable level for the valuation, reducing the risk of elevated volatility once trading begins.

"I don't think we need the headline 'oh my god, it is a trillion dollar IPO,' because I think what's actually more important is the secondary," Kettner told Bloomberg Radio. "If we get a dynamic like we had with SpaceX, that you get it on secondary and then stock rips for a couple hours, but then it dumps, in the current environment you don't want to have that."

Anthropic and its selling shareholders may start the formal marketing with a conservative size and valuation target and increase it based on a positive initial response from investors. Chipmaker Cerebras Systems Inc. and design software firm Figma Inc. both sold more shares than they initially marketed as bankers gauged rising demand. However, both are now trading well below their IPO prices.

Another, less palatable option is for Anthropic to delay its plans. Companies have to have their IPO filings available to the public for at least 15 calendar days before they can begin formal marketing, typically followed by pricing and trading a week later, but some choose to wait weeks or even months after filing publicly to kick off marketing, updating additional quarterly financial data to keep their disclosures fresh.

"The selloff poses a slight risk for the Anthropic IPO, of course, but when you think of it, maybe it's better to go to the market when the valuation excesses have already been purged," said Alexandre Baradez, chief market analyst at IG in Paris.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Strategist Who Warned Before Rout Sees Anthropic as Bigger Risk
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Matt Clinch, Anna Edwards, Guy Johnson and Tom Mackenzie

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- One of the few Wall Street strategists to turn cautious on stocks ahead of Thursday's selloff warned that a potential Anthropic PBC debut may prove a more decisive event than the US midterms.
Most Read from Bloomberg

HSBC Holdings Plc's Max Kettner cut his rating on stocks from maximum overweight to neutral two weeks ago, arguing that the narrative around tech had turned unfavorable regardless of how companies approached capital spending.

While he sees the artificial intelligence trade as fundamentally intact despite this week's heavy selling, he remains cautious after the vote, questioning how much risk could have cleared when investors had done little to hedge the election in the first place.

"The real risk clearing event is probably the Anthropic IPO in two weeks, if it happens. The best case would probably be you come, but you come with a $1 trillion valuation instead of $1.5 trillion valuation," he said.

Anthropic's planned initial public offering faces various hurdles. Recent selling in AI-related stocks has made the market backdrop less forgiving, while a changing of the guard in Washington also risks shifting expectations for Anthropic's ability to navigate the political landscape.
"You come with a reasonably low valuation, such that in the secondary market you actually start rallying. Or at least not dumping 20-30% in the first week — because that obviously would be horrible."

Kettner made a name for himself in recent years as one of the first to call the current bull run in stocks. But last month he cut back on his bet on stocks for the first time in months. He argued that sharp mood changes among investors warranted a more cautious approach ahead of the US midterms.

"Wednesday was really strange," he told Bloomberg, referring to the initial post-vote rally. "People were asking me, 'Why are you still cautious? Why are you still on the sidelines? What are you doing?'"

For Kettner, the explanations for the rally and then the sharp fall Thursday felt more like narratives being retrofitted to the price action that had genuinely surprised investors. The S&P 500 had its worst day since April 2025, while the Nasdaq 100 and chip index suffered their steepest declines since March 2020.

Kettner drew a parallel between the current environment and January-February 2018, when volatility products imploded, warning that the present selloff felt like a liquidation event driven by momentum unwinds rather than a genuine reassessment of fundamentals.

On the AI trade specifically, Kettner said hyperscalers were likely to find a floor because compute becoming scarcer and more expensive was probably positive for companies with existing capacity to rent out. He added that semiconductors could at some point "rip 20%, 30% in two days just because they squeeze higher," though he acknowledged he did not know when that moment would come.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/kenyan.headline: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years over 191 murders
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/kenyan.author: Carlos Mureithi

paragraphs.text: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in March 2023, when a man told police his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police rearrested him and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.
Reuters contributed reporting

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/ramp-data-show.headline: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/ramp-data-show.author: Rebecca Bellan

paragraphs.text: Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it.

A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.
As Anthropic gears up for its IPO, the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.

“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”

Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “AI-pilled” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said.
Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.

“If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Khazarian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.”
“The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued.
October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Khazarian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong.

Khazarian (who has published a series of blogs called “Cracks in the AI Thesis”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace.

“OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.
Khazarian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market.

Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Khazarian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition.

“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Khazarian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp.
“For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Khazarian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.”

The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty.

“As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Khazarian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.”
Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brr. Costs go ahhh.”

“A lot of the assumptions that we had about the trajectory of AI spend are starting to break down,” Khazarian said. “You can use more AI, but use it for less. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.”

Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.
Khazarian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.

Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend.

Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents. OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Meta have all released their own personal agents, alongside startups like Instinct. Khazarian is skeptical, though, that personal agents, which are “not as economically productive as coding,” will provide the boost the industry needs for nonstop growth.

“The projection is that there will be new products being introduced that will drive further growth,” Khazarian said. “But based on what we can observe today and the products available and what is commercially advanced, AI spend has started to slow down.”
