cnbc.com/2026/11/06/data-centers-ai-elec.headline: Data center double-down: Hassett says Blue Wave won't stop AI build-out
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/data-centers-ai-elec.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said Friday he expects data center growth to continue as projected, despite the blue-wave election that saw voters overwhelmingly favor limiting the tech infrastructure buildout.

Hassett, on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street," acknowledged the dozens of measures on states' midterm ballots seeking to constrain data centers, a crucial part of President Donald Trump's push to win the global artificial intelligence race.
In at least 46 of the at least 50 such initiatives on ballots in 2026, majorities voted to restrict development of the facilities, according to Ballotpedia's tally.

"We respect the localities that decide that's what they want to do," Hassett said. "But America is a big place, and right now, the data centers scheduled over the next couple of years aren't affected by these ballot initiatives."
"And the stuff after that, you know, there's plenty of room in the U.S. for for data center growth to continue, as it was projected ahead of the election," he said.
Hassett said he expects data centers will continue to expand in states with more welcoming governors, and he suggested that even hostile states will eventually come around.

"That's exactly what's going to happen," he said. "That, or what'll happen will be that the benefits of the data centers will be so obvious that people decide to change their minds about the way they regulate them."
Hassett also blamed Thursday's tech-driven market plunge on "uncertainty about what the political change is going to mean for data centers going forward."
"We've now got a ... new majority that maybe is going to go in there and muddle around in there, and I think that markets are anxious about that," he said.

"But I think that the economic strength that we see everywhere else is so strong, and of course, in the end, you could take something that's growing as fast as the data centers and make it grow a little bit slower, and you still have a blockbuster economy."
"And so, I think we're still very, very optimistic about what's going to happen going forward," he said.
The CNBC Voter Poll found 56% of midterm voters identified data centers as either a crucial or major issue — and of those who considered it crucial, 62% favored the generic Democratic candidate.
Trump has strongly embraced AI and data centers and has even tried to reverse their seeming unpopularity by rebranding the tech as "super intelligence," or SI.
In a Truth Social post Friday, Trump made clear that despite the midterm losses, his support for the nascent industry has not faltered.

"As President, I am 100% in favor of Super Intelligence (SI), and will work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them," Trump wrote. "They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say 'NO' to the riches they bring!"

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq62yy064vjpo.headline: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq62yy064vjpo.author: Henry Moore

paragraphs.text: European airlines have again been hit with a new wave of bomb threats - in the third such incident this week.
On Friday multiple flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia were targeted and the threats saw three planes escorted by Hungarian fighter jets, authorities said.

It also saw a number of high-profile media organisations, including Ireland's public broadcaster RTÉ, evacuated after threats were made against them - although there has been no concrete links between the messages against airlines and the broadcasters.
The disruption comes after nearly 30 aircraft and several airports across Europe were impacted by threats earlier this week, in what the UK called a "malicious hoax".

A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.
France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely.
No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday.
As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them.

Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.
In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".
While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".

In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public.
"Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.
Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.
Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week.
Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.

The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities".
"The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."
Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings.

Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.

"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c35ynnpzdq51o.headline: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c35ynnpzdq51o.author: Rachel Clun

paragraphs.text: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have started to climb following an enormous sell-off on Thursday that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
The Nasdaq Composite opened up 1.23% and continued to gain in early trading, reversing some of its 5.5% fall from Thursday.
The S&P 500 - home of the largest publicly-traded US companies that are not in the technology sector - also opened up slightly, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down.
Firms that experienced heavy losses on Thursday also began to bounce back in early trading.
Nvida, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday trading up more than 6%.
SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw more mixed gains, up more than 7% and nearly 3% respectively.
The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.

A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.

The increase in jobs was led by the professional and business services sector, which added 70,000 jobs. The healthcare sector added 42,000 jobs, and jobs were also added in transportation and warehousing as well as manufacturing.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Hassett Says No Economic Policy Shift Even After Election Rout
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Michael Sasso

paragraphs.text: Fri, November 6, 2026 at 10:37 AM EST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump's chief economic adviser said the administration won't be revamping its economic policies in the wake of Republicans' sweeping defeat in the midterm congressional elections.
Most Read from Bloomberg
"I don't think we have a policy change we need to plan," Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council, said in an interview on Bloomberg TV Friday. "The policies are working."

Hassett argued the Democratic victory in the elections wasn't a rebuttal of the president's supply-side policies, and reiterated Trump's threat to use vetoes to keep his agenda in place. Among other benefits, those measures have led to 120,000 people involved in building new factories, Hassett said, following an October employment report showing the nation added 165,000 jobs last month.

Trump "is concerned that the positive momentum that we've built could be upended by Democrats now that they've taken more power," Hassett said. "But I think they're going to have a really hard time repealing all the great policies which created the strong job market, because the president will veto it."

Hassett attributed recent stickiness in inflation to the Iran war and its effects on gasoline prices, rather than the administration's economic policies, which he suggested are having a downward effect on inflation. He contrasted that with what he called the inflationary impact of former President Joe Biden's agenda, "where they basically helicopter-dropped money down to people after the Covid crisis was over."

Joking that he had gotten a "veto hat" from the president, Hassett said the administration also has a "huge amount" of executive authority to keep pressing ahead with its program, including taking on over-regulation.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Goldman’s US Stock Panic Gauge Hits Extreme, Signaling Rebound
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Natalia Kniazhevich

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Goldman Sachs Group Inc. traders said the violent selloff in US equities has pushed market panic to an extreme level that historically signals a strong rebound over the medium term.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The bank's Vol Panic Index surged to 9.57 out of 10 on Thursday, crossing the 9.5 threshold that marks the panic zone. The roughly five-point increase was the third-largest daily jump on record. Coming on the heels of a huge decline Wednesday, the fourth largest, it resulted in the biggest ever two-day swing, traders including Lee Coppersmith wrote.
"The combined two-day swing was the largest on record, which I think shows how quickly the market went from relief to outright panic," Coppersmith said.

The sharp reversal followed an aggressive wave of demand for downside protection ahead of Wednesday's US midterm vote. Clients had sold hedges into the post-election relief rally, leaving portfolios materially under-protected when equities turned lower. As stocks tumbled and forced liquidations spread across hedge funds, investors scrambled to buy back the protection they had just shed, according to the traders.

The rush for hedges was reflected in options activity. More than 11 million puts traded on Cboe on Thursday, the highest daily volume on record, surpassing the previous peak in April 2025. Index puts accounted for much of the activity, while single-stock put volume ranked fourth-highest ever, highlighting the concentration of demand in broad-market protection.

Still, Goldman's historical analysis suggests the medium-term outlook becomes more constructive when panic reaches such extremes. Following the 15 previous signals in which its Vol Panic Index exceeded 9.5, the S&P 500 gained an average 4.6% over the subsequent three months, with an 80% hit rate. Over six months, the average gain was 9%, with stocks rising in 73% of cases.
"Yesterday was as much about an exceptionally poor technical setup and forced re-hedging as it was about a deterioration in fundamentals," Coppersmith wrote.

While there is still more positioning to work through as markets continue to search for a bottom, the historical pattern suggests that extreme volatility and forced selling can eventually create opportunities for investors willing to look beyond the near-term turbulence, according to Goldman's traders.

"The setup starts to look more interesting as forced selling runs its course," Coppersmith said. "Not necessarily a reason to rush back into risk, but it's getting harder to ignore the potential opportunity on the other side."

finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-co.headline: US Consumer Sentiment Unexpectedly Rises, Fueled by Independents
finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/us-co.author: Julia Fanzeres and Maria Paula Mijares Torres

paragraphs.text: Julia Fanzeres and Maria Paula Mijares Torres
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 10:00 AM EST 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- US consumer sentiment rose in November to a three-month high, bolstered by modest improvements in Americans' views of their personal finances and the economic outlook.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The University of Michigan's preliminary sentiment index increased to 51 in November from 48 in October, according to the survey released Friday. The median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of economists projected sentiment to hold at 48.
The improvement was concentrated among independents, who reported the strongest consumer sentiment in more than a year. Sentiment across both Democrats and Republicans deteriorated.
Cost of living concerns remain top of mind for many Americans. About 57% of respondents spontaneously mentioned that high prices had eroded their living standards -- the highest since May.

Despite limited layoffs and strong economic growth, household finances have been squeezed as prices rise faster than wages. Democrats' decisive victory in the midterm elections reflected deep voter frustration with the economy, particularly the high cost of food, gasoline and housing.

Inflation expectations in the year ahead improved but remained elevated. Consumers expect prices to rise 4.3% over the next year, a three-month low. They also saw costs climbing at an annual rate of 3.4% over the next five to 10 years, also a step down from the prior month.
In addition to inflation worries, "consumers' comments revealed growing anxiety over a possible AI bubble," Joanne Hsu, director of the survey, said in a statement.

"The personal finances of consumers with the largest stock portfolios dropped 12% this month to their lowest reading since April, likely due to agitation in stock values in recent weeks, while all other wealth groups saw modest improvements," she added.
A gauge of current personal finances climbed to a four-month high in November, while Americans' views of buying conditions for durable goods rebounded from a record low.
Gauges of current and expected conditions both rose to the highest since August.
The survey period includes responses from Oct. 20 to Nov. 2.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/fox-completes-.headline: Fox completes its $22B acquisition of Roku
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/fox-completes-.author: Lauren Forristal

paragraphs.text: Fox has completed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, wrapping up one of the biggest media deals in recent years and giving the company a major boost in the streaming and connected TV space.

Announced Friday, the deal brings the streaming company founded in 2002 formally under Fox’s ownership. Fox says the combined company now ranks as the third-largest television business in the U.S. by viewership.

“We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources,” Roku founder Anthony Wood said in a statement. “Our teams will keep building and innovating as they always have, now with the support and capabilities of Fox behind us.”

For Fox, the move provides direct access to Roku’s reach of more than 100 million households. The company expects that audience to help it improve advertising targeting, strengthen its position in the fast-growing connected TV market, and reduce its reliance on traditional TV distribution.

Today’s announcement comes two months after the Justice Department issued a second request for information, asking both companies to provide additional data and documents as part of its antitrust review. Earlier this month, reports suggested the deal was nearing U.S. regulatory approval.
The acquisition also closed much earlier than expected. When the deal was first announced in June, the companies projected it would be completed in the first half of 2027.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2d66n0lx1yo.headline: Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2d66n0lx1yo.author: Sarah Rainsford

paragraphs.text: The "Male State", an extremist misogynistic group named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, has denied any link to the false warnings causing flight disruption across Europe.

The comments to the BBC came as reports of more bomb scares to airlines began appearing, including on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome which was diverted to Venice.

Bomb threats were also reported to a number of high-profile Irish media organisations on Friday, prompting evacuations and a statement from the Irish government suggesting a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption".

Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.

"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"
The group was banned in Russia in 2021 and Pozdnyakov is now thought to live abroad. It has since renamed itself in some places as "Male Legion".
The initial hoax email, seen by the BBC, was sent on Thursday at 07:21 with the subject title: warning of a threat.

It was addressed to several offices and individuals at Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), the airport managing company in Rome, as well as accounts at the city's Fiumicino airport itself. The originating email address seems to be linked to the state health services in Bogota, Colombia.
It's not clear whether other countries' airports or airlines received the same or similar threat. At least one warning made on Friday appears to have come by phone, not email.

Written in word perfect Italian, the bizarre text sent to Rome on Thursday claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights in an attack on Italy's "feminist regime" that would be "remembered forever".

One flight was diverted as a result - ordered to land in France – another was escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, scrambled for the second time this week. No explosives were found on either plane, or any other that reported receiving bomb threats.
Asked why this particular email was taken so seriously, a source at ADR in Rome told the BBC that such warnings were extremely unusual. They didn't remember anything similar in recent years.
Despite the Russian group's denial, Italy's La Stampa newspaper appears in no doubt that "Male State" was behind the threats, asking in an article whether it is acting as "the regime's armed wing".
"Attacking, and being able to deny the attacks...is part of the Russian game plan," the paper writes, external.

One Telegram channel linked to Pozdnyakov is mainly filled with virulently pro-Russian messaging about the war on Ukraine and other posts highlighting problems and tensions in Europe, including recent youth protests.
The online investigation team at Bellingcat, who studied the group back in 2022, called it then a "vocal and vile online booster" of the Russian invasion, with a clear extremist far-right ideology.

As the Europe-wide hunt continues for who is behind the spate of hoax mails, and whether they are being co-ordinated - or could be the work of copycats - Italy's defence minister has warned of a "strategy to increase chaos".
Guido Crosetto noted that he had been talking of the "hybrid threat" to Europe for some years.

"It seems to me that, day after day, from incidents involving refrigerators to the blood supply in France and now these false alarms, there are those who have an interest in fuelling tensions," the minister said on Thursday, referring to a spate of recent cyber attacks that boosted supermarket fridge temperatures, destroying mountains of produce.
"Our interest is to do the opposite and ensure the country's security," Crosetto said.
Additional reporting by Davide Ghiglione

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-05/.headline: How Mayor-elect Nithya Raman will remake L.A. City Hall
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-05/.author: David Zahniser, Colleen Shalby, Itzel Luna

paragraphs.text: Bike lanes. Housing vouchers. A new police chief and many more new apartments, even in single-family neighborhoods.
And above all, data to find out if City Hall programs are working.

Mayor-elect Nithya Raman won’t represent a radical ideological break from her opponent, one-term incumbent Mayor Karen Bass. Like Bass, she’s a Democrat who believes in ending homelessness, keeping the city safe and delivering basic services.

But Raman is expected to push the city to the left on public safety, while also advancing urbanist policies that favor public transit, greater housing production and the redesign of city streets to improve safety and support alternatives to driving.

Rick Cole, a former deputy Los Angeles mayor who advised Raman throughout the campaign, said she’s dead serious about her campaign slogan “a city that works” — taking steps to ensure that streets, sidewalks and other parts of the city infrastructure are repaired, while also providing prompt responses to 911 calls.
Raman intends to be a hands-on manager, he said, improving coordination between city departments and analyzing ways to make them more effective.
“L.A. has been flying blind when it comes to measuring the impacts of the dollars spent,” said Cole, a Pasadena City Council member. “That is going to change.”

As mayor, Raman will have the power to hire and fire the managers of dozens of city agencies and appoint or remove hundreds of citizen commissioners — most of them volunteers — who will serve as an extension of her administration.

Cole is widely expected to supervise Raman’s transition team, sharing those duties with Andrea Conant, chief of staff for Raman’s council office. The mayor-elect will also have a close ally in City Controller Kenneth Mejia, the only elected official at City Hall to endorse her.

On the campaign trail, Raman has promised to let Mejia audit every dollar of city spending on homelessness, setting the stage for a potential overhaul of L.A.’s approach to the crisis. She said she would let his teams of investigators monitor encampment cleanups and operations aimed at moving homeless people indoors, something Bass resisted.

Raman has described the city’s use of hotel and motel rooms for temporary housing as expensive and ineffective, saying short-term rental vouchers are a better alternative. She has vowed to cut homelessness in half by the 2028 Olympic Games and entirely by the end of her four-year term.

Where Raman will land on public safety is murkier. She promised to replace Police Chief Jim McDonnell, saying he has lost the trust of Angelenos, while offering diverging answers on when that would happen. She told one news outlet she would keep him until 2030 and another she would start the replacement process on Day One.

When she began her mayoral campaign in February, Raman said the Los Angeles Police Department — which then had 8,700 officers — should not get any smaller. The LAPD has lost 200 since then. Raman has offered few strategies for rebuilding the force.
“I don’t think it should be shrinking indefinitely,” she said in August.

Raman, as part of her agenda for her first 100 days, said she will seek an audit of the Police Department’s efforts to follow L.A.’s sanctuary city law, which requires that city agencies treat information that can be used to trace a person’s citizenship or immigration status as confidential.

Once she takes office, Raman will be thrust almost immediately into salary negotiations with the Los Angeles Police Protective League, which waged an expensive campaign to defeat her. She opposed the union’s last contract, saying the package of raises and retention bonuses “bankrupted the city” and forced cuts to many taxpayer services.

Even though she is backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, the leftist organization that has supported her since 2020, Raman probably will govern in some ways as a fiscal hawk, said political science professor Fernando Guerra, who heads the Center for the Study of Los Angeles.

Raman opposed the $2.6-billion upgrade of the Los Angeles Convention Center, even as labor leaders and business groups said it would create jobs and help revive a struggling downtown, saying it would eventually add more than $100 million per year in costs to the city budget.

“When she voted against the raises for the police, she didn’t use arguments about defunding the police. She used a fiscal argument,” Guerra said. “When she was against the Convention Center, she didn’t say that it wouldn’t help the community. She used the fiscal argument [against it]. She understands numbers and their consequences.”

Raman was embraced by members of the YIMBY movement, which has been looking to ramp up housing production as a way of lowering rents. She promised to create a 60-day “shot clock” for the approval of new apartment projects that comply with city zoning laws.

She criticized Bass for opposing Senate Bill 79, the law that allows the construction of six- to nine-story apartments near rail stations and other transit stops. She vowed to bring “gentle density” — duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes — to single-family neighborhoods that are near public transit hubs.

“These are the kinds of homes that built L.A. and the kind of homes that many Angelenos want to live in,” said Scott Epstein, policy and research director at the nonprofit Abundant Housing LA, which endorsed Raman.
Epstein said his group appreciates some of the steps taken by Bass to speed up housing production. However, he sees “a lot more energy with Nithya,” he said.

Noah Suarez-Sikes, a member of DSA-LA’s steering committee, said his group expects Raman to follow through on her promise to create an Office of Tenant Protections to enforce the city’s laws protecting renters from harassment.
“They very rarely get used, but there’s many instances where tenants are being harassed by corporate landlords,” he said.

Raman is also expected to champion policies sought by the region’s transportation advocates. As a candidate, she criticized Bass for blocking a plan to install new bicycle lanes through Griffith Park, saying the improvements were urgently needed to reduce traffic deaths.

Hedge fund manager Aaron Sosnick, a bike lane advocate with homes in multiple cities, donated a combined $8 million to outside campaigns that promoted Raman and attacked Bass’ record. Some of those campaign ads were produced by the advocacy group Streets for All, best known for its success in 2024 in passing Measure HLA, which requires the expansion of bus lanes, bike lanes and other street improvements during major road repairs.

Michael Schneider, who heads that group, said he believes Raman will consolidate some of the city departments that are responsible for street maintenance, to make them more effective. He said it’s also likely she will pursue a ballot measure in 2028 — possibly a bond or tax hike — to raise money for sidewalk repairs, curb replacements, wheelchair ramps and other improvements.
Schneider predicted that Raman also will go much further than former Mayor Eric Garcetti, another transit enthusiast, on such issues as bike lanes, making tough decisions “even though it’s hard.”

“It doesn’t mean she’s going to railroad everything,” he said. “But I think she has much more of a political spine than Garcetti did when it comes to street safety, pushing projects through that may ruffle some feathers but are worth it for the safety benefits.”

Cole, the former deputy mayor, said Raman plans to place more emphasis on the commission system, which assigns citizen volunteers selected by the mayor to provide oversight of a number of city agencies, including the LAPD, the Department of Transportation and three proprietary agencies — the Department of Water and Power, the Port of Los Angeles and Los Angeles World Airports.

Raman will also join the 13-member Metropolitan Transportation Authority, where she will have the power to pick three of her colleagues. How she will interact with those other Metro board members — and the region’s other elected officials — is yet to be seen.
Times staff writer Noah Goldberg contributed to this report.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/pentagon-offer.headline: Pentagon offers battery startup 6K $250M loan to build U.S. factory
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/pentagon-offer.author: Tim De Chant

paragraphs.text: Batteries are everywhere, even on the battlefield, which helps explain the Pentagon’s recent interest in building more domestic manufacturing capacity.

The 12-year-old, North Andover, Mass.-based startup 6K announced Thursday that it won conditional approval for a $250 million loan from the Department of Defense to build a factory in Tennessee. The plant will use a unique microwave-powered process to produce battery materials that don’t rely on Chinese suppliers.

The company previously received a $50 million grant from the Department of Energy under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, though that 2023 grant was canceled by the Trump administration in a chaotic sweep of Biden-era awards, forcing 6K to reapply.
Initially, the factory was originally slated to open in 2024, but the grant cancelation and uncertainties in the EV market forced the company to rejigger its plans.

6K’s manufacturing process uses microwaves to heat metals into a plasma and then deposit them onto a surface, reducing the number of steps required to make cathode material, a key battery component. The company says the process can work on a number of different battery types, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP).

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/coreweave-bond-yield.headline: The AI ‘credit card’ is getting costlier as CoreWeave bond yield tops 16%
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/coreweave-bond-yield.author: Deena Zaidi

paragraphs.text: Debt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we're hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit.

That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: "The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away."

That isn't happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

The poster child for debt stress is neocloud Coreweave. The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave's five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank. The CDS eased 8% Friday to around 1,155.

"We've had plenty of warnings from the credit space," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note on Friday. Debt and equities are now moving more in sync, he added, "so we'll have to see if credit goes any further."
Investors are demanding more compensation to insure against default among even companies with the strongest balance sheets and credit ratings, including Nvidia, Broadcom, and Amazon.com.

CDS on Nvidia debt is up 76% in the last month. Broadcom's CDS is up 49%, while Amazon's has gained 44%. Their CDS remain low on an absolute basis; Nvidia's spread stood at roughly 139 basis points, compared with about 298 bps for Oracle and roughly 1,100 for CoreWeave. A large increase from a low starting point does not imply the same credit risk.
Still, rising CDS are a sign that markets want more protection against default among even the largest and healthiest debt issuers. And rising CDS imply higher financing costs down the line.

The market is now grappling with the prospect that at least some data center spending will be delayed or scrapped under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia, the three states with much of the planned capacity.

Moratoriums could impact 45% of planned capacity in the U.S. with a large amount of that in Texas, according to Goldman Sachs. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she's not opposed to data centers but wants a moratorium until the state legislature passes protections for communities.

None of these means AI debt financing is collapsing. Goldman tallies five AI bond deals totaling $67 billion since October 29, pushing total hyperscaler debt issuance this year to $296 billion. Goldman forecasts $440 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, plus an additional $300 billion of project-level issuance across investment-grade and high-yield.

The Trump administration is vowing to support data centers. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data center growth to continue as forecast, despite Democrats' big election wins.
What comes next

The big question now is how quickly AI spending will generate enough cash for hyperscalers to keep investors comfortable with future capex plans. For the neoclouds, any sign of consolidation or retrenchment in capex could result in fewer or shorter contracts for data center compute or delays in prepayments.
Goldman analysts said hyperscalers collectively reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter as capital spending exceeded operating cash flow.

"Delayed monetization and growth in purchase commitments—which we view as additional and sizable uses of cash, separate from Capex—are the key risks to more debt issuance, subject to market conditions," according to the bank.

Peak AI debt issuance may now be closer at hand. Bank of America analysts estimates that AI-related credit issuance will rise 31% from 2026 to 2027, hitting $685 billion, including public and private debt. They then see it falling 23% to $531 billion in 2028.

As for the risk? "Downside to these forecasts exists from a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure projects on the back of the Blue Wave, which will reduce capex needs and thus debt market funding," BofA said in a note.
-CNBC's Nick Wells and Michael Bloom contributed reporting

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx8dzzy8n713o.headline: Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx8dzzy8n713o.author: George Dabby

paragraphs.text: More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, according to the man behind Barack Obama's successful re-election bid.

Jim Messina, who led Obama's 2012 campaign, said that since Democrats saw major victories in congressional races as well as state elections, he's spoken to "over two dozen campaigns" that are actively considering running in 2028 and have begun the financing process and hiring staff.
"I think you're going to start having Democrats announce exploratory committees next week or the next couple of weeks, probably after Thanksgiving", Messina told the BBC's Americast podcast.
He said he already knows someone relocating to work on a governor's presidential campaign.
He also predicted that the number could shrink as candidates faced pressure to raise large sums needed for the primary contests that will decide the party's nominee.

Messina gave some insight into the conversations he's had, saying: "When I sit down with candidates or their campaigns, I say to them, 'Tell me your economic vision for the future of this country. What are you going to do on AI?'"
Then there's another factor: the outgoing president, Donald Trump, who will still be in office during the campaign season.
"And so, do the Democrats take the bait and talk about Donald Trump every day, or do you stay focused on your message?" he said.
"It's going be the most interesting presidential [election] since 2008."

Messina, who went on to become Obama's deputy chief of staff at the White House, said the party's success in the US midterm elections was down to their ability to stay focused on the economy and the effect of Donald Trump's tariffs, which were "devastating to rural voters".
"When you're a farmer and you're paying $7 for a gallon of diesel to put in your tractor, the economics just don't work, and at the same time you're paying more for everything," he said.
Staying on message about the economy helped them flip seats in traditionally strong Republican states like Iowa, Kansas, and Texas, he said.

"The common criticism of Democrats is that we can't stick to one message. And for the first time in a very long time, Democrats stuck to the economy. They didn't take the bait on the social wars," he said.
Messina cautioned Democrats that success in this year's midterm elections was not a ringing endorsement of the party and that "the MVP of the election for the Democrats was Donald Trump".
The hard part will now be bringing the party's progressive and centrist wings together in Congress, he said.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Berkshire’s Pivot to AI Bets Gets an Immediate Reality Check
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Alex Rajbhandari

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- In his first year as Chief Executive Officer of Berkshire Hathaway Inc., Greg Abel has pushed the conglomerate into an entirely new area of investment: artificial intelligence.
Most Read from Bloomberg

In a significant departure from Warren Buffett's famous reservations about technology stocks, the new CEO started cutting checks soon after he took on the job. In just a few months, he handed $10 billion to Google parent Alphabet Inc. to support its AI-related investments and plowed another $930 million into Bending Spoons SpA, an Italian conglomerate that uses the technology to transform businesses.
But with cracks in the AI trade starting to show, Berkshire's sudden push may appear ill-timed.
"I do think that part of this may be a conscious decision to increase their exposure," said Cathy Seifert, an analyst for CFRA Research. "One has to ask the question though, is it a little late?"

Since June, Alphabet's Class A and Class C shares have tumbled more than 24% and are now trading below the discounted price at which Berkshire acquired them — prompting some to wonder whether its bet on the firm is a stinker. And while Bending Spoons' stock surged after Berkshire added to its initial investment, the enthusiasm was short-lived: The stock has fallen over the past three weeks.

Still, for dedicated value investors and longtime Berkshire observers, such jitters may not really matter. After all, Buffett's 2016 investment in Apple Inc., derided at the time as being late in the iPhone maker's history, turned out to be one of Berkshire's most lucrative bets. Abel likely views Berkshire's AI investments as a long-term wager on the technology's potential, said Meyer Shields, an analyst for Keefe Bruyette & Woods.
"He's not trying to send a message to the markets," said Shields. The CEO "can consider these investments with all the conservatism that you would expect at Berkshire Hathaway."

And given AI's massive investment needs in the years to come, Berkshire, which was still sitting on a $365.5 billion cash pile at the end of the second quarter, is among the best placed to support the technology's development — and reap potential gains.

Investors will have to wait until mid-November to know whether Abel, in a typical value investor mindset, has decided to benefit from the market's concerns around AI, and the lower valuations, to put more money into the trade.
Meanwhile, Berkshire Hathaway is expected to release its third-quarter earnings Saturday, giving shareholders a peek into the conglomerate's financial standing.
The company, with its vast stable of businesses spanning insurance, energy and retail, may benefit from the health of the US economy in the period.
"It seems like overall economic growth in the quarter was pretty solid, and so much of Berkshire participates in the economy," Shields said.
But as high gas prices and inflation persist, investors may want to pay attention to the firm's collection of retail businesses.

"We're hearing a lot of anecdotal stories about the top-end investment portfolios, the wealth effect helping spending, but at the lower end, they're really squeezed," Seifert said. "We could see some of that in Berkshire's consumer businesses."

Investors are likely to pay attention to the performance of the firm's insurance businesses, including auto insurer Geico, as well. Last quarter, in sharp contrast to some of its peers, the unit reported lower earnings amid higher losses and advertising expenses.
"The overall personal auto insurance market has been rationally competitive," Shields said. "I think what we'll see is reports of a more aggressive growth strategy at Geico."
Across the rest of the group, strong traffic data and a fuel surcharge could support the performance of Berkshire's railroad operator, BNSF, according to analysts.

Investors are also expected to monitor whether Berkshire will buy back more of its own shares. After a hiatus that lasted more than a year, the conglomerate resumed share purchases in the first quarter, a sign that Abel and Buffett believe the stock was trading below its intrinsic value.
Since then, however, Berkshire shares have reached new heights. It's outperforming the S&P 500 this year.
"If that recent uptick in the shares may have quelled their enthusiasm for buying back more shares, I think investors may be a little disappointed in that," Seifert said.

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/mississippi-senate-t.headline: Mississippi Senate: Longshot Ty Pinkins says he aimed to spoil Hyde-Smith, boost Colom vote
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/mississippi-senate-t.author: Dan Mangan

paragraphs.text: Longshot Mississippi Senate candidate Ty Pinkins at first wanted to win — but says he stayed in to spoil.

Pinkins told a local TV station he remained in the race after an April poll showed he had no chance to boost Democratic nominee Scott Colom's chances of beating Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Pinkins' purported strategy might pay off.

Colom is narrowly leading Hyde-Smith in ongoing counting by just 1,936 votes, a margin of just 0.2 percentage points with 96.2% of the vote counted, according to the Associated Press. That margin is about one-tenth as large as Pinkins' 2.1-percentage-point share of the vote.
Pinkins has won just 20,010 votes so far out of the nearly 952,000 votes already counted.

"The only thing I did was stay in the race and let people shoot arrows at me," Pinkins said in an interview with WTVA in Mississippi on Thursday. "That is it. And that's a ... low price to pay to get someone in this race that I think can help people in the Delta and all across this state."
"The portion of the vote that I drew — and people were concerned about splitting the Black vote — what I actually did was split the Republican vote," he said.
Pinkins told the station in Tupelo that he intentionally avoided campaigning in areas with large Black populations to avoid cutting into the vote share of Colom, who, like Pinkins, is Black.
That tactic worked, he said, as the election results show he got most of his support from areas with relatively low Black populations.

"I'll be the boogeyman," he said. "But I'll tell you this: The independent in this race pulled most of his votes from a Republican, and for the first time since Reconstruction, a Democrat who is a Black man is leading."

Pinkins, a lawyer who previously ran for Mississippi secretary of state, was the Democratic nominee for Senate in 2024. He was crushed by Republican Sen. Roger Wicker, who won nearly 63% of the vote, compared to about 37% for Pinkins.
Despite that showing, the U.S. Army veteran decided to take another crack at the Senate in 2026.
But in the spring, he saw the writing on the wall for his candidacy.

"I got in this race to win," Pinkins told WTVA. "In April, I knew I was going to lose, but I also knew that I was pulling 70% of the Republican vote based on the [SPLC Action Fund and Impact Research] poll."
SPLC Action Fund, when it released the poll, said, "Sagging favorability numbers for Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith could open up a path to victory for Democrats.
"Independent Ty Pinkins has the potential to play spoiler for either candidate," SPLC Action Fund said in April.
In the WTVA interview, Pinkins said, "I probably attended maybe, maybe six events over the summer" as part of his campaign.
"Six events. I don't have to," Pinkins said. "Why? I'm not going to win. So why go to these Black communities that he's going to?"
"Some Republicans that say they're gonna that they're gonna vote for me," he said.

"They were literally calling me and sending me emails: 'We're gonna vote for you because we don't want to waste our vote on Cindy Hyde-Smith, we don't want to hold our nose and vote for her, so we're going to vote for you. Please stay in the race.'"
The campaigns of Colom and Hyde-Smith did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq1m41n3v7mmo.headline: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq1m41n3v7mmo.author: Bernd Debusmann

paragraphs.text: White House reporter
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.
Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.
But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.
No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.
The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways.
The 2026 winners who now have momentum
Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.
Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.
While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.
Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger.
Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.
Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.

California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.
On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.

Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.
JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressure
Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.
That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.
Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.
Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.
In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.
"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.
Left and centre Democrats in fight for future
Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.
Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.
El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.
His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.

"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.
Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."

Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.
This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.
Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.
Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.
Support of Hispanic voters must be earned
Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.
Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.
Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.

Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".
That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.
"Neither party owns these voters," she said.
The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.

Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.
"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.
"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq99zd93ryvko.headline: Judge blocks construction of Donald Trump's massive arch
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq99zd93ryvko.author: Nardine Saad, Isabella Jewell

paragraphs.text: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approval
A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in the nation's capital.
US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch in Washington which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.
Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch.

Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people.

The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.
The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment.

"The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission's decision to fully approve President Trump's historic vision to build a much needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, DC," a White House spokesperson told the BBC in a statement.
It is not yet clear when construction of the arch could begin, as several lawsuits seek to block the project.
The White House criticised the federal court that temporarily halted construction as an "activist district court."
"We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch," the spokesperson said.

A rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.
A website that the White House shared on social media on Friday also shows a video rendering of the arch that shows the structure emblazoned with the words "Golden Age of America" along one side.
It refers to the structure as "The Military Triumphal Arch".
The proposed structure is sprinkled with appliques that are visually similar to the golden embellishments Trump has added to the Oval Office.
The Trump administration has also said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.

"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.

Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments".
He and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended.
Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".
Opponents have strongly disagreed.
Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction.
"We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.
Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego – they've been rejected."

Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".
He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks.
Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.

Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves".
"This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.

Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch.

It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (£300m).
His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.
Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx30ee8018lvo.headline: US midterm results spark fears in Israel over future of two countries' ties
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx30ee8018lvo.author: Lucy Williamson

paragraphs.text: As the US midterm election results rolled in, long-held Israeli assumptions about the transatlantic alliance began to shatter.

"For us in Israel, this will be a generational sea change," wrote one prominent journalist in Israel's biggest-selling newspaper, right-leaning Yedioth Ahronoth. "The [prime minister, Benjamin] Netanyahu government sowed the wind and reaped the tsunami."
Israel's opposition leaders have lined up to blame their prime minister, with one saying the US results showed "just how toxic Netanyahu has become" among both Democrats and Republicans.
The prime minister himself has so far remained silent.

"Israel's political establishment understood intellectually that things have been shifting. They have not understood how much and how quickly," one US official with knowledge of the situation told me.
Israel's relationship with the US was a campaign issue in races across America.
Many Democratic candidates were sharply critical of Israel's actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, and the costs of the joint US-Israeli war on Iran was a key issue for many voters.
The US president himself blamed the Iran War for the Republican rout – a war that Israel's leader is widely seen as having promoted to him.

And US Vice-President JD Vance cited the US relationship to Israel as one of four key reasons voters had deserted the party, hammering home the message that the relationship is now seen as a political problem by its key ally.

"That might be even worse than what happened in the midterms," Israeli political and security analyst Yaakov Katz told me. "Because the Democrats we knew about, now [Vance] is pointing the finger and saying: 'Our voters want us to change our position on Israel' – and Israelis don't fully understand where this is going."
The question plaguing Israelis now is what this means for Israel's security and influence.

The sense of staunch US military and diplomatic support had remained unshaken in Israel despite growing anger among US voters, President Donald Trump's public insults to Netanyahu, and differences over Israel's actions in Iran and Lebanon.
Israel's prime minister continually boasted of his closeness to Trump, describing his "true friendship" and "unwavering support".

And just nine months ago, Israelis watched their armed forces wage war on Iran hand in hand with the US military, as the "unprecedented" coordination of the two allies became a daily mantra among military spokespeople and politicians.

So Trump's unexpected statement during a Fox News interview this week that he would stop $3.8bn (3.4bn euros; £2.8bn) in US military aid to Israel two years earlier than planned, caused shock here – not so much for the loss of aid as for what the move said about Israel's status as a diplomatic partner.
Israel's president said the announcement came as "a bolt from the blue".
"Nobody knows anything," was the headline in a report by Yedioth Ahronoth, adding that officials were still struggling to understand whether Trump's remark was serious, two days on.
The Israeli prime minister's office responded to the news several days later, saying that the shift from US aid to partnership showed "the strength and sophistication" of the bilateral relationship.

US military aid is less than 10% of Israel's annual military budget. But Yaakov Katz, author of several books about Israel's defence and security, said Trump's announcement was the tip of a much larger question around future funding, arms sales and joint military projects with Israel. All of this could be slowed or stalled by a Democrat-controlled Congress, even without the two-thirds majority it would need to overrule Trump.
"Everything that Israel used to get in a simpler, easier process will now potentially be much more complicated, and Israel has to be prepared that this is a new reality," he told me.

"Our entire Air Force is American-made military planes, we're dependent on American spare parts and American weapons. The last three years have shown us how dependent we are on American missile-defence systems. [If] those don't show up at the same pace, that's a real difference – that changes your calculation of what you're able to withstand if you go to war."
Katz believes the midterms could also translate into tougher demands on Israel over its actions in Gaza and Lebanon, and a requirement not to undermine an agreement with Iran.

"Something will change in the US-Israeli relationship, but it's a question of scale," said the US official I spoke to, who was not authorized to speak on the record. "It means shifting to [being] willing to criticise Israel when it's warranted, but the bedrock fundamental relationship will still be there."

In an interview on Israeli television, the US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee signalled little shift so far in core American positions, including on Israel's occupation of the West Bank, describing the sanctions imposed by other countries as "irrational" and counterproductive.

Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, told another Israeli channel that Trump would be in the White House for the next two years, and that Israel could "feel good" about the US veto in the UN Security Council – something Washington has repeatedly used in the past to block resolutions that target Israel.
"But we have to pay attention to the voices – not only in the Democratic Party but also the Republican Party – criticising Israel," he said. "It will be harder for us."

Questions over its key alliance have come at a particularly sensitive time for Israel, less than two weeks after its own parliamentary elections left neither government nor opposition with a clear majority. Discussions are now taking place with the country's president, who will decide whether Netanyahu or his centrist rival, Gadi Eisenkot, will get the first chance to form a governing coalition.
"Under my leadership, we will renew and deepen that [US] partnership, strengthen the bipartisan foundations that have long sustained it," Eisenkot said in a social media post.
Another member of his opposition bloc, Yair Lapid, said: "What do we do?"

"We go back to the rule that worked for us for seventy years, and which broke in 2015 when Netanyahu went to speak against [US president] Obama in Congress. Israel doesn't choose sides in America. We work with everyone."

Netanyahu's speech to the US Congress in 2015 is seen as a defining moment in Israel's relationship with the US, when the Israeli leader appealed over the head of America's Democratic president to urge Republicans in Congress not to back a nuclear agreement with Iran.
Since then, Netanyahu has increasingly anchored the alliance in Trump's Republican party, even as alienation among Democrats has grown.
The US official I spoke to said that, before the midterms, Netanyahu could have improved the relationship with Washington by getting rid of his two far-right ministers.
"I think everyone understands now it's bigger than [that]," he said.
How much the new tone in transatlantic relations will play into the task of building a new government in Israel is being closely watched.
Some government supporters argue it has increased the need for political stability, and that Netanyahu provides much-needed continuity and a deep knowledge of the US and its leaders.
"We cannot afford to be dragged into endless political disputes and election campaigns," said one opinion writer in Israel's largest-circulation daily, the right-wing Israel Hayom.
Whoever heads Israel's next government, its American ally may demand more than rhetoric.
In the noisy debate around what this will mean for Israel, the silence of its prime minister – once the whisperer of Washington's elite – is perhaps the most telling voice of all.

paragraphs.text: The 2026 midterm elections have profoundly altered the national regulatory environment, most notably with Democrats securing control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress and notching big victories in traditionally business-friendly states like Texas and South Carolina.

Over the past two decades, Southern states like Florida and Texas have attracted massive corporate migration from blue states. With less regulation and lower taxes. Those same benefits also attracted many people seeking lower taxes, lower housing costs, and better economic opportunities. With this political shift, relocated companies may now face a landscape increasingly focused on energy and building constraints, and tighter legislative oversight.

Information technology, semiconductors, and traditional energy sectors experienced immediate headwinds following the election. Companies at the forefront of the AI boom, such as CoreWeave, Tesla, and SpaceX, saw share prices slide as markets priced in tighter Democratic regulatory oversight and potential restrictions on AI deployment. Senator Bernie Sanders, for example, reposted his efforts to advance a data center moratorium proposal he co-authored with New York Congresswoman and socialist Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

The market is suddenly realizing that, between shifts in Washington and in states like Texas, the fastest-growing area of the U.S. economy might grind to a halt. Over half of the U.S. hyperscale data center pipeline could now face heightened regulatory friction. To build new facilities, even assuming they get permitted at all, developers may face tax increases, strict "bring your own power" mandates, or new air-permit delays for on-site gas plants. As all-in construction costs rise and timelines extend, immediate demand for advanced chips snowballs down the hardware supply chain.

Traditional oil and gas majors sank, while solar and green energy stocks surged, driven by expectations that a Democratic Congress will resume pushing subsidies for them. Also, the ongoing U.S.-Israel war with Iran has driven crude prices sharply higher throughout the year. With Democrats taking control of Congress, President Trump faces a legislative body that can severely constrain his military options and push back on defense budgets. Tehran almost certainly recognized that a politically weakened Trump administration would have a greater incentive to seek a negotiated deal, something Secretary of State Marco Rubio has now indicated is preferable to any escalating kinetic options. Consequently, crude prices plunged, with Brent dropping below $95 per barrel.

For similar reasons, defense contractors took market hits due to anticipated congressional resistance to the $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget. Although healthcare - as measured by XLV at least came in today, it remains above pre-election levels, along with grocery stocks such as Walmart, Costco, Kroger, and Dollar General, on expectations that a Democratic Congress might boost federal spending in those areas.

This may help explain why Costco was one of the relatively few stocks to close higher on Thursday, and why it also ranked as the 15th most active single-stock option (in notional terms), ahead of names like JP Morgan, Marvell, Oracle, Eli Lilly, and Dell.

At roughly 46x forward earnings, Costco (a perennial on the "Holly Index (MELLOY, CAN WE LINK TO THIS") isn't cheap, but then it is never cheap. The average forward multiple is actually a few turns higher at over 49x. So what were folks trading? Mostly short-dated call options. One possible reason? Costco isn't just trading at a relatively high multiple; as usual, it is also simply a high-priced stock in dollar terms, at over $1,065 as of Thursday's close. A "round lot" (100 shares) would therefore cost over $100,000 to initiate. Like many things packaged at Costco, that might be a little more than some buyers need (or want) to spend.

Alternatively, call options let investors gain exposure to 100 shares for far less than buying the shares. Buying the January 1060 calls, for example, would cost about $53.45, or $5,345 for upside participation on 100 shares of stock above the $1,060 strike price. That may seem more palatable, but a keen observer might notice that prior highs occasionally present some technical resistance, and Costco topped out at about $1,090 back in mid-May. By selling a call at or near that level, such as the January 1090s at 39.65, one could reduce the cost of the trade even further, expecting a pause before new highs. This would reduce the cost of the trade to $13.80, or just under 1.3% of the current stock price.

I won't pretend $1,380 is a small outlay for a one-lot call spread on a much-loved stock trading at 46x forward earnings. Nor is $520 for 8 6-ounce A5 Wagyu filet mignons (a Costco online only deal available now). But relatively, both the steaks at Costco and the options on Costco are very fairly priced. But it does provide participation in 100 shares of Costco between the strikes, for only 30% more than the cost of a single share of the underlying stock.
