nytimes.com/2026/11/06/science/science-d.headline: What a Democratic Congress Could Mean for Science

paragraphs.text: The Trump administration swept into office determined to undermine the postwar model of research spending that made the United States the world’s great engine of scientific discovery.

Much of that agenda — canceling studies, slashing scientific staff, imposing greater political oversight on grant making — went into effect without the cooperation of Congress, which even in Republican hands resisted the White House’s efforts to retool the country’s research machine.
Now Democrats are set to take control on Capitol Hill, and some are already promising to do more than play defense. They hope to begin reversing changes implemented under President Trump.
Whether that ultimately happens is unclear.

“The reality is, most of the shenanigans have been coming from the administration,” said Jeremy Berg, a former institute director at the National Institutes of Health. “And that will likely continue.”
From artificial intelligence to space exploration to the research juggernauts at the N.I.H., the American scientific enterprise is vast. Here are some trends to watch.
The Grant-Making Machine

Over the past two years, a Republican-led Congress rejected steep proposed cuts to the N.I.H. budget, blocked plans to formalize political control of the grant-making process and limited health officials’ power to more aggressively reduce the number of medical research grants.

But the Trump administration nevertheless turned to executive orders, staffing cuts, new layers of political review and obscure bureaucratic maneuvers to slow or impede some scientific research spending.
After this week’s election, Democratic lawmakers vowed to take back powers over federal spending that they said should have been exercised long before now.

“The power of the purse belongs to CONGRESS!” Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, wrote on X. “It’s NOT Trump’s money. Taxpayer dollars belong to the American PEOPLE.”

She and other lawmakers could, for example, ramp up oversight of the funding that the Trump administration has withheld. Congress could also more sharply limit reductions to the number of research grants being awarded.

Representative Zoe Lofgren, Democrat of California, who is seeking to lead the House Science Committee, said in an interview on Wednesday that lawmakers needed to be more “prescriptive,” and start delineating exactly how Congress intends for federal money to be spent.

“In some cases, the damage can’t be undone,” Ms. Lofgren said, noting that many younger scientists had left their fields or moved abroad because of the funding disruptions. “But we can prevent it from continuing.”

Equally consequential were the administration’s efforts to remake the process of vetting and awarding scientific grants. Under President Trump, the overall dollar figures for research spending have remained about the same. But his administration has exercised more discretion over how that funding is spent, changes that are mostly beyond Congress’s power to undo.

“The upheaval and damage has come from the White House, mainly O.M.B.,” said Sudip Parikh, chief executive of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, a major scientific advocacy group. “The change in Congress isn’t necessarily going to fix all that.”

Grants are now are screened for disfavored terminology, vetted in some cases by political appointees, and overseen by scientists sympathetic to the priorities of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other political leaders.
Under new processes, it has become harder for labs to predict when, or whether, their research proposals would be funded.

Ryan D. Enos, a political scientist at Harvard, said that American science has prospered in part because of how much federal funding had flowed to basic research at universities after World War II and during the Cold War.
But labs also depended on that funding remaining stable and predictable. And those norms have been so thoroughly shaken, Dr. Enos said, that a single election would not restore them.
“It’s a very different world right now,” he said.
New Investigative Targets

As the majority party in Congress, Republicans had the authority to hold oversight hearings and subpoena witnesses, a power they sometimes used to scrutinize scientists, including a contentious Senate committee hearing with Dr. Anthony S. Fauci this summer.

Those efforts may not end entirely with a new Congress. As chair of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Rand Paul, Republican of Kentucky, led an investigation into Dr. Fauci. He could continue to release damaging documents that he received from the administration while Republicans controlled the chamber.

But Mr. Paul is set to be replaced as committee chair by Maggie Hassan, Democrat of New Hampshire, a fierce Trump critic who has defended Dr. Fauci. She and other Democratic lawmakers will be in a position to end those hearings and investigate the Trump administration instead.

“A lot of how the new majority will try to drive change is through investigations and hearings,” said Mitch Benzine, senior counsel in the congressional investigations practice at the law firm Eversheds Sutherland.
Dr. Parikh said that could include investigations into the administration’s withholding of funds appropriated by Congress and changes made to the grant review process.

Lawmakers could even look to scrutinize universities that settled federal civil rights investigations or funding freezes with the Trump administration, even if only as a way to dig up evidence about the White House’s attacks on federal research funds.

Yet the elections also ushered out some stalwart defenders of medical research on the right, including Senator Susan Collins, Republican of Maine, a longtime champion of N.I.H. funding. Some scientists have already begun discussing the need to cultivate a new generation of supporters among Republicans in Congress.

Roger Severino, a vice president at the conservative Heritage Foundation and a health official in the first Trump administration, said that the election had hardly represented a rebuke of the administration’s efforts to cut medical studies related to race or gender.
“Trump had effectively won on this issue because the Democrats were petrified of pushing for a return to the halcyon days of D.E.I. funding and research during the election,” he said.

The White House Office of Management and Budget, he added, was “already very deeply involved in reviews of N.I.H. grant making,” and was already working to even more firmly establish the federal government’s power to terminate research grants.
A.I. Guardrails
On Tuesday, voters passed 40 out of 41 ballot initiatives that aim to halt or limit the development of the computer data centers used to build and deploy artificial intelligence.
While these measures are unlikely to have a major effect on the progress of A.I. in the near term, they could shift the direction of the field two to three years down the road.

Over the past several years, companies like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google could not have pushed A.I. forward as quickly as they did without the arrival of many massive new data center facilities designed specifically for A.I.
Building the most advanced A.I. systems typically requires thousands of specialized computer chips packed into a network of data centers in one location.

Increasingly immense facilities built for A.I. training are now coming online. But if some states push back on their development, it could increase the gap between the leading A.I. companies and the smaller players, said Harry Sudock, chief business officer at the data center developer CleanSpark.
“The bigger the company, the bigger the research lab, the more they will be able to navigate in what will be more constrained waters,” he said.
In other words, companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta will continue to have an advantage over everyone else, simply because they have more money and more leverage to build new facilities.

But mostly, these and other companies are building new data centers so that they can deliver their A.I. technologies to people across the globe. Scientists call this “inference,” as opposed to training.
If it becomes more difficult to build new data centers in certain parts of the country, Mr. Sudock said, the cost of using A.I. may rise even higher.

Separately, a Democrat-led Congress could introduce bills that restrict the development of the most powerful A.I. systems in the name of safety, something the Trump administration has been reluctant to do. Many experts worry that these systems are a threat to cybersecurity and could help build dangerous bioweapons.
These bills could also create new protections for copyright holders, which could affect the cost and the difficulty of training A.I. systems.
(The Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)
Safe Space
For NASA, the switch to Democratic control of Congress is unlikely to lead to significant changes in the nation’s space program, which has received steady bipartisan support.
Indeed, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have long been more likely to agree with one another about NASA than with the president.

When President Obama in 2010 canceled Constellation, a program started under President George W. Bush to send astronauts back to the moon, Congress pushed back and instructed NASA to develop the Space Launch System, the giant rocket used for Artemis, the current return-to-the-moon program.

When President Trump last year and this year sought to slice NASA’s robotic science programs by nearly half, Congress ignored the request and continued financing the space agency at roughly the same level as in earlier years.
Today there remains strong bipartisan consensus support for the Artemis missions and concern that the United States should not yield the moon to China.

nytimes.com/2026/11/06/science/scientist.headline: These Newly Elected Lawmakers Know Something Trump Doesn’t: Science

paragraphs.text: When he takes his oath of office next January, Daniel K. Biss will be among the most junior members of the House of Representatives. Even so, Mr. Biss, who was elected on Tuesday to represent the North Side of Chicago and nearby suburbs, is likely to be Washington’s foremost expert on matroid Grassmannians.
“I’ve pretty much cornered the market,” Mr. Biss joked in an interview.

Ominous name aside, matroid Grassmannians are just complex mathematical shapes — as well as the subject of the dissertation Mr. Biss completed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2002. Mr. Biss, now 49, taught math at the University of Chicago before moving to politics, first as an Illinois state legislator and then as the mayor of Evanston, a prosperous Chicago suburb. (His academic career has not been without controversy: Some of his work has been retracted or corrected, and this year he admitted to having a relationship in 2004 with an undergraduate student.)

Mr. Biss is one of several scientists and physicians who was elected to Congress on Tuesday. Like him, most are Democrats and most were elected to the House. They plan, they say, to use their knowledge to combat what they see as the anti-science policies promoted by the Trump administration.

The incoming scientists represent “a real repudiation of what has been two terrible years for science and public health,” said Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, a group that recruits Democratic doctors and scientists to run for office. Her group supported Democratic candidates who ended up winning in the House, as well as two incoming senators: Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, in Michigan and Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in South Carolina.
(In keeping with New York Times style, physicians and academics who stop practicing once elected to a political office are not given the courtesy title doctor.)

After World War II, the United States became a scientific powerhouse thanks to federal funding of research in the sciences. But decades of partnership between Washington and defense contractors, Silicon Valley and other sectors are being undermined by the Trump administration, according to a recently published Times investigation.

President Trump and congressional Republicans have enacted cuts to Medicaid and allowed the expiration of tax credits provided by the Affordable Care Act. His administration has sought cuts to science funding and has subjected research to political scrutiny.

Thousands of experts have left agencies like the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Department of Health and Human Services, now led by Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a vaccine skeptic whose Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement has been accused of peddling junk science.
“Now is a good time to course-correct and actually provide some oversight,” said Ms. Naughton of the new crop of science-minded Democrats.

Among those who hope to face off against Mr. Kennedy is Jasmine Clark, 43, who will represent parts of greater Atlanta in the House next year. Ms. Clark, a microbiologist at Emory University, said she was drawn to politics after Mr. Trump’s first presidential win in 2016.

She organized a pro-science march and criticized how Georgia reported coronavirus cases during the pandemic. Lately, she has watched with dismay as the C.D.C., which is based in Atlanta, has been drained of expertise. “The morale at C.D.C. is horrible,” she said.

Ms. Clark praised Mr. Kennedy for highlighting the prevalence of pesticides and processed foods but was critical of his inconsistent messaging about the safety and efficacy of vaccines and his handling of a growing number of measles outbreaks.
“It has been an absolute disaster,” Ms. Clark said of MAHA. “It’s making us sicker.”
Investigating the Trump administration will be one aspect of the Democrats’ agenda. Another will be to create policy of their own.

“The importance of having scientists, engineers and health professionals in national, state and local political positions cannot be overstated,” said Deborah D. Stine, an independent consultant who served as the executive director of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology during the Obama administration. She cited issues like artificial intelligence, climate change and national security, which legislators with scientific backgrounds may find easier to grapple with than their peers. “If the policy question is outside their own expertise they know how to call on the best experts,” Dr. Stine said.

Scientific expertise will be especially welcome on Capitol Hill, said Matthew Motta, an expert on health policy at Boston University, because of a 2024 Supreme Court ruling that said courts no longer needed to defer to agency interpretations of vague laws — meaning that Congress will have to be more specific in how those laws are written.
“One of the things that I think is going to be really important in the coming years is having legislators who have that expertise,” Dr. Motta said.

Other newly elected legislators with backgrounds in science include John Cowan, a Republican from Georgia who is a neurosurgeon and majored in physics as an undergraduate, and Rebecca Bennett, who has a chemical engineering degree from Cornell and will represent a district in northern New Jersey

Ms. Bennett, 39, said in an interview that she had many constituents who worked in the health care industry and were concerned about what she described as the federal government’s destructive interference in the workings of the scientific establishment.
Mr. Biss, the mathematician, said he believed that his colleagues with backgrounds in science would bring an important perspective on problem solving to Congress.
“The best habits of mind involve as few black boxes as possible and as much deep understanding as possible,” he said.

npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6032602/cyberat.headline: Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank
npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6032602/cyberat.author: Jenna McLaughlin

paragraphs.text: In a new security bulletin, the information sharing and analysis center devoted to the healthcare industry, Health ISAC, alerted members to a recent wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers — including one incident that affected a major French blood bank.

"This alert is issued for situational awareness, highlighting how recent operational technology (OT) attacks against specific refrigeration brands directly intersect with emerging threats to the health sector," reads the bulletin seen by NPR. Operational technology refers to the machines that control physical processes in the real world, from cooling systems to water pumps.

Cyberattacks on grocery stores and food processing plants everywhere from Europe and Israel to U.S. military bases have drawn headlines in recent months, particularly as attacks have resulted in spoiled food, fires, broken machinery, and major business disruptions. Attackers are clearly aware of the vulnerability of these systems and are taking advantage.

However, until news broke that the French blood bank, known as the French Blood Establishment, had also been targeted, there was less public attention focused on the potential consequences of refrigeration controllers failing in other industries, particularly healthcare, where lifesaving implements like blood and vaccines often require finely tuned temperature-controlled environments to remain viable.

"This incident underscores a stark operational reality: cybersecurity in healthcare is fundamentally about patient safety," wrote Errol Weiss, the chief security officer at Health ISAC in an email to NPR. "When threat actors manipulate operational technology like cold-chain storage and refrigeration units holding donor blood, plasma, or critical therapies, they aren't merely stealing data or locking down administrative files, they are directly endangering the physical resources required to sustain human life."

On Thursday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture published their own fact sheet about threats to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, tools they identify as critical to multiple industries from healthcare to chemical production, food and agriculture, and transportation.

The FBI Cyber Branch Operations director, Brett Leatherman, said the bureau is tracking bad actors targeting these systems "across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."

"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," Leatherman said.
Iran, Russia and the search for the culprits

The French blood bank confirmed in a press release Tuesday that one of its vendors used in cold storage rooms was targeted by malicious cyber activity, resulting in the defrost and temperature thresholds being raised dangerously high. The French Blood Establishment ultimately managed to detect the suspicious activity in time to rescue blood samples.
It remains unclear who is responsible for the global attacks on refrigeration controllers, and whether it's multiple actors or groups.

Iran has been linked to at least one incident in Israel earlier in the spring, though that breach involved a lot more sophistication and malicious activity. Investigators probing the disruptions at U.S. military bases are also considering Iran as the potential culprit.

Meanwhile, two pro-Russian hacking groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, belatedly released videos and posted on Telegram claiming responsibility for the attacks across Europe, publishing a sample of alleged hacked credentials that would've allowed them to access equipment including machines made by the Danish company Danfoss and the American company Copeland. Those machines can monitor and control temperature and other functions. The hacking groups have some history of targeting refrigeration controllers and other operational technology. However, it's unclear if the recent wave of attacks on refrigerators and freezers across Europe even required stolen credentials to execute, a factor that has led some cybersecurity experts to be skeptical of their claims.

Even so, it will require more evidence like access logs, configuration changes, and connections between maintenance accounts on the controllers to make any clear assessments, explained Tom Hegel, who leads threat intelligence research at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne.

"Russian-aligned actors are a credible hypothesis because there is a credible precedent, including the refrigeration-related attack DOJ attributed to CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn and NoName's history of politically motivated disruption. But that is only the context, not the missing evidentiary link to these European incidents," Hegel told NPR.
"It's important to note that such Russian threat actors often seek attention and claim to cause incidents even when false," he continued.
Regardless of who's responsible, the incident highlights how these nearly ubiquitous tools used to remotely manage critical systems are vulnerable to attack in several different ways.

For one, thousands of the refrigeration controllers in France alone were exposed to the open internet with almost no protection put in place before unidentified hackers went after them in October. Afterward, experts were still tracking hundreds of devices left unprotected. That's just a fraction of the tens of thousands of exposed operational devices online, many of them embedded in critical infrastructure.

Additionally, many of the major remote management systems used in refrigerators and freezers have security vulnerabilities. After alerting the companies to the problems, cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on vulnerabilities in multiple major refrigeration controllers, including those made by both the American manufacturer Copeland and by Danfoss.
While some of those vulnerabilities have been discovered and the vendors have designed patches to seal the hole, the problems don't stop there.

Experts warn it's difficult to patch operational technology because doing so often requires shutting systems down. In industries like healthcare, even minutes of downtime create extreme risk for patient safety. And for some aging models, it's impossible to patch, because the vendor is no longer offering updates — and companies can't afford to spring for a new model.
Sometimes, executives don't even know what machines are on their networks.

Additionally, for many companies, vendors that work with them demand remote access to systems like refrigeration controllers to regularly service them. It's often a requirement in the contract companies sign.

"Industrial chillers operate under vendor contracts that mandate persistent remote access," explained Nic Adams, CEO of 0rcus, a U.S. offensive security firm. "These commercial agreements leave national food and medical supplies defenseless against basic credential abuse."

Finally, hackers are now using AI to find these vulnerabilities faster than ever, and AI is also helping them to better understand the complex machines and the processes they control. Bad actors a world away no longer need to understand individual languages or industries, or even the physics involved to disrupt operations. In recent weeks, cyber incident responders tell NPR they're seeing a massive spike in attacks that are at least in part carried out by AI agents.
The good news is that a lot of these attacks, even if they incorporate AI, are not particularly sophisticated, novel, or stealthy.
Weiss of Health ISAC tells NPR there are basic steps the healthcare industry can take to prevent being a victim of these opportunistic attacks.

That process "begins" by "eliminating public internet exposure," wrote Weiss, then "enforcing strict network segmentation" in order to isolate refrigeration systems "from standard enterprise and guest networks" and finally adding on safeguards "that software overrides cannot bypass" like "hard-wired mechanical cutoffs" and "independent thermal alarms."

In the Health ISAC alert, the industry is urged to separate not just refrigeration controllers from hospital IT systems, but also medical gas monitors, for one, and train staff onsite on how to take physical manual control of machines in an emergency.
Finally, the alert urges hospitals to have offline backups of their systems.
Store managers on the frontlines
Sharing intelligence about these kinds of cyberattacks can help other potential victims avoid disaster.

While Estonian grocery stores were targeted in the most recent wave of attacks, many of those store managers were on high alert thanks to warnings issued by Estonia's Information Systems Authority, RIA. "When one Selver store was attacked on 2 November, the attackers managed to change the refrigeration system's temperature setting to +50°C. However, the service provider reacted quickly and prevented significant damage," said Annika Müür, a spokesperson for RIA. "So while we can't say that Estonia managed to prevent the attacks entirely, I think this case is a good example of the importance of monitoring threats internationally, acting on early warnings and working closely with businesses to minimise the impact."
Weiss of Health ISAC also urged companies across sectors that are being targeted by this recent wave of attacks to share information to help others defend themselves.
"The attack highlights why timely, trusted information sharing across borders and sectors is our strongest collective defense," he wrote.

"Rapid intelligence sharing allows hospitals and health facilities globally to recognize emerging attack patterns, verify vendor exposure, and harden critical infrastructure before threat actors can cause physical harm."

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/activi.headline: Activists break into building site of Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/activi.author: Ajit Niranjan

paragraphs.text: Activists have stormed the site of a Microsoft datacentre being built in Amsterdam, as the backlash to the social and environmental harms of the AI boom spreads across Europe.

Protesters from Geef Tegengas, a Dutch direct action group, clashed with police while breaking into a construction site at Westpoort Amsterdam, where some members climbed a crane, lit flares and tied helium balloons to equipment.

The action comes amid Europe-wide resistance to the rapid expansion of energy-hungry AI, with more than 100 groups involved in a two-day series of protests to demand moratoria on the construction of new datacentres.

The break-in at the Dutch site, where protesters hung banners objecting to Microsoft’s services to the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), was separate from the pan-European “Stop Dirty Data Centres” campaign, which targeted the same site but whose affiliated members stayed outside the perimeter fence.

“The police attempted to prevent [the occupation] and arrest protesters, but were unable to prevent it and force was used,” the police said in a statement to NOS, a Dutch public broadcaster. “An officer was slightly injured during the protest.”

Protesters from both groups said police used force and teargas to dispel the activists trying to enter the construction site. Organisers and local media reported hundreds of protesters on each side of the fence.

Smaller protests took place in the centre of Bristol, in the UK, at a datacentre in Berlin, Germany, outside the Polish parliament in Warsaw and at the main square in Zagreb, Croatia. Further protests are expected on Saturday.

Stop Dirty Data Centres, a coalition of independent groups that include national branches of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, said it had not coordinated or promoted the direct action that took place in the Netherlands, but that is was “understandable” communities would turn to a range of tactics when they were unable to meaningfully participate in decision-making.

“Big tech and government are racing ahead with large-scale datacentre development despite significant public concern about the impacts on local communities, natural resources and other industries,” said Owen Espley, campaign coordinator. “Many datacentre developments are planned with limited transparency or scrutiny, while communities across Europe are being shut out of decisions that will shape their local environments and futures.”

The ecological fallout of the datacentre boom has alarmed some climate scientists, while growing frustration with AI’s societal impact – from energy bills and job losses to the role of tech companies in undermining democracy – has increased public anger. In the US midterm elections this week, nearly every proposed moratorium on datacentres on the ballot was approved.

Roos Molenaar, an activist from Geef Tegengas, said the struggle against big tech was inseparable from the fight against oppression and fascism. “We won’t accept Amsterdam being used for the creation of AI slop and the facilitation of genocide,” said Molenaar. “This datacenter is gulping up our drinking water to make the rich even richer.”

A spokesperson for Microsoft said it was aware of the demonstration and that its first concern was the wellbeing of everyone at and around the site. “We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully. However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”
A spokesperson for Pure Data Centres, the site owner, said it respected the right to peaceful protest but that entering a live construction site was unlawful and dangerous.

“Our immediate priority is everyone’s safety, and we respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have,” a Pure DC spokesperson said.

Governments across Europe have supported the building of AI datacentres to boost tax revenues and catch up with the breakneck deployment of computing power in the US and China, with some framing the AI race as a matter of national security.

But datacentres have emerged as a flashpoint for public anger over issues from environment and energy to human rights and democracy. Last week, an investigation by the Guardian and Investigate Europe found evidence of dangerous conditions for some of the workers building them.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/hundreds-of-ar.headline: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/hundreds-of-ar.author: Zack Whittaker

paragraphs.text: Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.

The hacking software, called Artex, is an open-source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open-source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.”

In a blog post, cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in.

Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet.

The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.

Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September. Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies.

Artex was also used in an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise earlier in October, which allowed Chinese-linked hackers to spy on thousands of organizations whose data and files are hosted in Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft, which has visibility into the attack, said in a blog post that the hackers used Artex to break into customer’s cloud environments and steal their data at such speed that defenders had “little time to detect and respond.”
Many of the attacks linked to Artex involved exploiting simple vulnerabilities, such as guessing weak or known passwords, and a lack of multi-factor authentication.
The findings show that simple vulnerabilities, including misconfigurations, can expose both the attacker and their targets.

Artex has since announced it would go closed-source, effectively limiting further releases for paid customers. There are still dozens of copies of Artex’s code available on code-sharing sites that can still be used in active attacks.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.headline: Pamela Abdy feels rage after Warner Bros. exit, she says at WIF Honors
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.author: Laura Zornosa

paragraphs.text: Lately, Pamela Abdy has been feeling “pure, unadulterated rage.”
Abdy exited her role as co-chair and chief executive officer of Warner Bros. after the studio was acquired by Paramount Skydance in a controversial merger that closed last month.

The now-former studio executive received the inaugural Vanguard Award at the Women in Film Honors gala on Thursday evening. She thanked every single female director, producer and executive she has worked with throughout her career, including Greta Gerwig, Emerald Fennell, Zoë Kravitz, Margot Robbie, Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, whom she feels ever-growing gratitude toward.

“But lately, other feelings, and one in particular, have risen to the surface with undeniable ferocity, and that feeling is pure, unadulterated rage,” she said onstage in the Beverly Hilton’s opulent ballroom. “Rage for these women, rage for me and even more rage for the entire generation of women who deserve to have their potential recognized and elevated.”

“Rage at how women are under attack everywhere,” she continued. “Rage at how our health and our well-being always seem to come second to how we show up in a room. And here’s the problem: As a leader who happens to be a woman, I am supposed to sublimate this rage. And you know what happens when they tell you to tamp down a fever? Sometimes it just burns hotter.” (All remarks onstage were interpreted into ASL by Keturah Holiday and Amber Berteloot.)

She has been called difficult, emotional and combative, Abdy said. She’s been told to put on her “big boy pants,” to smile more. She’s been told that movies starring women and directed by women don’t make as much money as those made by men, that their audience is limited. (Even after “Barbie,” which she oversaw alongside Mike De Luca, grossed more than $1.4 billion.)

“It is getting harder, not easier, to be a woman in the business,” Abdy said. “We tell ourselves because a few of us made it into these chairperson seats, we broke through, that we paved the way for the next generation. But I don’t think it’s true.”

When Gerwig made “Barbie,” people consistently referred to her as a “female director,” Abdy said — not a “director.” But when people talk about the highest-grossing male directors, they don’t call them “male directors.” We still have the “Most Powerful Women in Hollywood” lists. But the men don’t have a separate list; they are the list, she added.

“So I have to ask: What business are we leaving for future vanguards?” Abdy said. “Is it a healthy industry for the next generation of storytellers and executives to step into? One that allows women to enter with an open heart and mind, without having to fight the fights we’re still fighting?”

“These are the questions I think about when I focus on funneling my rage,” she continued. “Rage can be destructive, but I think of it as fuel, as something that can burn bright, something that can be harnessed to fight on for what we think is right, what we believe in and what we deserve.”

Abdy then paused to acknowledge how heartening it was to see so many women elected in the midterms on Tuesday. Earlier in the evening, WIF Chief Executive Kirsten Schaffer shouted out Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman elected governor of a state, in Georgia; Gina Hinojosa, the first Latina governor elected in Texas; and the six transgender and nonbinary candidates who made history.

Filmmaker Nancy Meyers, who presented Abdy with her honor, praised Abdy and De Luca’s historic tenure: “Barbie” is the highest-grossing film in Warner Bros. history. “Sinners” set an Oscar record with the most nominations ever by a single movie. And last year’s best picture winner, “One Battle After Another,” was “another feather in Pam’s very crowded hat.”

After Meyers’ introduction, a highlight reel played Abdy’s greatest hits, including video submissions from some of her friends in the industry: Gerwig, Robbie, Kidman, Bullock and Ryan Coogler, among others.

Bullock cheekily reminded Abdy that, when she accepts her award, “remember that when they gave it to you, you were initially employed at the place where you are no longer employed.” Then, when Bullock “realizes” that this is the WIF Honors gala, she backtracks. “Never mind, forget everything I just said. Say everything you want to say, toot your own horn. They love you.”

This seemed, for the most part, true about the hundreds of women in attendance. As soon as Abdy turned her speech toward rage, a faint “preach!” rang from somewhere in the ballroom. The 15-minute speech was met with a standing ovation. (When Schaffer asked attendees to donate to WIF’s fellowship program, Skydance‘s “$25 donation” was among the contributions included in a video presentation, which prompted some disquiet, but this seemed like an ill-timed joke.)

“In the executive suites of Hollywood, in the past three months, we’ve lost 50% of our top women leaders, which has been a major blow, because it’s not like we had that many to begin with,” Schaffer said. “So what are we going to do about it? At WIF, we have a very simple answer: We keep going. We keep opening doors. We keep investing in each other. We keep hiring each other. We keep fostering the next generation of storytellers.”

Abdy wasn’t the only honoree Thursday evening. Jane Fonda presented Salma Hayek Pinault with the Jane Fonda Humanitarian Award for her philanthropic work, including with the Kering Foundation (established by her husband’s luxury group), which fights gender-based violence across the U.S., Mexico, France, Italy, Korea and the U.K. Hayek Pinault dedicated the award to Dolores Huerta, who attended the gala last year, and called Huerta “a womb for our community.”

Sharon Stone presented Hannah Waddingham with the Crystal Award for Advocacy in TV, and Maria Giulia Prezioso Maramotti (granddaughter of the founder of Italian clothing brand Max Mara, which sponsored the event) presented actor Adria Arjona with the WIF Max Mara Face of the Future Award. Emmy Rossum presented writer, director and producer Beth de Araújo and actor Gemma Chan (in absentia) with the Crystal Award for Advocacy in Film for their upcoming movie “Josephine,” about a young girl who has witnessed a sexual assault.

“In our film ‘Josephine,’ we attempt to transport you back to your youth, to a time before you understood the concept of sexual assault,” De Araújo said. “What happened to you once you became aware of it? How did this start to inform the way you moved your body through the world, the way you thought about your own safety?”

“For me, I certainly became very, very scared, and I hid. I locked myself inside so that there were barriers between myself and danger,” she continued, tearing up. “But I’m very tired of being scared. It is time for those who are committed to violence to be scared of us.”

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/meta-introduce.headline: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/meta-introduce.author: Lucas Ropek

paragraphs.text: Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works towards a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.

On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”

Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice, which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot, which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/06/binance-hack.headline: Fake job interview scams like the one that hit Binance are getting more sophisticated. Here are the new signs to watch for
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/06/binance-hack.author: Sarah Jackson

paragraphs.text: Job search scams can cost applicants hundreds or thousands of dollars. But one fake job interview recently impacted over $6 billion in assets.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, announced on Tuesday it recently experienced a security breach impacting $6.34 billion in digital assets. The hack was enabled in part by a job seeker's nightmare: bogus job interviews.

While the Binance hackers had their sights set on a much bigger target than an individual job seeker, job-related scams are on the rise. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) tallied employment-related losses amounting to roughly $363 million in 2025, up sharply from $264 million the year prior, and $70 million in 2023. The actual figure is likely higher, since many victims of such crimes do not report them.

Those orchestrating fake job scams have many potential targets today "because the job search is taking so long for so many right now," says Stefanie Fackrell, a former recruiter at Google and Nvidia. While October's jobs report showed promise as the U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs, far more than expected, many applicants have been struggling through a low-hire, low-fire market for months.
"With today's job market, people are anxious, they're tired, many are at their wits' end," says Garber. "A proactive inquiry can be something you just immediately respond to without thinking."
Artificial intelligence can also make scams more widespread and harder to detect.

"Cyber scams in general are becoming much more sophisticated just because they're evolving at the same speed as AI and public access to AI," says Leeza Garber, a privacy and cybersecurity expert and adjunct law professor at Drexel University's Kline School of Law. "AI is going to make things seem more and more real."
In 2025, victims reported losses of almost $13 million to AI-involved employment scams, according to the IC3.
What happened in the Binance hack

Binance's announcement included an abbreviated play-by-play of how its hack went down. Fackrell and Garber broke down some of the warning signs in how the events unfolded, including what job seekers can learn from the incident.

What happened: A software engineer, who was not named, was contacted through "a legitimate job-hunting platform" by someone posing as a project director, Binance said in its announcement. That person arranged for the engineer to have an initial interview with a purported HR representative and a second-round interview with the supposed CEO of a fake company.

Experts' red flags: A headshot that's clearly AI-generated or otherwise looks uncanny, as well as sparse profile information or activity, and few connections should give you pause, Fackrell says. On LinkedIn, for example, you can click the three dots on a person's profile to open an "About this member" pop-up, where you can see when they joined LinkedIn and if they've verified their identity, workplace and school.

Though some small startups may arrange for an interview with a C-suite executive, it's generally unusual, particularly for a second-round interview, unless you'd be reporting to that person, she adds.

What happened: In the first round, the fake HR representative had a live video interview with the software engineer, even sharing with him a social media account with personal photos and videos to build trust, Binance said. The tactic was "more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches," Binance added in its announcement.

Experts' red flags: A recruiter might bring up commonalities with a candidate like the same alma mater or ex-employer to "bring that human element into the conversation," Fackrell says. But sharing personal social media in a first-round interview is strange, she adds.
In video interviews in general, some red flags might include the person moving unusually slowly or not responding to one of your questions, or their visual skipping a beat, Garber says.

What happened: The second-round interview with the purported CEO of the fake company was conducted on "a popular social chat app," Binance said, and the software engineer was instructed to download "an 'assignment' containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer."

Experts' red flags: Interviews commonly happen over Microsoft Teams, Zoom or Google Meet, not a social chat app. "I don't know anybody that's FaceTiming or WhatsApping any of their candidates," Fackrell says.

While take-home assignments, particularly for technical roles, may use third-party systems, don't download software if you're not familiar with it, Fackrell advises. These assignments should be shared via email through a legitimate system, not over the phone. Job seekers should take interviews on a personal device, not a work computer.
Tips to avoid job search scams
Common job search scams today include:
• A fake recruiter reaching out to someone about a position and asking for their resume, only to say their resume must be rewritten, for a fee, to be considered

• Extending a fake job offer and asking the recipient to pay for job equipment, including by cashing a fake check to cover it and sending back "excess" funds; or asking the recipient to provide sensitive information, such as ID, bank account details, or Social Security number
• Text messages offering jobs that seem too easy, such as being paid to like social media content or leave positive reviews, as scammers typically ask these workers for their own money down the line
Job sites like LinkedIn and Indeed, and entities like the Federal Trade Commission and Better Business Bureau, also have more information about common scams.

You should not have to provide sensitive information or payment in order to get a job, according to the FTC. Legitimate recruiters will reach out from their corporate email addresses, not a personal address. Other red flags include pressure to move quickly through the hiring process or seeing multiple typos in communications.
"Do your research before clicking, responding or engaging with anybody," Fackrell says.
Take a minute to think about how you were contacted and what you're being asked to do to proceed, Garber suggests, and cross-check job postings against the company's official careers page.
"If seems too good to be true, it definitely is," says Garber.
