cnbc.com/2026/11/06/microsoft-moves-to-c.headline: Microsoft plans to use fewer neoclouds as AI buildout shows signs of strain
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/microsoft-moves-to-c.author: Jordan Novet, Seema Mody

paragraphs.text: Microsoft is shrinking its roster of neocloud partners as it focuses on work with a few key suppliers and builds out its own data centers, according to people familiar with the matter.

The software giant's plans pose another potential challenge for a corner of the artificial intelligence market that's showing signs of strain due to rising borrowing costs, hefty debt loads and concerns about whether the buildout will slow down.

Microsoft has forged relationships in recent years with a number of neoclouds, including CoreWeave, Nebius, Chronoscale, IREN, Lambda and Nscale, as well as with Oracle, which is pouring money into building out AI infrastructure.

Microsoft is now in the evaluation stage and hasn't decided which neoclouds it will stop using, said two sources, who asked not to be named because the talks are confidential. One of the people said Microsoft wants to prioritize its own data center footprint. Bloomberg reported on the plans earlier. Two people said that Microsoft opted not to renew a deal with Oracle.
A Microsoft spokesperson said in an emailed statement that its infrastructure strategy is "built on flexibility and choice."

"We combine Microsoft-owned datacenters, leased facilities and strategic partnerships with third-party providers to deliver the capacity our customers need, where and when they need it," the spokesperson said. "We regularly review these investments against customer demand. That includes tracking delivery and adjusting plans as circumstances change."

The neoclouds have been a turbulent trade on Wall Street in recent weeks as rising interest rates added to fears that many companies have become overly reliant on debt in rushing to build capacity. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all down by roughly half over the past month even after rallying on Friday.
A recent industry review counted 323 neoclouds, and experts have predicted that many of them won't survive.

In its earnings report on Thursday, IREN said it handed over data center capacity to Microsoft in August, but Microsoft requested a networking equipment upgrade that will result in the infrastructure coming online in January or February instead of this year.

Microsoft finance chief Amy Hood said on the software company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in October that some cloud contracts involving graphics processing units were delayed until the first half of 2027, affecting Azure cloud growth. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the latest quarter, and said capex spending will accelerate in the second half of the fiscal year.
Capital markets 'more selective'

CoreWeave and Nebius are both scheduled to report quarterly results next week. IREN shares popped 16% on Friday after the company said AI revenue more than doubled from the prior quarter to $200 million. IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told CNBC that there's a "disconnect between what we're seeing in public market and what we're seeing at the customer level."
However, he acknowledged the challenge that market conditions present.

"Capital markets have become more selective in the last few weeks, and the questions have undoubtedly moved from how big the contract is to whether it can be delivered, financed, and run at a profit," Roberts said on the earnings call.

Microsoft has already slashed its work with U.K.-based neocloud Nscale, walking away from a site that it had intended to use in England. Darren Hardman, Microsoft's CEO for the U.K and Ireland, told CNBC in October that the decision had to do with Nscale's ability to get access to electricity.

The Financial Times reported this week that Microsoft decided against renewing a contract with Nscale in Texas. Nscale filed to go public in mid-September but hasn't updated its prospectus since then. The company said in its IPO filing that it expects Microsoft to be a "significant customer in future periods."

Microsoft's big turn to neoclouds came after the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, which led to a surge in demand for GPUs. In looking elsewhere, Microsoft signed up CoreWeave, which was a privately held startup at the time with roots in cryptocurrency mining. When CoreWeave went public last year, it said 62% of its 2024 revenue came from Microsoft.
At the time of ChatGPT's release, OpenAI only used Azure. Now the company's cloud suppliers also include Amazon, Cerebras, CoreWeave, Google and Oracle.

Microsoft's spokesperson said that its approach to reviewing neocloud investments is "a normal and responsible way to manage large, complex infrastructure projects," and that "the pace of our new agreements reflects what we need today."
—CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed to this report.

nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/faa-floppy-dis.headline: F.A.A. to Phase Out Floppy Disks in Air Traffic Control Towers

paragraphs.text: When news arrived this week that the Federal Aviation Administration would phase out floppy disks used in air traffic control at the nation’s airports, the general reaction was: “Wait, someone still uses floppy disks?”
But there once was a time, decades ago, when the now-obsolete floppy was exciting new technology, heralded in The New York Times as “the cornerstone of the office of the future.”

The F.A.A. has been using systems for air traffic controllers, including floppy disks, that date to the 1980s. A planned new system will include a digital display board that will put in one place the information controllers need, with data about disruptions, weather conditions and advisories.
Airports in Atlantic City, N.J., Nashville and Rochester, N.Y., will be among the first to get the new tech, known as the Brand New Air Traffic Control System.
“The greatest nation in the world deserves a state-of-the-art air traffic control system,” Sean P. Duffy, the transportation secretary, said in a statement.

President Trump had promised to upgrade the F.A.A.’s equipment after a plane crash near Washington in 2025. Government officials at the time noted that flights were still tracked on strips of paper, and that some computers ran on the Windows 95 operating system.
At the moment, air traffic controllers use floppy disks to upload some data, including pilot reports and advisories, into their consoles, the F.A.A. said.

Most adults barely remember floppy disks, even if they are old enough to have used them. And the idea that such antiquated technology is still used for important jobs two decades into the 21st century seems laughable.
They were originally produced in the early 1970s at an eight-inch diameter, they shrank to 5 ¼ inches and then 3 ½ inches.
The original disk was indeed “floppy,” with a soft plastic case. Later versions that became popular in the mid-80s had harder plastic shells, and didn’t flop anymore, but the name stuck.
The disk inside, containing the data, was circular, but the casing around it was square.

In 1978, The Times breathlessly hailed floppy disks as an exciting new technology. It enthused that the disks held tremendous quantities of information: no fewer than 300 pages of manuscript on a single $8 one-megabyte disk.
Now people regularly download a megabyte of information, or much more, without a second thought. One standard high-resolution photo on a phone could blow past that mark.

“I think one megabyte is going to prove to be a magic number in this industry,” a manufacturer of drives retailing for $1,000 in 1978 was quoted as saying then. “Everybody and their brother are going to decide that now is the time to switch to floppy disks.”
Long ago, everybody and their brother abandoned floppies.

Still, the technology has been resilient in some places beyond air traffic control towers. Japan dropped regulations requiring floppy disks be used for administrative purposes only in 2024, even though the last disk was made there in 2011. (Fax machines and cash have also hung around in that country.)
As time has marched on and storage methods have shifted, older technologies like floppies have produced distinct problems.

A Times article sounded the alarm in 1993, noting that libraries were increasingly getting manuscripts in different formats: floppy disks of various sizes, cassette tapes, even rolls of perforated paper. Should readers of the future want to access the material, libraries “may need to preserve the software to run it. And not just the software, but all the obsolescent hardware as well,” the article said.

As it turned out, some libraries were able to mitigate this by digitizing old floppy-disk data. But concern about loss of archival material remains to this day. (In contrast, books from a millennium ago remain readable.)
As for the F.A.A., it plans to fully install the new system at 400 sites by the end of 2028.

theguardian.com/film/2026/nov/06/sebasti.headline: Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman and Gloria, dies aged 52
theguardian.com/film/2026/nov/06/sebasti.author: Benjamin Lee

paragraphs.text: Chilean film-maker Sebastián Lelio has died at the age of 52.
He was best known for the Oscar-winning trans drama A Fantastic Woman and his English-language films included Gloria Bell and The Wonder.

His partner Amalia Kassai announced his death on Instagram without specifying the cause of death but telling followers, in Spanish, that it was a painful time for his family. Chilean media reports that he died at his home in Las Condes, Santiago.

Lelio was born in Argentina but moved to Chile at the age of two. He studied journalism for one year before graduating from film school and then released 9/11 documentary Cero in 2003. His first narrative film The Sacred Family premiered at the San Sebastián film festival in 2005.

His follow-up, 2009’s Christmas, premiered at Cannes but it was 2013’s Gloria that provided him with a major international breakthrough. The drama, about a woman in her late 50s who starts dating again, premiered at Berlin and won its lead star Paulina García an acting award at the festival.

Lelio followed it up with A Fantastic Woman, a drama about the life of a trans woman, another breakout that became the first Chilean film to win the Oscar for best international feature. In a five-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw called it “a sublime study in the exalted ordeal of grief”.

“When we released it in 2017, a gender identity bill had been dormant in congress for seven years,” he said in a Guardian interview in 2018. “Somehow, the film’s release, and the year in which it became globally known, helped to reactivate the discussion in Chile.”

He made his English language debut with London-set drama Disobedience which told a queer love story between women played by Rachel Weisz and Rachel McAdams. It was nominated for five British independent film awards.

Lelio then remade Gloria as Gloria Bell, then set in America and starring Julianne Moore in the lead role. He followed it with a critically acclaimed adaptation of Emma Donoghue’s novel The Wonder starring Florence Pugh.

“I love working with actors, and need to know they trust me and can explore, get lost, be foolish or brave, and I’ll take care of them,” he said to the Guardian. “I love working on set – it is where the sparkle is.”
His final film was 2025’s The Wave, a musical protest drama that premiered at Cannes.
“Making a film is like a gift you leave somewhere – you then hide and see what happens,” he said.

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/long-term-unemployme.headline: A disturbing employment trend is hiding beneath the latest strong job numbers
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/long-term-unemployme.author: Alex Harring

paragraphs.text: Americans who lose their jobs these days are facing a harsh new problem: It's getting harder to find another one quickly.

The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to Friday's jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That amounts to a job search of nearly seven months, the longest outside of the pandemic period since 2016, when the U.S. labor market was finally getting back on track after the 2008 financial crisis.

About 2 million Americans have been without work for at least 27 weeks, the BLS reported. People in this category are referred to as the "long-term unemployed" and accounted for 27.6% of all jobless workers in October, the highest share since late 2021.

"This is a series that can be noisy from month to month," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed, a hiring platform. "But if you look over a longer time horizon, there is no mistake in the trend."

It's a troubling sign in an otherwise steady labor market. Workers stuck on the sidelines are a casualty of what's become a "low-hire, low-fire" job market, in which companies are hesitant to lay workers off, but aren't adding them either.
Research shows that Americans who experience long-term unemployment face depleted savings, lower earnings potential over time and declining mental health.
What's more, workers who are unemployed for extended periods risk falling into a self-perpetuating cycle, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond wrote earlier this year.

"Time spent unemployed may itself reduce the probability of finding a job, perhaps because skills depreciate, networks thin or employers interpret long unemployment durations as a negative signal," the researchers warned.

Workers stop being able to claim most, if not all, government unemployment benefits after 26 weeks in a year. Given that, a rising share of long-term unemployed people can explain in part why initial and continuing jobless claims have remained low.
"Now, the average unemployed person takes longer to find a job than their benefits would last," Stahle said. "That is a really key point of this."
A 'jarring' narrative
While jobless workers appear to be having a tough time, this week's employment data shows strength in other areas of the labor market.

Nonfarm payrolls blew past economists' forecasts for October and added 165,000 jobs, according to Friday's release. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, slightly lower than economists predicted.

Job openings came in much higher than economists expected in September, according to a separate report from the BLS released on Tuesday. The number of workers quitting jobs — a barometer of their confidence to obtain new employment — spiked to levels not seen since March 2025.

The BLS also said layoffs and discharges dropped to their lowest volume in more than a year. However, a recent string of high-profile workforce cuts could throw cold water on views among workers that the market is heating up.

CNBC reported this week that Disney is planning to axe thousands of jobs, the latest of several waves of layoffs at the media giant this year. American Express said last month that it was slashing head count by 5% as it reorients around artificial intelligence.

"It's difficult to separate what's happening to you or the people around you from the big picture," said Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360. "When your LinkedIn is filled with layoffs and your social circle features a few folks who have been job seeking for several months, positive narratives about the labor market can seem jarring."

npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6032795/stephen.headline: Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as Trump's chief of staff
npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6032795/stephen.author: Danielle Kurtzleben

paragraphs.text: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is being replaced by Stephen Miller, President Trump said Friday.
The change comes after Republicans were swept out of power during this week's midterm elections.
Miller currently serves as deputy chief of staff in the White House. Trump announced the change on social media today, saying that Miller will take over on Monday.

Wiles worked with the Trump 2020 campaign in Florida and has served as chief of staff in this White House from day one. She was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year, and but it was announced she was cancer free this fall.
Miller has been a fixture in Trump's circles since 2016 and is considered an architect of some of his core policies, including immigration.

npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6026702/pope-le.headline: Pope Leo begins a 12-day, 3-country South America tour after his cancer surgery
npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6026702/pope-le.author: Carrie Kahn

paragraphs.text: MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay — In his first trip following lung cancer surgery, Pope Leo XIV has left Rome for what will be his furthest and longest journey: a 12-day, three-country visit to South America. Vatican officials say the 71-year-old pontiff is exhibiting "fantastic" stamina.

Along the way Leo will take 12 flights, including two helicopter rides, give 36 speeches and visit 10 cities including Cusco, Peru, which sits more than 11,000 feet above sea level. Even the heartiest of travellers can experience altitude sickness there and may require supplemental oxygen.
Last month, Leo underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Vatican officials say he's completed the two-week long recovery period and requires no further treatment.

The Vatican's new communications chief Maria Montserrat Alvar said the pontiff was eager to begin his journey. "His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen," she said.
First stop Uruguay

It's a puzzling choice for the first leg of the pope's anticipated return to South America, where he spent two decades in Peru, first as a missionary then as Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo. Uruguay, a small nation of around 3.5 million people, where adoring crowds will be small, is famously Latin America's most secular nation.

When asked why go to Uruguay at all, given the high rate of atheists and strict separation of church and state, Communications Chief Alvarado answered simply, "Why Not?" Adding, "the Gospel is meant to go everywhere."

Few welcome banners are seen throughout the capital Montevideo, except for large posters of a waving Pope Leo adorning city churches. A huge banner drapes down the facade of the Blessed Sacrament Church, in Montevideo's upscale Pocitos neighborhood, where 70-year old retiree Ana Maria Saprissa was heading for quiet prayer.
We are thankful, agradecida, she says that the pontiff is coming to visit. "His visit gives us such joy because …he remembered us all here in this tiny country that has so many needs," she said.

Uruguay's tradition of separating religion from government and public life dates back more than a century. Christmas has long been officially referred to as Family Day, while Easter week is given the vacation-friendly name Tourism Week.
Only about a third of Uruguayans identify as Catholics and even less say they practice the religion, according to political analyst Mariana Pomiés , director of the public polling firm CIFRA.

But as a practicing Catholic, Pomies says sometimes Uruguayan and especially officials misinterpret what secularism is. "Secularism is not anti-religion, it's the neutrality of the state in religious matters. But here the neutrality se convirtió en un absoluto… it became an absolute."
Pope celebrates 'positive secularism.'

Dozens of volunteers cleaned streets, mowed lawns and erected a simple stage outside the tiny brick Our Lady of Guadalupe Church. It's the focal spot for many in the Casavalle neighborhood, a working-class city about a half hour north of Montevideo, where the pope is scheduled to visit on Saturday.

"I am very happy, very glad, very grateful … that eyes have been set here," where many are forgotten and stigmatized, said Father Pablo Coimbra who's served as the community's pastoral leader for the past six years

"For the first time many people live their lives always on the margins, on the margins of opportunities, of possibilities, of the future, on the margins of a loving gaze... well, today they are in the heart, in the center," he said.

A proposed papal address to the parliament triggered a swift rebuke from the public and politicos alike and was quickly scrapped. However, Uruguay's left-wing President Yamandú Orsi will oversee a welcome ceremony outside Montevideo's main cathedral, where Leo will later celebrate evening prayers, vespers with church leaders and laypeople.

Sunday mass will take place in Florida, about an hour outside the capital, a town replete with Catholic and national pride. Every Nov. 8, church goers commemorate the Virgin of the Thirty-five, a symbol of Uruguay's independence movement from the Brazilian empire in 1825.
A long awaited Papal return to Argentina
By Sunday, Pope Leo will be in neighboring Argentina, fulfilling a wish of his predecessor, Pope Francis, who had hoped to return to his homeland but never made the trip.
Before his death, Francis had said he didn't want a papal visit to become entangled in Argentina's intensely polarized politics.

Pope Leo's visit to Argentina offers an early test of how he will address the Catholic Church's differences with right-wing populist leaders gaining ground across Latin America. Those tensions have also surfaced in the U.S., where Leo has clashed with President Donald Trump over immigration and the treatment of migrants.
Far-right President Javier Milei's sweeping austerity measures, which have pushed millions of Argentines into poverty, could put him at odds with Leo, who has long championed the poor.

Milei has also embraced data centers and a largely unfettered approach to artificial intelligence regulation, while Pope Leo's inaugural encyclical called for ethical caution and safeguards to protect human dignity in the age of AI.
Saving the best for last?
The final leg of the trip will take Leo back to Peru in what has been billed as a homecoming.

As a missionary priest and later appointed Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo, Pope Leo spent two decades in the country. He became a naturalized Peruvian in 2015, and has said the country shaped his life more than anything else.
He will visit several cities and towns where he lived and will meet with President Keiko Fujimori, the daughter of former Peruvian dictator Alberto Fujimori.

As a priest during the Fujimori dictatorship, Leo was openly critical of military violence and human rights abuses and supported efforts leading to Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission following the return to democracy.

But for many Uruguayans Pope Leo is not very well known. Walking past the huge stage set up for Leo's welcoming ceremony, Juan Martin Guerreiro said he wasn't sure he would attend the pope's speeches.
"He doesn't feel as influential to me … as Pope Francis," said Guerreiro. But he said he's willing to give the new pope a change because he is South American.
When reminded that Pope Leo was born in Chicago, Guerreiro said he wouldn't hold that against him.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/06/ban.headline: Blue Colorado and Washington state ban transgender athletes in girls’ sports
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/06/ban.author: Annie Gowen, Todd Wallack

paragraphs.text: Voters in four states this week approved or strengthened limits on transgender athletes’ participation in girls’ sports, a rare win for conservatives during a historic blue-wave midterm.

More than two dozen Republican-led states have already adopted bans on transgender girls and women participating on female teams. Now two blue states, Colorado and Washington, are joining their ranks, and Arizona and Nebraska have strengthened their bans.
Colorado voters also narrowly approved a ban on gender-affirming surgeries for minors, a vote that was so close the Associated Press called the outcome only Friday.
Though in a fifth state, Missouri, a prohibition on gender transition surgeries tied to a ballot measure revoking abortion rights failed.

Conservatives had pushed for voter initiatives in those states after their legislatures had failed or not tried to adopt such policies. Now, proponents of the bans could turn to other states that lack such restrictions.
Erin Lee, the founder of Protect Kids Colorado, said in an interview that the ballot wins were victories for “common sense.”
“We’ve proven that these issues transcend party lines. Protecting children and safeguarding single-sex spaces isn’t Republican or Democrat — it’s common sense,” Lee said.

In both Colorado and Washington — with Democratic governors and majorities in the state legislature — LGBTQ+ advocates criticized Lee’s group and others for trying to do an end run around Democratic legislatures.

“It’s unfortunate this is the route we had to take,” Lee said. “I would have loved that the legislature had listened to the voting public on these issues. They’re not political, but they have been politicized.

Abigail Saguy, a sociologist at the University of California at Los Angeles and author of the book “Gender Flashpoints: The Power of Dialogue,” said the fact that Democrats and Republicans alike passed these measures during a midterm year that resulted in a historic blue wave “shows clearly how wrong the narrative has been on the left as well as on the right and how polarized a lot of the news reporting has been on these issues.”

Polls show that a majority of Americans oppose transgender athletes competing in girls’ sports, a number that has risen in recent years, according to Gallup surveys. Support for trans athletes playing on teams that match their gender identity dropped by around 10 percentage points between 2021 and 2025 among Democrats and independents, a Gallup poll showed last year.

“Voters overwhelmingly think it’s wrong for a transgender person to be fired or discriminated at work because they’re trans, but a large portion of those people also think eligibility for sports should be based on biology,” Saguy said. “Those two things can be true at the same time.”
Families Not Politics, the group that opposed the measures, said in a statement Thursday that the political campaign had turned transgender children into “statewide controversies.”

“Colorado’s kids will have to live with the consequences of this election — they will face new barriers to medically necessary healthcare and new, expensive barriers and exclusion from full participation in school,” the statement said.

Washington’s ban, heavily funded by a conservative private-equity mogul from the Seattle suburbs, will require verification from a health care provider of a student-athlete’s “biological sex, based on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels.”

The two sides each spent millions, sparring bitterly about what the initiative’s wording entailed. Opponents of the measure — including the Washington Academy of Family Physicians and the state nursing association — alleged it would require an intrusive genital exam, while proponents claimed the check would be routine.

The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association said in a statement this week that it would be “making all necessary changes” by Dec. 3, when the new law goes into effect, with implementation details, including updates to physical exam requirements, “under review.”
In Arizona and Nebraska, voters shored up or expanded restrictions already put in place.

Arizona voters approved expanding limits on transgender participation in girls’ sports to all schools and athletic associations, as well as restricting access to locker rooms to the sex listed on a person’s birth certificate.
Nebraska voters approved language for the state’s constitution that would shore up an existing transgender sports ban and make it harder for future legislatures to overturn.

Lee said public attitudes toward transgender competition in women’s sports has changed in recent years. She cited prominent athletes who have spoken out against transgender inclusion, including Sophie Cunningham, the WNBA player, who said this summer that women should not have to compete against “biological men.”
“So much has changed in the last five years,” Lee said. “The conversation has shifted. People are less kowtowed into staying silent. It’s okay to speak biological truth.”

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/06/meg.headline: Meghan Markle’s estranged father arrested on child porn charge
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/06/meg.author: Amy B Wang

paragraphs.text: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested Friday on a child pornography charge, according to the U.S. attorney’s office for the Central District of California.

The FBI raided two Los Angeles-area storage units that Markle had rented since 2008 after receiving notice that child sexual abuse materials had been found among Markle’s belongings in the Philippines, the office said in a statement Friday.

Federal agents seized 78 items from the California storage units, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse material. At least two of the images seized featured Markle with minor victims, according to the office.

“Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

Markle, 82, was arrested at his home in Lakeland, Florida, and is expected to make his first court appearance Friday in federal court in Tampa. If convicted, Markle could face up to 20 years in federal prison.

Markle could not immediately be reached for comment Friday, and a lawyer for him was not listed in publicly available court documents. Representatives for Meghan did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Markle’s arrest was first reported by the Daily Mail. The British tabloid also reported last week that child pornography had been found in a storage unit Markle had previously rented in Mexico.

“This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids — any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement Friday.
Meghan said last month that she had been informed of “disturbing allegations” about her estranged father in 2018 and had not allowed him any contact with her children to “protect them.”

Meghan’s relationship with her father broke down in the lead-up to her wedding to Prince Harry in May 2018, and her relationship with her father attracted intense tabloid interest. Her father did not attend the wedding.
Jeremy Roebuck and Victoria Craw contributed to this report.

washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/06/nat.headline: Nationals sign Jacob Young to extension, locking down another core player
washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/06/nat.author: Danielle Allentuck

paragraphs.text: The Washington Nationals have agreed to a contract extension with outfielder Jacob Young, according to a person familiar with the situation. The deal would lock in the center fielder for at least the next four years.
The person spoke on the condition of anonymity Friday because they weren’t authorized to publicly discuss the contract.
Young’s new deal — which is worth $23 million, according to reports — would buy out his three arbitration-eligible seasons and one year of free agency. There’s also an option for an additional year.

It’s the second extension handed out by Paul Toboni, the Nationals’ president of baseball operations, since he took over a year ago as the team invests in its core. Starting pitcher Cade Cavalli signed a four-year, $47 million extension in September.

Young, 27, debuted in 2023 and became a staple in Washington’s outfield a year later. He’s always been known for his strong defensive skills — his fielding range ranks in the 96th percentile — and he was named a Gold Glove finalist in 2024 and 2025.

Last offseason, Young put an increased emphasis on his hitting. He spent part of his offseason at Driveline, an advanced data-driven hitting lab in Kent, Washington. There, he worked on his swing with a trio of weighted bats. His average bat speed increased to 69.6 mph this season, up from 68.3 mph a year ago.
Those changes helped him hit a career-high 10 home runs in 140 games, compared to five in his previous 303. He also hit .252 with a .708 OPS last season, both the best marks of his career.

The Nationals’ outfield already seemed set for the long haul, with Dylan Crews, James Wood and Daylen Lile not becoming free agents until at least 2031. Now, they have at least one extra year of Young, who would have become a free agent in 2030.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/06/a.headline: Tech stocks rally as investors brace for more volatility
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/06/a.author: Victoria Craw, Miriam Waldvogel

paragraphs.text: American indexes and tech stocks picked up in the opening minutes of Friday trading as investors anticipated another day of volatility in an unsteady week for markets worldwide.

Asian and European stock markets dropped Friday, extending losses seen in U.S. indexes a day earlier amid investor concerns that Democratic control of Congress could increase regulatory scrutiny of AI development.

But major stock indexes rose slightly in the initial hours of Friday trading, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index and the S&P 500 both up. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost a little ground.

Chip stocks, which took heavy losses Thursday, opened Friday to an initial rebound. The iShares Semiconductor ETF, an investment fund tracking chips, rose about 5 percent. Nvidia, Taiwan Semiconductor and Broadcom all rose. Other technology stocks did not see as dramatic gains; Microsoft and Apple had slight dips by 10:30 a.m. Friday.

Early Friday, the price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, jumped back up to $99 a barrel, around 6 percent higher than a day earlier when the decisive midterm results boosted hopes of a renewed push to end the Iran war. It still remains below the $117 a barrel mark from one week ago.

Slides in European and Asian markets followed major U.S. stock markets tumbling on Thursday, largely erasing post-election gains, as investors processed the impact of Democratic success in the midterm elections.

The U.S. economy showed unexpectedly strong jobs numbers Friday morning, with the unemployment rate ticking down to 4.1 percent. The economy added 165,000 jobs in October, nearly triple what forecasters had expected.

The strong employment numbers buoyed expectations for the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates in December, potentially raising the cost of borrowing. The market jitters come as investors weigh the sustainability of America’s AI boom, with reports circulating Thursday that Anthropic, the maker of the chatbot Claude, may go public at a lower valuation than expected.

By Thursday’s close, the S&P 500, a broad index of 500 large American companies, had lost about 4 percent, while the Nasdaq lost around 5.5 percent amid fears that the election results could spur greater regulatory oversight of the AI-related development boom that has fueled market gains in recent months.

Tech stocks including Google parent company Alphabet, Apple, Meta, Space X and Nvidia — the chip company central to the AI boom — all lost ground in Thursday’s trade. South Korean companies Samsung and SK Hynix, which make AI chips, also saw their share price fall, though some tech stocks regained ground early Friday.

Dozens of ballot measures placing restrictions on data center development were approved in Tuesday’s elections, while states that have been hubs of data center development including Texas and Ohio will have new Democratic governors who have promised tighter regulation.

Priscilla Thiagamoorthy, a senior economist at the Bank of Montreal, said in a note after markets closed Thursday that the pullback was notable because stocks had for so long resisted “mounting economic headwinds.”
“But Thursday’s sell-off was a reminder that when expectations and valuations become stretched, even a modest shift in sentiment can trigger a swift repricing,” she added.
Ed Mills, a policy analyst at the firm Raymond James, said he expected to see continued volatility in AI driven by policy.
“We see very frequently after big moves, a recovery, [but] it’s too early to know exactly where that is,” he said.

Japan’s Nikkei and Korea’s KOSPI index both dropped about 6 percent, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng and the Shanghai composite index fell about 1 percent on Friday. Major stock indexes in the U.K. and Germany lost more than 2 percent, while France’s CAC 40 index fell nearly 1.8 percent.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/06/u.headline: U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, showing surprising strength
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/06/u.author: Lauren Kaori Gurley

paragraphs.text: The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, shattering expectations and suggesting strength in the labor market, especially for white-collar, health care and manufacturing workers.
The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent, extending low levels that have defined the labor market over the past year, according to a Labor Department report released Friday.
The labor market was stronger than originally reported in August and September, the report showed, with job gains revised up by 84,000 positions for those months.
Wage growth continued to be outpaced by inflation, in bad news for households.

The rosy job figures were unexpected, as soaring prices fueled by the Iran war, tariffs and immigration enforcement have dampened employers’ hiring plans this year. But spending by wealthier households flush with stock market gains has been propping up the economy.

“Today’s jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown,” wrote Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, in an analyst note. She added, “Job creation remains broad-based, pointing to an economy that is still absorbing labor comfortably rather than one beginning to buckle under tighter financial conditions.”

The White House, reeling from Tuesday’s midterm Republican wipeout, touted the job gains as a sign of a vigorous labor market. On CNBC, White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett called jobs number “through the roof.”
It’s “as good of a job market as you’re likely to see,” Hassett said.

But strong job gains appeared to have little impact on the stock market, which opened slightly higher Friday morning, after tumbling Thursday in reaction to concerns about whether country’s rapid AI build-out would continue with Democrats in power.
Jobs gains were spread across health care, professional and business services, manufacturing, and transportation and warehousing.

Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs, raising hopes of new growth in white-collar jobs. The sector averaged monthly job gains of around 15,000 over the prior 12 months. The job growth is welcome news for recent college graduates who have struggled to find work this year amid signs that artificial intelligence is zapping entry-level jobs.

The transportation and warehousing sector added 25,000 jobs, mostly delivery workers. Retailers and logistics firms are preparing for a robust holiday shopping season, with Amazon recently announcing the hiring of 300,000 workers for the season.

And manufacturing added jobs for the fifth straight month, including in metal production, which could be one of a few areas benefiting from the president’s tariffs. Manufacturing employers have added 101,000 jobs since hitting a recent low in December 2025.
Leisure and hospitality, and the federal government shed jobs.

Despite some pockets of job growth, many employers are still reluctant to bring on new workers. This year’s average monthly gains are much smaller than the average monthly jobs numbers added just a few years ago. During the first 10 months of 2026, job growth has averaged 86,000 positions per month, compared to the average monthly gain of 210,000 in 2023.

Indeed, there are underlying signs that many Americans are struggling in their job searches. The average duration of unemployment hit more than 27 weeks in October, the highest level since late 2021. Nearly 2 million Americans have been unemployed for more than half a year, the data showed, as new job opportunities are scarce in many sectors, especially in entry-level white-collar positions.

Recent college graduates are facing the brunt of this pain. The so-called underemployment rate for recent college graduates has risen to the highest rate since October 2020, according to data released Monday by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Underemployment measures the share of graduates working in jobs that typically do not require a bachelor’s degree.

Another dark spot is workers’ paychecks. Average hourly earnings grew to $38 an hour in October, an increase of 3.1 percent on an annual basis, the most recent data shows — well below inflation at 3.7 percent in September.

Many middle- and lower-income Americans have been feeling gloomy about the labor market and the economy, as war-fueled inflation outpaces workers’ wage gains eroding their spending power. That helps explain why Americans viewed the state of the economy as the top issue in midterm elections, in which voters delivered a wholesale rejection of President Donald Trump and his policies on Tuesday.

“What’s dragging the economy down right now is stubbornly high inflation driven by war in Iran and the shock to energy prices,” said Andrew Flowers, chief economist at Appcast. He added, “It’s also the long-standing structural in-affordability of health care and housing and premiums on health care rising quickly.”

But there are new data shows signs that the labor market could be picking up. In September, workers were quitting their jobs at the highest rate in over a year, according to the job openings report released Tuesday, signaling that some workers are newly confident in their ability to find better employment opportunities. Job openings also rose to the highest level since November 2024, and layoffs remain very low.

washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/06.headline: Jay Rockefeller, Senate voice on health care and security, dies at 89
washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/06.author: Louie Estrada

paragraphs.text: John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, an heir to a vast oil fortune and a liberal Democrat who entered politics in his adopted home state of West Virginia, serving as governor and a five-term U.S. senator and becoming a leading voice on health care, tax reform, social welfare and national security, died Friday at his home in Washington, D.C. He was 89. His family did not provide a cause.

Mr. Rockefeller was a great-grandson of billionaire industrialist John D. Rockefeller Sr., whose Standard Oil Trust monopolized the oil industry in the early 20th century and made him one of the world’s richest people.

Rockefeller descendants have figured prominently in philanthropy, business and politics. Mr. Rockefeller’s father was philanthropist John D. Rockefeller III; one uncle, Nelson A. Rockefeller, was elected governor of New York four times before being appointed vice president of the United States; another uncle, Winthrop Rockefeller, was elected governor of Arkansas twice; and yet another, David Rockefeller Sr., rose to become chairman and chief executive of Chase Manhattan Bank.

Having grown up a blue-blooded Northeasterner, Mr. Rockefeller made an unlikely public face of West Virginia. The rugged Appalachian state, long dependent on the coal industry, was beset by troubles: an aging population, high poverty, low-performing schools and a stagnant job market dominated by low-wage jobs.

Arriving on Capitol Hill in 1985, after two terms as governor, Mr. Rockefeller worked in the shadow of West Virginia’s long-serving senior senator, Democrat Robert C. Byrd, while burrowing deep into committee work and distinguishing himself as an earnest and dogged advocate for society’s most vulnerable.

His signature accomplishments included expanding eligibility of the earned income tax credit and establishing the child tax credit and the Children’s Health Insurance Program, a federal-state initiative that provides health coverage to children in low-income families. He also worked to protect Medicare, the federal health insurance program for the elderly and disabled, from proposed budget cuts.

Beginning in the late 1980s, he chaired a bipartisan commission established by Congress to study health coverage and long-term care. He was a key supporter in 1993 of the unsuccessful effort led by then-first lady Hillary Clinton to create a national system of universal health care. After that, he voted for and defended the Affordable Care Act, a step toward universal coverage that President Barack Obama signed into law in 2010.

Mr. Rockefeller successfully sponsored legislation to expand research into and treatment of illnesses related to military service. And, of particular interest to many West Virginians, he had a hand in writing legislation to protect the health benefits of coal miners and their families after mining companies shuttered operations. He was also a sponsor of 2006 legislation that updated mine-safety regulations.

Broadband internet access in rural communities and computer security were among Mr. Rockefeller’s other long-standing concerns. In one of his final legislative efforts, he sponsored the Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2014. The bill established a public-private partnership to set security standards and promote research and development aimed at protecting computer systems and networks involved in the operation of critical infrastructure.

Mr. Rockefeller, at various times, chaired the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, the Veterans’ Affairs Committee and the Intelligence Committee. In 2008, he led a bipartisan Senate investigation into the lead-up to the Iraq War. The committee report concluded that President George W. Bush’s administration had misrepresented intelligence on Iraq to justify the military invasion in 2003.

“There’s always talk in the Senate that members are either workhorses or showhorses,” said Donald A. Ritchie, historian emeritus of the U.S. Senate, in a 2022 interview for this obituary. “A showhorse is a senator who is on TV all the time. The workhorses — like Rockefeller — aren’t seen as much because they are in the committee doing the nitty-gritty work.”

Although Mr. Rockefeller voted with his Democratic colleagues more than 90 percent of the time, he wasn’t seen as ideological or partisan. “He was able to work with friends he made across the aisle,” Ritchie said.
Getting to know West Virginia

Mr. Rockefeller arrived in West Virginia as an idealistic 27-year-old community organizer with Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA), an anti-poverty program established by President Lyndon B. Johnson. The group required volunteers to take an oath of poverty before they went to live with host families in impoverished communities, mostly in the South and Appalachia.

His assignment sent him to Emmons, a remote mining town on the Big Coal River, about 20 miles south of Charleston, the state capital. It took months for townspeople to warm up to the 6-foot-6 stranger whose surname evoked a history of violent labor struggles in the early 20th century.

In Emmons, Mr. Rockefeller focused on youth and health care projects. He started the town’s first Little League team, led the construction of a community center and organized a mobile health-screening service for women.

Mr. Rockefeller decided to stay in West Virginia after his assignment ended, and then he began to climb the local political ladder — not as a Republican, in line with family tradition, but as a Democrat. His choice of political affiliation made national news at a time when “Rockefeller Republican” was shorthand for membership in the party’s moderate wing.

As a member of one of America’s most prominent families, much of his life was chronicled in the press. His 1967 marriage to Sharon Percy, daughter of U.S. Sen. Charles H. Percy (R-Illinois), made the cover of Life magazine. The next year, Mr. Rockefeller got a call from his uncle Nelson, then New York governor, offering to appoint him to the Senate seat of Robert F. Kennedy (D-New York), who had been assassinated while running for president.
“I said no immediately,” Mr. Rockefeller told The Washington Post years later, adding that he had ambitions of serving in the Senate but didn’t want the job handed to him.
Mr. Rockefeller served in the state House of Delegates from 1966 to 1968 and then was secretary of state through 1972, when he made an unsuccessful run for governor.

In the only political defeat of his career, he lost to Republican incumbent Arch Moore Jr., who accused Mr. Rockefeller of seeking to destroy the coal industry after the Democratic candidate called for a ban on strip mining, which has been linked to such problems as soil erosion and stream pollution.

For much of his career, Mr. Rockefeller’s political opponents derided him as a Yankee carpetbagger, an opportunistic outsider with deep pockets and a deeper sense of privilege. Moore ran TV ads that asked, “How’d you like to have a governor of New York from West Virginia?”

After losing the 1972 race, Mr. Rockefeller spent about four years as president of West Virginia Wesleyan College in Buckhannon before winning the first of two terms as governor in 1976. By that time, he had won over coal miners by reversing his stance on strip mining, reasoning that mining companies had taken steps to address environmental concerns.
During his tenure as governor, Mr. Rockefeller emphasized government ethics, affordable housing and infrastructure projects. He created the state’s first board of coal mine health and safety.

He was elected to the Senate in 1984, replacing Sen. Jennings Randolph (D), who was retiring. In 2013, Mr. Rockefeller announced his retirement from the Senate ahead of the 2014 election, which was won by Shelley Moore Capito (R), daughter of former governor Moore.

Survivors include his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller, the president and chief executive of WETA, Washington’s public broadcasting station; four children, John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Aldrich Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.
Elite schools and the Far East

John Rockefeller was born in Manhattan on June 18, 1937. He was one of four children and the only son of John D. Rockefeller III and the former Blanchette Ferry Hooker. His parents didn’t put the middle name Davison or the roman numeral suffix on his birth certificate, intending to spare him what they worried might be a burden.

“As a boy,” he told Life, “I was told that I should make up my own mind whether I wanted to carry on the full name, which I think stands for public service, a sense of responsibility, and a high standard of demand on oneself. When I was 21, I wrote a letter to my father saying I wanted the name and the responsibility.”

Amid the opulence of his youth — including a 3,000-acre family estate in suburban Westchester County — Jay Rockefeller had a strict Baptist upbringing. Idleness was considered a sin. If he wished to speak with his father, he had to schedule an appointment in the family study.

He graduated in 1954 from Phillips Exeter Academy boarding school, then majored in Far Eastern languages and history at Harvard. He had developed an affinity for Asian culture on family trips to Japan. But by his junior year, he desperately wanted to leave what he called his “privileged surroundings” and what looked to be the preordained trajectory of his life into the Northeast Republican establishment.

With the help of a sympathetic professor, Mr. Rockefeller obtained a temporary position teaching English at International Christian University in Tokyo. He lived with a group of Japanese students in a wood and paper shack in the middle of a rice field. During school breaks, he visited his friends’ families, many of whom worked on farms, struggling to rebuild their lives in the aftermath of World War II.

“It was a very personal experience for me, a very deep experience. It was the beginning of putting me on the track to public service,” Mr. Rockefeller said in the 2015 public television documentary “Jay: A Rockefeller’s Journey.”

He returned to Harvard in 1960, received a bachelor’s degree the next year and joined the nascent Peace Corps as special assistant to R. Sargent Shriver, its founding director. He also worked briefly for the State Department’s East Asian division.

But he grew restless in desk jobs and yearned to participate in grassroots community work. Through Action for Appalachian Youth, a program affiliated with VISTA, he traveled to West Virginia in 1964 on a one-year assignment to do social work in Emmons, where most of 250 residents relied on government assistance for food.
In the small town, he found a cause and a mission.
“My time there was transformative,” Mr. Rockefeller said in his 2014 farewell speech to the Senate. “It explains every policy I have pursued and every vote I have cast.”

correctionA previous version of this article incorrectly stated that Mr. Rockefeller's wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller, was the former president and chief executive of WETA, Washington’s public broadcasting station. She still holds those positions.

washingtonpost.com/education/2026/11/06/.headline: Low-income college students relied on campus child care. Then Trump cut it.
washingtonpost.com/education/2026/11/06/.author: Danielle Douglas-Gabriel

paragraphs.text: At the start of this semester, Larissa Saucillo was making great progress toward becoming a nurse.

Saucillo, 33, got into two popular evening lab courses that accommodated her full-time work schedule. And she secured a slot for her 5-year-old daughter in the college’s evening child care program, a service backed by a federal grant for low-income college students with children.

But a month into the current term, Saucillo learned the federal grant had run out, and the community college’s program was inexplicably denied new funding. Without child care, there was no way Saucillo could continue her classes, so she withdrew.

“It’s going to take me at least another semester now to complete my program,” Saucillo said. “That means more student loans, more debt when I could have just gotten it done and moved on to the nursing program. That program is so competitive that I may not be able to get in until 2028.”

The Trump administration’s controversial decision to cut the number of colleges awarded funding from the Child Care Access Means Parents in School (CCAMPIS) program has forced some students to cut back their college courses or stop attending. The $75 million federal program offers four-year grants to colleges and universities that provide child care on campus or in the surrounding community. It is a critical source of money for public colleges that educate large populations of students with limited financial means, advocates and school officials said.

Despite announcing plans this summer to provide 148 colleges with CCAMPIS funding through a new grant competition, the Education Department awarded only 40 grants in the fall. In its last grant competition in 2021, the department awarded funding to 327 colleges.

Advocates cried foul this fall after the Education Department gave all four years’ worth of funding to a few dozen colleges, instead of distributing the funding on a yearly basis to more schools from annual congressional appropriations.
The department typically avoids “front-loading,” but advocacy groups say the practice has become more common as the Trump administration tries to dismantle the Education Department.

Trump has twice proposed eliminating CCAMPIS, claiming it is misaligned with the Education Department’s purpose and would be best run by the Department of Health and Human Services. The administration off-loaded the child care program to HHS last year through an interagency agreement that left the Education Department in a supervisory role.
The Education Department did not explain the discrepancy between the anticipated and actual number of CCAMPIS awards, but said its decision is in line with the administration’s policy objectives.

“ED is forward funding successful applicants where the administration has not requested funding in future budget years to avoid interrupting projects partway into their project period,” Education Department spokesperson Ellen Keast said in an email. “We are ending the failed approach of previous administrations and funding high-quality grantees.”

Advocates argue there was no shortage of colleges offering high-quality child care. The department received nearly 300 applications, and public records show that 79 applicants earned perfect scores on their proposals. Yet many of those colleges were shut out of the awards.

Madison Area Technical College is one of them. The Wisconsin college, which has relied on CCAMPIS for the past eight years, received no explanation for the rejection, just glowing feedback from application reviewers. It had requested a little over the $2 million the college received in 2021.

Madison has two campus-based child care centers and has increased capacity three times since 2020 from 30 children to more than 120 children, as more students need a safe, convenient and affordable place to leave their children during class. Roughly 40 percent of full-time degree-seeking students at Madison are parents of young children.

With the loss of federal funding to subsidize the cost of care, six families have declined child care slots, three delayed starting care while seeking other funding, and two reduced their course loads to avoid the need for care in the past month, according to the college.

Madison President Jennifer Berne has been working with the college’s foundation to provide affected students temporary child care assistance, while rallying donors and the local government for additional financial support. But without federal funding, she said there is no way to guarantee the college can support parents through the completion of their education.

“This is a workforce issue,” Berne said. “We have the talent and motivation of the people who want to become nurses, mechanics, accountants … but without child care, they cannot access those programs.”

For college students with children — roughly 1 in 5 undergraduates — reliable and affordable child care can make or break their chances of earning a credential. In a 2024 survey conducted by the think tank New America, more than half of parenting community college students who dropped out said affordable child care would help them return to college. Only 38 percent of community colleges offer on-campus child care.

Demand for child care slots at many campuses has historically outpaced supply, leading to lengthy wait lists that have caught the attention of federal lawmakers. Congress increased CCAMPIS funding from $15 million to $75 million between 2017 and 2023, allowing more colleges and universities to access federal support. Still, the funding has never been enough to meet the full need.

When Madison lost its federal funding, graphic design student Christopher Rothe, 40, could no longer afford to send his 20-month-old son to the campus center five days a week. His boy now goes three days a week and spends the other two with Rothe, who had to cut back on his hours at work and his course load to stay home with his son.

“I’m really trying to get us to a point of being financially secure, into a better apartment, you know, just creating a better life for our family,” Rothe said. “I don’t know how long it’s going to take to finish my program now that I have to take fewer classes.”

In a letter sent earlier this month to Education Secretary Linda McMahon, Sens. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin) and Patty Murray (D-Washington), high-ranking members of the Appropriations Committee, criticized the Education Department’s treatment of CCAMPIS and other competitive grant programs that issued few awards and front-loaded congressional funding.

“It is perplexing that an administration that says it wants to improve affordability for Americans and help Americans find good-paying jobs would curtail a program that helps Americans afford higher education and workforce training,” the senators wrote.

Stephanie Baker, a senior policy manager in the higher education program at New America, said Congress could stipulate in the next appropriations bill that the Education Department hold another competition in 2027 for funding. Lawmakers, she said, could also direct the department to fund the slate of colleges that had strong applications but did not get grants.
But for now, colleges across the country are contending with the fallout of this year’s cut.

At Austin Community College, the $1.1 million in CCAMPIS funding from the previous competition has primarily been used to help students in its health science program, particularly those like Saucillo enrolled in night classes, said Cara Crowley, the special adviser to the chancellor for basic needs systems at the college.

She said the college began preparing students last year for the possibility that federal funding would not be renewed because there was so much uncertainty about the future of CCAMPIS under Trump. Some students qualified for a state grant that offset child care costs, but many others were left without any recourse.
ACC never received a response to its CCAMPIS application, and only learned that it was denied the federal funding after contacting Republican Sen. John Cornyn’s office in Texas.

About 30 percent of the 80,000 students at the community college are parents, and the wait list for child care slots has an average of 200 to 300 students every year. The college managed to reduce the wait list and open the nighttime program with its 2021 CCAMPIS award of just over $1 million, but now it is grappling with the loss of federal support.

Despite the setback, Saucillo remains resolute in becoming a nurse. She took a 75 percent pay cut to enroll full time and complete her program faster, but for now she can only take an online class without reliable child care.

“Everything is up in the air,” Saucillo said. “It’s unfortunate because I know I’m not the only parent going through this. We are all trying to provide better lives for our kids. … And the opportunity is being taken away.”

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/06/tex.headline: Texas’s new Democratic governor Hinojosa vows to undo policies she calls divisive
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/06/tex.author: Molly Hennessy-Fiske

paragraphs.text: AUSTIN — Texas’s first Latina governor pledged to abandon the extreme partisanship that she said has defined politics in this deeply red state for decades. But she has also made clear her determination to quickly undo many of her predecessor’s initiatives.

At a Thursday briefing where — unlike her predecessor, GOP Gov. Greg Abbott — she answered questions in English and Spanish, Gina Hinojosa said she had spoken with Abbott, who was “gracious” and assured her he would “fully cooperate” with the transition.

“People are tired of the divisions, of the fighting, of the culture wars. This is the time to come together in a way that is about just delivering for the people of Texas,” Hinojosa said at the University of Texas, just miles from the Capitol where for the next two months Republicans retain control of every state office.

Democrats flipped every statewide office and the Texas House. But Republicans still hold a majority in the state Senate where they can change rules to strip the new Democratic lieutenant governor, Vikki Goodwin, of agenda-setting powers before she takes office and effectively block Democrats’ priority legislation when the legislature reconvenes in January.
Hinojosa, 52, said she hopes Republicans work with, not against, her: “The people of Texas have spoken. I think it’s important as elected leaders that we respect what the people of Texas have said.”
“They want change. And I would hope the elected leaders don’t get in the way,” she said.

As the first Democrat to take the Texas governor’s mansion in almost four decades, Hinojosa faces a staggering to-do list, much of it focused on undoing GOP policies on health care, grocery and energy costs, public schools, public lands and data centers.
On the campaign trail, Hinojosa promised to declare a “high-cost emergency” in Texas and use executive orders to suspend state gas and diesel taxes and freeze electricity rates.

Hinojosa also vowed on her first day in office to declare a moratorium on data centers and to fire the state superintendent of schools, a software developer who has expanded state takeovers of local school districts and overseen a decline in student performance.

Hinojosa has said she plans to expand Medicaid (a provision of the Affordable Care Act that allows states to extend Medicaid health coverage to nearly all low-income adults), fully fund public schools including teacher raises, end state takeovers of school districts such as Houston, dismantle Abbott’s school voucher program and give every Texas household $1,500.

She predicted on Thursday those priorities could win support from Republicans in the legislature, pointing to a Republican former state representative, Ernest Bailes from South Texas, whom she had invited to join her team.
“I believe in Gina and I have faith that we will be able to do good things for the state of Texas. We will put partisanship aside,” Bailes said.
Hinojosa noted that they had worked together in the legislature on education issues and that “There are lots of issues where my good allies are Republicans.”

But there’s also a lot Hinojosa could do without Republican support, aided by lawmakers in the House, Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson and Comptroller-elect Sarah Eckhardt, state senators whom Hinojosa has worked with. Democrats took the Texas House with a comfortable margin, and are soon expected to elect a Democratic speaker and majority leader who can work in tandem with Hinojosa.
The new governor could also act unilaterally, although it’s not clear how far she’s willing to go.

Abbott used executive orders, emergency actions, disaster declarations, appointments, special legislative sessions and vetoes more than any previous governor, often to counter more liberal cities and counties.

He repeatedly renewed an emergency declaration at the southern border for the multibillion dollar Operation Lone Star, despite the number of migrant crossings dropping to record lows since the start of the second Trump administration. That move, along with other executive orders and disaster declarations, allowed Abbott to shift funds, pause regulations and award no-bid contracts. And he ordered the state law enforcement to assist federal immigration agents with the Trump administration’s crackdown.

Hinojosa largely avoided being drawn into the culture war during her campaign, saying that she preferred to focus on pocketbook issues. She has said the best place to fight the Texas GOP’s immigration measures is the bully pulpit and courts. In her victory speech, she rejected the GOP’s single party rule.
“This governor’s office does not belong to me, it does not belong to my party. We did not end one era of single party rule just to usher in another,” she said.

But just as Abbott worked with GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton to restrict abortion and LGBTQ+ rights, Hinojosa could work with Johnson to defend those rights — most immediately by dropping lawsuits Paxton will leave pending.

Johnson has said he will drop a lawsuit Paxton filed this year against a clinic that provides abortion medication by mail in Texas, and that he will not enforce restrictions on public restrooms for transgender Texans.

“Democrats are faced with something we haven’t faced in 30 years: Governance. Democrats need to do well and communicate well about what we’ve done,” Johnson said in an interview after his election, to “replace ideologues with public servants.”
Democrats will also have the Texas courts on their side, including a first-ever female majority and chief justice of the Texas Supreme Court and a majority on the Court of Criminal Appeals.
But some Republican lawmakers have already urged their colleagues to take action within the next 10 weeks to limit Democrats’ reach.

North Texas state Rep. Brian Harrison, a right-wing social conservative, posted a petition on X after the election urging Abbott to call a special legislative session before Hinojosa is sworn in “to rein in executive emergency powers.”
Harrison said he worked with Hinojosa in the legislature, where he heard her express opposition to Abbott’s executive actions.

“If she wants to pursue Democrat policies, she better follow the Texas Constitution and put that before the legislature,” he said in an interview. “We should use every tool we have to protect the freedom and liberty and Texans.”
But veteran GOP Texas Sen. Paul Bettencourt of Houston said he was not aware of coordinated plans by Republicans to strip the new lieutenant governor of her powers as Senate president.
Bettencourt said he advised colleagues, “It would be unwise to go and try to rip the president’s powers away from Ms. Goodwin after an election where the people put her there.”
