washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/06/thr.headline: Indiana, Florida and Alabama carried out executions on Thursday

paragraphs.text: Three states carried out the death penalty on Thursday, marking the second time in 2026 that three executions were carried out on the same day.

Jeffrey Weisheit, convicted of killing two children in a house fire, was pronounced dead in Indiana at 12:45 a.m. Gov. Mike Braun (R) had denied his lawyers’ request to change the sentence to life in prison.
Jesse Guardado, who had pleaded guilty to a fatal stabbing, was executed in Florida at 6:13 p.m. In his final statement, he apologized to the victim’s family, the AP reported.
Michael Taylor, who killed an elderly couple when he was 19, was executed an hour later in Alabama. Death penalty opponents had called for his sentence to be commuted given his young age at the time.
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) criticized Newsom’s decision in a statement to the AP, saying: “California may let their criminals escape justice, but not Alabama.”
The death penalty remains a divisive issue nationally, and executions have come under renewed scrutiny following Tennessee’s botched attempt to execute Christa Pike in September.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/05/new.headline: Newsom moves to commute 548 death sentences, emptying California’s death row
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/05/new.author: Katie Mettler, Hannah Knowles

paragraphs.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Thursday said he has started the process of commuting the death sentences of more than 500 state prisoners — a historic move that, if successful, would empty the nation’s largest death row and eliminate about a quarter of all death sentences nationwide.

Newsom, who has been weighing a mass commutation for months, announced the sweeping move just days after Democrats notched a resounding victory in the midterm elections, giving the party control of Congress and flipping several states blue. Newsom, who will leave office in January, is weighing a 2028 presidential run.

A longtime critic of capital punishment, the governor began his first term by ordering California’s first moratorium on executions, dismantling the state’s death chamber and repealing its lethal injection protocol. If approved by the courts, this mass commutation will cement Newsom as the most anti-death-penalty governor in the state’s history.
In a letter to California residents, Newsom said he is seeking to change the sentences of all 548 death row prisoners to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

He called the decision “among the most difficult” of his career. Newsom wrote in his letter that commuting the sentences “will always weigh heavily” on him, but that he felt “compelled to follow my conscience.”
“Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die,” Newsom said in his letter. “But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them.”
He called the state’s death penalty system “a failure” that “has not been and cannot be fairly applied and has resulted in the conviction of innocent people.”

“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundation of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” the governor said.

The state does not allow a governor to unilaterally commute the sentences of those with numerous felony convictions outside their capital murder cases, which account for about 70 percent of the state’s death row prisoners.
In those cases, the state Supreme Court will need to review Newsom’s clemency grants. At least four of the court’s seven justices must sign-off on the commutation for it to take effect.

Newsom wrote that he is “confident” the mass commutation is consistent with California law, but acknowledged this act of clemency requires the court to “participate in a weighty decision they did not choose to take up and with which they may personally disagree.”
California has not carried out an execution since 2006.

Newsom’s move was welcomed by Amnesty International and a mix of civil rights leaders, business officials, Hollywood actors and advocates for criminal justice reform. That included victims’ relatives like Annie Nichol and Jess Nichol, whose sister, 12-year-old Polly Klaas, was kidnapped and killed in 1993 by a man who remains on California’s death row.
“We don’t forgive the person that killed Polly,” Annie Nichol said in an interview Thursday. “But we also know that the death penalty is wrong.”

The Nichol sisters met with Newsom earlier this year at San Quentin prison, the former home of California’s death row, to discuss issues including their opposition to the death penalty. The family’s advocacy had helped reshape California’s justice system, but the sisters’ views on justice have evolved and they became uncomfortable with laws passed and upheld in Polly Klaas’s name.

“I believe that victims deserve the opportunity to heal and to grow, and the story of our loss and pain to change with time,” said Annie Nichol, who works as a survivor advocate with Crime Survivors Speak. “Just like people inside also deserve that opportunity, rather than having this capital punishment that’s irreversible.”

Other families of murder victims have viscerally opposed mass commutation, saying it feels like stolen justice. Ahead of Thursday’s announcement, some district attorneys and victim advocates urged the governor to leave death row alone — and hinted at legal challenges if he issued a mass commutation.

The move could have political repercussions, too, as critics come after Newsom and other Democrats for their criminal justice policies. But commuting the sentences could also win him credit with those weary of the justice system and reform advocates who have long been concerned about wrongful convictions and documented racial disparities in death sentences.

Newsom acknowledged that tension in his letter, writing that he understands his move will “anger and hurt some Californians.” He described seeking counsel from crime victims, public safety experts and religious and civil rights leaders.

“I deeply respect the views of those who will strongly disagree with my decision, including some families of victims who have suffered the worst possible loss,” Newsom wrote. “I hold this painful truth along with the belief that this is a righteous action.”
Governors in other states, including Oregon and Illinois, have commuted their own death rows, but none were nearly as large as California’s.

Shortly before leaving office, President Joe Biden commuted the sentences of 37 of the 40 people on federal death row, a move that has drawn sharp criticism from President Donald Trump and his allies.

While the death penalty used to be widely popular nationwide, support for it has dropped significantly. Still, despite a decline in executions nationwide, the pace of state-sanctioned killings has accelerated recently in some Republican-led states as the Trump administration has pushed for more capital punishment.
The District and 23 states have abolished the death penalty, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, but it remains on the books in 27 states and the federal system.

Five of those states currently have moratoriums blocking executions — including Tennessee, where Gov. Bill Lee (R) paused them this fall after prison officials botched the lethal injection of convicted killer Christa Pike. Her unprecedented survival of two doses of pentobarbital is the subject of ongoing litigation and an independent investigation.
In four death penalty states currently led by Republicans, Democrats will take over next year, potentially setting the stage for additional executive moves curtailing capital punishment.

Throughout his political career, Newsom has been clear on his strong opposition to the death penalty. He imposed a moratorium on executions in March 2019 and closed the state’s death chamber at San Quentin State Prison, moving those on death row into the general prison population.
“My ultimate goal is to end the death penalty in California,” Newsom said at the time.

His mass commutation effectively does just that, for now, though the death penalty remains legal and prosecutors in some counties are still pursuing capital cases. Capital punishment opponents in the state have tried, unsuccessfully, to end the death penalty by ballot measure.

In a letter to Newsom ahead of his decision, Dan Dow, district attorney of San Luis Obispo County, wrote that a universal act of clemency would rob victims’ families of the individual consideration their cases warranted.

Dow has also repeatedly emphasized his belief that any act of clemency — including this mass commutation — should explicitly acknowledge the names of the people killed by those on California’s death row.
In a statement Thursday, Dow lambasted Newsom for not naming any capital murder victims, including the three from his county.

“Governor Newsom just told the families of Rachel Newhouse, Aundria Crawford, Kesha Gurke and every other innocent victim of California’s 548 condemned killers that the killers’ lives matter more,” Dow said. “Juries chose justice case by case, voters chose it five times, and one outgoing governor is trying to erase it all with a pen. This is a sickening abuse of power.”
Nathan Hochman, the Los Angeles County district attorney, said in a separate statement that he will continue to pursue death sentences when he thinks the crime warrants it.
Before Thursday’s announcement, the governor had been openly wrestling with the idea and said on his podcast last month that he had lots of “people in my ear” saying not to do it.
But he told guest Bryan Stevenson, a prominent lawyer and death penalty opponent, that he was thinking hard about the issue.
“I have to prepare for my own conscience, my rocking chair test,” Newsom told Stevenson. “Do I commute the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere?”
“I think you do,” Stevenson answered, “and I think it becomes a really pivotal moment in this country.”

During their conversation with Newsom at San Quentin, the Nichol sisters said the governor seemed surprised by their perspective, asking them about their personal paths toward death penalty opposition.
Jess Nichol said she didn’t always feel this way, but the more work she did with other crime survivors, the more she felt herself letting go of vengeance.

“I may still have feelings of anger, but it’s not where I’m primarily living,” Jess Nichol said. “I believe our process of healing becomes our process of discovering justice for ourselves. It’s not just something you can prescribe to somebody. We need to discover for ourselves what true justice is.”

washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/05/inf.headline: Infant bleeding surged last year as parents refuse vitamin K shot for newborns
washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/05/inf.author: Daniel Wu

paragraphs.text: Cases of infant bleeding surged last year as more parents refused critical vitamin K injections for their newborns, according to new research released Thursday in JAMA Pediatrics.

While the research does not point to a cause, scientists note some of the change comes during a time of growing skepticism around public health fueled partly in recent years by President Donald Trump’s administration.
Cases of vitamin K-deficient bleeding have increased most years since 2017 and spiked last year, according to the study.

“We’ve gone generations without seeing this kind of increase in complications,” said Steven Woolf, a professor of family medicine and population health at Virginia Commonwealth University and a co-author of the study. “It’s very disheartening to see that progress in public health rolling back.”

Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Grace Jamison said in a statement that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention “recommends that parents give newborns a vitamin K injection within 6 hours of birth to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding.”

The statement acknowledged that uptake of the dose has declined in recent years and that “public trust in health care institutions has fallen,” but blamed “heavy-handed mandates and inconsistent messaging during the Biden administration” amid the covid-19 pandemic.

Vitamin K helps the body form blood clots. Newborns don’t have enough of it at birth or receive enough from breastmilk, and their digestive systems are too immature to make it, said Elizabeth Wolf, an associate professor of pediatrics at Virginia Commonwealth University and lead author of the study.
Infants deficient in vitamin K are at risk of uncontrollable bleeding and strokes.

“Babies who have these vitamin K deficient strokes, 20 percent of them will die, and then of the survivors, 40 percent will have permanent neurologic problems,” Wolf said. “So it can be very, very serious.”

Yearly cases of vitamin K-deficient bleeding increased from 189 to 903 between 2017 and 2024, according to the study. Then last year, they nearly doubled. There were 1,764 cases of vitamin K-deficient bleeding in 2025. Of those cases, a majority of infants had not received vitamin K shots. A small percentage of the cases led to hemorrhages in the brain.

The study analyzed electronic health data of more than 11 million infants in the United States and also found that between 2017 and 2025, the percentage of infants receiving a vitamin K shot fell from 98 percent to 95 percent.

Researchers said the rise in cases of shot refusals and of bleeding incidents coincides with the growth of vaccine skepticism. At least in recent years, that has been further fueled by moves from the Trump administration to overhaul childhood vaccine schedules and an erosion of trust in public health guidance, they say.

“As scientists, we can’t prove causality,” Woolf said. “But 2025 was a year where we saw a real escalation by the administration in messaging that eroded public confidence in public health interventions.”
The vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, but doctors said some parents confuse it for one because it is given as an injection.

Skepticism toward the shots may have “ramped up since the covid vaccine came out,” said Howard Gill, chairman of the pediatrics department at Holy Cross Health in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, who was not involved in the study. “And it became more of a political conversation.”

A separate study also published Thursday in JAMA by researchers at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia also found increases in infant bleeding between 2017 and 2025. The study found that bleeding increased both in infants who received vitamin K shots and those who did not, but observed that infants not receiving vitamin K shots was associated with a significantly higher bleeding risk.

Kristan Scott, a neonatologist and assistant professor of pediatrics at Emory University School of Medicine and senior author of the study, wrote to The Washington Post that it is “difficult to pinpoint exactly why some parents are declining vitamin K.”
“Our findings underscore the importance of ensuring that parents, particularly those who may be hesitant about vitamin K, have access to accurate, evidence-based information,” Scott said.

Democratic lawmakers have accused Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has not publicly supported vitamin K shots, of exacerbating the trend. Rep. Kim Schrier (D-Washington) and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland) sent a letter to the CDC in June describing the shift as a “growing and preventable public health crisis” and calling on the agency to track refusals of vitamin K shots and vitamin K-deficient bleeding.
When asked by Schrier to support the shots in a House subcommittee meeting in April, Kennedy denied he was connected to the refusals and said “I’ve never said anything about vitamin K.”
HHS did not respond to questions about the letter to CDC or criticism of Kennedy.

Vitamin K can also be given orally, and some parents opt for this instead of an injection, Gill said. But it is not the standard treatment because it is considered less effective than an injection. Infants sometimes require multiple vitamin K doses if given orally.
Wolf and Woolf wrote in their study that offering vitamin K orally may nevertheless be warranted as a “harm-reduction approach” if parents continue to refuse injections.
“It’s a hard time to be a pediatrician right now,” Wolf said.
“Sometimes it’s difficult to convey … information to the family and have them trust you,” she said.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/05/u.headline: Stocks tumble, erasing post-midterm gains as markets weigh future of AI build-out
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/05/u.author: Miriam Waldvogel

paragraphs.text: Major U.S. stock indexes tumbled Thursday, largely erasing post-election gains made the day before, as markets continued to absorb the broad impact of Democrats’ nationwide midterm success.
By market close on Thursday, the S&P 500, a broad index of 500 large American companies, had lost around 4 percent. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index was down around 5.5 percent.
Major tech stocks also took hits Thursday amid analyst concerns that the blue wave would snag America’s rapid AI build-out, with voters pushing back against data centers and the tech industry.

Dozens of ballot measures placing local restrictions on data center development were passed across the country Tuesday. States that have been hubs of data center development, including Texas and Ohio, will have new governors who have promised to regulate the projects more tightly.
Ira Jersey, chief U.S. interest rates strategist for Bloomberg Intelligence, said that could have consequences for the U.S. economy.
“With large states where people want to put a lot of data centers, if that pace of investment slows, that means the economy is going to slow somewhat,” he told Bloomberg Radio on Thursday.
“The market is getting a little bit worried and skeptical that the Fed is going to be able to continue to hike [interest rates], because maybe we’re going to have a slowdown,” Jersey said.
Investors sold off across the market, with shares of the bank JPMorgan Chase and manufacturer Caterpillar also down.

Companies linked to President Donald Trump and his political allies sold off more sharply than the broader markets. Elon Musk’s SpaceX, a major government contractor, was down around 9 percent Thursday afternoon. Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates the online platform Truth Social, was down around 10.5 percent.

Chip stocks took significant losses, with AI juggernaut Nvidia falling around 9 percent, enough to erase its year-to-date gains. Micron, a leading memory chip manufacturer, was down around 17.5 percent. Shares of Advanced Micro Devices, which reported strong earnings Tuesday, also fell around 17 percent.

Diane Swonk, chief economist at accounting firm KPMG, said on social media that she was considering the possibility that financial markets were experiencing either temporary wobbles or the start of a significant and long-lasting slump due to a bubble in expectations for AI.
“I hope our base case holds & that this is just another temporary setback,” she wrote. “Hope for the best but prepare for all outcomes.”
correctionA previous version of this article misstated the timing of the market drops. They occurred Thursday, not Wednesday.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/05/ind.headline: Indiana executes first of three men scheduled to die Thursday across U.S.

paragraphs.text: Indiana prison officials early Thursday morning executed death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit, who was convicted of killing two children in a house fire.
In the lead-up to his execution, Weisheit’s attorneys had lobbied Gov. Mike Braun (R) to commute the man’s sentence to life in prison without parole. Braun denied the request.

Weisheit’s legal team also asked the governor to grant a reprieve and launch an independent investigation into the state’s lethal injection protocol and drug acquisition practices amid concerns that the state purchased $275,000 worth of pentobarbital from a troubled pharmacy being investigated by the state’s attorney general for potential misconduct and safety violations.
But the governor rejected that bid, too, and the Indiana Supreme Court in a 3-2 vote denied an emergency stay of execution late Wednesday night.
Weisheit’s execution was the first of three scheduled for Thursday across the U.S.

In Florida, Jesse Guardado, who pleaded guilty to a fatal stabbing, is scheduled to die by lethal injection at 6 p.m. Guardado was abused as a teenager at the Dozier School for Boys, a notoriously violent state-run reform school.

In Alabama, Michael Taylor is set to be put to death an hour after Guardado, at 6 p.m. local time. Death penalty opponents have said Taylor received ineffective counsel and too harsh a sentence for his age at the time of his crime. He was 19 when he robbed and killed an elderly couple he knew.

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/05/h.headline: How the Texas blue wave came crashing down on Republicans
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/05/h.author: Karen Tumulty, Matthew Choi, Molly Hennessy-Fiske

paragraphs.text: AUSTIN — For three decades, Texas has been the white whale of Democratic politics — the most elusive of trophies, tantalizingly out of reach.

Not since 1994, before more than 40 percent of living Texans were born, had Democrats won a single statewide office. But on Tuesday, the party so long out of power swept every one of those races and flipped one chamber of the legislature in an epic feat with few if any parallels in modern politics.

“Texas is blue. That is a hard sentence to utter,” Sen. Ted Cruz — a likely 2028 presidential contender, who was not on Texas ballots this year — said on his podcast Wednesday. “As we sit here today, I am the only statewide elected Republican who remains in Texas. That’s not something I ever thought I would say.”

The tectonic shift that rattled Texas has far-reaching implications. Arguably the most influential conservative stronghold, Texas policies have rippled across the nation in recent years — from a program that bused migrants into Democratic cities, to a restrictive abortion law that put pressure on providers in other states, to a suite of legal challenges that bogged down the Biden administration. Many of its right-wing initiatives were copied by red-state governments nationwide. And its oil and tech billionaires have funded conservative campaigns and causes around the country, earning it the nickname “The Texas ATM.”
All of that seems about to change.

The durability of Democrats’ incoming government does remain in question. Texas voters are angry and impatient, yet still broadly conservative. Should Democrats overreach, they risk backlash from a Republican base already primed by the GOP’s incendiary rhetoric on social and cultural issues.

For now, however, at least some Republicans are willing to give them a chance. Kathy Montgomery, 78, a conservative Catholic, said she split her ticket and voted for the Democratic candidate for Senate on moral grounds and to address skyrocketing housing costs. Montgomery hopes that in the wake of perhaps the most divisive statewide election in modern history, Texans can work together to improve the place they love.
“You have to let go of prejudices, some of what you grew up with, and let people into your heart,” she said. “We’re not always going to see eye to eye, but give them room to be who they are.”

Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has promised to address issues Democratic and Republican voters both cited as being priorities, including investing heavily in public schools and pausing data center development. But Democrats will still face major structural challenges in governing for the first time in decades, from the balkiness of a Republican-controlled Senate to the sheer lack of Democratic muscle memory when it comes to operating the machinery of government.

“The good news is because of how badly Republicans have governed, there are so many quick victories in front of them: raising the minimum wage, expanding Medicaid, funding local schools,” said former congressman Beto O’Rourke, whose near miss in his 2018 Senate race against Cruz awakened his party to the possibility of resurrection. “If people earn more, can see a doctor and their kids are going to better schools, they will richly reward Democrats.”

At the outset of this campaign season, none of what happened in Texas’s statewide races seemed imaginable, much less inevitable, to most seasoned partisans on either side. Sen. John Cornyn and Gov. Greg Abbott, two fixtures with proven bipartisan appeal, were expected to lead the ballot. Democrats had also performed poorly in 2024, with the party’s performance decreasing in the presidential race that year for the first time since 2012.

The GOP Senate primary left Democrats elated, however — they learned they would face an opponent loaded down with years of baggage. Four-term incumbent Cornyn lost to scandal-scarred Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was carried to a landslide victory by an endorsement from President Donald Trump. The Republican legislature had impeached Paxton in 2023 for bribery and corruption, and his wife, a state senator, is divorcing him for what she said were “biblical grounds.”
“Ken Paxton is probably the worst major-party candidate in my lifetime, and I’m old,” said Matt Angle, a longtime Democratic operative whose work in Texas politics dates to the 1980s.

Democrats, meanwhile, elevated a candidate widely seen as giving them their best shot at being competitive: fresh-faced state Rep. James Talarico, a scripture-quoting Presbyterian seminary graduate with an uplifting, unifying message that brought national attention, scads of campaign contributions and the potential for GOP crossover votes.

If Talarico created a jet stream for other Democrats on the ballot, Republicans, led by Trump, were responsible for the undertow that dragged their side down. In races across the state, voters cited rising prices — brought on by Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran — as pushing them toward Democrats. And Trump’s immigration policies upended House races in districts state Republicans had gerrymandered to try to ensure victory.

In the Rio Grande Valley, where voters drifted toward Trump in 2024, Hispanic turnout surged, in part because of alarm over immigration sweeps that caught up hardworking, law-abiding people. Starr County, near the bottom tip of the state, where Latinos are close to 100 percent of the population, saw a 72-point stampede toward Democrats from two years ago, the nation’s largest margin shift.
Yet as sudden as it may have seemed, the Democrats’ victory was years in the making.

“Texas didn’t move away from Democrats overnight. Democrats aren’t going to win it overnight,” Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder said the weekend before Election Day, measuring his optimism against a history of losses.
One problem the party needed to correct: Even its best performances in the past had been conducted in a vacuum.

Coming off the near-wins of 2018, when O’Rourke came within three percentage points of defeating Cruz, state Democrats quietly began building infrastructure to topple Republicans’ monopoly on state power.

Although O’Rourke memorably visited all 254 Texas counties, reaching out to even the most ruby-red parts of the state, his operation was largely self-contained. Republicans, meanwhile, deployed their army of state lawmakers as surrogates to rally to Cruz’s defense.

Coming out of the 2024 losses, Democratic strategists gathered to create a slate of credible candidates who could run in even the most deeply Republican parts of Texas. O’Rourke, former gubernatorial candidate Wendy Davis, 2024 Senate nominee Colin Allred and other Democrats well known in the state, as well as the Texas Majority PAC (which backs Texas Democratic campaigns), began aggressive recruitment — and were able to put up contenders for every state and federal office.

Then, for the first time in over 40 years, candidates across the state operated in a coordinated campaign, pooling resources and hitting every corner of Texas. The party trained more than 1,000 precinct chairs spread out across rural areas.

“In order to win statewide, we need to lose by less in some of these areas. And in order to lose by less, we need to really legitimately campaign,” said Katherine Fischer, executive director of Texas Majority PAC and an alumna of the O’Rourke campaign. “Even a candidate like James, who’s so well resourced, can’t spend enough money to invest in 200 rural counties to really make a dent.”

Texas has the highest Black population of any state. And U.S. Rep. Christian Menefee of Houston, as he campaigned with Talarico in downtown Houston this past weekend at some of the city’s historically Black churches, said the party also made a concerted effort to reach out to Black voters.

“Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico have been out in the Black communities, and people have been really appreciative,” Menefee said, adding, “They are talking to everybody. And the Republicans are not doing that.”

Going forward, Fischer said the plan is to build up the party’s presence even in deep-red parts of the state, to help secure its wins in future races even without the gift of flawed candidates on the Republican side.

Angle, the Democratic operative, believes Republicans in the state will continue to struggle to find candidates with crossover appeal. GOP primaries have increasingly resembled MAGA purification rites that elevate darlings from the furthest-right reaches of the party, many of them backed by Trump. This has led to the rise of candidates like Paxton, who struggle in a general election, and Angle said the trend has no signs of stopping.
“The notion of a buttoned-down, normal business conservative, normal conservative Republican Party — just the notion of it is nostalgia,” Angle said. “That’s gone.”

At the same time, Democrats say they are aware of the impatience of voters who elected them for tangible results, as well as the limitations imposed by the Texas Senate, which still has a Republican majority.

Once the state legislature returns in January, Menefee expects Democrats to move quickly, and for the agenda to include “transformative” proposals to expand affordable health care and perhaps raise the minimum wage, with far less time spent on culture war issues.
State Rep. Gene Wu of Houston, who leads the House Democratic Caucus, agreed.
“What the public is mad about is finally in line with what Democrats are mad about,” Wu said, adding that while Texas Republicans “want to talk about drag queens, we’re going to talk about jobs.”
Now, Wu said, “we can stop being the laughingstock of the nation.” Or, put another way: The eyes of Texas are upon Democrats, and they hope they can deliver.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/05/dem.headline: In Democrats’ wins, some see a new era for the ‘religious left’
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/05/dem.author: Michelle Boorstein

paragraphs.text: Is the “religious left” back?

The election of five new Democrats to Congress on Tuesday who are clergy or seminarians, along with wins for other Democrats who talked often of their faith on the trail, has some watchers of religion and politics saying the midterms represent a historic shift.

After decades of focus on the rise of conservative Christians, these observers see victories by left-leaning candidates including Sens.-elect James Talarico of Texas (a Presbyterian seminarian) and Adam Hamilton of Kansas (a United Methodist mega-church pastor) as proof that the national narrative of religion and politics is being upended.

“The Christian left is here” was the headline Wednesday of a religion and politics story in Vox. Amy Sullivan, author of a popular 2008 book positing that Democrats were closing the “God gap,” posted on Facebook that she was taking a “victory lap. ... Democrats have leveled the praying field.”

But others who study religion and politics say this election, which included the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, was about the economy and the entire country moving left – not a sign of the Democratic Party becoming more overtly religious.

“It’s like Lucy with the football; every year it’s like ‘This is the year the religious left is coming back.’ No they’re not. To be religious in America is to be conservative,” said Washington University of St. Louis political scientist and religion statistician Ryan Burge, noting that the pattern applies to White Americans, not voters of color.

In Tuesday’s election, the largest “religious” group of voters were people with no religious affiliation – at 27 percent of the total. Seventy-eight percent of them voted Democratic on Tuesday, NBC News found.

Burge said he did see anecdotal signs that Americans were fed up with what they see as a lack of decency in politics, particularly from President Donald Trump and his MAGA movement. “It’s not a Christian morality. It’s called ‘civil religion’ —what we’ll allow and what we won’t.”

Northwestern University religious studies professor Robert Orsi said Talarico’s victory in particular signals the return of a “liberal Christianity” that was “the driving force behind the most important movements for social justice in U.S. history.”

Liberal Christianity has been “by its own choice in a position of resistance” in recent decades rather than in a cooperative dynamic with government, Orsi wrote in an email. Talarico, he added, is changing that.
Talking daily about faith
Talarico, a former middle school teacher who became a seminarian while serving in the Texas House, is the first Democratic senator-elect in 40 years from Texas, a stronghold of the religious right.

He won by talking daily about Scripture, his understanding of Christianity’s public obligations and how he sees Christian nationalism as heretical. He had a Sunday school teacher affect on podcasts and at rallies, describing his progressive Christianity, which he sees as focused on bringing up the downtrodden and disenfranchised and loving one’s neighbor.

“My faith teaches me that love is the strongest force in the universe,” he told supporters Tuesday night in Austin. “Love requires that we stand between the bullies and the bullied. Love requires that we look evil in the eye and not blink.”
Of Jesus, he said: “when the people at the top hurt his neighbors, that barefoot rabbi didn’t stay in his room and pray.” He “walked into the seat of power and flipped over the tables of injustice.”
High-visibility Islam
By becoming the first Muslim elected to the Senate, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed brings new prominence to an expression of Islam that is both observant and progressive.

El-Sayed was one of at least three Muslim Democrats to win seats in Congress on Tuesday, joining four incumbents — also Democrats — for a historic total of seven. (California Democrat Aisha Wahab, who was elected to Congress in an August special election, is leading in her race for a full term, which has not been called yet. She would bring the total number of Muslim lawmakers in Congress to eight.)

Along with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, these Muslim politicians are raising public awareness of their faith at a time of increasing anti-Muslim rhetoric and vitriol from parts of the Republican Party.

“American Muslims are no longer waiting for a seat at the table,” read the subject line of a Wednesday email from the advocacy group Muslim Public Affairs Council. The group also said Muslims seeking public office this year “were subjected to baseless accusations of extremism, attacks on their faith and patriotism, and efforts to portray their political participation as a threat.”

El-Sayed, a doctor and public health leader, spoke regularly during the campaign and in his victory speech about his faith — including stories about his Egyptian grandmother or the way the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks forced him to become more fluent about his religion.

“Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say ‘Inshallah’ or ‘God willing’ whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned,” he told his victory party Tuesday. “But today, tonight, we can turn that ‘Inshallah’ into a ‘Alhamdulillah!’” The latter phrase is Arabic for “Praise be to God.”

Attacks and polling during the campaign reflected some Americans’ skepticism and bias involving Islam. A Washington Post-Schar School poll released in September found that 45 percent of likely Michigan voters said they would not consider voting for a Muslim presidential candidate.
El-Sayed received 52.5 percent of the vote, according to preliminary returns, compared with 45.5 percent for his main opponent.

In a recent interview with “60 Minutes,” El-Sayed emphasized how he sees religious freedom operating in the United States. He cited instruction by the prophet Muhammad, Islam’s founder, to be charitable to neighbors, which he interpreted as a responsibility to the people around you and fighting to protect their rights.

Muslims in the U.S. are very diverse religiously and politically. For U.S. House races in Tuesday’s election, 62 percent voted Democratic and 35 percent voted Republican, according to a NORC poll. Still, El-Sayed was asked by “60 Minutes” if he sees tension between his faith and the more socially liberal positions of his party.
“I’m a constitutionalist, and I think rights are rights. The minute you assent to government taking anyone’s rights, you are assenting to the government taking everybody’s rights,” El-Sayed said.

He added that he tells both Muslims and LGBTQ+ advocates: “‘I don’t care whether you will ever use a right you’re fighting for. ... Whether it’s the right to put your face on the ground 34 times a day in a mosque or ... your right to love who you love.’”

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Supreme Court to Hear Goldman Sachs’ Bankruptcy Arbitration Bid
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Angélica Serrano-Román

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg Law) -- The US Supreme Court agreed to review a request by Goldman Sachs on whether bankruptcy courts can override arbitration agreements, setting up a high-stakes test of the Federal Arbitration Act's reach.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The court on Friday approved the multinational investment bank's request that the high court clarify whether, and under what circumstances, a bankruptcy court can refuse to enforce an arbitration agreement for claims under Section 362(k) of US Bankruptcy Code if a creditor violates the automatic litigation stay protecting bankrupt people and companies.
Goldman Sachs said that because Section 362(k) issues arise frequently in bankruptcy, a circuit split on this issue reflected lower-court confusion about the FAA's intersection with bankruptcy law.

Goldman Sachs lost a bid in the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit to compel arbitration in a suit alleging it violated bankruptcy law by continuing debt collection efforts despite the stay. The majority of the three-judge Fourth Circuit panel found that arbitration inherently conflicts with the core purposes of the bankruptcy code. Judge Robert B. King, in a dissent, found that the debtors' claims belong in arbitration.

The FAA creates a national policy favoring arbitration when parties have agreed to it. But bankruptcy law is designed to provide a collective, centralized resolution of a debtor's financial affairs. Courts are generally divided over the use of a test that considers whether issues are "core" or "non-core" and whether arbitration creates an inherent conflict.

The Supreme Court hasn't tested the tension between the two statutory schemes. The debtors in this lawsuit, two holders of Apple Card accounts issued by Goldman Sachs, argued the Supreme Court shouldn't take the case because its specific facts — involving a Chapter 13 stay — make it an unsuitable fit to properly resolve the broader legal question.
The American Bankers Association filed an amicus brief in support of Goldman Sachs.
Latham & Watkins LLP represents Goldman Sachs. Kellett & Bartholow PLLC and Giles & Lambert PC represent the consumer borrowers.
The case is Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, U.S., No. 25-1408, cert denied/granted 11/6/26.
To contact the reporter on this story: Angélica Serrano-Román in Washington at aserrano-roman@bloombergindustry.com

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Fed’s Daly Says More Rate Increases Likely Needed to Tame Prices
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Catarina Saraiva

paragraphs.text: Fri, November 6, 2026 at 12:24 PM CST 1 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco President Mary Daly said more interest rate increases are likely to be needed to tame inflation, but she said it was too soon to know how much higher rates will need to go.
Most Read from Bloomberg

"My expectation is we're going to have to tighten policy further," Daly said Friday in an interview on CNBC. "Exactly when and how much is still to be decided because we just have to take all the variables that are coming in."

Daly said she supported the decision last week to hold the Fed's benchmark rate steady amid uncertainty about the economy, and that she also backed the decision to raise interest rates in September for the first time since 2023. While two policymakers dissented from the decision to hold rates last month because they preferred to raise them instead, several officials have expressed support for moving them up gradually.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Walleye to Return $2 Billion to Clients in Stocks Trading Reset
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Nishant Kumar

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Walleye Capital plans to return about $2 billion to clients following its decision to cut back on equities trading.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The firm plans to shrink its hedge fund assets to about $10 billion, roughly the same level it started the year with, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. Walleye's separately managed accounts business Dockside will continue to run an additional $5 billion in assets, the person said, asking not to be identified because the details are private.
A representative for Walleye declined to comment.

The multistrategy hedge fund, which has about $17 billion in total assets, told clients on Nov. 5 it was returning a portion of its cash in a bid to revamp its internal equities business. Anil Gondi, the firm's head of equities, was let let go along with a "substantial" portion of the equities teams as part of the decision, Bloomberg reported.

Walleye finds itself competing in a hedge fund world dominated by industry giants from Millennium Management to Citadel that have attracted unprecedented investor interest and used that firepower to wage an expensive war for talent. Ten large multistrats tracked by research firm PivotalPath oversaw a total of $2.2 trillion in assets, including borrowed money, at the end of 2025, more than triple the amount in 2018.
With most of the largest firms now closed to new cash, challengers such as Walleye have grown too. The firm's assets have grown from about $4 billion at the end of 2023.

The firm is "going to lean into the businesses where we have a proven and differentiated right to win, including our Volatility, Quant and external businesses," Walleye's Chief Investment Officer Will England wrote in a letter to clients seen by Bloomberg.

He said while Walleye is not exiting equity long/short trading, its "competitive advantage" is not in trying to replicate the traditional multi-manager stocks trading model. The firm will continue the strategy through its external manager allocations as well as backing some of its "highest conviction" internal stock pickers.
Mike Scheer, a former Jain Global portfolio manager specializing in stock picking that the firm has hired, is joining to work directly for England, the person added.
Walleye lost 5.9% in October, bringing the total decline for this year through last month to 6.8%.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Microsoft Is Winding Down Oracle Deal to Rent AI Cloud Capacity
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Brody Ford

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Microsoft Corp. is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle Corp., part of a larger reassessment of billions of dollars in cloud partnerships.
Most Read from Bloomberg
In recent months, Microsoft has been turning off rented computing capacity from Oracle after declining to renew the contract, according to people familiar with the matter.

Over time, the computing Microsoft was renting became less useful because it no longer fit the company's specifications, said the people, who requested anonymity to discuss a private matter. The Oracle hardware used older-generation Nvidia Corp. chips, the people said.

An Oracle spokesperson said demand for the company's AI infrastructure remains strong, including for earlier-generation graphics processing units. Oracle said in September that it was renewing contracts for four-year-old GPUs at a 20% premium to the original deal price.
Microsoft declined to comment.

Under the arrangement, announced in 2023, Oracle agreed to sell Microsoft access to servers that would power a new AI-assisted version of the Bing search engine. The full size of the deal couldn't be determined.
The fact that Microsoft was prepared to rent servers from a major rival was seen as an early indication of the massive shortage of processing power that has come to define the AI era.

The world's largest software maker helped usher in a "neocloud" boom by signing massive contracts with upstart cloud businesses like CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius. In all, Microsoft committed more than $80 billion to rent capacity from other cloud companies to bolster its own AI efforts.

But Microsoft has been re-thinking its strategy. Key leaders at the company have grown frustrated with the neocloud providers over high costs and delays. In recent months, the company has tightened oversight of data center projects, stepped away from ones it deems risky and debated internally whether to ink new neocloud deals, Bloomberg previously reported.

Oracle's cloud businesses has expanded rapidly since 2023, fueled by big AI contracts with companies like OpenAI and Meta Platforms Inc. For the year that ended in May 2026, Oracle's cloud business posted $18 billion in revenue.

With Oracle developing data centers and expanding its cloud business, the company was initially seen as a major beneficiary of the AI boom. But investors have recently become concerned about heavy capital spending that has turned Oracle's free cash flow negative. The shares have lost more than half their value since hitting a high this year of $248.15 on June 1.
