npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6030645/mississ.headline: No one knows how many ballots are outstanding in Mississippi's Senate race
npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6030645/mississ.author: Miles Parks

paragraphs.text: In Mississippi's too-close-to-call U.S. Senate race, every ballot matters.
But no one can say for sure how many ballots there are left to count.

The razor-thin margin between incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom is shining a light on an election process in Mississippi that is among the slowest and most decentralized in the country.
"Mississippi is not a model of election administration," said Michael Morse, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania who studies voting.
As of midday Friday, fewer than 2,000 votes separated the two Senate candidates. But information about exactly how many ballots were outstanding was hard to come by.

The Colom campaign said late Tuesday it was aware of more than 15,000 provisional ballots, which require verification before they're counted. And the chair of the state Republican Party said Thursday he thought there were 20,000 outstanding ballots, including potential absentee votes that can legally be received by officials until Nov. 10 if they were postmarked by Election Day.

Mississippi's top voting official, Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson, said counties run their own elections, and even his office didn't know how many provisionals were left to count. He said Thursday nearly 7,000 of them had been processed, with "roughly 80% of them being accepted."

"Until we have the certified results, the individual counties will be the best source of the latest and most up-to-date information," Watson said in a statement. There are 82 counties in Mississippi, and they are not required to transmit election results to the state until next week.
Morse said he was shocked by the lack of good information available for such a high-profile race.
"Right now I would love to know a lot of things about the process and I am struggling to figure out what is unfolding here," Morse said. "I cannot tell you basic things."
Mississippi has a relatively high rate of provisional ballots

What is becoming clear is that the rate of provisional ballots, which are called affidavit ballots in Mississippi, may end up being among the highest in the country this election cycle. Those ballots are cast by people whose eligibility is questionable, according to local officials, so those votes are segregated and officials decide on a case-by-case basis whether they will be counted.
If the Colom campaign's estimate of 15,000 affidavit ballots holds true, that would represent roughly 1.5% of the total ballots cast in the Senate race, according to unofficial results.

In the last midterm year, 2022, just four states had a provisional ballot rate higher than that, according to federal data. And Mississippi looks to have a provisional rate close to double of that in North Carolina this year, based on the preliminary data in both states.
One potential reason is an in-the-weeds detail on how Mississippi does voter registration.

In most states, when voters don't cast ballots over a certain number of election cycles, or local officials come across data that indicates a voter has moved or is ineligible for some other reason, they move that voter to what's known as "inactive" status. But the voter is still able to vote normally for a period of a few years, mandated by federal law, before they either confirm their eligibility or are eventually removed.

Mississippi is one of the few states that makes those "inactive" voters have to vote provisionally. That means those voters need to fill out another form and their information needs to be reviewed after the fact by local officials before their votes are counted.

It's unclear at this point why so many voters had questionable eligibility when they showed up to vote, although the local outlet Mississippi Today has reported extensively on the state's experimental use of credit data to cull voter lists.
Morse said that list maintenance technique is garnering attention, but it's not the whole story.

"It's pairing the experiment with credit data, which could introduce some unreliability, with an undermining of the typical procedural process [in many other states], where a voter [marked "inactive"] could cast a regular ballot for at least the next two federal general elections," Morse said.
Watson, the Republican secretary of state, has already come out in defense of the state's registration process.
"The extra few minutes it may take to vote via affidavit ballot are well worth the election integrity added by having cleaner voter rolls!" Watson wrote Tuesday in a post on X.

But Kathy Boockvar, the former Democratic secretary of state of Pennsylvania, told NPR that while many people who have to vote with a provisional ballot are likely to be ultimately deemed eligible, the process doesn't breed trust from those who have to interact with it.

"It feels like you have to go talk to the teacher or something in the back room," Boockvar said. "It's a little bit of a suspicious-seeming thing because somebody who's going through it generally thinks that they're eligible to vote and feels like they're being asked to do something other than that."
Boockvar added that the fact that information has been so hard to come by is a sign Mississippi hasn't been in the limelight like traditional battleground states before.
"We all have to be prepared whether we expect it or not," Boockvar said. "Transparency and good data is one of the best solutions we have to combating all the suspicion and distrust."

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/robert-garcia-trump-.headline: Top House Oversight Democrat warns Trump family to 'lawyer up'
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/robert-garcia-trump-.author: Luke Fountain

paragraphs.text: Rep. Robert Garcia, the California Democrat poised to lead the powerful House Oversight Committee, doubled down on his warning to President Donald Trump and his allies Friday, releasing a video promising sweeping investigations into the administration.
"Oversight Democrats are ready to take on the crooks, the con men and the Trump crime family. Lawyer up," the California Democrat wrote on X.

"The American people have spoken, and they are tired of the unprecedented level of corruption coming out of this White House and under President Trump," Garcia said in the video, which ends with the words "LAWYER UP" splashed across the screen.

The warning comes three days after Democrats' sweeping midterm victories handed them control of the House. When the new Congress convenes in January, Democrats will gain control of the committee's subpoena power, allowing them to compel testimony and obtain documents in investigations that could target Trump, his family and his allies.

Garcia said the committee would investigate what he described as potential corruption involving the Trump family's business dealings, cryptocurrency ventures and Pentagon contracts, as well as alleged abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He also vowed to scrutinize individuals he said were connected to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
"Oversight Democrats are absolutely going to ensure that we investigate every single one of these instances," Garcia said. "Now let's get to work."
Garcia's approach may conflict with what some advisors are telling Democrats — to go after corporate interests rather than Trump and his family.
Garcia, currently the committee's top Democrat, formally launched his bid to become chairman Thursday. He is widely expected to secure the position.

The White House has dismissed Democrats' planned investigations as politically motivated, setting up a potentially contentious showdown between the Trump administration and the incoming Democratic congressional majority.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

persuasion.community/p/civilization-is-a.headline: Civilization Is About Settling for Second-Best
persuasion.community/p/civilization-is-a.author: Joseph Heath

paragraphs.text: During the brief period in which corporations thought it would be a good idea to indulge the political sensibilities of their junior employees, it became fashionable to adopt “mission statements” that expressed the supposedly higher purpose sought by the firm in its branches and divisions. This attracted a certain measure of ridicule, such as the case of Hellmann’s mayonnaise, which decided that its real purpose was not to produce mayonnaise, but rather to “reduce food waste” by transforming leftovers into “delicious meals.” The obvious objection to this, expressed in The Wall Street Journal and elsewhere, was the tacit assumption that the product itself could not be the purpose. This appeared to concede the essentially anti-capitalist idea that there was something unworthy or grubby about just making mayonnaise and selling it to people, which then created the need to identify a “higher,” non-pecuniary purpose in order to edify the entire operation.

The mayonnaise mission statement became the object of public controversy when a major shareholder in Unilever (the parent corporation) complained that “a company which feels it has to define the purpose of Hellmann’s mayonnaise has in our view clearly lost the plot.” I found this a bit uncharitable, since it’s not difficult to imagine why the company would have thought the mission statement to be not only good PR, but also good HR. For most people, sitting around at work every day thinking “I’m here to make money for Unilever” is less intrinsically motivating than “I’m on a mission to reduce food waste.”

I think about this episode sometimes as I’m driving to work. Technically, my job is to teach courses in philosophy. Students pay tuition, the university pays me, everyone goes home happy. The product is the purpose. No one thanks me, that’s what the money is for. I am, however, sometimes tempted by the idea that my work might have a loftier objective. Pressed to put it in the form of a mission statement, I might go with something like this: “reproducing the foundations of Western civilization, one lecture at a time.” Like the junior employees at Unilever, I find this more elevated statement of my task to be a greater source of motivation.

Of course, as in the case of mayonnaise, some people might find my mission statement a bit too lofty. In my defense, I should note that I don’t see myself making any particular contribution to human civilization or improving it in a noticeable way. I gave up on that a long time ago. Now I’m just trying to do my part to keep the show on the road, to discourage people from throwing away the stuff that works. Unfortunately, this leads to a natural follow-up question, which is why anyone would think that the reproduction of civilization requires help from the likes of me. That is something I also think about while driving to work, so here is my best response.
Allow me to kick things off with an observation made by Pierre Manent in his very interesting history of liberalism:

A singular feature of the present historical situation is that political thought and political life are, in modern times, intimately linked. This is something new. The political history of Greece or Rome can be related without referring to “ideas” or “doctrines.” In his work on the Peloponnesian War, Thucydides does not devote a single page to what we would call the “intellectual” or “cultural” life of the period … This fact is all the more remarkable since Greece was the birthplace of philosophy, and in particular of political philosophy. It was from the experience of life in the Greek city-state that Plato and Aristotle elaborated their interpretations of human life, which constitute the matrix of all subsequent philosophy. But these interpretations emerged after the great cycle of Greek politics occurred. The case of modern political philosophy is completely different. One is tempted to say that it was conceived and chosen before being implemented.

There are two points that I would add to this. First, because the ideas preceded their institutional realization, the reproduction of these institutions also requires the reproduction of the ideas. A generalized loss of conviction in our inherited principles of political philosophy would constitute a functional challenge to our institutions. Second, the ideas are unobvious; they do not coincide with anyone’s untutored intuitions. As a result, they must be explained to each new generation in order to carry any persuasive force. This has two enormous consequences. Sociologically, it means that the formal education system becomes an essential component of the core institutional structure of our society. Culturally, it means that cognitive elites become essential social actors, since they are the ones who do the explaining. (This has certain unfortunate byproduct effects, with perhaps the most important being that those who do not make it very far in the formal education system wind up being more or less out of the loop when it comes to the reproduction of civilization.)

What makes the reproduction of these ideas challenging is that the two sets of governing principles in our society—liberalism for the state and capitalism for the economy—are second-best arrangements. In other words, they do not coincide with most people’s sense of what an ideal world would look like. (Just to be clear, they are not second-best in the real-world sense. In the real world, they are the best that we can hope to attain, at least for the foreseeable future. The problem is that they are second-best with respect to most people’s personal values and moral ideals. They are not à la hauteur de nos espérances. This is why people got so annoyed at Francis Fukuyama for declaring the end of history. As Andrew Potter put it, “The suggestion that the endpoint of human development, the culmination of the ancient struggle for recognition, amounts to little more than the admixture of the Bill of Rights and Best Buy does not fill everyone’s heart with joy.”)

We have names for the first-best arrangements—those that most people come into the world wanting and wondering why we cannot obtain. In the domain of politics, the ideal is normally some form of communitarianism. People want to live in culturally rich communities with shared values and a dense network of high-trust social relations. In the economic realm, the ideal that corresponds to our everyday moral intuitions is socialism. Since the division of labor that characterizes our economic life is, fundamentally, a system of cooperation, it seems only natural that it should be governed by norms that directly enjoin cooperative behavior. We should all pitch in and do our part, selflessly devoting ourselves to the larger social project, sharing equally in the benefits.

And yet looking at the world we live in, what stands out most prominently are institutional arrangements that not only fail to promote these ideals, but in certain ways block their realization. In the political realm, we have a system of individual rights that recruits the power of the state to provide legal protection for self-evidently anti-social or self-destructive behavior. So we wind up living in a world of 4chan memes, Twitter Nazis, Russian trolls, Instagram thirst traps, mail-order drugs, etc. In the economic realm, instead of promoting cooperation, we instead strive to instill competition, creating winners and losers out of what should be a system of mutual benefit. And so we get a world marred by extreme inequality, environmental destruction, renegade billionaires, precarity for the young, etc.

When confronted by this spectacle, it is extremely natural to suspect that the profusion of anti-social behavior is elicited, to at least a large degree, by the legal protection that it is offered by our institutions. This leads many people to wonder why, instead of following this path, we do not use the power of the state to promote shared values or shared cooperative endeavors. Again, this is a perfectly natural thought. It is why, historically, the first pass at producing a political philosophy—whether it be in Plato or Confucius—came back with the same idea, that the law should be used to enforce morality and promote social cohesion, by rewarding the virtuous and punishing the wicked.

latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-06/tr.headline: Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles

paragraphs.text: President Trump on Friday announced his appointment of Stephen Miller as his chief of staff, to replace Susie Wiles.
Miller, the current deputy chief of staff, has helped design Trump’s immigration policies and spearhead his mass deportation campaign.

His appointment as chief of staff, a powerful position for driving the president’s policy agenda, managing his staff and twisting the arms of allies and opponents alike to bend to the executive’s will, ends speculation that Trump might ease back from his less popular policies or moderate following devastating losses for his party in the midterms. The losses were driven in part to losing Latino voters and many congressional seats along the southern border.
Miller is widely seen as among Trump’s more extreme advisors. But Trump on Friday called Miller one of his “most trusted advisors,” and said he would take over as chief of staff Monday.
Trump said Wiles “has done an outstanding job,” and will be moving to his political operation.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/06/for.headline: Former White House health aide accuses Trump advisers of catering to special interests
washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/06/for.author: Rachel Roubein

paragraphs.text: Calley Means, a former Trump White House adviser who quit last month, accused top administration aides and strategists of catering to special interests, and recommended that the president “clears house” in an extensive interview with podcast host Joe Rogan released Friday.

Means, who also served as a top aide of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., recounted for more than two hours his time inside the administration, frequently naming aides that he alleged blocked or hindered progress on policies popular within the Make America Healthy Again movement. Means quit his job roughly two weeks ago amid White House delays in enacting some of the food policies he and other top health officials had been seeking.

The interview comes as Democrats had a sweeping electoral victory this week, prompting Republican finger-pointing over the causes of the wipeout. Means claims the architects of Trump’s midterm strategy were “obsessed with redistricting” ahead of the November elections.

Several of Means’s allegations centered on some top Trump aides and allies, including Susie Wiles, his chief of staff, and Tony Fabrizio, Trump’s chief pollster. At one point, he claimed that Wiles blocked one of the health department’s food initiatives out of fear it would hurt political donations from the sugar industry. On Friday, after the podcast was released, Trump announced that Wiles would be replaced as chief of staff by his longtime aide Stephen Miller. Fabrizio did not provide comment.
“It is absolutely true that his administration has been infiltrated by the very people that he energized voters to say he would get out of D.C.,” Means said.

Later in the podcast, he said, “I think President Trump can save this presidency, can change staff, and get back on more of an America First fighting position against the swamp and get a lot done, and maybe even get some things done with Democrats.”
In a statement, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said “the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again.”

“The Administration has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming,” she said. “President Trump and Secretary Kennedy continue to work around the clock to deliver more wins for the American people.”
Some White House officials have countered that Wiles is a MAHA champion, and some of Means’s claims could not immediately be independently verified.

Means claimed that Trump is not fully aware of some of the decisions made by his top staff because he “can’t be everywhere at once,” saying that Trump asked “how the hell did this happen” after the Supreme Court restricted a massive wave of lawsuits against a major pesticide manufacturer. The administration supported the pesticide maker in the case, a switch from the Biden administration.
Means’s criticism of the administration comes as several policy priorities of the MAHA movement — which was born out of the political alignment between Trump and Kennedy — have stalled.

The MAHA movement is composed of multiple and, at times, competing factions, including ones pushing for healthier food, major changes to vaccines and less pesticide use. While at the White House and health department, Means pushed aggressively for MAHA policies, particularly related to food. This includes efforts to get food companies to drop synthetic dyes, changes to the dietary guidelines and advocating for states to adopt rules barring soda and candy from the nation’s food stamps program.

In the podcast interview, Means lamented a lack of midterm messaging around issues central to the MAHA movement, as polling has shown the majority of Americans agree there is insufficient regulation of chemical additives in food and pesticides used to grow crops.
Health and Human Services spokeswoman Emily Hilliard previously pushed back on the notion that Kennedy’s MAHA food agenda has been “stalled or slow walked.”

In his talk with Rogan, Means paints a portrait of White House staff who, at times, sidelined Kennedy and the policies his supporters are pushing. He claimed there was “tremendous energy to diminish [Kennedy’s] impact on the election.”

Democrats and medical experts have hammered some of the policies Kennedy, the founder of a prominent anti-vaccine group, have pursued, such as a sweeping reduction of the childhood vaccine schedule. Shortly after the election, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland) wrote on social media that “RFK Jr. must resign or be fired,” while prominent MAHA leaders argue the party should not seek to oust the nation’s top health official.
Throughout Rogan’s podcast, Means described his account of how key policies were crafted. He contended that Wiles has a “stranglehold” on such decisions.

MAHA activists have particularly been frustrated over the Trump administration’s handling of glyphosate, a widely used weed killer they say contributes to childhood health problems. Kennedy has previously called the herbicide “one of the likely culprits in America’s chronic disease epidemic” and was part of a team that won a $289 million judgment against chemical manufacturer Monsanto, which Bayer acquired in 2018, over claims the weed killer caused cancer.

Means alleges that Kennedy was not consulted on several major administration policies on glyphosate. In one such instance, Means recalled being told to review an executive order to boost production of glyphosate, and says he called the directive a “political disaster.” White House staff, including Wiles, made clear the issue was “not up for discussion,” Means said.
Means says he decided to leave the administration due to a White House delay in releasing the definition of ultra-processed foods and a new school lunch meal.

He also accused Wiles of blocking an initiative aimed at determining the safety of certain ingredients common in ultra-processed foods. The federal health department had been poised earlier this year to conclude that food companies should produce “any detailed safety studies” related to certain ingredients, The Post previously reported.

On immunizations, Means said that Trump advisers had urged Kennedy to avoid talking about vaccines ahead of the midterms. But, he said, Trump “wanted to go hard on investigating vaccines,” and removed the block.

“When President Trump heard about an issue, his inclination was right,” Means said. “And the people around him, I think, treat him horribly. They talk about him like a baby. They say it’s because ‘we’re the political experts.’”

As the Trump administration grapples with election’s fallout, Means argued that a future president should work to get corporate money out of politics. In the meantime, Trump should “go to war with Congress,” as well as meet with some of the progressive senators.

“I think the best chance the president has to get things done is meeting with Bernie, meeting with El-Sayed,” Means said, referring to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Michigan).

npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6032814/senate-.headline: The incoming class of U.S. senators is full of historic firsts
npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6032814/senate-.author: Saige Miller

paragraphs.text: When the newest class of U.S. senators are sworn into office in January, it will include some of America's firsts.

The 2026 midterm election resulted in a significant shift in the landscape of Congress as Democrats won in a big way up and down the ballot. While not all the races have been called, Democrats have flipped more than 40 House seats and picked up 7 Senate seats, giving them control of both chambers of Congress.
Here are some of the new faces to expect in the Senate who made history on Election Day.
Josh Turek of Iowa

Turek will be the first Paralympian to serve in the Senate. The Democrat is a two-time gold medalist in wheelchair basketball. Turek is paraplegic and uses a wheelchair due to spina bifida. He beat Republican Ashley Hinson in the general election.
Julia Letlow of Louisiana

Letlow has now made history twice. She was the first Republican woman elected to the U.S. House from Louisiana in 2021. Letlow ran for the House in a special election to replace her late husband, Congressman Luke Letlow, who died of COVID-19 in 2020. Now, Louisiana voters have decided to send her to the Senate, where she will be the first Republican woman from the state to serve. She will succeed Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, who Letlow beat in the primary election.
Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan

The incoming Democratic senator is the son of Egyptian immigrants and is the first Muslim person elected to the upper chamber. El-Sayed is an epidemiologist and the former health director for the city of Detroit. He beat Republican Mike Rogers for the hotly contested seat.
Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota

Minnesota's Democratic Lt. Governor is the first Native American elected to the Senate. Flanagan is a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe. She also made political history more than once. She was also the first woman of color elected to state office in Minnesota. Flanagan will replace outgoing Democratic Sen. Tina Smith.
Chris Pappas of New Hampshire

Pappas is the first openly gay man elected to the Senate and is also the first gay man to represent the state of New Hampshire. He served four terms in the House and beat Republican John Sununu in the election.
Annie Andrews of South Carolina

In one of the biggest election night upsets, Andrews pulled out an underdog win in deep red South Carolina. Andrews is the first woman elected to the U.S. senate from the Palmetto State. She beat Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham.
Texas and Kansas elect Democratic senators
Both states are reliably Republican and both states are sending pastors to Washington. This midterm election voters broke with the status quo and elected Democrats to represent them in the Senate.

In Texas, voters selected Democrat James Talarico as their next senator. It is the first time the Longhorn State has sent a Democrat to the chamber since 1988. Talarico won against Republican nominee Ken Paxton.

After nearly 100 years, Kansas elected a democratic senator to the chamber. Adam Hamilton will be the first Democrat that has served the state since 1932. He fended off a tough race with incumbent Republican Roger Marshall.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-06/.headline: Could Raman's win be a turning point for transit in Los Angeles?
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-06/.author: Colleen Shalby

paragraphs.text: Public transit is expected to be a top priority for Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, an advocate for expanding bus lanes and making the city friendlier for bicycles — and who campaigned on getting the Los Angeles International Airport people mover back on track after years of squabbles, delays and cost overruns.

As mayor, Raman will oversee the city’s transportation department and will have the power to appoint new members to the city’s Airport Commission. What’s more, she will have regional clout through L.A. Metro, the transportation agency that runs the county’s light-rail and subway lines.

Raman will take over as chair of Metro’s board of 13 voting members, a job now held by Mayor Karen Bass, whom Raman defeated for reelection this week. She will also get three appointees on the board, and can replace the current mayoral appointees — Councilmembers Katy Yaraslovsky and Imelda Padilla and community advocate Jaqueline Dupont-Walker — who all backed Bass in this week’s election.

Metro is currently in need of millions of dollars to fund a massive bus network for the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. Raman said that she would push Los Angeles’ congressional delegation to make this a key priority. In a statement to The Times ahead of the election, she said she will also prioritize Metro projects that “give the most benefits to the most riders and help make our network more useful” and plans to reinstate a project team in the mayor’s office to eliminate city delays on major capital projects.

Transportation analysts believe Raman, who has a graduate degree in urban planning from MIT, will be more aggressive in addressing transit issues than Bass, whose background was in healthcare and community organizing.

“I do think we’ll see a considerable amount of action on transit and multimodal transportation in the short run on a timeline that puts this work in the context of preparation for the summer of 2028,” said Juan Matute, deputy director of UCLA’s Institute of Transportation Studies.

Los Angeles voters also approved a charter amendment that will allow the City Council to disband the Public Works Board, a move that Matute believes will allow the city to streamline infrastructure projects. The charter change, combined with Raman’s election, will lead to “a shift in the foundation of transportation decision-making,” Matute said.

Among the transportation plans Raman has cited as priorities are the Sepulveda Transit Corridor project, which was approved earlier this year to connect the Westside to the San Fernando Valley; the East San Fernando Transit Corridor project to extend service along the E Line from East Los Angeles to Whittier; expansions of the K Line, to connect multiple communities from South Bay, Inglewood, Mid-City and Hollywood, and the D Line beneath Wilshire Boulevard; a new light rail connection in southeast L.A. County; and the Vermont Transit Corridor project.

That last project to add dedicated bike lanes along Vermont Avenue between 120th Street and Sunset Boulevard recently broke ground. It is also the subject of a lawsuit under Measure HLA that claims it requires a designated bike lane. Raman said she supports compliance with the measure, while supporting shared bike and bus lanes along narrower portions of the route.

Ahead of the election, Raman told The Times via written statements that her transit priorities as mayor would focus on safety, affordability and reliability so that people did not have to be as reliant on cars. She advocated for protected bike lanes and expansion of bus lanes during her campaign.

Raman also criticized Bass and the Los Angeles World Airports board of commissioners for not staying on top of the $3.3-billion Skylink people mover at LAX, a 2.25-mile train that is supposed to whisk passengers between the terminal and ground transportation. The project is years behind schedule and more than $1 billion over budget.

The contractor, LAX Integrated Express Solutions, or LINXS, has blamed the repeated delays on unsigned agreements between the city’s Los Angeles World Airports and the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power as one cause, along with nagging technical issues.

At a news conference near the airport last week, Raman told reporters that if elected, her first-week priority in office would be to convene airport and DWP officials and the contractor to determine who is responsible for each unresolved issue in an effort to break the logjam.
“Taxpayers deserve an advocate at the negotiating table, not another bill for someone else’s failure,” Raman said.
Michael Schneider of Streets for All, an advocacy nonprofit, said he expects Raman to convene a task force to address issues around the people mover project during her first 100 days in office.

He also foresees her consolidating some departments, such as the Street Services repaving division under the city’s transportation department, and directing city departments to implement Measure HLA. It’s also likely, he said, that she will initiate a bond or a tax hike to raise money for sidewalks repairs, curb updates and other street improvements.
“I think it’s the first election where safe streets has become a campaign issue, and real money has gone behind it to try to change the status quo,” Schneider said.
Streets for All’s political action committee took out ads to elect Raman and defeat Bass, powered largely by contributions from hedge fund manager and bike lane advocate Aaron Sosnick.

Over the summer, Raman slammed Bass for pausing a bike lane and street safety improvement project near two cemeteries along Forest Lawn Drive that had come under fire by some in Raman’s district. The debate became so heated that the state Legislature ultimately intervened and set a law that would require a public hearing and approval from the City Council and the mayor’s office before moving forward.

Raman has told The Times that she supported multiple bike lane and multi-modal projects including the 710 North Mobility Improvement Program along Valley Boulevard, Huntington Drive, and Eastern Avenue, plans to set priority bike lanes during peak hours along Sunset Boulevard and add bike lanes and reconfigure the intersection of Virgil, Sunset and Hollywood Boulevards.
It’s unclear how she will balance the push towards these types of endeavors when faced with community pushback.

Nadine Levyfield has advocated for more transparency and answers from Metro over a bus lane project through the center of Eagle Rock. The agency recently agreed to more community meetings to address ongoing concerns over how a reduction in lanes on a bottlenecked portion of Colorado Boulevard will affect traffic and parking through the area’s business district and surrounding neighborhoods. Levyfield believes the community’s asks align with Raman’s campaign.

“Running on a platform of accountability, transparency, improving efficiency, and making sure government agencies are accountable, we really hope she can help us ensure that Metro is prioritizing public safety,” Levyfield said.

Raman has said she is also committed to the city’s goal to eliminate traffic deaths and said she will treat an initiative that began under Mayor Eric Garcetti’s administration and faced significant scrutiny under Mayor Bass as a mandate.

“Angelenos look around and see faded crosswalks, busted pavement and darkened streetlights and wonder why the City can’t even take care of our basic transportation infrastructure,” Raman said in a statement to The Times before her election. “Traffic deaths are preventable and I’ll make sure we’re enforcing laws against dangerous driving, providing actual protection for people who walk and bike, and get our street lights back on and our streets fixed.”
“My priority is to make transit safe, affordable, fast, and reliable, so more Angelenos can avoid the high cost of car payments, insurance, and gas,” she said in the statement.

hightouch.com/blog/llm-judges-identity-r.headline: LLM Judges for Identity Resolution at 4x Lower Cost
hightouch.com/blog/llm-judges-identity-r.author: Albert Jin

paragraphs.text: We wanted to test whether LLMs and decision models, specifically Jev and Luna, could solve a hard problem that we encounter regularly (grading identity resolution results). We found that while both models performed okay out of the box (88.8–97.3% accuracy), implementing a hybrid model that combines Jev + Opus achieves frontier accuracy at > 4x lower costs.
Our other findings:
• Luna performs better than Jev out of the box, but the gap disappears on harder cases.

• Jev's confidence is better calibrated. Most of its mistakes come with low confidence its right. Most of Luna's mistakes come with high confidence. This enables Jev to perform better than Luna in a hybrid model harness.
• Frontier models are still more accurate than decision models

• Decision models are up to 90× cheaper and more than 10× faster out of the box. They cost $0.5 - $0.10 per 1,000 identities and answer in about 0.15 seconds, but trail Opus accuracy by about 6 percentage points on harder benchmarks.
