politico.com/news/2026/11/06/gop-reckoni.headline: Stephen Miller’s rise to chief of staff indicates Trump isn’t ready to move on
politico.com/news/2026/11/06/gop-reckoni.author: Meredith Lee Hill

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump's decision to name hard-line loyalist Stephen Miller as his top aide cemented what many Republicans were already privately fearing: There will be no party-wide GOP reckoning with this week's midterm bloodbath.

Instead, with Trump still in office for another two years, most have grown resigned to the reality that the president is going to lean in on a confrontational approach with Congress — and is not willing to change course.

Republicans on Capitol Hill and inside the Trump administration are questioning how and whether they can break with the president now after having green-lit much of his agenda, according to more than a dozen GOP lawmakers, senior aides and Trump officials interviewed for this story, some of whom were granted anonymity to speak candidly about the party’s future.
Trump's decision Friday to elevate Miller, the architect of his unpopular mass deportation policy and an advocate of fierce partisan confrontation, crystallized the frustration.

“There needs to be some self-reflection for Republicans,” Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) said in an interview about the midterm losses Friday morning. “There should be some heads rolling at the White House because we lost badly.”
Hours later, heads did roll. Trump announced Miller would replace Susie Wiles as his new chief of staff.
“Horrible decision,” Stutzman said in response.
One House Republican, when informed that Trump had named Miller his chief of staff, replied: “Please tell me you’re lying to me right now, just to get a reaction.”

The immediate aftermath of the election has sharpened the GOP’s core issue for the past decade: They are struggling to navigate the man who they reshaped their entire identity around, and whose record low approval with voters helped to fuel generational losses within the party.
The Iran war is another area where some Republicans are having regrets. Vice President JD Vance identified it as the main reason for the party’s defeat in his election post-mortem.
The problem with Vance’s assessment, one senior Hill Republican said, is, “we’ve been fucking voting for the war since March — because they told us to.”
Republicans and Trump advisers expect the president to wield massive influence in the 2028 GOP primaries, another reason many are staying quiet.

"Everyone is staring at each other and wondering who will speak up and blame Trump first," said one GOP operative who worked on a battleground race Democrats won. They, like others in this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. "But we've been here before. I'm not holding my breath. He still controls the party and its primaries, at least for now."
The White House responded to POLITICO's request for comment by referring to Trump's praise for Miller on Friday. The RNC declined to comment.

Miller wrote on social media that he is "honored beyond words to serve as [Trump's] White House Chief of Staff" and "the mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President."

How much lawmakers will distance themselves will be put to the test quickly: House Republicans will have an immediate opportunity to break with Trump and the war next week, when Rep. Thomas Massie said in an interview with POLITICO he will trigger his articles of impeachment against Secretary Pete Hegseth. “There are a lot of questions about Hegseth,” House Oversight Chair James Comer (R-Ky.) said Friday.

Some senior Republicans are privately nudging Trump officials to ditch Hegseth before the vote, according to two people with direct knowledge of the conversations. The White House is sticking by Hegseth so far, however.

House Republicans will also have a chance to elect new leadership next week, including a new chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee. But in a sign of what’s to come, none of the candidates — including Reps. Brian Jack (R-Ga.) and Rudy Yakym (R-Ind.) — nor any other GOP leadership candidates have publicly suggested doing more to break with Trump.

A small group of Republicans on Capitol Hill have privately declared, as of Tuesday night, that “MAGA is over,” and it’s time for a “reset,” as one House GOP aide put it — and yet it’s a sentiment no prominent Republican is willing to say publicly.

Rep. Chris Smith (R-N.J.), one of the longest-serving members of the House, said he wasn’t going to “blame” others for Tuesday’s losses, which left him as the sole GOP incumbent survivor in his home state. Asked if Republicans were dragged down by the president, Smith replied: “I don’t want to answer that.”

Rep. Warren Davidson (R-Ohio) went a step further. He declined to name Trump, but he said in an interview that he was tired of GOP leaders “ignoring” voters — a remarkable position for a party that Trump transformed into a working-class coalition.

"We had a lot of Republican leaders out there saying ‘everything's fine.’ And you kind of had the boomer generation saying, 'Well, yeah, back in my day, interest rates were 15%, so everything's good,’” said Davidson, a 56-year-old former Army Ranger. “Well, you had a lot of hardworking young people who felt really ignored, and they they went to the polls and said, 'Stop ignoring us.'"
Davidson said Republicans need to start discussing their problems quickly, or suffer the electoral consequences again.

"Bad news doesn't get better with time. So avoiding talking about something doesn't solve the problem," he said. He said Vance “walked a pretty good line” by being “candid” in his election post-mortem Wednesday.

Vance and other potential 2028 presidential contenders like Sen. Ted Cruz don’t have much time to waste if they want to chart a new path away from Trump. Cruz issued his own post-mortem that included a call to focus more on voters’ economic concerns. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said “this midterm was a rebuke of the president and Congress.”

French Hill, the powerful Financial Services Committee Chair who narrowly survived a strong Democratic challenge in his own deep-red Arkansas seat Tuesday night, pointed to “President Trump’s unfavorability” which hit “races across the country.” Hill added: “He will be considered a lame duck, and that often has members of both political parties looking out at who will be the standard-bearers in the 2028 presidential election.”
Most others have remained silent in public.
One thing is certain: The utter devastation in deep-red seats is stirring deep anger among many Hill Republicans, who believe something needs to change.

It’s fueling private recriminations at Trump’s political operation that his advisers didn’t take early warnings seriously about the extent of the damage in states like North Carolina. Trump’s now-former chief of staff Susie Wiles will join his political operation, the president announced Friday.
Trump's team has blamed "candidate quality" for the losses, instead of the president himself.

“Candidate quality matters. Unless you’re running for the U.S. Senate. They apparently don’t care if you would lose to a pinecone,” said a House Republican, referring to Trump's hand-picked North Carolina Senate nominee Michael Whatley.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee declined to comment.

Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), who leads the Senate campaign arm and saw Democrats flip a Senate seat in his own state, did not answer reporters’ questions on Thursday. The South Carolina Republican has a policy of not talking to reporters in the halls — and he didn’t start when POLITICO and others asked why Republicans lost so badly.

Back in August, some Republicans in seats Trump won by double digits were already telling the White House to keep the president away from their districts. Others publicly broke from the White House on mass deportations and the Iran war.
NRCC Chair Richard Hudson had largely dismissed those concerns when POLITICO asked him in a hallway interview on Sept. 1.

“Based on our polling, the president's a net positive in every district. And I've been encouraging him to get out and do events and do rallies. I'm going to continue to do that,” Hudson said. “I think the more he talks about his record and incredible achievements he's made over the last Congress, I think the better.”
Then, Hudson lost his own reelection bid. He is the first ever NRCC chair in history to be defeated in a general election.
Mia McCarthy, Andrew Howard and Samuel Benson contributed reporting.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/music/sto.headline: Mötley Crüe singer Vince Neil's girlfriend arrested on domestic assault
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/music/sto.author: Deborah Day

paragraphs.text: The girlfriend of Mötley Crüe frontman Vince Neil was arrested Sunday for reportedly striking the singer.

Rainbow Hannah Andreani, 45, was booked in Williamson County, Tenn., for alleged domestic assault, according to arrest records viewed by the Los Angeles Times. Andreani posted a $5,000 bond and was released Monday. She is due in court Dec. 3, according to the Williamson County Sheriff’s Office.
Andreani’s arrest occurred after she allegedly hit Neil, 65, TMZ reported.

The makeup artist, who goes by “Rain Hannah,” and Neil have been in a relationship since 2011, according to People. In 2025, she was aboard Neil’s Learjet when it was involved in a fatal crash in Scottsdale, Ariz. The aircraft left the runway when landing, collided with a parked plane and killed one pilot. Neil was not on the plane.

Neil wrapped up a 34-date North American tour on Sept. 26 in Washington with his Mötley Crüe bandmates, bassist Nikki Sixx, drummer Tommy Lee and guitarist John 5, who joined the group after Mick Mars’ 2022 departure. The Return of the Carnival of Sins tour celebrated two milestones for the band: the 20th anniversary of the 2005-2006 Carnival of Sins tour and the band’s 45th anniversary.

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/openai-bugging-alfoz.headline: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan pleads not guilty
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/openai-bugging-alfoz.author: Jordan Novet, Dan Mangan

paragraphs.text: The Saudi national charged with planting a listening device in the headquarters of OpenAI while he worked there pleaded not guilty on Friday during an appearance in San Francisco federal court.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was sent back to jail after the brief hearing. Alfozan has been held without bail since his arrest on a criminal complaint in early October.
He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted in the case.
A grand jury indicted Alfozan on Oct. 27 on a single count of interception of oral communications, court records show.
Prosecutors say that he put a recording device in a television in an executive conference room at OpenAI's offices in San Francisco on Sept. 28.
Alfozan's lawyer declined to comment after the hearing before Magistrate Judge Peter Kang.
The judge ordered Alfozan to next appear in court on Nov. 17.
Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm, Raed Ventures.
"He currently serves as Engineering Lead at OpenAI, with a focus on AI Agents and the data platform," Alfozan's bio page on Raed's site says.
Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of Saudi Arabia's royal family, is a venture partner in the same firm.

Alfozan's case comes as U.S. companies such as OpenAI are making rapid advancements in developing artificial intelligence agents, and as concerns grow about the potential theft of AI tech from those companies.In June, President Donald Trump, in an executive order on AI innovation, said it was U.S. policy "to protect American ingenuity and intellectual property from exploitation and theft by adversaries; and to cultivate America's advanced AI-enabled capabilities."Trump has had a close relationship with Saudi Arabia. But he has also taken steps during his second term in the White House to limit the number of visas for highly skilled foreign workers.OpenAI earlier this year held discussions with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the country's sovereign wealth fund, about investing in the company.
— Jordan Novet reported from San Francisco

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/openai-reporte.headline: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/openai-reporte.author: Lucas Ropek

paragraphs.text: OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.
In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.
OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market, with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/cramer-coreweave-neb.headline: Cramer’s week ahead: AI data center stocks face another hurdle and so does the Fed
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/cramer-coreweave-neb.author: Alexa LoMonaco

paragraphs.text: CNBC's Jim Cramer on Friday said that next week's earnings from leading neoclouds could test investor confidence in the battered data center trade.

Stocks rebounded to end a turbulent election week, which saw investors dumping companies tied to the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out after Democrats flipped the House and Senate and some key gubernatorial seats. Following the worst day on Wall Street in 19 months, Friday's gains were welcome but not to be trusted. Cramer remained skeptical of any recovery, as he also had been about what proved to be Wednesday's short-lived midterm rally.

Cramer argued that concerns about data center spending and financing have yet to be resolved. "It felt like a dead cat bounce," the "Mad Money" host said, referring to Friday's largely positive market. "I know we are never going to get an all clear. But it still feels like there are plenty of sellers lurking, just waiting for stocks to make a bigger recovery so they can get out."
With that backdrop, Cramer turned to the week ahead.
Monday
Constellation Energy reports before the bell, offering an early look at how political uncertainty could affect the power infrastructure supporting AI data centers.
Tuesday
On Holding reports earnings, but Cramer remains cautious on the athletic footwear. He said the industry feels increasingly crowded. "I am going to pass on this one," he said.

The consumer price index also arrives Tuesday morning, with Cramer looking for a meaningful slowdown in inflation. He warned that persistently high prices could prompt Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh to raise interest rates again. The Fed hiked rates in September for the first time in three years.

After the close, neocloud CoreWeave reports in what could be one of the week's most consequential earnings releases. Cramer said the heavily indebted neocloud needs to explain how it plans to finance its expansion and manage its borrowing costs.
Wednesday

Corteva reports in an otherwise quiet session. Cramer said the agricultural chemicals company has fallen sharply out of favor with investors and wants to better understand what's weighing on its stock.
Thursday

Nebius, another high-profile neocloud, reports before the bell, providing another major test for the AI infrastructure trade following results from CoreWeave. Cramer said investors will be looking for strong new orders, completed data centers and a robust pipeline of future projects. "What I don't want to hear is that the sites they are building are coming in late and overbudget," he said.
Cisco Systems also reports Thursday evening. He said the networking provider may be oversold, but would wait to see how the market responds to CoreWeave and Nebius before buying.

Applied Materials reports as well. Although the semiconductor equipment maker's shares have fallen sharply from their highs, Cramer cautioned that a steep decline alone does not make a stock attractive. "Remember, we don't care where a stock comes from. We just care about where it is going," he said.
Kraft Heinz holds an investor meeting Thursday. Cramer remains optimistic about CEO Steve Cahillane's ability to unlock shareholder value, citing his track record at Kellogg.

The producer price index comes in Friday, offering another important reading on inflation.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: When a single vowel stands in the path to victory, the stakes could not be higher for these spelling bee champions
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Caitlin Cassidy

paragraphs.text: Competing in a spelling bee is not for the faint of heart. Sometimes, the difference between victory and loss is one incorrect vowel and you’re undone, months of training reduced to nought.
At a small theatre hall in Sydney’s west on Friday afternoon, 34 primary school students sit stony-faced on a brightly lit stage, knowing this pressure only too well.

All have made it past about 200,000 students who competed in spelling bees across 1,070 public schools in New South Wales. The finalists earned their place at this year’s state competition after winning online regional finals in August. They represent the top 0.03%. And they’re not here to mess around.

Five are competing for a third time, having progressed to the last stage in the junior competition. Among them are year 5 student Wafiq Ayyash from the Hunter region, who won the junior state title in 2024, and year 6 student Bobby Ivaneza from the inner west, who was runner-up the same year.

Ewan Mattick from the state’s central west, Caleb Borg from the Riverina, and Alesha Kahfandi from the Hunter have also qualified for the state finals on three occasions. This isn’t their first rodeo.

The format is relatively simple. Contestants begin with “seen” words that they’ve been able to practise at home, before facing “unseen” words testing their broader skills and composure. Each round is sudden death.
To kick off, they’re introduced to the crowd by the host, ABC presenter Rae Johnston, with colourful details.

Archie Griffith likes the Parramatta Eels and his dachshund puppy. He doesn’t like his dad’s jokes. Ivaneza, who is wearing a bright red sweatband, admires Nicola Tesla, a Serbian-American engineer who died in 1943, for his genius. Ivaneza’s favourite food is camembert.
The students are as diverse as the schools they come from. Some 23 speak a language other than English at home, and 18 have travelled from outside Sydney.
Seven go down in the first round, stumbling over obscure words like “tourmaline” and “malapropism”. Another seven are out in round two – but you try spelling “lepidopterist” at home.
In the next four rounds, 13 students fall. Mattick nails “centurion” and gives a thumbs up to his family. Come round seven, Kahfandi begins to pray.
“Pernicious” and “sagacious” bring two more students down. And then there are five: Afeef Ahmed, Ivaneza, Kahfandi, Caroline Wang, and Maximilian Lumley, all in year 6. Two are returning finalists.

In round eight, they all spell their words correctly, though Ivaneza, usually breezing through with confidence, restarts on “whimsical”. Then, in round nine, he’s asked to spell “unserviceable” and omits the second “e”.

Ivaneza, visibly devastated, slumps into his seat and places his head in his hands. The remaining students spell their words correctly, and Ivaneza tearily returns to his family in the crowd and the comforting embrace of his father. The heartbreak is palpable.

Then, in an instant, after Ahmed correctly spells “immemorial”, the remaining three competitors fall. Kahfandi misses “antepenultimate”, Wang gets tied up by “parmigiana” and Lumley is one letter off getting “genealogy”. Ahmed has won.
But the show must go on.

“We are in an interesting situation,” Johnston says. “We need to play for a runner up.” Wang goes out straight away after being dealt the word “grandiloquent”. But Kahfandi and Lumley appear to be in lockstep. For the next five rounds, they’re either both correct or both wrong.
“We’re just going to keep on going,” Johnston declares. It begins to feel that the audience will grow old in this theatre, steadily working its way through the entire Macquarie Dictionary.
But then, Kahfandi misses the word “vociferous”. Lumley approaches the microphone and awaits his fate. His word is “apocalypse” and, after a deep breath, he nails it.

The crowd bursts into cheers, and Lumley returns to his seat and stares reflectively at the ground, looking like he has endured a war. His grandmother, Sue, is bursting with pride. “It was so stressful,” she says, “and he looked so calm.”
“He’s worked so hard. Some of those words, I didn’t even know what they were. We’re very proud.”

Kahfandi is proud of herself, too. “It was very tense in the room, there was a lot of pressure on everyone,” she says. “I feel a bit disappointed I didn’t get second and I was a bit tired after all those rounds, but getting third place is also really good.”
Ahmed is surprised he’s won, but his mother isn’t. She’s been helping him train for months – half an hour every night before bed.
“He reads a lot,” she says. “I knew he would win; he was three-time champion at school.”
Asked how he felt when he found out he’d won Ahmed says, at first, he “didn’t realise”.
“But then when they said we had a winner, I felt happy,” he says. “The runners-up words were harder than the ones I got.”

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-06/.headline: California says homes near former Exide plant are 'clean.' Soil samples raise questions
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-06/.author: Iris Kwok, Tony Briscoe

paragraphs.text: California has cleaned up lead-contaminated soil at thousands of homes in neighborhoods surrounding a shuttered battery recycling plant in southeast L.A. County, state officials say.

The former Exide facility in Vernon spewed toxic dust for decades as it melted down lead-acid car batteries for recycling. Its operations released lead dust across Boyle Heights, East Los Angeles, Commerce and Maywood while the state allowed the plant to operate for decades with a temporary permit.
“Every school, park, and childcare center in the affected area has been cleaned,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement Friday, “and nearly 6,500 homes have been made safer.”

The 6,500 figure, which was current as of Oct. 23, reflects roughly 80% of the 8,000 total eligible properties where owners granted access, according to the statement. That means there are about 1,500 properties left for the state to clean up.
“That is real progress for communities that waited far too long for justice,” Newsom said in the statement. “California will keep fighting to do right by the families of Southeast Los Angeles.”

In April, The Times reported on a study by a team of university researchers and a local environmental health organization that found some remediated homes still had lead levels above California’s standard for residential properties. The state Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) had committed to performing soil testing at homes where work was done early in the cleanup process.

Not long after, the state officials began sending letters to homeowners detailing these soil testing results. Over a dozen homeowners were notified that DTSC had found lead levels above the state’s standard in individual soil samples. Many of these samples were deeper underground and in harder to reach parts of the property.

DTSC officials told homeowners that “these areas could not be removed because of physical limitations,” such as tree roots, utility lines, power poles or nearby structures. They added that clean soil and other landscaping materials have been placed over properties “to prevent contact with lead in soil.”
The results raised long-standing concerns over the quality of work and whether the lingering contamination could present risks to the residents.
The department could not immediately be reached for comment on the status of those tests.

Jane Williams, executive director of California Communities Against Toxics, said the results suggest that DTSC may need to redeploy work crews to do additional soil remediation at some homes. However, she said DTSC needs to shift its focus beyond the 1.7-mile cleanup zone, where independent soil testing had also found excessive lead.

“The $700-million cleanup of the hundreds of homes affected by the Exide Lead Smelter has done a great deal to remove lead from the community and make homes safer inside the 1.7-mile cleanup zone,” Williams said. “It does appear from the data the state recently released that some homes may not meet the cleanup goals and that additional work may be needed to ensure these homes meet the standard.”
The effort to clean up the facility started about a decade ago, soon after testing revealed elevated lead levels in nearby residential soil, according to Newsom’s office.
In March 2015, Exide closed its Vernon plant in an agreement with federal prosecutors to avoid criminal charges, The Times reported.

Under the agreement, Exide was supposed to pay for the cleanup. But in 2020, a bankruptcy court ruled that the company could abandon its shuttered Vernon plant, leaving the cleanup to California taxpayers.
Newsom’s office said California had spent more than $700 million to clean lead-contaminated soil around the Exide plant.
State lawmakers, including Newsom, have pushed for the site to be designated a “Superfund” priority site in the hopes that it would bring in additional federal funding to accelerate cleanup efforts.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/06/i.headline: Why investors are dumping AI company stocks after Democrats’ election sweep
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/06/i.author: David J. Lynch

paragraphs.text: The Democratic Party’s takeover of Washington and key state capitals — coupled with an abrupt financing chill — threatens the artificial intelligence boom that has been driving U.S. economic growth and stock values.
Investors worry that Democrats, emboldened by their landslide win on Tuesday, will slow the nationwide buildout of AI data centers.
The shift in political power in states such as Texas, Ohio and Michigan comes as Wall Street’s willingness to finance the industry’s trillion-dollar AI plans was already waning.

Bond investors on Friday demanded yields of more than 16 percent to lend money to CoreWeave, a data center company that paid around 10 percent for borrowed money earlier this year. Several data center companies — including one backed by chipmaker Nvidia — abandoned plans for initial stock offerings this month as investor sentiment cooled.

Wall Street’s rethinking accelerated this month as it became clear that growth forecasts for top AI companies were overly optimistic. In advance of its planned stock market debut, Anthropic last week said its third-quarter revenue growth dropped to 47 percent from 144 percent in the previous quarter.

Some analysts expect that number to fall by half in the final three months of the year. Growing investor doubts about AI emerged on Thursday when a tech stock plunge erased roughly $2.5 trillion in wealth.
“Some of the cracks in the AI thesis are starting to emerge,” said Ara Kharazian, lead economist for Ramp, a spend-management company. “The market is trying to parse out the winners and losers here.”

If the AI industry’s investment math no longer works, the U.S. economy could take a hit. Sagging stock prices would threaten consumer spending on goods and services, which accounts for nearly 70 percent of the economy. Delays in AI infrastructure investment could knock out one of the props beneath strong recent growth in output and hiring.
On Friday, President Donald Trump weighed in, saying he was “100%” in favor of data centers and would “work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them.”
AI development for months has been shadowed by warring narratives.
Top executives at leading U.S. labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI describe the rise of machine intelligence as a seminal moment in human history that will reshape work, leisure, governance and health.

Yet amid the accolades and self-promotion, some analysts warned that the hype had inflated an investment bubble. Shares of Nvidia, the leading AI chipmaker, rose by more than 430 percent between October 2023 and October of this year before shedding nearly one-quarter of their value over the past month.
Chipmaker Intel has lost half its market value in the past month.

Since the debut of ChatGPT four years ago, AI has advanced from an economic curiosity to the center of the $33 trillion U.S. economy. In recent years, the “Magnificent 7” AI stocks — Amazon, Alphabet, Apple, Microsoft, Meta, Tesla and Nvidia — have been among Wall Street’s best performers.
Together, these seven stocks account for roughly one-third of the broader S&P 500 index’s market value.

Rising stock values paid economic dividends: Many Americans used investment gains to support their spending, according to the research firm JPMorgan Chase Institute. Between 2019 and 2025, the share of consumers tapping their portfolios for cash doubled. Investment gains now support roughly 7 percent of household spending.

That’s important because amid muted after-inflation income growth, consumers have been struggling to maintain their living standards. The personal savings rate is about half what it was in January 2024, according to the Commerce Department.

Unusually large tax refunds this year, thanks to the president’s signature tax legislation, helped boost spending. But as taxpayers adjust their paycheck withholding to take account of the new law, refunds should return to typical levels.
Seeking to juice their market gains, some Americans have borrowed money from brokerage firms to invest, a risky practice that can magnify gains or losses.
As of September, Americans had borrowed about $118 billion from their brokerages, up from $27 billion one year ago, according to Ian Shepherdson, chief economist with Pantheon Macroeconomics.
Investors can continue borrowing against their securities portfolio only if stocks keep rising.
“If you want to keep borrowing to keep spending more, you need stock prices to keep rising. Just leveling off isn’t enough. So that’s a very clear and present danger,” said Shepherdson.

It would probably take a serious stock market decline, well beyond the S&P 500’s more than 5 percent loss over the past month, to ignite broader economic problems, according to Joe Brusuelas, chief economist of RSM, a Chicago-based consultancy.
For now, that is a worst-case worry. The economy grew between July and September at a rapid 3.4 percent clip, and employers created 165,000 new jobs in October, the Labor Department said Friday.
Stock prices rebounded Friday, easing investor fears of an imminent crisis.
Still, many observers see the AI industry’s political problems and financial arrangements as reasons to worry.
“The boom is in its final innings,” Capital Economics in London told clients.

The Democrats who seized control of Capitol Hill and won gubernatorial races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia — states with major data center projects — are far more skeptical of the industry than the laissez-faire Republicans who preceded them.
Trump has pursued a largely hands-off approach to AI development. He has eased federal permitting for data centers and warned against “regulation that’s going to stifle a very important industry.”

The prospect of that changing smacked Elon Musk’s AI investments this week. After Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race, the stock of Musk’s Space X, which includes his Grok AI business, shed almost 13 percent of its value before recovering a bit on Friday.
Investors fear that Democrats’ response to public anger over proliferating data centers will derail profitable investments.

Half of the new data center capacity expected over the next year is located in four states that flipped to Democratic Party control, said hedge fund manager Dan Niles of Niles Investment Management in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. Excessive regulation could push the “hyperscalers” to take their investments elsewhere, he said.
“The biggest companies in the world can’t afford to just sort of sit there. They will put plants where they make the most sense. And there are plenty of places that would take them,” he said.
The industry’s financial outlook is drawing intensified scrutiny.

Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and other hyperscalers are in a “whatever it takes” posture on the investment required to compete. They plan to deploy a total of almost $1 trillion this year and perhaps more next year, seeing the global AI business as a revolutionary opportunity that can’t be missed.

These giants are likely to survive any AI winnowing. Along with operating data centers, they each have other products that bring in revenue to buttress them against costly AI setbacks, said Will Sommer, vice president of Gartner, a research firm in London.

But smaller AI providers called “neoclouds” may not be so lucky. Lacking other products, hundreds of these companies — with names like CoreWeave and Nebius — effectively represent concentrated bets on demand for additional data-crunching capability. There will not be enough revenue to go around, Sommer said.
By 2030, 80 percent of neoclouds will fail, be acquired or merge with a larger company, he said. At the current pace of investment, data center owners will need to write off $3.5 trillion in assets.

latimes.com/sports/story/2026-11-06/quen.headline: Quentin Lake texted apology to Justin Herbert for ‘deli meat’ comment
latimes.com/sports/story/2026-11-06/quen.author: Chuck Schilken, Gary Klein

paragraphs.text: Rams safety Quentin Lake says he texted Justin Herbert to apologize for comments he made about the Chargers quarterback on a podcast earlier this week.
So far, Lake said Friday afternoon, he hasn’t heard back.

“I don’t know if he read it,” Lake told The Times. “He probably says, ‘I don’t care about it anymore. I’m not trying to see this. It doesn’t matter. You said what you said.’ But at the same time I … felt like it was right for me to at least say,’ Hey, man, I didn’t mean it in any disrespectful way.’”

Lake and teammate Trent McDuffie each intercepted a pass thrown by Herbert during the Rams’ 24-9 victory over the Chargers on Sunday. During an appearance on the “St. Brown Podcast” this week, Lake mentioned that Herbert “was throwing deli meat” and “seeing ghosts” during the game.
The comments left Lake and the two hosts — Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown and his brother, former NFL receiver Equanimeous St. Brown — in stitches.
After his quotes went viral, however, Lake was left with a bad taste in his mouth.

“You know, I was with my boys,” said Lake, who played high school football with Amon-Ra St. Brown at Mater Dei. “I was in a comfortable environment. I was trying to say stuff funny. But looking back on it, they have a big platform. And when you say stuff like that, people are going to take it in ways that you may not mean it. ... In no way shape or form was it supposed to be disrespectful.”

The Chargers are 0-7 this season, and Herbert is seen as a key contributing factor. A two-time Pro Bowl selection who is just two seasons removed from throwing for 23 touchdowns and three interceptions over 17 games, Herbert has only five touchdowns and a league-high 10 interceptions this year. He ranks 31st in QB rating among passers with at least 100 attempts.
But Lake said he thinks Herbert is “still a great quarterback,” citing the seventh-year player’s arm strength, running skills and processing ability.

“Obviously there’s some things going on over there that they probably want to fix and probably want to polish up,” Lake said. “You look at their roster from top to bottom, [they’re] still very, very talented, him included.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/politics/susie.headline: Susie Wiles Is the Latest Powerful Woman to Exit the Trump Administration

paragraphs.text: Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff who stepped down on Friday, was one of the most powerful women to have served in Mr. Trump’s second term.

The first woman to hold the top staff job in the West Wing, she helped steer Mr. Trump to his election victory in 2024, playing a central role in his return to power. On election night on Tuesday, Mr. Trump blamed Ms. Wiles for the historic Republican midterms defeat in front of others.

Now, she is also the latest in a wave of women who have left the Trump administration in the past year, as The New York Times reported last month, and one of the first to depart since Tuesday’s elections. On Thursday, Harmeet Dhillon, a top official in the Justice Department, resigned after conflicts with department leaders.

Four of Mr. Trump’s eight female cabinet-level officials resigned or were fired earlier this year: Attorney General Pam Bondi; Lori Chavez-DeRemer, the labor secretary; Homeland Security Secretary Kristi L. Noem; and Tulsi Gabbard, the director of national intelligence.
Like Ms. Wiles, all four were replaced by men.

When Mr. Trump was putting together his administration for his second term, the president-elect tapped women for many cabinet-level jobs and high-profile positions in his inner circle. Among them was Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, who gained attention as the youngest person to serve in the position. She stepped down in August.
At a Women’s History Month celebration last year, Mr. Trump declared that he was “thrilled to say that we have more women in our cabinet than any Republican president in the history of our country.”

That is no longer the case. There are now three women remaining in cabinet-level positions: Brooke Rollins, the secretary of Agriculture; Linda McMahon, the secretary of education; and Kelly Loeffler, the head of the Small Business Administration.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/tr.headline: Trump’s Push for Data Centers on Public Land Faces Top Senate Democrat’s Scrutiny
finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/tr.author: Ari Natter

paragraphs.text: Fri, November 6, 2026 at 4:15 PM EST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- A top Senate Democrat is putting the Trump administration's moves to build data centers on public land in the crosshairs, foreshadowing a brewing fight when his party takes control of Congress next year.
Most Read from Bloomberg

In a letter to the Bureau of Land Management, Senator Martin Heinrich said the agency is considering at least 15 proposals to build data centers on related infrastructure on public land covering more than 17,000 acres stretching across six Western states. That comes after the administration approved an 88-acre data center site in Boulder City, Nevada this past June, according to Heinrich, who is poised to become chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee next year.

"I am extremely concerned with the Trump administration's actions to develop data centers on public lands,"Heinrich wrote in the letter to Steve Pearce, the director of the Bureau of Land Management, which has jurisdiction over hundreds of millions of acres of public lands.

In his letter Heinrich requested the Bureau of Land Management provide a list of all the authorities being used, related development proposals and the potential sites that were earmarked for data center development on public lands.

An Interior Department spokesperson said any right of way application involving public lands follows the established National Environmental Policy Act process, which includes rigorous environmental review, opportunities for public input, and full transparency.

"The Department's focus continues to be ensuring that any proposed use of public lands is evaluated carefully, openly, and in a way that protects communities, natural resources, and the long-term interests of the American people," the spokesperson said in an email.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order in July 2025 seeking to expedite the permitting of data centers on public land saying the facilities were a priority for the administration's goals of manufacturing and technical dominance.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Wall Street Sees US Hitting $41.1 Trillion Debt Cap in February
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Alexandra Harris

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Wall Street strategists are bracing for the US Treasury to hit against its borrowing limit as early as February, triggering the need for extraordinary measures before it faces a funding crunch in late 2027.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Strategists at Bank of America Corp., Barclays Plc and Morgan Stanley said that the Treasury's latest financing estimates along with a higher cash balance will pull forward the date it reaches the debt ceiling to mid- to late-February. Bank of America earlier saw the limit would be reached around May.

The US government is less than $800 billion shy of its $41.1 trillion borrowing cap. Treasury's estimates released last week call for roughly $800 billion of net borrowing in the January-to-March period. The department also projected an end-March cash balance of $1 trillion, a record quarter-end target.

The Treasury's increased cash balance likely reflects greater reliance on short-term bills to finance government spending and deficits. Because bill issuance results in larger and more frequent cash outflows during the month, officials generally seek to maintain a larger buffer. That, in turn, uses up the remaining borrowing capacity at a faster rate.

Unless there is an agreement by Congress to raise or suspend the debt limit, the Treasury can avoid breaching it by deploying extraordinary accounting measures that could add an estimated $300 billion to $350 billion before it runs the risk of default.

Strategists, including SMBC Nikko Securities America, expect that the so-called X date — the point at which the Treasury exhausts funds from its cash balance and extraordinary measures and is no longer able to meet all of its obligations — to be sometime between August and November.
The Democratic sweep of Congress raises the prospect of a prolonged confrontation with President Donald Trump over the government's borrowing.

Fitch Ratings warned last month that such an outcome would increase the likelihood of brinkmanship, unless the outgoing Republican-led Congress manages to raise or suspend the debt ceiling before its term expires at year's end.

Debt-limit constraints tend to ripple through funding markets as the Treasury begins drawing down its cash balance and reducing bill issuance. While that temporarily increases reserves in the banking system, putting downward pressure on overnight funding rates, those effects typically reverse once the debt ceiling is resolved. The Treasury will then ramp up bill issuance to replenish its coffers, draining reserves and driving funding costs higher.

An extended standoff next year could disrupt parts of the curve. During past confrontations, investors sold Treasury bills maturing around the date the government was projected to run out of money, while buying securities maturing before or after that date, creating a kink in the curve. Right now, the T-bill curve shows little sign of concern, with the government still months away from hitting the limit.
A delayed resolution could also prolong the Treasury's reliance on short-term borrowing for its overall financing needs and push back efforts to boost issuance of longer maturities later in the year.

"Given how significantly the debt limit could shape money markets next year, over the coming weeks we will be closely watching for progress on the reconciliation process," Barclays strategist Samuel Earl wrote in a note to clients on Friday.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/06/i.headline: Stephen Miller’s promotion angers industries reeling from immigration enforcement
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/06/i.author: Lauren Kaori Gurley

paragraphs.text: Industries that rely heavily on immigrant labor decried President Donald Trump’s promotion of his chief architect of deportations on Friday, just days after millions of Americans signaled anger about such policies.
The move elevating Stephen Miller to chief of staff starting Monday, left some leaders of groups representing the agriculture and construction sectors gobsmacked.

“When I got a text message, ‘Hey, have you heard about Stephen Miller?,’ my first thought was: Thank goodness he was let go,” said Chris Herr, president of PennAg Industries Association, which represents farmers and pork and poultry producers. Many of his members helped propel Trump to victory in 2024 but have soured on the president, as some farmers reel from the loss of workers to immigration enforcement, he said.
“The wild card now is what is the president going to do?” Herr said. “Is he going to be engaged or is the Stephen Miller policy going to rule the day?”

Last month, more than 40 farmers and agricultural industry groups wrote to Trump and congressional leaders, warning that the immigration crackdown was hitting the nation’s food supply, hurting farmers and risking higher grocery prices. The letter marked a strategy shift for an industry that had been reluctant to publicly criticize the immigration raids, preferring to lobby the administration behind the scenes. About 66 percent of the country’s farmworkers are foreign-born.

“Time will tell if Stephen Miller continues to wreck the economy, destroy families, tarnish the Republican political coalition and obliterate Trump’s legacy,” said Rebecca Shi, chief executive of the American Business Immigration Coalition, a bipartisan group that lobbies for immigration reform on Capitol Hill, which organized the letter.

For months, immigration raids have targeted construction sites across South Texas, resulting in significant project delays and labor shortages that helped deliver Democrats historic victories up and down the ballot in the Lone Star State this week.
Three-time Trump supporter Mario Guerrero, executive director of the South Texas Builders Association, said he was appalled to learn Miller would be taking a more significant role in the White House.
Guerrero said that when he saw the news, he thought, Trump “doesn’t live on this planet …”
“The reason the GOP lost across the board [on Tuesday] is because of the enforcement that Stephen Miller was pushing,” he added.
A request to the White House for comment on the business community pushback was not immediately returned.

Leaders of industries reliant on undocumented workers or those with temporary protections targeted by the Trump administration said they are hopeful that a Democratic-controlled Congress will create opportunities for bipartisan legislation to pass changes to immigration that have long been elusive.
Matt Teagarden, chief executive of the Kansas Livestock Association, said he was worried about what Miller’s promotion could mean.
“The potential for the president to sign [any immigration bill] may have gone down with Miller being named chief of staff,” he said.
“Doubling down on Miller to the extent that he has been the promoter of mass deportation tactics doesn’t fit the results that we saw in Kansas on Tuesday,” he added.
Rural counties and small cities in Kansas swung 20 points toward Democrats on Tuesday, helping elect the first Democrat to the Senate since 1932.
In September, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations near major meatpacking plants delayed cattle livestock operations, shipments and harvesting in southwest Kansas.
A request for comment from some of the nation’s largest business groups, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce was not immediately returned. The Business Roundtable declined to comment.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: Ben Roberts-Smith collaborates with gym business run by influencer that sold ‘war crimes’ pre-workout supplement
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Josh Butler

paragraphs.text: Ben Roberts-Smith has collaborated with a gym supplements company run by a right-wing influencer which recently sold a pre-workout product called “war crimes”.

Roberts-Smith, one of Australia’s most decorated living soldiers who is currently awaiting trial on war crimes charges, has recently launched an apparel brand, Epic 1 Two, producing t-shirts and gym wear.

In October, he also appeared in a social media video collaboration between his brand and Zero Limits supplements, co-owned by right-wing podcaster and fitness coach Chris Katelaris, also known as “Big Chocky”.

Roberts-Smith, Katelaris and others were filmed during a gym workout, with on-screen graphics reading “Zero Limits Supplements x Epic 1 Two”. Both brands were labelled “collaborators” on the video, which is also published on the Instagram grids of both brands.

Months earlier, Zero Limits had repeatedly posted online about a product titled “war crimes”, an energy supplement in the flavour “kill or capture cola”. Its label depicted a hooded captive on a chair in a room with an Australian flag on the wall, and a tall figure wearing a balaclava and military-style clothing.
In a video on 26 July, Katelaris promoted the product while holding a tub at the gym.
“You wanna drink out of a prosthetic leg? You wanna re-enact a Sparta kick? You wanna execute your workout?” he said.
“War crimes, it’s the pre-workout for you.”

Zero Limits, which says it is “veteran owned and operated”, does not currently list the “war crimes” product on its website, and Roberts-Smith is not shown endorsing, referencing or using that particular product.

The former soldier has praised another product from Zero Limits, posting an Instagram story – since shared by the brand – from Epic 1 Two’s Instagram page of himself drinking a separate pre-workout drink.

Roberts-Smith gave the brand a “massive shout out” and told followers to “get on their website and take a look”, sharing a link to its website. Roberts-Smith also last week appeared on the Zero Limits podcast, hosted by another founder of the supplements company of the same name.
Roberts-Smith was in April arrested and charged with five counts of war crime – murder, in relation to three incidents stemming from his service in Afghanistan in 2009 and 2012.

He has denied the charges, saying in a statement after his arrest: “As I’ve always maintained: I categorically deny all of these allegations … I will be taking this opportunity to finally clear my name. I’m proud of my service in Afghanistan.”

The three incidents allegedly involved Afghan nationals being shot dead by Roberts-Smith, or a subordinate under his command, while he was present, the AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said in April.

Roberts-Smith was previously found in a defamation suit – using the civil standard of the balance of probabilities – to have murdered unarmed civilians while serving in the Australian Special Air Service Regiment (SAS) in Afghanistan.

The federal court found to the lower civil standard that Roberts-Smith kicked Afghan man Ali Jan in the chest, sending him falling backwards over a cliff before he landed on the ground. The court found that Roberts-Smith then ordered another soldier to shoot him dead.
Roberts-Smith was also accused in media reporting of shooting an unarmed prisoner who had a prosthetic leg. The leg was later used as a drinking vessel by soldiers.
Zero Limits, Katelaris and Roberts-Smith were contacted for comment.
In a statement via a lawyer, Zero Limits did not respond to specific questions, only answering: “The products are great, make sure you check them out.”
In a statement via the same lawyer, Katelaris also did not respond to specific questions, but said: “If you thought this was wild, wait until next week’s campaign drops.”

Katelaris lists himself as a “co-owner” of the supplements brand in his Instagram bio. He also promotes a range of merchandise under his own name in support of Roberts-Smith, including “I stand with BRS” t-shirts, hats, hoodies and stubby coolers.

libghostty-vt 1.0 is here. libghostty is a portable, high-performance C library for terminal emulation, extracted directly from the core of Ghostty. The 1.0 release means both the library itself and the C ABI are now stable.

A little over a year ago, I wrote that libghostty is coming. At the time, the Zig module had just been merged, the C API didn't exist, and nobody but Ghostty was a consumer. Today, the C API is a complete terminal emulator, it runs in production for millions of people across hundreds of products, both free and commercial, and it has a real, enforced ABI stability policy.
This post is about how we got here and what 1.0 actually means.1
Who Is Already Using It

Since starting the Ghostty project in 2022, the most common question I've been asked is "why?". I already answered this in the libghostty is coming post, so feel free to read that if you wish. Today, I'd rather answer this by showing the broad industry impact libghostty has already had. I believe this strongly validates its existence.

A year ago, I used a bug in JediTerm, the terminal emulator in JetBrains IDEs, as an example of why terminal emulation is hard to get right. A year later, the terminal in JetBrains IDEs now runs on libghostty. Every IntelliJ, PyCharm, GoLand, etc. user now has a libghostty-powered terminal. Based on a report by JetBrains, that's over 12.5 million active users.

Neovim has an approved pull request replacing libvterm with libghostty-vt. Among other things, it closes a 10-year-old issue about reflowing scrollback on resize. The maintainers are waiting on a tagged release before merging so that distributions can package the dependency separately, and the release today should enable that.

KDE developers are experimenting with a Konsole replacement built on it. Vercel's Turborepo uses it to render task output in its TUI. devenv uses it to drive shells. Antithesis used it to fuzz TUI programs and found real bugs in btop and others. Ghostel brings it to Emacs. ghostty-web is the WASM build with an Xterm.js-compatible API. Commercial products like OrbStack embed it. And a whole wave of new terminals and "agentic" coding tools, such as herdr and cmux, have been built on it rather than writing yet another emulator.
There are community bindings for Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python, .NET, Elixir, Dart, Java, and more, and the awesome-libghostty list tracks well over a hundred projects.

More people today use a terminal powered by libghostty than use Ghostty the application, by a very large multiple. And libghostty is having a much larger impact than being "just" a terminal emulator.2
ABI Stability

1.0 means libghostty-vt follows semantic versioning and has strict ABI compatibility promises so that packagers across distributions and operating systems can be confident packaging libghostty-vt and program developers can be confident dynamically linking against it.

Beyond providing useful features, I believe the hallmark of a high-quality and enduring C library is ABI stability. So from the start, I took inspiration from C libraries I enjoyed working with and designed the API to have a strong, stable ABI that allows for future additions.

Every object is an opaque handle. The hundreds of values you might read or write go through a small set of enum-keyed getters and setters, so we can add new values easily without introducing a new symbol. Programs with newer headers linked against an older libghostty get GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED results instead of crashes or undefined behavior. The few non-opaque structs we have carry their size so that fields can be appended later, or contain reserved padding. Enums are pinned to int on every compiler, as much as the C standard allows.
Our CI enforces our ABI policy. Every change is checked with libabigail against a committed baseline on Linux, and against golden type manifests on macOS and WebAssembly.
On ELF platforms, every exported symbol is also versioned, so the dynamic loader refuses to load a mismatched library by name rather than failing in some mysterious way later.
Packaging

In addition to ABI stability, the 1.0 release brings along the proper build tooling, tarballs, dependency licensing manifests, documentation, and more to enable every major operating system and distribution to package libghostty-vt through standard official tooling.

Libghostty has its own release cycle, separate from Ghostty the application. And it has its own tarballs with only the files and dependencies libghostty needs, resulting in smaller sizes and simpler licensing verification and compatibility.

Each release publishes a signed source tarball along with a companion dependencies tarball containing every Zig package in Zig's own cache layout, so a distribution can build the library completely offline. The build installs the shared and static libraries with a proper SONAME, headers, pkg-config files, and a CMake package config, and it honors --prefix, DESTDIR, and lib64. Debug info is kept by default so distros can split it out. All of this is documented in PACKAGING-LIBGHOSTTY.md, which ships with the tarball.
Dependencies and Licensing
libghostty-vt is MIT licensed. At runtime it needs nothing beyond libc, and it can be built fully freestanding if you don't want that either.3

The library compiles in a small number of permissively licensed dependencies: simdutf and Google Highway for SIMD, a compact Unicode table for grapheme data, and Wuffs for image decoding in the Kitty graphics protocol. Both simdutf and Highway are built without libc++, so there is no C++ standard library dependency.

There is no copyleft code anywhere in the dependency tree. Every dependency is listed in a machine-readable manifest with its version, SPDX license, and hash, specifically so distros can fill in their bundled-library metadata more easily.
If a distro would rather dynamically link the system simdutf or Highway, there's a build flag for that.
Portability
libghostty-vt is highly portable. The table below lists all the platforms and architectures that we build and test (full unit tests plus running all examples) in CI:
There is a second set of platforms we build in CI but do not run tests for. These systems all have known users; we just haven't set up the machinery for automated testing:
Each of the tested platforms gets the artifacts it expects:
• Linux and FreeBSD get a shared library with a proper SONAME and versioned symbols, a static library, headers, pkg-config files, and a CMake package config.

• macOS and iOS get a dylib with an @rpath install name and compatibility version, plus an XCFramework covering macOS, iOS, and the iOS simulator that drops straight into Xcode or Swift Package Manager.
• Windows gets a DLL with a .pdb, an import library, and a static library. The library is built with the GNU ABI, but MSVC programs link against it through the import library and CI verifies this.
• Android gets a shared library built against the NDK with 16 KB page size support, as required by Android 15+.

• WebAssembly ships in two flavors, one optimized for speed and one for size, and the small one is under a megabyte with every feature enabled. If you only need a read-only viewer, subsystems like input encoding, search, selection, and Kitty graphics can be compiled out with a build flag, which roughly halves the module. Every function stays exported and simply returns GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED so your code doesn't have to change.4
Portability isn't just about the ability to build and run. It's also about resource usage and being able to work in a wide variety of resource environments.

For resource usage, the library creates no threads, allocates only through an allocator you can customize, and uses minimal compute and memory. I've run 10,000 active terminals, each with a live shell producing output, on a Linux server with 4 cores and 8 GB of RAM. In this test, I had to use dash because bash used far more RAM than libghostty-vt and wouldn't fit into the 8 GB budget.
What's Next
Libghostty 1.0 is a major milestone.

You can now create a terminal in ~1,500 lines of C that has more features and better performance than just about any terminal that existed in 2025, and most today in 2026.5 And thanks to the rich ecosystem of language bindings, you can do this in every major programming language. You get this for free. For almost no effort. You can just do it.

libghostty-vt is a generalized library, so we will focus on stability while implementing as many terminal protocols as exist (giving options to enable/disable them, of course) so that embedders have the luxury of choice.

Every bug any libghostty-vt embedder reports makes everyone else in the ecosystem better. Every feature we ship in libghostty-vt becomes available to everyone quickly and safely. Terminals can move faster with less fragmentation.

Thank you to everyone who contributed to the library, wrote bindings, filed bugs, and shipped something on top of it while the API was still experimental. As with all open source, this was the work of a large community.
Docs, examples, and downloads are at lib.ghostty.org.
Boo. 👻
Footnotes
• As usual, I hate that I have to do this for every post, but I want to note this post was completely hand-written with no AI assistance. ↩
• The numbers are rough because most consumers don't report usage, but JetBrains alone reports 12.5 million recurring active users, and that's before counting everything else on the list. ↩

• In the original post I wrote "not even libc!" The default build does link libc, because the SIMD paths use it and the default allocator is malloc. Turn off SIMD and the library is freestanding, which is how it runs on bare-metal RISC-V and ARM targets. ↩
• The feature flags aren't WASM-specific; they work on every target. They're likely useful for things like embedded devices too. ↩
• "Features" here means the set of terminal protocols and sequences understood, and "performance" means parsing throughput and memory usage, since those are the parts libghostty-vt provides. ↩

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-06/.headline: 18-year-old arrested in deadly Moss Landing shooting
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-06/.author: Iris Kwok

paragraphs.text: An 18-year-old man has been arrested in connection with a shooting in Moss Landing that left two students dead, authorities said Friday.

Greenfield resident Donald William Breeden was arrested and booked into Monterey County Jail on two counts of murder with criminal street gang enhancements, according to the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office. His bail was set at $2,035,000.
The sheriff’s office said there is no active threat to the community.
“No additional information will be released at this time,” Cmdr. Andres Rosas wrote in an email Friday.

The shooting took place early Monday morning at Moss Landing State Beach. When deputies arrived, they discovered the bodies of two boys — later identified as Marco Antonio Perez, 15, and Nathaniel Flores, 13 — along Jetty Road.
Both teens attended schools in the Salinas Union High School District. Nathaniel was involved in football, according to a fundraiser set up by Steinbeck Tigers Youth Football & Cheer.

Two other people were injured that morning, authorities said Friday. One had a gunshot wound, while the other suffered unspecified non-life-threatening injuries that were “subsequently determined to be unrelated to the shooting,” according to the sheriff’s statement.
Deputies said they executed two search warrants Thursday — one in the 900 block of Maple Avenue in Greenfield; and the other in the 45000 block of Crown Avenue in King City.
At the Greenfield address, deputies detained three people, authorities said.
Officials previously said they were aware of a possible party that occurred on the beach, though it was not clear if that was connected to the shooting.
Monterey County Sheriff Tina Nieto said information from community members helped them with the investigation, which remains “active and ongoing.”

“While an arrest has been made, our work is not over,” Nieto said in a statement. “We continue to ask the public for their assistance as we seek justice for Nathaniel and Marco Antonio and their families.”
The Monterey County district attorney’s office did not immediately respond to questions from The Times.
Anyone with information can contact Det. Sgt. Nick Kennedy at (831) 755-3773 or Det. Richard Geng at (831) 759-7279.

latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-06/20.headline: 2026 midterm election results map for Prop. 40, the billionaire tax
latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-06/20.author: Gabrielle LaMarr LeMee, Vanessa Martínez

paragraphs.text: Days after the midterm elections, Proposition 40 has yet to be decided. The ballot measure, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires to help fund healthcare, is failing by more than 8 percentage points.

Statewide, more than 4 million votes remain to be counted in this race, according to the Associated Press, which calculates the expected vote using returns and other data. That includes more than half a million from Los Angeles County, where the “yes” vote leads by more than 7 percentage points.

The proposition has so far found support in nine counties: Alameda, Humboldt, Los Angeles, Mendocino, Monterey, San Francisco, Santa Cruz, Sonoma and Yolo. In Southern California, Los Angeles is the only county leaning toward “yes.”
Propositions 41 and 42

While Proposition 40 focuses narrowly on taxing billionaires, competing Propositions 41 and 42 would have broader impacts on the state’s ability to enact new taxes. And the measures could undercut Proposition 40 if it passes.
As of Friday, the latest vote tallies showed “yes” on Proposition 41 trailing by more than 7 points, while “yes” on Proposition 42 was ahead by more than 6 points.

Proposition 41 would would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. If Proposition 40 passes and either of these measures passes with more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it would prevent the billionaire tax from becoming law.
A late October poll showed voter opposition to Propositions 41 and 42 had grown even as support for the billionaire tax declined.
The money behind the measures
Support for Proposition 40 has totaled to nearly $35 million, mostly from the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the healthcare workers union that proposed the tax.
Backers of Propositions 41 and 42 also opposed Proposition 40. Combined, they raised more than $300 million. Most of that money came from the billionaires who would be subject to the tax.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-06/.headline: L.A. D.A. won't charge Skipp Townsend, whose son now faces murder case
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-06/.author: James Queally, Libor Jany, Richard Winton

paragraphs.text: Prosecutors have decided not to file charges against a prominent South L.A. anti-gang worker, just days after he was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder by Los Angeles Police and the FBI, a defense attorney and three law enforcement sources told The Times on Friday.
But while 62-year-old Clifford “Skipp” Townsend was spared from prosecution, his son faces a murder charge instead, authorities said.

Townsend, executive director of the violence prevention group 2nd Call, was taken into custody by LAPD detectives and federal agents Wednesday. Prosecutors decided not to bring a criminal complaint against him by Friday afternoon, according to his attorney and the three law enforcement sources, who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the case.

On Friday afternoon, the L.A. District Attorney’s Office alleged Kody Townsend, 19, used an assault rifle to gun down Reginald Foreman, an employee of 2nd Call, in August. The men were members of rival factions of the Crips street gang, according to the district attorney’s office, which described the killing as “gang motivated.”
The younger Townsend had not been arrested as of Friday afternoon but faces one count of murder, the district attorney’s office said in a news release.
Jeremiah Abdelhameed, 25, was charged as an accessory after the fact in Foreman’s death. Abelhameed was one of several people arrested along with Skipp Townsend on Wednesday.

Detectives from the LAPD’s Robbery Homicide Division and federal agents descended on 2nd Call’s offices at La Brea Avenue and Obama Boulevard on Wednesday, where they seized several computers. Cellphone video circulating on social media captured the elder Townsend being led into a black-and-white LAPD squad car by officers.

“Obviously, we are pleased that charges were not filed in this case, but we remain confounded by the LAPD’s decision to arrest him. Skipp Townsend has been a leader in violence prevention for more than 20 years and is known for his work in Los Angeles and across the nation,” his attorney, Tiffiny Blacknell, said in a text message. “While he is eager to return to his violence-prevention work, the motivation behind his arrest remains unclear and continues to confound us.”
Skipp Townsend was expected to be released from custody later Friday. Blacknell did not know who was representing her client’s son.
A spokesperson for the district attorney’s office declined to answer a question about the decision not to charge Skipp Townsend. The LAPD didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The district attorney’s office can reject a case for a variety of reasons, including for a lack of evidence or on the condition that it will review the case again after police conduct a deeper investigation. Blacknell said prosecutors did not explain why they declined to charge Townsend.

Skipp Townsend is a former gang member who for more than two decades has been the head of one of the city’s largest intervention programs and often addresses the media and appears alongside city leaders. Founded in 2006, 2nd Call has sought to mediate gang disputes and provide alternatives to violence in the community.

News of his arrest quickly drew expressions of shock and disbelief from his colleagues — as well as condemnation from those who felt as though Townsend was being unfairly targeted by law enforcement because of the nature of his work.

Sean Garcia-Leys, executive director of the Peace & Justice Law Center, said the arrest and quick rejection of charges against the elder Townsend could hurt LAPD’s ability to collaborate with community members who legitimately can impact gang violence. Garcia-Leys also worried it could scare people off of intervention work.

“People who have been systematically impacted, been arrested and are trying to leave all of those problems behind, this can have a chilling effect on them becoming intervention workers,” Garcia-Leys said. “There’s a personal incentive in intervention work to make amends for bad things you’ve done, give back, but there’s also the desire to not ever get arrested or go to jail or prison again.”

Arrested along with Skipp Townsend on Wednesday were four others: Lenita Sinna Dee Lewis, 28; Shamond “Lil AD” Bennett, 49; Nichole Aaliyah Smith, 23; and Abdelhameed. Prosecutors did not file charges against Lewis, Bennett or Smith.
Foreman, 51, was fatally shot while working with Bennett and a 2nd Call team to clean up a stretch of Crenshaw Boulevard in Hyde Park.

Foreman — known as ”Big Ant” or simply “BA” — was removing weeds at a vacant lot near Crenshaw Boulevard and 60th Street. Witnesses said a youth in a medical face mask walked up to Foreman and Bennett and started shooting.

Foreman took off running, but the shooter caught up to him. Some witnesses said the gunman stood over Foreman and fired into his chest at point-blank range. Bennett was said to have escaped without injuries.

Some gang interventionists said the killing of Foreman may have stemmed from a simmering conflict between two neighboring gangs turned rivals: the 111 Neighborhood Crips that Foreman claimed growing up and Kody Townsend’s alleged gang.

Skipp Townsend has a reputation as the rare peacemaker who has the respect of generations of rival gang members while also earning the trust of senior LAPD officials and members of the city’s civilian Police Commission. A former member of the Rollin’ 20s Bloods, his upbringing included stints in prison.
In a Times profile on Skipp Townsend, Bennett, a onetime Rollin’ 60s member, said: “He is a Blood. He’s going into Crip neighborhood. There’s no more bigger sacrifice than that.”
Some observers of L.A. gang culture argued that the arrest fit a decades-long pattern of harassment by law enforcement of interventionists with criminal pasts.

This year, the LAPD arrested Miguel Angel Alvarez near MacArthur Park and accused the former 18th Street gang member of being a felon in possession of body armor. Alvarez, 41, had been working as a city-sponsored “peace ambassador” with Healing Urban Barrios. The “body armor” in his possession was a metal plate that he planned to use for an art project, his defense attorney said in court records. But prosecutors argued it was an element of a bulletproof vest, even though officers didn’t find a body armor plate carrier when they searched his car.
The case was tossed out in September based on a legal technicality.

In an interview with hip-hop chronicler DJ Vlad released a year ago, Skipp Townsend talked about the melancholy he felt upon learning that his two youngest sons had joined Crips gangs. Even though the boys, who were 17 and 19 at the time of the interview, had been around 2nd Call and its violence prevention efforts, both still had gravitated to the street life, Townsend said.
That “hurt me the most,” said the father of 12.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/crusoe-sells-t.headline: Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/crusoe-sells-t.author: Marina Temkin

paragraphs.text: Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion, confirmed Friday it has sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google.

Google, which Crusoe had tried and failed to land as a customer for the project, is taking over the development after reportedly raising concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe’s management.
Crusoe initially announced the project last year with Blackstone-backed infrastructure company Tallgrass, planning to eventually scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity.
Google did not disclose how much it paid Crusoe for the unfinished project, bu it announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus.

The deal highlights how difficult it can be for independent data center developers to deliver massive projects on time and within budget, given the challenges of securing equipment and power. Growing opposition from local communities can further complicate development.
Despite taking over the Wyoming facility, Google hasn’t walked away from working with Crusoe entirely. Crusoe is developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas.
The deal to sell the site to Google was first reported by Bloomberg in June, but the Wyoming setback didn’t stop Crusoe from raising a $3.9 billion round in September.
Crusoe makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.

Crusoe’s largest projects serve some of the biggest names in AI. Its campus in Abilene, Texas, is being built in phases for Oracle and OpenAI, and the company is also constructing a separate 900-megawatt campus next door for Microsoft, with its first building expected to come online in mid-2027. Meta is also a customer, and Bloomberg reported that the trading firm Jane Street signed a $13 billion, five-year cloud deal with Crusoe.

Crusoe was founded by Chase Lochmiller, now its CEO, and Cully Cavness, who started it as a cryptocurrency-mining business powered by natural gas that would otherwise have been burned off. In September, alongside its $3.9 billion funding round, the company added three board members, including JB Straubel, the Redwood Materials founder and Tesla board member who invested in Crusoe in 2021. Crusoe later became the first customer of Straubel’s energy-storage business.

Marina Temkin is a venture capital and startups reporter at TechCrunch. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she wrote about VC for PitchBook and Venture Capital Journal. Earlier in her career, Marina was a financial analyst and earned a CFA charterholder designation.
