nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/politics/homel.headline: U.S. Homeless Population Had Record Drop in 2025

paragraphs.text: The United States last year experienced the largest decline in homelessness since an annual count began nearly two decades ago, the Department of Housing and Urban Development announced late Friday.

The drop of more than 6 percent was the second consecutive year that the figure had fallen, and reduced the number of homeless people by more than 47,000. Homelessness still far exceeds prepandemic levels.

The reasons for the decline are contested, though the trend likely reflects in part the ebbing of a crisis that began in 2022 when a wave of people seeking asylumwere bused to Northern cities, where they flooded shelters. Most have since left.

The data comes from the annual point-in-time count, which hundreds of local groups conduct every January. While the housing department usually compiles the data into a detailed report before announcing it, the agency instead appeared to hurry a press release on Friday announcing the decline and crediting President Trump.

The department acted after learning that two nonprofit groups had tallied the data from many of the local groups and were releasing their own analyses during what has become a bitter policy debate. Both groups — the National Alliance to End Homelessness and Community Solutions — oppose sweeping changes the Trump administration is trying to make, and see the decline as evidence that progress is possible under current policies.

The Trump administration last year waited months later than usual to release its report on the previous year’s data, which showed a decline of 3 percent. The nonprofit groups seemed eager to avoid a similar delay.

The administration wants deep cuts in so-called Housing First programs, which provide long-term rental subsidies without demanding that homeless people enter treatment for mental illness or addiction. The housing department wants to shift the money to short-term programs with treatment mandates, to address what it calls the root causes of homelessness.

In separate analyses, both nonprofit groups found that the population of homeless people in shelters fell more than 7 percent last year. Unsheltered homelessness dropped nearly 5 percent. In addition, the alliance found that homelessness among veterans declined nearly 8 percent.

The decline “is not only continuing, it’s accelerating,” said Ann Oliva, the alliance’s chief executive officer. “The system is working for a lot of people. The administration’s efforts to gut these programs are way off base.”

According to the counts compiled by Community Solutions, nearly half of last year’s drop in homelessness occurred in four cities that became major destinations for people seeking asylum: New York, Chicago, Boston and Denver. That bolsters the argument that the surge of homelessness that began in 2022 had less to do with the merits of homelessness policy than cross-border flows.

But Adam Ruege, who wrote the Community Solutions report, said that last year’s decline in homelessness went well beyond those cities and amounted to a broader trend. Among the 182 local groups for which he had data, 57 percent registered declining homeless populations.
“More communities are seeing reductions, so that tells us there’s a trend here,” he said. “We believe the country has turned a corner.”

Many other forces might have fueled the drop, and varied greatly from place to place, Mr. Ruege added. He cited increased civic cooperation in cities including Denver, Atlanta and Oklahoma City, and a possible cooling of the housing market in some areas, which might have reduced the number of people entering homelessness.

Even a cursory look at the data Mr. Ruege compiled suggests how intensely local homelessness trends can be. Homelessness fell by 26 percent in affluent Montgomery County, Md., but rose by 3 percent in affluent Fairfax County, Va., just across the Potomac River.
It rose in Los Angeles (1 percent), Seattle (8 percent) and Las Vegas (14 percent), three large urban homelessness hubs. But it fell in two others, San Francisco (8 percent) and Honolulu (8 percent).

In percentage terms, the largest decline occurred in western North Carolina, where homelessness fell by about two-thirds during the ongoing recovery from Hurricane Helene — an up-and-down trend that says little about homelessness policy.

In a press release, Scott Turner, the housing secretary, attributed the decline to “President Trump’s actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities.” The press release placed the 2025 homeless population at 698,425 people.

Devon Kurtz, an analyst for the Cicero Institute, an administration ally, argued that the decline undercut the progressive argument that homelessness is mostly caused by high housing costs. “Housing remains spectacularly expensive in most of the country and yet homelessness still fell,” he said.
Chronic homelessness did not improve, rising about 1 percent, the alliance found. That is a concern, because the chronically homeless are by definition disabled.

But homelessness among veterans continued its long-term drop, falling 7 percent. It has now fallen nearly 60 percent since 2010. Much of that progress has occurred under a Housing First program called HUD-Vash, which Congress funds at much higher levels than other homeless programs. Advocates often cite the trend to argue for the effectiveness of well-funded housing programs.

Ms. Oliva made a point of praising the frontline workers who staff homelessness programs. Some conservatives have argued that the field attracts radical members of the “homelessness industrial complex” who want the problem to grow, to discredit the economic status quo.
“They have been doing incredible work, and they are a big part of the reason that we’re seeing declines two years in a row,” she said.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c68jzzvjgdy9o.headline: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c68jzzvjgdy9o.author: Victoria Bourne, Will Grant

paragraphs.text: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of a digital bank with links to his private business interests.

Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office due to a widening crisis triggered by the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this week.

He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The demise of the digital bank has left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions prompting widespread protests particularly in the capital, Asunción.

The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
Peña is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.
Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Paraguay's Vice-President Pedro Alliana was then sworn in as interim President.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as President until 2028.

Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history – a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".
In an address to the nation on Thursday, Peña said that he was sorry and that "it was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me".

npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6027897/how-oct.headline: How octopuses squeeze through teeny tiny holes
npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6027897/how-oct.author: Ari Daniel

paragraphs.text: MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:

Robots used for search-and-rescue operations need to be able to wriggle through narrow cracks and crevices. A group of researchers has turned to a natural contortionist for inspiration - the octopus. Here is science reporter Ari Daniel.
ARI DANIEL, BYLINE: After a disaster like an earthquake or a train crash, robots can be deployed in unpredictable physical environments to do critical lifesaving work.
WENCI XIN: First of all, try to find out where are the survivors, and then maybe after they reach the spaces that the peoples are, they can pass the water or the food to the survivors.

DANIEL: But four-legged robots and robots with wheels can have a hard time fitting into tight spaces to conduct these operations, says roboticist Wenci Xin, now at the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology. Even undulating, snake-like robots have their shortcomings.
XIN: Even with this kind of long cylinder shape, a robot still has the limited functionalities to do the tasks.

DANIEL: Because they're too narrow to hold emergency supplies or larger mechanical components and sensors, which is why Xin and his colleagues, like biologist Tamar Gutnick of the Vienna Zoo, turned to the octopus.
TAMAR GUTNICK: People are fascinated by the escape-artist aspect of octopuses.
DANIEL: Aside from a rigid capsule around the brain and a small hard beak used for eating, the octopus' body is soft and pliable.

GUTNICK: We know that they can squeeze through all these spaces, but nobody's actually looked at how they do this. So what we did was take octopuses and systematically make them go through different-sized holes.

DANIEL: The researchers enrolled a few common octopuses and several Mayan octopuses, each one the size of an apple, in an experiment at a public aquarium in Vienna. The team cut a hole in a clear] acrylic partition that slid into the tank and then analyzed the video footage of what the animals did next.
GUTNICK: Once they find a hole, they often just naturally will try and go through it.
DANIEL: First, the octopus reached a single arm through the hole to explore the other side. After determining the coast was clear, says Wenci Xin...
XIN: They usually move three to five arms to the other side.
DANIEL: If the hole was big enough, the octopus would then use those arms to pull the rest of its body through by pressing back against the partition.
GUTNICK: This is a sequence of actions that is consistent.

DANIEL: If the opening was smaller than the distance between the animal's eyes, Mayan octopuses wouldn't even attempt to slip through. The common octopus, though - it stuffed all eight of its arms into the hole before actively compressing its body cavity, along with its internal organs, to squeeze on through.
GUTNICK: It's very strange looking.

DANIEL: Tamar Gutnick says the octopuses appear to have a sense of their shifting size and shape and space. In terms of what comes next, Wenci Xin is trying to build a robot that mimics the behavior of the octopuses, which is no easy feat.
XIN: So we are thinking about whether we can bring this capability to the robots so that they can go through those kind of spaces that are really hard to reach.

DANIEL: Which might also include explorations of sunken shipwrecks - these results are published in the Journal of Experimental Biology. Mishu Duduta wasn't involved in the research. He's an engineer at the University of Connecticut who builds robots inspired by living things.
MISHU DUDUTA: Consistently, all those octopi would reach and then pull themselves through, and that kind of has big implications for how we think of robots for search and rescue.
DANIEL: Duduta says designing a robot that pushes versus pulls has been a long-standing debate. The octopus results strengthen the case for pulling. In addition...
DUDUTA: We usually want to send robots to do dangerous work, dull work or dirty work.
DANIEL: The octopuses, he says, point the way toward another kind of work - delicate. For NPR News, I'm Ari Daniel.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/sequoia-shutti.headline: Sequoia shutting down its Scouts program marks the end of an era
techcrunch.com/2026/11/06/sequoia-shutti.author: Anna Heim

paragraphs.text: Sequoia this week announced a broad overhaul in a memo posted to X, a move that includes closing its London office and shutting down its scout program. Observers warn that it would be a mistake to read too much into the London closure, since the British capital has a thriving AI scene. On the other hand, the decision to end scouts says more about where venture investing is headed.

That’s partly because 17 years ago, Sequoia pioneered the scouts model, in which select founders and operators write checks on the firm’s behalf. Amid increased competition for deal flow, many VC firms followed suit. But a consensus now seems to be emerging that the model has reached its limits in its current form.

Not everyone was sold on the model in the first place. “They pioneered the scout program but [to be honest] it never made sense to me!” VC Sheel Mohnot wrote on X this week. “The scouts themselves don’t really care that much about the investments, you can still miss (like they did with Uber), not sure what it gets you. I suspect other firms will shutter theirs too.” he added.

To be clear, Sequoia didn’t make a case against scouts in the memo. Instead, it framed its decision as part of a broader need for more focus. But its goal of “putting more energy behind fewer people and things” is likely to resonate with others who’ve questioned the ‘spray and pray’ approach to scouting.

Rival firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), for instance, rolled out a global scout network aimed at spotting opportunities in the U.S., but also in smaller European hubs. But a16z partner Gabriel Vasquez told TechCrunch earlier this year that the firm had revamped its program to double down “on the best people.”

Under this new approach, Vasquez explained, scouts get more resources but are also expected to be more active, such as by co-hosting dinners with the firm. “They get more budget, but we have reduced the number,” he said.

This also seems to indicate that it is VC firms who have been driving an overhaul of the model. For founders, being a scout is attractive: it brings them closer to firms they may want checks from someday, or even a partner role with, and being seen as someone who can write a check can raise their standing among other founders.

Some scouts will undoubtedly mourn the end of Sequoia’s program. Among them is Station F boss Roxanne Varza, who wrote on LinkedIn that she was “sad” to hear that the program was getting cut off, and “hope[d] that other funds [w]on’t follow suit.”

Varza, a former Sequoia scout from 2020 to 2025, told TechCrunch that she had no information beyond what had been shared publicly, but observed that becoming a scout had often been a stepping stone for aspiring investment managers.

“I cannot name all of the incredible scouts that have gone on to join or build funds, but there are quite a few. And the scout programs may have helped them get there — allowed them to build an investment track record, allowed them to build relationships with various funds directly, and more,” she wrote to TechCrunch.

According to Varza, the program’s impact went beyond the individual level, instead helping the entire ecosystem become more mature. “I believe they have helped to foster the investment culture and early-stage investment landscape that we now see in Europe, for example,” Varza said.

While others may agree with Varza about the role these programs have played, they may still have run their course for two reasons. First, seasoned operators may get more financial upside as angels. When it’s their own money, they get to keep the returns, too. Second, leading VC firms are now big and well-known enough that the best founders tend to come to them, so they worry less about missing deals, except at the very earliest stages or in niches and geographies where they have less reach.

Still, the pull of those early and niche deals is why scouts programs are much more likely to get revamped than to disappear entirely. “While Sequoia may be cutting the program, venture partner-style deals are likely to continue,” said Varza in her email to TechCrunch. “Scouts was just a way to scale the format. I don’t imagine Sequoia would end all forms of venture partners, but they are full of surprises.”
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.
Anna Heim is a writer and editorial consultant.
You can contact or verify outreach from Anna by emailing annatechcrunch [at] gmail.com.
As a freelance reporter at TechCrunch since 2021, she has covered a large range of startup-related topics including AI, fintech & insurtech, SaaS & pricing, and global venture capital trends.
As of May 2025, her reporting for TechCrunch focuses on Europe’s most interesting startup stories.

Anna has moderated panels and conducted onstage interviews at industry events of all sizes, including major tech conferences such as TechCrunch Disrupt, 4YFN, South Summit, TNW Conference, VivaTech, and many more.
A former LATAM & Media Editor at The Next Web, startup founder and Sciences Po Paris alum, she’s fluent in multiple languages, including French, English, Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx5ynly549njo.headline: Jehovah's Witness rules on blood transfusions have changed, but it's too late for my brother
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx5ynly549njo.author: Aleem Maqbool, Catherine Wyatt

paragraphs.text: In August this year, 26-year-old Isaac Valdez had an epileptic seizure while browsing in his local library, causing him to convulse and strike his head against the ground.
He lost consciousness. Later, in hospital, it transpired Isaac had hit his head with such force it had led to a brain haemorrhage.

Treatment was seriously complicated by the fact that, as a Jehovah's Witness, Isaac carried a "No Blood" card, an indication that he would not accept treatment involving any form of blood transfusion because of his religious beliefs.
As a result, a procedure to drain fluid from Isaac's brain did not take place.
But his family, from Waxahachie, Texas, were encouraged by the fact that he regained consciousness and even started to talk again. He was able to confirm that he stood by his "no blood" beliefs.
The family's relief at his apparent improvement was short-lived. Isaac slipped into a coma and his condition worsened rapidly.
A neurosurgeon told Isaac's family the only way to save his life was an emergency operation, but that it was one that required blood transfusion.
His family took the decision to abide by Issac's wishes as a lifelong Witness not to accept such a procedure.
Isaac - who his twin brother Jacob Valdez describes as an intelligent man who loved volunteering and helping the elderly - died on 26 August 2026 when doctors turned off his life support.

Just 23 days later, the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body announced a seismic change in teaching that would, in effect, have given Isaac the religious green light to have the life-saving treatment he had refused.

The change suddenly means the vast majority of medical procedures using donated blood are no longer prohibited to followers. Now, decisions on whether to accept such treatments are to be left to individuals.

Jacob, already dealing with the death of his twin, was angered at the Jehovah's Witnesses' leadership for not coming to their conclusion sooner. He told BBC News he believes Isaac could well still be alive if they had.

The original rule on blood transfusions dates back to 1945, towards the very end of a war during which the use of blood transfusions had been increasingly widespread. The leaders of Jehovah's Witnesses announced that their believers were not permitted to accept transfusions.

This was based on their interpretation of Bible verses from both the Old and New Testaments prohibiting the consumption of blood, including one from the Book of Acts that instructs believers to abstain from blood, from food offered to idols, and from things that had been strangled.
So, why has the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body, based in New York state, now decided to change the rules, 81 years after introducing them?
It comes after years of pressure from both within and outside the faith, but that is not how leaders of the faith describe the decision.

"The change is basically the application of Bible principles to modern medicine and its methods," says the Jehovah's Witnesses international spokesperson, Paul Gillies, who described it as both a fresh look at scripture and at medical advances.

We meet Gillies at the Jehovah's Witnesses UK headquarters set in 85 acres of Essex countryside. It is a vast modern complex where hundreds of volunteer followers of the faith live and work without pay.

He insists the basic teaching has not changed and that the transfusion of whole blood is still prohibited. However, for decades, most transfusions have not used whole blood, instead using the specific components of blood that are needed by the patient.
The change is being justified by permitting the use of blood components, like plasma and red blood cells and platelets, in the huge numbers of medical procedures that were previously banned.
Gillies says the Bible references "abstaining from blood" but not "various components that could be extracted from blood".
He says the Governing Body felt it their duty to avoid scriptural "overreach" and only apply what was specifically described in the Bible.

But that explanation has stunned many and led them to ask if it was not a huge overreach 81 years ago to ban blood transfusions in the first place, when transfusions are not specifically mentioned in the bible.
Others are then also asking why it has taken so long to come to this landmark decision, given that transfusions that do not use whole blood have been the norm for decades.
These are questions Jacob asked as soon as the ban was lifted, just days after a memorial service for Isaac.

Jacob, who had already left the Jehovah's Witness faith he was brought up in, texted prominent figures from Isaac's congregation in Texas after Isaac's death. The messages are full of angst, and painful to read.
He asked them to consider "the part you played in encouraging so many people to sacrifice their life for something that was never God's will".
Most did not reply, but one "elder" responded saying he could not understand why Jacob was so angry and fixated on the policy shift.
This all further infuriated Jacob, who particularly wants the faith's decision-makers to be accountable for all the lives lost.
"I want to ask them if they could apologise directly, I would like not to have a deflected answer, just straightforward apology," he says.

It is extremely difficult to say how many Jehovah's Witnesses, among the estimated nine million followers of the faith worldwide, died each year having refused treatment involving blood transfusions. But research in one medical journal in 2016, The Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey, put the figure at around 1,100.
"We're sympathetic to their feelings, and if individuals have lost family members and are concerned about some of these questions, they deserve to be heard compassionately," says Gillies.
But there was little clarity about why the change did not come earlier.
"Why has it taken this time? Well, I guess because it takes time, it doesn't necessarily mean that there is some magic change that's taken place," says Gillies.

And when asked, Gillies deflects calls for the leadership to apologise, saying that many lives had, in fact, been saved because faithful Jehovah's Witnesses had not been exposed to blood contamination scandals.

He also insists that even after the new edict, some Jehovah's Witnesses could still decide they did not want to accept a transfusion, and that may have been the case even if the edict had come years ago.

Indeed, the BBC spoke with Alex Ball, 58, a Jehovah's Witness from West Sussex, who says in 2012 a doctor told him he would not survive the chemotherapy he needed to treat his blood cancer unless he also had a transfusion.
"I wanted to adhere as closely to the scriptures as possible when I was sick, and I think I did that well."

With help from what is called "a Jehovah's Witness Hospital Liaison Committee", Alex found an American consultant who could perform a treatment to boost Alex's blood cells without the need for any products from someone else. His UK consultant agreed to treat him using the new method and it worked.
More than a decade later, Alex says he would make the same decision again, despite the change in blood policy that would have permitted the transfusions he had been told he needed.
It is not just receiving blood which has been an issue.
Elisha Cummings, 50, a Jehovah's Witness from Trinidad and Tobago, was unable to donate blood to her aunt, who died, because of the rules.

They also cost her her marriage too, with her husband of 10 years leaving the faith and divorcing her after it came to light that he had had a blood transfusion as a child, something that was looked down upon in her Witness community.
"Since the blood policy change, I have not been myself," she says. "It left me in a sort of depressed mode."
"How many houses did I go to trying to convince people about the blood doctrine? And you're coming now and it's something totally different," Elisha says.
Elisha says her beliefs as a whole have been shaken, yet she feels reluctant to leave the faith, partly because it is what provides her with her community and she fears isolation.
In the past, those who disagreed with "blood doctrine" were ostracised or felt like they needed to leave the faith. Will they now be able to come back?
"Any individual that wants to come back to the faith is warmly welcomed," says Gillies, speaking of those who had left the faith because they had accepted a transfusion for themselves or a relative.
"If they would like to become one of Jehovah's Witnesses again and would like to speak to the elders, then they're very welcome to do so."

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq0k0lg48705o.headline: Mogadishu tourism: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees her city
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq0k0lg48705o.author: Fardowsa Hanshi

paragraphs.text: As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.

This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.
Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.
Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes.
"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.
The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara.

But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers.
Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea.
Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity.
"Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says.
At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species.
Guiding tours runs in Sucdi's family. Her father worked in the profession for over three decades, taking journalists, photographers and visitors from different countries around Somalia.
He introduced her to the business nearly three years ago.
"I started this job as a hobby, but it has become something that I like and am passionate about," she says.
She now works alongside her father and a team of guides, building on his experience while using social media to reach a wider audience.
She shares videos of her tours on TikTok, offering people outside Somalia a glimpse of places they may never have imagined visiting.
She is also considering producing content in English to reach audiences who do not speak Somali.
Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu.

The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow.
However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security.

Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down.

But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation.

Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital.
Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life.
About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department.
Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city.
But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive.
"What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says.
Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue.
She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen.
"I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says.
Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.
Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade.
For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking.
American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice.
His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media.
"I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says.
What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere.
"It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says.
During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes.
"The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says.
Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage.
"If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines."
But visiting the country challenged those perceptions.
"Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says.
Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia's natural beauty.
Although she has spent only a few hours in Mogadishu, she has already visited the sand dunes and taken in the Indian Ocean coastline.
"The desert was so beautiful to see. I have also enjoyed the beach, and the ocean. It is inspiring," she says.
Having travelled to Somalia from neighbouring Ethiopia, she says she has been struck by the people's friendliness.
"I don't see anything dangerous. I feel safe and the people are warm," she says.
An experienced traveller, Mihaela says she prefers to visit new countries without having preconceived ideas.
"I travel the world to see new places, to see countries, to see the differences. I don't take a picture in my mind to compare the reality with. I'm just expecting the new to come to me," she says.
She hopes to share her experience and encourage others to visit Somalia.
"I'm going to post my pictures and say good things about what I'm experiencing. I'm going to promote it," she says.
For Sucdi, that potential is personal.
She is continuing a family profession while building a business in an industry with few women and using digital platforms to reach audiences far beyond Mogadishu.
"Somalia still has a long way to go before tourism becomes a major industry," she says.
"Through my tours, I am giving visitors an opportunity to experience its landscapes, our culture and people beyond the familiar negative headlines."
For her, every visitor is another opportunity to tell a fuller story of Mogadishu.
