bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60e0001ve9wo.headline: Pope Leo in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60e0001ve9wo.author: Sarah Rainsford, Victoria Bourne

paragraphs.text: Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.
The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.
The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.
The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru, which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop.
"I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay.
"Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.
Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.
On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.
In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".
He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.
He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral.
Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.
On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.
The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology.headline: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology.author: Anish Nangia

paragraphs.text: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash brings 15-second clips, stronger consistency, and faster, more cost-effective generation.
Product Manager, Google DeepMind
Your browser does not support the audio element.

Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.
Here’s an overview of what’s new:
Fast and cost-effective at scale

Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
Longer clips up to 15 seconds

You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.
Better reference adherence

You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.

Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.
More consistent results

You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.

Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.
Easier editing in conversation

You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating.

Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact.
More natural speech

You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in Flow, creating video explainers in Gemini for business, or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in Google Vids.

Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene.
More controllable, cinematic look

You can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look.

Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts.
Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistency

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts.
15 second long clips: Turns one style frame into a 4-shot, 15-second macro science explainer with accurately spelled, motion-tracked callouts.
Multi-turn motion transfer: Generates a rippling octopus in Turn 1, then replaces it in Turn 2 with a dancer whose gown mirrors the exact fluid motion.

First-to-last frame consistency (1.1 vs. 1.2): Connects an exterior start frame and interior end frame in one continuous camera push in 1.2 Flash. You can see subtle differences like the cats on the roof, the soup ladle turning into chopsticks, and some other minor changes.
Unbroken crash zoom-out: Pulls continuously from a tight shoreline close-up to an aerial island vista in one 10-second shot with natural scale and zero cuts.
Real-world results, from creatives to global brands

Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.
Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash

While development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms:
• For developers using the Gemini API: Prototype in Google AI Studio, explore interactive starter apps, and check out the developer documentation and pricing.
• For businesses: Try it in the Google Cloud console, and build enterprise solutions with the API.

cnbc.com/2026/11/07/hoax-bomb-threats-fl.headline: Why a wave of bomb threats is proving so difficult for Europe's aviation authorities to contain
cnbc.com/2026/11/07/hoax-bomb-threats-fl.author: Jenni Reid

paragraphs.text: A spate of bomb threats against passenger flights has forced diversions, emergency landings and military escorts across European airspace this week, stoking fear among passengers and heaping pressure on airlines.

Authorities have described the more than two dozen threats as malicious hoaxes, and no actual attacks have been carried out. But the incidents have highlighted the huge impact that even false claims can have on a tightly scheduled aviation network.
"This is really quite exceptional, I've never seen this before in my whole career," Wilfried Covent, head of security firm Covent Consulting with a specialization in aviation, told CNBC by phone.
"We've had bomb threats in flights and towards airports, but usually maybe a single copycat, one or two max. What we see now is a systematic attack on airlines and airports."

An email sent to European broadcasters on Friday claimed to be from the leader of the group behind the plane hoaxes and also said bombs had been placed in their buildings, prompting evacuations. No bombs were found at the sites.
"What happened this week is just a small part of what awaits Europe in the near future," the message said, according to Reuters.
The news agency said it could not verify the sender's identity, where the emails originated or whether they were linked to the threats against flights.

Covent said the "criminals" — who many security analysts say are likely to be state-backed actors working in coordination to disrupt public life for Europeans, but have not been identified — were well aware that the "weakest point of aviation is targeting it in-flight."

"With a threat on an airport or a general threat to aircraft, you can assess the situation without fully disrupting operations. When the threat is called on a specific flight number that is in the air, even with a hoax, that triggers international regulations which ensure you don't ignore it — it means a quick landing, evacuation and searches by specialist forces," he told CNBC.

"For the context of an assessment, you cannot say that 20 times before it has been a hoax so this time it is a hoax, the safety of passengers and crew is priority number one. The criminals know that."
Coordinated response

Responsibility for dealing with hoax attacks is split, international agencies told CNBC. Assessing security threats and implementing aviation security measures primarily falls to national authorities, working in coordination with airport operators, airlines and law enforcement.

Air traffic control will also be involved in finding aircraft with an appropriate place to land, while the European Union Aviation Safety Agency, or EASA and U.K.'s Civil Aviation Authority more broadly set aviation safety rules and set how airlines prepare their crews to respond to security threats. Within the European Union, the European Commission is involved in aviation security policy and coordination between member states.

The operational decisions also depend on where the threat arises. Joji Waites, director of flight safety, policy and regulation at the British Air Line Pilots Association, said airline assessors grade a threat as red, amber or green, but that an amber verdict would never be given if the plane is airborne.

If assessors judge a threat credible, the crew is informed and the captain takes command of decisions for the aircraft, guided by company procedures. On the ground, that may mean an evacuation, while in the air the priority is to land as soon and as safely as possible.
As well as the fear and disruption to specific flights, each diversion can then affect the next flight scheduled to use that aircraft, the crew's working hours and passengers with connections.

The network effect can be significant. Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University, told AP that a single diversion could cost an airline as much as $250,000, including replacement crews, missed connections and disruption to the rest of the day's schedule.

"Diversions necessitated by these bomb threats are a disturbance to a system designed for predictability and efficiency, and lead to increased workload for pilots, Air Traffic Controllers and airports," an EASA spokesperson said in emailed comments.

"As these staff have all have been trained to cope with such unexpected developments, the immediate safety threat from individual hoax threats is low. However, the higher number of diversions places an additional strain on the system."
What can change?

National governments will already be looking at their aviation authority regulations and frameworks and there will be discussions at the European and global level, John Edwards, senior consultant at Gates Aviation in London, said by phone.

"Bomb threats to aviation have been going on for decades, what they'll need to be looking at is what's different. Why have there been so many, why have so many been considered sufficiently credible to warrant the kind of action that it's warranted?"

"There's a range of questions they should be able to work through fairly quickly to establish a broad-brush level of credibility. If there is some characteristic that is new, every time there is an event of this kind, it triggers a big collaboration to ensure recurrence is prevented going forward."
"In theory, he said, "the vast majority should be able to assessed and considered non-credible based on routine risk assessment processes and well established procedures."

However, Eric Schouten, a former intelligence liaison officer at the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service and CEO of security consultancy Dyami, said that changes to existing procedural regulations would take some time and require balancing the views and responsibilities of countries, airports, safety authorities and the European Union, with geopolitics also playing a role.
"There is a high likelihood even more flights are going to be canceled or diverted. It's possible that next to be targeted could be railways and highways," he said.
"But they will figure it out. It's not the first time airlines have had to deal with hoax calls because there are always copycats."
"Whatever measures they come out with to address it, they won't share publicly" for risk of alerting the bad actors, he added.

Wilfried Covent said that while there would not be any quick changes to assessment protocol, "if this is really going on for ever and ever something will need to change or you'd have to stop flying completely."

"Based on what we've seen in the past with other kinds of threats, time goes on and the type of attack may change and move on," he continued, pointing to the wave of cyberattacks that has recently hit supermarket fridges and blood banks.
"As Europeans we need to be prepared."

cnbc.com/2026/11/07/proxima-fusion-power.headline: The race is on to build the first fusion power plant — and Europe is looking to Japan for help
cnbc.com/2026/11/07/proxima-fusion-power.author: Ian King

paragraphs.text: The race is on to build the world's first commercial fusion power plant — and one of Europe's leading contenders in the field has just received a boost.

Munich-based Proxima Fusion signed memoranda of understanding with two Japanese industrial partners, Fujikura and Kyoto Fusioneering, in Tokyo on Oct. 28. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — who was visiting in a bid to deepen trade ties — were both in attendance.

Ann Mettler, president of Catalyse Europe, a Brussels-based clean-energy think tank, and a former vice president of Breakthrough Energy, said developing the technology should be a strategic imperative for Europe.

"Europe is a resource-poor geography and we are very dependent on China. The world is in competition for technological supremacy — this is a zero-sum game," Mettler told CNBC, speaking in a personal capacity.
"Fusion is a silver bullet because the promise is abundant, clean, limitless energy."
Fusion energy seeks to replicate the way the sun produces power, using super-heated plasma to fuse two light atomic nuclei into one heavier one, releasing vast amounts of energy in the process.

There are two main approaches: one uses high-powered lasers, while the other uses powerful magnets to confine the plasma. Proxima is developing a type of magnetic device called a stellarator, which is designed to hold the plasma in place for long periods.
The agreement with Kyoto Fusioneering will expand existing work on next-generation gyrotrons — devices that generate high-power microwaves used to heat the plasma.
Why HTS tape matters

Proxima's agreement with 141-year-old Fujikura will explore plans for industrial-scale manufacturing in Germany of high-temperature superconducting, or HTS, tape, a specialized metallic tape that is superconducting at relatively high temperatures and can carry electrical current with virtually no resistive losses.
The tape is wound into coils to form powerful magnets that confine and control the heated plasma inside the stellarator.

Francesco Sciortino, CEO and co-founder of Proxima Fusion, told CNBC that Fujikura, which employs over 50,000 people worldwide, was a leader in manufacturing high-temperature superconductors, having built its reputation in optical fibers. "They think this tape has the potential to be the next optical fibre," he said.
He said Proxima, which is studying plans to build a manufacturing facility in Lower Saxony, hoped to make around 5,000 kilometers, or 3,100 miles, of tape annually by 2030.

The 140 million euro ($160 million) facility would be financed partly by the proceeds of a $468 million funding round in July, which valued Proxima, whose backers include Alphabet-owned Google, at $2.7 billion.

Proxima expects to need around 20,000 kilometers (12,400 miles) of the tape for its "Alpha" fusion demonstrator and a further 40,000 kilometers (24,900 miles) for its planned "Stellaris" fusion power station.
Europe’s fusion supply chain

Sciortino said that establishing production of the tape in Germany was crucial as it would help Europe create the expertise and supply chains needed to turn its fusion research leadership into industrial capability.
This is where Europe has historically struggled, according to Catalyse Europe's Mettler.
If Europe is first to develop this technology, it will give us a huge advantage, but key to that will be building the supply chainAnn MettlerCatalyse Europe
"Every geography wants to turn leadership in science into industrial leadership and this is where Europe has traditionally been not so good — turning that scientific leadership into euros," she said.
While Europe had industrial giants to be proud of, disruptors tended to be more successful in frontier technologies, according to Mettler.
"If Europe is first to develop this technology, it will give us a huge advantage, but key to that will be building the supply chain," she said.
Commercial fusion competitors
Sciortino said he remains confident Proxima will be the first company to turn on a pilot plant — but stressed the key to profitability would be making that plant as simple as possible to operate.

"You can have complexity in the design, manufacturing and operation of the plant," he said. "We can take care of the complexity in the design and manufacturing, but our view is that there needs to be simplicity in the operation. We are aiming for net energy gain during the early 2030s."

But Proxima has some well-heeled competitors. They include U.S.-based Commonwealth Fusion Systems, which is also backed by Google, and Helion Energy, as well as Canada's General Fusion. China has a number of state-backed players, most notably China Fusion Energy Co., while Tokyo-based Helical Fusion leads Japan's push.
"The supply chain in fusion energy needs to be built years before — people often think of frontier technologies as a switch that can be thrown," Mettler said. "That is not the case here."

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/card-pokemon-grading.headline: Inside the card-grading empire shaping the price of Pokémon cards
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/card-pokemon-grading.author: Matthew Tan

paragraphs.text: Collectors may have more grading options than ever, but many still turn to Professional Sports Authenticator, or PSA — even as the industry leader works through a backlog of millions of cards.
Demand for grading — an act of verifying a card’s authenticity and condition — has grown as collectors increasingly treat trading and vintage sports cards as alternative investments.

PSA reported a backlog of 7.2 million items on Oct. 20, down from 12.4 million in July. The company suspended cheaper submission services in June to ease the backlog before reopening its Value service on Oct. 29.
Even so, some sellers would rather wait for a PSA label than send their cards to a competitor, dealers told CNBC.
“It really all comes down to secondary market values,” said Geoff Wilson, founder and CEO of CardsHQ, which operates one of the world's largest sports card shops.
PSA-graded cards typically command higher prices than equivalent grades from competitors, Wilson said, giving collectors and investors an incentive to choose PSA in hopes of a stronger return.
The financial difference can be substantial.
A 1999 Base Set Charizard graded PSA 9 sold for about $3,440 on eBay on Sept. 29, compared with roughly $1,890 for a CGC 9 copy sold the same day, according to CNBC's review of PriceCharting records.
That pricing gap reinforces PSA's lead and gives its decisions about fees and submission services considerable influence over the resale market.

PSA had not responded to CNBC’s detailed questions at the time of publication. In published updates, the company has attributed service restrictions and pricing changes to demand exceeding capacity, and outlined investments intended to reduce the backlog.
The 'gold standard'

Grading companies verify a card’s authenticity, assess its condition and seal it in a protective plastic case, known as a slab. PSA uses a 10-point scale, with its highest grade, Gem Mint 10, reserved for cards it describes as "virtually perfect."
Like a credit rating in bond markets, a card grade gives buyers and sellers a common benchmark for assessing condition.
That can reduce friction in transactions by giving both sides a reference point based on past sales of the same card at the same grade.

That capability has helped open the trading-card market to more global participation and made cross-border transactions easier, according to an unnamed spokesperson for Singapore-based submission dealer Oxley Grading.
The spokesperson attributed PSA’s position as the industry’s “gold standard” to its early start, brand recognition and extensive history of completed sales.
“They've just built up such a strong branding and a lot of sales records,” the spokesperson said.
They estimated that roughly 90% of the graded cards offered to Oxley Grading for purchase carry PSA’s label.

The dominance creates a self-reinforcing cycle: buyers seek out PSA-graded cards, giving sellers an incentive to use the company. The abundance of PSA slabs in shops and online marketplaces further reinforces the brand's visibility and demand.
For a seller choosing a grader, that established resale demand can outweigh a competitor’s lower fees or faster turnaround times.
The collectible empire
PSA sits within a larger collectibles business.

Its parent company, Collectors, also owns rival grading brands Beckett and SGC, pricing-data platform Card Ladder, the PSA Vault and financial services. The vault links storage with selling through external marketplaces, including eBay.
Together, those businesses span much of a card’s commercial journey — grading, pricing, storage, sales and even financing against collectibles.

Collectors' three card-grading brands accounted for roughly 71% of August grading volume among the major firms tracked by industry analyst GemRate. PSA alone represented about 65%, while the next-largest player, CGC, represented about 28%.
Collectors' consolidation has also drawn legal scrutiny.

A proposed class action filed in April challenges Collectors’ acquisitions of SGC and Beckett, alleging that the deals unlawfully reduced competition in card grading. The allegations have not been proven in court.
Collectors has defended the Beckett acquisition as a way to strengthen a trusted brand while preserving collectors’ ability to choose the grading service that best suits their items.
“We believe that strong, well-supported brands help grow access to the hobby,” Collectors CEO Nat Turner said in the company's 2025 acquisition announcement.
Cost of market dependence
For sellers who prioritize PSA's resale premium, changes to its fees and submission services can alter the economics of grading a card.

PSA raised fees across several existing tiers in February, including Value Bulk from $21.99 to $24.99 and Value from $27.99 to $32.99. It also lengthened estimated turnaround times for some services, saying the changes would help balance submission demand with grading capacity.

The suspension of cheaper tiers in June further narrowed affordable options, while higher costs have made customers more selective about which cards they submit, according to Oxley Grading's spokesperson.
Meanwhile, Wilson said the restrictions have particularly affected collectors and dealers who buy cards ungraded, send them to PSA and then resell them at a higher price.
For cards worth a few hundred dollars or less, that strategy has become harder to justify, he said.
“You're seeing more raw cards bought and sold at card shows,” Wilson added, using the industry term for ungraded cards.
PSA has acknowledged that customers are waiting too long.

In an Oct. 28 update, the company said submissions in April and May were 2.5 times the volume received in the same months a year earlier. It also announced shorter turnaround estimates for Standard and Priority services, while saying new Value submissions would be processed behind existing orders.
“We have added an incredible amount of capacity, but we still have work to do,” Ryan Hoge, president of PSA and grading at Collectors, said in the statement.
For Wilson, those investments in capacity are part of PSA's appeal.
“They've made the collector experience better by doing that,” he said.
Limited bargaining power
The leading graders' dominance may leave collectors with little room to push back.

Collectors' preference for PSA's resale value can make switching graders less attractive, the Oxley Grading's spokesperson said, adding, "PSA's lead comes from resale demand and liquidity, and other labels are still building that."
Overseas customers can face fewer practical grading options as many major graders are based in the U.S., Amber Chuah, operations manager of trading-card platform TCG Marketplace, told CNBC.
The complaints she hears most often involve long waits and disappointment when cards receive lower grades than customers expected.
Challenging a grade can require another round of shipping and waiting, discouraging some collectors from disputing the result, she added.
"If you're really keen on selling, that's a lot of time."
PSA did not respond to CNBC's questions about the sources' claims.

PSA’s terms allow customers to request a paid review of disputed grades, with customers responsible for grading and applicable shipping fees. The company also offers defect notes for eligible submissions to provide more detail on how a grade was determined.
CardsHQ's Wilson said some variation between assessments is an inherent challenge in a process that involves human judgment.
Challenging PSA
Wilson pushes back against the suggestion that PSA’s position leaves customers without alternatives.
“First of all, there are alternatives,” he said, pointing to CGC, Beckett and smaller grading firms such as TAG.

CGC’s grading volume in August was more than double its level a year earlier, according to GemRate, showing that rival graders are attracting business. Beckett also recorded strong growth, although it is owned by Collectors.

Oxley Grading's spokesperson said there may be room for lower-cost services aimed at collectors who care more about a card’s artwork, sentimental value or preservation than maximizing its resale value.
Competing for sellers focused on the strongest financial return remains more difficult.
Building comparable resale acceptance would require substantial investment, with no guarantee that buyers would ultimately value a newcomer's label as highly as PSA's, the spokesperson said.
For Wilson, broader acceptance in the resale market is key to shifting that balance.
“If the market as a whole starts to respect the value of the other grading companies' cards more, then collectors will increasingly submit to those companies,” he said.

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/defense-military-tec.headline: Drones are changing warfare. But defense giants are still making billions from old-school weapons
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/defense-military-tec.author: Elsa Ohlen

paragraphs.text: Drone technology and artificial intelligence are rapidly reshaping modern warfare, but the world's biggest defense contractors are finding that demand for tanks, fighter jets and other traditional military equipment remains strong.

Recent earnings from U.S. and European defense companies show conventional weapons continue to drive year-on-year growth, even alongside surging demand for advanced sensors, autonomous systems and counter-drone technology.
Rather than displacing traditional weapons manufacturers, the rise of drones and autonomous warfare is creating new business for many of the same companies.

From counter-drone defenses to advanced sensors integrated into tanks and fighter jets, the technologies transforming the battlefield are also changing, or even expanding, the markets served by legacy defense giants.
Legacy defense remains strong

Lockheed Martin reported a 24% jump in revenue from its missiles business in the third quarter, while RTX secured multibillion-dollar contracts for established missile systems. In Europe, German defense supplier Renk saw orders for its military vehicle business surge 46% in the first nine months of the year.
Yet, the same earnings also show how the boundaries between legacy weapons and emerging defense technology are increasingly blurred.

German defense electronics company Hensoldt reported a 52% jump in revenue from its optronics business, with its chief financial officer telling CNBC that much of the growth came from conventional military equipment, including tanks and armored vehicles.
Meanwhile, Rheinmetall's air defense business, which includes counter-drone systems, reported 63% revenue growth, even as the wider company cut its full-year outlook, citing project delays.
A changing battlefield

The rise of drones is transforming traditional military platforms rather than replacing them, with tanks and other weapons increasingly integrated into connected, data-driven battlefield networks, according to Morningstar.
Over the past five years and since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, defense primes have seen their order books swell amid higher military spending among governments globally.

Yet, analysts mostly say that the rearmament boom is structural, and even an end to wars in Ukraine and Iran won't derail it. Crucially, Europe now has to play catch-up amid increasing uncertainty over U.S. security guarantees and Russia's next move, after decades of military underfunding.
However, concerns that valuations had run ahead of the industry's ability to deliver dented defense stocks this year amid several instances of project delays and contract cancellations.

Advancements in modern warfare and technology – as proven by Ukraine's use of drones on the front lines – further hit investor confidence in defense contractors amid worries that new technologies may displace demand for traditional military equipment.

Beyond the front line, NATO plans to invest more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities over the next five years, as Secretary General Mark Rutte warned that drones have fundamentally transformed modern warfare.
Even so, Hensoldt CFO Christian Ladurner told CNBC on Thursday that demand for traditional military equipment remains a key driver of growth.

Its fast-growing optronics business, which supplies optical and sensor technologies, is benefiting from European governments' efforts to replenish conventional military equipment, even as newer battlefield technologies attract increasing attention, Ladurner said.

He also highlighted growing demand for air defense systems, as militaries confront an expanding range of threats, from small drones to ballistic missiles, adding that the air defense market is "underinvested" despite growing by 20% a year.

Limits to Patriot interceptors produced by Lockheed Martin are being felt hard, not least in Ukraine, after the U.S. depleted much of its stockpile of the state-of-the-art system able to take down high-speed missiles in the Iran war.
U.S. midterm fears
More recently, defense stocks have come under pressure amid concerns that the Democrats' U.S. midterm victories could squeeze American military spending.

While the result has dampened expectations for defense spending, with Democratic control of Congress making a proposed $1.5 trillion budget unlikely and potentially weighing on military spending growth through 2029, nothing has materially changed the geopolitical calculations, TD Cowen analyst Roman Schweizer told CNBC's "Morning Call" on Thursday.

"This is a multi-year picture, and I think we've seen those changes both in the U.S. and also Europe," he said, referencing internal budgetary difficulties and questions around NATO's hiked spending targets.
Morningstar analyst Loredana Muharremi told CNBC Wednesday's weakness in European defense stocks was largely sentiment-driven.

"Some investors may now see a greater chance of stronger US backing for Europe, easing the pressure on European governments to spend more [but] even with stronger US backing, we expect Europe to stick to its spending plans," she said.
"It takes years of investment to close the gaps in Europe's own military capabilities and build the industrial capacity it needs to deter Russia."

nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/tesla-wind-cy.headline: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production after years of poor sales in few markets
nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/tesla-wind-cy.author: Reuters

paragraphs.text: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks that ultimately only sold in just a handful of markets because of its heavy, angular design.

Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla's robotaxi ambitions.

While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model's specialized components.
In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era."
Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours.

The US EV maker only began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Before the pickup truck launched, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.
"It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same."
"It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves."

Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Its angular design was mocked by pickup truck purists and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.
The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them - only to leave massive cracks in two of them.
During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future."
But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations.

Automotive analyst Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pick-ups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market.
"All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said.

But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact.
"Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said.
The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker.
Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis.

After years of delays to Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards.
"Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/06/bett.headline: Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’
theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/06/bett.author: Ian Sample

paragraphs.text: As an early stab at rules for conversation, Cicero did a fine job: watch your tone, never look bored, never lose your temper and never ramble on, particularly about yourself, he advised.

Now scientists have followed in the great orator’s footsteps and discovered a telltale signature of an enjoyable chinwag. The secret of a mutually satisfying exchange is a healthy dose of pink noise, they say.

The colour of noise tends to animate physicists more than linguists, but researchers at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire in the US found the concept provided fresh insights into what makes a good conversation.

Kathryn O’Nell, the first author on the study, said: “In physics, people talk about pink noise as existing on the edge of chaos, where you can stay at a stable point, but you’re not stuck there for ever.
“It’s particularly cool for conversation, because you can stay somewhere long enough to really get to know each other, to understand the topic, but you’re not stuck there while it gets stale.”

The researchers analysed more than 1,000 conversations between strangers, who answered questions on the chats afterwards. People enjoyed conversations more, wanted to continue chatting, and felt a stronger sense of connection when the tête-à-têtes exhibited more pink noise, they found.

To see whether the effect applied beyond strangers, the researchers ran a similar analysis on conversations between friends about their formative experiences. Again, more pink noise meant more enjoyment.

The effect had real-world consequences, too. When the scientists turned to speed-dating conversations, they found that more pink noise predicted which pairs met up for a second date. Details have been published in Science Advances.

Nailing down what makes a great chat is notoriously tricky, the researchers said. In a bold opening statement to their paper, the authors write: “Good conversation is like pornography – it is difficult to define, but we know it when we see it.”

Colloquially, people talk about being in sync, but the metaphor misses something, said Dr Emily Finn, a neuroscientist and senior author on the paper. “In sync can be incredibly dull,” she said. People can be in sync when they repeat each other’s words and circle a single subject. They might well be immensely bored.

In the study, the scientists took conversations and fed each side into an AI called MPNet. The program scored every turn of the chat on 768 different criteria, covering aspects such as meaning, tone and context. This allowed the scientists to quantify how conversations ebbed and flowed over time.

Conversations exhibit white noise when people fail to follow what has just been said: the chat might jump all over the place, or be dominated by a person who seems oblivious to the other person’s responses. Other conversations can have red noise, which arises when people mirror each other’s language and fall into a conversational rut.

Pink noise lies somewhere in between: a conversational Goldilocks zone that balances stability and flexibility. People will synchronise as they explore a topic, then drift apart as they pull in fresh ideas before converging again to explore those.

The pinkiness of a conversation depends on the people involved, but O’Nell said she suspected the skill could be learned and developed. As part of the study, the team analysed podcasts fronted by two hosts and found that the pinkiness of their conversations increased over the first 50 episodes.

Prof Elizabeth Stokoe, a conversation analyst at the London School of Economics, praised the researchers for moving beyond the idea that “more similarity is better”. But asking whether a conversation is enjoyable risks missing the point, she added.

“There’s a lovely study of a phone call in which a father and his daughter, a young woman with learning disabilities living in residential care, take a long time to say goodbye, and the ending is painful and poignant,” she said. “Reducing conversations to whether they are ‘enjoyable’ can feel bloodless, since many of the conversations that matter most in our lives are like this.”

theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/07/hom.headline: Home Office sued after stripping almost 1,500 EU citizens of right to live in UK
theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/07/hom.author: Lisa O’Carroll

paragraphs.text: The Home Office is being sued for alleged breach of the Brexit withdrawal agreement after stripping almost 1,500 EU citizens of their full rights to live in the UK.

Campaign group the3million lodged papers at the high court on Friday after several cases emerged of EU citizens who were granted pre-settled status to remain in the country after Brexit but were told recently those decisions were an “error”.

According to the statement of claim, the Home Office decision to remove all or some rights from citizens granted pre-settled status was made without “procedural protections” required under the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA).

These protections include a right of an appeal and an assessment of “proportionality”, which would establish whether removal of rights was appropriate given the EU citizens in question built their lives in the UK on the basis of the Home Office’s original decision.

Among the people affected by the Home Office policy was a 33-year-old Brazilian Italian engineer who has been in London since 2018. He was originally told that he should not have settled status: he could stay but his Brazilian wife could not, a decision that was reversed in the last few weeks after objections were raised.

Another EU citizen who raised her case with the3million is a woman working in the NHS and studying for a PhD in dentistry. She has said the Home Office’s notification had “turned her life upside down”.

In October 2026, the Home Office accepted that where a person provides evidence of their Italian citizenship, together with evidence that this was obtained through jure sanguinis, they would now accept that this person was an Italian from birth.

Previously it told a number of Brazilian Italians they were granted status “in error” because they had not presented an Italian passport at the time of their application, merely stating they were Italian citizens.

Monique Hawkins, acting CEO of the3million, said: “The Home Office is putting the cart before the horse. It denies people the safeguards the withdrawal agreement guarantees – a fair assessment and a right of appeal – because it says they are ‘clearly’ not covered by the agreement. That’s like saying someone doesn’t need a trial because they’re ‘clearly’ guilty.”
She said the Home Office U-turn on jure sanguinis Italian nationals showed it could change its policy when its errors were exposed.

Hawkins said: “This is a simple matter of providing proper due process. Despite our advocacy efforts since early 2025, the Home Office refused to change course, so we have no option but to challenge the policy in court.”

The campaign group is asking the court to declare that the “grant in error policy is unlawful, by breach of the WA and/or common law” and make whatever order is necessary to “excise the offending parts of the published policy”

Many complained that although they were jure sanguinis (direct and unbroken Italian relative), they could not get a passport because the public institutions were in lockdown during the coronavirus pandemic.

Lawyers have also argued that the apparent generosity of the UK, which minimised the evidence required by any EU citizens applying to stay after Brexit, “compounded” the current Home Office policy of removing rights.

The unlawfulness of the policy is compounded by the nature of the EU settlement scheme itself. The UK deliberately implemented a scheme that, in a number of respects, operated more generously than the minimum requirements of the WA.
Hawkins said: “Grants were also made through processes involving evidential flexibility and, in some cases, discretionary decision-making.

“As a result, many status holders cannot know, and are given no means of knowing, whether their status was granted because they satisfied the substantive requirements of the WA, because they satisfied the requirements of Appendix EU as a matter of domestic law, because a caseworker exercised evidential flexibility or discretion in their favour, or because the grant was genuinely erroneous.”

Several cases have come to light of Brazilians who have Italian parents or grandparents. Under Italian law these citizens are Italian by birth but the Home Office alleged they were not because they did not have an Italian passport at the time.
This is not the first time the Home Office has been sued over its implementation of the withdrawal agreement.
In 2022 it was taken to court by the statutory watchdog set up to ensure the Home Office implemented the withdrawal agreement properly.

The Independent Monitoring Authority, backed by the3million, accused the Home Office of putting EU citizens at risk of losing their rights to work or rent a home by forcing them to reapply for settled status once their pre-settled status expired.
High court judges ruled in the IMA’s favour concluding the conditions imposed by the Home Office were unlawful.
A spokesperson for the Home Office said they could not comment as proceedings were ongoing.

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/07/desp.headline: Despite midterm rebuke of Trump, allies see U.S. turning further away
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/07/desp.author: Greg Miller

paragraphs.text: LONDON — After two years of rocky relations with President Donald Trump, America’s allies had reason to revel in the midterm rebuke of a commander in chief who targeted them with tariffs, threatened to seize their territories and often seemed more enamored with his autocratic peers in Moscow and Pyongyang.

Instead, the drubbing of Trump and Republicans in congressional races has drawn a muted response from U.S. allies, many of whom see the election as the latest political spasm in a country that, no matter how mighty, can no longer be trusted as a reliable defender of global democracy, Western officials and experts said.

In recent days, officials in Canada, Europe and Asia voiced relief that U.S. democratic mechanisms were not derailed and, in interviews and social media posts, they expressed cautious optimism that Trump’s penchant for attacks and threats might be curbed.

Yet many described the election result as offering limited comfort, as voters turned against a combative president but not his America First agenda — a nation turning further inward, officials said, with scant regard for the fate of allies and partners or any discernible longing to resume its former role as leader and defender of the free world.

“We are reassured by the strength of democracy,” said a senior Canadian official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to express candid views about U.S. political developments. “But we will not contemplate a shift in our own course. Folks here don’t believe the old ways are ever coming back and are conducting themselves accordingly.”

While Trump has been the main driver of ruptures in the transatlantic alliance, he is accelerating a decoupling that Americans broadly favor, Gérard Araud, who served as French ambassador to the United States during Trump’s first term in office, said in a social media post.
“Americans are leaving a Europe they see more and more as a periphery of the world,” Araud said.

Disengagement is now the default across the U.S. political spectrum, he said, “the Democrats politely but inexorably and Trump brutally. They both close the door behind them but he slams it on our fingers.”
Surveys of voters appeared to substantiate these interpretations, showing that their decisions were driven overwhelmingly by concerns about the economy and other domestic issues.

The war in Iran was a singular exception, registering as a “top national issue” for one-third of the more than 90,000 midterm voters surveyed this week by the research firm NORC in partnership with The Washington Post.

But even that conflict was viewed mostly through the prism of domestic politics, with voters aggrieved to be paying higher fuel prices with little regard for ripple effects on allies, such as the soaring energy prices in Europe and months of deadly, damaging missile strikes on partner nations throughout the Middle East.

The Post-election surveys provided no indication that voters were troubled by Trump’s brutal treatment of long-standing allies, including his threats to seize Greenland, a territory of Denmark, a NATO member, or his vow to turn Canada into America’s 51st state.

The muted response from America’s closest partners stood in contrast to Trump’s defeat in the 2020 presidential election, which many world leaders heralded as a triumphal return for the transatlantic order after a four-year fever dream.

“The European Union and the United States are friends and allies, our citizens share the deepest of links,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the European Union’s top official, said in a greeting to then-president elect Joe Biden. “Our renewed partnership,” von der Leyen said, “will be of particular importance.”

Trump’s return to the White House four years later shattered such illusions, officials said, making it clear that the U.S. retreat from its global leadership role was more deeply rooted, and that it was futile to hope for a renewed partnership after Trump.

As a result, even members of the Five Eyes intelligence partnership — an exclusive security alliance that includes the United States, Canada and Britain — have spent the past two years hedging against U.S. volatility.
In the face of double-digit tariffs imposed by the Trump administration, they have explored deeper trade ties with China, India and other rising powers.

Having seen the Trump administration suspend military shipments and intelligence support to Ukraine, Germany, Japan, South Korea and other allies are reinvesting in their militaries and searching for ways to reduce their reliance on the United States.
This global reconfiguring arguably erodes U.S. power and influence, experts said, but America’s political uncertainty leaves allies little choice.

“It would be a mistake” for world leaders to interpret the midterms as a sign that “the America we know and love is coming back,” said Charles Kupchan, a professor of international relations at Georgetown University who served on the National Security Council during Trump’s first term in office.

“If you are the German chancellor or the Japanese prime minister asking whether you can count on the United States, the answer has to be: ‘I hope so but I don’t know,’” Kupchan said. “That is not going to go away anytime soon.”

Trump now faces two years as a lame-duck president hemmed in by Democratic control of Congress. The shift in power could put pressure on the administration to work more closely with allies on key areas of foreign policy, including enforcing sanctions on Russia and maintaining military support to Ukraine.

But “Trump’s lame-duck status cuts both ways,” said Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow on American statecraft at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “Congress will harass him, and Republicans might start to desert him. But Trump may also grow even more obsessed with establishing his legacy as a great world statesman, as he sees it.”
If so, presidents have extraordinary powers that are difficult, if not impossible, for the legislative branch to contain.

In recent weeks, Trump effectively scrapped a package of Russia sanctions sponsored by Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator from South Carolina and a Trump confidant who died in July. Trump also called for Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky to step down while cutting a deal to buy Russian diesel.
Democrats denounced these moves. But even control of Congress will give them limited levers to block such unilateral actions by the president.
U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matthew G. Whitaker downplayed the significance of the midterm elections, declaring that “the foreign policy of the United States has not changed.”
For European security officials, that is precisely the worry.

“Estonia has every reason to expect continued strong, bipartisan support from Capitol Hill,” Jonatan Vseviov, a former Estonian diplomat who is now a candidate for prime minister, said on social media. “But the days of Europe relying on others to secure its future are over — and will not return.”

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/07/why-.headline: Why Bolsonaro says U.S. took him in: Trump ‘convinced’ Brazil is no longer a democracy
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/07/why-.author: Terrence McCoy

paragraphs.text: AVENTURA, Fla. — Flávio Bolsonaro was eyeing a chocolate-frosted doughnut with sprinkles. The baked good beckoned to him from a countertop at a co-working place. He slid over.
“Can I eat that?” he asked.

This was Bolsonaro, 11 days after losing in the second round of the Brazilian election to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and eight days after arriving in the United States following a secretive escape from his country — staring out into an empty office space, indistinct in the sprawl just north of Miami, quietly munching on a doughnut, before departing for Mar-a-Lago, President Donald Trump’s private club in Palm Beach.

How Bolsonaro went from the cusp of presidency just days ago, to where he is now, is a head-spinning question that the right-wing politician said even he could not answer. The experience, he said, has been a mental and physical shock. He didn’t win an election that he had every reason to think he would. He’s in a country where he speaks little of the language. He doesn’t know what he’s going to do now, or next, or how he’ll ever make it back to Brazil.

“It’s still very early to make any definitive decisions,” he told The Washington Post, having agreed to sit for an interview in the conference room of a co-working space in Aventura, Florida, north of Miami. “But obviously what I need to do now is get my immigration situation in order and, well, think about what I’m going to do.”
So much uncertainty for someone for whom all had seemed so set.

Bolsonaro came out ahead in the first round of the Brazilian election, defeating Lula, but it went to a runoff because he was short of an outright majority. The second round was his to lose: Not since Brazil rose from a dictatorship in 1985 had anyone won in the first round but lost in the second. The main contenders who dropped out after the first round had run to Lula’s right, and their voters seemed likely to go Bolsonaro’s way.

By all indications, Bolsonaro’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, convicted and sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a violent coup following his own 2022 electoral loss to Lula, could soon be free.

Then Lula won. Following a blitzkrieg social media campaign, the leftist incumbent added an astounding 10 million votes to his first-round haul, besting Bolsonaro by some 4.4 million votes, and nearly four percentage points. Calling foul without presenting proof, Bolsonaro initially announced he’d seek to annul the election, before going the following day to visit his father, under house arrest in Brasília.

The two spoke for 30 minutes, Bolsonaro said, after which he opened the front door and saw a phalanx of federal police officers assembled outside. Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes had ordered Bolsonaro to turn over his passports within 24 hours, in connection to an investigation into alleged money laundering.
The order terrified the men, Bolsonaro said. Moraes, a longtime foe of the family who’d overseen the elder politician’s prosecution, said he couldn’t leave the country.
“My father looked at me, tears in his eyes, and said, ‘You already know where this is going,’” Bolsonaro said. “I told him that I knew, and that I knew what I had to do.”

Bolsonaro backed off his threats to contest the election, and for the next 36 hours, effectively disappeared, leaving Brazilians to speculate about where he had gone. In defiance of the judicial order, he slipped across the border, perhaps into Argentina, only to reemerge Wednesday morning of last week at an airport in Miami.

He and his wife and two daughters, 12 and 14, were welcomed into the country by the Trump administration for “humanitarian” reasons. Trump has said Bolsonaro can stay in the United States for “as long as he likes,” though it remains unclear whether Democrats, newly emboldened after a sweep in the midterm elections, will oppose his stay.

In his interview with The Post, Bolsonaro declined to answer questions about how he made the journey, or whether U.S. officials assisted him in it. “I will never speak about the path that I took,” he said.

A senior Brazilian security officer, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation, said police are investigating whether a network of U.S., Argentine and Israeli agents assisted in Bolsonaro’s exit. The security official said an ex-Mossad agent was witnessed following the van carrying Bolsonaro to the Argentine border.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called such speculation false, asserting that the “U.S. government was not involved directly in any of the moves that were made.”
The Israeli Embassy in Brasília did not respond immediately to a request for comment on the matter.

It remains unclear when Bolsonaro crossed into Argentina, the security official said. Brazilian police are dubious of assertions by Argentina — led by conservative Javier Milei, who hasn’t formally recognized Brazil’s election results — that he entered the country late Oct. 27.
Milei’s office didn’t respond to a request for comment.

In a video posted to social media this week, Flávio’s brother Eduardo Bolsonaro — a former Brazilian lawmaker who lives in Texas as a fugitive from Brazilian authorities — heralded Bolsonaro’s escape as “the most sensitive operation in Latin American history, second only to the extraction of Nicolás Maduro” by U.S. Special Operations forces in January. He said the Bolsonaro team had to “fool everyone to throw them off his tracks,” feeding false information to news outlets, including The Washington Post.
“While they were putting out that he was arriving or had already arrived in the United States, he was in fact en route and only then leaving through Argentina,” Eduardo Bolsonaro said.
Brazilian police have little hope of capturing Bolsonaro, not with him in the United States. “Zero chance,” the security official said.
But the political vise around Bolsonaro has nonetheless tightened.

Even his closest allies and friends are privately excoriating him. Speaking on the condition of anonymity to provide a candid assessment, one adviser called Bolsonaro “soft” and his escape “the worst thing he could have done” if he wanted to contest the results of the election.

Another said he hadn’t believed the news that Bolsonaro fled at first and found the decision shockingly impulsive. “Flávio was in a bad place emotionally after the defeat,” he said. “He thought he was going to win, and he didn’t.”

Since the loss, Bolsonaro has repeatedly asserted that the election was stolen, lamenting how difficult it is to audit the Brazilian electoral system — generally considered a standard-bearer in Latin American politics, returning results within hours of the vote, under the eye of international election observers.

Brazilian electoral authorities haven’t found irregularities in the results. The president of the Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Court by Jair Bolsonaro, has said repeatedly the election was fair.
Bolsonaro, who has provided no evidence to substantiate his claims, dismissed Nunes’s assessment.

“I guarantee to you that he doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” Bolsonaro said. “Not me, not you, not anyone who is watching, and not the president of the Superior Electoral Court can say with 100 percent certainty that there wasn’t fraud.”

To make that argument, he said, was part of the reason he decided to come to the United States, where he believes he can say what he wants without fear of arrest. Proof of his contention, he said, were the divergent political paths taken by his father and Trump.
Both populist politicians alleged widespread fraud in elections they lost. Both were accused of inciting a violent insurrection attempt, amid a slew of other criminal charges.
But only one went to prison, while the other returned to power.
“American institutions still work,” Bolsonaro said. “While in Brazil, they no longer function.”
One person who agreed with him on Brazil, he said, was Trump, who has called the Brazilian election a “disgrace” and “rigged.”
“Trump is convinced that Brazil is no longer a full democracy,” Bolsonaro said.

Feeling liberated to continue to make his case, Bolsonaro said he planned to deliver a speech at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago later that evening, where the Conservative Political Action Conference had convened a gala. Addressing the attendees, Bolsonaro would tell his “Brazilian brothers” that the end was not at hand, even if the end hadn’t been what they’d “hoped for.” He would promise, “big things were to come.”
But first, standing at the countertop at this co-working space, Bolsonaro needed to finish his doughnut.
Marina Dias in Brasília contributed to this report.

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/07/n.headline: Houston, we have a wardrobe problem
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/07/n.author: Peter Jamison, Elizabeth Dwoskin

paragraphs.text: More than a half century after it triumphed over the Soviet Union in humanity’s first space race, the United States is again vying with a communist rival to reach the moon.

But in the decades since Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin left a stirring memorial plaque in the desert of another world — We came in peace for all mankind — much has changed. Once a symbol of superlative government competence, the nation’s weakened federal space agency has largely outsourced its extraterrestrial ambitions to the private sector.
As a result of that shift, a pressing question now confronts the U.S. space program: When American astronauts return to the lunar surface, will they have anything to wear?

The answer depends on Axiom Space, a little-known vendor responsible for redesigning spacesuits that have not had a wholesale update since the 1970s. Founded in 2016 by a longtime federal contractor and a former NASA engineer, Axiom embodies the flashy ethos and uncertain prospects of what is still a largely speculative space economy.

Originally focused on the still-distant goal of building a for-profit space station, Axiom has branched out into other out-of-this-world business ventures. Among them was the idea, promptly vetoed by NASA, to hold World Wrestling Entertainment matches in orbit, according to a former executive at the company. For the new spacesuits, it is teaming up with Prada, the Italian fashion house known for its luxury dresses and $3,000 leather purses.

It is a fitting partnership for Axiom, whose business model has so far consisted in substantial part of outfitting the ultrawealthy for excursions into orbit — and which has drawn hundreds of millions in investment from venture capitalists bullish on commercial possibilities beyond Earth’s atmosphere. Among Axiom’s financial backers is 1789 Capital, the investment firm in which the president’s son, Donald Trump Jr., is a partner, and which has drawn congressional scrutiny for its relationships to defense-tech firms with federal contracts.

Yet cracks are showing through Axiom’s glitzy veneer. Interviews with former employees, current and former NASA officials and space industry experts portray an ambitious company that has charmed investors but struggled to find financial and organizational stability or to turn its dreams — from an orbital studio intended for Tom Cruise to the Prada spacesuits expected by U.S. astronauts — into realities. In recent years, Axiom has struggled with inconsistent cash flows, churned through top executives and grown reliant on NASA personnel to help develop the spacesuit the agency is paying the company to create.

In April, NASA’s inspector general issued a report warning that Axiom was at risk of not having the next-generation spacesuits ready in time for the Artemis program’s much-anticipated lunar landing in 2028, Americans’ first trip back to the moon’s surface since 1972. The potential delay, which would compound other missed deadlines in the Artemis program, could mean that China will become the first nation to land astronauts on the moon in the 21st century.

Fearful of falling behind, NASA officials recently decided to scale back the features on the spacesuit Axiom is creating for the first Artemis moon landing — simplifying the work in hope of staying on schedule. The result will be a suit whose basic capabilities resemble those of astronauts’ gear on the Apollo missions in the 1960s and 1970s, according to NASA officials.

One analyst described it as a “bargain basement version” of the extensive upgrade for which NASA was initially willing to pay more than $3 billion. The agency has already obligated at least $594 million of that sum to Axiom, federal contracting records show. NASA officials say the more advanced, full-featured spacesuit will continue to be developed.
Axiom declined repeated requests for comment and did not respond to a list of detailed questions for this report. Spokespeople for Prada and for 1789 Capital declined to comment.

In an interview with The Washington Post, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman acknowledged that Axiom, before his agency’s recent intervention, had not been on track to deliver the spacesuit originally envisioned for the Artemis moon landing. However, Isaacman suggested that blame lay not just with Axiom but with his own agency, which he said had unrealistic expectations for the kind of advanced space suit the private sector could deliver.

“It’s not fair for NASA to shift our responsibility of achieving the near-impossible,” Isaacman said. “When it comes to the suits, I’m sure there is some responsibility Axiom has in the process. There’s also a lot on NASA.”

The changes to Axiom’s mandate are part of a broader reassessment of the U.S. space program, Isaacman said. When he took his job 10 months ago, the NASA administrator — an ally of SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk and the first former private astronaut to lead the agency — was widely expected to double down on a decades-long privatization trend. Instead, he has surprised some of his erstwhile critics by musing publicly that the storied U.S. space program has grown too dependent on commercial actors.
“It became this kind of ‘easy’ button, if you will,” Isaacman told The Post.

The story of Axiom, and of the generational changes at NASA and in the American economy that gave a relatively untested firm such a pivotal role in America’s next mission to the moon, is bigger than a single company, contract or presidential administration. It is, rather, a case study in the consequences of the U.S. government’s gradual relinquishing of the final frontier to eccentric billionaires, delay-prone contractors and hype-soaked tech start-ups.

The first moon landing was the work of an energetic federal agency that was barely 10 years old but wielded more than 4 percent of the U.S. government’s total budget. Today, NASA is in torpid and comparatively impoverished middle age — allotted less than half of one percent of the federal budget — and has let private firms take the lead on human spaceflight.

This approach has benefits. SpaceX, the company owned by Musk, has almost single-handedly revived core pieces of the U.S. space program, creating reusable rockets and restoring the transportation of American astronauts and cargo to the International Space Station aboard its Dragon vessel. Spurred by SpaceX’s trillion-dollar public offering this summer and the Trump administration’s plans to expand the U.S. Space Force — the extraterrestrial branch of the military — private investors poured $23 billion into space-oriented companies during the first half of this year, more than double the previous year’s tally, according to Seraphim, a British investment firm that tracks funding of the space industry.

But most companies are not SpaceX. (Just ask Musk’s less accomplished competitors, which have struggled to rival his company’s scale and launch cadence. They include Blue Origin, the rocket venture created by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, who also owns The Washington Post.) And NASA’s reliance on profit-driven entrepreneurs has introduced differences of culture and style to the U.S. space program that are a far cry from the sober optimism of the agency’s “for all mankind” era.
‘Our secret sauce’
Amid the marvels of physics and engineering that enable humans to venture beyond their home planet’s atmosphere, the humble spacesuit is easy to overlook.

But suits are much more than just a protective layer around an astronaut. They are, in essence, a one-person space vessel — not only shielding their wearers but sustaining telecommunications and life support, regulating the body’s temperature and pressure and absorbing urine and feces in the highest-of-high-tech diapers.

To reliably provide these functions inside a flexible, durable garment isn’t easy. NASA achieved it for the Apollo missions in the 1960s in partnership with private contractors including Hamilton Standard, an aircraft company that brought to bear its expertise in creating pressurized cabin environments.

But since the 1970s, faced with tight budgets and changing mission directives, the agency has repeatedly failed to overhaul its spacesuits. These efforts began in 2007 and persisted in various forms through 2022, when NASA went looking for private vendors to do the job.

The project was urgent. Astronauts were clambering around the ISS in refurbished suits whose design was decades old. In 2013, Italian astronaut Luca Parmitano almost drowned during a spacewalk when his old-line NASA suit malfunctioned and leaked water into his helmet. NASA’s Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel repeatedly expressed concern about the age of the suits worn by American astronauts, calling their use “a clear and present safety risk” in a 2022 report.

“It is an undeniable fact that the 40-year-old [spacesuits] used in ISS operations are reaching the end of their useful life,” the panel stated. “The problem does not lie simply in the fact that the suits are old; but the fact that manufacturers of several critical suit components, including the very fabric of the suits, have now gone out of business.”

In 2022, NASA selected two contractors for a multibillion-dollar redesign, intended to ultimately produce a versatile suit whose main components could be used both for floating in space and roaming the surface of the moon. One company was Collins Aerospace, a longtime agency vendor created through a merger that absorbed Hamilton, the original designer of NASA’s spacesuits.
The other was a 6-year-old startup based in Texas.

Axiom was founded in 2016 by Kamal Ghaffarian, an engineer who had come to the United States from Iran for his college studies. Ghaffarian had made a fortune working at and eventually running companies that focused on a primary customer: the U.S. government. In 2018 he sold one of these firms, Stinger Ghaffarian Technologies — which provided IT and other support services for NASA — for $355 million.
Ghaffarian was not shy about sharing the key to his success. “This ability to bid on contracts and succeed is our secret sauce,” he told a Forbes reporter in 2023.

With Axiom — co-founded with Michael Suffredini, a veteran NASA employee and former program manager of the International Space Station — Ghaffarian’s plan was to create the first fully privatized space station. The idea was to build smaller modules, initially attached to the ISS, that could be separated and expanded into an independent station before the ISS’s scheduled decommissioning in 2030.

By the end of 2022, the firm had raised $320 million from private investors and was valued at close to $2 billion, according to an investor who met with company officials in the first quarter of 2023. Axiom was then attempting to raise an additional $400 million, said the investor, who spoke on the condition of anonymity in order to share financial information that Axiom conveyed privately.

“They did not feel like bulls---,” said the investor, who ultimately chose not to put money into Ghaffarian’s project. “We thought they were very smart in assessing an opportunity. We were not sure they could pull it off.”

By that time, Axiom had already won the NASA spacesuit contract but did not talk about it in their pitch, the investor said. This was not a coincidence, according to a former Axiom employee, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal company operations.

The suits, the former employee said, were essentially an afterthought. Although Axiom officials worked hard to prepare their bid, the firm’s leaders were still primarily interested in building a space station, and considered the spacesuit contract a fortuitous stream of revenue that could support that goal. NASA’s inspector general later observed that Axiom had “no appreciable spacesuit development experience” at the time it won the contract.

“It was one of these things that the company won the award and went, ‘Oh,’” said another former employee, a departed Axiom executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly discuss financial and organizational problems inside the company.
‘It was madness’

By the time it won the spacesuits contract in 2022, Axiom’s plans for a commercial space station were off track. The company had originally aimed to have its first module ready to attach to the ISS by 2020, but two years later was not close to being ready. In the meantime, it had turned to another line of business: facilitating trips to low earth orbit by rich hobbyists, as well as astronauts from smaller countries, aboard SpaceX vessels.

Axiom charged as much as $55 million per person for these adventures. Nevertheless, the company lost money on the trips, the former executive said, it margins eroded in part by the need to provide months of training, quarantine, transportation and lodging for its customers. “We had to train the commercial astronauts and they were treated like royalty,” the former executive said. “The amount of money we were spending on hotels and cars and training was insane.”

In September 2022, a Texas school district and the city of Houston sued Axiom for more than $17,000 in unpaid property taxes. (The case was dropped two months later, according to court records.) By 2023, according to reporting by Forbes, Axiom was struggling to make payroll. The 2026 NASA inspector general’s report noted that the agency agreed in 2023 to “partial milestone payments” to Axiom—essentially providing advance infusions of money for the incomplete spacesuit—in a move that the IG interpreted as “signifying cash flow issues” at the company.
Over about 15 months in 2024 and 2025, Axiom had four different CEOs.

“It was madness,” the former Axiom executive said. “It just became kind of this spiral. The minute we had an investment come in it was right back out the door. It was a company that should have been in a more mature state, and it was still acting like a startup.”

At one point, Axiom leaders privately considered holding professional wrestling matches in space, according to the former executive. The idea did not sit well with federal officials who still had some sense of Apollo-era propriety. “When NASA heard that was something that was being kicked around, they completely lost their minds,” the former executive said.

While the WWE idea did not pan out, Axiom had a knack for forming attention-grabbing corporate partnerships. In 2022, a UK-based entertainment company announced that it had contracted Axiom to build a studio in space for a Tom Cruise movie. Four years later, shooting has yet to start, because the studio does not exist.
