Officials at the UK company, Space Entertainment Enterprise, did not respond to a request for comment. A representative for Cruise did not respond to a request for comment.

When it set out to redesign NASA’s spacesuits, Axiom teamed up with marquee brands including Prada and Oakley, the high-end sunglasses company. (Spokespeople for Oakley did not respond to a request for comment.) In 2024, Axiom revealed some sleek-looking prototypes of the suit at a conference in Milan. In June of this year, at Prada’s store in Manhattan’s SoHo neighborhood, the company unveiled an elegant gray bodysuit—what a Prada executive called “super nice pajamas”—that will serve as the underlayer of the new moon garments.

“Prada leads the world in development of luxury items,” Axiom CEO Jonathan Cirtain said, according to the New York Times. “Why would you choose to do it on your own when you could work with the best?”

Earlier this year, Axiom announced that it had raised $350 million in an investment round led by Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund and Type One Ventures, a venture capital firm specializing in space companies. Another investor in that round was Donald Trump Jr.’s firm, 1789 Capital.

The president’s son has had no direct involvement with Axiom and was not part of the decision to invest in it, according to three people who are familiar with 1789 Capital’s relationship with Axiom, and who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations. The venture-capital firm is led by investors Omeed Malik and Chris Buskirk, a prominent ally of Vice President JD Vance.

1789 made a small investment in Axiom after an introduction from a Mar-a-Lago member involved with Type One Ventures, two of the people said. The 1789 investors wanted to establish a stake in Axiom in case the company becomes a prominent player in the space economy. Among the firm’s other investments is a large stake in SpaceX.

Isaacman told The Post that no representatives of 1789 have ever spoken to him about Axiom’s spacesuit contract and that the White House has never pressured him to treat the company favorably. He noted that the company won the spacesuit contract during the Biden administration, four years before 1789 invested.
For all mankind, in rented clothes

By tapping multiple vendors for the suit redevelopment project, NASA intended to reduce the risk of relying on just one contractor. The combined maximum value of the contracts was more than $3 billion, according to federal records: a ceiling for the total amount that could be split among the chosen firms.

But the daunting specs for the sort of spacesuit the agency wanted — capable not only of floating around outside a space station but of repeated exposure to the sharp rocks and highly abrasive dust (more like powdered glass) on the moon’s surface — had, from the start, scared off most firms.

“If everybody could build a spacesuit, we’d have a ton of vendors, just like we do with space vehicles,” said a former NASA official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to publicly discuss the agency.

In 2024, facing complaints from NASA about its work, Collins gave up on the suits in order to prioritize other contracts. That left NASA reliant on a single vendor, Axiom, which had now become a linchpin in America’s quest to return to the moon.
That quest was already beset by other challenges.

The first Trump administration announced the Artemis missions in 2019, laying out an aggressive jump-starting of human space exploration. American astronauts planned not only to return to the moon, but to build a permanent base at the lunar south pole. This, in turn, could be a stepping stone for humans’ first crewed mission to Mars.
NASA had originally hoped to get an American astronaut back on the moon in 2024. It is now aiming for a lunar landing by the end of Trump’s second term, in 2028.

Even that delayed timeline is questionable. SpaceX is behind schedule on its Starship vessel, intended to land humans on the lunar surface. The NASA inspector general’s office, in its April report, estimated that Axiom, if it experienced the sorts of delays typical of other agency projects, might not have the next-generation spacesuits ready until 2031.

Wary of this risk, NASA has now tasked Axiom with designing a pared-back “sortie suit” for the 2028 moon landing. Isaacman told The Post that the simplified suit will be capable of excursions of about two-and-a-half hours — similar to the suits worn on the Apollo missions. Axiom’s contract had originally called for a spacesuit that could be used for six hours at a time, he said.

“It’s certainly going to be modern, and it will be inherently more safe, because we’re building in more redundancy and fault tolerance,” Isaacman said of the sortie suit. “But the requirements are going to be more in line with a ‘step one.’”
The NASA administrator said that the more advanced suit will still be created, although he could not say when.

“Everything now is being done in a much more logical, iterative approach,” Isaacman said. “If everything was right to the dream state, if everything had to [be] Apollo 11 on steroids, it’s not going to be done on time or on budget.”

America’s next spacesuit may well be appropriate for lunar recreation such as Alan Shepard’s golf swing or Eugene Cernan’s bunny hop. But it probably won’t be ready for the Ultimate Warrior’s Gorilla Press Slam, to say nothing of Sabu’s Triple Jump Moonsault.

Charlie Precourt, a former astronaut and member of the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel, said at a panel meeting in August that NASA has also taken a much more hands-on role in developing the new spacesuits — dispatching its technical experts to work with Axiom employees, offering the company the use of government facilities and performing “increased day-to-day insight through embedded personnel,” according to minutes of the meeting.

Don Platt, director of the Spaceport Education Center at the Florida Institute of Technology, said that, even with NASA’s direct involvement and the decision to settle for what he called a “bargain basement version” of its new spacesuit, it’s an open question whether the Artemis missions can stick to their latest timeline.
“I see very little chance, honestly, that NASA will have humans on the moon by the end of 2028,” Platt said.

The mission’s timing will be closely watched, and measured, against the nation’s chief geopolitical rival. China’s ambitious space program, after successful lunar excursions using robots, is now attempting to land its own astronauts on the moon by 2030. (China’s Tiangong space station, in orbit since 2021, is already on track to become humans’ only permanent extraterrestrial abode after the ISS shuts down.)

The competition’s outcome could be interpreted as a verdict on two very different paradigms of 21st century space exploration. China, a country whose industrial and technological progress is closely superintended by its authoritarian government, is — somewhat ironically — taking an approach to its moon missions that resembles the American government’s top-down efforts in the 1960s, said Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at the nonprofit Planetary Society.
This government-centric approach has distinct benefits, Kiraly said.

“There is no profit-driven motivation for fundamental research, space science, space exploration. It’s a very difficult endeavor,” Kiraly said. “There’s a reason it’s the domain of nations, not companies.”

Isaacman doesn’t disagree. He told The Post that for well-established technologies, such as spacecraft launches or telecommunications, buying the services of commercial vendors can make sense. In other areas, he said, government has a more central role to play.

“I’m happy to have competitive forces make the product better and cost less,” Isaacman said. “And then there’s some areas, where to simply say, ‘Well, I’m going to put the commercial label on it, and therefore it’ll work and cost less,’ is just not well thought through, at all.”

For the moment, the U.S. is still betting its lunar fortunes on a heavily commercialized space program. One potential drawback of that approach may be evident even if the Artemis missions — and the spacesuits needed to perform them — are a success.
The spacesuits in which astronauts first stepped onto the moon in July 1969 may have served a mission for all mankind. But they belonged to the American people — specifically, to NASA.
Under the current terms of the contract awarded to Axiom, however, the U.S. space agency will not actually own its new Prada space gear. Axiom will.
The company’s job is to create “spacesuits as a service.” That’s a fancy way of saying that when future American astronauts walk on the moon, they will be doing so in rented clothes.
Andrew Ba Tran and Aaron Schaffer contributed to this report.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/07/m.headline: Men see more career advancement in jobs with AI, as women lose ground
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/07/m.author: Julia Carpenter

paragraphs.text: There’s a new gender gap in the workplace. It’s not about men commanding higher salaries or well-qualified women losing out on promotions to their male counterparts. This time, the gender gap is all about artificial intelligence.

Female workers tend to use AI tools less often than men, according to a recent analysis from the Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard University. Women also say they have comparatively less access to AI training, mentorship and other workplace support that would enable and empower them to use it.

“It isn’t that women are less competent using it, only that they are less confident, often thanks to lack of support in their workplace but also because they just trust it less overall,” said Shorenstein Center Director Nancy Gibbs. “And that skepticism is a valuable part of the larger debate over AI safety and guardrails and value and usage.”

The gender gap in AI adoption is closing, but slowly, according to research from Solène Delecourt, an assistant professor of management of organizations at the University of California at Berkeley. Women still report feeling more apprehensive or cautious about integrating AI into their work, she said, and when it comes to the newest AI tools, the vast majority of early adopters are men.
“Anecdotally, I hear a lot of women say they are so tired of AI,” Delecourt said. “They feel like it’s taking away some of the joy of their work.”

Women also report feeling more time-constrained than men, Delecourt said. At home, they tend to shoulder a larger share of housework and family caregiving responsibilities, and at work, they are often saddled with invisible labor in addition to their regular job duties.
“When you tinker with a tool, there is a lot of wasted time initially,” she said. “So women probably feel like, ‘I have all these tasks to accomplish and I just don’t have this extra spare time.’”

The verdict is still out, of course, as far as whether AI will on balance help people expand their skills — or eliminate their jobs entirely. But it appears that men’s employment has grown faster than women’s in occupations with significant AI exposure — such as software development and financial management — which is creating a gap in job growth, according to data from the Pew Research Center.
Because training, mentorship and workplace support can lead to greater adoption and more excitement among workers, Gibbs said, she encourages employers to incorporate women’s input in these programs.
“When women’s voices are missing from spaces where decisions are made, then arguably we have less cause to trust those decisions,” she said.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261105.headline: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk

paragraphs.text: Your daily cup of coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up in the morning. A long-running study of U.S. adults suggests that drinking caffeinated coffee regularly is associated with a substantially lower risk of dementia and better cognitive health as people age.

Researchers found that adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee developed dementia at considerably lower rates than those who rarely or never drank it. The findings were based on follow-up periods extending as long as 43 years, offering a valuable look at how everyday drinking habits relate to brain health over time.

The strongest associations appeared among people who drank two to three cups of caffeinated coffee each day. Tea consumption was also linked to better cognitive outcomes, although the amount associated with the greatest benefit was somewhat lower.
Interestingly, decaffeinated coffee did not show the same benefits, raising questions about whether caffeine itself might help explain the connection.
Coffee Drinkers Showed Much Lower Dementia Rates
One of the most striking findings involved the difference in dementia rates between regular coffee drinkers and people who consumed little or no coffee.

Among U.S. adults who drank higher amounts of caffeinated coffee, researchers recorded 141 dementia cases annually for every 100,000 people. In comparison, the rate was 330 cases per 100,000 people each year among those who rarely or never drank caffeinated coffee.

Dementia is a general term for conditions that progressively interfere with memory, thinking, reasoning, and the ability to perform everyday activities. Alzheimer's disease is its most common cause, although several other brain disorders can also lead to dementia.

While occasional forgetfulness can be a normal part of aging, dementia involves cognitive difficulties severe enough to disrupt daily life. Identifying lifestyle habits associated with lower dementia risk is therefore an important area of research, particularly as populations grow older.

The findings suggest that regular caffeinated coffee consumption may be one such habit. However, the results show an association rather than proving that coffee directly prevents dementia. Other differences between coffee drinkers and people who avoid coffee could also contribute to the observed results.
Coffee Was Also Linked to Better Cognitive Health
The potential benefits were not limited to diagnosed dementia. Participants who drank more caffeinated coffee were also less likely to report that their memory or thinking abilities had declined.
Researchers found that 7.8% of adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee reported subjective cognitive decline, compared with 9.5% of those who rarely or never drank it.

Subjective cognitive decline refers to changes in memory or thinking that people notice themselves, even when those difficulties have not necessarily been confirmed by formal cognitive testing. Someone experiencing it might feel that remembering information, concentrating, or finding the right words has become more difficult.
Such complaints do not automatically indicate dementia. Nevertheless, they can provide useful information about how people perceive changes in their cognitive abilities as they grow older.
The lower percentage among caffeinated coffee drinkers adds to the evidence linking coffee consumption with healthier cognitive aging.
How Much Coffee Offers the Greatest Benefit?
The researchers also examined whether the amount of coffee consumed was related to the strength of the observed benefits.
Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee per day was associated with the most favorable outcomes for dementia risk and cognitive functioning.

Notably, this association remained apparent regardless of participants' genetic risk of developing dementia. In other words, the relationship between coffee consumption and brain health was observed even among people whose inherited characteristics might make them more vulnerable to the disease.

Genetic risk refers to the influence of inherited variations in DNA that can increase or decrease a person's likelihood of developing certain conditions. Although genetics can play an important role in dementia, they are only one part of a much larger picture that includes age, general health, and lifestyle.

The results also suggest that drinking larger amounts of coffee is not necessarily better. Consumption beyond the range associated with the strongest benefits did not appear to provide additional protection.
Tea Drinkers May Benefit Too, but Decaf Was Different
Coffee was not the only beverage associated with better brain health. Researchers found that drinking tea was also linked to lower dementia risk and better cognitive functioning.
For tea, the strongest associations appeared among participants who consumed one to two cups per day. As with coffee, drinking more than this amount did not appear to produce further benefits.

However, the study did not distinguish between caffeinated and noncaffeinated tea. As a result, the findings cannot establish whether caffeine was responsible for the association observed among tea drinkers.

The results for coffee offered an additional clue. While regular caffeinated coffee was associated with lower dementia risk and better cognitive outcomes, decaffeinated coffee did not demonstrate the same benefits.

Caffeine is a naturally occurring stimulant found in coffee, tea, and several other plants. It acts on the central nervous system and is best known for temporarily increasing alertness and reducing feelings of tiredness.

Whether caffeine also contributes to better brain health over many years is a separate question. The difference between regular and decaffeinated coffee makes this possibility worth investigating, but it does not establish caffeine as the cause of the observed benefits.

Taken together, the findings suggest that moderate consumption of caffeinated coffee and tea may be associated with healthier brain aging. For coffee drinkers, two to three cups daily appeared to offer the strongest association, while one to two cups of tea showed the most favorable results among tea drinkers.

Although additional research is needed to determine whether these beverages directly influence dementia risk, the long-term findings offer encouraging news for people who already enjoy coffee or tea as part of their daily routine.

cbsnews.com/news/paraguay-president-arre.headline: Paraguay's ousted president under house arrest after bank collapse leaves millions locked out of accounts

paragraphs.text: November 7, 2026 / 5:12 AM EST / CBS/AP
Paraguay's president has been placed on house arrest on Friday after the collapse of a government-linked bank that locked nearly half the country's population out of their accounts.

Paraguay's Senate voted to remove Santiago Peña for misconduct in office, making him the second president ousted by impeachment since the end of Gen. Alfredo Stroessner's 35-year dictatorship in 1989.
Regulators had seized Ueno Bank just three days earlier, sending shock waves through the financial system and setting off the country's worst political crisis in more than a decade.

Peña was ordered to remain at one of his homes in Asunción until he appears before prosecutors Saturday morning on charges of breach of trust, influence peddling and using public office for personal gain, the most serious of which carry up to 10 years in prison. Lawmakers accuse him of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending.
The Paraguayan president denied wrongdoing.

When regulators seized the bank, Ueno customers could no longer withdraw cash, access their savings or use their cards to buy anything. The digital lender had aggressively courted the poor and unbanked with generous supermarket rebates, and more than 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there, according to Ueno. Even players on the national soccer team, which Ueno sponsored through its run to a World Cup upset of Germany this year, say they can't reach their money.

The fallout has spread well beyond savers. A ride-hailing app that relied on Ueno shut down, leaving 3,000 drivers without work. The state power company says $21 million in loans from the Inter-American Development Bank and Taiwan, earmarked for public works, is trapped at the bank. Paraguay's bonds have posted some of the worst losses in emerging markets this week, and the guaraní has slid against the dollar.

Some depositors began recovering their money Thursday, starting with those holding up to 10 million guaraníes (about $1,500). Deposits are insured up to about $35,000, which the central bank says covers 97% of Ueno's customers. It calls the collapse an isolated case and insists the broader financial system is safe.

livescience.com/animals/cats/why-do-most.headline: Why do most cats hate it when you touch their belly, feet or tail?
livescience.com/animals/cats/why-do-most.author: Clarissa Brincat

paragraphs.text: Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."
But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?
Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.
Off-limits petting zones

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."
Petting rules and exceptions

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.
Related mysteries

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.
She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."
How much of a cat fan are you? Find out by taking our cat quiz!

npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-6007770/data-ce.headline: An unexpected activist emerged to help block a $5 billion data center in Maryland
npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-6007770/data-ce.author: Jenny Abamu

paragraphs.text: The overgrown grass and weeds seem to stretch into the horizon on nearly 90 acres of empty land in Landover, Md. It used to be Landover Mall, but that closed in 2002, and the site has been mostly vacant since.
In 2024, the developer that built the mall won approval from county planners for a $5 billion data center campus, and word began spreading through the largely Black community nearby.

"I was like, 'Oh, hell no,'" said Taylor Frazier McCollum, describing the moment she learned about the project. She lived less than a mile away from it. "Why would you want to bring water-polluting, diesel-generating data centers right down the street from where people live, work, play? It just didn't make sense to me."

Frazier McCollum is one of a number of Americans whose political awakening was triggered by data center development. Across the country, community members have taken to local council hearings to voice their opposition. They've prompted — though estimates vary — about 500 moratoriums on data centers nationwide.
A different kind of land-use activist

Unlike a lot of land-use activists trying to protect their homes from threats in their backyards, Frazier McCollum does not own a home. In 2024, she and her young daughter were evicted from their apartment. She was working at a waxing center that cut wages, and she could no longer cover her rent.

"It was difficult," Frazier McCollum recalled. "Because I created the ideal life paying for us to live in this apartment and have our own space ... and then to have it taken away ... It felt like something that wasn't ever going to end."
They've moved around and were living in her grandfather's home when she learned about the proposed project less than a mile away.

She created a petition that gathered over 25,000 signatures, leading to widely attended protests and culminating in multiple local moratoriums imposed on data centers throughout the county. It blocked the $5 billion project that was set to break ground between 2026 and 2027.

The fight pushed Frazier McCollum to the forefront of local politics. She went to county meetings, testified before Maryland legislators and endorsed political candidates. She found herself in a coalition of socialists, environmentalists, people angry about their electric bills and neighbors new to organizing.
Local media interviewed her, and people in data center circles called her "the Landover girl."
After some losses, the county needs revenue, and data centers could help
Staci Hartwell, a longtime local environmental activist, says she spent years struggling to get traction on the data center issue before Frazier McCollum came along.
"This is something that was happening in her neighborhood, and it was really like her awakening," Hartwell said.

But with data centers paused, some in Prince George's County worry about declining tax revenue. Last year, a local Six Flags closed. The NFL's Washington Commanders announced plans to return to neighboring Washington, D.C. Thousands of federal workers have lost their jobs. The county faces a budget deficit.

In September, Frazier McCollum appeared at a county council meeting to advocate for a fund for roof repairs, something her grandfather's home needs. Council member Wanika Fisher, who supports moving some data center projects forward, reminded her that the county needs development.

"Our county has an economic future that we have to grapple with," said Fisher, addressing the request. "I don't see where the money is coming from. I think we have to have a real conversation. And I'm not saying that a data center is the answer, but I'm saying it's worth the hard discussion."
Now Frazier McCollum is broadening her activism and going to new places

With the Landover project on hold, Frazier McCollum now wants a full ban on that and other data center projects. And with grants Hartwell and others have found, Frazier McCollum has taken her message to Black communities fighting data center growth in Atlanta, Memphis and even across the globe in Zambia.

"I feel like so many people are depending on this fight to be successful," Frazier McCollum explained. "Not just for myself, but even across the country, to set precedent for other people that are fighting against hyperscale data centers."
She's lost out on work to attend public meetings or knock on doors, and she's relied on family for rides and childcare.
Her father, Lacy McCollum Jr., sees the data center fight as rooted in civil rights.

"We're talking about the right to water, the right to clean air, the right to a place to live. That's everybody's fight, right?" Lacy McCollum Jr. said. "While I'm afraid for her, we need those people. We needed the Medgar Everses. We needed the Martin Luther Kings. We needed the Malcolm X's. People like Taylor, they jump out here so the people behind them get to make progress."
Some urge her to run for office. She says she wants to pay off her debt and traffic tickets and find a home first.

"I didn't want to have to focus on housing and the campaign and doing everything else," explained Frazier McCollum. "Now is not maybe the moment for it, but I do have aspirations to run for something."

In the meantime, she's pitching plans to turn the old Landover site into a sports complex or affordable housing, or to use some of it to support heritage tourism in the county. But none of those ideas, she acknowledges, would be as lucrative as a data center campus.
Jenny Abamu is a reporter for WAMU.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv8ezz9yn6pyo.headline: Spate of bomb threats poses serious challenge to airline industry
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv8ezz9yn6pyo.author: Marc Ashdown

paragraphs.text: With no fewer than 32 bomb threats affecting a dozen airlines in the space of four days, the aviation industry is facing another potential crisis.
Some of the threats apparently came from phone calls, others via email, and although they have all turned out to be hoaxes, they were each clearly serious enough to force emergency action.
Some planes had to be escorted by military jets, others were quietly inspected mid-air by cabin crew - desperate not to cause alarm.

A number had to be re-routed from their original destinations, landing at different airports, sometimes in different countries. An Aer Lingus flight had to land at an airbase 1,000 kilometers from its intended destination after running low on fuel.
All this poses a serious challenge to the airlines, who have little idea who is causing the severe disruption they have faced almost every day this week.
Although so far all threats have turned out to be hoaxes, airlines have no choice but take each threat seriously.

"They have a triage system, but follow the same protocols for each until they are absolutely sure there is no threat," says Marco Chan, a former commercial airline pilot and aviation expert at Kingston University.
"That could involve a mid-air inspection, but definitely a search once the plane has landed.
"Passengers might not even know there is an issue until they are told to disembark. It can cause disruption, but that is a small price to pay when safety is at stake", he adds.
The sight of sniffer dogs and specialist teams on the tarmac searching for explosives on commercial planes may cause alarm.
So far, the disruption too has been limited to the few thousand passengers who have been directly involved.
Paul Mason, an aviation security expert, says there will be a financial cost to the airline involved, but planes get diverted every day.

"The number can sometimes run to over a hundred planes daily, for things like technical issues, medical emergencies, even the weather," he adds. "They far outweigh the few which have been diverted due to hoaxes. So airlines are well equipped at dealing with the unexpected."
It is also unlikely that customers will be able to get refunds, he explains, because these incidents are not the fault of the airlines.
The more worrying aspect over the past few days will be the seeming random nature of the targets and the lack of any credible intelligence regarding who is behind the threats.
Aside from emails suggesting that an extremist misogynist group had claimed responsibility for a handful of the incidents - although since denied by its founder - there appear to be few leads.
With 20 years of military experience as well, Paul Mason says the incidents bear the hallmarks of hybrid warfare, which involves unconventional methods such as cyber attacks.
"It does feel co-ordinated," he says. "Russia has said it's got nothing to do with it, but it could be proxies. It's a very easy way to create disruption and chaos, with plausible deniability."
"That's the problem. Someone can have an opinion on who is behind it, but if the perpetrators are using sophisticated technology, it will be very hard to trace them."
He does say however that if misguided individuals try to copy the threats they could find themselves in serious trouble.

The Aviation Security Act 1982 states that "intentionally communicating false, misleading, or deceptive information that endangers - or is likely to endanger - the safety of an aircraft in flight is a serious criminal offence".
The maximum sentence is life imprisonment.

There is precious little that airports and airlines can do to guard against actually receiving threats, as they can come from a vast range of sources. But the punishment is designed to act as a deterrent.
As Paul Mason warns: "Someone might think it's a laugh and very easy to do, but unless they are very sophisticated, they are highly likely to be traced. And find themselves facing prison."

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261104.headline: Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined

paragraphs.text: Picture the wilderness of central Europe 100,000 years ago, or even a million years ago. You might imagine an endless expanse of towering trees, with thick canopies blocking sunlight from reaching the ground. But according to a major new study, that familiar image of Europe's ancient forests is probably misleading.

Instead, much of the continent was a vibrant landscape of scattered trees, open woodlands, grassy clearings, and colorful wildflower meadows. Birds and butterflies flourished in these sunlit habitats, while enormous grazing animals helped prevent trees and shrubs from taking over.

Researchers led by Aarhus University have found that this mixture of habitats dominated Europe's landscapes for more than 20 million years. Far from being the continent's original natural condition, the dense, dark forests common in many parts of Europe today appear to be a relatively recent development in its ecological history.

Published in Biological Conservation, the findings challenge a longstanding assumption about what Europe's wilderness looked like before widespread human intervention. They also raise important questions about modern reforestation programs, which often prioritize planting dense forests to combat climate change and protect biodiversity.

"The study shows that current reforestation practices are on the wrong track - both here in Denmark, where subsidies are only granted for planting dense forests, and elsewhere in Europe. This will not only be harmful for biodiversity; it will be in direct contradiction to the type of ecosystems that Europe's species have evolved in over millions of years," says Professor Jens-Christian Svenning from the Center for Ecological Dynamics in a Novel Biosphere (ECONOVO), Department of Biology at Aarhus University, senior author of the study.
Challenging the Myth of Europe's Ancient Forests

For decades, conservation strategies have been influenced by the "closed-forest paradigm." This is the belief that dense forests with nearly continuous tree canopies were Europe's natural landscape before humans began clearing land for agriculture and settlements.
Under this view, restoring nature often means allowing trees to reclaim open areas or planting forests where they no longer exist.

The new research suggests that this approach may overlook a crucial part of Europe's ecological history. Rather than being uniformly covered by dense forests, the continent was characterized by changing combinations of grasslands, shrubs, and woodlands with different amounts of tree cover.

These landscapes supported a rich variety of species adapted to both wooded and open environments. Large plant-eating animals also played a major role in maintaining this diversity by grazing, browsing, and disturbing vegetation.
What 23 Million Years of Evidence Reveals
To reconstruct Europe's ancient environments, the researchers examined an unusually extensive collection of evidence spanning millions of years.

Previous studies have generally concentrated on more recent periods. This investigation extended much further into the past, examining paleoecological records from the Miocene epoch (which began around 23 million years ago) through the pre-industrial era.

Paleoecology is the study of ancient ecosystems using clues preserved in fossils, sediments, and other natural records. Because no single type of evidence can provide a complete picture of the distant past, the team combined several independent methods.

These included fossilized pollen and larger plant remains, charcoal left by ancient wildfires, and chemical signatures preserved in the teeth and bones of plant-eating animals. The researchers also examined fossil insects and mammals, along with ancient environmental DNA recovered from sediments.

Environmental DNA consists of genetic material left behind by organisms in their surroundings. When preserved in ancient deposits, it can help scientists identify plants and animals that lived in an area long ago.

Together, these different sources of evidence allowed the researchers to reconstruct not only what types of vegetation existed, but also how ecosystems changed over time and how animals influenced their surroundings.

"Each type of proxy offers its own perspective, but together they let us see whether the landscapes were covered by dense forests, open grasslands, or a mix of the two. By combining these datasets across time - from the Miocene to the pre-industrial era - we could trace long-term changes in vegetation and the role of large herbivores with much greater confidence than earlier studies that used only one method," explains the study's lead author, ECONOVO PhD student Szymon Czyzewski of Aarhus University.

The evidence points to a consistent pattern. Across more than 20 million years, Europe's landscapes were typically a shifting mosaic of trees, open spaces, and flowering plants rather than continuous stretches of closed forest.

Importantly, these mixed landscapes were not limited to one particular climate. They existed under temperate conditions comparable to those in much of Europe today, as well as during warmer and colder periods.
Elephants, Rhinos, and Bison Shaped Europe's Wilderness
One of the most striking findings concerns the influence of large wild herbivores.

Ancient Europe was home to animals such as elephants, rhinoceroses, aurochs, and bison. By feeding on vegetation and disturbing the ground as they moved, these animals helped keep parts of the landscape open.
Their activities created opportunities for grasses, wildflowers, and other plants that might otherwise have struggled beneath dense tree cover.
This constant interaction between animals and vegetation helped sustain a diverse mixture of habitats, providing suitable conditions for many different species.

Modern Europe, however, is missing much of this ecological influence. Many of the large wild herbivores that once shaped its landscapes have disappeared, and traditional grazing practices have also declined.

"The ecosystems we see in Europe today lack the large wild herbivores that not only shaped landscapes but also sustained its biodiversity for millions of years. The most dramatic shift has largely taken place within the last hundred years, when traditional extensive grazing disappeared from large parts of the landscape," says Czyzewski.

This loss of grazing pressure has changed how vegetation develops across much of the continent, helping explain why present-day European ecosystems differ so dramatically from those of the distant past.
Europe's Ancient Woodlands Were Full of Wildflowers
The research also offers a different perspective on species commonly associated with farmland and other human-managed environments.

Birds such as larks and jackdaws, along with mammals such as the European hamster, are often regarded as characteristic of agricultural landscapes. Yet the researchers suggest that their evolutionary histories likely extend back to the open woodland environments that existed long before modern farming.
Even familiar wildflowers have connections to these ancient ecosystems.
Wild poppies, now frequently seen growing in agricultural fields, also thrived in areas where large grazing animals disturbed vegetation within ancient woodlands.
These findings challenge the sharp distinction between "forest" and "open habitats" that often guides conservation planning today.

In Europe's ecological past, trees, meadows, shrubs, and grazing animals were not necessarily separate parts of nature. They frequently existed together, forming interconnected habitats that supported a wide range of wildlife.
Why Planting More Trees May Not Always Help Nature
The findings arrive as European countries continue expanding forests to capture carbon dioxide, address climate change, and restore biodiversity.

Although forests can provide important environmental benefits, the researchers argue that planting large areas of uniformly dense woodland may not be the best approach when the goal is to restore Europe's native ecosystems.

Many European species evolved in landscapes containing a mixture of trees and open areas. Converting these habitats into continuous closed-canopy forests could therefore reduce the variety of environments available to wildlife.
The study suggests that restoration efforts should focus more strongly on maintaining diverse landscapes, including open grasslands, scattered woodland, and areas shaped by natural grazing.

"Instead, restoration efforts should place greater emphasis on creating and maintaining mosaics of woodland and open habitats - not least through the restoration of natural-living large herbivores," Svenning concludes.
The findings add to a growing body of research from the same scientific group suggesting that large animals played a far greater role in shaping Europe's ecosystems than previously recognized.
They also reinforce the idea that Europe's ancient landscapes were generally brighter, more open, and more varied than the dense primeval forests often depicted in popular imagination.

Rather than restoring nature by simply planting more trees, the researchers suggest that protecting biodiversity may require recreating the complex balance of woodlands, meadows, and grazing animals that shaped the continent for millions of years.
The familiar image of Europe as a vast, dark, unbroken forest may be deeply rooted in our understanding of nature, but millions of years of evidence are painting a very different picture.

washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/07/dem.headline: Democrats could use new power to challenge Trump’s D.C. golf project
washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/07/dem.author: Rick Maese

paragraphs.text: Democrats’ takeover of Congress could present new obstacles to President Donald Trump’s plans to overhaul East Potomac Golf Links, with lawmakers preparing to use their control of federal spending and congressional committees to scrutinize — and potentially block — parts of the project.
Some Democrats are considering acting even sooner.

Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), the top Democrat on the House Appropriations subcommittee that oversees the Interior Department and National Park Service, said lawmakers are discussing whether restrictions on the golf project could be included in spending legislation during the lame-duck session that begins next week.

“There would certainly be an opportunity to insert some language regarding the golf course and stopping the president’s project if we can get some agreement from the Republicans,” Pingree said in an interview.

The federal government is operating under a temporary spending measure that expires Dec. 11, and Congress has not completed a full-year spending bill for the Interior Department and Park Service. That leaves lawmakers facing another funding deadline during the lame duck — and potentially, an opening for Democrats to seek restrictions on Trump’s plans.

If Republicans seek to finish the spending bill before Democrats take over, Pingree said Democrats could press for restrictions on East Potomac as part of the negotiations. If Congress instead extends temporary funding into next year, Democrats would take control with the Interior spending bill still unfinished — giving them greater power to impose restrictions, but also giving the administration more time to advance the project.
“We’ve been talking a little bit about language that we could do in the lame duck for that very purpose,” she said.

The shift in power could also complicate other high-profile projects Trump has pursued in Washington, including his White House ballroom and proposed monumental arch near Arlington Memorial Bridge. Democrats have challenged the projects’ funding, approval and contracting processes and, beginning in January, will control committees with the power to issue subpoenas, conduct investigations and pursue restrictions on federal spending.
Pingree said she wants to block the arch before construction begins but was more circumspect about the partially built ballroom, saying it would be harder to undo construction already underway.
“If we need lawsuits to do it, if we need to use subpoena power, investigative power, we’ll use every tool in our toolbox,” Pingree said.

Pingree said Democratic control of the House would also give lawmakers standing to pursue litigation over Trump’s projects, providing another potential avenue for challenging them. She said Democrats also intend to use the appropriations process to restrict Trump’s projects if they are unable to do so during the lame duck.

“We will absolutely include language to block the president’s vanity projects and his moving around of funds from different places in the National Park Service, a variety of other things, including the golf course,” she said.

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-California), the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, has already outlined one possible approach. Last week, he urged congressional appropriators to place restrictions on a $500 million administration request for National Park Service construction that includes work on the East Potomac seawall and World War II Memorial.

Huffman proposed barring federal money from being used for the golf-course redevelopment and requiring any East Potomac seawall funding to be spent exclusively on the seawall. Asked whether she supports those restrictions, Pingree said, “absolutely,” adding that her staff intends to work with Huffman on potential legislative language.
Other Democrats set to take gavels on committees overseeing public lands and federal spending have similarly signaled that Trump’s projects will face new scrutiny.

A spokesman for Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico), who is in line to lead the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, said that while committee leadership has not been finalized, Heinrich would focus on “ensuring that public lands stay in public hands.” And Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon), the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations subcommittee overseeing Interior, said Democrats would seek to hold the administration accountable for its use of federal money.

“Instead of wasting folks’ hard-earned tax dollars on Trump’s ego-driven vanity projects, we should be focused on protecting our nation’s parks — not destroying them — and reversing cuts to national parks staffing,” Merkley said in a statement. “With Democrats taking back control of Congress, now is the time to hold his Administration accountable for its misuse of federal dollars and fund our parks, not the President’s pet projects.”
The emerging congressional push comes as the administration is already fighting on a separate front to make Trump’s vision for East Potomac a reality.

The administration plans to close the golf course and most of the Hains Point peninsula Nov. 15, citing in part safety problems with the deteriorating seawall. Preservation groups asked U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes on Thursday to block the closure, arguing that the stated safety concerns are a pretext for clearing the way for Trump’s planned championship golf course. Reyes is scheduled to consider the request Nov. 13.
Trump’s plans at East Potomac are also subject to review by the National Capital Planning Commission, whose composition will change when Democrats take control of Congress.

Two of the commission’s 12 seats belong to congressional committee leaders — the chairs of the House Oversight Committee and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. Those seats are held by Republicans but are expected to shift in January to Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California) and Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), who are in line to lead the committees.

The potential significance of those two seats was illustrated Thursday night, when the commission voted 8-4 to approve Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch. The four commissioners representing the District opposed the project, while the eight other commissioners supported it. Had the two congressional representatives joined the District commissioners in opposition, the vote would have been deadlocked, 6-6 — not enough votes to approve the project.

East Potomac is headed for review by the same commission. The administration’s plan is expected to be presented at its Dec. 3 meeting but would not likely receive a vote for final approval until after the revamped commission is in place.

Pingree acknowledged that Democrats may be racing against an administration eager to advance several projects before the new Congress takes office. She said actions taken in the coming weeks could make some changes harder to reverse.
“It’s a little harder when he’s cutting down trees on the golf course to put them back,” she said. “But we will use whatever powers we have.”

npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6026662/the-eco.headline: The economy propelled Democrats to victory. What can they actually do about it?
npr.org/2026/11/06/nx-s1-6026662/the-eco.author: Barbara Sprunt

paragraphs.text: After a sweeping set of midterm victories, Congressional Democratic leaders say they're clear-eyed about their mandate come January.

"We're going to fight to make sure that we make this country affordable for every single American," said Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is the presumptive House speaker, on Tuesday night. "This is a change election, and we understand as House Democrats we need to deliver dramatic change."

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., added "relief is on the way" but acknowledged some of the public may be skeptical that Democrats can deliver on the economic message that catapulted them to recapturing both chambers of Congress.
Democrats will control the legislative branch, but won't have a large enough majority to overturn a presidential veto and will likely face Republican filibusters in the Senate.

"That doesn't mean that nothing can happen, but it means there are real obstacles," said Bobby Kogan, senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank based in Washington, D.C.
Matt Bennett of Third Way, a center-left think tank, said those obstacles create the potential for voters to be disappointed by the limitations inherent in divided government.

"What Democrats were really promising was: return us to power, we will put a check on Trump for two years, and then when we get the White House in 2028, we can actually make your lives better. It isn't clear to me that voters heard the entire message," Bennett said. "They might have just heard the last part, and so there is some risk that voters will be disappointed."
The power of playing offense
An important power that comes with being in the majority is controlling which bills make it to the floor for a vote.

"There will be plenty of bills where the purpose is contrast — Democrats are for this and Republicans are against that," Kogan said. "But what is special about controlling both chambers is that legislation where the public is on [Democrats'] side and it's very difficult for Republicans to argue why they're against it, those sorts of things become real."

As an example, he points to the release of the Epstein files. President Trump and Republican leadership worked to prevent the measure from reaching the floor last year. Once it was brought to a vote in the House via a legislative end run around Speaker Mike Johnson, lawmakers were forced to go on the record and voted nearly unanimously to release the files.
"The difficulty was just getting it there," Kogan said. "And what Democrats can do is they can make popular things get there."

Forcing votes on popular issues has been a winning strategy in previous divided governments. After Democrats won control of Congress in the 2006 midterm elections, they made raising the minimum wage a signature issue, and Republican President George W. Bush went on to sign it into law.
Democrats have signaled plans to put forth bills to help Americans with health care costs, bring back enhanced premium tax credits, and undo Medicaid cuts.

"I think that's going to be critically important — that when you vote for a Democrat, your life improves," said Rebecca Cooke, the Wisconsin Democrat who unseated GOP incumbent Derrick Van Orden in the state's 3rd congressional district.

Democrats also have the ability to use budget reconciliation, a tool that bypasses the threat of a Senate filibuster by allowing certain budget-related bills to pass with a simple majority. Democrats used reconciliation to pass some health care changes in 2010. Republicans used it to pass tax cuts in 2017, and it was used to pass Trump's signature tax and spending bill.

Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren is already calling on her party to embrace reconciliation, writing in Time this week that Democrats should use it to "reverse Republican health care cuts, expand health care coverage, and fund universal child care."
Embrace the veto
Trump has sent mixed signals about what kind of leader he'll be in divided government, saying he'll "veto everything" and that he could "make deals" with Democrats.
Congressional Democrats are already pushing back at the idea that a veto is a deterrent.

"If we have a bill that is bipartisan to restore healthcare for the people who lost their Medicaid or to improve access to affordable medicines and other things, like, I dare him to veto that," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand told Morning Edition. "If he decides to veto the common sense things that get groceries down or housing prices down, then '28's going to be very favorable for Democrats."
Embracing the veto – rather than running away from it – can be an effective political tool.

"You might see legislation that is meant to address the effects of the tariffs that Democrats could pass, then dare President Trump to veto and use that as a mechanism for signaling to the American people where Democrats are versus where the president is," said Molly Reynolds, a Congress expert at Brookings.
Lindsay Owens, president of the think tank Groundwork Collaborative, adds voters want to see action.

"I don't think the American people sent this many Democrats to Congress to hear a bunch of talk about what they can't do. That will go over like a lead balloon," Owens said. "Democrats need to send those bills to the president's desk. If he vetoes them, that news cycle will be good for Democrats – like, 'Trump vetoes bill that would have lowered your health care cost.'"
Bennett, of Third Way, said delivering legislation fast will help Democrats long-term.
"They need to be caught trying, as Bill Clinton would say. And then they can turn to voters and say, look, this is what we would do for you if it wasn't being blocked by Republicans," he said.

Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill., said in divided government, it's important to make sure voters know exactly what Democrats are trying to do — to ward off any disappointment that priorities face GOP roadblocks.
"We have to constantly communicate where we are," said Schneider, who chairs the New Dems coalition. "Make sure people understand what we're doing, when, and why."
What about the war and gas prices?
A change in legislative power won't bring down fuel costs anytime soon. Lawmakers don't have a direct path toward lowering the price of oil, which is shaped by a complex global market.
Democrats plan to reassert the legislative branch's authority over tariffs and bring new votes on a war powers resolution, to force an end to the Iran war, which has raised the price of fuel.

"We can advance strong war powers resolution that the president will have to take up. Get it to his desk and then explain himself to the American people if in fact he decides to use his veto pen," Jeffries said in an interview Friday with Morning Edition.
But the war powers resolution has largely been ignored by presidents of both parties, with administrations sidestepping its requirements.

An alternative option for Democrats to address the war is through appropriations bills that fund the government, with a provision that prohibits funds from being used to carry out military operations in Iran.
Sam Gringlas contributed reporting

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/07/whe.headline: When the great-grandson of an enslaved man beat the grandson of a president
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/07/whe.author: Maegan Vazquez

paragraphs.text: Speaking to an auditorium full of Clevelanders in the closing days of a heated mayoral campaign, Democratic candidate Carl B. Stokes said the quiet part out loud.
“I am going to be brutally frank with you,” Stokes, a Black man, told a crowd that The Washington Post described as “1,500 hostile white faces.”
The experts, Stokes said, were predicting that his Republican opponent might win the election only because “his skin happens to be white.”
The audience, The Post reported, roared in outrage. The newspaper called Stokes’s comments a “major political blunder.”

But not a fatal one. Fifty-nine years ago Saturday, Stokes, the great-grandson of Seaborn Brinson, an enslaved man, defeated Republican Seth Taft, the grandson of President and Chief Justice William Howard Taft.

The World War II veteran and lawyer took 50.4 percent of the vote on Nov. 7, 1967, to become the first Black person elected mayor of a major U.S. city. Black Democrat Richard G. Hatcher, meanwhile, was elected mayor of Gary, Indiana.

The Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., who was in Cleveland on election night, called the victories of Stokes, Hatcher and civil rights-minded Boston mayor-elect Kevin White a “one-two-three punch against backlash and bigotry.”

Election analysts told The Post shortly after the election that 80 percent of White Democrats in Cleveland and 90 percent of White Democrats in Gary “broke with Stokes and Hatcher and supported their white Republican rivals.”
Stokes won reelection in 1969 by a similarly narrow margin. As mayor, he worked to hire Black people and women at city hall, revitalize neighborhoods and address industrial pollution.

On the night King was assassinated, as other cities erupted in violence, Stokes rushed to a local television station to urge calm: “I appeal to all Clevelanders to do honor to the memory of MLK by reacting to this tragic loss in the peaceful manner in which he lived.”

He then ordered White police officers out of Black neighborhoods — a decision that would further strain a tense relationship with the police department — and assembled what he called a “peace patrol”: “Clergymen, athletes, street clubs, militants out patrolling, working to keep the lid on,” he wrote in a 1973 autobiography. He joined them in walking the city through the night, “calming people, talking them into cooler emotions.”

Stokes declined to seek a third term in 1971. After leaving office, he became an anchorman with WNBC-TV in New York, a municipal judge and, under President Bill Clinton, U.S. ambassador to the African island nation of Seychelles.
(His brother and law partner, the civil rights attorney Louis Stokes, was the first Black congressman from Ohio. He served 15 terms from 1969 to 1999.)

In the years since Carl Stokes’s victory, Black people have occupied all levels of public office in the United States up to the presidency. The National Conference of Black Mayors says it now represents more than 640 municipal chief executives across the country.
Photo Almanac is an occasional series from The Washington Post, using photo archives to examine where we’ve been to understand where we are.

thehill.com/homenews/administration/6205.headline: Trump sends ‘clear message’ to Democrats with Miller promotion
thehill.com/homenews/administration/6205.author: Julia Manchester

paragraphs.text: President Trump sent a blunt message to the incoming Democratic majority on Capitol Hill by tapping Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff, setting up what is likely to be a contentious two years between both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue.

Miller is loathed by most Democrats, many of whom view him as xenophobic and racist. Additionally, the incoming chief of staff is not known to compromise with the other side of the aisle, preferring a combative approach to pushing the Trump agenda.
Many see the move as Trump signaling to congressional Democrats that he is not thinking about compromise and will implement his agenda through executive authority.

“They are not going to slow down on executive power, executive orders, and regulations,” said Joe Grogan, former director of Trump’s Domestic Policy Council in his first administration and senior adviser at Covington & Burling LLP. “Stephen is going to move aggressively on all of that.”
Mick Mulvaney, who was Trump’s chief of staff during his first term, said the president’s pick of Miller sends “a clear message.”
“The White House will continue to prioritize executive authority in the next two years,” Mulvaney told The Hill.

“Stephen is a good choice on many levels, but face it, if the president was looking to build bridges with the new incoming Democrat majorities, he would probably have gone in a different direction,” he continued.
Not everyone in Trump’s orbit and the broader GOP universe is thrilled about the decision.

“We’re cooked,” said one former Trump administration official. “It’s exactly the opposite direction voters are begging Republicans to go. Susie was the best thing that happened to President Trump,” the former official continued, referencing chief of staff Susie Wiles, who resigned Friday.
Another former Trump White House official who worked with Miller described the incoming chief of staff as “smart and opinionated, but does not have many close friends on the White House staff.”
“Most of his colleagues view him as somewhat of an arrogant lone wolf,” the former official said.

“Trump likes him because he’s been a hard-liner on immigration enforcement in both his terms, but Trump has also gone against Miller when his ‘no holds barred’ approach goes too far like in Minneapolis earlier this year,” they added.

The violent optics of the clashes between federal immigration enforcement and protesters in Minnesota earlier this year led, in part, to the ouster of former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. Border Patrol officer Gregory Bovino, who served as commander at large of the law enforcement arm, was also removed from his position following the unrest.
However, Miller, who strongly defended the operation, kept his role in the administration.
His promotion comes after the president said Wednesday that he would “probably get along with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive, adding that he wields “the power of the veto.”
“They’ve already called, and they want to talk about things, and that’s fine,” the president said.
Democrats, however, say Trump’s promotion of Miller has thrown that possibility out the window.

“Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said in a post on the social platform X. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor.”
“Fire him today,” added Jeffries, who is likely to be the next House Speaker.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) responded to Miller’s promotion by saying Trump has “learned nothing from his historic defeat.”

“Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice,” Schumer wrote on X. “Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”
One Republican lobbyist warned the move to promote Miller will only worsen relations between the White House and Capitol Hill.

“The president has two directions, one was to work with the Democratic Congress to try to get some things done. The other is to go to war with them. Stephen is more of a go-to-war guy,” the lobbyist said.
But Grogan argued that Trump’s move to tap Miller as his chief of staff could be seen as a negotiating tactic in itself.
“Trump is a negotiator and by picking Miller he is negotiating because he’s projecting strength, not weakness,” Grogan said.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/07/her.headline: Her Statue of Liberty tour was supposed to be upbeat. Then she erupted.
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/07/her.author: Danielle Paquette

paragraphs.text: NEW YORK — On the day she would finally snap, Isabelle Garbani wore jeans and a bright yellow T-shirt. She wanted to look cheerful. Approachable. Her streak of five-star reviews depended on it, she thought.

The clients she led to the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island had praised her as “fun,” “enthusiastic” and “a real charmer.” Most were on vacation from across the country — small towns, big cities, opposing realities — so Isabelle, 59, tried to unspool her message diplomatically.

Four in 10 of you, she liked to say, probably have an ancestor who passed through this gateway to America. As for her, she had come in 1984 from a tiny French village, which explained her accent, but her last name is Italian, and her paternal grandmother was Polish.
“This tour,” she’d explain, “is focused on immigration.”

Focusing on immigration lately made it harder to stay charming. Since President Donald Trump returned to office and ordered what he touted as the “largest mass deportation operation of illegal aliens in history,” Isabelle had read reports of federal authorities making arrests without reasonable suspicion, entering homes without judicial warrants and deporting people in spite of protective orders to nations they had never visited. Agents who had sworn an oath to uphold the Constitution had detained U.S. citizens unlawfully and killed people who Isabelle thought seemed innocent.

She had heard the conservative arguments about undocumented criminals overwhelming the borders, distributing lethal drugs, spreading gang violence and “poisoning the blood of our country,” as Trump had put it. But in her 42 years here, two decades as a citizen, Isabelle had never felt as unsafe as she did now, and what she feared was the government abusing its power.

She hadn’t mentioned any of that on a tour. Some sightseers, she guessed, might support what disturbed her — including, she assumed, the client who’d said his Mexican family had relocated to California “the right way.”

There used to be no wrong way, Isabelle had replied in what she hoped was a playful tone. Millions arrived before the United States had a national screening system, she pointed out. (The man didn’t leave her a review.)

Now she waited near the Battery park ferry terminal with a sign that read “TOURS BY LOCALS,” wondering what she would hear next. Isabelle scanned the crowd. On this October morning, a family of five was supposed to meet her for a four-hour exploration of what the National Park Service called a “memorial to all who pursued the American dream and have made this nation their adopted home.”

For seven years, this gig had subsidized her passions: art and acting. Isabelle listed improvisation as a “special skill” on her résumé, and adapting to the energy of any group, politically right or left or apathetic, helped her book enough $396 tours to cover the rent for her Bay Ridge apartment.

All she knew about today’s clients were their names: the Espinozas. Perhaps they were immigrants, too. That didn’t mean they’d sympathize with her anger. Reading the room meant stifling the urge to blurt out: Did you know that, yesterday afternoon, about 14 miles from where we’re standing, a federal agent shot a Dominican man right in front of his 5-year-old son?
“Hellooo!” Isabelle called out to the young woman waving at her.
“How are you?” chirped the woman, who introduced herself as Carina.
“This is Samantha,” Carina said, nodding to her 17-month-old daughter.
“Hiii Samantha!” Isabelle cooed.
The toddler stared up from her travel stroller.
“And this is Sam, Karla and Deisy,” Carina continued, pointing to her husband, niece and sister-in-law.
“Where are you guys coming from?” Isabelle asked in her singsongy autopilot.
“San Diego,” Carina replied, tucking a section of wavy black hair behind her ears.
“Oh!” Isabelle exclaimed. “It’s so beautiful out there.”
This crew seemed friendly, she thought, if a bit tired. She guided them to a ferry named MISS FREEDOM, where passengers were lining up for the 11:30 a.m. ride to Liberty Island.
Check out the Manhattan skyline, she said. Workers from at least four continents forged those skyscrapers.
“New York became what it is because of immigrant labor,” Isabelle said, watching her clients’ faces.

AS A TEENAGER in rural Longueil-Sainte-Marie, France, Isabelle couldn’t picture her future. “Only blankness,” she recalled. Maybe she was depressed. Her father had pressured her into studying science, an academic track she found boring.
Then he got a printer technology job near Boston, and Isabelle landed in what she saw as a world of possibility.

She started painting. She got cast as a hula dancer in her high school’s production of “Get Smart.” She got into puppetry. She got into poetry. She met her partner of three decades, Daniel Collins, and he followed her in 2005 to New York, where she earned an MFA in sculpture.
“This is the rest of my life,” she had thought.

The couple agreed to prioritize freedom — she didn’t want kids, and he didn’t want marriage — and indulge each other’s ideas, no matter how outlandish. Like his Dungeons & Dragons vlogcast, and her sense that stuffed animals had feelings. (“Well, obviously,” Daniel replied.)

Isabelle became a tour guide in 2019. Shepherding visitors to America’s most famous landmark — a gift from France, by the way — felt as natural to her as pronouncing the statue’s original name: La Liberté éclairant le monde. Liberty enlightening the world.
Now, she worried the president of the U.S. could get angry at Emmanuel Macron and decide to deport all the French.
“There are no rules anymore,” Isabelle complained.
“It’s chaos,” Daniel agreed.

When Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests tripled in the first months of the second Trump administration, Daniel’s union at Kingsborough Community College, where he teaches math and computing, posted a callout for “court support.” He volunteered to guide asylum seekers through a busy federal immigration office in Manhattan. Some had missed hearings, a colleague told him, because they weren’t notified of a room or time change. The penalty could be deportation.

Isabelle joined a Signal group dedicated to helping immigrants and handed out “Know Your Rights” fliers at Yemeni restaurants, Palestinian bakeries and halal grocery stores in their Brooklyn neighborhood. That felt empowering until January, when federal agents in Minnesota shot and killed two American protesters — a poet with three children and an intensive care nurse.
“What is the point of knowing your rights?” Isabelle asked.

She and Daniel had lived in the same apartment for 21 years. Only a massive rent hike, they’d reasoned, could force them out. Yet on an August trip to Copenhagen, both were relieved to be far away. Getting married, Daniel half-joked, would make it easier for him to obtain a European passport.

Isabelle, though, wasn’t ready to leave New York. Someone had just paid her $50 to read lines from a rough-draft script, and she would soon audition to play a concerned rabbi in a show about Trump’s ICE surge in Minnesota.
The range of creative outlets thrilled her, but she felt most at home on the subway, where she thought everyone looked and sounded different. “An array of colors and languages,” she marveled.

The Yemeni cafe two blocks from home made the best ice cream sundae. The Muslim mayor she voted for spoke to his constituents in Mandarin. Her favorite poem in English was inscribed on the Statue of Liberty.
ISABELLE LED THE ESPINOZAS off the ferry to Liberty Island, where everyone stared up at the green copper icon.
“She has broken shackles and chains at her feet,” the tour guide said, “so she has broken the chains of tyranny.”

Below that sculpted metaphor, on a bronze plaque inside the stone pedestal, was the 1883 sonnet by Emma Lazarus. The New York poet, Isabelle said, had cast the Statue of Liberty as “Mother of Exiles.”
“Ahhh,” Carina murmured.
The paralegal, 30, was interested in this history, really, but she was also watching her toddler, who was stomping in pink Velcro sneakers around the brick pavilion.
“Maaa!” the 17-month-old screeched as she crouched over a yellow leaf. Carina scooped her up as Isabelle recited “The New Colossus.”
Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free...
Carina didn’t recognize what she caught of the poem, but she could relate to “yearning to breathe free.”

When she was a baby, Carina’s mom brought her from Tijuana, Mexico, to San Diego on a tourist visa. They never left. Carina had no memory of Mexico. She had gone to American schools, married an American man and given birth to an American daughter, but she might never be American, not technically.

Pursuing citizenship would require leaving the country while her case was pending with no guarantee of when or if she could return. So every two years, Carina renewed papers that authorized her to work anywhere in the country under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program. That was also supposed to protect her from deportation. But during Trump’s second term, dozens of “Dreamers” like her, with no criminal record, had been deported. Two had been arrested at what sounded to Carina like routine appointments.
She was so nervous she could barely speak when she reported in January to an immigration office for her latest round of fingerprinting. The woman operating the biometric scanner must have noticed.
“Honey, it’s okay,” she had told her. “Just relax.”

Now, Carina struggled to relax under the Statue of Liberty. She had expected to feel awe and was annoyed to feel sad. Angry, even. The chains of tyranny were broken up there, sure, but the headline that had flashed on her husband’s phone the evening before was: ICE agents shot at man in car with his 5-year-old son.
What if that had been Samantha terrified in the back seat?
Gratitude, Carina reminded herself. Her family was here and healthy. Holding her baby for the first time, she’d thought, “My lucky girl.”
Turning back toward her tour guide, Carina appreciated the tenderness in Isabelle’s voice.
Send these, the homeless, tempest-tost to me,
I lift my lamp beside the golden door!
Lazarus wrote those lines, Isabelle said, after Congress passed a law that barred Chinese laborers from entering the U.S.
What she wanted to add was: See how dumb that was! And what did we learn? Instead, she summarized a mainstream view from that era, one she found unnervingly recurring.
“People blamed the immigrants,” Isabelle said, “for everything bad that was happening.”
“Well,” Carina chimed in, squeezing Samantha, “we’re pro-immigrant.”

TWO HOURS IN, Isabelle had detected no tension she needed to banter away. Some of her previous clients looked uncomfortable when she mentioned darker parts of America’s past. She’d heard a few variations of: My ancestors followed the rules.
The Espinozas had been nodding along. Pro-immigrant, Carina had said.
“These guys get it,” Isabelle thought.

The issue now was they were hungry. Up next was what she’d advertised as a “melting pot picnic” on Ellis Island. Unfortunately, hundreds of people waited ahead of them to board the next ferry to that prime tourist destination.
“We’ve got at least 25 minutes,” Isabelle estimated, eyeing the crammed dock.
The group was quiet for a moment, gazing out at the glittering water.
“I guess I could do my Ellis Island spiel,” Isabelle offered.
She started like she usually did.

“So Ellis Island opens in 1892...,” she said. She breezed through the island’s backstory to 1924, when the U.S. enacted a law that sharply limited immigration from nations lawmakers deemed threatening to the “racial status quo.”
“Specifically designed to exclude the Italians,” Isabelle said.

All around her, she realized, more people were listening. One red-haired man seemed to be scowling. Did the shameful facts of a century ago irritate him, she wondered, or was that the sun in his eyes?
“Those quotas existed until the 60s,” Isabelle continued.
