She moved on to 1965, when Lyndon B. Johnson, standing at the base of the Statue of Liberty, signed the law that abolished that system — “a cruel and enduring wrong,” he called it — and allowed immigrants from around the world to join their families in the U.S.

Approximately 12 million immigrants, mainly Europeans, traveled through what used to be America’s busiest processing station. Most entered before any visa was required. They just needed to pass a medical evaluation and answer some questions.
“Then you could walk in and do whatever you wanted,” Isabelle said.

She enjoyed how that line surprised some people. The Espinozas simply listened. So did a woman behind them wearing a foam Statue of Liberty headband, Isabelle noticed, and a man in a Rip Curl cap, and another in tactical shades, and another with a Canon camera dangling around his neck.
“A whole theater of people,” Isabelle thought. She would normally stop there to guide her clients to the museum, but they were still stuck on the dock, and was that guy scowling?
Perhaps her habit of scanning for cues was throwing her off. Or riling her up. That guy couldn’t leave her a review, Isabelle thought. That guy’s going to listen to me.

She could have stayed “fun” by asking if anyone wanted a photo. She could have transitioned into talking about the unseasonably warm weather. But wasn’t this place supposed to be a memorial to all who had made America their adopted home? How was that going for immigrants now?
Maybe it was the silence she reflexively tended to fill, or the adrenaline she felt while speaking publicly, or the anger she could no longer contain to conversations with Daniel.
Isabelle ditched her spiel.
“Now, it’s a goddamn mess,” she snapped.
That might have been her first curse word on Liberty Island. She spoke louder and faster.
“Let’s just be clear,” she said. “People are being deported left and right. People who are here legally are being deported. People are being deported to countries they don’t even know.”
Isabelle looked around. Yeah, that guy was scowling.
“ICE agents are actually grabbing people from the courthouse. So people who are trying to make their situation legal — people are being dragged directly from the courthouse.”
Now, dozens were just watching.
“They are making things confusing for people,” Isabelle said. “‘Oh, we sent you a letter to change your appointment. You didn’t get it? Too bad. You’re deported.’”
She wouldn’t mention the bloodshed, like the shooting from the day before. There were children around.
“So, it’s a horrific thing happening in the U.S.,” she concluded.
Nobody clapped. The tourists turned back to their groups and phones. But Carina’s husband nudged her arm, and she understood what he meant: She’s cool.
“EVERYONE DOING OKAY?” Isabelle asked as they finally headed to lunch.

Still amped, she redirected her attention to her guests, shifting back into her singsongy autopilot. This way to the Ellis Island museum. That way to the cafeteria. Bathrooms are on the left. We can fit at that table in the corner.

Decades of riffing onstage had conditioned her not to dwell on whether a performance had bombed, but what about a rant as a tour guide? Had she gone too far for a family trying to enjoy themselves on vacation?
“I laid it on thicker,” she told the Espinozas, “when I saw that guy scowling.”
Carina hadn’t seen the man Isabelle described. With red hair, though, she imagined his ancestors were immigrants who had been lucky enough to seek a better life before ICE existed.
“They immigrated 500 years ago, so they are special,” Carina said sarcastically.
“They were on the Mayflower,” Isabelle quipped back. “Like, good for you!”

The ferry wait had delayed their meal by an hour, but the group seemed looser than they had all day. Isabelle laid out a spread of croissants, turkey, hummus, guacamole, tomatoes and potato chips. “What the immigrants brought, food-wise,” she said as everyone dug in.

Carina didn’t tell Isabelle, but the tour guide’s candor had impressed her. “This is a safe space,” she had thought. They could joke about pilgrims, and Carina didn’t have to worry about not sounding grateful for her place in the only country she’d ever known. This was a pleasant diversion from monitoring the news and worrying about getting torn from her toddler.
“I don’t even believe in borders,” Isabelle confessed while they ate.
Nine days later, she received her 55th straight five-star review.
“Hands down,” Carina had written, “the best tour we’ve been on.”

washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/07.headline: Martina Arroyo was a luminous star of opera who broke racial barriers
washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/07.author: Matt Schudel

paragraphs.text: In a celebrated career as an international superstar of opera, the soprano Martina Arroyo appeared on many of the great stages of the world, from La Scala in Milan to Covent Garden in London, from the Vienna State Opera to the Paris Opera and Teatro Colón in Buenos Aires. But, in some ways, her longest journey never left Manhattan, where she was born and lived for most of her life.

Ms. Arroyo, who died Oct. 13 at age 90, grew up in Harlem at a time when few Black singers imagined that a career in opera could be possible. As a child, she took dance lessons, sang in church choirs, attended concerts and listened to opera broadcasts on the radio. But she had little expectation of becoming an opera singer in her own right, let alone one of its most luminous stars.

Ms. Arroyo began taking vocal lessons in earnest at 14, studied languages in college, and was a teacher and social worker before she became a professional singer, performing in Europe and in occasional small operatic roles. Her breakthrough came at New York’s Metropolitan Opera in 1965, when she took on the lead role in “Aida” at the last minute after an ailing soprano dropped out. She received a standing ovation and was praised by New York Times music critic Raymond Ericson for having “one of the most gorgeous voices before the public today.”

Ms. Arroyo was promptly signed to a contract by the Metropolitan Opera, completing her sojourn from 111th Street in Harlem to the world’s most prestigious opera company, then in Midtown Manhattan. The Met would become her primary musical home for two decades.

She would win renown in the 1960s and 1970s as one of the busiest sopranos in opera, performing many of the greatest roles in the repertoire, including Cio-Cio San in Giacomo Puccini’s “Madama Butterfly,” the title role in Puccini’s “Tosca,” Elsa in Richard Wagner’s “Lohengrin” and both principal soprano parts in Mozart’s “Don Giovanni,” Donna Anna and Donna Elvira.

Ms. Arroyo shared the stage with such acclaimed singers as Joan Sutherland, Plácido Domingo, Luciano Pavarotti and Sherrill Milnes. Renowned conductors, including Leonard Bernstein, Eugene Ormandy and Zubin Mehta, sought her out for concert performances.

Above all, Ms. Arroyo was known for her interpretations of major roles in the operas of Giuseppe Verdi, including “Aida,” “La forza del destino,” “Il trovatore,” “Un ballo in maschera” and “Macbeth.” She was regarded as one of the leading “Verdi sopranos” of her generation for her clear, soaring tone, particularly in the upper register, and for her ability to project her voice above the orchestra, with a commanding yet lithe presence.

“It’s such a rich, rotund and luscious sound,” the operatic tenor George Shirley told The Washington Post’s classical music writer Anne Midgette in 2013, when Ms. Arroyo was awarded the Kennedy Center Honors.
“There was a quality of the tone and her artistry that made her distinctive,” Shirley added.

What also made her distinctive was that she was a Black woman triumphing in an art form that had been an almost exclusively White domain for well over a century. It wasn’t until 1955 that Marian Anderson, then in her late 50s, was the first Black singer to perform at the Met, in a secondary role in “Un ballo in maschera.” Leontyne Price became a featured soprano at the Met in the early 1960s, followed by Ms. Arroyo, Grace Bumbry and Shirley Verrett.
Ms. Arroyo said she encountered little overt discrimination in the opera world, in part because she had grown up in New York.

“I had never been an outsider,” she told The Post in 2013. “It gives you a type of fearlessness because you don’t know you’re going to run into the problem, and I didn’t run into it. Or if I did, I didn’t know about it.”

Martina Arroyo was born Feb. 2, 1936, in Harlem, the younger of two children. Her father, Demetrio Arroyo, was a mechanical engineer who had grown up in Puerto Rico. Her mother, the former Lucille Washington, was originally from Charleston, South Carolina, and played piano. Ms. Arroyo’s brother, 16 years her senior, became a minister.
Despite her father’s Puerto Rican heritage, Ms. Arroyo considered herself African American and attended Baptist churches in Harlem.
“I am what you see: a Black woman,” she told The Post. “I’m a New Yorker through and through.”

Ms. Arroyo learned piano from her mother, and both parents emphasized education and cultural awareness. She was admitted to Hunter College High School, then a selective public school for girls with an emphasis on the arts. While sitting in on an opera workshop at nearby Hunter College, Ms. Arroyo and some of her fellow high school students began to imitate the older singers. The director of the workshop, Josef Turnau, told them that if they liked singing so much, they should audition.

“I sang what I thought was the Jewel Song” — from Charles Gounod’s “Faust” — Ms. Arroyo told The Post, “in what I thought was French.” Amateurish as her effort may have been, the quality of her voice impressed Turnau, who allowed her to attend his college-level workshop. He recommended that she take lessons from Marinka Gurewich, who remained Ms. Arroyo’s vocal coach throughout her career.
Later, while attending Hunter College, Ms. Arroyo studied Italian and other Romance languages but began to neglect her vocal training.

“And there came a time when Madame G. warned me that if I didn’t take my voice more seriously she’d drop me,” she told the New York Times in 1972. “This was a turning point for me. Up to then, I must have been, in my mind, treating singing as a hobby, a lark — something I loved that I was dabbling in. … But Madame G.’s warning made me face up to myself as a professional.”

Ms. Arroyo graduated from Hunter in three years, in 1956, taught English at a Bronx high school for a year, and then spent two years as a social worker in New York. All the while, she continued her vocal studies and sang in small productions.

In 1957, she failed a Metropolitan Opera audition, but the next year she was accepted, winning a scholarship to the company’s training school, where she studied drama, diction and even fencing. She made her operatic debut at Carnegie Hall in 1958 in the U.S. premiere of Ildebrando Pizzetti’s “Murder in the Cathedral,” then had a small role as the Celestial Voice in Verdi’s “Don Carlo” at the Met in 1959.

With only four days’ notice, Ms. Arroyo stepped into the lead role in “Aida” on Feb. 6, 1965, after Birgit Nilsson withdrew. It was a career-making performance, leading to 199 appearances at the Met, plus many more at the world’s leading opera halls. In a fitting bookend to her career, Ms. Arroyo gave her final performance at the Met — and her final performance as Aida — in 1986. She continued to sing in recitals until 1992 before devoting herself to teaching, primarily at Louisiana State University and later at Indiana University.

While at Indiana, Ms. Arroyo developed a course on how to prepare for an operatic role. That course helped lead to the creation of the Martina Arroyo Foundation, which has helped launch hundreds of students on careers in opera and music. In addition to her Kennedy Center Honors, Ms. Arroyo was a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and a Carnegie Hall board member.

Known for her effervescent sense of humor, Ms. Arroyo made more than 20 appearances on Johnny Carson’s “Tonight Show” and played herself in a 1975 episode of the sitcom “The Odd Couple,” singing an aria from “Il trovatore” and Stevie Wonder’s “For Once in My Life.”
She was sometimes coy about her age, once remarking, “The 10 years between 29 and 30 are the hardest.”

Her first marriage, to Italian musician Emilio Poggioni, ended in divorce. She was married to French banker Michel Maurel for more than 35 years until his death in 2011. Ms. Arroyo’s death, at her home in Manhattan, was announced by the Metropolitan Opera. She had no immediate survivors.

Ms. Arroyo was meticulous in her preparation for roles. The vocal part was relatively easy, but the more difficult part was reaching the emotional and psychological depth required of such dramatic roles as Lady Macbeth, Tosca or Amelia in “Un ballo in maschera.”

“If people think a kind of magic happens on stage, they ought to know that what they’re seeing is a lot of work,” she said in 1972. “To me, ‘charisma’ is just a fancy word for rehearsals. And if I catch you using the word ‘effortless’ about me, I’ll laugh in your face.”

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/07/h.headline: How to turn your retirement savings into a steady income stream for life
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/07/h.author: Michelle Singletary

paragraphs.text: For decades, you exercised financial discipline, sacrificing immediate wants to ensure you have a secure retirement.
But once you retire, you’re left with a daunting new problem: how to spend down what you’ve saved and invested.

Concerns about rising inflation, the financial stability of Social Security, and the likelihood of exorbitant health care expenses create a paradox: Even when retirees have built a healthy nest egg, the dread of depleting it keeps them from enjoying it.
So how do you spend the money without regrets or anxiety?

I’ve got a book for that. For this November’s Color of Money Book Club, Jean Chatzky addresses the withdrawal years in “The Forever Paycheck: The New Retirement Strategy to Spend More, Worry Less, and Never Run Out of Money.” Chatzky offers strategies to turn the money you’ve put away into a steady paycheck so you can relax, spend what you earned and actually enjoy life.

Chatzky shares a personal story that resonated with me because I already know I’ll have trouble drawing down on my retirement savings when I’m no longer getting a steady paycheck. I wrote about my anxiety when my husband retired three years ago.

When Chatzky’s father died in 2005, her mother was 63, and she had $1.6 million in retirement and taxable accounts. Her mother’s fixed income included Social Security and a modest pension from her husband’s years as a college professor. Her home was paid off, and she had a long-term care policy.

“What became more clear with each passing year was that she was comfortable spending her Social Security, the pension dollars, and the interest on her brokerage accounts — but nothing more,” Chatzky wrote.
When Chatzky’s mom died in 2024 at 83, she didn’t have the $1.6 million left. Her retirement balance had grown to $1.7 million.
“She would not spend the principal,” Chatzky said during an interview for my podcast.
Here’s a sobering statistic: 67 percent of Americans are more afraid of running out of money in retirement than of dying, according to a study by the Allianz Center for the Future of Retirement.
In the book, Chatzky highlights research that found retirees with guaranteed income from an annuity typically spend twice as much as those relying on lump-sum retirement accounts.
What made the difference in spending comfort?
“I think it’s because they just knew that those paychecks were going to continue to come,” she told me.
In her research, Chatzky explains how many people can feel more at ease spending what they’ve saved.
“The paycheck-to-paycheck mentality that we work so hard to escape during the early stages of our career turns out to be the key to living more comfortably in retirement,” she wrote.
Before she gets to the strategies for creating a retirement paycheck, Chatzky recommends that you know your numbers.
Here’s a game you should try: List the major expense categories you have, then, without checking your bank or credit card statements, guess how much you spend in each category. How well would you do?

“As spending money — with swipes, clicks, dips, taps and so on — has gotten more and more frictionless, it’s also become more invisible,” Chatzky points out in the book. “Only when the bills pour in at the end of the month do we get a sense of how much we’ve spent.”
You need this preretirement baseline to help you create your retirement budget. This will give you a better understanding of what you can live without, so your money lasts longer.

“In retirement, as in life before retirement, money is a limited resource,” Chatzky wrote in the book. “That means making conscious choices about what’s a need, what’s a want, and what’s a wish — and getting very specific about the ones that are deal breakers.”

Next, of course, you’ll build your base retirement paycheck by maximizing Social Security and any pension you have. The hardest part of Social Security is deciding when to claim it. Claiming at 62, when you’re first eligible, can mean a 30 percent reduction. If your full retirement age is 67, waiting until 70 will give you an 8 percent annual increase.

Chatzky offers a thorough discussion of when to take your benefits. Early might make sense for some; late might be a better choice for others. If you haven’t already, create a Social Security account to get an estimate of your monthly benefit.

If you’re fortunate enough to have a pension, you’ve got some choices to make as well. If you’re married, do you want a survivor benefit? (You can’t leave the benefit to someone else unless your spouse signs off on it.)
At the heart of the book are additional strategies for structuring your retirement income so it feels like a paycheck.
For those comfortable with market movements, you can build a self-managed structure with cash buckets, CDs, Treasury bonds and dividend-paying stocks.
For risk-averse individuals, Chatzky suggests creating a paycheck by purchasing an annuity that will provide income for the rest of your life.

“In the simplest form, you take a chunk of money and give it to an insurance company, and in exchange, they give you a paycheck that either starts immediately or starts down the road. And because they pool risk … they actually can give you a better return than you’re likely to get with something like a CD or a Treasury.”

Chatzky concedes she grew up in personal finance journalism, very wary of annuities. Many types of annuities come with high commissions, surrender charges if you want to exit the contract early, and other fees that can make them more expensive than investing in a mutual fund.
“If you’re raising a skeptical eyebrow, you’re not alone, ” she wrote. “For many years, I did as well … The fees were too high, the terms mind-bogglingly confusing.”
But she says her research for the book changed her perspective. She now views them as a useful tool when used properly.
Like much of retirement planning, you need to figure out what’s right for you.

“I still don’t like all annuities,” Chatzky wrote in the book. “But I do believe that if you’re a person who wants to know that you’ll have income that flows for the rest of your life … they can provide guarantees that other products cannot.”

I’m still in the wary camp. However, I agree an annuity makes sense for some people. But as Chatzky stresses, you must be very careful about what you buy, when you buy it and how much money you allocate to them.

If you decide an annuity is right for you, buy only from insurance companies rated A or better, and potentially spread your risk across multiple companies to stay within state guaranty fund limits, Chatzky said.

“I am going to buy an annuity,” Chatzky told me. “I never thought I would say that, but I’m actually gonna take some of my money — not all of it, just a chunk — and buy a paycheck that I know will continue to come for the rest of my life, and then I’ll invest the rest.”

In “The Forever Paycheck,” written in collaboration with AARP, Chatzky doesn’t prescribe a single “one-and-done” solution. She guides you through a range of options to turn your money into a steady stream of income, tailored to your financial goals, lifestyle, and risk tolerance.
To prudently enjoy your retirement savings, you need a strategy. Fear isn’t a plan.

Follow Michelle’s financial advice show, Dollars & Sense with Michelle Singletary, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts. Want Michelle to answer your money question on the show? Email dollarsandsense@washpost.com.

washingtonpost.com/education/2026/11/07/.headline: Texas remade education in the GOP’s image. Hinojosa plans to undo it.
washingtonpost.com/education/2026/11/07/.author: Lauren Lumpkin

paragraphs.text: Democratic Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa is barreling into office with a pledge to shift away from the conservative education policies that have set Texas apart from other red states — and the rest of the country.
Hours after the polls closed this week, Hinojosa repeated one of the promises central to her plan to shake up education in Texas: “In case you have not heard, on day one, I will fire Mike Morath.”
Morath, the state’s top education official, appointed by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, has been on a 10-year crusade to remake education for the state’s 5.4 million students.

During the tenures of Morath and Abbott, Texas has earned a reputation as a testing ground for conservative education policies that have been replicated in other states, but nowhere quite as aggressively. Texas officials in recent years have encouraged prayer in schools, passed a law requiring classrooms to display the Ten Commandments, and allowed chaplains to offer spiritual counseling to public school students. School districts can get extra funding for adopting a curriculum that includes Bible passages.

In the state’s public universities, Republicans have wielded their control to ban diversity, equity and inclusion programs. Some campuses have cut courses and eliminated majors in ethnic, women’s and gender studies.
And the Texas Education Agency has taken control of seven school districts because of academic underperformance, mostly in Black, Latino and Democratic swaths of the state.
Morath also is credited with overseeing a nationally recognized program that pays teachers more for boosting students’ test scores, and with helping to launch a new $1 billion voucher program.
Hinojosa will be able to start trying to undo much of that when she takes office in January. Some changes will be easier to tackle than others, experts say.

The state representative and former Austin school board member has said less about how she will address culture war topics, such as religion in classrooms and diversity, equity and inclusion. But she has vowed to peel back some of the foremost pieces of Abbott’s education plan, including ending contested state takeovers of school districts and halting his landmark voucher program. Hinojosa has also promised to do away with Texas’s standardized test, pause the statewide school accountability system and increase teacher pay.

“We are taking our children’s education back from a government that has failed them,” she said to a crowd of cheering supporters Tuesday. “Schools will not be taken out of our control. They will not be shuttered or suffocated.”

Soon, she will be able to appoint regents to public universities’ governing boards, a task that will need the approval of the majority-Republican state Senate. Along with the new Democratic majority in the Texas House and the State Board of Education, which is poised to lose its GOP majority, a crop of new leaders could roll back policies that Abbott’s administration championed.

“I would expect to see a lot less of the culture war policies and politics even kind of surfacing for a time now,” said David DeMatthews, a professor in the educational leadership and policy department at the University of Texas at Austin. “Questions around book bans and transgender bathrooms and the Ten Commandments, I would expect to see that kind of push go.”
Still, Hinojosa could face an uphill battle, and it is unclear how exactly she will fulfill her campaign promises.
Hinojosa’s office did not respond to requests for comment.
Libby Cohen, executive director of Raise Your Hand Texas, an education advocacy group, said the state Senate will pose a challenge.
“Certainly, a lot of her ability to move on a legislative agenda is going to depend on her ability to find common ground with the Republican Senate majority,” Cohen said.

Hinojosa’s promises to end state takeovers of public schools are already stirring hopes in the Austin Independent School District, where families at two middle schools have advanced a controversial plan to close their own schools rather than cede control of the district to state officials.

In Texas, the state can take control of a school district if a single low-performing school gets five consecutive “F” ratings from the state’s education agency. During a takeover, the education commissioner can replace a district’s locally elected school board with a board of managers and install a new superintendent, among other changes.

Burnet and Webb middle schools, two predominantly Hispanic schools serving some of Austin’s lowest-income neighborhoods, received their fifth “F” in a row this summer. For months, families have feared that state officials would take over the district.
That appears unlikely when Hinojosa is in office, said Ken Zarifis, a Burnet parent and president of the district’s teachers union.
“I’m super excited,” Zarifis said. “Her whole campaign was about schools, about taking care of them, taking care of the kids.”

The Texas Education Agency did not respond to questions about whether it will take control of Austin’s schools before Hinojosa assumes office. In a message to families, Austin Superintendent Matias Segura said school leaders are evaluating how the election will affect the district.

Hinojosa is bound by law to intervene in a struggling district, so using the legislative process to end state takeovers would require bipartisan support. But the person she installs as the next education commissioner will have wide latitude over the process.
“The takeover doesn’t have to feel or look anything like what it has looked like under Morath,” DeMatthews said.

Researchers have found that, on average, school takeovers can be disruptive for students and do little to improve math and reading scores. Supporters say the intervention, which has surged in Texas, puts pressure on districts to turn around chronically underperforming schools.

Critics, however, argue that state takeovers leave schools worse off. Since the state took control in 2023 of the Houston Independent School District, Texas’s largest school system, the district has seen an exodus of 21,000 students, higher teacher turnover and a federal probe into the district’s handling of special-education students.

F. Mike Miles, the state-appointed superintendent in Houston, said test scores have been on the rise since he took over. He pointed to state data showing that achievement gaps between Black and White and Hispanic and White children have shrunk, and noted that enrollment is declining in districts across the country.

“I don’t think people should just throw up their hands and say, ‘Well, you know, local control.’ I think, at some point, if the elected board and the administration haven’t done what they need to do for kids, then there should be an intervention,” Miles said. “It’s been a good thing for kids in Texas.”
Miles cut hundreds of teaching positions to remove educators he called ineffective and to rightsize after enrollment losses, he said. He added that 87 percent of teachers returned this school year.
At least 14 other Texas school districts are at risk of being taken over, according to an analysis by the Texas Tribune.
Hinojosa is also going after Abbott’s banner voucher program.

The Texas Education Freedom Accounts program pays families $10,474 per student, money they can use for private school tuition or other education-related expenses. Children with disabilities and home-schooled students also qualify for cash.
The program has more than 111,000 participants this year, state data shows.
It would take legislation to undo the voucher system. Hinojosa could, however, use line-item veto power to eliminate funding for the program or veto future voucher-related legislation.
“That is definitely a very meaningful piece of leverage that she now holds as she gets ready to step into the office,” Cohen said.
Changes on the State Board of Education could also help propel Hinojosa’s agenda.

Democrats this week gained a stronger foothold on the board, which lost its 11-4 Republican majority. The balance of power is now split 7-7; a final race had not yet been called as of Friday, according to the Texas Tribune.
No matter the outcome, Texans can expect to see a school board less mired in clashes over social issues, said Gustavo Reveles, a board member since 2025.

“It was a call from people, most of them Republicans, who said extremism went too far. Extremism did not help us at all,” Reveles said. “So this is not the right time for us as Democrats to swing it back to the other side. It’s time for us to really come to the middle, collaborate.”

This year the school board adopted hotly debated social studies standards that emphasize the influence of the Bible on America’s founding and include a mandatory reading list with stories from the Bible.

Nationally, education advocates are taking notice of what’s happening in Texas. Michael Petrilli, president of the Thomas B. Fordham Institute, a conservative think tank, predicts that there will be “less shenanigans on the culture war front” but worries about Texas losing steam on policies that have shown promise.

He called the Teacher Incentive Allotment, a program launched in 2019 that boosts pay for high-performing teachers, “one of the most promising policies in education today.” He added that state takeovers have been controversial but are necessary to turn schools around.
“I do think that the governor and commissioner deserve credit for the political courage to do something,” Petrilli said.

The path forward for other parts of Hinojosa’s plan is unclear. The governor-elect’s campaign platform called for replacing the state’s standardized test and pausing the accountability system that assigns every school and district a letter grade between A and F. Those grades are used to determine whether campuses should close or districts should be taken over by the state.
Federal law requires public schools that receive federal funding to administer some form of standardized test.
Hinojosa’s campaign did not respond to a question about what other assessments the governor-elect is considering.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/07/doe.headline: Does Florida’s narrow escape from the blue wave hold lessons for Republicans?
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/07/doe.author: Alex DeLuca

paragraphs.text: There weren’t too many Republicans cheering their party’s performance in the aftermath of the nationwide thumping they experienced. But Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis probably came closest to a victory lap.

DeSantis, who plans to run for president in 2028, said that election night would have been an “extinction-level event” for the Republican Party if it weren’t for the Sunshine State. “Really, Florida is the last main anchor standing,” he said.

GOP strongholds such as Texas and Ohio saw both the governor’s office and a U.S. Senate seat flip blue this week. Of the nation’s 10 most populous states, Florida will be the only one where Republicans control the governor’s office and the state legislature when newly elected officials take office in January.

Even in Florida, the blue wave reached down the ballot. Democrats flipped 15 seats in the state House, ending the Republican supermajority, and picked up a seat in the state Senate. In Miami-Dade County, which President Donald Trump carried in 2024, voters swung back blue.

But statewide, Republicans held on. Republican Byron Donalds beat Democrat David Jolly by 1.3 percentage points in the governor’s race to succeed DeSantis, while the Republican incumbents for attorney general, chief financial officer and agriculture commissioner won by similarly close margins. In the U.S. Senate race, Republican Ashley Moody defeated Democrat Angie Nixon, 51 percent to 48 percent.

“Now it’s going to take a lot of time and effort to rebuild. It will not happen in just one election cycle. But Florida shows how you can build a coalition, not only to convert on all your promises in good times, but also to withstand the bad times,” DeSantis said.
So, how did Florida Republicans hold on?
Big lead going in
Political analysts said, among other reasons, the party had a “cushion” before the campaigns even began: a sizable lead over Democrats in voter registration.

“There was no secret little thing they did here in Florida that allowed them to stay in power,” said Brad Coker, managing director of Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy. “It’s strictly the cushion, and that cushion got pushed to the limit.”

At the end of 2020, Democrats outnumbered Republicans among Florida’s active registered voters by about 97,000. But by the end of September, Republicans led by roughly 1.55 million, according to state figures.

Much of that lead is attributed to people moving to Florida after DeSantis promoted it as a haven from pandemic restrictions, said Aubrey Jewett, a political science professor at the University of Central Florida. The newcomers helped reshape the electorate, he said, giving Republicans an edge even in an election favorable to Democrats.
“As long as they didn’t have exceptionally low turnout, as long as they were just solid, they were going to have an advantage,” Jewett said.
Huge fundraising advantage
As with elsewhere across the country, Republicans in Florida also had an edge on the money side.

Donalds’s campaign and political committee spent more than $165 million through Oct. 29, compared with almost $25 million for Jolly’s campaign and political committee, according to a Florida Politics review of state filings. In the U.S. Senate race, Moody’s campaign reported spending $13.7 million through Oct. 14, compared with $8.1 million for Nixon’s, according to Federal Election Commission data.
Kathryn DePalo-Gould, a political science professor at Florida International University, said a lack of national Democratic funding and support hurt the party’s chances in Florida.
She credited Republicans, especially the Donalds campaign, with canvassing and a “really great ground game.”
“They didn’t take the state for granted,” DePalo-Gould said.

Donalds’s focus on affordability also resonated, she said, in a state where younger voters worried they couldn’t afford to buy a home and older homeowners feared they couldn’t afford to stay in theirs.
The lure of low taxes

Voters also weighed in directly on costs of owning a home. On Tuesday, they approved Amendment 3, a DeSantis-backed measure to increase Florida’s homestead exemption for nonschool property taxes. DePalo-Gould said the prospect of lower property taxes may have drawn enough reluctant Republican voters to the polls to help the party win statewide.
“I think Republican voters might have stayed home in greater numbers had Amendment 3 not been on the ballot,” she said.
DeSantis made the same case: “The existence of Amendment 3 on the ballot is one of the reasons Florida averted the fate of other red states. It drew more voters to the polls.”
A popular governor

DeSantis also endorsed all five Republicans who won statewide races Tuesday. An early October Stetson University poll found that 55 percent of likely voters in Florida approved of the governor’s job performance.
In the governor’s race, Coker said, DeSantis’s support helped Donalds when Trump had become somewhat of a liability.

Ahead of the August primary, Donalds trumpeted Trump’s endorsement in a campaign ad. But by September, as he faced Jolly, his campaign had scrubbed several prominent references to Trump from its website.
The following month, Donalds released two ads on the same day, one featuring Trump’s endorsement and the other touting DeSantis’s.
“DeSantis bailed him out,” Coker said of Donalds.
For the next election, Coker urged Republicans to keep the focus closer to home.
“If you are a Florida Republican right now, stay away from national stuff,” he said. “Just stay away.”

livescience.com/health/flu/i-almost-died.headline: I almost died from flu. My life didn't go back to normal after.
livescience.com/health/flu/i-almost-died.author: Hannah Osborne

paragraphs.text: In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.
Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.
I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.
With thanks to Families Fighting Flu, a non-profit organization that promotes flu vaccination and raises awareness of the severity of the infectious disease through families that have been affected.

bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-league/articles/cm.headline: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Kalyn Ponga-inspired New Zealand power past Tonga to reach final
bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-league/articles/cm.author: Steve Sutcliffe

paragraphs.text: New Zealand (12) 34
Tries: Nikora, Gagai, McLean, Hughes, Willison, Nicoll-Klokstad Goals: Isaako 5
Tonga (10) 10
Tries: Fifita 2 Goals: Katoa
Just 23 days after breaking his arm, Kalyn Ponga returned to inspire New Zealand to a 34-10 victory in a pulsating encounter with Tonga as they reached their first World Cup final since 2013.

Ponga had been named initially in reserve and then as one of the interchange players in the build-up to this contest - and the expectation was that he would be eased back into action and play a limited role.

Instead, head coach Stacey Jones stunned many with his decision to include Ponga in New Zealand's starting 13 but was repaid in full as the Newcastle Knights talisman starred on home turf at the McDonald Jones Stadium, in New South Wales,
Ponga's impact from full-back was almost immediate as he sent Briton Nikora over in the right corner inside four minutes.
He was also involved in the Kiwis' second try of the game - as his contest with his opposite number Lehi Hopoate was crucial to Dane Gagai grounding the ball.
And while the swirling wind made conditions almost unplayable at times, he repeatedly gathered high kicks and made several telling defensive contributions.

One of those included throwing himself in the way of Tonga's juggernaut second row Demitric Vaimauga to prevent a certain try, while his ability to stall Hopoate's run and prevent him from offloading to Isaiya Katoa stopped another at a key stage with New Zealand only 12-10 ahead.
The prelude to this fixture was almost every bit as gripping as the main event.

Tonga's traditional war dance, the Sipi Tau, was met by New Zealand's Haka and a long stand-off between the players provided the perfect backdrop to a contest brimming with athleticism, power and superb ball-handling skills.
For the second week running, Tonga fans turned out in force with the stands a sea of red.
And they witnessed their side's participation in a wonderful advert for rugby league with Jojo Fifita scoring two excellent tries.

However, the match ultimately swung away from them in a five-minute period after the break when New Zealand's outstanding centre Casey McLean surged over in the left corner and the wily Jahrome Hughes darted in to score.

On this occasion, Kristian Woolf's team, who effectively torpedoed England's hopes of reaching the last four with a 30-12 in their opening match on 17 October, were unable to stage the same sort of fightback that helped them defeat their Pacific Island rivals Samoa last weekend.
With the scoreboard, time and a gale-force wind against Tonga, Xavier Willison punished them further when they failed to gather a short drop out.
And when Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad superbly grounded Erin Clark's kick, it put the gloss on a fine New Zealand performance.

phys.org/news/2026-11-polar-vortex-falte.headline: Polar vortex faltering weeks earlier than ever recorded
phys.org/news/2026-11-polar-vortex-falte.author: Issam Ahmed with Peter Hutchison, Laurent Thomet

paragraphs.text: edited by Andrew Zinin

Meteorologists said Friday they were observing an unprecedented early disruption of the polar vortex, raising the risk of cold snaps across the Northern Hemisphere, though there remains significant uncertainty.
The polar vortex is a vast region of cold, low-pressure air that normally circulates from west to east high above the Arctic.

It generally strengthens through autumn and peaks around January. It can weaken in the second half of winter, typically between January and March, sending bitterly cold air spilling south into Europe, North America and Asia.
But scientists say the vortex is already weakening in early November.
El Niño effects

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told AFP.

Judah Cohen, a climatologist at MIT, explained that the vortex is disrupted from below. Large atmospheric waves in the lower layer of the atmosphere, the troposphere, known as Rossby waves, can surge upward, and a big enough surge into the polar stratosphere triggers a rapid warming known as sudden stratospheric warming (SSW).
This weakens or even reverses the vortex's west-to-east winds, which can split it apart and cause it to spill southward.

"That really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, U.S., Europe and East Asia," Cohen told AFP.
Grahame Madge, a spokesperson for Britain's Met Office, told AFP: "This is very early, and possibly that earliness is triggered by the amplitude of the El Niño event in the Pacific."

This year's El Niño, a pattern of warmer-than-normal sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific that has ripple effects through the atmosphere, is exceptionally strong and could be amplifying those waves.
Stockdale and Vitart said they did not know why the disruption came so early, but agreed the El Niño "could have been a factor in making it more likely."

But Cohen was more circumspect, explaining the current disruption appeared more linked to a record-breaking high-pressure system over Scandinavia and northwestern Russia, which are more favored in La Niña years.
The polarvortex.earth dashboard, which visualizes ECMWF modeling, currently shows a full breakdown of the vortex—when the westerly winds turn easterly—by Nov. 20.
A November SSW has happened only three times in records dating back to the 1950s—1958, 1968 and 2025—all on Nov. 28.
France's Meteo-France agency told AFP the current disruption is "an unprecedented event."
How severe any cold snaps will be is far from clear.
Climate change link?

Because the disruption is coming so early, air temperatures in "places like Siberia or over the Arctic are not as cold yet as they will be," which could make outbreaks less "severe," said Madge, who called the event "exceptional" but "not necessarily worrying."
El Niño, which tends to bring milder winters, could also help. Cohen said it could "moderate or modify" the impacts, but said this remained uncertain.

"At this stage, the potential consequences for France remain highly uncertain," said Meteo-France. "They will depend on how the disruption evolves, its positioning, and whether or not it propagates down to the lower layers of the atmosphere."
Cohen said climate change could be playing a role, though he stressed this was speculation and no research has yet confirmed the link.

Rapid sea ice loss around Scandinavia is warming that region, while more snow in East Asia is cooling it, he said. That could be sharpening the temperature contrast across Eurasia, which in turn would amplify Rossby waves and make the polar vortex more likely to be disrupted.

thehill.com/homenews/analysis/6205560-tr.headline: The Memo: GOP fumbles for way forward in a world beyond Trump
thehill.com/homenews/analysis/6205560-tr.author: Niall Stanage

paragraphs.text: A historic election week is ending, but the debate about the future of the Republican Party is just beginning.
On one side are those who see the midterms as a wholesale repudiation of President Trump — or at least a startling reminder that neither he nor his party is immune to the laws of political gravity.
According to this theory, everything from Trump’s war on Iran to his solipsistic rhetoric about White House renovations weighed heavily on voters who were mostly concerned with the cost of living.

On the other side of the internal divide are those who urge their party colleagues not to overreact or overcorrect. This faction believes that, while some minor course corrections may be necessary, the right-wing populism that Trump espouses retains broad appeal.
These aren’t just abstract debates, of course.

Since Tuesday’s cataclysm — where GOP-held Senate seats were lost even in crimson strongholds like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina — potential 2028 standard-bearers have been offering their prognosis about what went wrong. The implicit message in the responses from Vice President Vance, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), among others, is that they are the people to put it right.
Vance, on social media, wrote, “The reason we lost is the war” — a very thinly veiled reminder that he is perceived as a skeptic about the conflict.
DeSantis lamented at a press conference that the results were “close to an extinction-level event” — but noted that his Florida was “the one state that was able to hold the line.”
Cruz, in a lengthy post on social platform X, highlighted how the GOP had alienated Hispanic voters and emphasized his record in winning their support.
The battle to define the GOP’s future direction, and to determine who leads it into the 2028 election, looks set to be fierce.
For the moment, Trump critics are feeling validated.
Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson (R) told this column that the election results were a manifestation of “defiance” from the electorate against Trump’s “style and chaos.”

Hutchinson, who ran a long-shot campaign against Trump for the GOP nomination in 2024, said that his party now had an opening to “not simply be a mirror image of President Trump, which it has been, really, for the past 10 years.”

Beyond questions about Trump himself, Hutchinson argued that a change in direction was imperative for the Republican Party’s electoral self-preservation — and that such a move was possible without any abandonment of conservative values.

“We have to be in a position to win the votes of those in the middle — and the new generation of voters,” he said. “That takes change and adjustment, but it’s not a violation of fundamental principles.”

At the other end of the GOP’s spectrum are the Trump loyalists who disdain such anxieties and say the best response to Tuesday’s results is to keep rolling down the MAGA road — regardless of how much liberal outrage or media criticism this generates.
This camp takes heart from Trump’s announcement Friday afternoon that Stephen Miller is to become White House chief of staff, replacing the departing Susie Wiles.
To say Miller is controversial is an understatement.

He is widely seen as the main architect of the administration’s immigration enforcement policies, an advocate of extremely expansive executive powers, a fierce critic of judges who have the temerity to rule against the president, and a pugnacious cable-news brawler — among other things.

“I’m going to miss Susie [Wiles] a lot, but we’re now at war and Stephen Miller is a wartime consigliere,” longtime Trump adviser Michael Caputo told this column, suggesting there is a need to gird for battle with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Caputo, who demurred on discussing the battle for the 2028 GOP nomination, argued that the Trump administration needed to intensify its focus. He said this pattern had already been seen in the past from Democrats, when then-President Obama endured significant midterm defeats for his party.
“I would counsel that, like Obama, we double down,” Caputo said. “And there’s nobody better to double down with than Stephen Miller.”

Others draw different lessons from the midterms — even if they acknowledge such talk is taking place against the backdrop of a president who reacts volcanically to criticism and a GOP base that is still supportive of him.

“Everybody is delicately weighing in, everybody’s discussing this privately — consultants, candidates, everyone,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based GOP strategist who is also the CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI.

“Clearly, Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio and JD [Vance] and Ron DeSantis are doing similar: ‘What are the takeaways from the election? What are we confident in saying about the election? If we feel the need to be more critical of the president, is it a bad idea if we step out?’ Everyone is having those conversations.”

The strategist said his view was that the cost of living hurt the GOP more than anything else, but that a host of other topics — from the war to the exponential growth of data centers to concerns about corruption — also played on voters’ minds.
But Steinhauser was frank in admitting it’s too early to say what it all means for 2028.

“I don’t want to overstate it,” he said. “There are all these articles saying ‘MAGA is dead’ but the base is going to be with Trump. It’s so hard to predict, but it would be the wrong analysis to think they want a George W. Bush-type figure.”
The mere fact that Trump suffered such an electoral rebuke in the midterms perhaps complicates Vance’s position more than anyone else’s.

His message blaming the war for the GOP’s defeat was widely seen as an effort to create distance from Trump without seeming disloyal. It’s not clear if it’s possible to thread this needle over a longer period.
Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and former communications director of the Republican National Committee, noted that Vance was hardly the first vice president to face this challenge.

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris’s remark, during an interview with ABC’s “The View,” that there was “not a thing” she would have done differently from then-President Biden came to haunt her.
“These are very difficult waters,” Heye said. “It’s like watching the Olympics — sometimes it’s hard to say whether something is possible until someone does it, until someone sticks the landing.”
“That’s where Republicans are right now,” he added. “They’re in the air, spinning. And we don’t know how, or who, can stick the landing.”
The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

persuasion.community/p/martin-wolf-3.headline: Martin Wolf on Democratic Capitalism After Trump
persuasion.community/p/martin-wolf-3.author: Yascha Mounk

paragraphs.text: Martin Wolf is chief economics commentator at The Financial Times. His latest book is The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism, now out in paperback with a new chapter on Donald Trump’s second term.

In this week’s conversation, Yascha Mounk and Martin Wolf discuss whether democratic capitalism can recover from the damage done by populists like Donald Trump, how artificial intelligence might upend both the economy and humanity’s control over its own fate, and whether a bursting AI bubble or France’s fiscal woes could trigger the next financial crisis.
Note: This episode was recorded on November 3, before the election results were available.
This transcript has been condensed and lightly edited for clarity.

Yascha Mounk: It’s always a pleasure to talk to you, Martin. I’m really excited to talk about a bunch of the contemporary economic issues facing the United States, Europe, and the world today. But I want to start by revisiting The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism, your really magisterial book about the relationship between capitalism and democracy. It is now a few years old and has just come out in a paperback edition with a new chapter.

Looking back from today’s vantage point, do you remain optimistic that, for all of the challenges we face, we are capable of continuing to reconcile our capitalist system with our democratic institutions, and that we will be able to avert the threats that risk undermining each of those elements?

Martin Wolf: Overall, I’m a little less optimistic. Not dramatically less optimistic, but less optimistic. Very briefly, I feel two things. The first relates to a basic theme of my book. Quite apart from the benefits of moral development in some sense, education and so forth, the capitalist economy that we created in the 19th century and roughly the first three quarters of the 20th century quite naturally generated a redistribution of power in society.

We moved, as it were, from feudalism and pre-modern structures based around land ownership to the modern capitalist economy, with an increasingly organized and powerful working class. Workers were genuinely powerful because they had education and they could easily coalesce and coordinate. That was an environment in which there was a very real risk of major war, and we saw that linked with the formation of the nation state. But there was also tremendous democratic pressure.

In the end, we seem to have reconciled all of that in the post-Second World War period, which was really very important. That underpinning has very obviously been cracking, and that was a theme of my book. But when I wrote it, I still thought that if we understood how damaging and how dangerous this was for living tolerably, we would prevent the worst.

That leads to the second theme, which is very much the theme of this revision. It contains an extra chapter on the Trump experience, Trump’s second term and so forth. What has become obvious is that we do now elect really quite radically reactionary governments. Maybe that’s not the right word, because they’re more complex than that: radically demagogic, populist governments. And we seem likely to do so now in other countries in Europe, which also seemed to be stable. The more I think about it, the more difficult it seems to undo that, because of the damage that is done.

You start not with something that is mildly damaged but with something that is, in some respects, wrecked. Finally, there are changes in technology and society, of which AI is obviously the most important and the most recent. But we’ve had others before that, social media and all the rest of it, which make it so difficult for people to organize politically in the way they used to. The parties of the left and right are just different institutions from what they were when I was young.

So I now begin to think that reversing all this and going back to the things we were familiar with is just a pipe dream. What that means for the future is really open, but in this respect I’ve become more concerned. We’ll see about the Trump experience in the next few years, perhaps. But undoing the damage he has done domestically and internationally—and the U.S. is so pivotal—is going to be an immense task.
One very last comment on this. The Polish experience, which I discuss, is actually live right now as we talk because of the argument with the president. It shows just how difficult it is to reverse.

Mounk: I’m struck by how much more negative and pessimistic the tenor of this added chapter is compared to the overall tenor of your book. The book was obviously written in alarm and with concern, but it still seemed to have a certain baseline confidence that, in the end, the enormous advantages and achievements of democratic capitalism would allow it to persist.

Perhaps we’ve gone on slightly different trajectories over the course of the last 10 years. Perhaps I was much more alarmed in 2017 than you were, and perhaps I’m a little less alarmed than you are today. Your book came out, if I remember correctly, before Donald Trump was reelected.
Wolf: Yeah, it came out in early ‘23.

Mounk: So obviously the fact that Trump was able to get reelected was very concerning and upsetting. But look back at January 2025, when Trump was taking office. He seemed to have a much more efficient staff than in 2016. He had control of a much more unified Republican Party. He seemed to be implementing Project 2025 and other plans for remaking the state very quickly. The Department of Government Efficiency was trying to dismantle large parts of the federal bureaucracy.

He was talking about taking possession of the Panama Canal and of Greenland. He wanted to introduce sky-high tariffs across the board. He had total control of the government. That felt like a very perilous moment. Internationally, it was a moment in which Narendra Modi was riding high in India, and in which there was good reason to believe that democracy had basically been abolished in Hungary by Viktor Orbán, in Serbia by Vučić, and in other places.

A couple of years on, it feels to me that Trump is now finally fading from the American political system. Many of my colleagues have written this once a week for the last 10 years, but I only wrote it for the first time a few months ago. He is at record-low approval ratings. We happen to be recording this on the day of the midterms, and it is very likely that Democrats will win the House of Representatives, and probably the Senate.

Most of the governorships are going to go to Democrats, so it’s going to be very hard for Republicans to skew the vote in 2028, because the vote will be administered by and large by Democratic governors and secretaries of state. More broadly, Trump has done a lot of damage. He has been enormously corrupt and has shot his own country in the foot. But the Supreme Court has struck down a lot of the tariffs. The U.S. economy continues to be surprisingly robust. The attempt to dismantle the federal bureaucracy quickly stalled. They have effectively managed to abolish USAID, but beyond that there haven’t been changes as big as were expected.

Internationally, Viktor Orbán has gone as a result of free and fair democratic elections. Even Vučić appears to be stepping aside. Modi looks more vulnerable than he did recently because of the cockroach movement.

So perhaps we need to move away from the idea that there’s a functioning set of democracies facing threats from populism outside, and either we win or we lose. Instead, we’re going to be in a period of much lower-quality governance, with many more irrational policies and bad governments that do really damaging things. But perhaps the threat to democracy and to the capitalist system is a little less existential than I might have thought five or 10 years ago. Am I really naive to try and see this optimistically, in this vein?
Wolf: I don’t think you are, because the truth is we don’t know. I’ve tried to think hard about historical analogies, and there’s never one that’s perfect.

So I’m beginning to think that maybe the best model for how politics might work in many countries is South America. They have dictatorial regimes, but those regimes don’t last very long. At some point they’re cajoled into elections, partly because of outside pressure, though a lot of the pressure has come from within. Then there is a democratic government, and there’s some respect for civil rights. But the fundamental problems aren’t resolved.

At one stage I called this a populist cycle, but perhaps you could call it a populist-democratic cycle. It goes on. Government is never really efficient, because institutions don’t last long enough. They’re not stable enough. The people in them aren’t secure enough or valued enough to be really very good. But on the other hand, they’re not catastrophic either.

You go on like this. When I look at the government of my own country since the financial crisis, it increasingly feels like that. We’ve had a succession of governments, none of which is really in control. They’re not really effective. All over Europe, I think it’s similar. They will quite possibly be replaced at some point by some sort of populist government of the right or left, but that won’t end democracy. It’s just dysfunctional. That’s much worse than what we had before, but it’s not a properly functioning autocracy.

In many of these countries—India is another example—you won’t end up with a Putin-type regime, because that’s very specific. But you will end up with regimes that oscillate between attempts to create a properly functioning, old-fashioned democracy and, on the other hand, decidedly corrupt, ineffective, but still malevolent populist dictatorships, which could be of the right or the left.

That now seems to me quite a plausible future. In that respect, the parallels I once saw with the 1930s don’t seem right anymore. But at the same time, I don’t feel that the stable, self-confident democratic systems of my youth will survive, except perhaps in countries like Switzerland. Maybe the Netherlands, though that’s not so clear. Scandinavia, I think—small, very solidly bourgeois countries. But in the rest of the world, it doesn’t look like that. You could think of this as optimistic or pessimistic, but it’s not what I would prefer.

Mounk: I think we’re converging on a shared interpretation of a glass of water that is a quarter full or three quarters empty. One way of thinking about this from the perspective of political science is through regime types. I’ve been saying for a very long time that it’s not helpful to think about democracy and dictatorship as ones or zeros.
Wolf: Yes, of course. That was the Cold War scenario.

Mounk: Yes, but no system is perfectly autocratic and no system is perfectly democratic. There’s a huge range of gradations between them. One helpful political science concept is that of competitive authoritarianism, or at least of an uneven playing field, where somebody like Orbán or Vučić is able to capture power. They make the playing field uneven, and they favor themselves in all kinds of ways. That makes it hard for the opposition to displace them. But there is a genuine competition between the government and the opposition, and when the government becomes sufficiently unpopular, the opposition might be able to come in. And perhaps the opposition is great and democratic for a few years. But perhaps they themselves start to emulate the same norms and govern in abusive ways. And at some point a party that really doesn’t care about democratic norms is going to be back in power.

Another way of thinking about it is perhaps as what my colleague Roberto Foa and I once called a “dirty democracy.” Instead of the rules being set for everybody and everybody competing to get into government by the existing rules, a lot of the game consists in influencing, manipulating, and exploiting the rules of the game in such a way that you’re more likely to stay in.

That’s still a game, right? You’re not able to capture the rules to such an extent that the opposition can never win. But a lot of the effort in this polity is then taken up not with putting forward the better ideas for governance, not even with a battle of values, but with trying to maneuver in complicated ways to shape the rules of the game in your favor, to make it more likely that you then win the next election.

Wolf: But there is an important point, at least I as an economist would insist on. What you’re describing is a massively costly regime type, particularly for any functioning economy. So what makes a functioning economy work? People have to make really long-term, risky investments. And by long-term, I mean decades.

If they are to do that, they need to feel that the rules of the economic game, by which I mean the rule of law, their ownership of property, and the ability to trust contracts, are secure. They need to be able to assume that the government services they will need will be provided reliably, consistently, and without corruption, and that the trade regime and the monetary regime they’re operating under are predictable. And if those are changed, they’re changed as a result of a legislative process that involves serious debates and discussions.

It’s a slightly naive way of defining it, but this is pretty close to what was created in the West after the Second World War. And it launched a period of just staggering economic advance. I was lecturing about this yesterday to a group of Chinese business people, and I said that the world order created after the Second World War is incomparably the most successful in world history. And it was because of this, and because of the opportunities that it also extended to people in developing countries, including China.

Now, the world you describe—the world of South America, which, by the way, has done particularly badly in this period relative to what it should have done—is very, very far from that. It’s a world in which you constantly have autocrats and their coteries coming along and acting in whimsical, willful, and corrupt ways. Whether you can go ahead with your project will depend to some extent on whether you can seduce or corrupt some bunch of bureaucrats to help you. Of course, that means you will use them to help you against your rivals, whom they will have to act against.

So everything is politicized, as opposed to everything happening in accordance with well-established principles. The support for science, technology, free inquiry, and genuine free debate will again be politicized. And societies like this—indeed, this is mostly what we have in the world now—in my view don’t perform very well.

I agree with you that the U.S. is doing reasonably well economically, but I would say that’s because it is pursuing a radically unsustainable fiscal policy in the long run, which is, of course, generating demand in the short run. And there’s the AI boom, but the AI boom is the fruit of decades of technological development that happened to come to this crescendo right now. It’s got nothing to do with what this administration is doing.

So I would say you’re absolutely right: there are far worse things than this. It’s far better to have this than Stalinism or Hitler, obviously. On the other hand, it’s going to be pretty unpleasant, and everything will be, as it were, for sale. Everything will be unpredictable in every possible dimension.

And this comes back to the point we were discussing. I think the damage from the Trump experience has been bigger than you suggest. Telling people “we’re going to go back to the way it was before,” when they’ve lived in these circumstances I’ve just described—well, they’re not going to believe it. They’re not going to behave as they used to, because they’ll ask: “Can you promise us that there won’t be someone like Trump, or worse, soon? Can you promise us that the bureaucrats I’m going to be dealing with will be honest, honorable, non-corrupt people, which they used to be?” And I think the answer to that is no, you can’t.

So I think you’re absolutely right that there are far worse things. And it’s very encouraging that these would-be autocrats have had their wings clipped, and I assume that’s going to happen now in the midterms. But it’s very far from what we had before, when we could be confident that the system would work.

Mounk: Look, I think that’s right. Living in Argentina is a hell of a lot better than living in North Korea, or for that matter in Russia. But at the same time, while a hundred years ago it famously might not have been clear whether you’d rather emigrate to Argentina or to the United States, today, if you have a choice between living in the United States, with its economic opportunities, or in Argentina, it’s relatively obvious that you would choose the United States, because the country has done a lot better. And as you’re pointing out, that’s not because of the governance we’ve had for the last 18 months—or the last 24 months—it’s because of the governance we’ve had for the last 60 or 200 years. So I think we’re on the same page about that.

One of the ironies I find about this moment is that the world is being radically and fundamentally transformed by artificial intelligence, and we’re going to have to think very hard about the kind of government response we need. That’s partially about regulation, to make sure that people can’t steal financial information and bankrupt you through cyberattacks. It’s partially about making sure that people can’t manufacture viruses that are going to kill millions, or tens or hundreds of millions, of people. But it’s also about thinking about how to preserve and reinstitute the basic structural preconditions for a middle-class economy and for inclusive political institutions.

Now, 20 or 25 years ago, it feels to me like a lot of the major democracies in the world might have had the self-confidence, and perhaps the lack of polarization, to go about that in a rational way. Perhaps that was never really the case, but at least there would have been grand commissions by think tanks involving a bipartisan set of people that would have done briefings for top officials. There would at least have been the expectation that there would be some rational analysis of the problem, a set of proposals being debated and discussed, and policy made on the basis of that.

It’s very hard to imagine that world today, right? And so we’re confronting this huge challenge of artificial intelligence at a time when our collective self-confidence in being able to govern it is much lower than it would have been 25 or 50 years ago.

Wolf: Yes, I think that’s clearly right. I’ve suggested this in a few of my writings on AI. The first column I wrote on this, and I still think the best, started off with the history of the horse, which is quite well documented. I pointed out that up until the end of the 19th century, the horse was really—we could argue a bit about the sailing ship—the most important transport technology in the world. And now horses are just for entertainment.

So it seemed to me that there’s a lesson. Of course, my economist friends say, “Well, of course, we’re much more complicated than the horse.” Yes. But if it turns out that the most important thing human beings can do is to think, which I think is true—and that doesn’t just mean thinking intellectually, it means thinking in everything we do—and we can create AI and robots (I was just talking to somebody who does robots yesterday), then it doesn’t seem impossible to imagine a world in which everybody who has any money would rather have, apart from their few loved ones, machines around them. It’s an interesting question what having money will even mean in the future, but let’s leave that aside.

So what is the rest of humanity for?
