I sometimes begin to wonder whether the really deep reason why nobody’s having any children anymore is that, at some deep psychological level, they’ve realized that there is no future for their children, so they are acting preemptively. I’m not suggesting that’s true, but it does seem fascinating that there is this coincidence in time.

But the fundamental point you make is obviously right. This is a revolution. Now, here it interacts with politics in the following way. The most striking feature of the politics of the last 30 years—and it was essential in my book, though lots of others have written about it—is the rejection by the body politic of “experts,” of intellectuals, who have come to be seen and portrayed as the enemy.

I understand why, because the sort of policies the intellectuals and experts recommended, very much including economists, don’t seem to have worked from the point of view of most people. And so that opened room for people to get into power essentially by running against them. The most striking feature, in some sense, of the Trump revolution, or attempted overthrow of the old order, or whatever it is, is the war against universities. It’s a war that was possible because the intelligentsia here discredited itself. I think it did so.

Now, 40 years ago, the idea that any government in America would plausibly run against Harvard, or here against Oxford and Cambridge, would have been unthinkable. So that comes back to our thinking about AI. The process you are discussing should have involved ordinary people. I very much believe in citizens’ assemblies; it’s one of my democratic romanticisms. But of course, in discussing AI we’d need very high-level expertise, and indeed a royal commission would be the obvious thing to do if you were Britain or the equivalent. In the same way—though I know all the differences—when in the ‘50s and ‘60s they were thinking about how to control nuclear weapons, they talked to people like Thomas Schelling, very famously. And I think if we’d really been asked, we could have thought at least moderately intelligently about the real risks.

The idea—I’ve got this in my column for tomorrow—that Anthropic would put out in its IPO, for a business that seems likely to be valued in the trillion-dollar range, that, well, one of the risks is that we might end humanity, as it were, en passant Anthropic IPO risk disclosure. It’s a reductio ad absurdum of learned helplessness. I do think the reason we can’t do it is that, somehow or other, the intelligentsia has discredited itself, and it has been successfully discredited by its enemies. Running a really sophisticated, complex modern polity embedded in this complicated world, while being against the intelligentsia—any form of it—just seems crazy. It’s a theme of one of the things in my book.

Compare it with what the New Deal was like. I wrote a bit about Dean Acheson recently. And then you look at what the Trump administration has done to the State Department or the intelligence services. And then you look at what they’ve been saying about the Iran war. It’s all crazy stuff. Admittedly, it was pretty crazy in Vietnam too.
But the point is, I don’t think we can recover that confidence in our ability to control these things. So they are uncontrolled and uncontrollable, and the Anthropic IPO shows that.

Mounk: If they’re likely to be uncontrolled, what do you think the economic impacts of this AI revolution are going to be? On the one hand, if intelligence was the ingredient of the economy that was scarce, then suddenly having a country of geniuses in your laptop, or whatever the phrase is, should unleash huge amounts of productivity and that might produce more goods and services in ways that make us all wealthier.

At the same time, there’s deep concerns about the distribution of those goods and services, and there’s deep concerns about whether or not human workers will still be needed in the ways they are today, and what that might do to the size of the middle class, which is something that I’ve been thinking and worrying about. Stepping back, to what extent can we predict what’s going to happen? How should we go about thinking about what this totally uncharted territory might look like?

Wolf: I think all those questions are the right questions. But I actually begin to think they’re not the most important questions. I may be completely wrong, but perhaps because they’re so predictably economic sort of questions, I’ve been wondering whether we’re not being radical enough in our thinking about what this means.

First of all, we live in a world in which literally everything is run through the digital economy. I mean, just everything. It seems to be absolutely inevitable that AI-enabled computing, which will be everything, will take this over. They’re gonna run it. We’ve already seen pretty clear signs—to which, of course, Dario Amodei has been referring—that they’re not necessarily gonna run it in ways that we would think are sensible or right or moral or anything. They seem to be extraordinarily willful and erratic and out of control. So in some sense, they can do anything, whether on their own or when guided by hackers.

In Europe just today, in Sweden, I think it is, we’ve got a story about some hackers—might be an AI bot, might be some hackers—that have got control of the freezers in supermarkets and have decided to raise the temperature to levels that rot all the food. These all look like terrorism.

What happens if that’s the normal state? My nightmare—and it just seems impossible—is that we wake up one morning and discover that every single bank account in the world has been nullified. Everyone’s. In which case, the world economy stops. Period. It’s done. Can we guarantee that won’t happen in this world? I don’t see how.
Mounk: I’ve been thinking about whether I should take printouts of my bank accounts regularly, so that in such a world you at least have some kind of proof.

Wolf: Yeah, I think you probably should. Every day, the businesses of the world—every single business—are doing trillions of dollars, collectively, in financing on a daily basis. They can’t do that without the system. The electric power systems of our world, everything else, can’t do that. So we are going to lose control of the core institutions, the core operating system of our world. I don’t think it is possible to guess what that will mean.

The second thing I was thinking about—we have this idea that at the end of this, we go back, as an extreme, and it’s suggested by your model, to a sort of feudal economy, but accept that the vast majority of human beings actually have no labor value, because machines will do all that stuff. We won’t even need serfs, as it were. Most human beings are completely redundant. The machines that run the economy will be owned by a tiny elite of super wealthy people—the likes of Elon Musk and so forth—and all the goodies will go to them.

I don’t see why that should happen, because why should these machines pay the slightest attention to these notional ownership claims of these fragile little human things? They have their own purposes and aims. Why should we assume—I’m being very, very science fiction—that... So I think everything you say is right, these are all good questions, but I think AI is more radical, potentially more destabilizing, less controllable than that.

But, of course, just one last thing: it’s perfectly possible to imagine an upheaval which will make the deindustrialization process, itself radically destabilizing, look like a garden party, because people won’t be doing what you or I do. Most physicists and others will be replaced by brilliant machines. How quickly that will happen, I have no idea. Maybe human originality will survive. But the fundamental question, of course, is: what value do humans have? An even more fundamental question is: do human beings continue to control things?

Mounk: No, and I think those questions about existential risk—which come in different forms—are absolutely fundamental. One way it could go is that a machine decides to eradicate humanity, either because it wants to take over or because it’s misaligned in some kind of way. Another is just that machines might have some kind of use for us, or perhaps they want to keep us around as a museum of their own prehistory, of their creation, or something like that. But they’re going to be the ones in control.

It’s very interesting to think about bullfighting in this respect. I went to a bullfight many years ago; I was kind of dragged there by somebody, I wasn’t particularly keen to go. But I did actually enjoy it greatly, because I started to realize at a certain point during the event that, when it’s done really, really well, it’s not about celebrating the person with the biggest muscles, or the person with the biggest cojones. It’s not just about muscles or bravery, though those things are involved.

It is principally about the triumph of the human spirit and of intelligence. It is a human standing in front of a beast that is greatly stronger and more powerful than any human being can be—greatly more powerful and stronger than Arnold Schwarzenegger or anybody else. But it is through our intelligence that we are able to master the bull. So that raises the question: why should we expect that, in the long run humans, even if we created these AI machines, which might give us some kind of advantage for a while, should continue to be able to govern these weird creatures that are already about as intelligent as us, and in many ways more intelligent, and probably one, three, five years from now will be vastly more intelligent than we are? Why should we have all of that confidence? I think that we should both be thinking about those questions and thinking about the question of how, if we do manage to control AI, it’s still going to transform our social and economic world in deep, deep problematic ways—because both of those are deep threats to our world. But I certainly take the existential risk points very seriously.

Wolf: Well, one thing that is clear is in the world that you described—assume away the existential stuff, just look at the economics—I think in the world we can imagine, in which AI is the dominant instrument of organizing production and so forth, if humanity is to continue in some sense collectively to be the master of its fate, collectively and individually, then there’s going to have to be a far greater degree of socialization of the means of production and distribution and exchange than any of us have thought about. Because it’s very easy to imagine that the marginal product of a great many human beings, compared to the most efficient alternatives, will be negative, or at least not really at what we would consider subsistence level. What are people for in this situation?

Now, there are clearly some things we would still want other people to do—I’m assuming here that there are still people in charge. But I think we’d have to start thinking that the assumptions we have about how the economy will work, how the output we are potentially able to produce will be distributed, and what you need to do to get the things you need to survive and lead a good life—whatever that means in this context—how that will be done, would be radically different from the ways we have organized them.

One way I thought about this is that essentially this could be a world, at the most extreme, in which everybody lives like the aristocrats of old. The aristocrats of old didn’t do anything, basically. They owned land, and they owned the fruit of the labor of the people on the land, and they had soldiers who were theirs who controlled the latter. Well, they could live without actually producing anything. They were rentiers. In the world of AI, if all the production is essentially done by AI, we all become rentiers, and a decent society would share the rents. So we would live not on our ability to produce, but on our right to consume. I’ve never actually written about this. I suggested this in a seminar about 15 years ago in Washington. You could imagine a world in which everybody became an aristocrat. If we’re rich enough, we could organize that world. Everybody could enjoy lots of stuff. They couldn’t enjoy everything—you can’t all have the most beautiful view in the world—but you could imagine that sort of world. Politically, though, it involves a complete transformation of the fundamental assumptions of our economic, social, and political order.

Mounk: Let me ask you about two things here. The first is that I find that analogy imprecise in two ways. The first is that many aristocrats had a lot of leisure, but they were actually responsible for something. In some ways, they were running, in our language today, small- or medium-sized enterprises. A profligate duke could spend money and not care about his fields falling into disarray, and then he would leave a relatively destitute heir. But their social role was to make sure that the heir would get about as much money and fields and so on as they did. So they were responsible for managing, essentially, hundreds of thousands or tens of thousands of employees. Now, they did that in a relatively arm’s-length way, and the people they employed to go around and look after that did most of the dirty work. But they were actually, in that sense, running little enterprises.

They had a sense of responsibility, and were judged on whether or not they were able to pass on to their heirs what they had received from their parents. The other point you hinted at is that, of course, the lives of aristocrats—insofar as they were happy, and if you read Brideshead Revisited and other kinds of works, there are good questions about the extent to which they were happy; many of them probably had quite empty lives and felt that emptiness—but insofar as they had meaning, they had meaning in part because they had high social status. They had a high positional good. They could go around and say, “I’m a duke.”

I have a whole social world of which I’m a part, and in which I play an essential role in the legitimization of this strange political order, because of my social position. I’m somebody. But not everybody can be somebody by virtue of who they are by birth.

Wolf: That is right. That is something we can’t arrange. We can only arrange that they consume. We can’t arrange to give them this exalted status. I agree with you absolutely, of course. A book that influenced me a lot in thinking about how the morality—the sense of purpose in life—of people like that might collapse, because it’s a brilliant book, is Les Liaisons Dangereuses, whose idea was, in a sense—here are these signs of the French aristocracy; of course, when it was written is important—who basically thought, particularly the male ones, that all they can do in life is destroy the lives of young women by seducing them and abandoning them. That’s clearly part of how they lived. So it can be very, very destructive.

I think I’m obviously one of those people—a classic modern person, perhaps pre-modern given where we are now—who thinks that the value in life consists of fruitful work and contributing to society and being part of it. I justify what I’ve done in my life as contributing in some way to political and economic life. That’s value, and I’m paid for it, and I feel very good about it.

In a world in which those functions wouldn’t exist, because they will be done better by an AI program, or because there’s no political system left to advise, then I don’t know what I would do. I do think that without some sense of contributing through one’s own efforts to society... You’re right, of course, dukes felt that too, in the way they did things. Certainly people who held serious positions in the state as a result of their rank. If you take that away from human beings, they basically never grow up. They’re never adults. They are perpetually looked after. That’s not a life. This is, of course, what Brave New World was about.

There are lots of major contributions to literature which play around with exactly this theme: what do you do if there’s no struggle, no effort, and no reward for effort, when you’re basically playing, and you know you’re playing? Well, I think it’s poison. I’m in complete—poison, which is why, as I said, if I were dictator of the world and invited to this commission, I would say this whole thing should be banned, closed, finished. I’ve said this many times. It’s what I believe. But of course it’s not gonna happen.

Mounk: I’m not sure I agree with you on that, for I am very conscious of the dangers of AI, but I actually want to ask a question that brings the conversation a little bit full circle, back to the concerns of your book. You rightly defend the triumph of democratic capitalism in your book, and explain the dangers that await us if that system breaks down. But let’s try and imagine the world fifty or a hundred years from now, if the AI revolution totally takes place. If it does turn out that a lot of the ingredients to productivity that used to be scarce, and that therefore needed to be distributed by markets, no longer are scarce in that way—we have much greater material plenty, nearly unlimited compute, and we have intelligence at our beck and call for negligible or nonexistent prices—most people can be idle, perhaps happily, perhaps unhappily, and live in material splendor where we find it hard to imagine, and yet we somehow keep control of the AI.

I know these are all very, very large “if” statements, and I think there’s good reason to think a bunch of them don’t turn out to be true. But let’s take that as a premise, as a question, for a moment. Do we still need capitalism in that world? Is capitalism still the right economic system, or will we have to envisage a totally different economic system to govern that kind of a world?

Wolf: The answer, in a way, would relate to where I would challenge the assumptions—and, implicitly, the assumption you’re making, and this, of course, goes back through a whole history, including the prophecies of Karl Marx about the future. It’s been picked up strangely in a very popular recent book, which I’m sure you’ve read, on abundance.

The idea of limitless abundance seems to me to be very difficult to imagine. The reason is there are things that are intrinsically scarce. As long as the things that are intrinsically scarce exist, they have to be allocated in some way. The market is only one way, and some of them probably don’t want to be allocated in that way.

Let’s think about what might not be abundant. First, in your world of limitless abundance, you’re assuming away resource constraints—that means we have limitless energy, we can recycle things freely, as it were, at zero cost, and the basic raw materials for production, metals and all the rest of it, will be freely available. But the most important of these things, unquestionably, is energy. So the world you imagine must, I think, have a limitless energy source, and it probably would have to be fusion. So there are quite big technological problems to solve, which may or may not be soluble.

Then the second set of things—if we don’t solve them, things will continue to be scarce, and we have to have a mechanism for allocating them. It’s either through markets, in some way, which is capitalism, or it’s through hierarchy of some kind. The hierarchies are political, and we have to discuss how those will be organized.

Then the other set of things, which was introduced into my thinking by a magnificent book published in the ’70s by a man called Fred Hirsch, which you might know, called The Social Limits to Growth—which is basically about what are called positional goods. There are a vast number of things that are valuable because they’re intrinsically scarce.
Mounk: Well, and that goes back to the idea that not everybody can be an aristocrat, because the core of being an aristocrat is to be superior to most people in the relevant social hierarchy.

Wolf: Not everybody—for example, think about houses. Land is not freely available. Land is intrinsically constrained. We need houses, and I live in a particularly nice suburb of London, and everybody can’t live here. The result of that—the fact that everybody can’t live here—is that houses cost millions. They didn’t when I bought mine, but they do now.

The point is, everybody can’t live here. Everybody can’t have the perfect view. Everybody can’t own a Swiss lake or a beautiful island in the Caribbean. In other words, there are positional goods which are intrinsically limited by virtue of the demand from all the other humans. Somebody has to allocate this somehow, through social status or market competition. We do it through a mixture of the two. Above all, market competition generates the wealth. If you win in market competition, then you can buy the island in the Caribbean. But these are not things that can become abundant, and positions in society can’t be, by definition. Only one person can be the president or the prime minister at any time. We could imagine a competition which isn’t through voting, as we do it now, but one can manage.

Essentially, a world in which goods are freely available—that is imaginable for many goods anyway—but there are lots of things we really care about which will remain scarce, and they’re really important because they’re about social status. If they’re not done through the market, which is perfectly possible, then you have to manage them through some other allocation, and, by and large, historically, it’s been done through force.

That was, of course, Marx’s great mistake. He thought that if we got rid of private property, all these problems would be solved. I’ll leave aside his problem about abundance, but the problem he found was that it wasn’t solved, because somebody with the biggest gun—and the largest number of guns—simply took whatever he wanted and allocated the rest to the people who supported him. So I think the problem is much more profound than you suggest, even in this world.

In the rest of this conversation, Yascha and Martin discuss whether we are in an AI bubble, what would happen if it burst, and the state of the European economy. This part of the conversation is reserved for paying subscribers…

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-07/.headline: Stephen Miller rises, but California hopes it can blunt his force
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-07/.author: Grace Toohey, Suhauna Hussain, Karen Garcia

paragraphs.text: President Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller — the architect of the administration’s extreme crackdown on immigration — to White House chief of staff is sparking alarm among immigrant advocates and politicians across California.
But also, this week’s sweeping Democratic victories are giving immigrant communities hope that control of Congress will give them more tools to fight Miller’s policies.

Miller grew up in Santa Monica but has become a relentless critic of California, specifically its immigration policies, protections and, in many ways, identity. Southern California was the first city targeted by widespread immigration raids last year, upending the region in ways that continue to reverberate, particularly for immigrant communities.

President Trump announced Miller’s promotion Friday. The move is seen by many as an indication that the president has no intention of backing away from some of his most polarizing policies during his last two years in office, despite devastating midterm losses for Republicans across the country. Many viewed the nationwide Democratic swing — in South Carolina, Texas, California’s Central Valley and across the Midwest — as a rebuke of the administration’s first two years, particularly the major immigration crackdown that went far beyond Trump’s promise to focus on the “worst of the worst,” instead arresting thousands without criminal convictions, many of whom had lived in the country for decades.

“We’re concerned that this means the president may be doubling down on his domestic agenda of ICE crackdowns and on deportations if Stephen Miller is at the helm,” said Jamal Abdi, the president of the National Iranian American Council. “He thinks that every problem starts with the immigrant community — and that getting rid of them is the solution.”

Abdi worries that Miller’s latest promotion will further anti-immigrant policies, which have long painted Iranians and other immigrant communities as threats. He is hopeful Miller will help end the military’s war in Iran but fears that may mean more focus domestically on immigrants, especially Iranians, who have been demonized as a political tool amid hostilities. The diaspora is highly concentrated in Los Angeles, which is home to the largest group of people of Iranian descent outside of Iran.
“We are definitely not out of the woods, and it seems like maybe the president might do less damage abroad but will really focus energy domestically,” Abdi said.

Angelica Salas, executive director of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights in Los Angeles, said seeing more power in the hands of Miller — who she said was behind the Trump administration’s strategies that included “warrantless arrest, racial profiling, excessive use of force, medical neglect in detention centers, people deported illegally” — is concerning.

“Now he’s the chief of staff, and so that means that he has access to every single cabinet secretary to unleash his reign of terror on our people,” Salas said. During the midterm elections, she said her team was aware of an influx of Department of Homeland Security sightings and activity in the Southland.
“We saw people arrested the day after the election in a massive way and it almost feels very vengeful,” she said. “Almost [like saying], ‘You know you can’t stop us.’”
Now, she and other immigration advocates are preparing themselves for “even more abuse from this administration,” Salas said.
But Ahilan Arulanantham, faculty co-director of UCLA’s Miñana Family Center for Immigration Law and Policy, said Miller’s promotion doesn’t change anything for him.

“He’s been adopting the most extreme authoritarian and racist views and espousing it publicly… for the entire two years of this administration,” Arulanantham said. “Whether he does it as the deputy chief of staff or chief of staff ... I don’t have a view of the difference.”

Despite widespread backlash to the immigration raids last year, particularly after federal agents killed two civilians in Minnesota, the administration did pull back some of its most aggressive tactics. But Miller has remained intensely focused on his goal to limit immigration dramatically and deport undocumented migrants.

Miller’s new role will come as the administration prepares to face a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate, which could provide the strongest check yet on the executive branch since Trump began his second term.

“Congress has tremendous opportunity to constrain what the federal government can do in the form of abusive immigration practices,” Arulanantham said. “Congress has a huge amount of leverage that it could choose to use to force the administration to change its conduct — in the way that voters have clearly demanded.”

He hopes Congress will pass laws that limit how the Department of Homeland Security enforces immigration laws, including how agents use warrants — or don’t, what they wear while on duty and what factors they can consider when stopping someone.
Members of Congress appeared to agree with that approach.

“Stephen Miller should lawyer up,” U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Long Beach), who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee once the next Congress is sworn in, wrote in a statement Friday. He and his colleagues are committed to fighting “against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts.”

“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” Garcia said. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”
Sen. Alex Padilla (D-California) characterized Miller as “the man most responsible for this Administration’s failures and most harmful policies” in a statement Friday.

Miller is “the architect of the cruelest immigration policies this country has seen in modern times: family separations, detainment of babies and children, militarized raids, arbitrary arrest quotas, and the horror unleashed in communities across the country,” Padilla said. “Trump is doubling down — so will we.”

“We will use every tool at our disposal — oversight, investigations, subpoenas, and our leverage over federal funding — to expose this Administration’s abuse of power and hold those responsible accountable.”

Standing up to the administration was a similar response for lawmakers in Los Angeles. City Councilmember Eunisses Hernandez, whose district was targeted by some of the most extreme immigration sweeps last year, called Miller’s appointment an act of desperation by Trump.
The council member said it won’t deter her office or the community from pushing back against harsh immigration policies and continued activity in L.A.

“We’re going to fight back,” Hernandez said. “Even when we were on the losing side, when we didn’t have the majority in the Senate or the House, many of us were still fighting against those raids, fighting for our communities, fighting to make sure people are fed and housed.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/06/trump-stephen-miller.headline: Trump says Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
cnbc.com/2026/11/06/trump-stephen-miller.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump on Friday announced White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will be promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Trump revealed the stunning shake-up just three days after Democrats won a landslide victory in the midterm elections, gaining majority control in the House and Senate and scrambling the trajectory of Trump's last two years in office.

Elevating Miller, an architect of Trump's controversial mass-deportation efforts, is bound to raise the hackles of the incoming class of congressional Democrats, who have already vowed to investigate the government's immigration policies.
"It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff," Miller said on X later Friday.
"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic," he said.
Miller will take over starting Monday, Trump said in a Truth Social post, praising his longtime aide as "one of my most trusted advisors."
Wiles, "who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation," the president wrote.
Asked about the move later Friday afternoon, Trump said, "I wanted to make a change."
"I think Susie's done a very good job, great job. But I just wanted to make it," Trump told reporters as he left the White House for an event in Cape Canaveral, Florida.
"Stephen's been great," Trump said, adding, "Sometimes in life you have to make moves."

Wiles resigned Thursday night, a senior White House source told MS NOW. Wiles told Trump, who was said to be angry with her following the GOP's huge election losses, "let me make this easy on you — I am going to resign," MS NOW reported.
"Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff," Wiles said in an X post Friday afternoon. "Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime."
"While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will," she wrote.
Senior administration officials were quick to congratulate Miller.

"Patriots in control," read an X post from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose job security has come into question after some Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, blamed the midterm results on the Iran war.
Vance also praised Miller on X, saying he "will do great things."
The official X account for Trump's political operation celebrated the announcement by posting a black-and-white photo of Miller under the caption, "It's Miller time."
Democrats and other critics, meanwhile, filed in to denounce the pick.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who could be elected House speaker next year, called Miller "a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands."
"His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today," Jeffries wrote on X.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., wrote that Trump "learned nothing from his historic defeat."

"Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn't have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way," Schumer wrote.
Others took Miller's promotion as a sign that Trump, who seemed to express some willingness to negotiate with a blue Congress, will instead remain combative.

"For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water," wrote David Axelrod, a former senior advisor to President Barack Obama.

The White House reshuffle follows multiple resignations of senior staff in the Department of Justice since Election Day. They include Harmeet Dhillon, a leader in the DOJ's civil rights division, John Eisenberg, who headed the national security division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who had been in charge of conspiracy investigations related to Trump's foes.

Wiles oversaw Trump's winning 2024 presidential campaign and has wielded major influence in his second administration, while largely staying out of the spotlight. She drew focus in late 2025, when Vanity Fair reported that Wiles admitted that Trump had pursued "retribution" as president and that he had an "alcoholic's personality."
Trump, and many other top administration officials, defended Wiles at the time, underscoring her status in the White House.

While Wiles is not fully leaving Trump's orbit, her resignation follows a pattern of other top female officials who have left or been fired from Trump's second administration, and then replaced by men.

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/07/h.headline: Historic voter turnout powered Democrats’ blue wave
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/07/h.author: Lydia Sidhom, Luis Melgar, Laura Beveridge

paragraphs.text: Turnout in the midterm elections reached its second-highest peak in more than a century — only slightly behind the 2018 midterms, during President Donald Trump’s first term — with the greatest number of voters casting ballots in states where Democrats won unexpected victories.

Across the United States, 49 percent of eligible Americans voted, the second-highest turnout since 1914, when neither women nor African Americans could vote in many states, according to preliminary data from the University of Florida Election Lab.

Three states with the highest turnout — Maine (65.7 percent), Minnesota (65.2 percent) and Michigan (63.2 percent) — held competitive Senate races where Democrats prevailed. All three also elected Democratic governors.

National turnout increased by three percentage points compared with 2022’s midterm elections. It was only slightly lower than in 2018, during the first Trump presidency, when 50 percent of eligible voters turned out.

Despite setting high marks for a midterm, turnout was lower than the 2024 presidential election by 15.2 percent. But the gap was smaller in the most competitive races, including in Maine, where Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson ousted Sen. Susan Collins (R), and Texas, where state Rep. James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, in the race for U.S. Senate.
Across all states with competitive Senate races, turnout averaged 52 percent, higher than the national average.

“When it comes to turnout, Trump has had more of an impact than anyone of the last century. He has the ability to mobilize both sides, for and against him,” Tom Bonier, an analyst and former Democratic political strategist, said of the president.
“What was different this time around [compared with 2018] was that he was repellent to Republicans as well, so that many just chose to stay home,” he said.
Turnout is often lower in wave elections because one side stays home.

Daron Shaw, a Republican pollster and politics professor at the University of Texas at Austin, said he expected Republicans would benefit from higher turnout because it would counter Democratic enthusiasm.
“In fact, it was exactly the opposite,” he said.
Lower-propensity voters showed up because they were “upset over the economy, perhaps a little anger over the Iran war and it’s relationship to higher gas prices.”
“Trump is an incredible mobilizer,” Shaw said. “But he also happens to be one of the great counter-mobilizers of all time.”

8rank.ai/game/apple-intelligence-persona.headline: Anatomy of Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph

paragraphs.text: What if I told you that every Mac since 2022 ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about you and the people around you: who you are, who you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, with whom, what you do and when. This graph is built on device by cross-referencing pretty much everything on the machine: Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, Screen Time and a long tail of behavioral signals. And, more importantly, it is held as a queryable store that LLMs retrieve from (allegedly). Would you believe me?

Well, that's what is happening, and interestingly enough, there is little documentation of how this whole mechanism works on your Mac. The closest thing to an official description is the man page (man 8 knowledgeconstructiond), and this is all you get:

Previous work: To be fair, Apple's own researchers did publish a paper on the techniques behind this graph construction, back in 2023. But there is next to nothing on how it is integrated into macOS: which versions run it, and the exact list of what is collected and inferred. And not a word about the "kinship" inference discussed below. Also, we personally ran into it while doing some security research on the Apple Intelligence bundle in macOS 26 in August 2026; but a few months before, Nic Lydon came across the same database and wrote it up in I Built a Personal Knowledge Graph. Apple Had Already Built One on My Laptop.
But we go a bit deeper.

This blog post is an account of some analysis work we carried out on what the knowledge graph actually does, so that you (the user) can get a better understanding of how this mechanism works, and some clarity on what the graph holds about you and your family and friends. Everything in it was collected on macOS 26 (26.6.2 at the time of writing).
To this end, we open-source a local dashboard (iKnow) you can use to read the content of your personal knowledge graph on your Mac.

Finally, we derail a bit and look into what we do best: weaponizing and exploiting. We run a thought experiment (one that applies to any such personalized system) and show what happens if such a knowledge base ends up in the wrong hands, and how a "privacy single point of failure" can be exploited to threaten you in ways you may not have considered before (when combined with an abliterated LLM).
What's in the personal knowledge graph?
The two daemons keep their work in ~/Library/IntelligencePlatform, a directory of SQLite databases (fifty-one databases) stored in plaintext but located in a zone protected by TCC Full Disk Access.

Likely, the most interesting is graph.db. It is a triple store written in a vocabulary of 181 entity classes and 278 predicates: every row is a subject, a predicate and an object. The subject is an entity (a person, an app, an event); the object is either a plain value (a name, a handle, a date) or another entity, which is where the graph gets its edges. The predicate is the interesting part: it says what kind of relationship the system believes holds between the two.

Most of what the two daemons do is populate those predicates, and the tables kept beside them, from everything the OS will let them read. Into the graph go Contacts; Photos (faces); Calendar (titles and attendees); Family Sharing (including the age of every member); the Medical ID emergency contact in Health; events and contacts Siri Suggestions finds in Mail and Messages; people donated by apps through App Intents; and installed apps. Beside it, in tables of their own, sit who appears with whom in your photos; the communication log (who, when, which app, which direction; no content), which also pulls from your other devices; location and movement; and a long tail of device signals (screen locked, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, charging, ambient light, and a stream named ContextualUnderstanding.PhysicalSocial whose record format lists people by name, phone and email, each with a start and an end time; it reads like a log of who was physically around you, though we never saw it filled in).
What is inferred
The complete list of the 181 entity classes:

Fifty-seven of the 181 describe an activity: sleeping, exercising, mindfulness, going to bed, commute, dining, most of them with a matching type class beside them, so nearly a third of the vocabulary went on what you are doing rather than on who or where you are. That said, it is not clear that every class is actually used; some may be placeholders that are declared and never filled. In the table, we flag as implemented the classes for which we could locate a mechanism that might be responsible for the class, but those are to be taken as inference work rather than ground truth.
And this is the complete list of predicates (same disclaimer applies):
How it is inferred

The methods run the whole range. Most of the vocabulary is filled by plain copying (a name from Contacts, an attendee from Calendar) and rules over the copies; the interesting rows come from models: a pair of XGBoost classifiers decides who is family from 144 mostly behavioral features, two embedding models are one of ten signals the system uses to decide when two records are the same person, twelve analyzers in Photos score partner, parent, child, coworker and friend from who appears in your pictures with you, on which trips and holidays, and Apple's on-device LLM reads your messages to put a name and a relationship on a face (if Apple Intelligence is active).
Whatever the method, every row lands in the graph with a confidence attached, a number between 0 and 1.

The family scores live apart. Two CoreML models ship next to the ontology, EntityTagging_Family.mlmodelc and EntityTagging_FamilyAndFriends.mlmodelc: binary XGBoost classifiers that take 144 features and return a class and a probability over it. Their scores do not go into the triple store but into a table of their own (entityTagging.db, one row per person, seventeen relationship columns from family to mother to coworker, recomputed every day), which is what the iKnow scorecard further down reads. Only two of those seventeen columns have a shipped model behind them; what fills the other fifteen, and how any of these probabilities would become a confidence in the graph, we could not trace.
The feature names are in each model's metadata.json, in plain text. They are the clearest statement of what this system is that I have found anywhere. All 144:

The identity group is the tidy story: same surname, same home address, an iCloud Family flag — and it is the small half. The bulk of the model is the other two: who you message and who appears in your photographs, conditioned on the day of the week and the time of day, and then on both at once. photosPersonPosteriorProbabilityGivenSaturdayNight is a shipped feature name in a shipped classifier whose job is deciding whether someone is family.
Deleting something does not delete it everywhere.
The live graph forgets. Delete a contact and nothing re-derives them; the next run replaces the table wholesale.

But the store keeps a second table, expired_stable_graph, beside the live one. The retracted row moves there and keeps its confidence and its sources. How long it stays there is not clear from what we could see. It seems to go after about 48 hours (the store keeps a prune watermark, and a recent snapshot of the table reached back no further than that); but on my own Mac, I could still read very old records in it.

And a conclusion can outlive the evidence for it. On my Mac, the scorecard still scored two people the graph had dropped the day before, both of them known to it only from a calendar invitation. Well, if you want your partner not to discover some contacts you might have deleted and their "closeness" to you, better to drop some rows from expired_stable_graph too (unfortunately, you have to do it manually). But I am sure you have nothing to hide (just joking).
Look into your own data

Is any of this sensitive? We'll leave that to you, since "sensitive" means different things to different people (though I think you have plenty to choose from here). However, the thing is, none of it lives in isolation. It is built to be joined and correlated; the nodes are there to be linked:

The most important point, though, is that this is not only about you (the person using the Mac). The people around you are in it too: your family, your friends, "anyone" you have talked to through your device. None of them was asked, and the store links them to you and, through the events and groups they share, to each other. A relationship is intelligence one level above the rows it was inferred from. For instance, by correlating across my own store, I (well, an LLM working for me) could easily work out the following:

• That there is a child in the household, and roughly how old. The family-member types and a family circle give the household. The scorecard's child and son/daughter columns give the child's place in it. Beside it sits an age, copied from Family Sharing; and dates of birth in the store can carry the system's own word imputed, though what the system means by it is not clear to us.

• Which daycare the child goes to, and both of the numbers that reach it. Copied off contact cards. Note what is not there: the calendar has no school-run event, so the store holds the institution and its lines but not the hour the child is dropped off. That is still enough to call a parent from a number their phone already trusts.

• Where the family will be, on which days, between which hours. One calendar event, a place, two stored time slots and a title that names the family (so the guest list is in the string even where the attendee rows are empty).

• Which of the family will be there. The scorecard names the ones scored as family, a household entity holds them together, and a Family Sharing circle says which of them are in the same family group.
• And, in the same file, what is installed on the machine, down to the password manager.

It is easy to see how this could be weaponized if this single point of failure for your privacy ends up in the wrong hands. We play that (hypothetical) scenario out in a second write-up. The good thing is that this knowledge is meant to stay local on your machine, protected by the Full Disk Access permission; although it can be consumed by other services (but it is not entirely clear to us how and what can be accessed).

The reality is that the amount of information in this store is really something else: every time we dig into what the daemons infer, and how, a few new lines of investigation open up. Whatever you would rather no one knew about you or your family may well be in there somewhere, and we think you have the right to know whether it is. What you get instead: no documentation, no way to inspect the store and no general way to correct an inference that is wrong.

So we give you two tools. The first is iKnow, a local dashboard for browsing your own graph without anything leaving your Mac (the next section walks through it). The second is for going deeper. The iKnow repository ships a manual for your own agent that tells it where the databases are and how to read them, so it can go looking for whatever you are after. (Please point a self-hosted model at it, not a cloud one.)
iKnow
We designed iKnow as a web dashboard implemented in the Python standard library; no npm and no CDN.

It is meant to be run directly on your Mac, where the databases are stored. When executed, it binds 127.0.0.1, locates the databases in your file system (granted the necessary permissions), opens them read-only, collects the info on the fly and represents it on a dashboard. Nothing is written and nothing is logged; values go from the stores, over loopback, into a browser tab; it can be run air-gapped if you want.
We have tested it on macOS 26.6.2 and 26.7.1, and, only partially, on 27.0.1.
iKnow has a dozen pages.
Start here
What your Mac knows. The landing page: the graph of people around you. Below it come the faces in your photos, your family, your handles, your correspondents and where you will be next.
Its graph is the same household as the one at the top of this post, this time drawn by the tool's own renderer:
The graph is the overview, and an overview is easy to shrug at. The pages behind it are not.
Social graph. Who the store links to whom through shared meetings, group chats and a closeness score. Each circle opens to its members and to the evidence behind it.
What it concluded
Kinship scorecard. The family bindings inferred by the daemon.
Its card on the landing page is cut down to the people it names:
The card is a summary of one table, and iKnow draws the whole table too:

The scores in these two shots are invented, and more generous than the real thing. On the Mac we took apart, only mother reached the top of the ladder; the few others it scored at all got one small vote on every family label at once, father and brother alike. What the fixture keeps is the table's grain: it only ever writes a handful of values (0.125, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.96), and most people sit on one default.
The face index. A face cluster for everyone in your photos.
Its co-occurrence graph does not use a single contact, message or calendar entry. It is built from your photographs alone:

This is the page's own honest point: the graph points at the face clusters and can name almost none of them (three of the twenty-nine, in the fixture). It does not need to. Who stands next to whom, how often, and which groups never meet is all there without a single name, and whoever knows the household can put the names back on in a second.
Guessed or given. What you typed in and what the Mac worked out for itself live in the same table. A confidence score is the only thing separating them.
What it recorded
A year of contact. Who you talked to, when, and not a word of message text (and it does not need any to tell when you are asleep).
Its card on the landing page is the one that gets the reaction, and it contains no inference at all.
iKnow draws that line too, from the same log folded onto a single week:
That is the general shape of this store: almost nothing in it had to be collected, because almost everything in it is a consequence of something that was.
The calendar. The one layer that knows where you will be: the hour, the room, the attendees and the dial-in.
What you withdrew. Withdrawing a fact does not remove it. The row moves to an expired table and keeps its confidence and provenance.
The machinery
The store. The file itself: what it models, and two real rows expanded into everything they touch.

Device fingerprint. Every app installed on the Mac is written down in plain text, next to a token that is an unsalted SHA-256 of that same app identifier, so the page recomputes it in your browser and you can watch it match.

Who else reads it. The graph is the first copy, not the only one. This page maps the views that subscribe to it, the databases they publish into, the tables that repeat the same facts, the streams coming in from hardware paired with the Mac, and the machinery that is set up but has not run yet.

A note on macOS 27. macOS 27 was released on September 14, 2026. After the upgrade to 27.0.1, the graph withdrew most of the rows it had built from Contacts, Calendar, Siri Suggestions, Family Sharing and the app catalog, and rebuilt them over the following day. Some pages of iKnow may not work fully on macOS 27 yet.

thehill.com/homenews/education/6198820-s.headline: Schools scramble after Google gives AI ultimatum
thehill.com/homenews/education/6198820-s.author: Lexi Lonas Cochran

paragraphs.text: Schools are scrambling after Google said Tuesday that education leaders need to either accept some AI in classrooms or lose access to its search engine.
School officials trying to push back on an encroaching AI are in a bind. The tech giant dominates search online, and it didn’t give much time for districts to make their decisions.
District leaders say a fight would be a big undertaking, but some may be up to the challenge, especially as public outcry after the announcement grows.

Google announced that early next year its Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will automatically be turned off for school districts and administrators will have to choose to opt into the features. However, the company said Search and AI are “deeply integrated”, and it will not be possible to turn on Google Search without accepting AI.
The company is updating its Search feature, so AI Overviews “will offer step-by-step guided learning” instead of instantly giving students the answers, but that does not offer comfort to the public.
“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”

AI in schools has become a growing issue as parents and school leaders contemplate how to integrate a technology that is increasingly used in the workforce but viewed with extreme skepticism by critics.
New York City is among multiple localities that has banned AI completely for younger students but still makes it available in some capacity for high schoolers.
“It’s a small microcosm of the issue of AI in our world and AI in school districts, and then how school districts operate,” said Clay Lavercombe, freshman principal at Springboro High School in Ohio.

“To change anything in the middle of a school year, big or small, I think is a challenge. I would hope that leaders would consider that, and maybe even Google would consider that — to allow school districts to determine what they want to do, but I’m sure that there’ll be some school districts, big and small, who say, ‘We cannot use Google, and we’ll have to figure something else out,'” he added.

But abandoning Google is not as simple as just switching search engines. An estimated 60,000 K-12 schools use Google Workplace, meaning teachers and students have integrated their work in Google emails, sheets and slides, according to Tech & Learning. Around 93 percent of U.S. public schools either use or plan on using Google Chromebooks in classrooms, About Chromebooks reported.

“I really think Google risks undermining its own position. They’ve had a tremendous amount of market share, but they’re ultimately forcing these schools and districts to choose between access to the information that they already have and controlling over how students use AI,” said Eric Gibbs, vice president of education at AI detection company Copyleaks, which works with schools around the country on AI usage.
Google did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Advocacy groups had been pushing for the company to turn off its AI features on Google Search after discovering the platform would easily complete a homework assignment for students or give them all the answers.

“We were really calling on Google to turn it off, recognizing that was probably the best way to ensure that kids were safe online and that we ensured that AI was not doing homework and schoolwork for kids,” said Yvette Renteria, chief programs officer at Common Sense Media.

“And so, when Google puts out this choice of ‘You can only use Google Search with AI or you don’t use it at all,’ it’s really disturbing because, again, it takes away the opportunity to provide critical thinking skills, which is so important in education,” she added.
A May 2026 Gallup poll said 50 percent of the U.S. workforce uses AI at least a few times a year and 15 percent uses the technology daily. That usage is expected to increase in the future.
Schools have tried several times to ban the technology due to cheating concerns, and some teachers have even switched assignments from online to in-person writing to avoid AI.
AI supporters don’t think the fight is worth having.

The Google announcement “doesn’t bother me tremendously. I actually think AI is a useful tool. That, but we also have to have to teach our kids how to use AI. It’s a tool that has to be taught, similar to how to use safe internet practices or how to search on YouTube, use YouTube in appropriate ways. But it’s a tool that’s only going to get bigger, and … that genie’s not going back in the bottle,” said Dustin Strickland, an administrator at North Murray High School in Florida.

“AI is here. It’s part of what is going to be part of our students’ lives. So rather than burying our head in the sand, I think we have to learn, have to teach our kids how to use it effectively,” he added.

nytimes.com/2026/11/07/world/middleeast/.headline: Why Israel’s Ex-Army Chief’s Next Mission Could Be Mission Impossible

paragraphs.text: Gadi Eisenkot, Israel’s former military chief, is all but certain on Sunday to be given a chance to form a new government, after he was recommended for the task by parties that won 67 seats in the 120-seat Parliament.
But completing that mission and replacing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may well be the toughest assignment of Mr. Eisenkot’s career so far.

The ideologically and ethnically diverse factions that recommended him for prime minister include left-wing, right-wing, centrist and predominantly Arab parties. Most would have to break seemingly ironclad campaign promises in order to unite behind Mr. Eisenkot, no matter how he arranges them into a governing coalition.
But the pressure is on him and his allies to do just that because the alternatives, in their view, are far worse.

A failure to form a government could send Israel to another round of elections. It would leave Mr. Netanyahu in his job as prime minister in the meantime, with all of the advantages of incumbency. And the opposition would be unlikely to perform as well as it did in October, when thousands of expatriate Israelis flew home to vote.

A unity government in which Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Netanyahu share power, such as by taking turns as premier, seemed far-fetched before Election Day and seems unthinkable now. Some of Mr. Eisenkot’s campaign promises left wiggle room, but he was adamant in saying that Mr. Netanyahu, as the person with ultimate responsibility for defending the country on Oct. 7, 2023, when it suffered its worst attack in history, was unfit to continue in government.

Since the election, Mr. Netanyahu’s efforts to delegitimize the result — by accusing Arab parties of stealing votes — have hardened those views. And the lopsided result of the U.S. midterm elections underscored the urgency of replacing Mr. Netanyahu, opposition leaders have argued: Israel’s standing with lawmakers in both the Democratic and Republican parties is so dismal, and Mr. Netanyahu so loathed, that only a new prime minister could possibly begin to repair it.

“Israel is already in the midst of a dangerous diplomatic tsunami,” Mr. Eisenkot said on Friday. He added that a situation in which Mr. Netanyahu “continues to exercise authority over Israel’s security system and law enforcement agencies is dangerous and must not be allowed to continue for even one more day.”
But what kind of government can Mr. Eisenkot form?

He starts with 48 members of Parliament, thanks to his own center-right Yashar party (21), Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s centrist Together party (12), Yair Golan and the left-wing Democrats party (8), and Avigdor Liberman’s right-wing but secular Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) party (7).

That is more than Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition can count on: After an ultra-Orthodox party, United Torah Judaism, refused to recommend him for prime minister, Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition has only 46 seats.

To form a bigger coalition, let alone a majority in Parliament, Mr. Eisenkot’s options include partnering with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which together have 13 seats, or the Arab parties, which won a record 19 seats. Either route is deeply problematic, according to opposition lawmakers, operatives and advisers, most of whom insisted on anonymity to discuss coalition talks.
Here is a look at Mr. Eisenkot’s possible path forward, and at one major roadblock standing in his way.
First, Take Control of Parliament

Until a new government is formed, Mr. Netanyahu remains a caretaker prime minister. But Parliament is another story. Lawmakers will be sworn in on Tuesday, and Mr. Eisenkot is working to arrange for the election of a new speaker to replace Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu loyalist.

If he is successful, that could put Mr. Eisenkot’s allies in charge of key legislative committees. And it could allow his anti-Netanyahu bloc to begin enacting legislation — fulfilling key campaign promises and demonstrating Mr. Eisenkot’s ability to get things done.

The lowest-hanging fruit, insiders say, would be to repeal laws passed by Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition, such as controversial judicial changes allowing more political control over the appointment of judges and curbing the attorney general’s powers.

Equally important would be to deliver on a core campaign promise by all the opposition leaders to establish a national commission of inquiry to investigate the security failures that preceded the Oct. 7 attack.
Liberman Rules Out the Arab Parties
Mr. Eisenkot this past week began speaking of the need to form a “national emergency government” — an important rhetorical shift.
“If it’s an emergency, you do things you wouldn’t do otherwise,” said Nimrod Novik, a senior fellow of the Israel Policy Forum who was an adviser to Shimon Peres when he was prime minister.
The Arab parties’ 19 seats would give Mr. Eisenkot a solid majority, but bringing them into a government could cost him other allies.

For now, the question is moot: The Joint List, an amalgam of three smaller Arab parties that together won 11 seats, has ruled out joining a government, though it could provide support from the outside and enable a minority government to function. The United Arab List, or Raam, which won eight seats, has not. But Mr. Eisenkot has insisted that any party joining his government must declare Hamas a terrorist organization.
Raam’s leader, Mansour Abbas, has refused to do so, though he condemns all terrorist acts. But he did say on Thursday that Hamas and all other Palestinian factions should be disarmed.

Even if Mr. Abbas were to satisfy Mr. Eisenkot, however, Mr. Liberman, the Yisrael Beiteinu leader, has repeatedly ruled out a government that includes Arab parties or even relies on their support from the outside.
That leaves relying on the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties.
A Deal With the Ultra-Orthodox?

This, too, is fraught with peril. The most important issue for the Haredim is to protect their young men, who now account for about one in four draft-age teenagers, from conscription into the military and punishment for draft evasion. But with the Israeli Army overstretched, a core campaign promise of Mr. Eisenkot and his opposition allies was to compel Haredi men to share the sacrifice of defending the country.
Mr. Liberman has now chosen to break that promise but not his vow to keep Arab parties out of government.

On Friday, he wrote on social media that while he remained dead set on replacing Mr. Netanyahu, avoiding new elections and spurning any partnership with the Arab parties, “on all other issues, it is permissible and desirable to be flexible and compromise, and to understand that you cannot have it all. This includes the issue of the conscription law as well.”

Mr. Eisenkot was not entirely absolutist in his campaign rhetoric about drafting the ultra-Orthodox, but Mr. Bennett, of the Together party, was adamant about it and would have to accept going back on that pledge.

Mr. Eisenkot could also find it difficult to strike a deal with the Haredi party leaders, who are far more experienced at coalition negotiations than he is, and whose voters have grown steadily more right-wing and nationalist in recent years.

David Makovsky, an analyst at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said the fact that United Torah Judaism had declined to recommend Mr. Netanyahu for prime minister was a positive sign. “It means the store is open,” he said. “But how much they’re willing to go against their base, which is really right-wing — that’s the $64,000 question.”
Eisenkot Considers a Minority Government

With 48 votes to Mr. Netanyahu’s 46, Mr. Eisenkot said on Friday that he planned to form a minority government, at least initially. That would mean that the Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties abstain from the vote to form the government.

But he also said he would invite every political party — without exceptions — to join his government, now or later, provided it embraced his terms: recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accepting the values in the Israeli Declaration of Independence, requiring universal national military or civilian service, and agreeing that Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be dismantled.
Mr. Liberman, however, is again standing in the way. On Friday, he ruled out forming a government with anything less than a 61-seat majority.
Gayil Talshir, a political science lecturer at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem who is advising the opposition, said it was unclear whether Mr. Liberman really wanted Mr. Eisenkot to be successful.

Mr. Liberman has complained publicly that Mr. Eisenkot ended his campaign by cannibalizing support for his allies in a way that Mr. Liberman contends cost both Yisrael Beiteinu and the anti-Netanyahu bloc several seats.
Ms. Talshir said Mr. Liberman may fear the wrath of his right-wing voters if he agrees to a partnership with Arab parties.
He also may be angling to take a shot at becoming prime minister himself.

Should Mr. Eisenkot fail to form a government, Mr. Netanyahu would be given a chance next. But if he failed, there would be a short period before new elections are called in which anyone in Parliament — including Mr. Liberman — could become prime minister by enlisting the support of 60 other lawmakers.
On Friday, Mr. Eisenkot appeared to allude to Mr. Liberman’s resistance — and possible ulterior motives.

“Anyone who seeks to delay or sabotage the formation of a government for personal rather than substantive reasons,” he wrote on social media before the start of the Sabbath, “will be remembered by history as someone who failed to rise to the occasion and failed to act to save Israel in a time of national emergency. They will not be forgiven.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/07/us/politics/midte.headline: The Good, the Bad and the Cringe: 10 Ads That Defined the Midterms

paragraphs.text: Campaigns spent billions of dollars on ads this year. Some worked. Some didn’t. Some were stirring. Some were cringe.
Most will be quickly forgotten. A few will be remembered.
Here are some of the most memorable, influential and sometimes incoherent spots of a 2026 midterm election that resulted in one of the biggest Democratic landslides in modern history:
“Pick another protein?” The affordability ad that defined a Senate race.

Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Republican of Mississippi, wasn’t supposed to even be in a competitive race. But in the closing stretch, national Republicans redirected money and President Trump made a trip for a rally to try to save her.
But it was one of her missteps in a TV interview that her Democratic challenger, Scott Colom, packaged into a viral clip about her dismissal of the price of beef.
“You know you have so many proteins to choose from,” Ms. Hyde-Smith had said.
The spot features a parade of Mississippians mocking the idea.
“Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator,” one woman says.

The spot did not run on television. But Mr. Colom’s post on X featuring the video was widely viewed. And in perhaps the nation’s closest Senate race — as of now still uncalled but with Mr. Colom narrowly leading — it drew attention to the Democrat on one of the year’s defining issues: costs.
An early hit on Epstein
By the end of the election, there was more than $120 million of advertising referring to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

But one of the earliest Democrats to seize on linking Mr. Epstein to his Republican opponent was the former Senator Sherrod Brown, Democrat of Ohio. He ran an ad in the spring accusing Senator Jon Husted of having “taken the most money from associates of Jeffrey Epstein” of all 535 members of Congress. (The ad highlighted more than $100,000 in campaign contributions Mr. Husted had received in the past from Leslie Wexner, who was the source of much of Mr. Epstein’s wealth; Mr. Husted’s campaign noted that Mr. Brown himself had received campaign donations in the past from Mr. Wexner’s wife.)

In a year when Democrats tried to push a message that Republicans were serving themselves and the elites over everyday Americans, the closing line foreshadowed the hits to come: “Who’s he really working for?”
Mr. Brown won the race.
The most brutal, and best-testing, House Democratic ad
Some admakers still produce spots on instinct and intuition. But many are rigorously tested both before and after for how much they move voters.

Of all the ads that the House Majority PAC, the top House Democratic super PAC, ran this year, one stood alone as the most effective: This spot highlighting allegations Representative Max Miller, Republican of Ohio, faced from his ex-wife. The ad ticks through some of her accusations, including that he scalded her with hot water from a skillet and fractured his daughter’s collarbone. (Mr. Miller has denied the domestic abuse allegations and claimed that his ex-wife has mental health challenges.)
The ad moved Mr. Miller’s favorable rating by 15 points, and shifted the race itself nearly 10 points, according to testing data shared by the House Majority PAC.

The race was one of the ugliest in the country after many Republicans — including Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, whose daughter is Mr. Miller’s ex-wife — tried to get Mr. Miller to quit the race. Mr. Miller lost.
A memorable grandparent embrace
Mr. Trump launched Islamophobic attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, calling him a “jihadist” while Republicans suggested he had ties to terrorists.
The El-Sayed campaign countered in many ways — including with a memorable ad.
“Where did Abdul El-Sayed come from?” a wide-eyed older white woman intones ominously, shot in noirish black and white.
Then the ad shifts to color.
“Here!” she shouts gleefully, sitting on a sofa with another older white man. “We’re his grandparents!” The words “Livingston County, MI” appear on the screen.
The cheeky spot had $1.8 million spent on it, according to AdImpact, starting right after the Democratic primary, in a bid to neutralize the coming attacks.
Mr. El-Sayed won the race.
Parlez-Vous blue to red?
As of Friday, former Gov. Paul LePage of Maine was one of the few Republicans ahead in the vote counting to flip a Democratic seat that had not been redrawn.
In a district that borders Canada and has pockets of French-speaking populations, Mr. LePage ran a memorable ad in which he took a hard line on illegal immigration.

The spot showcased the depth of his ties to the community — he says in French that French was his first language in Lewiston — and worked in his record as governor, while pitching himself as a supporter of legal immigration, but opposed to illegal immigration.
James Talarico’s experience ad

One perennial challenge for candidates is to push back on accusations from rivals without repeating the allegations. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in Texas, took a creative approach to that: He ticked through how his experience was different from Ken Paxton’s, his Republican rival, and then he unloaded on Mr. Paxton.

“Ken Paxton says I don’t have his experience and he’s right. I’ve never been indicted for fraud,” he says, walking through a warehouse as 3-D words flash across the screen, “I’ve never been reported to the F.B.I. for bribery. I’ve never been impeached by my own party. ”
Mr. Talarico on Tuesday became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988.
Roger Marshall goes rogue
Even Senator Roger Marshall’s own team knew this one was a bad idea.

But when they said no, Mr. Marshall, a Kansas Republican, went ahead anyway. Without his senior campaign team’s knowledge, he arranged for a film crew to produce a spot defending his past lawsuits as an obstetrician against his patients, some of whom eventually faced arrest.

Mr. Marshall was determined to clear his name in the closing days — and thus drew more attention to the story. (The New York Times reported in September that Mr. Marshall had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients, seeking payments of their debts, and at least 81 were arrested for missing court dates. Others faced wage garnishments and Mr. Marshall routinely charged an 18 percent interest rate on the outstanding debts.)
“I never had anyone arrested,” Mr. Marshall says in his would-be ad.

He had sent it to some campaign aides and top leaders moved to block its release. Mr. Marshall began personally texting it to people and it was posted by a local talk-radio host. Mr. Marshall was defeated on Tuesday, as a Democrat won a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time in nearly a century.
Ramaswamy’s ruthless ad
An ad from Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor of Ohio, quickly rocked his race, divided Republicans across the country and became a symbol of the ugly tenor of the midterms.
The explosive spot shows the estranged mother of Mr. Ramaswamy’s Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, describing her as a liar and urging voters not to support her.

Ms. Acton said she had not spoken to her mother since she was 12, after her stepfather was charged with raping her. The sitting governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, a Republican, said he found the ad “deeply, deeply troubling” and “just plain wrong.”
Other Republicans, including Mr. Trump, closed ranks around Mr. Ramaswamy.
Vice President JD Vance, a former Ohio senator, said he was “disgusted” to see Republicans “whining” about the ad.
Former President Barack Obama, visiting Ohio to campaign, said he did not “know what’s happened where the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run an ad like that.”
Mr. Ramaswamy lost to Ms. Acton on Tuesday.
An attack on Cooper that boomeranged
In North Carolina, an ad for the Republican Senate nominee, Michael Whatley, appeared to boomerang and boost Democrats.

The ad, from the flagship super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, the Senate Leadership Fund, featured Ronald Hayes, whose son had been murdered. It blamed the Democratic Senate nominee, former Gov. Roy Cooper, for crime in North Carolina.
The ad had a flaw, Mr. Hayes, a Democrat, told news outlets. He had no problem with Mr. Cooper, he said, and had been misled by Republican operatives about the subject of the commercial.
Mr. Cooper’s campaign rushed out an ad to highlight Mr. Hayes’s account.
“Michael Whatley: Lies, deceit,” a voice in the Cooper campaign’s ad says. “He should never be in the Senate.”
The Cooper campaign spent more money on the pushback ad than anything else all cycle, according to AdImpact’s data, nearly $3 million.
Carter Wrenn, a Republican strategist in North Carolina, said Mr. Cooper’s ad was effective in tarnishing Mr. Whatley’s credibility.
“Because it was true what Cooper was saying,” Mr. Wrenn said, adding that Mr. Whatley’s allies looked “sloppy.”
Mr. Cooper won by a wide margin.
A dismissive ‘cord of wood’ mention drew accusations of elitism
In the waning days before the election, Senator Susan Collins of Maine ran an ad that stunned some Republicans and that Democrats quickly promoted.

The ad showed a retired Maine telecaster, Bill Green, dismissing the Democratic nominee Troy Jackson’s work as a logger. “We’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here,” Mr. Green says. “We’re sending someone to the U.S. Senate.”

Democrats said it was elitist. Mr. Jackson used it to focus attention on a crisis facing Maine residents: heating oil costs that were soaring because of the war in Iran. Half the homes in Maine are heated with fuel oil, and the rising prices became a central issue in the race.

Mr. Jackson said the race was “about a cord of wood” and about Mainers’ struggles to heat their homes. On Halloween, Mr. Jackson walked the streets of Portland, Maine, dressed as a cord of wood, mocking the commercial.

Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist in Maine and a former aide to Ms. Collins, said the ad carried a “tone of condescension” and left an impression that Ms. Collins was out of touch on a crucial issue.
“How that got on the air, I have no idea,” Mr. Dutson said.
Mr. Jackson defeated Ms. Collins.

nytimes.com/2026/11/07/us/politics/democ.headline: Democrats, Newly Ascendant, Begin a Fight to Shape the Party’s Future

paragraphs.text: A pastor in Kansas. A Paralympian in Iowa. A former Presbyterian seminarian in Texas.
Democrats expanded their map this week with big wins in traditionally red states that the party had all but written off for years by making appeals to moderate, independent and Republican voters.
At the same time, progressives won key races in two purple states, Michigan and Maine.

The combined victories amounted to a sweeping triumph that will send an ideologically diverse crop of new Democratic lawmakers to Congress in January, but internal debates are already emerging about what lessons the party should draw ahead of the 2028 presidential campaign.

For centrists, the results demonstrate that the best way to flip conservative strongholds where their party has long struggled is through embracing moderate candidates and positions that appeal to a broader array of voters. Progressives argue that the victories in Maine and Michigan show that left-wing populists can energize the party’s liberal base and win back some of the working-class voters who had flocked to President Trump.
The debate arrives at a moment of unusual opportunity for the Democratic Party, which will hold large majorities in Congress next year and will seek to carry its midterm momentum into the 2028 cycle.

The discussion over the party’s direction is already playing out as donors, officials and politicians converge at party meetings and liberal gatherings across the country to take a victory lap and plan for the future.
