And as potential presidential contenders accelerate their quiet planning, they are using the results to make a case for the next nominee — and, possibly, themselves.

“There’s a ton of non-MAGA Republicans and independents that are giving Democrats a second look and a second chance,” Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor, who is considering a presidential run, said in an interview. “I don’t happen to think socialism is the way to win their hearts and minds.”
He added: “We don’t want to be identified with that anymore.”
Representative Ro Khanna, a California progressive who has also been teasing a bid, had a different assessment.

“The results show that there is no electoral penalty for being a progressive,” he said in an interview. “The stale talking points of the establishment, which lost twice to Trump, about who they deem electable or not electable is totally out the window.”
Revenge of the Moderates
The early skirmishes are the latest round of a decade-long dispute over the Democratic Party’s direction and strategy.

In the first few months of this year, it appeared as if progressives had the upper hand. Liberal insurgents knocked off moderate rivals in blue districts in New York, New Jersey and Colorado, and they prevailed in Senate primaries in Maine, Michigan and Minnesota.

But in the general election, the moderates roared back, using explicitly bipartisan appeals to win by notable margins in states that had not elected Democrats to the Senate in years or, in the case of Kansas, nearly a century.

In Iowa, Josh Turek, the party’s nominee for Senate, ran a closing-stretch TV ad about how he opposed transgender athletes participating in youth sports. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a pastor who until this year had been a registered Republican, offered direct appeals to Trump voters and described himself as “a liberal conservative and a conservative liberal” who was above party politics. And in Texas, James Talarico embraced a “politics of love” that leaned away from partisanship and focused on “top versus bottom,” or the rich and powerful against ordinary Americans.

While all three men embraced economic populist platforms that promised to lower costs and raise taxes on billionaires, they also denounced what Mr. Hamilton called the “hyperpolarization in Washington.”

“Those candidates ran on that kind of pragmatic platform, saying we’re going to focus on the issues that impact our community, and we’re going to be independent voices, not putting parties and politics first,” said Representative Adam Gray of California, a Democrat who is the chairman of the moderate Blue Dog PAC. “They did better than their progressive counterparts. I think you’re going to see that in the data.”
Victories for the Left
Progressives rode a different path to victory.

The party’s Senate candidates in Maine, Michigan and Minnesota placed left-wing rallying cries at the center of their campaigns, promising to establish “Medicare for all”; calling to dismantle the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency; and accusing Israel of committing genocide in Gaza.
In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed combined some of those promises into a call-and-response slogan: “Money out of politics, money in your pocket and Medicare for all.”
In an interview, he credited his victory to his willingness to try to upend the political system. He suggested that not everyone in his party was on board with that idea.

“I think one of my big critiques of Democrats has often been that we just treat the symptom and not the disease,” he said. “Some people want to treat the disease without treating symptoms, right? You’ve got to treat both.”

He wasn’t the only progressive feeling bullish. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, the dean of congressional progressives, claimed near-total victory in an interview. Of the candidates he endorsed, the only one who did not win was Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist who fell just short in the Florida Senate race.

Mr. Sanders said Democrats should not hesitate to press a progressive agenda next year in Congress. He argued that Americans had voted for major changes, including wealth taxes, a higher minimum wage, universal health care and ending foreign wars.

“They want a government that stands up to the working class, that takes on the oligarchs, that delivers for working families,” he said. “We can no longer engage in same old, same old, status quo policies.”

In the House, Representative Greg Casar of Texas, the chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, boasted that his group would expand its ranks by 25 members next year. He cast the midterms as a generational victory for the progressive movement.

Progressive winners of House races included Will Lawrence, a co-founder of an environmental group, the Sunrise Movement, who flipped a Republican-held district in Michigan; Brian Poindexter, who defeated a scandal-tarred Republican in northeast Ohio; and Randy Villegas, who prevailed in a redistricted House seat in California.

“This election cycle, the progressives made a big new bet that by endorsing populist candidates in seats Trump won big, we could show that a populist progressive message can win anywhere,” Mr. Casar said in an interview. “And that paid off.”
He added, “Progressive ideas won.”
‘They Were Saying the Same Things’
With so many Democratic wins, not all the ideological lanes were quite so clear.

Both moderates and progressives claimed some credit for the party’s flips of Republican-held seats by Sam Forstag, a union leader and smoke jumper in western Montana; Bob Brooks, a Pennsylvania union leader; and Rebecca Cooke, a Wisconsin political fund-raiser.

Democratic leaders have tried to downplay the party’s divide. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, who is widely expected to become the next majority leader, and Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to become speaker, stressed unity. They said all of the party’s candidates had run by focusing on the cost of living, corruption and the Iran war.
“Whether they were progressives or moderates, they were saying the same things,” Mr. Schumer told reporters.
Still, some officials in both wings of the party interpreted the results through the prism of what kind of Democrat would be best to nominate for president in 2028.

With the jockeying for the presidential race escalating this week — Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois released a memo on Wednesday promoting his proposed agenda for the next two years — the fight over the party’s direction will unfold both in Congress and in the early primary states.
A chief target of the centrist scrutiny was Mr. El-Sayed, who won in Michigan after his party sent its full armada to help him.

Former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris stumped for him. Mr. Schumer’s super PAC invested $67 million into the race even though Mr. El-Sayed said he would not back Mr. Schumer to be party leader.

In the final weeks, some party officials quietly grumbled that a more centrist candidate would have cost less and freed up money for Democrats to expand their playing field of competitive races into places like Florida and Mississippi, where a moderate candidate leads a Senate race by just over 2,000 votes as counting continues.
Progressives, for their part, noted that Mr. El-Sayed had been undercut by his moderate primary rival’s surprising late endorsement of the Republican nominee.

Broadly, centrist Democrats have argued that progressive candidates, despite winning, underperformed in blue or purple states. Democrats are on track to win the national popular congressional vote by about 13 percentage points, according to estimates by The New York Times. Mr. El-Sayed won his Senate race by seven points, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota by 10 and Troy Jackson of Maine by six.

“The people who won handily in states Democrats haven’t won in decades were the people who practiced the politics of addition, not the politics of subtraction,” said Neera Tanden, the president of the center-left Center for American Progress.
Some other Democrats were already looking ahead to the next race.

Even before the polls closed on Tuesday, aides to Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York released a five-page memo detailing her contributions to midterm Democrats and again articulating her thinking about whether to seek the 2028 presidential nomination.

“In the coming days and weeks, much will be discussed about the future of the Democratic Party and 2028. You may be asked whether you support her running for president or for Senate in New York or staying in the House of Representatives,” the memo concluded. “We’d recommend you rely on the details of this memo and answer that Rep. Ocasio-Cortez will continue to do what she’s always done: look for ways to do the most good for the most people.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/07/world/europe/ukra.headline: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Reverse Some Russian War Gains

paragraphs.text: A steady hum of activity filled the underground bunker in eastern Ukraine. Soldiers called across one another as they monitored banks of screens showing livestream video feeds from the battlefield one morning last month.

“Guys, let’s fight the war first and deal with our stuff later,” the commander, Yuriy Horobets, shouted, quieting the room. “Our FPV is coming in now,” he said, pointing out a tiny, pale object, a first-person-view drone, moving across the screen of a reconnaissance feed. The drone, a remotely piloted quadcopter, was homing in to attack.

His brigade, the 66th Mechanized Brigade, had multiple drones in the sky that day to strike Russian positions as its troops prepared to storm a tree line. The assault was at the tail end of a monthslong operation that recaptured a sizable portion of eastern territory.
That operation, called Vivaldi, thwarted Russian efforts this year to encircle the last cities of Donetsk Province, the prize that Moscow insists it wants to end the war.

After months of operational silence, the Ukrainian brigades involved have begun to reveal details of how they managed to turn a losing defensive fight against Russian forces into a successful offensive along parts of the front line. They allowed a team of New York Times reporters to embed with them for two weeks and see their work firsthand.

Ukrainian troops had been losing ground to the far more numerous Russian Army for the best part of two years. But the wider use of drones and remote-controlled vehicles, and changes in the command structure and culture within parts of the army, enabled Ukraine to shift gears.

Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky, the overall commander of the operation, claimed that the tactics were so successful that his troops had wiped out Russia’s 144th Motor Rifle Division in the fighting and reversed Russia’s gains of a whole year.

“What we are seeing now looks more like desperate attempts to establish a defensive line — an agony, rather than organized, systematic military operations,” he told journalists in a briefing in October.

Alongside several of his commanders, he had gathered members of the news media in an underground bunker to announce the end of Operation Vivaldi, the main thrust of which he said began in May, and to sum up its results.

In October, for the second consecutive month, Ukraine gained more territory than Russia, and Russian forces suffered their highest monthly casualty toll — more than 54,000 killed or seriously wounded — of the war, according to the Institute for the Study of War.

Military analysts and Russian military bloggers have confirmed Ukrainian gains, as Russian forces lost a key salient north of the city of Lyman and an equal amount of territory on the Zaporizhzhia front line in southern Ukraine.

The 66th brigade was essential to that success. Its challenges were typical of many Ukrainian military formations, like struggling with old equipment and shortages of personnel and resources. Many of its infantry soldiers are in their 40s or 50s, like Mr. Horobets, 45, a battalion commander.

Last year, the brigade, vastly outnumbered by Russian forces opposing them, was steadily losing ground, Mr. Horobets said. Their supply routes were under fire, preventing them from bringing in ammunition and evacuating the wounded.

Yet it was from that maelstrom, fed up with being destroyed by Russian firepower, that a few battalion commanders said they took things into their own hands. They seized critical Russian positions on high ground above a village from which Russian troops were directing the strikes against them.

Once they controlled the heights and knocked out Russian communications, they found they had an advantage. The Russian soldiers in the village did not know what had happened and could not replace equipment because the Ukrainian forces were bringing down the Russian supply drones and preventing vehicles getting through on the roads, several commanders involved in the operation said.

“At that point, we had superiority over the enemy in terms of both strike drones and aerial reconnaissance,” said Nazar Kinash, 25, the acting commander of a mechanized battalion. The Russians “had effectively been blinded,” he said.
The 66th brigade began infiltrating soldiers into the village and setting up ambushes, Mr. Horobets said. Within a month, they had taken the village, and six weeks later, they seized another.

“For now, you see silence,” Mr. Horobets said as he gestured at a bank of video screens in his underground command post. “A month ago, there was a terrible war here because the enemy was trying to regain its positions and counterattack,” he said. “But, for now, they are exhausted.”

The operation is the first sign of a new direction under General Biletsky, who took command of the Third Army Corps in summer 2025, bringing a unity of command and coordination among six brigades along their part of the front line, several battalion commanders said.

Decision making was given to commanders on the ground rather than being relayed from a command post, while the senior commanders focused on the broader operational level to disrupt the Russian command, they said.

Working in sync for the first time with the units around them, the commanders of the 66th brigade said they had cracked the problem of Russian infiltration, sealing the gaps between units where Russian soldiers had been slipping through to set up positions behind Ukrainian lines.

Drone warfare has transformed the front line in Ukraine into a miles-wide kill zone, where vehicles are so easily targeted that soldiers mostly move on foot in small groups. The Russian Army has largely abandoned full-frontal armored assaults in favor of a stealthy advance by inserting foot soldiers.

For months, the 66th brigade hunted down and destroyed every Russian position it could find, including single soldiers holed up in dens behind Ukrainian lines, infantry in trenches and drone pilots in bunkers, Mr. Horobets said.

“Overall, it comes down to coordination,” he said. He showed two areas of scrubby woodland outlined in red on a video screen. Russian soldiers were still dug in there and were his target for the afternoon, he said.
“We will destroy the antennas first, then destroy the generators,” he said. “It will turn out that we destroy the pilots, too.”

As the Ukrainians began advancing, the value of their middle-range drone strikes became clear. The Third Army Corps was striking up to 50 Russian vehicles a day, sometimes as deep as 100 miles behind Russian lines, General Biletsky said.

“It became normal for the enemy to unload 40 to 50 kilometers from the front line and then continue on foot,” he said. Sometimes a soldier would carry a single artillery shell 20 miles, he said. “Their logistics have effectively been paralyzed.”
Russian soldiers were running short of fuel, ammunition and food. Some began holding up cardboard signs outside their positions, saying they were hungry and thirsty, several commanders said.
Critically, when Russian reinforcements were called in, Ukrainian drones struck them as they dismounted from vehicles miles before they could reach the front line, Mr. Horobets said.

The wider use of battlefield robots to beat Russia’s superiority in numbers has steadily grown. A 27-year-old former Ukrainian assault trooper said he had been put in charge of building up a special battalion of remote-controlled strike vehicles since last fall. He asked to be identified by only his call sign, Makar, for security reasons and according to protocol.

The Ukrainians cannot outnumber the Russians in terms of personnel, he said in an interview. “But we can outperform them technologically,” he said, “in terms of quality and scale, if we consistently stay several steps ahead of them.”

By now, ground robots are vital. In several underground command posts our team visited, Ukrainian soldiers watched livestream videos of tracks and undergrowth as the vehicles trundled through the kill zone carrying cargo. Sometimes they brought out the bodies of dead soldiers.
Many of the vehicles break down or get attacked by Russian drones, and their cameras showed the wrecks of other vehicles.
But many of them get through. General Biletsky said his brigades were delivering three times as much cargo to their soldiers on the front line as other brigades that recently came under his command.

“That means a soldier in the Third Army Corps has considerably more resources and capabilities available to them: food supplies, ammunition, equipment, power sources, batteries and so on, compared with a soldier elsewhere,” he said. They were even receiving diggers to help build underground bunkers, he said.

Makar said he had focused on using remote-controlled vehicles as tools of attack. Soldiers of his unit, NC13, part of the Third Assault Brigade, were at the forefront of Operation Vivaldi, piloting such strike vehicles on the battlefield.

The Times met a group of them, 20-year-olds with nine months’ experience in the army, during a live-fire training exercise, in which they directed remote-controlled buggies armed with rocket-propelled grenades and a Browning machine gun. Another team piloted a reconnaissance drone to supply a constant video feed.
The next day, their trainer, who uses the call sign Bar, was at the controls, guiding a robot vehicle into a tree line in a real attack.

The machine, visible in a video stream from a surveillance drone, was moving clumsily back and forth, tangled in the undergrowth as it approached the entrance of a bunker. Then suddenly the screen filled with a cloud of smoke.
It was unlikely that anyone inside the bunker had survived the blast, Makar said as he watched the video replay, “That’s 20 kilos of explosive.”

As Vivaldi was drawing to conclusion, Mr. Horobets was still focused on stragglers in his area. On a livestreamed video, a soldier carrying a backpack and a weapon moved cautiously from the trees into an open field. When he reached a patch of tall grass, he stopped and crouched low, barely visible.
“He’s Russian,” Mr. Horobets said. “We have work to do.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/07/technology/whistl.headline: Jeffrey Wigand, Who Blew the Whistle on Big Tobacco, Takes a Lot of Calls

paragraphs.text: Every day, people call Jeffrey Wigand and say they really need to talk.

They are people with a secret, people who think they have information that can blow their town or their company or their country wide open. Maybe they need a little help. Sometimes they want reassurance that their life won’t be ruined. They’re frightened, so they’re reaching out to someone who has been through the whirlwind.
Dr. Wigand, a corporate insider turned implacable adversary, talks them through it.

“Make sure you have your family tightly bound to you,” he says. “Do you have a strong marriage? Are you a churchgoer?” Sometimes they’re enormously angry. “Vengeance without evidence is bad,” he says. “The only thing that protects you is 100 percent truth and the facts that support it.”

Often the callers are in their late 40s or mid-50s, have young children, haven’t quite hit the moment to do what they think is right. But if they are looking for uplift and sweet talk, they should have dialed another number.
“You’ll never be the same,” Dr. Wigand warns.

He certainly wasn’t. In the early 1990s, Dr. Wigand was a scientist at Brown & Williamson, one of the big tobacco companies. Middle-aged with a family, he was hired to make a healthier cigarette. Through an unlikely chain of events, he became a whistle-blower or, to use the term he prefers, “person of conscience.”

He testified that cigarettes were manipulated to make them addictive, an enormously consequential act. He was the recipient of death threats, appeared on “60 Minutes,” was played by Russell Crowe in a big Hollywood movie called “The Insider,” lost his marriage, lost his career and became a high school science teacher.

Now 83 and suffering from severe osteoarthritis — “I move like I’m dead” — Dr. Wigand has become a sort of pro bono Whistle-Blower Central at a moment when the world seems eager to see more of them. Pollsters say the perception of corruption in the U.S. government is practically universal and drove voters in the midterm elections. Dr. Wigand lives in north-central Michigan with his wife, Hope Elizabeth May, and gets calls from all over. The internet has his phone number.

A worker in a big U.S. lab says data is being manipulated for publication. A young researcher in Japan says he has proof that his company’s products do not do what the company claims. An employee of a hospital chain says there is an organized billing scam involving its patients. Someone from an agency charged with defending the country says there are things the world needs to know.

“I believe I have a duty to help others in return for what has been given to me,” Dr. Wigand said. “I don’t like the corruption in our world. There’s more moral decay than before, on all levels. I’m not going to go out on a box and preach, but this is something I can do.”

The first thing Dr. Wigand does is make sure the callers are on the level. “No one likes to be manipulated,” he says. Those who are deemed authentic might talk for an hour or more. Often they call again. He’s talked to the Japanese researcher five times, a process aided by the fluent Japanese he learned early in his career.
He sees his role as less pushing the callers to go through with it and more encouraging them to ask themselves if they can survive it.

“Some are almost there. Some are scared to death. Some are both,” Dr. Wigand said. “They start talking and you can hear their voice changing, and there’s a sob. They’re exploding.”The social media trials in the spring and summer brought him back into the public eye. Meta, owner of Facebook and Instagram, has been defending itself against suits by state regulators and former users. Whistle-blowers helped build the cases. Activists are optimistic that the tide against social media, and maybe screens themselves, is turning.

For Dr. Wigand, all this is familiar. “The tech industry deliberately and conspicuously manufactured a product that was addictive, just like the tobacco companies. And they also geared it to children,” he said. The tech industry denies this, but courts are finding it guilty. In August, Meta settled a suit with California and other states for up to $17 billion, a deal that echoed the $200 billion Big Tobacco settlement in 1998.

If there are useful parallels, there are differences, too. One element that accelerated the push against tobacco was the dangers of secondhand smoke. Smokers were seen as imperiling the health of others, who were outspoken as a result.

In other words, society wanted to change, which seems less clear with social media. Social media is also in the midst of shifting as it becomes subsumed into artificial intelligence, which makes it a more elusive target.

The biggest problem for social media critics reaching back to the tobacco battles for inspiration might be this: They weren’t entirely successful. Smoking in public has largely disappeared, but consumption of nicotine through vaping and other methods is still very much with us.
Dr. Wigand has outlived Brown & Williamson, which was absorbed in a merger, but the tobacco industry itself has survived and even prospered since the big settlement.

“It turned out to be only a symbolic victory,” Dr. Wigand said. “The industry easily came up with the money. They passed the price on to the victims, who will pay what they can to get the addictive product.”

The road ahead for social media is equally uncertain. “What social media needs more than anything else is the truth,” Dr. Wigand said. “The incriminating documents had to be extracted from the tobacco industry through legal proceedings. We’re in the earliest stages of that with social media.”

When Dr. Wigand went public with his accusations against Big Tobacco, there was minimal legal infrastructure to support people making accusations of wrongdoing against their own employers, and not much in the way of public support, either.

“Whistle-blowers were then called ‘snitches,’” recalled Ralph Nader, who held the first conference on insiders and informants in the early 1970s. The most famous whistle-blowers of the era included Frank Serpico, a New York cop who made Police Department corruption into a major issue; Karen Silkwood, a nuclear lab technician in Oklahoma; and Deep Throat, a then-anonymous government source for the Watergate reporter Bob Woodward (later revealed to be an F.B.I. official, Mark Felt).

These individuals — whose lives were enshrined, like Dr. Wigand’s, in big Hollywood movies — might have been inspirational, but their stories offered little practical guidance. In any case, people of conscience are rare. Threats of retribution are a very effective deterrent.

“After the way the company went after me, nobody wanted to follow,” Dr. Wigand said of his Brown & Williamson colleagues. Money plays a role, too. “When you get paid $500,000 a year, you don’t want to upset the apple cart.”
Since the 1990s, support for whistle-blowers has been institutionalized. By one count, there are now 66 countries with national whistle-blower laws.

The United States, once a leader in this regard, has gone in another direction under President Trump. A government whistle-blower who called attention to a phone call in which the president tried to coerce Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, to investigate Hunter Biden directly caused his first impeachment attempt, which in turn helped inspire a backlash on the right.
“Republicans, with few exceptions, have turned on whistle-blower rights,” said Tom Devine, the legal director of the Government Accountability Project, a Washington nonprofit.

The U.S. Office of Special Counsel, which reviews disclosures of wrongdoing from federal whistle-blowers, has recorded 11 cases so far in 2026. A few years ago, the annual number of cases was 60. With the Democrats regaining the House and the Senate, whistle-blowers may suddenly have a receptive ear in Washington.

If government has been less welcoming and in some cases outright hostile, the media is eager to give a hearing to allegations of wrongdoing. This is particularly true in the tech sector. Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic, caused an uproar in September when he announced he was leaving the industry over what he described as disregard for safety.
“Whistle-blowers are among the few people who can get the truth out to the public, and the public is aware of that,” Mr. Devine said.

There is even a new whistle-blower movie, “The Social Reckoning,” Aaron Sorkin’s quasi-update of “The Social Network.” The latter film, released in 2010, explored the origins of Facebook. The new film dramatizes the story of a company whistle-blower, Frances Haugen, who disclosed tens of thousands of internal documents.And the movie that seems to be filling theaters, “You Can See Everything,” would not exist were it not for a whistle-blower. Tyler Shultz, an intern at Theranos, endured threats and extraordinary familial pressure when he helped expose fraud at Elizabeth Holmes’s blood-testing start-up. (Mr. Shultz still feels that Ms. Holmes is once again getting away with things.)

Mr. Wigand has yet to see either movie. But then, he doesn’t spend a lot of time rewatching the movie about him. “The Insider,” directed by Michael Mann, came out in 1999. Mr. Crowe’s portrayal of Dr. Wigand — uncertain whom to trust, worried about his family, beset on all sides — won an Oscar nomination.
“It brings back a lot of bad memories,” Dr. Wigand said. “If you got a death threat to your children, how would you feel?”

His story had a relatively happy ending, but it could have gone in another direction. While many whistle-blowers succeed in publicizing their issues, a few come to unfortunate ends, leading to speculation they have been silenced, or at least that the burden was too much to bear.

The 1974 case of Karen Silkwood, a plutonium plant worker who had reported safety and record-falsification violations to regulators, still haunts potential whistle-blowers. Ms. Silkwood’s car hit a concrete culvert while she was on her way to meet a New York Times investigative reporter. The official verdict ruled it an accident. Her family and others say they have spent decades searching for the truth.
A Boeing whistle-blower was found dead from a gunshot wound in 2024, as was an OpenAI whistle-blower. Both deaths were ruled self-inflicted.
Dr. Wigand doesn’t keep track of how many calls he gets. His younger brother James says that when he comes to visit, they’re a persistent backdrop.

“The phone rings and he says, ‘I need to take this call.’ I go to another room or go outside,” said James, a retired endocrinologist. “Most 83-year-olds are like, ‘I’ve had enough.’ They’re worn out. But my brother is a persistent fighter. To use a Yiddish term, he has really good chutzpah.”
He also has his bone-deep understanding of what’s ahead. Fewer than half of his callers go through with it, Dr. Wigand estimates.
“Given how hard whistle-blowing is,” he said, “I think that’s a lot.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/07/business/economy/.headline: U.S. Cleared Nvidia Chips to Chinese Firms With Empty Offices and Troubling Ties

paragraphs.text: In a recently built industrial park on the northwest fringe of Beijing, the listed address of a company called New Matrix stands empty, a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration approved this Chinese firm to assemble Nvidia’s advanced chips into the computers that create artificial intelligence. President Trump allowed the sale of the chips, called the H200, to China late last year. But before they could be sold, the Commerce Department was required to review the companies involved for national security risks.

New Matrix passed that review. Yet recent checks by The New York Times found that, within China, there is little evidence the firm actually exists, raising questions about who in China is behind the company.

Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.

According to Chinese corporate records, New Matrix’s owners have ties to a prominent Chinese private equity fund that the U.S. government placed on a trade blacklist in 2024. Two analysts who examined the corporate records and other Chinese-language information said they believed New Matrix may be a front for firms associated with that fund.

The sale of chips to New Matrix appears to be part of a pattern that has concerned technology experts inside and outside the government: The Commerce Department is giving clearance to buy and handle Nvidia’s chips to Chinese companies with ties to firms that have been subject to national-security-related trade restrictions.

Nvidia’s chips are the crucial technology in A.I. data centers and now one of the world’s most coveted commodities. They are also at the heart of the economic and geopolitical competition between the United States and China.

Corporate records show that several other Chinese companies approved to purchase H200 chips or assemble them into servers have ties to firms that have been blacklisted by the U.S. government, or that work as military contractors in China.

Liza Tobin, the former China director for the White House National Security Council in the first Trump and Biden administrations, said the approvals raised questions about how rigorously the Trump administration is policing who can get their hands on Nvidia’s chips.
“I have a ton of concerns that neither the Commerce Department or Nvidia is doing the due diligence needed to ensure that the licensing terms are being followed,” she said.

During the Biden administration, the United States began more broadly restricting sales of A.I. chips to China out of concern the technology would help China advance militarily. But Mr. Trump eased some of those limits after lobbying by Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, with whom he has grown close during his second term.
In December, Mr. Trump gave Nvidia permission to sell the H200, an older but still powerful A.I. chip, to China, as long as the U.S. government was given a cut of the sales.

In an unusual arrangement, Mr. Trump is requiring these chips, which are assembled in Taiwan, to be routed through the United States on their way to China, so that the government can collect a 25 percent tariff on their value.

Nvidia is now selling only small amounts of H200 chips to China. The Chinese government has been slow to approve its companies for the purchases, partly because it is trying to promote domestically made chips.

In total, the Commerce Department appears to have approved roughly two dozen Chinese firms to buy or handle Nvidia’s H200 chips, including major Chinese companies like Baidu, BYD and Tesla Shanghai, according to people familiar with the approvals. The firms received approval to purchase tens of thousands of the chips each, but have not yet met that quota, the people said.
Reuters previously reported that the Commerce Department had approved major Chinese companies like Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance and ZTE Kangxun Telecom for the licenses.

A spokesman for the Bureau of Industry and Security, which reviews licenses inside the Commerce Department, said it carefully reviews all applications for national security risks. The agency also said it had imposed $324 million of penalties on companies for export violations in 2025 and hired more than 90 officers this year to enforce technology rules.
New Matrix did not respond to requests for comment.

John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said that “it makes no sense for the Chinese military to depend on American technology,” and that Nvidia sells the “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”

He added that the Chinese government has strictly limited imports of the H200 in favor of its own chip companies, but that even Nvidia’s limited sales of the chip support American jobs and manufacturing.

Although China is a potentially huge market for A.I. technology, sales directly to the country currently account for only a tiny percentage of Nvidia’s revenue. In the quarter that ended in July, H200 shipments to customers based in China made up less than 1 percent of Nvidia’s revenue from data centers. The company also said in August that it was not assuming any sales to China in its estimate for data center revenue for the current quarter.

But many Chinese companies are gaining access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Southeast Asia, and the chips still appear to be a critical focus for Beijing. The Times reported last month that Mr. Huang of Nvidia had a close relationship with a woman who American spy agencies concluded was an intelligence asset for China. The company she worked at, Megaspeed, operated data centers in Southeast Asia that served Chinese clients and was being investigated for smuggling some chips into China.
Another Empty Office

When the Commerce Department granted its approval to New Matrix this year, the company’s registered address was at a compound on the outskirts of Beijing used for corporate registrations, where thousands of other firms are also registered on paper, according to the Chinese corporate information site Qichacha. But this fall, New Matrix’s address changed to the empty office in the industrial park visited by The Times.

New Matrix’s website does not name any staff members, advertise any jobs or include information about its history, as of Nov. 6. But two of its primary owners appear in the records of companies connected to a Chinese private equity firm under sanctions and its founder, a man named Li Bin, according to WireScreen, a data platform.

In 2024, the U.S. government added the private equity firm, Wise Road, to the Commerce Department’s “entity list,” which restricts companies from doing business with the United States. The department said Wise Road had helped the Chinese government acquire strategically sensitive companies with chip technology.

Mr. Li is also the chairman of Tsinghua Unigroup, a technology conglomerate with government ownership. In 2021, one of Tsinghua Unigroup’s subsidiaries, New H3C Semiconductor Technologies, was added to the entity list for working with the Chinese military.
New Matrix is the second Chinese company approved to handle Nvidia’s H200 chips that does not seem to have any physical presence at its listed address.

In September, The Times reported that another recently created Chinese firm called Maginfra had also received a license for H200s. Like New Matrix, Maginfra appears to have been approved not as the ultimate buyer of the chips, but as a company that would assemble them into A.I. servers for another customer.

But when a Times reporter visited Maginfra’s listed address in China in September, it also appeared deserted. A few chairs and empty desks sat inside a small locked room with no signs. Workers on the floor said they had not seen anyone use the office, and building receptionists said they had not heard of Maginfra.

Analysts said they believed Maginfra was an offshoot of Inspur, a company whose headquarters were near Maginfra’s listed address. The U.S. government has added Inspur to the entity list for working with the Chinese military. Maginfra and Inspur share personnel and patents, and both have government ownership.
Military Ties

Other Chinese companies that have been approved for licenses to buy Nvidia’s H200 chips also have ties through their corporate owners to military suppliers, according to people familiar with the approvals and documents viewed by The Times.

One, called Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology, has ties to a cloud computing giant that has sold services to military contractors, called Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group. Yindun is partly operated from a data center owned by Range, and several of its executives are family members of Range’s founder.

Range serves as the cloud computing provider for a satellite program run by the defense bureau of Hebei province, which it has described on its website as serving the strategic needs of “national defense development.” It also started a subsidiary in 2016 to focus on quantum communications for the Chinese government and military. Part of the subsidiary is owned by a firm that the United States added to the entity list in 2021 for acquiring American items for the Chinese military.

Another company licensed to purchase H200 chips, Shanghai Jiatang, grew out of a state-owned enterprise called Datang Telecom, a chipmaker that provides technology to the Chinese military. Datang is controlled by the China Academy of Telecommunications Technology, a state-owned enterprise that has developed cryptography for the Chinese military.
Shanghai Jiatang, Yindun Cloud and Maginfra did not respond to requests for comment.

nytimes.com/2026/11/07/style/illeana-dou.headline: Illeana Douglas Looks Back on Hollywood’s Biggest ‘Cat Fight’

paragraphs.text: At the dawn of feminism, I assumed that cat fights would soon be history.
We were all going to be sisters, supporting each other and keeping our claws sheathed.
How naïve I was.

As they fought for equality, women were competing not only for mates but for jobs, desperately trying to infiltrate the room where it happens. Even the pioneers of feminism, Gloria Steinem and Betty Friedan, feuded.

But cat fights, as it turns out, are great for business. From “Dynasty” to the “Real Housewives,” “The Bachelor” and “Love Island” franchises, from “Mean Girls” to “Bridesmaids,” women scratching each other’s eyes out has been an amazing moneymaker, mostly for the men who still largely run the entertainment industry.

Cat fights are big in politics, too. Witness the tabloid delight in the “Democrat fight” between Nancy Pelosi and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in 2019 and the recent hair-pulling at the White House, with President Trump’s recently ousted chief of staff, the “ice maiden” Susie Wiles, sparring with the West Wing aide Natalie Harp and the short-lived press secretary Katie Zacharia.

So, naturally, I wanted to go to Connecticut to talk with Illeana Douglas about the biggest cat fight movie of all time and one that helped popularize the term — Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer’s 1939 classic, “The Women,” based on the Clare Boothe Luce Broadway hit of the same name. (Luce, the wife of Henry Luce, the founder of the Time-Life magazine empire, later became a congresswoman from Connecticut.)

Douglas, a 65-year-old actress, writer and director, has a glossy new book, “Jungle Red!”, on the making of the movie — the only lavish studio film, she says, ever produced with no men onscreen — and the rivalries offscreen among the famous actresses.
Even the animals in the film, dogs and horses, were female. George Cukor, the director, told the press that male visitors were barred from the set — an order defied by Joan Crawford.
“In all the publicity and in the press, they had people coming to the set, like, ‘This is going to be the world’s best catfight,’” Douglas said. “So from the very beginning, they set it up.”

In case anyone possibly missed the point, Cukor’s opening credits included animals corresponding to the film’s main characters — a leopard for Crawford and a hissing black cat for Rosalind Russell, while Norma Shearer and Joan Fontaine were prey, a doe and a lamb.
Crawford embraced her inner predatory feline. “I wanted this role more than anything in my life,” she said. “I like playing bitches. There’s a little bitch in all of us.”

Douglas and I are sitting in her renovated kitchen of her colonial farmhouse, which looks like one of the dreamy film sets depicted in her earlier book, “Connecticut in the Movies.” She grew up mostly in nearby Old Saybrook, where Katharine Hepburn also lived.

She made pancakes with maple syrup and turkey sausage and reminisced about her grandfather, the urbane Melvyn Douglas, who starred in Ernst Lubitsch’s “Ninotchka” with Greta Garbo and “The Candidate” with Robert Redford.

He went on to win two late-in-life supporting actor Oscars for “Hud” with Paul Newman and “Being There” with Peter Sellers. Melvyn’s second wife was the actress and politician Helen Gahagan Douglas, who lost the 1950 Senate race to Richard Nixon in California, after Nixon smeared her as a Communist sympathizer.

Illeana Douglas had memorable film roles in “GoodFellas,” “Cape Fear,” “To Die For,” “Grace of My Heart” and “Ghost World,” as well as the TV shows “Six Feet Under” and “Law & Order: SVU.” She played Gary Shandling’s girlfriend toward the end of “The Larry Sanders Show” and hosted a show on female filmmakers for Turner Classic Movies.

Her house is filled with gorgeous movie posters, including her grandfather’s Hollywood classics “A Woman’s Face” (with Crawford), “That Uncertain Feeling” (with Merle Oberon) and “Ninotchka.” There’s also a picture of her former boyfriend of eight years, Martin Scorsese, and a library of books about Hollywood.

Douglas was a nepo baby, given her legendary grandfather, but she had to work her way up. After attending the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York for a year, she was an assistant to the notorious publicist Peggy Siegal, decades before Siegel got tarred in the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

“People would jokingly say, ‘You work for the devil’s publicist,’” she recalled. “And I would say, ‘Oh, that’s why it’s so hot in the office.’ My job consisted of calling people like Walter Cronkite on the phone and inviting him to a party.”
Scorsese was editing “The Last Temptation of Christ” nearby and needed someone to dub in screams for Mary Magdalene. Douglas pitched in and the two began dating.
Douglas has complained that she always gets asked about Scorsese, but he never gets asked about her.

“Would you want to be identified with one relationship you had in your life?” she asked me. “Except for privately, I never get to talk about other great relationships I’ve had and influences I’ve had on them.”
What influence did she have on Scorsese?

She said that during the filming of the 1990 movie “GoodFellas,” she suggested making the scene with all the wives a Mary Kay party, after Scorsese couldn’t get the rights to make it a Tupperware party. “And a lot of the improv lines that we were coming up with that day at my house went into the movie,” she said.
Douglas was married to the late Jonathan Axelrod, a producer and writer, for three years until their divorce in 2001. Would she want to remarry?
“No,” she said flatly. “I used to always want to be married, but unfortunately I don’t think there’s anything in it for women. Having been married once, I don’t think it’s a good idea.”

The title of Douglas’s book comes from a signature line in “The Women,” when Shearer’s character, Mary Haines, resolves to go on the offensive against Crawford’s Crystal Allen, a vampy shopgirl who has stolen her husband. Haines gets in fighting trim by growing her nails into “claws” and having them painted a fierce shade: “Jungle red!” she cries, showing off her manicure as violins swell.
When Douglas recounted the scene, I noticed that her nails were done up in the same deep shade.

The stars of “The Women” did not care for each other offscreen either. Crawford felt that Shearer got all the good roles because of her marriage to MGM’s “Wonder Boy” executive, Irving Thalberg, who died in 1936. Crawford mockingly called Shearer, the classy first lady of MGM, “the Widow Thalberg.”

As Anita Loos, the screenwriter, put it: “Norma and Joan could never have been personal friends — they came from different worlds. Norma thought Joan crude and pushy, and Joan considered Norma overbearing and uppity — but they both knew the ‘feud’ was good copy, and so they helped it along.”

Things came to a delicious head when Crawford read lines with Shearer while engaging in her cacophonous hobby, knitting. Norma genteelly asked Joan to put away the clacking knitting needles, but the whole point was needling Norma, so Joan didn’t.

As the movie’s hair stylist, Sydney Guilaroff, recalled, “Crawford went home, drank six martinis and fired off a telegram to Norma informing her in no uncertain terms exactly what she thought of her.” At Cukor’s insistence, Crawford sent an apology telegram to Shearer, but she doubled down by listing all the slights she felt she had endured.

After that, Crawford bailed on the first day of shooting with Shearer, saying she had arsenic poisoning. She also skipped the cast luncheon after the film wrapped, sending word that she had ironing to do.
“So many people say Norma and I don’t like each other,” Crawford purred to the gossip columnist Hedda Hopper. “Who are we to disagree with the majority opinion?”

Cukor, who was known in Hollywood to be gay, had something to prove. He had recently been fired as the director of “Gone With the Wind” after Clark Gable fretted that his approach was too feminine, favoring Vivien Leigh.
“I thought it was kind of interesting that he got fired from ‘Gone with the Wind’ for being gay and then hired for ‘The Women’ because he was gay,” Douglas told me.

Rosalind Russell soared as Mary’s backbiting friend, playing the role as high camp. “I relate, obviously, to Rosalind Russell, who was stuck in these second leads, but she persisted,” said Douglas, who has played her share of supporting roles.

Tensions bristled between Russell and her fellow cast member Paulette Goddard, a longtime girlfriend of Charlie Chaplin who showed up at the soundstage each day in her custom Rolls-Royce. “There was no sisterhood,” Goddard said.

The mutual antipathy spilled over into what the producer Hunt Stromberg hailed as “the greatest catfight of all time,” a fight scene at a ranch in Reno, Nev., which escalated to the point that a doctor was called to patch up Goddard after Russell bit her.

It should have been a mere stage bite, Douglas writes, “but during one of the takes, Russell sank her teeth right into Goddard’s thigh. Loos, who was watching the scene, said, ‘Blood began dripping from her leg.’”
“The Women” was such a hit that studio suits began inserting cat fights in other movies, Douglas noted, saying, “‘Oh, it worked with Rosalind Russell. Let’s see Marlene Dietrich now!’”
Douglas added dryly: “You know, if Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock had had a catfight in ‘Practical Magic,’ it would have done so much better.”
Some people objected to Luce’s portrayal of women in “The Women.” Eleanor Roosevelt dismissed it as unpleasant.

But Douglas said she was relieved, when she saw screenings of the film with younger women, that they got into the fur-is-flying spirit and were not put off by female characters who devote so much energy to discussing husbands, ex-husbands and suitors. (The movie’s tag line was “It’s all about the men!”)

Douglas acknowledged that some women these days might be skeptical of a movie centered on female characters who talk so much about men. “But what should they be talking about?” she said. “Their diet?” And when you think about it, the girls in “Girls” and “Sex and the City” talk a lot about men, too.

“As soon as the leopard comes on and you see Joan Crawford, the audience starts laughing,” Douglas said. She added: “People seem to be relieved, like, ‘Oh, OK, we can just laugh at women all being bitches.’ ”

She said she follows the Elaine May rule, that there’s no point trying to disarm men who think you’re scary-smart by trying to be likable. (That’s where Hillary Clinton went wrong in her debate with a lurking Donald Trump; as she recently acknowledged, she should have just turned around and said, “Back up, you creep!”)
“You wrap yourself up like a pretzel trying to please people and navigate and then you can’t take it anymore,” Douglas said. “It’s better to just be unlikable from the get-go.”
She said that all the actresses in “The Women” “used the tools in their tool kit to scare the hell” out of Cukor and the producers.
“That’s why I wrote the whole book,” Douglas said. “But I think we’re so afraid of it because we want to be liked. But I absolutely know that you get more done with men if they’re afraid of you.”

She continued: “And, yes, people are going to dislike you. And, yes, unfortunately, a lot of times it’s women. ‘Who do you think you are, standing up for yourself?’ That’s what I do find a little odd in the female empowerment game — that we don’t celebrate other women becoming successful.

“I do think that women are way too sensitive to criticism. And that has ended many of my friendships.” Douglas said, adding, “Women will stop being friends with you simply because you confront them about something they did that hurt your feelings.”

Douglas made headlines in 2018 when she told Ronan Farrow of The New Yorker about being assaulted and retaliated against by Les Moonves, then the powerful head of CBS. Moonves admitted to trying to kiss Douglas in his office but denied her other allegations. He ended up losing his job and his severance after revelations by Douglas and other women.

“I was attacked by Les Moonves when I was doing a television show,” she recalled. “And, again, nobody talked about it, but it was something that everybody in my life knew, and we even sort of comically talked about it.
She added: “So I’m glad I stood up for myself. It was extremely cathartic.

She said that making her case against Moonves “did put the nail in the coffin of the predatory behavior at the top level.” But she added, “I don’t think that the #MeToo movement did anything for the relationships between men and women. If anything, it’s like men solidified, and women became terrified.”
She noted “an odd unnaturalness” between men and women in Hollywood meetings these days.
“There always is going to be that weird, awkward thing of, ‘Is she going to say I attacked her?’ or ‘Is he going to say … ?” she said.
Now she’s working on a book about Hollywood in the ’90s.

Back then, she recalled, “There was this environment where you were told to go in — the agents, the managers, everybody’s involved in it — you’re supposed to go in and wear a short skirt, and you’re supposed to flirt with the leading actor, to a certain extent, to get the part.”

The casting couch was installed on the first day of Hollywood. As Douglas writes in her book, Louis B. Mayer, the head of MGM, would tell Crawford he felt paternal toward her. “Mayer would always say, ‘I feel about you like I feel about one of my own daughters,’” Crawford said, “‘but usually, when he was saying it, he would have his hand on my tit.’”
Douglas said that when her grandfather got to MGM in the 1930s, “he said they gave you a list of people that you could take out to dinner, and then people you could have sex with.”
She felt that the #MeToo movement “did seem to be hijacked away from what the initial scream of pain was.”
“I’m like, wait a minute,” she said. “Can we focus? And so, part of the reason that I had friends who wanted me to come forward was to put it back on track to workplace harassment.”

Given the comebacks of several men in the entertainment industry who had been banished for sexual misconduct, and given the recent purging of women executives at studios, what is her advice for young women trying to make it in Hollywood?

“I think they should be a bitch right off the bat,” she said. “You don’t have to be mean. You don’t have to say, ‘Your hair is receding’ or anything like that. But I think that being very strong and very direct always works better.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/politics/steph.headline: What to Know About Stephen Miller, Trump’s New Chief of Staff

paragraphs.text: Stephen Miller is one of President Trump’s longest-serving and most influential aides, and the architect of many of the president’s most aggressive border and immigration policies. His rise to White House chief of staff elevates a hard-line policy adviser to a position of pre-eminent power and influence in Mr. Trump’s inner circle.

An unabashed champion of Mr. Trump and his agenda in high-profile media appearances, Mr. Miller rose to become a public face of the Trump administration — and a perennial target of critics of Mr. Trump, who have highlighted his right-wing views.

Mr. Trump did not explain his decision to fire Susie Wiles, his current chief of staff, and replace her with Mr. Miller, noting only that “Stephen’s been with me from the beginning” and was one of his most trusted advisers.

Mr. Miller, 41, has advised Mr. Trump for nearly a decade, and has either authored or significantly contributed to many of the president’s most high-profile moves. Those include separation of migrant families at the border; the 2017 Muslim travel ban; directing the government to stifle critics of Mr. Trump; the ending of nearly all U.S. refugee programs; the widespread pressure campaign against American universities; extrajudicial boat strikes that have killed hundreds; and purges of officials deemed insufficiently loyal to Mr. Trump.

But perhaps Mr. Miller’s most wide-reaching influence can be seen in Mr. Trump’s mass deportation campaign, which Mr. Miller has overseen. Mr. Miller helped set in motion militarized operations on the streets of American cities, pitting masked, heavily armed immigration agents against residents of cities like Minneapolis and Chicago.

Many of those raids have targeted immigrant communities that Mr. Trump has denigrated, including Somalis. Mr. Miller has also fixated on accusations that Somali-Americans have committed fraud and are spending public money on luxury cars, mansions and first-class travel.

Mr. Miller has earned Mr. Trump's trust by validating the president’s impulses and his worldview, particularly on immigration. Mr. Miller, once an aide to Senator Jeff Sessions, an immigration hard-liner, was drawn to Mr. Trump by his anti-immigrant rhetoric that dominated his 2016 presidential campaign. Mr. Trump, in turn, was impressed by his ideas on immigration policy and the fervor with which Mr. Miller would rile up crowds during campaign rallies and defend Mr. Trump in media appearances.
“I love watching him on television,” Mr. Trump said of Mr. Miller last year.

Republicans in Washington have said that they consider Mr. Miller to be channeling the president when he speaks. The two spent the four years that Mr. Trump was out of power speaking on nearly a daily basis, “talking about what a second term agenda might look like before many of us even dreamed that there would be a second term,” said Senator Jim Banks, Republican of Indiana.
Mr. Miller, who has now amassed considerable power in the second Trump administration, has continued to serve as a fiery surrogate for the president’s most divisive moves.

Earlier this year, as Mr. Trump publicly toyed with the idea of invading Greenland, Mr. Miller laid out a vision of American imperialism in which the United States could freely overthrow national governments and take foreign territory and resources so long as it was deemed in the national interest.

“We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else,” Mr. Miller told Jake Tapper of CNN. “But we live in a world, in the real world, Jake, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world since the beginning of time.”

Mr. Miller has also echoed Mr. Trump’s efforts to undermine the legitimacy of the federal judiciary. When judges blocked the president’s tariffs last year, Mr. Miller attacked the decision as a “judicial coup” on social media. He has also blasted other judges scrutinizing Trump administration policies as Marxists and “crazy” communists.

livemint.com/global/iran-war-threatens-r.headline: Iran war threatens record annual drop in global LNG supply, IEA says

paragraphs.text: Gas markets are facing a major squeeze, with liquefied-natural-gas output set for its steepest annual decline on record as the Iran war chokes off supplies and intensifies competition among importers, the International Energy Agency said.

Global LNG supply is forecast to fall by 3% this year, or nearly 20 billion cubic meters, as disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz—which used to carry around 20% of the world’s LNG flows—and Iranian attacks on key regional infrastructure sharply curtailed exports from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.

The forecast assumes that trade flows through Hormuz will remain largely disrupted at least until the end of the year, according to the Paris-based energy agency, which represents a group of Western nations and their allies.

Higher production elsewhere helped soften the blow. New projects in North America and Africa—along with increased gas supplies to existing LNG plants in Africa, Asia and Russia—pushed production outside the Persian Gulf up 14% between March and October. That made up for roughly two-thirds of the lost Gulf supplies.

Still, global LNG production fell around 6% during the war, the Paris-based agency said. The loss of supply is expected to intensify competition among buyers in the coming months, especially during periods of strong consumption.
European gas storage levels are a particular concern.

Storage sites across the European Union are entering the 2026-27 heating season with inventories at their lowest levels since 2013, increasing the region’s dependence on global LNG supplies to meet winter demand, the IEA said in its latest report on Tuesday.
In order to rebuild depleted reserves over the summer, Europe could also need to buy significantly more LNG, potentially keeping global supplies tight well into next year.

The supply shortfall comes as global gas demand is also expected to weaken this year, declining by around 1.5%, or close to 65 billion cubic meters, driven by demand destruction in the Middle East, lower industrial gas consumption in Europe and a shift from gas to coal in the power sector across several Asian countries.

For airlines in the United States, going bankrupt is practically a rite of passage. Since the airline industry was deregulated almost 50 years ago, dozens of airlines have filed for Chapter 11, including each of the so-called Big Three carriers—United, American, and Delta. A notable exception has been JetBlue, which until recently was one of the industry’s few success stories. But after The Wall Street Journal reported last month that the airline’s mounting debt obligations moved senior creditors to hire restructuring advisers, some investors began assuming that bankruptcy was on the way.

JetBlue’s CEO, Joanna Geraghty, insists otherwise. On the company’s most recent earnings call, in late October, she at least temporarily assuaged investor anxieties with claims that the airline was not at risk of going under, and was on track to return to profitability next year. Even so, JetBlue is undoubtedly struggling. The carrier has lost more than $3 billion since 2019, the last year it turned a full-year profit, and its debt load has risen swiftly to about $8.4 billion. The proximate cause of the company’s current woes is obvious: Fuel costs have soared since the Iran war began. But the challenge the company faces is more fundamental than that. JetBlue has been struggling because it finds itself in what’s sometimes called the “mushy middle,” caught between discount airlines on the low end and the big legacy carriers, which have lots of expense-account-wielding business travelers and lucrative transatlantic routes, on the high end.
[Read: An SNL sketch to make airlines feel ashamed]

When JetBlue began flying, in 2000, being in between was a strength: The company explicitly positioned itself as a stylish and plucky alternative to the ultra-low-cost carriers and the legacy carriers. It offered more legroom, good snacks, free satellite television, and leather seats to every customer, but still managed to be significantly cheaper than the big airlines. It was able to pull this off because its jet fleet was made up of only one type of plane, which kept maintenance costs down, and its workforce was not unionized. The carrier also initially offered just one class of seat, which helped it maximize space, even with the extra legroom.JetBlue’s marketing leaned into the idea that the company offered a new model for the industry, promising to “bring humanity back to air travel.” The carrier was so successful so quickly that legacy airlines tried to adopt this model for themselves: Delta and United started lower-cost, would-be JetBlue competitors in the 2000s, but both quickly failed. Meanwhile, JetBlue expanded its relatively low-cost, high-value offerings; in 2014, it launched a premium cabin for transcontinental routes called Mint, featuring lie-flat seats and fares well below those of the big carriers. By the late 2010s, it was the fifth-biggest airline in the country.

Over much of the past decade, though, that sweet spot in the market that JetBlue had made its own has shrunk. On the low end, new discount airlines have sprung up, offering no frills but also very cheap fares. On the higher end, the legacy carriers have gotten better at exploiting their lucrative revenue sources, jacking up prices on business travel and transatlantic routes, and using their giant customer bases to partner with credit-card companies willing to pay them billions.

JetBlue has found it hard to keep up. Even if the carrier had wanted to slash prices to compete with the discounters, its costs are now far too high for it to do so. Those jets that were brand-new when the company launched are aging, driving up maintenance costs, and its workforce began unionizing in 2014, driving up labor costs. (It also does not want to give up on the premium amenities that have made it so distinctive.) At the same time, JetBlue has struggled to compete with the legacy carriers for more profitable business travelers because most of its planes lack business- or first-class cabins, and the company doesn’t fly to nearly as many cities as the legacy carriers do. Nor has it been able to leverage its loyalty program, TrueBlue, the way the big carriers have leveraged theirs. TrueBlue will generate about $1 billion in revenue for the airline this year, which seems impressive until you realize that Delta makes more than $8 billion annually from the SkyMiles credit cards issued by American Express.
[Read: The only thing worse than Spirit Airlines]

These problems are in some respects specific to the airline industry. But JetBlue’s troubles are also emblematic of a basic fact about American business, which is that it has simply become harder for companies targeting the middle of the market to succeed. Traditional department stores such as Macy’s and Kohl’s have found themselves squeezed between big-box retailers and e-tailers such as Walmart, Target, and Amazon on the low end and premium retailers on the high end. Casual sit-down restaurants including Applebee’s and TGI Fridays have gotten edged out by fast-casual restaurants and fine dining. The disappearance of the American-made passenger car is also part of this story: Cars such as the Chrysler Sebring and the Chevy Malibu weren’t cheap enough, relative to their perceived level of quality, to compete with the perennially reliable Toyota Camry and Honda Accord, but they also weren’t fancy enough to compete with Lexus and Tesla. Consumers have become more price-conscious and are better informed about quality and cachet. So offering a pretty-good option at an almost-premium price doesn’t cut it anymore.

JetBlue is not doomed. It still has valuable assets, including most notably its brand, which remains surprisingly strong—even if it’s now doing many of the things that annoy people about traditional airlines, such as raising baggage fees. Its planes still have more legroom and free Wi-Fi. And next month, the carrier is going to be rolling out first-class cabins on many of its domestic routes, which should boost revenue. When fuel costs come down, the company may well turn a profit again. But being JetBlue is never going to be easy. It’s stuck in the middle, and these days, that’s the toughest place for a business to be.

phys.org/news/2026-11-diwali-celebration.headline: Diwali celebrations coincide with worsening air. Here's how to stay safer
phys.org/news/2026-11-diwali-celebration.author: Sibi Arasu

paragraphs.text: edited by Andrew Zinin
For people across South Asia, especially in northern India, Diwali celebrations coincide with the return of hazardous winter air, raising concerns about how to celebrate safely.

Winter also brings severe smog to parts of Pakistan and China, where warmer air can act as a lid, trapping colder air and pollution near the ground. In eastern Europe, burning coal and wood to heat homes also adds to winter pollution. Western Hemisphere countries, meanwhile, face their own seasonal air-quality problems, as summer wildfires send smoke across vast areas of the United States and Canada.

Experts say no matter where you live or when you face pollution, simple steps such as checking the air quality index, wearing a well-fitting mask and using air purifiers can reduce exposure to harmful pollutants.

An estimated 1 billion people worldwide celebrate Diwali, a holiday of Hindus and Jains with ties to ancient epics such as the Ramayana. Fireworks traditionally set off during the holiday, which starts Sunday, can make polluted air more dangerous.
As Diwali approaches, here are ways to reduce exposure to polluted air.
Check the air before heading out

Fireworks add a sharp burst of pollution to a much bigger problem. Across India, Pakistan and other parts of South Asia, traffic, factories, dust from construction and burning of crop residues and waste foul the air. Weak winds and stagnant winter air allow that pollution to build up.
"Poor air quality is our all-year-round problem in our country," said Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance. Narayan said firecrackers add to the problem.

India's air quality index turns pollution measurements into a health warning. AQI readings of 201–300 mean "poor," 301–400 "very poor" and 401–500 "severe." Severe levels can harm even healthy people.

Check pollution levels on government or privately run websites before heading outdoors. Look for data from a nearby monitoring station and the time of its last update. A citywide average can conceal a polluted neighborhood.

The problem is especially bad in Delhi, where fine particle pollution averaged about 19 times the World Health Organization's annual guideline last year. Air pollution monitors have reached the maximum reading they can display multiple times in recent years.

City authorities have responded with temporary construction, industrial and vehicle restrictions. Public health experts said such measures often fail to address the root causes. The city of more than 20 million people is also implementing a long-term plan to promote use of electric vehicles.
Make your mask fit

Dr. Arvind Kumar, a chest surgeon at Medanta hospital near Delhi and founder trustee of the Lung Care Foundation, recommends using properly fitted N95 or N99 masks outdoors during periods of heavy pollution. These masks are available at pharmacies, hardware stores and online retailers.
N95 filters are designed to capture at least 95% of airborne particles; N99 filters are made to capture at least 99%. The particle respirator masks do not filter harmful gases.

Cover your nose, mouth and chin. Shape the nose clip and check the seal every time. Facial hair can break that seal. The aim, Kumar said, is to ensure "all the breathing is through the mask and not around the mask."
Replace disposable masks when dirty, damaged or hard to breathe through. Never put a mask on a child younger than 2. People with heart or lung disease should seek medical advice about mask use.
Loose surgical masks, cloth masks and scarves offer unreliable protection against fine particles.

Kumar said pollution can cause persistent coughing, inflame the airways and trigger asthma-like attacks. He also cited increased risks of pneumonia, heart attacks and strokes, while linking prolonged exposure to impaired lung development in children and lung cancer.
Kumar said people should avoid strenuous exercise outdoors during heavy pollution, including early mornings, when pollution levels can be high.
Match the purifier to the room
Using the right air purifiers indoors can help. The devices draw in air to filter out pollutants, then recirculate the cleaner air.

A purifier needs enough capacity to clean the air of the room where it runs. Look for a high-efficiency particulate air, or HEPA, filter. Then check its clean air delivery rate, which is the volume of filtered air it supplies.
Place the purifier where you spend the most time, such as the bedroom. Keep its airflow clear and run it consistently.

HEPA filters trap particles. Substantial activated-carbon filters can remove some gases. No purifier removes every pollutant. Avoid machines that deliberately produce ozone, which irritates the lungs.
Cleaner indoor air reduces exposure, but a purifier cannot eliminate pollution's health risks, Kumar said.
Celebrate with less smoke

Kumar said it's important to avoid incense, mosquito coils and candles. Their particles can linger indoors for hours, especially in poorly ventilated rooms, while fireworks pollution can persist overnight, depending on the weather. When many households set off fireworks, their combined emissions can worsen air quality across neighborhoods and entire cities, exposing people who are not taking part. Electric lights can be another way to celebrate Diwali, avoiding toxic gases and smoke from firecrackers.
"If one wants to celebrate and really enjoy the festival of Diwali, avoid bursting firecrackers," said Narayan, the public health expert.
• A worker sweeps the area outside a construction site as authorities use water sprinklers to curb air pollution in New Delhi, India, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Credit: AP Photo/Manish Swarup
• Traffic moves through evening smog in New Delhi, India, as air quality across the capital region deteriorates ahead of winter, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Credit: AP Photo/Manish Swarup
• People light firecrackers to celebrate Diwali, the festival of lights, in Ahmedabad, India, Oct. 20, 2025. Credit: AP Photo/Ajit Solanki, File

India's health ministry also recommends reducing smoky cooking and using a kitchen exhaust that vents outdoors. Damp-mopping floors and wiping dusty surfaces, instead of dry sweeping, can avoid stirring up particles that worsen air quality.
Personal precautions have limits. Narayan said people who earn their livelihoods outdoors cannot simply stay home. Many families also cannot afford air purifiers.

She called for sustained action on pollution sources and affordable health care for those already suffering. Masks and filters can reduce exposure, but lasting protection requires governments to clean the air.
"It's our responsibility to hold our governments accountable," Narayan said. "There's no other way about it."
