npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-152225/princess-.headline: This teen boy set out to get people talking about periods. He's now a Diana honoree
npr.org/2026/11/07/g-s1-152225/princess-.author: Kamala Thiagarajan

paragraphs.text: Can a teenage boy change the way people think about menstruation?

At just 14, Aadvik Jain, studying in India's capital city, Delhi, set out to do exactly that. It all began when he had to watch a close friend struggle with debilitating menstrual pain that wasn't being taken seriously.

This year, he's among the 198 young people from 44 countries who were honored with the Diana Award, an international recognition for young changemakers working to improve lives in their communities. The awardees were announced on November 4 at a virtual ceremony streamed internationally.

Established in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales, the international award recognizes young people ages 16 to 25 for their social action and humanitarian efforts. This year, India accounted for nearly a quarter of the recipients, with 49 honorees.

Among them are Shiv Mandlik, who invented a bendable pole to help construction workers avoid working at dangerous heights and who developed an app to detect falls; Krish Aggarwal, who created an inexpensive filter that can be fitted onto ordinary fans to reduce indoor air pollution; and Kushal Sachdeva, who at age 11 began feeding a starving street dog. His organization, Protect Paws, has reportedly helped more than 1,500 stray dogs by arranging for medical treatment, vaccinations and reflective collars.

And then there's Jain. Now 18, he leads Team Period, an initiative he started in 2024 with three close friends. Together, they are challenging menstrual stigma through workshops, street performances, awareness campaigns and efforts to improve access to menstrual pads and products. He's also set to start studying medicine and public health at the University of Bologna in Italy in February.

NPR spoke to Jain through a video call about the experiences that inspired him, the challenge of persuading boys and men to join the conversation on periods and what he has learned about changing deeply entrenched attitudes.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
You were just 14 when you became concerned about menstrual health. What happened to make you realize that something needed to change?

It started with something that happened to a very close friend of mine in 2023, when we were in the tenth grade. We had been friends since the fifth grade. She used to call me her brother and would tie a rakhi every year [a sacred thread that girls tie around the wrist of a brother or brother-like figure, as a symbol of their bond, during the Indian festival of Raksha Bandhan].

During our midterm examinations, I noticed that she was struggling. She was in so much pain. I could not put a finger on it. What's happening? Does she have a fever? What's going on? So I checked in on her, and she said "I'm on my period, and I'm having really bad cramps." And then she just started crying. We took her to the medical room, where she was given a painkiller, and her parents were called to take her home. In India, menstruation is something that is very concealed. It's a very hush-hush topic. Not a lot of people talk about it openly in their families.

She had been experiencing severe cramps for six to eight months, and before that, her periods had been very irregular. But the next day, she was back in school, with the same pain. Her parents thought she was trying to get out of her examinations.
She is such a bright person, but for one or two weeks every month, she would become like a wilted rose. She couldn't concentrate in class or do well in her tests.
I went home and asked my mother what we could do. My mother spoke to our teacher, who contacted my friend's parents and encouraged them to take her to a doctor.

She was subsequently diagnosed with PCOS [now referred to as PMOS, or polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome], and doctors were also investigating the possibility of endometriosis. She received treatment, made changes to her lifestyle and gradually improved. She's so much better now, because of her own efforts, and because she got the help she needed at the right time.
That experience really stayed with me.
Why did her experience affect you so deeply?

I remember once breaking my little toe against the edge of my bed. My father left his office, which was two hours away, came home and took me to the emergency room. I had an X-ray, and my foot was bandaged.
I thought, what if we responded to menstrual pain with the same concern?
What if a girl could simply tell her father, "Dad, I'm having really bad cramps, and I can't go to school today," and he would say, "Okay, let me get you a heating pad"?
But because menstruation is such a hush-hush topic, especially around the men in a family, that kind of conversation often doesn't happen.
And sometimes, even the women in a family aren't able to support other women in the way they deserve.
I realized that this was something that needed attention.
How did that concern and empathy develop into Team Period?
I studied at Amity International School, and our school runs a program called Youth Power through its student newspaper, The Global Times. [the only registered school newspaper in India].

Schools form teams of four students, choose a social cause and spend several months working to create change in their communities. Then the schools compete with each other [to see who has the best ideas]. Our team consisted of me, Shivansh Arora, Aaratrika Jha Anand and Navya Manglik — so we're two boys and two girls.
Initially, Team Period began like any other school competition. We spent about six months working on the issue. But when the competition ended, I didn't want the work to end.

There is a certain feeling you get when you're talking to people, knowing that what you are saying matters, and maybe one day it could even change someone's life. But it wasn't just about that feeling. It was about the change we were creating at the grassroots level.

I have always been interested in public health, and I hope to work with an organization like the WHO or the United Nations one day. But as a 16- or 17-year-old, you can't just show up at the WHO and say you want to change things.
You have to start somewhere.
As a teenage boy, did you encounter resistance when you began talking about menstruation? Did girls ever accuse you of mansplaining?
Of course, people were surprised that a 15-year-old boy wanted to tackle menstrual shame.

But our friends were very supportive because we never approached the issue as experts. We approached it as learners. I never thought that I could explain what happens to a woman's body better than a woman herself.

At times, I was the face of the campaign. I was the spokesperson delivering speeches and talking to young women about menstruation. But it never came from a place of thinking that I knew more than they did. It came from a place of wanting to help solve a problem.

Everything we did was approached with empathy, sensitivity and respect. One girl might be completely comfortable talking about her periods in front of a classroom, while another might be deeply embarrassed.
Our goal is to end that shame, but we don't want to do it by shaming the person herself.
Were there moments when you realized that it might be harder than you thought to include boys in this conversation?
Yes. There was a workshop we organized at a school where the boys were asked to leave the room, so the girls could discuss these issues freely.
Initially, I was very upset because the whole point of our project was that boys should learn about menstruation, too.
But once the boys left, I saw girls who had been completely silent suddenly asking questions, laughing and speaking openly.
That was a learning experience for me.

Sometimes, girls need their own space to talk about these things. You can't force everyone to be comfortable immediately. We later held a separate session for the boys and eventually brought everyone together for a discussion. So at the end of the day, boys and girls were able to talk about it openly. I learned that creating an open environment is a process.
Can you describe an experience that convinced you your work was making a difference? Anything that really surprised you?
We once held an activity with middle-school students where we taught them to make simple heating pads using socks filled with lentils or chickpeas.

There was a boy, about 12 years old, who was very disruptive. He kept interrupting us and asking why he needed to learn about periods. His attitude was essentially that this had nothing to do with him. The teacher wanted to send him to another classroom, but we said no. We wanted him to stay and participate. About a year later, after I had finished school, I returned to visit my teachers and met that boy again.

He told me that his younger sister, who was barely 9 years old, had got her first period when they were alone at home. She was terrified. She had gone to the bathroom, seen the blood and started crying and screaming for help. But because of our workshop, he knew what was happening. He called his mother and asked where she kept the sanitary pads. He reassured his sister, helped her get cleaned up, made her a heating pad and even ordered chocolates for her.
By the time his mother returned, his sister was feeling much better.
He came up to me and thanked me. He said that when we first held the workshop, he couldn't understand why he needed to know any of this.
But when his sister needed help, he knew what to do. The fulfillment I felt in that moment was incomparable. To know that you've touched even one life is such a big honor.
You have used some unusual ways to get people talking about menstruation, including dance performances and flash mobs. How did those work?
We wanted to tackle menstrual shame from different directions, including through culture and performance.
One of our productions was a dance drama set during Durga Puja [a major Hindu festival honoring Goddess Durga's victory over a demon].

In the story, a young girl is performing the aarti [a Hindu ritual where a lamp is lit and prayers are offered] when her grandmother notices a menstrual stain on her clothes. The grandmother immediately excludes her from the prayers.

But Durga [the goddess] sees what has happened. She appears, comforts the girl and brings her back. I came up with the story, but the whole school helped put it together — the dance teachers, art teachers, costume designers, students and everyone involved in the production.
We performed it before an audience of more than 500 people in April 2025, and we've since performed or screened it at other events.
We also organized a flash mob at a mall and held activities at our school's winter carnival, where students, parents and grandparents participated in games about menstrual health.

One game involved picking colored chits containing questions about menstruation. People had only a short time to respond, which encouraged spontaneous answers instead of rehearsed ones. Sometimes a young boy would play, pick up a question and ask, all confused, "What is PCOS?"
We would stop the game and spend 10 minutes explaining it.
Our goal was to spark conversations.
You conducted surveys. Did this give you an insight into the way people think about menstruation?
We have been conducting surveys among students, parents and the wider community. At this point, we have collected around 4,000 responses.
One response that really struck us came from an eighth-grade girl.
She was angry that nobody cared if someone got a vegetable stain or ketchup on their clothes, but if a girl had a red menstrual stain on the back of her uniform, it became a huge issue.
Until then, our approach had been to teach boys to be sensitive — if a girl had a stain, you could quietly tell her or offer her your jacket.
But her response made us question that approach. Why should a menstrual stain be so embarrassing in the first place?
So we decided to normalize it.

We began wearing red stains on our uniforms. Some were stitched from red cloth, while others were stickers. At first, everyone laughed at us. Even the school objected because we were ruining the look of our uniforms with these big red patches.
But over the course of a week, more and more students joined in.
By the end, there was a sea of students wearing red stains. Some wore them on their backs, others on their shirts or identification cards.
When we conducted another survey months later, many students said they no longer felt that it was such a shame to spot or have a red stain.
We can't change attitudes across all of India immediately, but we were able to change something in our school.
In addition to changing attitudes and addressing stigma, what other aspects of menstrual care are you looking into?
There are several aspects to our work.

One is cultural — breaking down taboos and stigma. Another is logistical. How do you ensure that girls and women have access to menstrual products without feeling ashamed to ask for them? We installed a sanitary pad dispenser at our school.
Now we're talking to companies about how we could make dispensers available to other schools at a nominal cost. We are also exploring the possibility of developing our own design.

Disposal is another major issue. Used sanitary pads are often wrapped in newspaper and thrown into the garbage. But think about the people who sort that waste. How are they supposed to know what is inside the newspaper?

We're exploring a disposal system in which used pads can be sealed in specially designed bags, with clear warnings and illustrations in different languages. We want to think not just about the people using menstrual products but also those who handle the waste.
Your work has largely been concentrated in Delhi. Any plans to expand?
Until now, we've worked in government schools, orphanages, underserved neighborhoods and our own school in Delhi. We've also organized health camps.
But we were students, and our budgets were limited. We couldn't simply fly to Chennai or another city to replicate everything.
Now we want to decentralize Team Period and create local chapters.
Our team members are already spreading out to different cities and countries for their studies.
We'd like to bring in volunteers who speak different regional languages so that we can communicate more effectively with communities.
What does winning the Diana Award mean to you? Does it provide funding to help expand Team Period?
The Diana Award doesn't come with prize money.
But I think what it gives us is something equally valuable: recognition that our work matters.

When you're young and approaching potential sponsors or partners, people naturally have questions. They want to know whether you're legitimate and whether your work is making a difference. An international recognition like the Diana Award helps establish that credibility.
It gives us a platform to take our work to a larger audience.

For me, personally, it's deeply meaningful because we've faced moments when people questioned why boys were talking about menstruation. We've received strange looks from older people and even people of our own generation.
But this recognition tells us to keep showing up, even when things are difficult.

Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, South India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times , The British Medical Journal , the BBC, The Guardian and other outlets. You can find her on X: @Kamal_t.

Despite this week’s unseasonably warm weather, turning the clocks back is like shifting into winter gear. The sun peaces out at 4:45 p.m. as if saying, You don’t have to go home but you can’t stay here. And go home we do, helpless to disobey the darkness. Why are we eating dinner at 6 p.m.? Why this sudden urge to make soup? Where are my slippers?

The urge comes on strong to hibernate, to melt into layers of fleece and quilts. Here comes the cozy season — what will we watch and read, what about a hot cider or a hot buttered rum or something, anything, steaming in a mug? Warmblooded animals hibernate. Their body temperatures, heart rates, metabolism, all drop. Posted up in the burrow or the cave or the hollow tree — winter quarters known as the hibernaculum — they stay unconscious for weeks or months.

It’s a tempting model, but I’ve come to be skeptical of it for humans. Hibernating feels like comfort for those of us who see cold and dark as things to endure. But hibernation is missing an essential energy. Hunker too long and it can tip over into lethargy, detachment, a seasonal case of the blues.

If we want to indulge in the pleasure of indoor coziness without totally going to sleep, we might take inspiration from the wintertime behavior of coldblooded animals. Where woodchucks and bats hibernate, reptiles and amphibians brumate. Brumation also involves bodily functions’ slowing down to conserve energy. But brumating animals don’t go totally unconscious: A lizard might emerge on warm days to bask in the sun. A snake might have a drink of water.

“The most important distinction between brumation and hibernation is awareness,” is how a website that sells enclosures for reptiles explains it. “A hibernating animal is in a deep, continuous sleep and generally doesn’t wake until the season changes. A brumating reptile remains somewhat aware and responsive to their surroundings.”

What does it look like to remain aware and responsive as fall seeps into winter? It’s questioning the cues: Do I feel like staying in because it’s restorative, or am I shutting down early just because the sun did? It’s continuing to participate in the splendor of the world even if it’s icy outside.

If you have a tendency to go dark in the colder months, might I suggest acting a little more reptilian this year? We might slow down when winter comes, we might feel most comfortable in our own tree hollows, but we remain aware — aware of the way our energy and appetites shift as the light does; aware of the world inside and outside our hibernacula; aware that this winter, like all winters, is still a season of our lives that we don’t want to miss.
I’ll be on vacation for the next two Saturdays. See you after Thanksgiving. (I can’t believe it either.)
TRUMP’S NEW CHIEF OF STAFF

Days after the Republican rout in the midterm elections, President Trump ousted his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and replaced her with Stephen Miller, his policy adviser and architect of his controversial immigration crackdown.
Miller had been pitching himself for the job for weeks, saying he would advocate winding down the war in Iran.

There had been signs Wiles was on shaky ground with the president. He cut her out of some decisions, like picking a television pundit as his press secretary (which turned out to be a disaster). He also blamed her for Tuesday’s losses. On Friday, Trump told reporters that Wiles had done a “great job” but that “sometimes in life you have to make moves.”
Wiles, one of the most powerful figures in Trump’s orbit for years, is the latest in a wave of powerful women to leave his administration.
THE LATEST NEWS
• Scott Colom, the Democratic Senate nominee in Mississippi, held a slim but growing lead as the ballot counting continued.
• Young voters, alienated by Trump’s policies and an older generation of politicians, powered many of the Democratic victories this year.
• Prediction markets tout their accuracy. Did they pick the right midterm winners?
• After Texas flipped blue, Houston’s mayor told the city’s police officers to limit their cooperation with ICE.
• Voters in four states chose to bar transgender athletes from competing on female sports teams.
• The U.S. attorney who helped oversee Trump’s retribution campaign has resigned, adding to a list of abrupt departures from the Justice Department since Election Day.
Around the World
• Saudi-led forces bombed a home in northern Yemen, killing nine family members, five of them children, their relatives said.
• A Tanzania court sentenced the country’s main opposition leader to four years in prison. Human rights groups say the case is part of a pattern of repression.
• What was once a popular nightclub in Haiti is now a makeshift shelter for families fleeing gang violence. Click to watch.
• Employers in the United States added 165,000 jobs in October, and the overall unemployment rate fell. (Is A.I. boosting the job market?)
• The Cornell faculty senate passed a resolution of no confidence in the school’s administration, urging change in how the university handles sexual assault.
• The U.S. experienced the largest drop in homelessness last year since an annual count began nearly two decades ago.
GAME OF THE WEEK

College football rivalry: Can Michigan State football find its way out of its deepest hole ever? The Spartans are rocking an embarrassing 2-6 record. In their home conference, where the team has played its worst stretch of football in almost 75 years, it’s 0-5. Tonight at 7:30 p.m., Michigan State faces off against its rival, the University of Michigan Wolverines, who are 5-3 (2-3 in their conference).

There will be a parallel competition on the sidelines that scientific researchers are calling “The Piss Off.” For a project across both campuses, researchers will collect urine from tailgaters, pasteurize it and isolate nutrients for use in fertilizer pellets. So fans should feel free to have another beer! — Evan Gorelick
THE WEEK IN CULTURE
Film and TV
• Close-up shots of Elizabeth Holmes, Nathan Fielder and Billy Evans give “You Can See Everything” its signature look. Our film critic asks: What do their faces say?
• Jordan Firstman, known as an Instagram troublemaker, becomes a sentimental filmmaker with his debut feature, “Club Kid.”
• The Canadian sketch show “SCTV,” whose archives are now available on Netflix, featured a murderer’s row of comedians like John Candy and Catherine O’Hara. Our critic explains what made it so funny.
• Sometimes, Dominic Fike sounds like Weezer, or like John Mayer and Jack Johnson. Other times, he raps. Is the mess part of his appeal? Listen to his interview on “Popcast.”
• The composer John Luther Adams, long attracted to extreme environments, left the U.S. for inspiration in the arid heart of Australia.
• “The Nutcracker” has entered virtual reality: Audience members in Detroit watched the ballet on a borderless, 87-foot-diameter LED dome.
• The Booker Prize will be announced on Monday. See the nominated novels, and vote for your favorite.
• Lucien Smith, the young artist who skyrocketed to fame before his death this year, died from an accidental drug overdose, the New York City medical examiner’s office said.
RECIPE OF THE WEEK
Crispy Tofu Tacos

Alexa Weibel’s deeply spiced crispy tofu tacos are a masterpiece — fragrant and savory, with heft and crunch. The tofu crumbles are versatile, too. You can skip the tacos and spoon them over rice or sprinkle them onto salads. The key is to really let the grated tofu bits roast until the sizzle is audible. That’s when you know the crunch will be, too.
REAL ESTATE
The Hunt: She loved her Brooklyn apartment, but there wasn’t much nature nearby. What did she find for $500,000 in the Catskills?
What you get for $1.5 million around Cuernavaca, Mexico: A four-bedroom in Palmira, a contemporary home in Chapultepec or a Mexican colonial in Acapantzingo.
Calculator: How old will I be before I own a home?
LIVING
Snowfall effect: A super El Niño is here. What does that mean for skiing?
First-lady-worthy: Whom did Rama Duwaji, Zohran Mamdani’s wife, DM for a haircut?
Never left: Long after the pandemic, people are still using weekend and seasonal homes year-round.
ADVICE FROM WIRECUTTER
Order your Thanksgiving turkey in the mail

Yes, you can outsource your holiday bird. My advice, in fact, is that you do. A good smoked turkey — we found several in our taste-testing — can be a delightfully tender and wonderfully juicy centerpiece. All of the Rockwellian vibes, close to zero work. You’re not babysitting a bird all day, which frees up more time to go all out on sides and desserts. Because it arrives fully cooked, this turkey won’t hog oven space, nor require you to maneuver around a raw bird brining in the fridge. Maybe best of all, it gives you scrumptious, smoky leftovers for gumbo, my family’s favorite tradition. Just make sure you give yourself plenty of time for shipping, plus an additional day or two to let it thaw. Another shortcut? One of these actually good store-bought pie crusts. — Abigail Bailey

nytimes.com/2026/11/07/us/turning-point-.headline: Turning Point Bet on the Midterms and Lost. Some Republicans Are Furious.

paragraphs.text: Turning Point USA bet big on Arizona.
Leaders of the right-wing activist organization founded by Charlie Kirk said the state’s contest for governor was “the most important race in America.”

The group’s handpicked candidate, Representative Andy Biggs, a MAGA-aligned Republican, was one of the last politicians Mr. Kirk personally endorsed before his assassination last year. Its political arm spent nearly $20 million to support Mr. Biggs’s campaign.
But on Tuesday, Turning Point’s bet went bust.

In the group’s home state, where registered Republicans outnumber Democrats, Mr. Biggs lost to Gov. Katie Hobbs by more than 10 percentage points, and Democrats thumped Turning Point’s chosen candidates for statewide and congressional races. The same happened in Nevada and New Hampshire, states where the group hoped to build conservative power and lay a foundation for the 2028 presidential contest.

Instead of vindicating a polarizing organization that has pitched itself as the future of the G.O.P., Tuesday’s results set off recriminations from establishment Republicans who have been exiled by Turning Point’s political machine.

“Turning Point is driving us to extinction,” said Gina Swoboda, the former Arizona Republican Party chairwoman who has feuded with the group. “They have become a destructive force in Republican politics.”

In the days since Republicans’ blowout loss, Turning Point leaders have been left to sift through the rubble of the “red wall” they had pledged to build in Arizona, Nevada and New Hampshire, states they view as critical battlegrounds. Despite the group’s significant investment, the only high-profile candidate in those three states who won with its backing was Kelly Ayotte, the incumbent governor of New Hampshire.

Turning Point and its allies have defended the group’s strategy, blaming Republican losses on a brutal national political environment stemming from President Trump’s deeply unpopular war with Iran. And they note that many other Republican candidates who ran without Turning Point’s backing lost by similar margins.

“I think it’s clear that we were up against a national wave that impacted every state,” Andrew Kolvet, Turning Point’s spokesman, said in a statement. “One of the mistakes you can make after a result like we had Tuesday is to learn the wrong lessons. Any suggestion that a more moderate candidate would have fared better is plain wrong.”

In a social media post, Erika Kirk, Mr. Kirk’s widow and Turning Point’s chief executive, said it was clear voters were “concerned about the state of the economy and the war in Iran.” The group’s leaders, she said, were poring over election results and would “spend the next two years making the case for how conservative, free market solutions, and a renewed focus on our country’s founding principles can address the problems the American people face.”

Turning Point, which is headquartered in Phoenix, has thousands of chapters at high schools and college campuses across the country, but its leadership has long considered Arizona to be the most important battleground for setting up national Republican victories. The group has honed its get-out-the-vote operations there and worked to remake the state’s G.O.P. in its image, championing hard-right primary challengers while muscling out the type of moderate Republicans exemplified by the late Senator John McCain.

But Arizona’s general election voters have repeatedly passed over Turning Point-supported candidates like Kari Lake and Blake Masters, allowing Democrats to take control of most major statewide offices and both U.S. Senate seats, even as Mr. Trump won the state in 2024.

This year, some Republicans warned that Turning Point had not learned from past mistakes. One misstep came in April, when the group’s unusual involvement in an obscure public utility election prompted a backlash that allowed a slate of liberal candidates to triumph.
And as the midterms approached, Turning Point elevated some candidates despite warnings from fellow Republicans that most voters would see them as too extreme.

The group’s operatives helped clear the primary field for Mr. Biggs by relentlessly attacking his chief competitor, the more moderate Karrin Taylor Robson, who dropped out early in the race after lagging in polls.

And Turning Point sparred publicly with Ms. Swoboda, who first planned to run in one of the state’s most competitive House districts before pivoting to an unsuccessful bid for secretary of state. Turning Point worked against her in each primary contest.

Both of the group’s favored candidates in those races lost on Tuesday — Jay Feely, a former N.F.L. kicker, for Arizona’s First Congressional District, and Alexander Kolodin, an election-denying lawmaker, for secretary of state.

Ms. Swoboda and other longtime Turning Point opponents could barely contain their schadenfreude this week. She likened the group’s relationship to the Republican Party as akin to “a parasite on a host.”

“It’d be one thing if you were a parasite that could function in a symbiotic way,” Ms. Swoboda said. “But if you’re a tick that keeps sucking on a host until the host is dead, then you’re useless and a negative.”
Some Turning Point critics argue that more moderate candidates would have performed better. Others struggled to think of a Republican who could have withstood the blue tide that swept the country.

“It might be satisfying to me to say Turning Point snatched defeat from jaws of victory,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican and former Maricopa County recorder who lost his 2024 primary to a candidate backed by Turning Point. But, he said, “President Trump owns this loss.”
Still, Mr. Richer said, Turning Point has “missed the message” several cycles in a row.
Mr. Kolvet said those denouncing Turning Point were “irrelevant, disgruntled local political malcontents.”
But even some Republican base voters have grown tired of the combative political environment the group has fostered.

“This whole nonsense about insulting other conservatives because they don’t agree 100 percent with their views is really dumb, and it’s cost us dearly here,” Tom Abood, a real estate developer who has voted for Mr. Trump three times, said after casting his ballot for Republicans on Tuesday in the suburb of Paradise Valley. “It should be an easy slam dunk win in this state.”
On the day after the election, Turning Point staff members arrived early at their office near the foothills of Phoenix’s South Mountain Preserve to take stock.

The shift to Democrats among young men — who had moved sharply right in 2024 — was especially concerning, said Alex Clark, who hosts a health and wellness podcast for Turning Point and was at the office that day.

College-age voters should be the group’s top priority going forward, Ms. Clark said, and Turning Point should invest in more polling on campuses to keep tabs on the constituency before it drifts further left.
“That should be a really sobering reality for the G.O.P., that if you do not work to rebuild trust with these voters by 2028, you will have built a super-Democrat party,” Ms. Clark said.

Mrs. Kirk has already endorsed Vice President JD Vance for president in 2028. But Ms. Clark said Turning Point would be wise not to tie itself too closely to any one president. The group should promote conservative values while remaining neutral in 2028 and beyond, she said.
“The base could turn on a president, conservative or not, at any time,” Ms. Clark said. “You don’t want to be stuck in the middle of that.”
The group’s leaders say they plan to analyze state-level polling, redouble their efforts on college campuses and strategize about how to best allocate their resources ahead of 2028.

Sean Noble, who was Mr. Biggs’s top campaign strategist, saw a silver lining for Turning Point in the sweeping Republican defeat. The group now has a chance to become the leading voice of resistance to new Democratic leadership on Capitol Hill, he said. Mr. Noble compared the moment to the early 1990s, when Rush Limbaugh surged in popularity and became a hero to grass-roots conservatives.
“One of the best things that could have happened for Turning Point,” Mr. Noble said, “is they now have the foil of Democrats in charge of Congress.”

fortune.com/2026/11/07/wall-street-banks.headline: Wall Street banks brace for ‘political theater’ as Democrats return to power—but few expect major change anytime soon
fortune.com/2026/11/07/wall-street-banks.author: Morgan Chittum

paragraphs.text: The giant blue wave that swept Congress this week has left Democrats in a celebratory mood. The vibe on Wall Street, however, is less upbeat as lawmakers like Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), who have expressed pointed hostility towards the financial industry, prepare to wield oversight power. This would seem to bode ill for behemoths like JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. But the banks can take comfort in the view of analysts and legal experts, who say that the fallout from the mid-term election is likely to amount to little more than “political theater” and public shaming—at least for now.

For Wall Street, the first signs of the new political order are already appearing. Just days after the election, CNBC reported that Senate Democrats are gearing up to investigate JPMorgan for the bank’s relationship with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, citing a source familiar with the matter. JPMorgan declined Fortune’s request for comment on the matter.
Before that, on the same evening that polls closed, Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat who is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee, posted a simple message on X: “Subpoenas.”
It was a one-word preview of the scrutiny Wall Street could face when Democrats take control early next year.
“I think there’s going to be a tremendous amount of political theater,” Joann Needleman, head of the financial services regulatory and compliance practice at law firm Clark Hill, told Fortune.

That could mean subpoenas, investigations, hearings, and more strongly worded letters demanding answers from top executives. Among the lawmakers expected to lead that charge is Warren, who is widely expected to become the new chair of the powerful Senate Banking Committee.

“Elizabeth Warren is going to bring all of these firms in and talk about all the billions that they’ve made and all the things that they have charged consumers,” Needleman said. “The bigger banks will just be called in and be put to shame by various committees that want to inquire about them.”

Warren has already shown how aggressively she is willing to challenge the financial industry. She has previously called for criminal probes into banking execs, described the private-equity industry as legal “looting” and even written a bill that could make it easier to prosecute executives. Longtime Wall Street watchers, though, say any upcoming investigations or oversight hearings are par for the course.
“The people who were elected have mandates, and you have to expect them to follow through on those mandates,” said Mike Mayo, Wells Fargo’s head of U.S. large-cap bank research.
But that doesn’t mean all of this will result in significant disruption to how the big banks operate on a day-to-day level.

“We could certainly see tougher language, more congressional hearings, and increased scrutiny of industries … but translating that rhetoric into meaningful legislation is an entirely different challenge,” Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management, said in a statement to Fortune.

After all, President Donald Trump still has veto power. Plus, financial regulators such as the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency remain under Trump-appointed leadership. Those agencies still have the authority to enforce the rules for banks, so a change in the congressional majority would not reverse the administration’s agenda.

Wall Street has already benefited massively from Trump’s second term in the White House. The FDIC rolled back Biden-era merger policies, making it easier for big banks to facilitate megadeals. Regulators have also relaxed key capital constraints, giving banks greater flexibility to deploy their balance sheets.

“The legislative leaders, at a minimum, have a full pulpit to relay their messages,” Mayo, who started his career as a bank analyst at the Federal Reserve, told Fortune. “The degree that those messages translate to actual laws or regulations is a lot less. So I think it’s a matter of setting a tone, or the pace and degree of deregulation, as opposed to changing the direction.”

Citi analyst Ben Gerlinger echoed that view. “They can subpoena companies. They can bring in management. But it really, frankly, can’t change their business models too much without a regulatory agency being that acting figure,” Gerlinger told Fortune. “They can make life difficult, but they can’t necessarily change the overall tenor of where the banks are projected to go.”
“But at the end of the day, earnings drive banks,” he added. “I think earnings are still in a really good spot, in addition to capital levels.”
If the blue wave outlasts Trump and brings new regulators to Washington, that’s a different story—but not one for today.

cnbc.com/2026/11/07/snap-social-media-te.headline: Tech companies face mounting child safety lawsuits while pushing AI into schools
cnbc.com/2026/11/07/snap-social-media-te.author: Jonathan Vanian

paragraphs.text: Tech companies have spent years telling parents they're working to make their products safer for children. But ongoing jury trials, settlements and related litigation against the likes of Meta, Google and Snap suggest that they're not doing enough.

The latest examples landed this week. Snap confidentially settled a case claiming that its technology caused severe psychological distress to two teenage users. Meta, TikTok and YouTube previously settled with the plaintiffs in the same suit. And Google was sued this week by the parents of a child who allegedly suffered a psychological crisis after chatting with the Gemini AI chatbot in Google Classroom.

Concern is intensifying as artificial intelligence companies pursue trillion-dollar valuations, and established internet giants pour money into developing advanced AI models while pushing them into the classroom. Products and features intended to maximize engagement can have detrimental effects on users, thus warranting "broader systemic changes in tech design, particularly when children are using them," said developmental psychologist Kate Blocker.

"I think it's so so important that children's safety is being considered when these products — AI, social media, et cetera — are being designed, and not after the fact as these problems emerge," said Blocker, the director of research and programs for the nonprofit Children and Screens.

Snap's settlement this week, which spared CEO Evan Spiegel from testifying in a Los Angeles court, continues a general trend of tech companies attempting to shield themselves from public scrutiny due to the various high-profile child-safety related trials this year, said Joseph McNally, the director of emerging litigation at McNicholas & McNicholas.
The case was one of several lawsuits related to the social media personal injury trial that Meta and YouTube lost earlier this year. More trials are slated to commence in March.

"I view this settlement and the other settlements in this space as an effort by tech companies to turn a corner, not only because I think that there were real legal challenges, but also the reputation of their products, the reputation of their companies has really been hit," said McNally, a former acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California.
"The parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner," a Snap spokesperson said in a statement.

"We've built safeguards, launched safety tutorials, and partnered with experts and because safety is never finished, we remain committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community," the Snap spokesperson said.

But there remains a federal case involving Meta, TikTok, Snap and YouTube and a litany of nationwide school districts, along with various state attorneys general suits. In August, Meta agreed to pay nearly $17 billion to settle with a group of state AGs in a child mental health case. Some AGs are still pursuing similar suits against Meta's rivals.
The social media lawsuits have helped inform parents and the public about how the industry designs products used by teenagers and children, McNally said.
"It's the technology arms race that continues," he said. "What is oftentimes missing is how you balance that participation in the arms race with utility and then product safety."
More scrutiny in the classroom

Google ran into more criticism this week for moving too fast. The New York Times reported on Tuesday that K-12 schools that don't allow use of Google's AI tools for students will lose access to search. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that, "Search and AI are deeply integrated."

That coincided with the new lawsuit against Google centering on a teen's alleged suicidal crisis that the parents attributed to the company's Gemini AI. The plaintiff's attorneys allege that "despite Gemini's known risks, Google hastily integrated" Gemini into Chromebook computers for school children.

"We are reviewing the claims in the lawsuit and we take this very seriously," a Google spokesperson said in a statement. "We've worked extensively with medical professionals and academic experts to build features that help young people find critical support and trusted resources when they need it."
Google and its internet peers have for decades been able to rely on Section 230.

Passed in 1996, the federal legislation has protected social media companies from being sued over content posted by their users. That's why plaintiffs' attorneys and state AGs have been focused on alleged harms stemming from the design of the tech platforms as opposed to their content.

Some plaintiffs are using the same tactics against AI companies. OpenAI faces several lawsuits from state AGs and plaintiff attorneys, taking cues from the social media suits in alleging that the design of ChatGPT can pose risks to children.

The litigation could become a growing financial risk as the company plans for a potential blockbuster IPO. OpenAI competitor Anthropic, which is planning to go public this month, highlighted the issue in its prospectus, even though the Claude creator prohibits children from using its product.
"This is a clear indication that tech companies anticipate more litigation risks than they did a decade ago," said Michele Neitz, a professor at the University of San Francisco School of Law.

Blocker said that the highly personalized nature of current AI-powered chat apps makes it "a little bit unpredictable" to determine exactly what the apps will say to kids. She stressed the importance of testing and evaluating these products for children's developmental safety from the start, "not after harms start happening."
This collective litigation has helped educate the public on the potential pitfalls of poor product design choices, Blocker said. And it could be a catalyzing force for change in the tech industry.
"Certainly there's a hope that this will motivate real systemic change, both from a regulation standpoint and internal company decision-making standpoint," Blocker said.
If you are having suicidal thoughts or are in distress, contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 for support and assistance from a trained counselor.

infohawk.com/news/2026-11-05-scamwich-re.headline: Scamwich: Inside a Restaurant Delivery Payment-Skimming Campaign

paragraphs.text: When customers order food online, they expect a familiar experience: find their restaurant, choose their meal, and pay. Increasingly, criminals are exploiting that familiarity by creating convincing clones of restaurant ordering websites, right down to the original site's underlying code.

In early November 2026, InfoHawk researchers investigated a collection of suspicious websites that appear to be part of one or more coordinated restaurant impersonation and payment-skimming operations.
Across two research passes, we identified 820 domains impersonating 35 restaurant brands. Of those, 808 use the .delivery top-level domain, and the rest use .com or .shop.
The scale is concerning, but what makes these sites particularly dangerous is how convincing they can be.
These aren't ordinary fake websites
The investigation began with a suspicious domain: mlckessejersstey[.]delivery.
The site impersonated Jersey Mike's, the popular sandwich chain, and reproduced its online ordering experience.

Rather than simply displaying a crude imitation of the restaurant's website, the attackers used a more sophisticated approach: reverse-proxying the legitimate site while replacing the checkout payment form with a malicious one.

A reverse proxy can retrieve content from a legitimate website and present it to visitors under a different domain. This allows an attacker-controlled site to display genuine pages and assets while selectively modifying the parts of the experience that matter to the attacker.
In this case, the malicious checkout requested credit card information and also asked customers for the SMS verification code sent by their bank.

This is a particularly dangerous combination. Capturing a credit card number is valuable to criminals; obtaining a one-time verification code could also help them authorize fraudulent transactions, depending on how the victim's bank uses that code.

For consumers, the experience can appear nearly indistinguishable from ordering directly from the restaurant. The site looks familiar, the menu and ordering flow can behave normally, and the fraudulent payment form appears at the moment a customer expects to pay.

Importantly, this does not require the legitimate restaurant's website to have been hacked. The attackers can operate on infrastructure they control while using the authentic restaurant website as the source of the content they display.
Impersonated brands

Mostly .delivery typosquats, plus a few look-alike .com and .shop names, found across two research passes. "Seen" is the range of registration or scan dates we have for a brand's domains, all in 2026. Open a brand to see its domains.

How the attack works

Each clone is a reverse proxy: a server that sits between the victim and the real restaurant site, fetches every page from the real site as it is requested, edits it on the way through, and passes it on. Menus, prices, store hours, and the cart are live and correct, because they come from the real site. Only the payment step is replaced. Described from mlckessejersstey[.]delivery (Jersey Mike's); we believe the clones of the other brands run the same kit.

• The victim arrives from a search ad A Google Search ad imitates the restaurant's listing and shows a look-alike domain. The domain is behind Cloudflare, so its real server is hidden, and Cloudflare gives it a valid certificate automatically (Google Trust Services here), so the browser shows "Connection is secure".

• Every page is fetched live from the real site The proxy forwards each request to the restaurant's own servers, adjusting the host name and cookies, and relays the answer. The real site's headers come through (on Jersey Mike's, x-powered-by: Nuxt and Amazon CloudFront headers), which is how we could tell which paths came from the real site and which from the scammer's server.

• Addresses are rewritten to keep the victim on the fake domain The proxy replaces the brand's own host names in pages, scripts, and redirects with the fake domain, and maps each backend to a path on it, such as /__bapi__/ or /__payments__/. Store lookup, menus, login, and cart all work, because those calls go back through the proxy to the real APIs. Even the brand's own bot-detection script still runs, with its endpoints rewritten.

• Three scripts are injected into every page A script blocker patches HTMLScriptElement.prototype.src so that listed scripts never load (on Jersey Mike's, the OneTrust cookie banner and Branch, which could send phone users to the app or the real domain). _jmu() finds the real checkout payment frame and points it at /js/index.html on the fake domain; a MutationObserver puts the fake one back whenever the page restores the real one. _chkT() reads the order total from the "Place order" button every half second and saves it, so the fake form shows the right amount.

• The card form is the scammer's A few paths are answered by the scammer's server instead of the real site: /js/* (the card form and its scripts) and /payment/socket.io. The form looks like part of checkout. On submit it collects every field (card number, expiry, CVV, name, phone) and sends it, with the site name, to the operator over a live socket.io connection.

• An operator gets past the bank's check live We believe a person watching a control panel uses the card elsewhere and, when the bank challenges that payment, tells the victim's page what to show next: "card declined, try another", a page asking for the SMS code (/js/confirmation/), an "approve in your bank app" page (/js/app/), or "invalid code, try again". We believe the code the victim types is what lets the operator's charge through 3-D Secure.

• The victim is sent away When the operator marks it a success, the page sets a cookie valid=77777 lasting until 2038 and sends the victim to another chain's real site (href.li/?https://www.jimmyjohns.com/; href.li hides where they came from). No order reaches the restaurant: the real payment step never runs, so there is no confirmation email and no food. We believe the victim's card is then charged for whatever the operator bought.

Why this design. The clone never goes out of date, the victim builds a real order with a real total before anything looks wrong, and one kit works against any restaurant by changing the target site, the domain, and a few path rules. The scammer's server does very little work, which makes it cheap to move. Some variants skip the payment wording and only pin the frame's address, re-setting it every time the page changes it.
Distribution of the Delivery Scam

Searching Google's ad archive (Ads Transparency Center) for the domains in our first sweep found at least 47 Google Search text ads between July 7, 2026, and October 20, 2026, run under at least 46 separate advertiser accounts with at least 43 different, unrelated-looking business names (construction firms, a reptile rescue, a watch company). The ads below are a sub-sample: we searched only for the domains in our first sweep, so there are likely more. Each ad imitates a restaurant's search listing and shows a look-alike domain. Most ran for 1–4 days, usually starting days after the domain was registered.

Status: On November 4, 2026, 367 of the 820 domains still served a site, so they could be getting traffic through means other than ads. None of the ads below were still running on November 3, 2026, but this scam may also be running through other ads, or other means. Google's public Ads Transparency pages now show "Can't find ad" for the creatives and "No ads found" for the domains we checked, which suggests Google has taken them down; the "Ads Transparency page" links below will likely not load. The images and text here come from InfoHawk's own capture of Google's archive, made on or before November 3, 2026. Of the 47 ads below, 41 have Google's rendered image; the rest show the text from Google's ad preview. Domains in the image ads were read from the image and may contain small reading errors.
Hosting

Most of the clones sit behind Cloudflare (AS13335), which hides the real servers: 761 of the 820 domains use Cloudflare nameservers, 11 use other nameservers, and 48 have none. Another cluster of 68 domains is tied to an Amazon Web Services (AWS) server. Some of its sites are served straight from that server, in Frankfurt (3.79.192.101) through my-ndns.com nameservers, and its pages carry a different injected script (/static/<name>-fix.js). It uses the same cloning technique, but we found nothing that shows the same people run it, so these sites may come from more than one operator using the same kit.
In our first sweep of 255 domains, 251 were registered at Dynadot, spread across 111 Cloudflare nameserver pairs.
What this means for restaurant brands

These clones don't need to break into a restaurant's systems. They borrow the real site, page by page, and insert the attack only at the moment a customer pays. That makes them hard to spot from the outside, but it also means the brand's own servers see every page the clone serves. Brands and their ordering providers that watch for their site loading under someone else's domain, or for checkout sessions that never reach the real payment provider, are well placed to catch these sites early.
Is your brand being cloned? Let's find out.

bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cmy4x9.headline: JJ Gabriel: Manchester United forward says 'my dream is to win Ballon d'Or'
bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cmy4x9.author: Ben Ramsdale

paragraphs.text: The 16-year-old is still registered at United but has been training on his own in Spain after walking out on the club and relocating with his family.
He has subsequently reached a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid but no deal has been signed as yet.

On Friday, following one of his sessions, the teenager was approached by Spanish news outlet Marca who presented him with a copy of their newspaper, which featured a front-page story about his expected move to Los Blancos.
The newspaper reported he told them in English: "My dream is to win a Ballon d'Or."
United would be due compensation should Gabriel leave, although the figure will be lower if he signs for a club outside the Premier League.
Though no club-to-club talks have been held, sources have told BBC Sport that Real have verbally agreed a deal with Gabriel and his representatives.
Gabriel, who scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut, has secured a European Union passport, which is expected to make it easier for him to sign for a club outside England.
He was named the Premier League's Under-18 player of the season last term, despite being only 14 when the season began.

theatlantic.com/newsletters/2026/11/mike.headline: Mike Johnson Will Tend To Your Lawn Now

paragraphs.text: “Heaven forbid, if we lose this majority or whatever, I don’t know what my next chapter of life is, I’m just open to it. And if God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I’ll do that with equal fervor. I mean, I just want to be of my highest and best use to God and to my country.” — Mike Johnson, to Fox News’s Aishah Hasnie

Mike Johnson finished his circuit of the lawn on his riding mower, dismounted, and stared at the tree. It was an old tree, large and ornamental. Yet something about the branches was wrong. But what? If only he could ask Donald Trump for advice!

No—this was his new job, his lawn-care business. It was going to be a lot more work than he had anticipated. There should be more jobs like speaker of the House, without any major responsibilities except to sit at the feet of the president and gaze at him in silent adoration. Now Johnson felt like he was working all the time. And, worse, he had to direct his own activities.

But after losing the majority, he had been left with no choice. He could not seek election to the minority leadership. Minority leadership? That smacked of DEI. The lawns of Shreveport needed him, and he would answer.
The biggest question had been what to call the business. Finally, he decided on Mike Johnson Total Landscaping, an homage to his former patron.

It was hard to figure out how to begin without Trump’s guiding hand. He knew some things about Trump’s attitude toward lawns, but not all. Grass, he knew, had a life, like people. And trees were bad. Trees were the enemy. To cut down 400 trees as quickly as possible was a great act. Pools were generally good—some, but not others. He had made notes of all of this, but there were still so many blanks to fill in. Were grassroots movements good or bad? How could you tell if something was a weed? It was hard to think for himself after so many months out of practice.

Occasionally he thought of the time when he had been speaker of the House. What a strange time! It almost felt like a dream. What a strange job, too. He had understood that the speaker of the House was third in line to the presidency, and therefore it behooved him to remain in careful seclusion from any kind of disturbing news, so that if he were called upon to serve, he would be rested and ready. Yet people were always asking him frustrating questions, as though he were meant to be keeping up on things, approving or disapproving of events, or even taking an active role in them. But he had known better: His purpose was to serve the president. Such a funny title, given that! “Speaker of the House.” He wondered what house it was. The White House, maybe.

Since leaving that role, he’d had much more time to catch up on news. Astounding how much had happened in the country since he left Shreveport! He had been wondering why he saw so few other landscapers. He heard from his friends at Greenwater Services that there had been some roving gangs of masked men making people frightened to leave home. He also heard that there was a war of some kind? Gasoline was certainly expensive, but he had to keep his mower running somehow.
Now that he had finally caught up on all the news, he’d started listening to a book on tape: the U.S. Constitution. What he’d learned disturbed him.
“Did you know about this?” he had asked his wife, at the end of his first day trimming hedges.
“What?”
“Apparently, there are three equal branches of government. Congress is actually the first one mentioned. Before the president, even. Article I!” He frowned. “I had no idea. Equal branches.”
“What do you think it means?” she said. She sounded worried.
He’d kept listening. “Did you know?” he said, the next afternoon. “The leader of that equal branch of government—do you know what that job is called?”
She shook her head.
“The speaker of the House,” he said. “Isn’t that funny?”
She frowned. “But that’s the same name as your old job,” she said.
It was a strange coincidence, he thought. Nothing more. Still, sometimes, he wondered.

Now he stared at the tree. Something was the matter with its branches, but he did not know what to do to fix it. Cut the strong one? Cut the weak one, maybe? If only Donald Trump were here. He would be sure to know what to do.

cnbc.com/2026/11/07/cosm-immersive-movie.headline: Cosm rides premium moviegoing wave with more immersive screenings and a wider library
cnbc.com/2026/11/07/cosm-immersive-movie.author: Sarah Whitten

paragraphs.text: The next big thing in premium large format theatrical viewing takes inspiration from the stars.

Cosm, an immersive entertainment technology company, got its start programming planetariums — its name a combination of "cosmos" and "colosseum." The company's massive, domed screens first offered guests a view of the universe, now they mimic courtside seats at sports venues around the world and drop film fans into some of Hollywood's most iconic sets.

At a time when the theatrical industry is seeing its biggest growth from the sale of premium large format, or PLF, tickets, Cosm seeks to offer a fresh take on an elevated viewing experience. And it's quickly expanding both its footprint and its content library.

Since 2024, Cosm has opened four theaters — near Los Angeles, Dallas, Atlanta and Detroit — with a Cleveland hub set to open in 2027. These experimental venues have garnered the attention of sports fans, screening live matchups in an arena-like environment. Showings often sell out, according to Cosm.

More recently, Cosm has partnered with Hollywood studios like Warner Bros., now a part of Skydance, to bring the likes of "The Matrix," "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" and "It" to its locations. Cosm recently signed a deal with Universal, which will bring "Shrek" to its domes in December.
The agreements mark a lucrative new chapter for the privately held Cosm, expanding its audience reach and viewing opportunities beyond timed, live events.

As a privately held company, Cosm doesn't disclose its financials. Tickets cost anywhere from $18 for a matinee to around $70 for prime seats or in-demand showings. That doesn't include added fees for concessions or items from special, themed menus tied to screenings.
Sony invested $100 million in the company in June, taking a minority stake and placing Sony Pictures Entertainment Chairman and CEO Ravi Ahuja onto its board of directors.

Cosm also counts among its investors Cosm chairman Steve Winn's firm, Mirasol Capital; former Milwaukee Bucks co-owner Marc Lasry's Avenue Sports Fund; Rocket Mortgage co-founder Dan Gilbert's Rock; and David Blitzer, managing partner of the New Jersey Devils and Philadelphia 76ers, who invested through his firm Bolt Ventures.

"Cosm is really early in its growth trajectory at the moment, and we saw an opportunity to partner with the company at, what I would say is at, a very important stage in its development," Jay Levine, chief strategy and business operations officer at Sony, told CNBC. "They have about five locations with the goal of a pretty significant rollout. And the real reason why we did it was it gave us a lot of exposure to a growing distribution and what we deem an experiential platform that we think has long-term potential."

Sony has made several plays in the theatrical space in recent years. It bought Alamo Drafthouse in 2024 and entered a long-term lease to reopen and restore the iconic Cinerama Dome in Los Angeles in July of this year.

"Our experiences strategy is around tech, it's around fandom, and it's around new and innovative approaches to content distribution," Levine said. "For us, we're all about these differentiated experiences."
What sets Cosm apart

Cosm's 87-foot-diameter, concave screens drop viewers into the middle of the action, whether it's an NFL game or inside the world of "The Matrix." The company's forthcoming Cleveland location will have an even bigger dome, at 100 feet in diameter.
The experience is akin to that of the Sphere in Las Vegas, which has garnered headlines since opening in 2023 for hosting high-profile concerts and events.

"People absolutely love to live out what they love in fandom, just like wearing a sports jersey," Alexis Scalice, head of Cosm Studios, told CNBC. "And I love that I'm seeing that same behavior happen with cinema."

Stadium-style seating is nestled within each Cosm dome, with booths and tables set on each level. The dome's width is such that it fills much of the viewer's periphery, giving the sensation that they are part of the on-screen environment.

The Los Angeles and Dallas locations have capacity for around 350 seats each, while the newer domes in Atlanta and Detroit have up to 500 available seats. Cosm has not shared how many seats the Cleveland location will have, but with its larger screen it is expected to have a larger number of seats.
For live sports events, Cosm has specialty cameras mounted in arenas that broadcast back to the dome, creating the illusion of being on the field of play.
For theatrical features, the film is played in a large rectangle in the center of the dome and the background is transformed to extend the scene.

In Cosm's presentation of "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," for example, during the iconic scene where thousands of Hogwarts acceptance letters flood through the fireplace and into a living room, the background is swarmed with animated envelopes.

Cosm has partnered with experiential production company Little Cinema and creative studio MakeMake to create the visuals and environments for each scene of a film released in the dome. From storyboarding to post-production, this process can take up to a year as Cosm, the participating studio and the visual effects artists craft and render each moment.

"We really work hard not to take away from the story, so the film remains the hero in the narrative," Scalice said. "Working very closely with Warner Bros. and our creative partners to make sure that we're not detracting too much from the story, but we're enhancing those moments for more elevated emotional response."
With the exception of "It," which was released in 2017, Cosm's theatrical offerings thus far have been films that were released decades ago and that typically have long-established fan bases.
That helps Cosm leverage what Scalice called "that nostalgia factor" — "parents coming in that ... grew up on this, and they want to share it with their children."
"We can reinvigorate these legendary films," she added.
Cosm has dabbled across genres — horror, fantasy, science fiction — and also demographics — family-friendly and R-rated. "Shrek," set to debut Dec. 16, will be its first foray into animation.

"The thing that's so incredible about it is everybody thought initially it's just going to be working for sports, and when you look at what they've done, a lot of the titles with 'Harry Potter,' with 'Shrek,' and some of the other ones, I mean, the fill rates are actually incredible," Sony's Levine said.
The future is premium
Studios and theatrical exhibitors alike are looking for innovative ways to showcase Hollywood's product to moviegoers, especially as major shifts in viewing habits have disrupted the business.
In the post-pandemic era, the cinema space has been defined by fewer screens and fewer moviegoers, but those declines have been masked by higher movie ticket prices, particularly for PLF experiences.

These elevated offerings — think Imax, Dolby Cinema, ScreenX and 4DX — have bigger screens and better sound or introduce a unique experience, such as moving seats and fog machines. They're particularly popular with Gen Z and millennials, who've yet to be deterred by rising average ticket prices.
While an average standard movie ticket costs around $13, premium tickets average more than $18 each, according to data from EntTelligence.
Prices for Cosm's events fluctuate based on showtime and venue, but on average it's "higher than I think anybody really would have thought," Sony's Levine said.
Unlike Cosm's sports offerings, which can also be viewed from outside the dome from its hall and deck viewing areas at a lower price, theatrical presentations are only available in the dome.

"They have no problem selling these tickets because people want to experience these things, like an immersive format," said Mike Polydoros, CEO at cinema marketing firm PaperAirplane Media. "That is something they can't get at home."

engadget.com/2309200/engadget-review-rec.headline: Engadget Review Recap: Apple Devices, Googlebooks And Kindles
engadget.com/2309200/engadget-review-rec.author: Billy Steele

paragraphs.text: It has been another jam-packed two weeks here at Engadget. In a fortnight, we've published 13 new reviews, and there's even more on the horizon. You'll be forgiven if you missed a few, so we've rounded up the best of the baker's dozen for easy weekend reading. Be sure to keep your eyes peeled next week as we've already got six more reviews on the docket, and there's a good chance we'll add others to that tally in the next few days.
MacBook Pro(s), iMac and iPad mini

Apple added to its late 2026 gadget tally last week, debuting a trio of new Macs alongside an overhauled iPad mini. The main attraction is certainly the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, the first touchscreen Apple laptop with a very awkward name. It's an excellent machine, but it's also very expensive, and senior reporter Devindra Hardawar argued the marquee feature doesn't add enough to the overall experience.

Devindra also put the new MacBook Pro M6 through its paces, and this device was the highest-scoring of the bunch. The only thing new here is the upgraded Apple silicon, and of course, a higher price. If a desktop Mac is more your style, there's a new iMac in town. Associate editor Steve Dent lamented the lack of a larger refresh on this model, noting that the price increase makes the enhanced performance a tough sell. Last but not least, deputy news editor Nathan Ingraham tested the iPad mini with an A20 Pro chip. But, yet again, the device is more expensive, plus the display refresh rate is still 60Hz and there's no Face ID.
Googlebooks have arrived

We have entered Googlebook era, which is proving to be a new period of Google-powered laptops with familiar issues. Nathan wrote an in-depth guide to the devices, but we've also reviewed two models so far. The consensus amongst our team seems to be that despite the presence of great hardware, Googlebook OS isn't fully baked just yet. Senior reporter Sam Rutherford tested the Lenovo Googlebook 15 while Devindra reviewed the Dell XPS Googlebook, which both cost around $1,000.
Two new Kindles

Amazon has a bunch of new Kindle devices this fall, and the first two we could get our hands on were the Signature Editions of the Colorsoft and Paperwhite models. I'm a big fan of the Paperwhite devices, and that continues on the new version. However, I'm not sure the pricier option adds enough to warrant the extra cost. Executive editor Cherlynn Low felt similarly about the Colorsoft Signature Edition.
Fitbit Edge and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2

The steady arrival of new wearables continues. First, Cherlynn spent some time with the elegantly designed Fitbit Edge, noting that Google may have finally struck the right balance between looks and features. We had to wait for the most attractive new features to arrive on the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, but as soon as Samsung delivered those, UK bureau chief Mat Smith went to work. That device's bright display, excellent battery life and bevy of health and fitness tracking tools are the highlights.

phys.org/news/2026-11-soil-acidity-crop-.headline: Why treating soil acidity crop by crop is no longer enough for prairie farmers
phys.org/news/2026-11-soil-acidity-crop-.author: Bev Betkowski

paragraphs.text: edited by Gaby Clark, reviewed by Andrew Zinin

To protect their future harvests, Western Canadian farmers need to manage soil acidity across their entire multiyear rotation rather than crop by crop, long-term research from the University of Alberta suggests.

In a study to address the challenge of how modern agricultural practices affect soil acidity, the consequences for crop production and how farmers can manage those changes before they become a serious problem, researchers found that proactively managing soil pH levels pays off across the entire rotation. The work is published in the Canadian Journal of Plant Science.

The researchers looked at how decades of fertilizer use, crop rotation and corrective lime applications affect soil acidity and nutrient availability over time. Their most important finding was that liming legume forages not only boosts their growth but also unlocks vital nitrogen for grain crops planted in future rotations.

"Managing soil acidity is about more than simply maintaining the productivity of individual crops," says soil scientist Dr. Miles Dyck, a professor in the Faculty of Agricultural, Life & Environmental Sciences and a co-author on the study with Dr. Linda Gorim.
"It can also help preserve important biological processes."

Historically, soil acidity hasn't been a major concern for many farmers in Western Canada, but agricultural practices have changed considerably over the past several decades, making it more of an issue, notes Dyck, who recently discussed the problem in a podcast.
Beneficial practices, unintended consequences

"Farmers are growing more diverse and productive crops, applying more fertilizer and removing larger quantities of nutrients from their fields through harvests. These practices have many benefits, but they can also gradually increase soil acidity, often over decades. That means producers may not notice a problem until soil acidity reaches a level that begins to affect their yields. By that point, restoring favorable soil conditions can require considerable time and expense."
As soil becomes more acidic, it can become less favorable for plant growth and crop productivity by affecting the availability of nutrients and the activity of beneficial soil microorganisms.

"The main prairie crops—cereals like wheat, barley and oats, oilseeds such as canola, pulses like peas and lentils, and forages such as grasses and alfalfa—vary in their sensitivity to soil acidity. If one crop in a rotation is affected by soil acidity, the crops that follow will also be affected," Dyck notes.

Drawing on data gathered between 1980 and 2020 from the U of A's Breton Plots, the researchers examined how synthetic fertilizer, manure and lime—a crushed limestone powder used to neutralize soil acidity—affected soil health, yields and nitrogen cycling within a five-year crop rotation of wheat, oats, barley and an alfalfa-brome grass mix.

Results showed that legumes like alfalfa benefit most directly from liming. In fields treated with synthetic fertilizers, applying lime boosted forage yields, biological nitrogen fixation in the alfalfa and the absorption of essential nutrients.

Although cereal crops like wheat and oats were less sensitive to soil acidity and didn't see direct grain yield increases from liming, they did gain indirect benefits by taking up more nitrogen when they followed alfalfa grown in limed soil.

"We believe this occurred because reducing soil acidity improved alfalfa growth and likely increased the amount of nitrogen fixed by beneficial bacteria associated with its roots," Dyck notes. "Some of that nitrogen subsequently became available to the wheat and oats."

Dyck says this shows an important relationship between crops in a rotation and why producers should evaluate the potential benefits of liming for all crops in their rotation on time scales of two or three rotation cycles, which span ten to 15 years.

"Managing soil conditions to benefit one crop can also improve the growing conditions for others planted in subsequent years. And in some cases, the benefits may be indirect and become apparent only over several growing seasons."
A surprising finding

However, the researchers also found a surprising contradiction: alfalfa can contribute to soil acidification. As the plant's roots absorb large quantities of positively charged nutrients like calcium and magnesium, they release acid into the soil. When the crop is harvested, a large amount of those essential nutrients is removed from the field, accelerating pH decline.

"This shows how a crop can improve one aspect of soil fertility while at the same time contributing to changes in another," Dyck notes, adding that it doesn't mean farmers should avoid growing alfalfa or other legumes.
"These crops offer important benefits, but their effects on soil acidity need to be considered when planning rotations and nutrient management."

The experiments also showed that soil acidification was most rapid in plots treated with synthetic fertilizers, even when lime was applied, suggesting that it shouldn't necessarily be viewed as a one-time solution.

At the same time, the study showed that manure slowed soil acidification more than synthetic fertilizers by returning nutrients like calcium and magnesium to the soil, helping maintain the capacity to resist changes in pH levels.
The findings point to the importance of considering long-term consequences of different nutrient management strategies, Dyck says.
"Various types of fertilizers and soil amendments can have quite different long-term effects on soil chemistry."
Regular monitoring and management of soil acidity are becoming increasingly important in cropping systems in Western Canada, he adds.

Soil testing carried out by farmers usually focuses on plant-available nutrient levels in the top 6, 12 or 24 inches (15, 30 or 61 centimeters) of soil. Under modern zero- or reduced-tillage systems, soil acidity mostly occurs in the top 3 inches (8 centimeters) where seeds and fertilizers are placed every year, Dyck notes. Sampling soil in layers, testing repeatedly at the same locations and depths over time, and liming strategically to protect acid-sensitive crops like alfalfa and pulse legumes can help to catch the issue early, he says.
"To be able to identify and manage soil acidity before it begins limiting crop productivity, it's important to pay closer attention to soil pH and how it changes over time," Dyck notes.
"Soils are continually responding to the way we manage them, and understanding these gradual changes is essential to maintaining productive, sustainable agricultural systems for future generations."

Jedida Chirchir et al., Perennial legume forages drive soil acidification and nitrogen availability to subsequent crops in a cereal–forage rotation, Canadian Journal of Plant Science (2026). DOI: 10.1139/cjps-2025-0168
