bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g1nq8158po.headline: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g1nq8158po.author: Olivia Ireland, Dan Johnson

paragraphs.text: Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.
Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.
Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".
Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.

"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.
"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."

In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.
The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.
Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.
The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.
She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhihia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.
Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.
He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.
"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."
Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.
Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-6023225/perspec.headline: Perspective: Simon Winchester was here to tell a story
npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-6023225/perspec.author: Scott Simon

paragraphs.text: I met Simon Winchester decades ago, covering a big story in a small town. The Menominee Warrior Society had seized an abandoned Catholic monastery in Gresham, Wisconsin, and other indigenous rights activists - including the actor Marlon Brando - came to join them.

I was a young reporter who had traveled up from Chicago. Simon Winchester was there for The Guardian newspaper, wearing a Sherlock Holmes-style hat and a tweed cape. We wound up in the same local rooming house, and I would creep onto the stairs at midnight to hear Simon, on a payphone, read his elegant copy to an editor in London between quaffs of brandy.
"Analysis is just so much gabble," I remember him remonstrating to an editor one night. "I'm here to tell a story."

Simon Winchester, who died this week at the age of 82, told so many stories. He covered Bloody Sunday in Derry, Northern Ireland; the Watergate scandal in Washington DC; and the Falklands war - during which Argentine authorities accused him of spying for the British government and threw him in jail for three months.
"Who on earth would make me a spy?," he used to ask in re-telling the story. "As if I could keep a secret!"

Simon Winchester went on to author dozens of bestsellers that ranged around the world, and humanity. He wrote about earthquakes and cities, explorers on open seas, mountains, and in laboratories, the English language, and the human mind and soul.
"It was a brave man," Simon wrote in his book about the Atlantic Ocean, "who ate the first oyster."

This week, as exit polls show so much human anxiety over Artificial Intelligence, I wondered if Simon Winchester might want people to hear some of the final, surprisingly buoyant thoughts from his 2024 book, Knowing What We Know.
"An existential intellectual crisis looms," he wrote. "If machines will acquire all our knowledge for us and do our thinking for us, then what, pray, is the need for us to be?...
"But what if the opposite is true?" asked Simon Winchester. "What if mental leisure gives us the time and space to suppose, ponder, ruminate, consider, assess, wonder, contemplate, imagine, dream?...
"And by doing so perhaps come to know not simply what we do know, but what we should know, in order to be fully human."

theatlantic.com/newsletters/2026/11/less.headline: Americans Are Spending Less Time With Friends

paragraphs.text: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.

What does your ideal night look like? Maybe it’s dinner with friends or a quiet evening at home with family or a partner. If you picked the latter option, you are part of a growing contingent of Americans who are spending less time with friends and, by some measures, more time with family.

Although enjoying the company of loved ones can be deeply fulfilling, something may be lost when our household makes up the majority of our social life. In a recent Atlantic story, my colleague Faith Hill explores why friendship is taking a back seat to family time. In one survey, nearly 40 percent of respondents who said they wished they saw friends more cited a lack of money as an obstacle; others pointed to busy schedules and exhaustion. “More Americans are hanging out with family—by choice, but also by necessity,” Faith writes.

Friendships offer a type of companionship that family life can’t always provide. But unlike family ties, friendships depend on our continued attention to nurture them, making them meaningful—and easier to lose.
The Socializing That’s Replacing Friend Time
More Americans are hanging out with family—by choice, but also by necessity.
Read the article.
We all want more time with our friends, but we’re spending more time alone. (From 2024)
What If Friendship, Not Marriage, Was at the Center of Life?
“Our boyfriends, our significant others, and our husbands are supposed to be No. 1. Our worlds are backward.” (From 2020)
Still Curious?
• Another symptom of growing isolation: A recent study found that people spoke fewer words a day in 2019 than in 2005, Olga Khazan wrote.
• The new age of endless parenting: More grown kids are in near-constant contact with their family. Some call this a failure to launch—but there’s another way to look at it, Hill wrote in 2024.

My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “Where I live is often crispy and dry by early summer; everything loses its greenness and turns golden to brown. But a week or so ago we got some great rain, so I moseyed down to the river, to a spot I frequent often, and was enamored by the vibrant pops of green lichen and moss on the boulders and trees next to the river,” Allie S. from El Portal, California, shared. “The contrasting textures and colors were an absolute delight. And there is something truly special about returning to a place again and again and then one day seeing it in a new way and appreciating it once more.”
We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks.
— Rafaela

cnbc.com/2026/11/07/berkshire-shares-sur.headline: Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
cnbc.com/2026/11/07/berkshire-shares-sur.author: Alex Crippen

paragraphs.text: (This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears

Berkshire Hathaway shares roared past the S&P 500 index this week as investors moved money away from slumping tech stocks and moved into what appears to be the relative safety of a traditional conglomerate with relatively little exposure to artificial intelligence amid fears massive spending on data centers won't pay off.
One month ago, Berkshire's widely held B shares were underperforming the S&P by 13.6 percentage points for the year.
With help from three more record-high closes this week, Berkshire is now 5.8 percentage points ahead of the benchmark.
Berkshire was up more than 5% this week while the S&P fell almost 2.7%.
The contrast is even sharper with the Nasdaq Composite, which fell 3.4% on the week.

Thursday's especially heavy tech selling pushed the index down more than 10% below its most recent high in what is commonly referred to as a "correction," but it did make up some of its lost ground Friday.

Two weeks ago, Berkshire's share prices completely erased all of the roughly 15% drop they suffered in the three months following Warren Buffett's surprise announcement at the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year.
Now they are up 6% from the record high closes they hit the Friday before Buffett's revelation on May 3, 2025.
Alphabet's slide cited as example of 'disappointing' stock picks
Berkshire is not completely removed from the convulsions around AI.
Abel told us in early September he sees a "significant opportunity" ahead for Berkshire Hathaway Energy to provide electricity to data centers.

He also expected Berkshire would benefit from its big bet on Google parent Alphabet, saying he and Warren Buffett knew AI was "going to have a significant impact on America and businesses," and "we saw Google as a significant player."
Now that investment is getting negative reviews this week as the stock slumps along with other companies related to AI.

As of the end of June, Berkshire reported it owned almost 106 million shares of Alphabet, including 28.6 million shares it bought directly from the company in June: $5 billion of its Class A shares (GOOGL) for $351.81 each and another $5 billion of Class C shares (GOOG) for $348.20 each.
They are around $284 per share now.

It bought another $7 billion of Alphabet shares on the open market during the second quarter, adding to the position it started building in last year's third quarter, an investment initiated by Warren Buffett.
Bloomberg suggests that "with cracks in the AI trade starting to show, Berkshire's sudden push [into AI] may appear ill-timed."
On June 30, the position had a market value of $37.8 billion and it was the third largest equity holding in Berkshire's portfolio.
Since then both the Class A and Class C shares have dropped by around 20% and the stake is now valued at $30.2 billion, falling behind Coca-Cola's $38.3 billion to the portfolio's #4 position.
(In just over a week, we'll find out whether Berkshire made any changes to its Alphabet position during the third quarter ending September 30.)

Bloomberg quotes CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert as saying, "I do think that part of this may be a conscious decision to increase their exposure. One has to ask the question though, is it a little late?"

But the article notes that "for dedicated value investors and longtime Berkshire observers, such jitters may not really matter," with Keefe Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields saying Abel probably sees bets on AI as a long-term wager on the technology's potential, in keeping with the "conservatism that you would expect at Berkshire Hathaway."
At Barron's, however, Andrew Bary sees what he estimates is a $3 billion loss on Alphabet as part of a "disappointing" long-term trend in Berkshire's stock choices
"The company hasn't created much value from stock picking during the current decade" even though the "S&P 500 has returned 150% since the end of 2019 and tech stocks have quadrupled."
While Berkshire's investments in five Japanese "trading houses," Chevron, and Chubb have done well, "there have been plenty of losers or simply mediocre investments that have been closed out."
He cites Verizon, HP, Paramount (now Skydance), General Motors, Constellation Brands, and Pool.
While he estimates Berkshire's Occidental Petroleum investment is up about 20% from what it paid, OXY is "far behind most energy stocks" amid this year's big increase in crude prices.
Bary also lists stocks that have continued to rise in price after Berkshire cut its stakes, with Apple being the worst offender.
That stake has been reduced by 75% since 2023 at what Bary calculates is an average selling price around $200 per share, well below AAPL's current $342.

Despite those sales, Apple is Berkshire's largest equity holding with a market value of $78 billion. The stock is up 1200% since Berkshire started buying it at the beginning of 2016, at a time when many thought the company had already seen its best days.
Bary thinks Abel will probably keep Berkshire's core equity investments but may concentrate more on his strengths going forward: improving Berkshire's operating companies and making new acquisitions.
His conclusion: "Barring a market rout, equity investing may not be central to Berkshire anymore.
"And if any new Berkshire holdings are revealed soon, it may not be a good idea to buy them. The record hasn't been great."
Small buy helps lift Sirius XM shares

Berkshire Hathaway's disclosure that it had made a relatively small $27 million addition to its $4.1 billion Sirius XM position helped fuel an ongoing rally that lifted the satellite radio company's shares to a 52-week high this week.
On Thursday morning last week, Sirius XM reported a 14% increase in its Q3 free cash flow, 5,000 more self-pay subscribers, and it raised its 2026 full-year financial guidance.
The stock ended 4.9% higher that day at $28.67.
On Friday, Monday, and Tuesday, Berkshire bought more than 924 thousand shares at an average price of $29.10 as the stock continued to gain ground, ending Tuesday at $30.80.
Berkshire disclosed the buys late Tuesday evening, apparently helping to fuel an additional 8.4% gain as the stock closed at $33.40 on Wednesday.
It hit a 52-week intraday high of $33.76 on Thursday but finished lower Friday at $32.40.
Overall, Sirius XM is up 18.6% since the earnings release and has gained 62.0% so far this year.
It's the first addition to Berkshire's stake since late-July and early-August last year.
In 2025, it bought a total of 7.3 million shares at an average price of $21.86.
The position is likely one of portfolio manager Ted Weschler's stocks.
Berkshire utility asks for 57% rate hike in Northern California
Pacific Power, a unit of Berkshire Hathaway's PacifiCorp, is asking California regulators for a 57% rate increase that would raise the typical residential electric bill by $120 a month.
The Wall Street Journal calls it a "stunning request even in an era of rising electricity costs."
The utility says the hike would be partially offset by a 14% decrease taking effect on January 1.

A lot of the $103 million that would be generated by the increase is already being spent on efforts to make power equipment in the sparsely populated and heavily wooded area more resistant to wildfires.
The utility is facing around $637 million in liability claims for fires in 2020 and 2022.

This week, Reuters reports, Oregon's Supreme Court heard arguments on whether to revive a jury verdict that could expose PacifiCorp "to tens of billions of dollars of potential damages over its role in four Oregon wildfires in 2020."
BUFFETT & BERKSHIRE AROUND THE INTERNET
Some links may require a subscription:
HIGHLIGHTS FROM CNBC'S BUFFETT ARCHIVE
Work in the age of artificial intelligence (2017)
Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger share their opinions about how artificial intelligence could affect the economy, the government, and how much time people spend on leisure activities.
ANDREW ROSS SORKIN: Thomas Kimay (PH) is here. He's a 27-year-old shareholder from Kentfield, California.

And I should preface this question by saying that he was here 17 years ago at 10 years old, asked you a question from the audience asking you if the internet might hurt some of Berkshire's investments.
At the time, you said you wanted to see how things would play out. He's now updated the question. (Buffett laughs)
"What do you think about the implications of artificial intelligence on Berkshire's businesses, beyond autonomous driving and GEICO, which you've talked about already? ...
WARREN BUFFETT: I certainly have no special insights on artificial intelligence, but I will bet a lot of things happen in that field in the next couple of decades, and probably a shorter timeframe.
They should lead, I would certainly think — but again, I don't bring much to this party. But I would certainly think they would result in significantly less employment in certain areas.
But that's good for society.
And it may not be good for a given business, but let's take it to the extreme.
Let's assume one person could push a button and, essentially, through various machines and robotics, all kinds of things, turn out all of the output we have in this country.
So, everybody's — there's just as much output as we have. It's all being done by, you know, instead of 150-some million people being employed, one person.
You know, is the world better off or not?
Well, certainly we'd work a lot less hours a week — of work per week and so on.

I mean, it would be a good thing, but it would require enormous transformation in how people relate to each other, what they expect of government, you know, all kinds of things. And, of course, as a practical matter, more than one person would keep working.
But pushing the idea that way is one of the — you'd certainly think that's one of the consequences of making great progress in artificial intelligence.
And that's enormously prosocial, eventually. It's enormously disruptive in other ways. And it can have huge problems, in terms of a democracy and how it reacts to that...

CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, you're painting a very funny world where everybody's engaged in trade. And the trade is, I give you golf lessons and you dye my hair. And that would be a world kind of like the royal family of Kuwait or something.
And I don't think it would be good for America to have everything produced by one person and the rest of us just engaged in leisure.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7/pro-russian.headline: Pro-Russian hackers leak Italian foreign minister’s data on dark web
aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/7/pro-russian.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has said his personal data had been disseminated on the dark web, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blaming pro-Russian hackers for the leak.

Tajani announced in a social media post on Saturday that “for days now, cybercriminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation”.
Recommended Stories

The threats against Tajani, who is also vice prime minister of Italy, come amid a spate of hoax bomb threats across Europe that have forced flight diversions, security alerts at broadcasters, and attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems.

“They are also targeting my family; they are willing to pay for more details about me and my loved ones,” Tajani added in his X post. “My response is very simple: I will not be intimidated in any way.”
‘Matter of grave concern’
Meloni expressed solidarity with Tajani “following the revelations about the activities of pro-Russian hackers, and the publication on the dark web of personal data”.
She called attempts to sell confidential information about government officials “a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination”.

Tajani added in his statement that Italy’s “position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted: defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation’s democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities”.
He also suggested that the cyberthreats may also be a reaction to the Italian government’s efforts to strengthen the Foreign Ministry’s digital defences.
Tajani did not specify what kind of information had been shared, but suggested that the cyberthreat was ongoing.
He added that the ministry was taking the threats seriously and was coordinating its response with allied countries.

aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11/7/atletico-.headline: Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: La Liga – predictions, team news, lineups
aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11/7/atletico-.author: Manasi Pathak

paragraphs.text: Who: Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona What: La Liga, match day 12 Where: Riyadh Air Metropolitano, Madrid, Spain When: Sunday, November 8, at 9pm (20:00 GMT). How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 17:00 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream
A top-of-the-table clash headlines Sunday’s La Liga action, with Barcelona looking to retain their top spot before the international break as they face challengers Atletico Madrid.
Recommended Stories
With only two points separating the teams, the blockbuster clash could well be the turning point in the 2026-27 title race should Atletico upset Barcelona.
Diego Simeone’s side have been in terrific form all season and take on Barcelona, bolstered by a seven-game winning streak in the Spanish top flight.

Atletico’s striker Julian Alvarez struggled to find his feet early in the campaign, with a dramatic transfer saga involving Barcelona adding to the uncertainty. But the Argentinian has since rediscovered his form, scoring in each of his last two league outings.
If Atletico have been impressive, Barcelona have been irresistible.
Hansi Flick’s team have netted an incredible 46 goals in just 11 league games; the only team to score more in their first 11 matches of a campaign were Athletic Club in 1930-31 (49).

Raphinha and Lamine Yamal have been the architects of Barca’s lethal attack, with the Brazilian winger leading the goal-scoring charts this season with 15 league goals in 10 games. He is just the second player to reach this tally within 10 games at the start of a campaign after Real Madrid icon Cristiano Ronaldo, who did so in 2014-15 (18 goals in 10 matches).
Ahead of Atletico vs Barcelona, here’s everything to know:
How have Atletico played this season?
Atletico are second in the La Liga standings, with 28 points from 11 games. They have won nine matches, lost once and drawn as many.
How have Barcelona played this season?
Barcelona lead the La Liga points table with 30 points from 11 games. They have won 10 games and lost only once, suffering a 2-1 Clasico defeat to bitter rivals Real Madrid last month.
Raphinha thriving where Barca envisaged Atletico’s Alvarez
Raphinha is back to his devastating best as Barcelona’s centre-forward, suggesting the Catalan giants have little reason to regret missing out on Atletico’s Alvarez this summer.

The Argentina international tried to force his way out of Atletico to join Spanish champions Barca, whose attempts to engineer a deal angered the Rojiblancos. Barcelona were fined about 600 euros ($675) for their approach for striker Alvarez by the Spanish football federation in October.

Alvarez stayed and later apologised to Atletico fans to try and rebuild bridges, while Barcelona moved on fast, with winger Raphinha developing into an unstoppable force in a previously unfamiliar number nine role.
Raphinha’s form has made the chances of Barca returning for Alvarez next summer remote, and, after penning a new contract until 2030 on Thursday, he will look to underline that against Atletico.
With the Brazilian firing on all cylinders, Flick’s side won 11 games straight across all competitions at the start of the season.
Currently, he has 19 goals in 13 games across all competitions, including a brace each in the last two games.
After joining Barcelona from Leeds United in 2022, the winger grew frustrated under coach Xavi Hernandez, who did not seem to trust him completely.

However, Flick’s arrival and his high-pressing game suited Raphinha to the ground, and the winger has gone from strength to strength, becoming one of the team’s most influential players and one of the captains.
What happened the last time Atletico played Barcelona?
The last time the teams met was in a 2025-26 Champions League knockout game on April 14.
Although Barcelona defeated Atletico 2-1 in Madrid that day, Atletico edged their Catalan opponents 3-2 on aggregate and reached the semifinals.
Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: Predictions
Opta’s supercomputer gives Barcelona a 49.3 percent chance of winning, while Atletico’s probability of a win stands at 27.5 percent. There is a 23.3 percent chance of a draw.
Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: Head-to-head
Atletico have won two of their last five games against Barcelona in all competitions (L3), all of which have taken place in 2026.

The teams faced off twice in the Copa del Rey semifinals in March, with Atleti grabbing a solid first-leg 4-0 win at home before holding on for a 4-3 aggregate triumph, while they also won 2-0 at Camp Nou in the Champions League quarterfinals in April, going through 3-2 on aggregate on that occasion.

In La Liga, though, Barcelona have won in each of their last four trips to the Metropolitano. They are bidding to become just the third team in La Liga history to clinch five straight away wins over Atletico, after Athletic Club in 1955 and Real Madrid in 2013 (both runs of six).

bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cmq.headline: Ireland Rugby Social: Ireland 'going from strength to strength'
bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cmq.author: BBC Sport

paragraphs.text: Ireland began their autumn series of Nations Championship matches by scoring six tries in a comprehensive 42-12 win over Argentina at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin on Friday night.

Afterwards on the Ireland Rugby Social podcast, BBC Sport NI's Gavin Andrews spoke to Ireland second row Joe McCarthy about his thoughts on the game and then chatted to co-presenter and former Ireland scrum-half Conor Murray to break down the analysis of the home side's performance.

With matches against Fiji and South Africa to follow over the next couple of weeks, there was much to dissect after the win over the Pumas and assess what may be to come for the remainder of November.
You can watch the podcast now on BBC NI YouTube, external or listen on BBC Sounds.
Here are a few highlights of what Murray had to say.
On Hugo Keenan, who scored a hat-trick of tries: "Hugo stood out but he's always going to do that. He talks so much on the pitch and makes it way easier for the players around him.
"He's always marshalling the wingers and that kind of back-field system. That's Hugo in a nutshell. He's the ultimate team player.
"He looked incredibly fit, incredibly quick, explosive. He looked back to his best."

On fledgling half-back partnership Sam Prendergast and Craig Casey: "Craig and Sam marshalled the game really well. Not that there were question marks but they were a relatively new combination and it was their first time getting a big Test start together.
"Sam can forget what he's been through, I suppose the rocky start to his international career and the public scrutiny on him.
"He looks like a player who has just soaked it all in and is using it as a weapon now. He looked really sharp. He looks like he has bulked up, which is great to see too.
"There'll be a target on his back, there was already but there definitely will be now as he is such a big influence.
"We know what Craig Casey can do in terms of quick ball and magical moments but now in terms of the control of the game.

"His passing was on the money and his kicking is top notch. The overall control is probably the test that Andy Farrell gave him. He knows what he can do in loose play but in terms of controlling a Test game I thought the half-backs were brilliant."

On an impressive performance by the forwards: "[Tadhg] Furlong went really well, he's always a standard-bearer anyhow and you get top-notch performances from him, but [Andrew] Porter, another player who came back from an extended period out with injury, he's come back and showed what he's about.
"His explosiveness in open play and his fitness, he's like another back row on the field.

"Dan Sheehan, Tadhg Beirne, Joe McCarthy, Ryan Baird, the back row, across the board, all really good. I think Nick Timoney and Josh [van der Flier] are in a real battle as regards that number seven jersey."

On strength in depth: "The depth we have now is really impressive. Over a year ago there were a good few injuries and people were worrying, not that there was panic, but wondering, 'where's the depth?' Not that we had no depth, but Andy had to blood a few players quickly.
"Those players are now in the squad and they are pushing lads across the board, pushing the other boys to perform.
"I think Irish rugby is going from strength to strength and it's really impressive to see."
On facing Fiji next week and then South Africa: "They [Ireland] should beat Fiji. I don't think that's getting ahead of ourselves. I think that's where Ireland rugby is at now.
"The lads coming in next week will be thinking they have a chance to perform and will want to be in Andy and the coaches' minds for selection for the South Africa game.

"That's how competitive the squad is. It's a real difference now that the guys coming out against Fiji aren't just saying, 'I'm getting a run out here', but rather, 'I'm actually in the mix here', which is really healthy.

"Lads deserve a chance but Andy will expect the same level of performance. When there are changes, there can be a dip because the combinations change but it's a big week of prep now and those guys will sniff an opportunity that they can stay involved.
"They won't say it but everyone wants to be involved against South Africa.
"There'll still be a core to the team that will be really, really strong, because you respect Fiji and you want some sort of consistency and some sort of momentum."

engadget.com/2304942/black-friday-fake-t.headline: November Is The Month Of Fake Black Friday Tech Deals
engadget.com/2304942/black-friday-fake-t.author: Husain Parvez

paragraphs.text: That Black Friday discount you’re excited about might not be as good a deal as it seems.

Black Friday falls on November 27 this year, but retailers like Amazon and Best Buy will have sales running well before then. Some of these sales may be well worth taking advantage of, while others may seem like bargains until you compare prices. Then there are outright scams, including fake storefronts and phishing emails posing as retailer promotions.

For example, a 2025 study by UK consumer organization Which? tracked 175 products across eight retailers (including Amazon) from May 2024 to May 2025. The results showed that 83 percent of these items were available for the same price or less at least once outside the four-week Black Friday sales period. That doesn't prove retailers intentionally raised prices, but it's a reminder that a discounted price tells you little on its own. Similarly, Bitdefender found that scams accounted for 53 percent of the Black Friday-related spam it analyzed between October 1 and November 10, 2025. These included fake Amazon coupons and messages impersonating familiar retailers.
Check the price history, not the discount percentage

If you're buying from Amazon, the best way to check whether a discount is actually worth it is to copy the product URL from Amazon and paste it into an Amazon price tracker like CamelCamelCamel or Keepa. Similarly, Amazon's Alexa for Shopping assistant (previously called Rufus) can display up to 365 days of price history for eligible items without requiring a Prime membership. Google Shopping compares prices from retailers and, for US shoppers, can indicate whether the current price is high, low or typical for the product. Slickdeals discussions can give you additional information regarding past sales, but community member comments are not verified price records.

If you see a sharp price increase just before a November sale, it deserves a closer look. Take the Samsung Jet Bot robot vacuum, which UK retailer John Lewis advertised for £350 on Black Friday 2024, down from £500. Which? found it had sold for £299 on 29 days in May and June, while the £500 price had only been in place since October. Suddenly, that discount doesn't seem so good. Shipping costs and coupon requirements can also raise the final price, making a potential deal much less appealing at checkout.
Do, however, bear in mind that historical lows aren't guaranteed to return. RAM prices, for example, are expected to stay high through 2030, so you likely won't get a massive deal anytime soon.
Fake storefronts and sellers are a different problem

Inflated discounts are annoying and misleading, but a fraudulent retailer can ruin your Black Friday experience entirely. That's why you shouldn't immediately jump on a heavily discounted GPU or gaming console from a vendor you don't recognize. Many scammers will use the same logos and product descriptions as legitimate retailers, lulling you into a false sense of security to acquire your financial information or sell you fake goods. Some may take your money and then cut off contact, never sending you anything at all.

So instead of clicking on links in unwanted emails or questionable sponsored ads, visit the retailer's site directly. It's always a good practice to check the full web address, seller reviews and return policy before buying. Even a professional-looking storefront doesn't necessarily mean the retailer is legitimate. Whenever possible, the FTC suggests using a credit card so you can dispute charges for products that never arrive. Also, don't hesitate to walk away if a seller demands gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency payments.

The same applies to Amazon: Check who's selling the item and not just who's shipping it. Even products listed as "Ships from Amazon" can still be sold by a different company, which would be listed under the "Sold by" heading.

npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-6029659/democra.headline: Democrats plan to widen their probes of fatal ICE shootings
npr.org/2026/11/07/nx-s1-6029659/democra.author: Meg Anderson

paragraphs.text: The morning after Tuesday's midterms was gloomy and rainy in Minneapolis, but people still gathered at the place where Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a VA nurse and U.S. citizen, last January. All week, community members have come here to place their "I Voted" stickers at the memorial.
Nicki Adams, who dated Pretti and was his close friend for nearly 17 years, watched quietly as a woman added her sticker to a street lamp completely covered in the red decals.
"I wanted to see all the stickers. I just wanted to be here," she says. "It just means a lot to me. I think it would mean a lot to Alex, too."

A few blocks away, people left their stickers where an ICE officer killed Renee Good, a mom of three and a U.S. citizen, just a few weeks before Pretti's death. In Houston, they left them where an ICE officer killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a father of three and a Mexican immigrant, in July.

Adams says these stickers, and the election results this week, send a clear message to Congress: "You work for us, and please carry on these values that we care about … We want to be seen and heard and taken care of and have our neighbors taken care of."

The deaths of Pretti and Good during the ICE surge in Minneapolis marked a pivotal moment for the country, sparking intense public backlash to President Trump's aggressive deportation efforts. But federal law enforcement officials have given little indication they're progressing in investigating their deaths, or the deaths of at least seven other people killed by federal immigration agents since Trump took office again last year. DHS did not respond to an NPR request for the status of those investigations.

Now, after Democrats' sweeping wins this week, their deaths at the hands of immigration agents will likely be the targets of renewed investigations. With a majority in Congress, Democrats can issue subpoenas to the major players in Trump's mass deportation plan, compelling them to testify under oath before the legislature.

That could include White House Border Czar Tom Homan, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, among others.
Congress can also demand internal documents like use-of-force reports.
"They can dissect these individual shootings, and really unravel the story of what happened," says Naureen Shah, who leads the ACLU's immigration policy work.
Democrats have already held shadow hearings on the ICE shootings, during which they've called in family members and witnesses to testify.
But Shah says now Congress can ask key questions of top decision makers: What orders were given to immigration officers in the field? What was training like for these officers?
Who made the decision to paint Good and Pretti as threats, including calling Pretti a "would-be assassin" and a domestic terrorist, when video showed otherwise?

"It's like we can turn the faucet on and actually find out so much more," Shah says. "There's an aspect of this that is really about a kind of reckoning with how it's possible that things that seemed unthinkable could happen on American streets. How do you have that reckoning if you don't actually have the ability to force people to explain themselves?"
Democratic leaders have already said that's the plan.

Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is expected to lead the House Judiciary Committee, told NPR in a statement that Congress will use "every tool" at its disposal to investigate ICE and that it is time for the agency to "start answering to the American people."
California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to lead the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, vowed to take on DHS and ICE abuses in a two-word statement: "Lawyer Up."

Mississippi Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, expected to lead the House Committee on Homeland Security, sent a letter on Wednesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, demanding the agency "comply with all document preservation requirements."
Illinois Democratic Rep. Delia Ramirez wrote on social media that Noem, Miller, Homan, Bovino and Mullin should "clear" their schedules.
In response to that, DHS general counsel James Percival said Democrats are "more interested in political shenanigans than in governing" but said the agency is prepared to "deal with this nonsense."
There are key limitations to what Democrats in Congress can do with their majority when it comes to ICE accountability, says Rachel Moran, a professor at the University of St. Thomas School of Law.
Major changes, like clawing back funding for the agency, would require a veto-proof majority, something the Democrats don't have.
"You still have a president who has shown a complete lack of interest in accountability for federal agents and in fact, a great deal of knee jerk defensiveness about their conduct," Moran says.
In a statement, a White House spokesperson told NPR "if Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."
Democrats, the statement added, "should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."

But that's not true. Congress has its own powers, one of them being the ability to compel testimony. Moran says a deeper probe into the shootings could still serve important purposes, like making evidence available for states to use in their own criminal investigations.
Minnesota officials, for instance, have been fighting with the federal government to get evidence related to the Pretti and Good killings.

Brent Ganger, Renee Good's brother, says learning more information about his sister's death will be hard to hear, "but I think it's also super important for us to understand what happened that day. I don't want history to keep repeating itself."

It was painful, he says, to watch immigration agents kill more people after his sister. He thought her death would be a turning point. In a way, it might have been the start of one. After the surge in Minneapolis, most Americans said ICE had gone too far.

Ganger, who considers himself a moderate, was happy to see the Blue Wave this week. On election night, he was scrolling Instagram when he saw a photo of his sister's memorial site, with all the "I Voted" stickers.
"I was very grateful to see the repudiation of this administration from the country. It felt very supportive of my entire family," he says.
The next morning, in his home in Colorado, he got up and made biscuits and gravy, his sister's favorite breakfast.

aljazeera.com/features/2026/11/7/buildin.headline: Buildings damaged in Israeli bombings risk collapse as rain inundates Gaza
aljazeera.com/features/2026/11/7/buildin.author: Lina Ghassan Abu Zayed

paragraphs.text: Gaza City – Rana Adnan Hmeida, 29, stands at the entrance to her tent in al-Mina camp in northern Gaza, holding her two-month-old daughter as she tries to keep her warm after rainwater has flooded their shelter overnight. The family’s bedding, blankets and clothes are all soaked, with her children exposed to the cold and wind of Gaza’s latest storm.

Hmeida, her husband and children have been awake since midnight as heavy rain and strong winds swept through the camp. Water seeped into the tent and drenched their belongings. With all their clothes wet, Hmeida had to ask neighbours to help dry their clothes.
Recommended Stories

“Since midnight, we have been sitting awake. Water came into our tent, and the bedding, blankets and everything else got soaked. In the morning, I found my son and little daughter shivering. My two-month-old baby was freezing,” Hmeida told Al Jazeera.

“What am I supposed to do? Hold my children or try to stop the water? I was trying to keep them warm while carrying my little girl, but the water kept coming in. The wind was so strong that we felt the tent was about to be ripped out of the ground.”
Her husband, Sameh Hmeida, 30, said the family’s tent is particularly exposed due to its close proximity to the sea. It has no tarpaulins or insulating materials that might have helped in the storm.

Heavy rain has flooded camps and cities across Gaza over the past days, where many Palestinians are spending the fourth winter outside their homes since Israel began its genocidal war on the enclave in October 2023.
Water levels have risen by 30 to 40cm (12 to 16in) at several camps in Gaza due to Saturday’s rain, with Gaza’s civil defence agency receiving hundreds of calls.
Rainwater has flooded many tents in al-Mina camp, where about 1,700 Palestinian families live, turning the ground into pools of muddy water.
Raed Abu Amsha, 40, said his tent collapsed on top of his family during the storm. The clothes and blankets of all nine children in his care, four of them from his late brother, were soaked.

“I am responsible for orphans as well as my own children, and I cannot provide for their needs. This storm lasted only two hours, and look what it did to us. We need tents, tarpaulins and anything that can protect our children. How long are we going to keep living like this?” he said.
In Nuseirat, a decades-old camp in central Gaza with permanent structures, rainfall also threatens families living in buildings damaged by Israeli bombardments.

Nasser al-Hajj, 54, lives in a tower block that was hit in an Israeli strike in September 2025. Debris from upper floors fell onto his home, leaving a large hole in the ceiling where water now enters every time it rains.

Although the ceiling has been reinforced with support beams, an engineer has warned al-Hajj that the apartment is dangerous, with the risk of further rubble falling from the building if more bad weather hits Gaza.

During the latest storm, al-Hajj took his children to a neighbour’s home and waited for the debris to stop falling from the roof. Two of his children, who have autism, sleep in the tower block’s guard room, away from the damaged area.

“I am forced to live somewhere that could collapse over our heads at any moment. But where am I supposed to go? Rent is expensive, and a tent is not safe either,” he told Al Jazeera. “I know how dangerous this place is, but I have no other option,” he added.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding. Low-lying locations and sites near the coast are particularly vulnerable, with more than 400,000 people living in areas considered at high risk of flooding.

About 44,000 Palestinians are living in structurally unsafe buildings, while more than 4,000 buildings across the territory are estimated to require full or partial demolition due to damage caused by Israeli air strikes. About 294,250 families need shelter assistance ahead of winter, but the available supplies cover only 18 percent of their needs.

The Gaza Municipality is also struggling to respond to the storms. About 15 kilometres of rainwater drainage lines and 212 kilometres of sewage networks have been damaged. Eight pumping stations and three main stormwater collection basins are out of service.
The remaining system can handle no more than 20 percent of rainwater under the best of circumstances, according to municipality spokesperson Hosni Muhanna.
“[We] continue to clean drainage systems in preparation for the rainy season,” Muhanna said.
The municipality has deployed workers to clean drains and manholes, remove rubbish and clear water channels, repair damaged sections of drainage lines and operate water pumps.
But Muhanna warns that these efforts cannot restore the network’s capacity amid shortages of fuel, equipment and spare parts.
More than 2,000 buildings in Gaza City alone are at risk of collapse, he said, and the volume of rubble in Gaza City has exceeded 25 million tonnes.

Emergency committees in displacement camps are also struggling with shortages of shelter supplies. Adli Awad, an official with the emergency committee in Nuseirat refugee camp, said his team is trying to distribute tents and tarpaulins, particularly to families affected by the rain. But the number of people in need far exceeds available stocks.
“We are trying to provide as many tents and tarpaulins as possible. We are also helping families dig channels to divert rainwater away from tents and reduce flooding,” Awad said.

fortune.com/2026/11/07/alignable-ai-assi.headline: Big Tech’s AI race will save small business owners time. It won’t find them customers
fortune.com/2026/11/07/alignable-ai-assi.author: Eric Groves

paragraphs.text: Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are racing to become the small business owner’s AI assistant. Meta brought its Muse agent to small businesses in September. Anthropic and OpenAI now package tools aimed squarely at owners, and Google is building the same features into tools millions of them already use.
That competition is good for Main Street. But it’s a race to save owners time, and time isn’t what keeps them up at night. What keeps them up is where the next customer will come from.

A word on where I sit. I run Alignable, a network of 10 million small business owners, so I have a stake in this argument. Alignable also co-hosts small business AI training with Anthropic, one of the companies named here. Read what follows with that in mind. But I also have something the assistants don’t: 13 years of data on how small businesses actually find work.
Fifty beats 500
Start with where customers come from. In our surveys, members say about 85% of their customers come through referrals. Not ads, not search, not cold email. People who already trust them.

Across 35,000 local communities, our members have formed 226 million business connections. Most of them never become a relationship that sends work either way. The owners who grow through their networks aren’t the ones with the most connections. I’ve told owners for years that 50 warm relationships beat 500 cold contacts. That’s a rule of thumb from experience, not a number we’ve measured. But the owners who win do keep a small set of relationships active and leave the rest alone.

And most owners are sitting on more opportunity than they know. When members tell us what their ideal customer looks like, we can count how many of those businesses sit one introduction away: connected to someone the owner already knows. Among members whose ideal customers show up in their extended network, the typical one has about 190 of them a single introduction away. For one in four, it’s more than 600.
The next customer is rarely a stranger. They’re one relationship away, through someone the owner hasn’t talked to in months.

Those relationships aren’t random, either. In my experience, three kinds do most of the work: customers who talk you up, businesses that serve the same customer without competing with you, and a handful of people who open doors. The best referral partner usually isn’t a peer in your own industry. It’s the business your customer calls right before or right after they call you: the realtor and the home inspector, the accountant and the financial planner.
What a general assistant can’t see

Ask any of the big assistants how to get more referrals and you’ll get a solid list of best practices. Ask an assistant that sits on a map of business relationships and it can tell you something specific: three nearby businesses serve your ideal customer, one of them already knows two of your clients, and you haven’t spoken to your best referral partner in four months.
That’s the difference between advice and action. A general assistant can’t answer that question, because the answer lives in data it doesn’t have.

The early numbers bear this out. In Bluehost’s 2026 study of 350 U.S. owners, 78% said AI saves them time every week. But 43% have seen no change in revenue. Time saved only matters if it goes somewhere that pays.

Too often it goes into volume. Forbes recently told the story of Paul Birrell, a New Jersey owner whose automation loop sent roughly 400,000 emails in three days. His reaction: “I don’t have 400,000 customers.” Everything we see says growth comes from the opposite: judgment about the few people who matter.
Three kinds of AI, not one
AI will reach small business owners in three forms. The first is the personal assistant the giants are fighting over. It delivers time, and the assistants are converging fast.

The second is AI built into the systems that already hold the business’s own data. Intuit knows the books. Shopify knows the store. That AI delivers control: it can flag a cash crunch six weeks out or spot the product quietly losing money.

The third is AI built on the relationships between businesses: who knows whom, who serves the same customers, who sends work to whom. That’s the one that delivers growth, and it’s the one almost nobody is talking about. At Alignable, ours is called Allie.

The giants have real advantages, and they’ll connect to the other two kinds. Meta’s Muse already plugs into QuickBooks, Shopify and Stripe, and the others are adding similar connections. The open question is who the intelligence works for. Meta makes nearly all of its money selling ads, and an assistant built by an ad company will tend to find that the answer involves more advertising. The data that actually works for the owner describes how their business runs and who in their community can help it grow.
What owners should do now
Use a personal assistant every day. The time savings are real.

Then decide, in advance, where the reclaimed hours go. Put them on the calendar against the work that generates revenue, and the most neglected item on that list is relationships. Write down the 50 people most likely to send you business. Most owners can name 10 without trying. Those 10 are where AI should be pointing you.

There are about 36 million small businesses in the U.S., and more than 80% of them have no employees. For those owners, AI isn’t a department upgrade. It’s a capability they never had. Owners should take the better tools the giants’ race produces. But the biggest gains won’t come from saving an hour. They’ll come from knowing which 50 relationships to spend it on.
The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

theatlantic.com/politics/2026/11/ice-mid.headline: The Blue Wave Can’t Stop ICE

paragraphs.text: “Deportations will continue,” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote in a post on X the day after voters punished his party in the midterm election. The three-word statement appeared to be aimed at quieting an incipient debate among Republicans over whether President Trump should ease his ICE crackdown. Two years after he won back the White House promising the largest mass-deportation campaign in U.S. history, Trump and his party suffered monumental losses in states such as Texas, Georgia, and North Carolina, where voters—especially Hispanics—swung hard to Democrats. More moderate Republicans have urged the administration to adopt a quieter enforcement approach, focusing more narrowly on criminal offenders.

Although the president has reportedly expressed concern to those close to him that some ICE tactics have gone too far, he has not ordered specific policy changes, according to three senior officials I spoke with at DHS. Those officials and others I’ve talked to told me they aren’t expecting a pullback, either. Trump’s decision to name Stephen Miller as his chief of staff yesterday places the chief architect and principal ideologue of the ICE campaign in charge of his administration. Miller’s promotion will give him even more power to mobilize other federal agencies to help ICE maximize deportations.

Since Trump’s return to the White House, Republicans in Congress have given the administration nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars for the crackdown, aiming for 1 million deportations a year. ICE has obtained upwards of $110 billion, more than 11 times its annual budget, and the funding surge has created a powerful inertia. Absent a major policy reversal from Trump or a successful intervention by Democratic majorities in Congress—a longshot, experts say—Trump’s mass-deportation campaign will continue with its mandate to add more officers, more deportation flights, and more immigration jails. The campaign includes handing out wads of cash to local police and sheriff departments, which help the agency boost arrests. Prior to the midterms, ICE launched a hiring push to add 5,000 more employees—mosty deportation officers—by the end of the year.

“Regardless of the political pressures that the White House may be feeling on immigration enforcement, the money creates a huge amount of momentum on its own,” Sarah Pierce, an immigration policy expert at the center-left think tank Third Way, told me. ICE has so much money that it will have to double its rate of spending to use it all before its deadline at the end of the 2029 fiscal year, she said. “Pulling that back would be extremely difficult for the White House.”
[Read: Losing the ‘big-ass truck’ vote]

Despite the midterm results, there hasn’t been a broad consensus in the Republican Party that overzealous ICE tactics were a vulnerability, and some right-wing commentators have pointed to exit-poll data showing that immigration was the top motivating issue for Republican voter turnout.

At a polling place in the Dallas suburbs where I spoke with voters on Tuesday, several of the Republican supporters I met said they wanted Trump to stay the course. “Gotta keep locking it down,” said Danny, a 32-year-old hospital staffer I met outside a public library in Plano, north of Dallas. Danny told me he didn’t want his last name published, because he worried that he’d be harassed. His hometown and surrounding Collin County were reliably Republican when he was growing up, he said, but the region’s economic boom had brought in more transplants. “They keep voting for Democrats,” he said. “Democrats vote for more immigration. It’s a vicious cycle.”

James Talarico, the Democratic winner of the Senate race in Texas, won Collin County by 12 points on Tuesday, a 23-point swing from Trump’s 2024 victory. It was the first time this century that Democrats have won statewide races in the county. Trump won nearly half the Hispanic vote nationwide in 2024, but this year Hispanics are estimated to have voted for Democrats by a 69–29 percent margin.

Could Democrats use their large majorities in Congress next year to force the administration to rein in ICE? Claire Trickler-McNulty, an attorney who has held several high-ranking roles at ICE, most recently during the Biden administration, told me that it will be hard for Democrats to change the trajectory of ICE spending. If Democrats pass an appropriations bill with language constraining or shifting ICE funds, Trump would have to sign it. “I don’t have a lot of confidence that he would sign that, but people I’ve talked to on the Hill feel like there may be a window or a path to a clawback, if you combine that with something he cares about,” Trickler-McNulty said.

Trump has said he doesn’t want to spend the next two years “vetoing everything,” although the White House has also circulated a photo of a red VETO hat sitting on the Resolute Desk with the president in the background. Trump told Politico late Tuesday night that he’d be willing to work with Democrats on immigration reform if it were “appropriate and good for the country.” But the possibility of such negotiations could reduce the likelihood that Trump orders a different tack for ICE in the meantime.

Mark Krikorian, the executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies, a leading immigration-restrictionist group, told me that the Trump administration has already shifted tactics, and could do so again. After the killings of two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis in January, Trump demoted Greg Bovino, the performative Border Patrol commander who was leading the crackdown in the city, and replaced Kristi Noem with Mullin, who said he wanted a more low-key ICE approach. That change marked the end of what Krikorian described as “theatricality,” generating ready-for-TV images of masked federal forces staging operations that thrilled the president’s base. But Krikorian said that an “imbalance” remains between “body-armor enforcement versus briefcase enforcement.”

Trump could direct ICE to conduct more enforcement at worksites—not necessarily with raids that would send people running, Krikorian said, but with mundane audits that check Social Security numbers and other documents. “Worksite enforcement is something that has been very much lacking in this administration,” he said. It’s a lot less photogenic and a lot less politically tumultuous to just send in some bureaucrats.”
[Read: The secretary of homeland]

ICE continued to ramp up, with less fanfare, after Minneapolis, and the agency is now making more than 50,000 arrests a month, its highest rate ever. Officers have achieved those levels in part by using automated technologies, such as license-plate readers, and powerful database tools to make more traffic stops. Those public encounters deepened the backlash to ICE over the summer when officers shot several unarmed immigrants—two fatally—as they attempted to drive away. City and state governments have joined in that backlash, a trend that could accelerate with the widespread Democratic victories this week. The mayor of Houston announced yesterday that the city’s police will no longer contact ICE about nonviolent offenders who lack legal status.

White-collar enforcement would not necessarily lead to arrests and deportations, but it would make it more likely for immigrants who are in the United States illegally to leave on their own, Krikorian said. The frustrations that Trump has been hearing from business owners may weigh against a crackdown on employers.

Vice President Vance, who is considering running for president in 2028, appeared to signal a preference for that approach on Wednesday in a lengthy X post that assessed the party’s defeat. Vance wrote that he was “open” to shifting ICE’s focus to businesses that “hire illegal labor,” but said he didn’t support “amnesty,” the catch-all term used by immigration hard-liners who oppose creating a path to legal status for the estimated 12 million to 15 million immigrants who are illegally present in the United States. “Anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” Vance wrote.

Pierce told me that she interpreted Vance’s post as a defense of the administration’s crackdown that was aimed at Republicans who view the midterm results as a rebuke. She said she’ll be watching to see if pressure on the administration to change tactics builds in the coming weeks or if the White House remains defensive and determined to follow the same course.
[Read: Repudiation]

There were also signs in Vance’s post of the conundrum that he and other potential Republican presidential candidates will likely face if they try to succeed Trump. Although there is broad support across the electorate for the deportation of immigrants who commit violent crimes or pose a threat to public safety, those immigrants represent only 10 to 20 percent of ICE arrests. Trump officials have spent the past two years appealing to the most ardent members of the MAGA movement, especially those who want DHS to be a tool of social and demographic transformation through the removal and “remigration” of millions of immigrants. Those views are too extreme for most voters in a general presidential election. But to win the party’s primaries,
Vance, or any other potential Republican candidate, may need to embrace them.
Ashley Parker and Michael Scherer contributed reporting.

sports.yahoo.com/articles/pittsburgh-pen.headline: Pittsburgh Penguins Ville Koivunen’s NHL Performance is Beginning to Impress

paragraphs.text: An overtime goal against the Nashville Predators has made many realize that Ville Koivunen projection for his future NHL performance is clearly making him a fixture in the lineup. He is showing a well-round game, early on in his NHL career. Let’s discuss the details.
An Expected Contract with an Unexpected Price

A 23-year-old restricted free agent with just 47 NHL games under his belt was the resume Ville Koivunen possessed when general manager Kyle Dubas and the Pittsburgh Penguins decided to extend him eight years on a contract with an average annual value of $4 million. He had scored just two NHL goals at the time of the deal.
The Penguins have re-signed restricted free agent forward Ville Koivunen to an eight-year contract.— Pittsburgh Penguins (@penguins) August 6, 2026
AHL-Level Excellence and Arriving Just When He’s Needed

While Koivunen hadn’t yet lit up the NHL, he has long established himself as a top-level producer at the AHL level. Coming over from the Carolina Hurricanes as part of the Jake Guentzel trade, Koivunen quickly established himself with the Penguins’ farm team, the Wilkes-Barre/Scranton Penguins. After scoring 21 goals and 56 points in 2024-25, a 13-goal, 43-point season in 2025-26 meant that Koivunen had done all he could at that level and just needed to find a way to break into the NHL lineup.

His chance came as a result of a ton of injuries to Pittsburgh’s forward group. Veterans like Evgeni Malkin, Rickard Rakell, as well as younger players like last year’s star acquisition Egor Chinakhov, have all found themselves falling out of the lineup. A team already struggling to find their flow, the Penguins responded to this adversity with increased opportunity for players like Koivunen, another trade acquisition, Rutger McGroarty, who came over from the Winnipeg Jets, and also, the Hendrix Lapierre trade, who was with the Washington Capitals. A general theme has emerged, and spots opening up for players like Koivunen and Lapierre have led to unexpected chemistry between the pair. They’ve been dominant in their time together.
Finally Putting it All Together

Ville Koivunen’s overtime winner may have put more attention on his performance, but he’s already been playing better than the credit he’s given for this season. A speedy and skilled winger capable of playing some defence, the biggest criticisms of Koivunen’s game have been his lack of physicality and his decision-making. The young forward would routinely get knocked off the puck when in transition or driving into opposing zones. Additionally, his decision-making had been lacking, with less-than-ideal passes to teammates or driving at inopportune times. This season, it’s evident Koivunen has worked hard on these issues, as he’s consistently able to make the smart play, using his speed and skill to keep possession or get his linemates better opportunities.

With two goals and five points in 14 games, Koivunen has made a marked difference wherever he’s placed in the lineup, playing stout defence and acting as a fast, speedy transition winger. His latest goal was a game-winner in overtime, a clean shot after extended time holding onto the puck that beat elite goaltender Juuse Saros after making a fantastic move to get away from the Nashville defence.
The Last Word

With injuries and rumours of veterans on the way out, the Penguins are primed to get younger and need players to emerge as staples in the line-up. Pittsburgh is not an organization that is interested in a full teardown rebuild just yet, and still needs players that can produce, develop, and become legitimate threats. Ville Koivunen seems primed to finally establish himself as one such player this season. Having cleaned up his deficiencies and focused on his strengths has evolved Koivunen’s game. Meanwhile, Head Coach Dan Muse and the coaching staff have all shown belief in the young star, with time on the power play, penalty kill, and overtime. In the 2026-27 NHL season, Ville Koivunen is establishing himself in the NHL.
