theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/07/blacko.headline: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/07/blacko.author: Luke Harding

paragraphs.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.

Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said.

Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.

The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.

The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.

They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.

In a series of social media posts, Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.

Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.

Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”

Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.

Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-07/.headline: California's Great America theme park is closing for good. Here's when
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-07/.author: Rong-Gong Lin II

paragraphs.text: The Santa Clara theme park’s final day of operation will be next Labor Day, ending a 51-year run as an attraction once seen as Northern California’s version of Disneyland — and a rite of passage for local teenagers.

The closure has long been expected, ever since Cedar Fair sold the park’s 112-acre footprint to San Francisco logistics real estate company Prologis in 2022 for $310 million — a considerable gain from when the former owner purchased the land from the city’s redevelopment agency for $150 million three years earlier.

The new owner continued leasing the land under the park to Great America, with the term ending in mid-2028 and an option to extend through mid-2033. But with Great America’s latest corporate owner, Six Flags, struggling financially after its merger with Cedar Fair, there have been clear signs that the park probably was going to close sooner rather than later.

Last year, Great America canceled most live entertainment and its seasonal Halloween- and Christmas-themed events. The park’s vice president and general manager, Barbara-Lea Granter, also left the company as Six Flags moved to a regional operating structure centralizing certain responsibilities at the corporate level. Six Flags closed its theme park near Washington, D.C., and named a new chief executive. The company sold seven more parks this year.

Great America originally was opened in 1976 by the Marriott Corp. and considered a jewel in the string of theme parks built as smaller, regional venues to give people more convenient — and less expensive — places to visit. The Great America branding was a nod to its opening during the nation’s bicentennial, with themed lands recalling periods of American history, including Orleans Place and 1920s-era Hometown Square.

At its entrance is Carousel Columbia — a rare double-decker attraction, reputedly the tallest in the world, that is also notable for having an array of animals besides horses to ride on, including pigs and rabbits. Amusement Today ranks the park’s Gold Striker among the top 20 wooden roller coasters in the world.

But the theme park had a history of failing to meet financial expectations, a reason why Marriott soon opted to sell. News reports at the time said Marriott had hoped the park would attract 3.5 million visitors a year, but actual attendance was only 2 million.

The city of Santa Clara bought the park through its redevelopment agency and later sold the assets to Kings Entertainment Co. The assets were sold again to Paramount Communications in 1992, then to Cedar Fair in 2006.

The city’s redevelopment agency kept the land on which the park sat until 2019, when it was forced to sell after the state abolished redevelopment agencies, and the city was not in a financial position to outbid Cedar Fair for the land.
Great America’s sister park near Chicago — Six Flags Great America — remains open.
The announcement of Great America’s closure follows recent headlines regarding ride safety concerns at other Six Flags parks.

Last month, a 42-year-old man fell to his death at Six Flags Over Georgia after being ejected from a roller coaster. Six Flags temporarily closed several attractions across the U.S. and Canada “out of an abundance of caution,” including the Goliath roller coaster at Magic Mountain in Valencia.
In September, Magic Mountain announced its famous X2 coaster would permanently close following a history of injuries, including some that led to deaths.

“We have launched a comprehensive review of ride safety across our entire portfolio, supported by independent third-party engineering and inspection specialists,” the president and chief executive of Six Flags, John Reilly, said in a statement Thursday.

cnbc.com/2026/11/07/iran-war-midterm-ele.headline: Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic sweep in U.S. midterm elections
cnbc.com/2026/11/07/iran-war-midterm-ele.author: Spencer Kimball

paragraphs.text: The U.S. and Iran are careening toward renewed war despite growing hopes this week that the Democrats' decisive midterm election victory will bring the conflict to an end, analysts say.

Crude oil prices fell more than 16% over the last five trading days after Vice President JD Vance publicly blamed the Republicans' stinging loss on the war. Vance's remarks raised questions about whether there is still support within the administration to continue the conflict with Iran.

The Democrats plan to use their comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress to pass a war powers resolution that demands President Donald Trump end the war. But tensions in the Middle East have not eased since the election, and the Democrats aren't sworn in until January, the analysts say.

"Throughout the week, we were struck by the divergence between deepening escalation concerns in the Gulf and the headline driven off-ramp optimism of market participants thousands of miles away," Helima Croft, head of global commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets, told investors in a note Friday.
More attacks

Several oil tankers have come under attack near Oman since the election, killing one seafarer, according to maritime security agencies. Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen continue to fire missiles at neighboring Saudi Arabia.

Meanwhile, the U.S. military buildup continues, with a third carrier strike group en route to the region. The consulting group Rapidan Energy sees an 80% chance that fighting will resume as diplomacy stalls.
President Donald Trump told reporters Thursday that he will make a decision soon on whether to attack Iran again.
"I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible but maybe I'll have to," Trump said in the Oval Office. "You'll know soon enough."
"We're locked and loaded," the president said. "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we're very much locked in."
Price risk

Crude oil prices will vault above $100 a barrel again in response to renewed fighting, said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading above $97 on Friday while U.S. crude was around $90.

"President Donald Trump is determined as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Friday.

"The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it," the analyst said. The escalation dynamic remains in place so long as that core difference between the U.S. and Iran persists, he said.

The risk of war is still alive, especially since Trump doesn't face anymore future elections, said Amos Hochstein, a former energy advisor to President Joe Biden. Gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices would all surge as a consequence, Hochstein told CNBC's "Power Lunch" Friday.
Iranian taunts

Tehran has been taunting the Trump administration since the election. The social media account of Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the "process of the U.S.'s collapse has accelerated" after the midterm results.
And Congress is unlikely to pass a war powers resolution until Democrats take control in January. Trump can veto such a resolution in any case.

The main leverage Congress will have is the power of the purse, Croft said. Government funding expires on Dec. 11 and negotiations for another continuing resolution could drag into 2027, she said. This would give Democrats more leverage when they take power in January, the analyst said.

"Importantly, deferring funding decisions would not immediately constrain Trump's ability to conduct military operations, but could significantly reshape the administration's longer-term funding outlook," Croft told investors.
Trump discussed diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the region with the emir of Qatar during a Friday phone call, according to Qatar's state news agency.

An unnamed senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Tehran sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar. Tehran will only discuss the proposal after the U.S. meets its demands, the Iranian official told Reuters.
Trump seemed to dismiss the diplomatic efforts Thursday.

"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," the president said. "They're not doing anything without our approval. It doesn't make any difference what they're looking at," he said of the diplomatic efforts.

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/07/r.headline: Two House Republicans battle to lead the party’s diminished ranks
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/07/r.author: Mariana Alfaro

paragraphs.text: House Republicans, shell-shocked by historic defeats Tuesday, will return to the Capitol next week for another election: one to determine who will shepherd their diminished ranks for the next two years, and shape the role they will play in the minority.

As it became clear that Democrats had won the majority back by a margin far beyond what most election prognosticators suggested, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) said Wednesday that he would not seek to stay on as minority leader.
By stepping away, Johnson set the stage for a rematch between two longtime rivals: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana) and Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio).
Jordan and Scalise are the only two running for the seat — members were given until Friday afternoon to file their intention to run for leadership.

While the two have publicly stood united behind Johnson during his tenure, they have both been chasing the top seat in the House GOP for years. Their most recent attempt came in 2023 during a chaotic speakership race, when an aggressive push by Jordan left both him and Scalise sidelined in favor of Johnson.

The two men have divergent styles — with Jordan seen as a firebrand and Scalise as a pragmatist. Jordan allies question whether Scalise, who served as Johnson’s No. 2, would represent a real change from the status quo. Scalise’s backers, meanwhile, ask whether Jordan has the temperament to rebuild a shattered conference.

Their campaign for the top spot began even before Johnson’s announcement; both men traveled widely this election, fundraising and campaigning for colleagues as they tried to build a base of support. Now, with the leadership election only days away, Jordan and Scalise are making their final pitches to their colleagues.

Jordan is suggesting that the party adopt an aggressive strategy to defend President Donald Trump against Democrats’ planned investigations in the next two years. Scalise is asking for unity in the wake of the major losses, and after four years in which the squabbles of an unruly GOP majority sometimes made it difficult to get Republican priorities passed.

In a letter to colleagues Wednesday, Jordan touted his record as a veteran of both the Oversight and Judiciary committees — both of which are expected to play key roles in any Trump investigations — and argued that he is the best-positioned candidate to fight back against the incoming Democratic majority.

“I know what it will take to lead our conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the Democrats’ tactics,” he wrote. “We need a leadership team that is active and engaged, forward-thinking and straight-shooting.”

Scalise, in his own letter Thursday, said his “number one goal as Republican Leader will be to win back the majority and I expect you to hold me accountable to that mission.” He also argued that the GOP needs to do more than battle Democrats.
“To succeed, we will need to be effective in both the oversight and legislative fights ahead, but we will also need to lay out a clear and optimistic vision for America,” Scalise wrote.
Jordan, a founding member of the right-wing House Freedom Caucus, will probably receive the support of many of its members.
Freedom Caucus chairman Andy Harris (R-Maryland) has endorsed Jordan, telling Newsmax on Thursday that the Ohio lawmaker is “the type of communicator we need.”
While the Freedom Caucus — which has about 30 members — suffered some losses Tuesday, the majority of Republican members who did not get reelected were part of the party’s larger, more-moderate wing.

That moderate wing contains many of Scalise’s closest allies, and its reduced numbers could complicate Scalise’s bid. Still, his backers told The Washington Post that the longtime No. 2 enjoys widespread support in the conference.

Several Republicans backing Scalise told The Post that he is the candidate most likely to lead the party back to a majority in 2028. One of those supporters, Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart (R-Florida) said that Scalise will be able to recapture the majority by turning the party “back to basics.”
“The basics are: the economy, national security,” he said.

The chief of staff of a member who was ousted Tuesday, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the election’s aftermath, noted that Jordan is well-equipped to handle defense on investigations.

But the staffer questioned Jordan’s recent efforts to present himself as a unifier, citing his history of engaging in procedural fights, including his participation in the effort to push out former Speaker Kevin McCarthy in 2023.

“Breathing fire, sure, but then what?” this aide said. “The new conference is going to have a different composition, and it’s still going to have people that aren’t necessarily all fire breathers. They’re workhorses.”
Jordan’s backers dismiss those concerns, and say a vote for Scalise would be a vote for the team that led the House GOP to one of its worst defeats in recent history.
Rep. Marlin A. Stutzman (R-Indiana) said Thursday on Newsmax that he is going to support Jordan because the party needs “new leadership, new voices.”

“I appreciate everything they’ve done and tried to do, but it didn’t work,” Stutzman said, later adding, “I’m a business guy, and if in business all of a sudden you lose that much of your work to your competitor, you’re going to fire people.”
Besides the race for minority leader, Republicans will choose a new No. 2 and No. 3 this week.
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minnesota), the current No. 3 House Republican, is running for minority whip — the No. 2 spot.
House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Michigan) is running to keep her position, and would be the No. 3 House Republican if she wins.
Both are facing relatively unexpected challenges from younger members of the party, who are arguing that it is time to swap out the leadership at all levels.
Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas) is challenging Emmer for the whip position, and Reps. Erin Houchin (R-Indiana) and Greg Steube (R-Florida) are challenging McClain.

Harris, the Freedom Caucus chairman, told Newsmax he thinks Emmer will remain as whip, “but I think a lot of the other positions will undergo changes, which is expected when you get a drubbing in an election.”

Although McClain, as is expected of conference chairs, was heavily involved shaping the GOP’s messaging and often campaigned on behalf of Republicans this cycle, some members say she should not be blamed for the losses. And several said that she ought to stay in her role as well.
“Her experienced leadership is needed now more than ever,” said Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois).
Some members told The Post that House GOP leaders are not to blame for the midterm results — or the two years of slow governing in the House.

“Anybody that blames our leadership for the losses that Republicans suffered in this election is misguided,” said Rep. Mike Simpson (R-Idaho). “When you look at the things that we couldn’t do, it wasn’t the Democrats’ fault; it was the Republicans’ fault that wouldn’t vote [to move legislation forward].”

Others were more direct: “In my race, yes the district changed. The district is really difficult, but my opponent wasn’t my opponent. My opponent was Trump, every time he opened his mouth,” said a House Republican who survived a competitive race, and who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the leadership races.
Whoever led the conference, and whatever their message was, this member said, “just didn’t matter.”

decoded.legal/blog/2026/11/running-a-law.headline: Running a law firm on Free software (2026 edition)

paragraphs.text: Published on: 2026-11-06 12:18:47 by Neil Brown

I started running decoded.legal - a small English law firm, focussing on Internet, telecoms, and tech law - on Free software, both client and server side, around five years ago. I have used Free software in my personal life for a lot longer than that.
Back in 2022, I wrote about my experiences after the first year or so.
I wrote an update in 2024.
Someone asked me recently what I am doing now, and, while it is mostly the same, some bits have changed. So here is the 2026 update.
Client-side stuff
I am still using Debian, with GNOME, and it works well for me.

I’m using it on a ThinkPad X1 Yoga Gen 6, as my primary machine, and, being a “Yoga” version, I rather like being able to fold the screen back and write on it to mark up documents. (Here are my thoughts on the different “Active Pens” available for it.)

However, the machine itself seems to have a hardware problem with the Thunderbolt / USB-C ports (fine for power, very flaky for data), and so I might need to replace it. And I have no idea what laptop I might get.

• Email (MUA): Thunderbird and mutt, depending on what I am doing Quick Folder Move and Move Message And Yourself are particularly useful add-ons for Thunderbird, for rapid filing of email with keyboard shortcuts Thunderbird seems to be having a problem with some recurring calendar invitations, while ikhal is handling them fine. I’ve not dug into it, but it is a nuisance.

• Document production: LibreOffice’s Writer if I want a “Word” document (e.g. I am exchanging documents with other lawyers), and I am using pandoc and typst to convert Markdown files that I tend to write in vim for some other bits. I’d like to explore tex at some point, as I have a client who likes diffs to their .tex files, and that looks rather neat.

• Presentations: reveal.js I absolutely love this. I have a bash script which sets up a template for a new presentation, and then I just write the presentation using Markdown. I get a nicely-formatted presentation (using a css template) with very little effort, and no distracting GUI Blogpost about reveal.js Here are some presentations I’ve given, using reveal.js
• File manager: Nautilus Mainly because it is GNOME’s default, although, especially when combined with some useful bash scripts, it works well for my needs
• PDFs: evince for most reading; Xournal++ for marking up PDFs; PDFarranger and pdftk for interfering with PDFs
• Text expansion: espanso This is a fantastic shortcut for me, saving me from typing the same thing multiple times. I have loads of shortcuts set up, and I’d be lost without them.

• Browser: Firefox or links I am still using Firefox. It is … fine? I should probably look at LibreWolf or another fork, as I’m not enamoured by Mozilla’s direction of travel but, for now, Firefox it is. I use Firefox for joining people’s Teams and Zoom etc. meetings, if someone else sets up the meeting, and that works fine
• Local wiki / knowledge management: vimwiki because I use vim so much, vimwiki was quite an obvious choice. I use this for keeping track of my professional development, and for various notes
• Disk encryption: LUKS
• Client-side encryption of files before syncing them with Syncthing: Cryptomator

• Fediverse: I tend to use the Mastodon advanced web UI or, when I want fewer images, the TUI toot. I schedule toots - for example, about blogposts, using a simple bash script and a cron job; it has moved on a bit since I wrote that post, but it is the same principle
• Password manager: Bitwarden, using the vaultwarden server, with YubiKeys for managing more sensitive credentials
• Markdown editor (for blogposts; I do presentations in vim or gedit): Apostrophe
• Scanning: paperless-ngx
• Label printing: there’s a great FOSS web UI for Brother (and perhaps other) label printers. I don’t print many labels, as we aim to be paperless, but it’s convenient when I need to do so

Why so many terminal-based tools? The simple answer is that I am very comfortable in a terminal, and I like them. They have fewer distractions and, when compared with most GUI software, are just - IMHO - easier to use, especially when I don’t need to move my hands away from the keyboard. So, while I don’t use them exclusively, I use mutt, vim, ikhal, ncmpcpp, newsboat, toot, links, and various other TUIs, frequently.
Server-side stuff
Everything here - other than Signal - is self-hosted, and I’m mostly using Intel NUCs now. I still have some Raspberry Pi devices, but fewer than I did.
(Again, this doesn’t list everything; just the main applications.)
• Email (MTA): postfix / dovecot I need to move our mail infrastructure at some point, and I want to look at Stalwart.

• File synchronisation: Syncthing One of the bigger changes since last time was moving away from Nextcloud. I just was not getting on with it, and it was causing me more problems than it solved. So I switched to Syncthing for file sync, and radicale for CalDAV / CardDAV. I’ve been more than happy with this combination.

• Video conferencing: Signal I ran jitsi for years, but stopped using it a few months back. Jitsi is great, and I remain a fan, but most of the time I am joining other people’s Teams or Zoom meetings, so I was running the Jitsi server for very little usage. I turned it off, and instead offer Signal. I have had no grumbles.
• Invoicing and tracking payments: InvoicePlane, just for generating PDF invoices. Clients don’t interact with it
• Time tracking: Kimai v2 of Kimai is excellent, and I had a very pleasant exchange with the developer, which is always nice.
• “Case management” / “Matter management”: EspoCRM
• VPN: WireGuard, using trailofbit’s algo ansible scripts on one machine, and PiVPN on another (albeit not on a Pi)
• Vulnerability scanning: greenbone/OpenVAS
• Monitoring: Uptime Kuma I implemented this not long after the last update. It … just works?

• Forge / hosted git repository: Forgejo I use this for version tracking the website, and for a couple of template projects I do not host anything particularly important on it - for that, I have a git process running on another machine, which is not accessible over the Internet, and I just push to that
• SIEM: Wazuh
• Password manager: vaultwarden

• Website: it is a static site built via mkdocs, hosted on apache2 It got even simpler and even faster to load. Yes, it’s basic, but I like it! We still have an .onion version. If you visit decoded.legal in Tor Browser, it should re-direct your automatically

• Blog: BSSG After a couple of annoyances with hugo, I moved to BSSG - a bash static site generator. The developer, Stefano, is amazing, and it is working incredibly well. I’ve gone for a very basic, easy to read, theme - which should be very similar to what was there before - and there’s still an RSS feed for it, of course I blog quite frequently, and, rather than keep private / internal “knowhow” files, I tend to just blog things and share the learnings I tend to use my personal blog for posts about the more technical bits and pieces I have automated the most common actions - templates, and publishing - using bash scripts, so that I can focus on writing (in Markdown); getting it online is the easiest bit

• Fediverse: I am using the *glitch-soc Mastodon** fork Switching from normal Mastodon to glitch-soc Mastodon was easy I stopped using Markdown in toots, even though I like the rendered output (i.e. as html not as markdown), but this is not supported consistently well across clients, so I stopped using it. I turned off decoded.legal’s own fedi instance. I had been on the fence as to whether this is worthwhile or not for a while, and decided that, really, it was not.
• Knowledge management, and managing our law firm’s (numerous) policies and procedures: dokuwiki with the Markdown plugin
• DNS: unbound, with Pi-Hole in front of it I used to run a doh server, but I’ve stopped doing that.
• Backups: restic and rsync Notes on restic

• Forms: LiberaForms I have been really happy with LiberaForms, for easy-to-create and easy-to-use forms, especially since they implemented encryption, so that the form responses are stored encrypted on the server. I still delete them as soon as I can, but knowing that they are encrypted in the database is welcome. I use LiberaForms for our “Know Your Client” pre-engagement questionnaire, and for various other bits
• Collaborative document editing: I don’t. I used to run CryptPad, but it just didn’t get much use, so I turned it off.
AI tools
None, for various reasons.
Mobile device
I’m using a Pixel running GrapheneOS for my mobile device.
I use F-Droid as the main app store.

Using Android doesn’t thrill me, especially given Google’s direction of travel, but at the moment - despite trying quite a lot of different OSs and devices, including postmarketOS and Ubuntu Touch, as well as SailfishOS previously - I have not found something that does what I need better than GrapheneOS.
Working with others (who don’t use FOSS tools)
No change here: zero problems.
Many of my clients use Microsoft’s software, or Apple’s software.
All posts CC BY-SA-NC 4.0 or any later version, unless otherwise stated.
This blog is for interest only; nothing here is legal advice.
This blog was written by a human, without AI.
This site was generated with BSSG, a Bash Static Site Generator.

engadget.com/2305270/samsung-one-ui-9-co.headline: 10 Of The Coolest Features In Samsung's New One UI 9 Update
engadget.com/2305270/samsung-one-ui-9-co.author: Max Sheridan

paragraphs.text: Your Samsung device has a lot of new tricks to explore.

Samsung One UI 9 recently started rolling out to more devices, and it gives everyone from the seasoned power user to the lock screen enthusiast something to be excited about. As with all system updates, some of the new tech you'll find under your Samsung device's hood is just plain fun. The One UI 9 kit added some neat background styling options for Favorites tiles and an AI-enhanced clock that blends into your lock screen photo.
But One UI 9 isn't just bling; there are quite a few useful new features you'll want to take for a spin. You just have to know what to look for.
1. More Quick Panel customizations

Yes, it's an enhanced control center. But given how many times your fingers go there every day, being able to make the space your own makes it more functional. One seemingly tiny detail of Samsung's Quick Panel overhaul makes this clear: dark mode is now a standalone button, separate from the display slider. For dark mode fans, this is a super useful way to override system settings with a single tap.

One UI 9 also makes reorganizing and sizing controls easier with granular vertical and horizontal resizing, which includes the media playback widget. Organizing shortcut widgets also became easier, as you can now drag and drop them into whatever order you want. To start customizing, tap the pencil icon at the top of the Quick Panel.
2. Camera improvements galore
Shoot in 24MP

Samsung added a mid-range 24MP resolution option for photos in One UI 9 when previously, we had to pick between 12MP and 50MP. 12MP can feel skimpy for photos that need to look good, while 50MP pics can eat up too much storage. So 24MP is a Goldilocks pixel density that should feel just right.

To enable this, install Good Lock if you haven't already, then search for and enable the Camera Assistant module within Good Lock. Then open Camera Assistant, access the Advanced Resolution Options and enable 24 MP resolution.
Turn your Samsung device into a webcam

Samsung phones have traditionally been great for shooting video, so you might have wished you could ditch your less-than-stellar laptop webcam for the higher-resolution phone camera. While this was possible before, it required clunky workarounds with extra apps and account logins. Now, you can achieve it with a direct USB connection.

After connecting your phone to your computer with a USB cable, pull down the notification shade and tap the USB for entry to change how your phone is connected. Choose Webcam, then you're ready to select your phone as a camera in your video calling app of choice.
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is perfect for this because it balances on surfaces by itself. For non-folding phones, you'll likely need some kind of stand or clip.
Own TikTok with My Fan Cam

My Fan Cam is a new AI-powered feature that lets you resize a video's aspect ratio (its width and height proportions). This means if you shoot a video of your daughter's ballet troupe and want to focus on only her, you can zoom in on her and crop the rest of the video out, turning a 16x9 pageant into a 9x16 one-woman TikTok show.

For photos, the object eraser has also gotten smarter. Tap the pencil icon while viewing a photo to access the eraser, then your device can identify unwanted elements without you having to draw over them manually. This makes it easier to remove everyone but your daughter from the stage.
3. Gesture Wake-up and multi-finger gestures

If you need some info in a pinch and don't feel like saying "hi" to Bixby, Samsung has given you a quicker way to summon your AI assistant. The setting to enable is Gesture Wake-up: go to Settings > Advanced Features > Bixby to find it.

After toggling Gesture Wake-up on, all you have to do is lift your phone to your lips (an inch away will do; you don't have to kiss Bixby) and start talking. Bixby, who has gotten a lot chattier lately, should snap out of its slumber and respond.

One UI 9 also offers perhaps the most ornate swiping experience in modern mobile history with its new Multi-Finger Gesture library. Two fingers, three fingers, five fingers — you can use all these gestures to unlock up to five personalized actions. For example, you might set swiping left with two fingers to bring up your screenshots, while swiping right with four fingers splits your screen in two.

To use these, install the Home Up module inside Good Lock, then open it, select Multi-finger gesture and configure as desired. If there is such a thing as too much swiping, you will find that limit with this feature.
4. Live data speed monitoring

To understand why Samsung's latest status bar addition is so great, we only have to hark back to the old days of, say, One UI 7. Imagine you were at Bojangles and couldn't open up Engadget to read our review of the iPhone Duo. Is the problem your phone, the website, your mobile provider or something else? At your wit's end, you would have to fall back on a third-party speed test app to realize you were stuck because Bojangles' Wi-Fi was moving at dial-up speeds.

One UI 9's Live Data Speed monitor makes this assessment much easier by showing your real-time connection speeds (Wi-Fi and cellular) right in the status bar at the top of your screen. Enabling this feature is slightly cumbersome for how useful it is. As with many of the other tweaks here, you'll need the Good Lock app if you don't have it already. Inside that app, find and enable QuickStar, then look for Visibility of Indicator Icons and toggle it on. Network speed should now appear among your status bar options; activate it and you're set.
5. Better privacy controls

It's easy to grant apps permissions when you're not paying attention. But it's trickier to remove them, since doing so involves tapping through multiple menus. While One UI 9 doesn't fix this completely, it makes one common permission type easier to manage.

The new Privacy Indicator is a blue button that sits in your status bar and tells you which apps are currently sharing your location. Tap the pop-up to see what's tracking you, which gives you a shortcut to control its access if needed. This joins the green Samsung dot that lets you know your camera is in use.
Hopefully, Samsung's next feature drop will include even more privacy indicators, since our phones have many other ways to monitor us.
6. App multitasking tweaks

As Samsung device screens get bigger and bigger, especially with wide foldables like the Galaxy Z Fold8, you have more real estate for showing multiple apps at once. There are various ways for this to be useful, like checking your calendar while you're on the phone booking an appointment with your dentist. Or you can have fun instead of being productive, like playing Vampire Survivors while watching someone else play Vampire Survivors.

One UI 9 gives multitaskers the option to fit up to three apps onto their screens at once. So now, you can play Vampire Survivors while watching someone else play Vampire Survivors and follow an eBay auction at the same time. If that's not enough multitasking for you, One UI 10 will be here soon enough.
7. Searchable screenshots

Screenshot innovations aren't something you would expect from a major update, but you'll probably end up using these. Often, we amass screenshots of all kinds that just sit there in our images folder helter-skelter.

One UI 9's AI-fueled Gallery app turns the previously unwanted screenshot into something more by organizing them into useful, clickable categories like QR codes, receipts, boarding passes and similar. That means all those screenshots you've taken over the years have more utility and are easier to surface.
You can also search for screenshots just by typing keywords. To give it a spin, open the Gallery app, tap Albums, then choose Screenshots.
8. Game Booster while you game

About 84 percent of gamers play on their phones, with more than a third of those playing exclusively on mobile. This explains why Samsung, after updating its Mobile Gaming Hub, has made accessing its Game Booster controls easier in One UI 9. To make them appear, just swipe right from the left of the screen while you're playing.

While the tools themselves haven't changed, you can now call them up while you're playing instead of pausing your game to track them down in app settings. So if you want to ramp down performance to save battery life, the button is right there. The same goes for system CPU/GPU monitoring, screen sensitivity and recording and commenting while you're playing.
You can also block Bixby from interrupting your games with a weather or stock market announcement. To have a look, visit Gaming Hub > More > Game Booster.
9. Now nudge everywhere

Now nudge, Samsung's AI suggestion prompt engine, originally shipped at the beginning of the year with One UI 8.5. Its latest iteration in One UI 9 isn't much smarter, but you will find it in more places.

Until One UI 9, Now nudge communicated mostly while you were messaging. If you were chatting with a friend about dinner plans, it would prompt you to save the date in your calendar: tap the prompt, make a calendar item and you were all set without leaving the messaging app.

Now, those nudges aren't restricted to the keyboard. You'll find them in other places, like chat notifications and even as a floating button. To serve you those prompts, Samsung's AI butler needs access to heaps of your personal data. The more it knows, the better it can "nudge" you about details you would otherwise have to double-check yourself.

This is definitely neat, but it's also a potential privacy concern. To enable Now nudge, you need to turn on Personal Data Intelligence (Settings > Security and privacy > More privacy settings). Samsung clearly states that all data is processed on your phone "unless you consent to share it with Samsung or its partners for better recommendations." It's unclear, however, where and when you'd be giving your consent, so keep your eyes open. Samsung's Personal Data Engine has been running since One UI 7 and it's fueled by user data.
10. A revamped scanner
Samsung has had a fairly reliable scanner built into its cameras for years. With One UI 9, it received an AI boost.

The major improvement with the latest system update is a scanner that intuitively knows how to remove creases, folds and even curves from documents. The result is a much smoother scan, which is especially useful when you have a book with a spine and are scanning two pages at once.

Samsung's revamped scanner will also remove your thumbs — well, not your actual thumbs, but it will erase "thumb shadows" produced when you attempt to wrangle a book or crumpled document into submission on a flat surface. Use the Finger Eraser option for that.

The improved scanner also does a better job compensating for glare and moiré, an undulating pattern produced when black and white lines are slightly off-kilter. For scanner super-users, One UI 9 has even added a Home screen shortcut.

cnbc.com/2026/11/07/socialism-elections-.headline: America doesn't like socialism. So why are socialists winning?
cnbc.com/2026/11/07/socialism-elections-.author: Luke Fountain, Alex Harring

paragraphs.text: Democratic socialists just had their biggest election night yet.
There's just one complication: Most American voters don't actually like socialism.

Six candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America won House seats Tuesday, giving the movement its largest foothold yet in Congress and greater clout in a Democratic Party already divided over how far left to go.

The victories, coming on the heels of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's rise to power, mark another milestone for a movement that has spent years challenging the party establishment. Now, with Democrats sweeping control of Congress, the question is whether those electoral gains will translate into actual political power.

The results of the new CNBC Voter Poll show the potential hazard of handing too much power to the party's left flank. The survey of roughly 80,000 midterm voters found that 53% view socialism unfavorably, compared with 33% who viewed it favorably. Capitalism fared considerably better, with 56% expressing a positive view. Just 18% of voters identified themselves as democratic socialists.

That disconnect underscores both the opportunity and the challenge facing Democrats and their growing left flank. How the party reconciles the divide between reforming capitalism and fundamentally overhauling it could shape its legislative agenda in Congress, its economic message to voters and, ultimately, its direction heading into the 2028 presidential election.
A mixed night for the left
The DSA's presence in Congress will be quadrupled when Tuesday's victors, all of whom won in safely Democratic districts, are sworn in.

But the projected Democratic landslide of more than 250 House seats could dilute their influence. Party leaders could afford to lose all eight DSA votes on most measures, leaving the group with far less bargaining power than it would wield in a narrowly controlled chamber.

Still, the movement is building financial muscle. While the DSA relies on membership dues, wealthy donors are now backing its candidates through outside groups. The 12 largest donors to American Priorities, a super PAC supporting some DSA-backed candidates, gave nearly $5.9 million this cycle, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings through Oct. 31.

"We've had success with more donors but also we have an even stronger ground game to spread our message," said Megan Romer, co-chair of the DSA. "Mailers and ads alone just don't do it anymore. You have to knock on more doors and make more phone calls and talk to more people at work and in your union."
The more revealing tests on Tuesday came outside of liberal enclaves.

In Florida, DSA member Angie Nixon came within three percentage points of an upset in a state where Democrats haven't won a Senate race since 2012 and President Donald Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. But she lost by a wider margin than Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly, who took a more moderate approach.

Michigan told a similar story. Progressive Abdul El-Sayed – backed by self-described democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., – won his Senate seat by seven percentage points. Yet he lagged nearly four percentage points behind Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson's winning margin.
El-Sayed shares many DSA priorities but neither belongs to the group nor received its endorsement. He says he favors reforming capitalism over replacing it.

State ballot initiatives offered an equally mixed ideological verdict: Nearly two-thirds of voters in ruby-red Montana backed limits on corporate political spending, while deep-blue California rejected a billionaire wealth tax by roughly 10 percentage points, even as voters approved higher income taxes on the wealthy.

The results sharpen the dilemma over Democrats' identity heading into 2028, as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., the DSA's most prominent standard-bearer, seemingly weighs a White House bid: Can left-wing populism expand the party's coalition without alienating the swing-state moderates it needs to win a presidential election – especially in a less favorable political environment?
"I think a lot of people did vote for Democrats who would not ordinarily and who probably did it ... with their teeth gritted," Romer told CNBC.
Capitalism or socialism?
But it's clear that even voters who reject socialism aren't satisfied with capitalism as it stands.

Three out of every four participants in the CNBC Voter Poll said the condition of the U.S. economy was poor or not so good, compared with just 2% who described it as excellent. And 70% said the economic system favors the wealthy rather than treating most Americans fairly.

That frustration helped fuel a populist message far beyond the socialist left, with victorious Democrats from Adam Hamilton in Kansas to James Talarico in Texas tapping into anger over rising costs, economic inequality and the political influence of wealthy elites. Eighteen Sanders-endorsed candidates also won, including in traditionally right-leaning states like Ohio and Montana.

"The real fight in this country is not left versus right. It is top versus bottom," Talarico, who flipped a Senate seat for Democrats in the Lone Star state, said in his victory speech. "The people at the top work so hard to keep us angry and divided because our unity is a threat to their wealth and their power."
Even politicians who weren't on the ballot took note. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a video posted to X Friday that "Democrats won by being populist economic fighters."

Economists have pointed to measures showing increasing wealth concentration and a shrinking share of the U.S. GDP heading to workers in the form of pay as signs that the divide between the country's rich and poor is widening. Coming out of the pandemic, the "K"-shaped economy has become a common descriptor for the unequal recovery seen by income classes.
Americans displayed their economic dissatisfaction well before they headed to the polls this week. The University of Michigan's closely followed consumer sentiment index hit all-time lows this year.
"We have a rising tide that is not equally lifting all boats," said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, a tax firm. "That's not what we used to tell ourselves when we were young."

Rather than signaling a distaste for capitalism as a whole, Brusuelas said this week's results show voters want a system that also includes populist policies like Medicare for all. Or, as he calls it, "capitalism with a human face."
"These things are not mutually exclusive," said Brusuelas, who regularly briefs members of Congress on policy issues. "We can walk and chew gum at the same time."
Wall Street readies

Tuesday's Democratic sweep left some on Wall Street racing to prepare their clients' portfolios for potential policy shifts. Bank of America analysts detailed what heightened scrutiny of social media platforms or artificial intelligence data centers could mean for the shares of companies in those industries. CIBC built a basket of stocks that should benefit from a Democratically controlled Congress.
Still, the reaction of Wall Street veterans and New York City business moguls to this week's election was relatively subdued compared with Mamdani's victory in the mayoral race last year.

After Mamdani clinched his party's nomination, Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman said he was "a bit depressed." Ahead of Mamdani's victory, Kathryn Wylde, who leads the Partnership for New York City, a nonprofit group of business executives, told CNBC that "terror is the feeling" as he rose in the polls.

Wall Street magnates wondered how a city known as the epicenter of financial markets and global capitalism could survive under a self-described socialist. Some questioned if billionaires would flee the city or whether corporations would move their headquarters — fears that largely haven't materialized since Mamdani took office.

With roughly 10 months of Mamdani's term in the rearview mirror, Anthony Chan, the former chief economist at JPMorgan, said finance moguls have realized that politics don't necessarily result in material policy changes. Chan said it's a message they've carried with them exiting this week, with many understanding that any incoming lawmakers in Washington aligned with democratic socialist policies would be a small minority.

"Many of the people that I meet that were very adamantly against and opposed to his candidacy now are sending their kids to his free daycare centers," Chan said, referencing Mamdani's partnership with the state to expand no-cost programs for 2-year-olds in New York City.

"I thought you felt that the world was going to end if this mayor came in," said Chan, who's also an alumnus of Barclays and the New York Federal Reserve. "Now, you're sending your kids to his free daycare centers."

But the DSA has even bigger ambitions for 2028. With growing political clout, infrastructure and financial backing, the movement is looking to expand its influence nationwide, while one of its most prominent allies, Ocasio-Cortez, weighs a White House run.
"That infrastructure is there, and that will make a big difference for a potential left presidential candidate," Romer said. "It's really kind of do or die time. We really have to deliver."

theguardian.com/law/2026/nov/07/court-of.headline: Court rules against Home Office in asylum seeker kidnapping case
theguardian.com/law/2026/nov/07/court-of.author: Diane Taylor

paragraphs.text: The court of appeal has rejected claims by the Home Office that being kidnapped for ransom is not exploitation of trafficking victims.

The ruling means that many people who have been kidnapped for ransom, whom officials have previously excluded from being victims of exploitation under trafficking rules, will now have to have these claims considered. They may be eligible for the support and recovery package trafficking victims are entitled to.

Being kidnapped for ransom is a common hazard for asylum seekers passing through Libya on their journey to Europe. Many are fleeing conflict in countries such as Sudan and Eritrea as well as some Middle Eastern countries.

The legal challenge was brought by a Syrian asylum seeker who cannot be identified. The 25-year-old fled forced military conscription in July 2021, knowing he was likely to be imprisoned and tortured in Syria for refusing to fight.

He arrived in Libya, ultimately hoping to reach the UK. He and other Syrians were abducted by armed men and held in captivity for a month between August and September 2021. His money and phone were seized and they were driven through the desert for 24 hours, hearing gunshots, with no food and little water.

They were told they would not be released until their families agreed to pay a ransom of several thousand dollars. He was tied up and often beaten on his hands and feet by his kidnappers. He and the other captives had to phone their families to beg them to pay their kidnappers the ransom money. While they were on the phone, the kidnappers beat them so their families could hear screams. He was terrified that even if his family paid his captors, he might not be released and that his organs might be harvested.

The man was released after his family paid his kidnappers, and he made his way to Europe, crossing the Mediterranean from Libya to Italy by boat. He crossed the Channel from France to the UK on 16 May 2022 and claimed asylum.

The Home Office rejected his trafficking claim, arguing that because he had not been subjected to forced labour by his kidnappers, his experience did not meet the definition of exploitation in the trafficking rules. He challenged the decision in the high court, which ruled in his favour. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, appealed against the ruling.

While the government has pledged to support trafficking victims, the decision to exclude asylum seekers kidnapped for ransom in Libya has denied many the support the judges ruled they may be entitled to. Recent freedom of information data relating to asylum seekers who were confirmed to be genuine trafficking victims found that of the 1,778 confirmed victims between July 2024 and July 2025, 89% were forcibly removed from the UK, putting them at risk of being trafficked again.

While each trafficking claim must be considered on the facts of the individual case, the judgment found: “The secretary of state erred in not considering the question of whether kidnapping amounted to exploitation.”

The ruling could help thousands of potential trafficking victims, not only those who arrive in Britain in the future but also those previously rejected as being trafficking victims who were kidnapped and held to ransom in Libya. They can now get a fresh referral into the national referral mechanism for a new decision on whether there are reasonable grounds for them to be considered a victim of trafficking.

Jeremy Bloom, a consultant solicitor at Duncan Lewis, who represented the Syrian man, welcomed the ruling. “This judgment is a vindication of my client’s claim to be a victim of trafficking. The Home Office sought to restrict the definition of exploitation,” he said.

“We hope that it will also assist other victims of trafficking who have experienced similarly horrendous treatment to gain access to the leave and support that they need to recover from those experiences. Those individuals may include people who have had their claims to be a victim of trafficking refused, and who might now be able to ask for a new decision based on the law as set out in this judgment.”

Home Office sources said it would not be appropriate to comment on legal proceedings. A Home Office spokesperson said:“We are simplifying and strengthening protection and immigration routes, ensuring they are clear, targeted and focused on their intended purpose, while maintaining fairness and public confidence.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/06/world/asia/new-ze.headline: New Zealand’s Election ‘Too Close to Call’ as Voters Turn to Minor Parties

paragraphs.text: New Zealand went to the polls on Saturday to decide who will lead the country at a moment of economic sluggishness and widespread political discontent. Preliminary results showed no clear front-runner, with many disgruntled voters choosing smaller parties over the major players.

Both Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s National Party, which is governing in a conservative coalition, and the main opposition, the center-left Labour Party, had been polling at near historic lows, signaling voters’ lack of faith in their ability to steer the nation out of its malaise.

Early results after polls closed at 7 p.m. local time showed the National Party neck and neck with Labour, both around 29.4 percent, with about 78 percent of the vote counted, according to the Electoral Commission.
Whichever party finishes first will almost certainly need to build a coalition to form a government under the country’s mixed-member, proportional electoral system.

The makeup will depend on the votes garnered by the libertarian ACT party and the populist New Zealand First on the right, and the Green Party and Maori Party on the left. A newly ascendant, centrist Opportunity Party is most likely to end up playing the role of kingmaker after clearing the 5 percent threshold to enter Parliament for the first time.

All votes are counted by hand, and the official result will not be released until Nov. 27. Negotiations for the formation of a government could take days or weeks, and may even stretch into the new year.
Here is what to watch for:
Cost of Living Worries

The victors will have a daunting task to turn around a dire economic picture that has many New Zealanders feeling bleak about their outlook and increasingly viewing moving overseas as the only option for making a decent living.

A surging cost of living is a leading concern, with four in 10 New Zealanders saying in a recent survey by the University of Otago that they were struggling to pay for essentials. Unemployment has edged up to 5.7 percent, the highest level since 2013. The country saw nearly 40,000 more citizens moving away than returning annually over the past two years.
Mr. Luxon and the National Party have sought to persuade voters to give them another chance at tackling inflation and government debt.
Chris Hipkins, who has led the Labour Party since Jacinda Ardern’s resignation in 2023, has centered his messaging on commitments to bring down health care and transportation costs.
Both parties were polling under 30 percent across multiple surveys leading up to the election.

“What we have seen from the two Chrises is a distinct lack of leadership, charisma and hope,” said Shamubeel Eaqub, the chief economist at Simplicity, a New Zealand fund management company. “This election, I think, will be remarked upon as one that was unsettling for its lack of vision and lack of hope at a time when people were really looking for it.”
Minor Parties, Major Roles
Lackluster support for the two major players has meant increased backing for the minor parties, each with its own priorities, personalities and political strategies.

All but one of the governments formed since the country adopted its current system in 1996 have been a coalition. Even so, the smaller parties will most likely play a larger role this time, with polls indicating that many will take a larger share of votes as people look for alternatives.

One contender that has emerged as a possible kingmaker is the Opportunity Party, headed by Qiulae Wong, a Fiji-born 38-year-old former business consultant. She has said Opportunity would be willing to work with either of the major parties to form a government.

Shortly after polls closed, Ms. Wong said it was “looking very likely” that the party could “make history tonight.” If Opportunity can hold its current share of the party vote, 5.8 percent, it will enter Parliament for the first time after contesting three elections.
“You guys have voted for unity over division,” Ms. Wong told a room of cheering and clapping supporters. “You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good.”

New Zealand First, which is led by the firebrand Winston Peters and has pledged to curb immigration, and the environmental Green Party have also seen their support increase. Voters in New Zealand cast ballots for both a local representative in Parliament and a party.
‘Division and Toxicity’

With bread-and-butter issues dominating, foreign policy has hardly figured into the race. New Zealand has to balance its heavy trade dependence on China while wrestling with the country, making its military heft increasingly felt in the region.
The National Party was voted into power in 2023 vowing to solidify relationships with the country’s traditional partners, the United States and Australia, and increase defense spending.
Asked in the final debate about managing relations with the United States, Kieran McAnulty, Labour’s campaign chair, said his party would approach the Trump administration differently.
“We saw yesterday with the results in the U.S. that the American people wholeheartedly rejected the division and the toxicity that we’re seeing in their politics over there,” he said on Thursday.

fortune.com/2026/11/07/fast-fires-wildfi.headline: ‘Fast fires’ were just 2.7% of U.S. wildfires but destroyed 78% of the structures lost — and up to 449,000 could be lost by 2060
fortune.com/2026/11/07/fast-fires-wildfi.author: Virginia Iglesias, The Conversation

paragraphs.text: As temperatures rise and development expands, the number of homes and other structures damaged or destroyed by wildfires across the U.S. is on pace to triple by mid-century, my colleagues and I found in a study just published.

The 2026 wildfire season has been a sharp reminder of that risk and why making homes and properties less vulnerable to wildfires is increasingly crucial. Fortunately, strategies to lower the risk of losing a home to wildfire don’t have to be overly expensive.
The 2026 western fire season

The 2026 wildfire season began with historically low mountain snowpack, early snowmelt and exceptional warmth across much of the West. Even before the nation’s hottest summer on record intensified drought and dried vegetation, fires were breaking out.

Colorado’s Aspen Acres Fire destroyed hundreds of structures in June. Four firefighters died from injuries suffered when the fast-moving Knowles Fire overtook them near the Colorado–Utah border in July. In August, wind-driven fires swept into neighborhoods in Spokane, Washington, damaging more than 800 homes and forcing tens of thousands of residents to evacuate.

In Colorado, the summer monsoon season brought rainfall, helping firefighters gain ground. Across the Rocky Mountain region, lightning continued to start fires, but rain helped keep many fires small in many areas despite above-average temperatures.

Despite this reprieve, Colorado fires had burned more than 318,000 acres by late October, nearly twice the annual average since 2000. Nationally, the total area burned was also well above average. The U.S. spent 48 consecutive days at Preparedness Level 5 – the highest level, indicating that firefighting resources were stretched nationally – compared with a 10-year average of 25 days annually.
Reasons for rising fire risk

Fire is a natural and often beneficial part of many ecosystems, shaping vegetation and supporting biodiversity. However, a century of fire suppression has allowed dry vegetation to accumulate in forests that historically had frequently burned.

Rising temperatures caused by human activities such as burning fossil fuels have increased the rate at which the atmosphere pulls moisture from the land, drying soils and vegetation. Researchers estimate that this drying nearly doubled the area burned in western U.S. forests between 1984 and 2015 compared with what would have burned without human-caused climate change.

More people also now live in and at the edges of wildland areas, raising the risk of fires reaching neighborhoods. Human activity has extended the fire season beyond summer, when most lightning-caused fires occur, too. Power lines, vehicles, machinery, burning of debris and campfires can spark fires year-round.
These interacting factors have helped nearly quadruple the annual area burned in the western United States since 2000.
They also contribute to the growing threat of fast-growing fires, which can overwhelm emergency response.

In a 2024 study, my colleagues and I used satellite imagery to measure daily fire growth across the contiguous United States from 2001 to 2020. “Fast fires,” defined as those that burned more than 4,000 acres in a single day, represented just 2.7% of fires analyzed but accounted for 78% of documented structures destroyed and 61% of reported firefighting costs.

A brief burst of growth, often fueled by strong winds or highly flammable materials, can matter enormously, even if a fire’s eventual size is relatively small. And in many ecosystems, fires are getting faster.
More homes in harm’s way
The number of people and buildings in harm’s way has also been increasing in the U.S., raising the risk of damage.

Between 1945 and 2015, development in regions of the country with the highest wildfire risk expanded tenfold, increasing the amount of human exposure to wildfires while also introducing ignition sources and buildings that can burn. Once embers enter a neighborhood, fire can spread quickly from building to building.

My team’s new research suggests that without further action to reduce wildfire risk, the annual number of structures damaged or destroyed nationwide could nearly triple by mid-century. That would mean up to 449,000 structures lost between 2026 and 2060.

We used historical data about development patterns, wildfire area and the fires’ effects to reconstruct the past fire risk, then modeled future fire risk by incorporating weather, climate and housing-density expectations.

We found that roughly one-third of western neighborhoods facing the greatest future risk are low-income communities. In these communities, people may struggle to afford measures to protect their homes, maintain insurance coverage and recover financially after a fire.
How to lower your wildfire risk
These projections are sobering, but actual losses will depend partly on the choices people make now.

For example, homes can be made less likely to ignite with Class A fire-resistant roofs and ember-resistant vents that reduce the potential for burning particles to enter homes. Removing flammable debris, mulch, firewood and vegetation from around buildings also reduces the risk of fire spreading to the home. Community programs are available in many areas to help low-income homeowners reduce their home’s fire risk.

Building homes to be wildfire-resilient can also cost less than people may expect. In a study of new home construction, my colleagues and I found that meeting the two protection levels established by the Colorado fire code increased minimum construction costs by approximately 0.6% and 4.2%. Access to lower-cost materials and homeowner education can help make wildfire resilience more affordable.
Wildfire-resilient construction can lower the risk of losing a home, but it does not completely eliminate it.

Beyond individual buildings, prescribed burning and appropriately designed forest-thinning operations can reduce fuels and alter fire behavior before flames reach neighborhoods. Utilities can strengthen infrastructure and reduce the probability of ignition while limiting disruptions from preventive power shut-offs. Insurance companies can reward measurable risk reduction and help sustain coverage in communities working to become safer.

These measures work best when they reinforce one another. The odds of losing a home to wildfire depend on its construction, its immediate surroundings and the broader neighborhood. There is no one-size-fits-all solution to wildfire risk. As the threat grows, strategies tailored to the environmental, social and economic realities of each community are more important than ever.
Virginia Iglesias, Earth Lab Director, University of Colorado Boulder

sports.yahoo.com/articles/knicks-defend-.headline: Knicks Defend Taylor Swift After Two of Their Own Players Suggest She's a 'Fake' Celebrity Fan

paragraphs.text: The New York Knicks have defended Taylor Swift after two of their players questioned her support for the team. Guards Tyler Kolek and Miles "Deuce" McBride singled her out during a discussion of celebrity spectators at Madison Square Garden.
A Knicks spokesperson told Entertainment Weekly that Swift had supported the team for years. The organization was "incredibly appreciative of her support," the representative said.

The exchange appeared in a November 5 installment of the NBA 2K League's Deflected series. Kolek and McBride were answering questions while playing the basketball video game when the subject turned to familiar faces in courtside seats.

Swift, 36, was among the celebrities attending New York's NBA Finals games in June. EW said it had contacted her for comment but had not received an immediate response when its November 6 report was published.
Kolek Calls Swift's Appearances 'a Little Performative'

Kolek suggested that some celebrities attend Knicks games because they want to be photographed rather than because they follow the team. Asked to name someone, he offered, "Maybe Taylor Swift," according to Billboard. He said he couldn't recall seeing her at other games.

McBride agreed, then warned that Swift's fans would not appreciate the answer. Kolek acknowledged that her schedule might prevent frequent visits, prompting his teammate to joke that he was trying to soften the criticism. Kolek nevertheless concluded that her attendance seemed "a little performative."
McBride named Ben Stiller and Tracy Morgan as examples of dependable celebrity supporters. Both have been regular courtside presences beyond the team's recent championship run.
Swift Explained Her Knicks Connection in a 2014 Interview

Swift was photographed attending the October 29, 2014, game against the Chicago Bulls with Karlie Kloss. Entertainment Tonight's coverage from the following day noted that she also sat near Stiller and his son. The Knicks lost that regular-season game 104-80, according to the accompanying Getty Images record.

In a November 2014 interview with TIME, Swift linked her interest in the team to friendly encounters with then-Knicks player Amar'e Stoudemire and his wife, Alexis, at the Met Gala. She also recalled performing in Madison Square Garden's halftime talent competition when she was 12 or 13.
When the interviewer pointed out that the Knicks weren't playing well, Swift replied, "I love them, though. Why does that matter?"
Alana Haim Made Her 'Stevie Knicks' Shirt at Home
View this post on Instagram A post shared by HAIM (@haimtheband)

For Game 4 of the Finals on June 10, Swift joined Este and Alana Haim in blue shirts with orange lettering. Hers read "Stevie Knicks," combining the team's name with Stevie Nicks'. Este's shirt referenced Nicole Kidman, while Alana's nodded to Nickelback. Mariska Hargitay also wore a shirt matching Swift's.

Alana told Vogue that Swift had texted asking her to make the design and came up with the pun herself. She printed the shirts at home, using orange ink with a puff additive on blue tees that cost $2.99 each.

The band later shared an Instagram reel of Swift and the sisters showing off their shirts while dancing to Cyndi Lauper's Girls Just Want to Have Fun. Nicole Kidman reposted the clip on her Instagram Stories, as PEOPLE documented.

On the court, New York erased a 29-point deficit to beat the San Antonio Spurs 107-106, the largest comeback on record in an NBA Finals game, according to the NBA. The Knicks then won Game 5 to secure their first championship since 1973.
